scripts.name: saros-arithmetic
scripts.title: one Saros family, 6585.32 days at a time
scripts.text:
/* ============================================================================
saros-arithmetic.epher -- one Saros family, 6585.32 days at a time

Takes the next solar eclipse after a knob date (the chapter 54
machinery of next-solar-eclipse.epher, Jean Meeus, "Astronomical
Algorithms" 2nd ed.) and steps it by the Saros: 223 synodic months,
6585.3213 days, 18 years 10.3 days (11.3 across leap years), three
members backward and three forward in time. Each step lands on the
next eclipse of the same family - the Sun-Moon-Earth geometry
repeats almost exactly because 223 lunations and 19 draconic years
(242 node passages) close to within a few hours, which is why the
dates, eclipse kinds and gamma values below march in step. The
series is the one Meeus, "More Mathematical Astronomy Morsels"
(2002), its chapter on solar-eclipse periodicities, calls the Saros;
Espenak's canon tables number these families: the default anchor,
2026 Feb 17, is Saros 121's member, a series of 71 eclipses that
opened in 944 AD and whose annular stretch runs from 1863 to 2044 -
the 2044 member printed below is its last annular eclipse, and the
two following members have turned partial as gamma drifts past the
central limit.

Accuracy: the member times and gammas carry the chapter 54 mean
series grade - about a minute and 0.002 (next-solar-eclipse.epher
works the comparison against NASA's canon).

Knobs: the start date and the search span.
============================================================================ */

// ---- the knobs ----------------------------------------------------------------
const day = {2026, 1, 1}     // search from here for the family's anchor eclipse
const maxscan = 25           // lunations to try
const members = 3            // steps backward and forward from the anchor

// ---- Meeus ch. 49/54 mean elements in T = k / 1236.85 --------------------------
def e3(t) = 1 - 0.002516 * t - 0.0000074 * t ^ 2
def mp(k) = 201.5643 + 385.81693528 * k + 0.0107582 * (k / 1236.85) ^ 2 + 0.00001238 * (k / 1236.85) ^ 3 - 0.000000058 * (k / 1236.85) ^ 4
def ms(k) = 2.5534 + 29.10535670 * k - 0.0000014 * (k / 1236.85) ^ 2 - 0.00000011 * (k / 1236.85) ^ 3
def mf(k) = 160.7108 + 390.67050284 * k - 0.0016118 * (k / 1236.85) ^ 2 - 0.00000227 * (k / 1236.85) ^ 3 + 0.000000011 * (k / 1236.85) ^ 4
def node(k) = 124.7746 - 1.56375588 * k + 0.0020672 * (k / 1236.85) ^ 2 + 0.00000215 * (k / 1236.85) ^ 3
def base(k) = 2451550.09766 + 29.530588861 * k + 0.00015437 * (k / 1236.85) ^ 2 - 0.000000150 * (k / 1236.85) ^ 3 + 0.00000000073 * (k / 1236.85) ^ 4
def kb(j) = (j - 2451550.09766) / 29.530588861
def f1(k) = mf(k) - 0.02665 * sin(rad(node(k)))
def tmax(k) = base(k) - 0.4075 * sin(rad(mp(k))) + 0.1721 * e3(k / 1236.85) * sin(rad(ms(k))) + 0.0161 * sin(rad(2 * mp(k))) - 0.0097 * sin(rad(2 * f1(k))) + 0.0073 * e3(k / 1236.85) * sin(rad(mp(k) - ms(k))) - 0.0050 * e3(k / 1236.85) * sin(rad(mp(k) + ms(k))) - 0.0023 * sin(rad(mp(k) - 2 * f1(k))) + 0.0021 * e3(k / 1236.85) * sin(rad(2 * ms(k))) + 0.0012 * sin(rad(mp(k) + 2 * f1(k))) + 0.0006 * e3(k / 1236.85) * sin(rad(2 * mp(k) + ms(k))) - 0.0004 * sin(rad(3 * mp(k))) - 0.0003 * e3(k / 1236.85) * sin(rad(ms(k) + 2 * f1(k))) + 0.0003 * sin(rad(299.77 + 0.107408 * k)) - 0.0002 * e3(k / 1236.85) * sin(rad(ms(k) - 2 * f1(k))) - 0.0002 * e3(k / 1236.85) * sin(rad(2 * mp(k) - ms(k))) - 0.0002 * sin(rad(node(k)))
def pang(k) = 0.2070 * e3(k / 1236.85) * sin(rad(ms(k))) + 0.0024 * e3(k / 1236.85) * sin(rad(2 * ms(k))) - 0.0392 * sin(rad(mp(k))) + 0.0116 * sin(rad(2 * mp(k))) - 0.0073 * e3(k / 1236.85) * sin(rad(mp(k) + ms(k))) + 0.0067 * e3(k / 1236.85) * sin(rad(mp(k) - ms(k))) + 0.0118 * sin(rad(2 * f1(k)))
def qang(k) = 5.2207 - 0.0048 * e3(k / 1236.85) * cos(rad(ms(k))) + 0.0020 * e3(k / 1236.85) * cos(rad(2 * ms(k))) - 0.3299 * cos(rad(mp(k))) - 0.0060 * e3(k / 1236.85) * cos(rad(mp(k) + ms(k))) + 0.0041 * e3(k / 1236.85) * cos(rad(mp(k) - ms(k)))
def gamma(k) = (pang(k) * cos(rad(f1(k))) + qang(k) * sin(rad(f1(k)))) * (1 - 0.0048 * abs(cos(rad(f1(k)))))
def uval(k) = 0.0059 + 0.0046 * e3(k / 1236.85) * cos(rad(ms(k))) - 0.0182 * cos(rad(mp(k))) + 0.0004 * cos(rad(2 * mp(k))) - 0.0005 * cos(rad(ms(k) + mp(k)))
def kind(k) = (if abs(gamma(k)) < 0.9972 then (if uval(k) < 0 then "total" else if uval(k) > 0.0047 then "annular" else "hybrid") else "partial")
def is_eclipse(k) = abs(sin(rad(mf(k)))) <= 0.36 and abs(gamma(k)) <= 1.5433 + uval(k)
def next_hit(k, n) = if n == 0 then -1 else if is_eclipse(k) then k else next_hit(k + 1, n - 1)

// ---- the anchor eclipse and its Saros siblings ---------------------------------
const saros = 223 * 29.530588861   // the Saros in days: 223 lunations = 6585.3213 d
const saros_k = 223                // ... or 223 in lunation count (same step)
const kanchor = next_hit(ceil(kb(jd(day[1], day[2], day[3]))), maxscan)
def member(n) = kanchor + n * saros_k
def mdate(n) = iso(tmax(member(n)) - delta_t(tmax(member(n))) / 86400)
def mkind(n) = kind(member(n))
def mgamma(n) = gamma(member(n))

// ---- results -------------------------------------------------------------------
print("one Saros =", saros, "days = 18 y 10.3 d (11.3 over leap years)")
print("anchor: next solar eclipse after", iso(jd(day[1], day[2], day[3])), "is lunation", kanchor)
print("member", -members, ":", mdate(-members), "UT,", mkind(-members), ", gamma", mgamma(-members))
print("member", -2, ":", mdate(-2), "UT,", mkind(-2), ", gamma", mgamma(-2))
print("member", -1, ":", mdate(-1), "UT,", mkind(-1), ", gamma", mgamma(-1))
print("member", 0, ": ", mdate(0), "UT,", mkind(0), ", gamma", mgamma(0), "(anchor)")
print("member", 1, ":", mdate(1), "UT,", mkind(1), ", gamma", mgamma(1))
print("member", 2, ":", mdate(2), "UT,", mkind(2), ", gamma", mgamma(2))
print("member", members, ":", mdate(members), "UT,", mkind(members), ", gamma", mgamma(members))

/* The family portrait: kind and gamma stay close across the seven
members, while the dates slide 18 years 10-11 days per step and the
time of day shifts by the Saros's 0.3213-day excess - about 7.7
hours per member, which carries the eclipse path about 115 deg of
longitude westward each Saros. Gamma drifts slowly across the
family's life (printed below as the mean drift per member), and
when it passes the partial-eclipse limit the family dies; a solar
Saros family lives roughly 70-80 members, 1226-1550 years. */
print("gamma drift per Saros member:", (mgamma(members) - mgamma(-members)) / (2 * members))

/* ---- expected output ----
= one Saros = 6585.321316 days = 18 y 10.3 d (11.3 over leap years)
= anchor: next solar eclipse after 2026-01-01T00:00:00 is lunation 323
= member -3 : 1972-01-16T11:02:46 UT, annular , gamma -0.936764996047
= member -2 : 1990-01-26T19:30:59 UT, annular , gamma -0.945577692586
= member -1 : 2008-02-07T03:54:50 UT, annular , gamma -0.957523181072
= member 0 :  2026-02-17T12:12:48 UT, annular , gamma -0.973790137956 (anchor)
= member 1 : 2044-02-28T20:23:18 UT, annular , gamma -0.995407602172
= member 2 : 2062-03-11T04:25:03 UT, partial , gamma -1.02320473231
= member 3 : 2080-03-21T12:17:30 UT, partial , gamma -1.05778080248
= gamma drift per Saros member: -0.0201693010714
*/

scripts.name: semidiameters
scripts.title: angular radii of Sun, Moon and planets
scripts.text:
/* ============================================================================
semidiameters.epher -- angular radii of Sun, Moon and planets

The apparent (angular) radius, or semidiameter, that each body's disk
subtends at the Earth on a knob date. The Sun and the Moon come
straight from the engine's built-in diam accessor (the angular
diameter in degrees, solar-ephemeris crate, JPL-validated; half of
it is the semidiameter). The planets' disks are far smaller than the
ephemeris tracks, so their semidiameters come from the classical
formula s = 206265 x R / d arcseconds: the body's physical radius R
in kilometers (NASA Planetary Fact Sheet values, nssdc.gsfc.nasa.gov/
planetary/factsheet) divided by its geocentric distance d in
kilometers, read from the engine's dist accessor in AU times the au
constant. As a cross-check the Sun's radius-formula value is printed
against the engine's diam, which agree to the size of the radius
constant (a few tenths of a percent).

The last line prints alpha, the Moon/Sun semidiameter ratio: alpha
under 1 means the Moon's disk is the smaller one and any central
solar eclipse that day is annular, alpha over 1 allows totality. On
the knob date, 2026 Feb 17, the canon's eclipse was annular - the
printed alpha explains why.

Accuracy: the Sun/Moon diameters are the engine's (arcsecond class,
and the radius-formula cross-check below agrees to 0.003 arcsec);
the planets' radii are rounded fact-sheet values, so their
semidiameters carry about 0.1-0.5 percent (Venus's disk, for
instance, is a few hundredths of an arcsecond larger or smaller
with the radius's last digit).

Knob: the date (the instant is 12:00 UT of it).
============================================================================ */

// ---- the knob ----------------------------------------------------------------
const day = {2026, 2, 17}    // the 2026 Feb 17 annular eclipse day

// ---- the model ---------------------------------------------------------------
def sdarc(rkm, b, j) = 206265 * rkm * 1000 / (dist(b, j) * au)   // s = 206265 R / d, arcsec; radii km, au constant in m
// the engine's constants come in meters (au = 1.495978707e11 m, r_sun = 6.957e8 m)
def sdmoon(j) = diam(11, j) / 2 * 60                      // Moon semidiameter, arcmin (engine diam, deg)

// ---- results ------------------------------------------------------------------
const j = jd(day[1], day[2], day[3], 12)
print("geocentric semidiameters at", iso(j), "UT")
print("Sun: ", diam(10, j) / 2 * 3600, "arcsec =", diam(10, j) / 2 * 60, "arcmin")
print("Moon:", diam(11, j) / 2 * 3600, "arcsec =", sdmoon(j), "arcmin")
print("Mercury:", sdarc(2439.7, 1, j), "arcsec (radius 2439.7 km)")
print("Venus:  ", sdarc(6051.8, 2, j), "arcsec (radius 6051.8 km)")
print("Mars:   ", sdarc(3396.2, 4, j), "arcsec (radius 3396.2 km)")
print("Jupiter:", sdarc(71492, 5, j), "arcsec (radius 71492 km)")
print("Saturn: ", sdarc(60268, 6, j), "arcsec (radius 60268 km)")
print("Uranus: ", sdarc(25559, 7, j), "arcsec (radius 25559 km)")
print("Neptune:", sdarc(24764, 8, j), "arcsec (radius 24764 km)")

/* Cross-check the Sun: the same radius formula with the built-in
r_sun constant against the engine's diam accessor - the two agree to
the roundness of the radius constant. */
print("Sun cross-check: radius formula", 206265 * r_sun / (dist(10, j) * au), "vs engine", diam(10, j) / 2 * 3600, "arcsec")

/* The eclipse geometry ratio: alpha = Moon semidiameter / Sun
semidiameter. Under 1 the Moon's disk is smaller than the Sun's and
a central eclipse is annular; over 1 totality fits. On 2026-02-17
the eclipse was annular, which the printed alpha predicts. */
const a = (diam(11, j) / 2) / (diam(10, j) / 2)
print("alpha (Moon/Sun semidiameter ratio):", a)
print("verdict:", if a < 1 then "Moon smaller: annular geometry" else "Moon large enough: totality possible")

/* ---- expected output ----
= geocentric semidiameters at 2026-02-17T12:00:00 UT
= Sun:  970.6805 arcsec = 16.1780083333 arcmin
= Moon: 932.04285 arcsec = 15.5340475 arcmin
= Mercury: 3.36019094535 arcsec (radius 2439.7 km)
= Venus:   4.97042758463 arcsec (radius 6051.8 km)
= Mars:    1.98638348459 arcsec (radius 3396.2 km)
= Jupiter: 22.0883584715 arcsec (radius 71492 km)
= Saturn:  8.04329944502 arcsec (radius 60268 km)
= Uranus:  1.80917029667 arcsec (radius 25559 km)
= Neptune: 1.11152699295 arcsec (radius 24764 km)
= Sun cross-check: radius formula 970.677850414 vs engine 970.6805 arcsec
= alpha (Moon/Sun semidiameter ratio): 0.960195295981
= verdict: Moon smaller: annular geometry
*/

scripts.name: body-almanac
scripts.title: one body's full almanac panel for tonight
scripts.text:
/* ============================================================================
body-almanac.epher -- one body's full almanac panel for tonight

Prints the whole observing panel the almanac apps lead with (the
Heavens-Above Sun & Moon panels, the timeanddate ephemeris tables,
hpcalc.org's "Effemeridi" and "Real Time Ephemeris" programs) for one
solar-system body, one instant and one place: right ascension,
declination, distance, magnitude, phase angle and illuminated
fraction, angular diameter, rise / transit / set for the local day,
and altitude and azimuth at the instant. Every number comes from the
built-in accessors (solar-ephemeris crate, VSOP2013 planets and
ELP-MPP02 Moon, JPL-Horizons-validated; guide 1.29).

Accuracy: JPL Horizons agrees with the engine to about 1 arcsecond
in position and 1e-5 AU in distance (checked for this very panel);
rise and set follow the engine's event convention (upper limb on the
geometric horizon).

Knobs: body (guide 1.29 numbering), instant `tm`, and the observer's
`lat` and `lon` (degrees, east positive). All four sit below.
============================================================================ */

// ---- the knobs ----------------------------------------------------------------
const body = 4                 // Mars
const tm = jd(2026, 6, 1, 3)    // 03:00 UT
const lat = 51.4779            // Greenwich
const lon = 0

// ---- panel --------------------------------------------------------------------
print("almanac for", iso(tm), "at lat", lat, "lon", lon)
print("ra:", deg2hms(ra(body, tm)), " dec:", deg2dms(decl(body, tm)))
print("distance:", dist(body, tm), "AU")
print("magnitude:", mag(body, tm))
print("phase angle:", phase(body, tm), "deg, illuminated:", illum(body, tm))
print("angular diameter:", diam(body, tm) * 3600, "arcsec")
print("rises:", iso(rise(body, tm, lat, lon)))
print("transits:", iso(transit(body, tm, lat, lon)))
print("sets:", iso(set(body, tm, lat, lon)))
print("at the instant: alt", alt(body, tm, lat, lon), "az", az(body, tm, lat, lon))

/* Self-check: at its transit a body stands on the observer's
meridian, so its altitude must equal 90 degrees minus the span
between observer and body declination (the topocentric one, which
for Mars differs from geocentric by well under an arcminute). */
const tt = transit(body, tm, lat, lon)
print("alt at transit:", alt(body, tt, lat, lon), "vs 90 - |lat - dec|:", 90 - abs(lat - decl(body, tt)))

/* ---- expected output ----
= almanac for 2026-06-01T03:00:00 at lat 51.4779 lon 0
= ra: 2h 30m 36s  dec: 14° 10' 26"
= distance: 2.1837735787 AU
= magnitude: 1.27
= phase angle: 21.58 deg, illuminated: 0.965
= angular diameter: 4.2801 arcsec
= rises: 2026-06-01T02:34:13
= transits: 2026-06-01T09:51:59
= sets: 2026-06-01T17:10:16
= at the instant: alt 3.1756137 az 71.092283
= alt at transit: 52.7646496 vs 90 - |lat - dec|: 52.765335104
*/

scripts.name: bright-limb-pa
scripts.title: the position angle of the bright limb
scripts.text:
/* ============================================================================
bright-limb-pa.epher -- the position angle of the bright limb

Prints the position angle of a body's bright limb for one instant -
the angle, measured from the celestial north point through east,
that says which side of the Moon or a planet is lit. The lit side
faces the Sun, so the bright-limb PA is the sky position angle of
the direction from the body toward the Sun - the standard two-body
position angle (the formula the double-star observers use, and the
one behind Meeus ch. 48 and Duffett-Smith's "Position angle of the
bright limb"):

  tan(theta) = sin(as - ab) cos(ds)
             / (cos(db) sin(ds) - sin(db) cos(ds) cos(as - ab))

with (as, ds) the Sun's and (ab, db) the body's right ascension and
declination, evaluated with atan2 for the right quadrant (some
printings of ch. 48 give the antipodal convention, measured from
the dark side). Positions come from the built-in accessors
(solar-ephemeris crate, JPL-Horizons-validated; guide 1.29).

Accuracy: arcsecond-grade positions make the angle good to a few
thousandths of a degree; the printed illumination is the engine's
model value.

Knobs: the body (11 = Moon) and the instant tm below.
============================================================================ */

// ---- the knobs ----------------------------------------------------------------
const body = 11                // Moon
const tm = jd(2026, 9, 13, 19)  // an evening crescent test

// ---- Meeus ch. 48: bright-limb position angle, from precomputed ra/dec ------------
def pa(sra, sde, bra, bde) = deg(atan2(sin(rad(sra - bra)) * cos(rad(sde)), cos(rad(bde)) * sin(rad(sde)) - sin(rad(bde)) * cos(rad(sde)) * cos(rad(sra - bra))))

const sra = ra(10, tm)
const sde = decl(10, tm)
const bra = ra(body, tm)
const bde = decl(body, tm)

// ---- results ----------------------------------------------------------------------
print("at", iso(tm))
print("bright-limb PA (north through east):", pa(sra, sde, bra, bde), "deg")
print("illuminated fraction:", illum(body, tm))

/* Self-check: the phase picture must be consistent - this is a
young crescent, so the Sun (which the lit side faces) is below the
horizon for Greenwich at the instant, and its azimuth tells which
way the crescent points. */
print("Sun altitude at the instant:", alt(10, tm, 51.4779, 0), "deg")
print("Sun azimuth at the instant: ", az(10, tm, 51.4779, 0), "deg")

/* ---- expected output ----
= at 2026-09-13T19:00:00
= bright-limb PA (north through east): -61.4724326937 deg
= illuminated fraction: 0.0808
= Sun altitude at the instant: -7.0771504 deg
= Sun azimuth at the instant:  284.8611349 deg
*/

scripts.name: ecliptic-position
scripts.title: ecliptic longitude and latitude of a body
scripts.text:
/* ============================================================================
ecliptic-position.epher -- ecliptic longitude and latitude of a body

Converts a body's geocentric equatorial position (the engine's ra and
decl, solar-ephemeris crate, JPL-Horizons-validated) into ecliptic
longitude and latitude with the spherical rotation about the
obliquity - Meeus, "Astronomical Algorithms" 2nd ed. ch. 13 (eq. 13.3
and 13.4):

  tan(lambda) = (sin(alpha) cos(eps) + tan(delta) sin(eps)) / cos(alpha)
  sin(beta)   = sin(delta) cos(eps) - cos(delta) sin(eps) sin(alpha)

The obliquity is the mean value of Meeus ch. 22 (eq. 22.2). The
ecliptic frame is the astronomers' answer to "how far off the
ecliptic does Mars wander this month" - and it is the frame the old
ephemerides and the calculator classics (Effemeridi, EPHE) work in.

Accuracy: engine positions are arcsecond-grade; using the MEAN
obliquity (nutation omitted) costs up to about 9 arcsec of
longitude. Latitude is unaffected at the same grade.

Knobs: the body (guide 1.29 numbering) and the instant tm below.
============================================================================ */

// ---- the knobs ----------------------------------------------------------------
const body = 4                 // Mars
const tm = jd(2026, 9, 10, 2)

// ---- mean obliquity of the ecliptic in degrees (Meeus eq. 22.2) ------------------
def epsdeg(j) = 23.4392911 - 46.8150 * ((j - 2451545) / 36525) / 3600 - 0.00059 * ((j - 2451545) / 36525) ^ 2 / 3600 + 0.001813 * ((j - 2451545) / 36525) ^ 3 / 3600

// ---- the rotation (Meeus ch. 13), on precomputed ra/dec pairs ---------------------
def eclon(ar, dr) = deg(atan2(sin(rad(ar)) * cos(rad(epsdeg(tm))) + tan(rad(dr)) * sin(rad(epsdeg(tm))), cos(rad(ar))))
def eclat(ar, dr) = deg(asin(sin(rad(dr)) * cos(rad(epsdeg(tm))) - cos(rad(dr)) * sin(rad(epsdeg(tm))) * sin(rad(ar))))

const mra = ra(body, tm)      // Mars right ascension, computed once
const mde = decl(body, tm)    // Mars declination
const sra = ra(10, tm)        // the Sun's right ascension
const sde = decl(10, tm)      // the Sun's declination

// ---- results --------------------------------------------------------------------
print("at", iso(tm))
print("Mars   ecliptic lon:", eclon(mra, mde), " lat:", eclat(mra, mde))
print("Sun    ecliptic lon:", eclon(sra, sde), " lat:", eclat(sra, sde))

/* ---- expected output ----
= at 2026-09-10T02:00:00
= Mars   ecliptic lon: 109.093783646  lat: 0.67567275331
= Sun    ecliptic lon: 167.40045609  lat: 0.000497719747027
*/

scripts.name: elongation
scripts.title: how far each planet sits from the Sun, east or west
scripts.text:
/* ============================================================================
elongation.epher -- how far each planet sits from the Sun, east or west

Computes the solar elongation of the Moon and the planets at an
instant: the angle body-Sun-Earth seen from Earth, signed by side.
Ecliptic longitudes of body and Sun come from the built-in accessors
ra and decl (solar-ephemeris crate, JPL-Horizons-validated; guide
1.29) rotated into the ecliptic with the mean obliquity; the
elongation is their difference wrapped to -180..180. Positive means
east of the Sun (sets after it, evening sky), negative west (rises
before it, morning sky); 0 is solar conjunction, 180 opposition.

Method and source: the ecliptic-coordinate rotation is Meeus,
"Astronomical Algorithms" 2nd ed. ch. 13 (eq. 13.3), the signed
elongation is Duffett-Smith & Zwart, "Practical Astronomy with your
Calculator or Spreadsheet", 4th ed., "Solar elongations". Note the
two senses of the word: this signed difference of ecliptic
longitudes is what the morning/evening question needs, while the
great-circle angle (separation.epher) differs from it by the
body's ecliptic latitude. The same signed quantity is what
almanac apps list beside each planet.

Accuracy: ephemeris-grade - JPL Horizons matches the engine's
positions to about an arcsecond here, so the elongations are honest
to a few hundredths of a degree.

Knobs: the instant `tm` below (jd of 2026-06-01 12:00 UT).
============================================================================ */

// ---- the knob -----------------------------------------------------------------
const tm = jd(2026, 6, 1, 12)

// ---- ecliptic longitude of a body, Meeus eq. 13.3 (degrees, 0..360) -----------
def centuries(j) = (j - jd(2000, 1, 1, 12)) / 36525
def obliquity(j) = 23.4392911 - 0.0130042 * centuries(j)   // mean, degrees
def eclon(b) = deg(atan2(sin(rad(ra(b, tm))) * cos(rad(obliquity(tm))) + tan(rad(decl(b, tm))) * sin(rad(obliquity(tm))), cos(rad(ra(b, tm)))))

// ---- signed elongation: longitude difference wrapped to -180..180 -------------
def wrap180(x) = x - 360 * floor((x + 180) / 360)
def elong(b) = wrap180(eclon(b) - eclon(10))

// ---- results ------------------------------------------------------------------
print("solar elongation, degrees, at", iso(tm))
print("Moon:", elong(11))
print("Mercury:", elong(1))
print("Venus:", elong(2))
print("Mars:", elong(4))
print("Jupiter:", elong(5))
print("Saturn:", elong(6))
print("Uranus:", elong(7))
print("Neptune:", elong(8))

/* Self-checks. The Sun's own elongation is 0 by construction. The
Moon's elongation must agree with its illuminated fraction k through
const k = (1 - cos(elong)) / 2, the phase law of Meeus ch. 48 - which the
built-in illum reports independently. The two agree only to about
half a percent, and the slack is real: the phase law assumes both
bodies ride the ecliptic, while the Moon runs up to 5 degrees off it
(the same reason a full moon's illum tops out at 0.9986, see
full-moons.epher). */
print("Sun elongation (must be 0):", elong(10))
print("Moon illum from elongation:", (1 - cos(rad(abs(elong(11))))) / 2, "vs built-in illum:", illum(11, tm))

/* ---- expected output ----
= solar elongation, degrees, at 2026-06-01T12:00:00
= Moon: -167.603103654
= Mercury: 18.9875091925
= Venus: 34.9681795246
= Mars: -30.8871525524
= Jupiter: 43.1451622895
= Saturn: -58.7303376883
= Uranus: -8.92388319764
= Neptune: -66.9469715787
= Sun elongation (must be 0): 0
= Moon illum from elongation: 0.988341954447 vs built-in illum: 0.9868
*/

scripts.name: light-time
scripts.title: how long light takes to reach us from each planet
scripts.text:
/* ============================================================================
light-time.epher -- how long light takes to reach us from each planet

Computes the one-way light-travel time from the Sun, the Moon and the
planets to Earth at a given instant: distance from the built-in
ephemeris accessor dist (the solar-ephemeris crate, VSOP2013 planets,
ELP-MPP02 Moon, JPL-Horizons-validated; guide 1.29) divided by the
speed of light c. The 499.00478 s the light of 1 AU takes is the
yardstick astronomers quote distances in: "Mars is 18 light minutes
away tonight" is this script's answer for a planet.

Method and source: distance / c, the standard of the nautical and
amateur almanacs (Duffett-Smith & Zwart, "Practical Astronomy with
your Calculator or Spreadsheet", 4th ed., section "Distance, light-
travel time and angular size of a planet"; on the calculators, the
hpcalc.org program "Distance from the Sun & Orbital Speed").

Accuracy: the ephemeris distance is JPL-grade (Horizons agrees with
the engine to microns of an AU here), so the light time is honest to
well under a second. Pluto rides approximate elements, so its
minutes are good to a few seconds only.

Knobs: the instant `tm` below (jd of 2026-06-01 12:00 UT).
============================================================================ */

// ---- the knob -----------------------------------------------------------------
const tm = jd(2026, 6, 1, 12)

// ---- light time in minutes: distance in AU -> metres -> / c -> / 60 -----------
// au and c are the constants (guide 1.29); dist is AU and c is m/s.
def lt(b) = dist(b, tm) * au / c / 60 in min

// ---- results ------------------------------------------------------------------
print("light-time one way, Earth at", iso(tm))
print("Sun:", lt(10))
print("Moon:", dist(11, tm) * au / c in s)
print("Mercury:", lt(1))
print("Venus:", lt(2))
print("Mars:", lt(4))
print("Jupiter:", lt(5))
print("Saturn:", lt(6))
print("Uranus:", lt(7))
print("Neptune:", lt(8))
print("Pluto:", lt(9))

/* A yardstick and a self-check: 1 AU / c = 499.00478 s (the light
second of the ephemeris), and the Moon's distance must come out near
60 Earth radii - about 1.3 light seconds. Both lines below. */
print("1 AU in light seconds:", au / c in s)
print("Moon in light seconds:", dist(11, tm) * au / c, "s =", dist(11, tm) * au / r_earth, "Earth radii")

/* ---- expected output ----
= light-time one way, Earth at 2026-06-01T12:00:00
= Sun: 8.43287925086 min
= Moon: 1.35537939717 s
= Mercury: 9.0855301898 min
= Venus: 10.4202317104 min
= Mars: 18.1549160825 min
= Jupiter: 49.567431747 min
= Saturn: 82.818041105 min
= Uranus: 170.19495175 min
= Neptune: 251.692030036 min
= Pluto: 290.508580775 min
= 1 AU in light seconds: 499.004783836 s
= Moon in light seconds: 1.35537939717 s = 63.7784525192 Earth radii
*/

scripts.name: parallax-demo
scripts.title: geocentric vs topocentric: the Moon's parallax
scripts.text:
/* ============================================================================
parallax-demo.epher -- geocentric vs topocentric: the Moon's parallax

Shows the ~1 degree lesson of the Moon's geocentric parallax: the
altitude a geocentric observer would compute for the Moon against
the topocentric altitude the engine reports for a place on Earth's
surface. The geocentric value comes from the standard hour-angle
formula

  sin(a) = sin(phi) sin(delta) + cos(phi) cos(delta) cos(H)

with H = local sidereal time - right ascension, and the horizontal
parallax HP = asin(r_earth / d) from the engine's distance (Meeus
ch. 40; Duffett-Smith, "Geocentric parallax"). For an object seen from the surface the topocentric direction is
the geocentric one rotated toward the observer's nadir, so the
topocentric altitude lies BELOW the geocentric by up to HP at the
horizon and zero at the zenith - the gap obeys

  topocentric - geocentric = -asin(sin(HP) * cos(altitude))

Accuracy: the engine's topocentric value is the ground truth (its
ephemeris models the observer on the ellipsoid); the geocentric
formula below uses the geodetic latitude unchanged (flattening and
the ~0.7 degree topocentric correction terms omitted), good to
about a tenth of the parallax itself - which is the point: the
printed gap is of order one degree for the Moon.

Knobs: the instant tm and the observer's lat/lon below.
============================================================================ */

// ---- the knobs ----------------------------------------------------------------
const tm = jd(2026, 9, 10, 12)  // the Moon rides high at noon here
const lat = 51.4779            // Greenwich
const lon = 0

// ---- helpers ----------------------------------------------------------------------
def wrap(x) = x - 360 * floor(x / 360)
def spread(x) = if wrap(x) > 180 then wrap(x) - 360 else wrap(x)

// ---- the two altitudes and the parallax --------------------------------------------
const mra = ra(11, tm)
const mde = decl(11, tm)
const mdist = dist(11, tm)
const h = spread(15 * lst(tm, lon) - mra)          // local hour angle, degrees
const ageo = deg(asin(sin(rad(lat)) * sin(rad(mde)) + cos(rad(lat)) * cos(rad(mde)) * cos(rad(h))))
const atopo = alt(11, tm, lat, lon)
const hp = deg(asin(r_earth / (mdist * au)))      // horizontal parallax, r_earth and au in km

print("at", iso(tm), "lat", lat, "lon", lon)
print("geocentric altitude: ", ageo, "deg")
print("topocentric altitude:", atopo, "deg")
print("horizontal parallax: ", hp, "deg")
print("gap (topo - geo):    ", atopo - ageo, "deg")
print("exact model:         ", -deg(asin(sin(rad(hp)) * cos(rad(ageo)))), "deg")

/* ---- expected output ----
= at 2026-09-10T12:00:00 lat 51.4779 lon 0
= geocentric altitude:  45.0982479109 deg
= topocentric altitude: 44.4042815 deg
= horizontal parallax:  0.975262609983 deg
= gap (topo - geo):     -0.693966410879 deg
= exact model:          -0.6884145954 deg
*/

scripts.name: rise-set-azimuth
scripts.title: where a body comes up and goes down
scripts.text:
/* ============================================================================
rise-set-azimuth.epher -- where a body comes up and goes down

Prints the azimuth of a body's rise and of its set for one place and
day - the compass numbers a photographer or a radio operator wants
beside the horizon times (timeanddate prints the same two columns
beside its rise and set times; Meeus ch. 15 derives them from the
rise geometry). The azimuths are read off the engine's own event
instants: rise and set are defined by an altitude crossing, so the
azimuth at that instant IS the rise (or set) azimuth.

Accuracy: the events land within seconds of the true crossing and the
azimuth moves well under a degree in that time, so the printed values
are good to a few hundredths of a degree. The engine's convention is
apparent altitude: the altitude at the event reads about -0.83 deg
for the Moon (-34 arcmin of standard refraction minus the Moon's
semidiameter) and about -0.57 deg for the Sun.

Knobs: the body (guide 1.29 numbering), the day tm and the place below.
============================================================================ */

// ---- the knobs ----------------------------------------------------------------
const body = 11                 // Moon
const tm = jd(2026, 9, 10, 0)    // the local day
const lat = 51.4779             // Greenwich
const lon = 0

// ---- the events and their compass bearings --------------------------------------
const tr = rise(body, tm, lat, lon)
const ts = set(body, tm, lat, lon)
const azr = az(body, tr, lat, lon)
const azs = az(body, ts, lat, lon)

print("rises", iso(tr), "at azimuth", azr)
print("sets  ", iso(ts), "at azimuth", azs)

/* Self-check: at the event instant the altitude must read about
-0.83 deg for the Moon, i.e. the upper limb on the apparent horizon
(-34 arcmin refraction minus the semidiameter). */
print("altitude at rise (about -0.83 for the Moon):", alt(body, tr, lat, lon))

/* ---- expected output ----
= rises 2026-09-10T04:24:24 at azimuth 75.3570601
= sets   2026-09-10T18:03:36 at azimuth 278.7558128
= altitude at rise (about -0.83 for the Moon): -0.8333433
*/
