scripts.name: separation
scripts.title: the angle between two bodies on the sky
scripts.text:
/* ============================================================================
separation.epher -- the angle between two bodies on the sky

Computes the great-circle separation of any two solar-system bodies
at an instant, from their geocentric right ascensions and
declinations given by the built-in accessors ra and decl (solar-
ephemeris crate, JPL-Horizons-validated; guide 1.29) and the cosine
law of spherical trigonometry: cos(d) = sin(d1) sin(d2) +
cos(d1) cos(d2) cos(a1 - a2). This is the number that answers "how
far apart are the Moon and Venus tonight" - the conjunction watcher's
question, the one hpcalc.org's "Angular Distance Between Stars"
program and Meeus ch. 17 both compute.

Method and source: Meeus, "Astronomical Algorithms" 2nd ed. ch. 17
(eq. 17.1); Duffett-Smith & Zwart, "Practical Astronomy with your
Calculator or Spreadsheet", 4th ed., "The angle between two
celestial objects". The worked pair below was cross-checked against
PyEphem: both engines agree to about a hundredth of a degree (the
bodies' apparent places differ by a few arcseconds between the two
ephemeris models).

Accuracy: a few hundredths of a degree (ephemeris-grade positions,
formula exact).

Knobs: the instant `tm` and the body pair below (Moon 11 and Venus 2).
============================================================================ */

// ---- the knobs ----------------------------------------------------------------
const tm = jd(2026, 6, 19, 21)
const b1 = 11
const b2 = 2

// ---- Meeus eq. 17.1: great-circle separation in degrees ------------------------
def sep(p, q) = deg(acos(sin(rad(decl(p, tm))) * sin(rad(decl(q, tm))) + cos(rad(decl(p, tm))) * cos(rad(decl(q, tm))) * cos(rad(ra(p, tm) - ra(q, tm)))))

// ---- results ------------------------------------------------------------------
print("the two bodies:", iso(tm))
print("Moon-Venus separation:", sep(b1, b2), "deg")
print("               in dms:", deg2dms(sep(b1, b2)))
print("where they are:")
print("Moon  ra", deg2hms(ra(b1, tm)), " dec", deg2dms(decl(b1, tm)))
print("Venus ra", deg2hms(ra(b2, tm)), " dec", deg2dms(decl(b2, tm)))

/* The Moon-Sun distance tells the phase story from the geometry side:
the Moon was new on 2026-06-15, so the 19th finds it 65 degrees east
of the Sun and the phase law k = (1 - cos 65) / 2 gives 0.289 lit -
the built-in illum reads 0.2901 from the real phase angle. */
print("Moon-Sun separation:", sep(11, 10), "deg, Moon illum:", illum(11, tm))

/* ---- expected output ----
= the two bodies: 2026-06-19T21:00:00
= Moon-Venus separation: 26.2716488378 deg
=                in dms: 26° 16' 18"
= where they are:
= Moon  ra 10h 21m 59s  dec 10° 1' 38"
= Venus ra 8h 41m 37s  dec 20° 20' 29"
= Moon-Sun separation: 65.0521692041 deg, Moon illum: 0.2901
*/

scripts.name: subsolar-sublunar
scripts.title: the ground points beneath Sun and Moon
scripts.text:
/* ============================================================================
subsolar-sublunar.epher -- the ground points beneath Sun and Moon

Computes the point on Earth's surface directly below the Sun (the
subsolar point) and below the Moon (the sublunar point), then the
great-circle distance between them. Latitude: the geocentric
declination of the body (the point where the body is at the zenith
has geocentric latitude equal to the declination; the geodetic
latitude differs by well under a degree). Longitude: the meridian
whose local sidereal time equals the body's right ascension, i.e.
const lon = ra - 15 * GMST hours, wrapped to +/-180 degrees east.

Accuracy: positions arcsecond-grade; the stated latitude
simplification (geocentric vs geodetic, and for the Moon a
topocentric shift of up to ~1 degree) dominates - the points are
good to about a degree, fine for the "who is overhead right now"
question the weather-satellite apps answer for the Sun.

Knobs: the instant tm below.
============================================================================ */

// ---- the knobs ----------------------------------------------------------------
const tm = jd(2026, 9, 10, 22)

// ---- helpers ----------------------------------------------------------------------
def wrap(x) = x - 360 * floor(x / 360)
def lonof(ar) = if wrap(ar - 15 * lst(tm, 0)) > 180 then wrap(ar - 15 * lst(tm, 0)) - 360 else wrap(ar - 15 * lst(tm, 0))  // east positive
def sep(a1, d1, a2, d2) = deg(acos(sin(rad(d1)) * sin(rad(d2)) + cos(rad(d1)) * cos(rad(d2)) * cos(rad(a1 - a2))))

// ---- the two points ----------------------------------------------------------------
const sunra = ra(10, tm)
const sunde = decl(10, tm)
const moonra = ra(11, tm)
const moonde = decl(11, tm)

print("at", iso(tm))
print("subsolar point:  lat", sunde, " lon", lonof(sunra), "(east positive)")
print("sublunar point:  lat", moonde, " lon", lonof(moonra), "(east positive)")
print("separation:", sep(lonof(sunra), sunde, lonof(moonra), moonde), "deg on the sphere")

/* Self-check: the subsolar longitude must be near -15 * (12:00 - UT)
+ equation-of-time terms at the instant; cheaper and stronger: the
Sun is overhead only where its hour angle vanishes, so the subsolar
point's local sidereal time equals the Sun's right ascension - the
construction above guarantees that by definition. The printed
sanity line is the sublunar point's LST vs the Moon's ra. */
print("sublunar LST:", lst(tm, lonof(moonra)), "h  vs Moon ra:", moonra / 15, "h")

/* ---- expected output ----
= at 2026-09-10T22:00:00
= subsolar point:  lat 4.661386822  lon -150.790596618 (east positive)
= sublunar point:  lat 4.492071972  lon -154.020384517 (east positive)
= separation: 3.22393450336 deg on the sphere
= sublunar LST: 11.0619718889 h  vs Moon ra: 11.0619718889 h
*/

scripts.name: weekly-track
scripts.title: a body's weekly almanac track
scripts.text:
/* ============================================================================
weekly-track.epher -- a body's weekly almanac track

Prints six weekly rows of right ascension, declination, distance and
magnitude for one solar-system body - the almanac-table layout that
timeanddate's ephemeris tables and the yearbook pages use. Every
number is a built-in accessor readout (solar-ephemeris crate, VSOP2013
planets, JPL-Horizons-validated; guide 1.29); the script only lays the
table.

Accuracy: the engine's own - about an arcsecond of position and 1e-5 AU
of distance; magnitudes are the standard model magnitudes, good to a
few hundredths.

Knobs: the body (guide 1.29 numbering), the starting instant t0 and
the week step below.
============================================================================ */

// ---- the knobs ----------------------------------------------------------------
const body = 5                 // Jupiter
const t0 = jd(2026, 9, 10, 0)  // first row, 00:00 UT

// ---- the track: one print per row -----------------------------------------------
print("Jupiter, weekly track from", iso(t0))
print("week  date                 ra            dec           dist (AU)  mag")
print(0, iso(t0), deg2hms(ra(body, t0)), deg2dms(decl(body, t0)), dist(body, t0), mag(body, t0))
print(1, iso(t0 + 7), deg2hms(ra(body, t0 + 7)), deg2dms(decl(body, t0 + 7)), dist(body, t0 + 7), mag(body, t0 + 7))
print(2, iso(t0 + 14), deg2hms(ra(body, t0 + 14)), deg2dms(decl(body, t0 + 14)), dist(body, t0 + 14), mag(body, t0 + 14))
print(3, iso(t0 + 21), deg2hms(ra(body, t0 + 21)), deg2dms(decl(body, t0 + 21)), dist(body, t0 + 21), mag(body, t0 + 21))
print(4, iso(t0 + 28), deg2hms(ra(body, t0 + 28)), deg2dms(decl(body, t0 + 28)), dist(body, t0 + 28), mag(body, t0 + 28))
print(5, iso(t0 + 35), deg2hms(ra(body, t0 + 35)), deg2dms(decl(body, t0 + 35)), dist(body, t0 + 35), mag(body, t0 + 35))

/* Self-check: after its June 2026 station Jupiter is in direct
motion, so right ascension must increase week over week. */
print("ra advancing week over week:", ra(body, t0 + 7) > ra(body, t0) and ra(body, t0 + 14) > ra(body, t0 + 7))

/* ---- expected output ----
= Jupiter, weekly track from 2026-09-10T00:00:00
= week  date                 ra            dec           dist (AU)  mag
= 0 2026-09-10T00:00:00 9h 12m 46s 16° 41' 35" 6.12978019676 -1.81
= 1 2026-09-17T00:00:00 9h 18m 21s 16° 17' 19" 6.06837526653 -1.83
= 2 2026-09-24T00:00:00 9h 23m 42s 15° 53' 33" 5.9985358869 -1.85
= 3 2026-10-01T00:00:00 9h 28m 48s 15° 30' 31" 5.92083511095 -1.87
= 4 2026-10-08T00:00:00 9h 33m 37s 15° 8' 27" 5.83581722345 -1.9
= 5 2026-10-15T00:00:00 9h 38m 7s 14° 47' 36" 5.74416128873 -1.93
= ra advancing week over week: true
*/

scripts.name: blue-moon
scripts.title: which months of a year hold two full moons
scripts.text:
/* ============================================================================
blue-moon.epher -- which months of a year hold two full moons

Lists the calendar months of one year that carry two full moons (the
traditional "blue moon": the second full moon in one month) from the
full-moon series of chapter 49 of Jean Meeus, "Astronomical Algorithms"
(2nd ed., Willmann-Bell, 1998): the mean phase (eq. 49.1), the periodic
corrections of table 49.A full-moon column and the planetary
corrections of table 49.C - the same series full-moons.epher carries.
Each full moon is bucketed by its calendar month with the date built-in
(guide 1.18), and equal neighbours mark the doubled month.

A year with thirteen full moons (twelve lunations straddling the
calendar, 365 days versus the 354.4-day twelve-moon year) always has
one month with two; two such months appear when February holds none
(2018 did: Jan and Mar doubled, Feb moonless). Meeus discusses the
calendar spread in "Mathematical Astronomy Morsels", in the essay on
months with five lunar phases.

Accuracy: the series fixes each full moon to about a minute for
2000-2100; only a full moon within a minute of a month boundary could
move to the neighbouring month, and none does in 2026.

Knobs: `year` below (2026 has its doubled month in May).
============================================================================ */

// ---- the knob ----------------------------------------------------------------
const year = 2026

// ---- Meeus ch. 49: mean elements, angles in degrees (eq. 49.3-49.7) -----------
def e3(t) = 1 - 0.002516 * t - 0.0000074 * t ^ 2      // Earth's orbital eccentricity (no unit)
def mp(k) = 201.5643 + 385.81693528 * k               // Moon's mean anomaly, degrees
def ms(k) = 2.5534 + 29.10535670 * k                  // Sun's mean anomaly, degrees
def mf(k) = 160.7108 + 390.67050284 * k               // Moon's argument of latitude, degrees
def node(k) = 124.7746 - 1.56375588 * k               // Moon's ascending node, degrees

// ---- mean full-moon instant in JD: k counts lunations, full moons end in .5 --
def base(k) = 2451550.09766 + 29.530588861 * k + 0.00015437 * (k / 1236.85) ^ 2 - 0.000000150 * (k / 1236.85) ^ 3 + 0.00000000073 * (k / 1236.85) ^ 4

// ---- periodic corrections in days, table 49.A full-moon column, by size -------
def corr_a(k) = -0.40614 * sin(rad(mp(k))) + 0.17302 * e3(k / 1236.85) * sin(rad(ms(k))) + 0.01614 * sin(rad(2 * mp(k))) + 0.01043 * sin(rad(2 * mf(k))) + 0.00734 * e3(k / 1236.85) * sin(rad(mp(k) - ms(k))) - 0.00515 * e3(k / 1236.85) * sin(rad(mp(k) + ms(k))) + 0.00209 * e3(k / 1236.85) ^ 2 * sin(rad(2 * ms(k))) - 0.00111 * sin(rad(mp(k) - 2 * mf(k)))
def corr_b(k) = -0.00057 * sin(rad(mp(k) + 2 * mf(k))) + 0.00056 * e3(k / 1236.85) * sin(rad(2 * mp(k) + ms(k))) - 0.00042 * sin(rad(3 * mp(k))) + 0.00042 * e3(k / 1236.85) * sin(rad(ms(k) + 2 * mf(k))) + 0.00038 * e3(k / 1236.85) * sin(rad(ms(k) - 2 * mf(k))) - 0.00024 * e3(k / 1236.85) * sin(rad(2 * mp(k) - ms(k)))
def corr_c(k) = -0.00017 * sin(rad(node(k))) - 0.00007 * sin(rad(mp(k) + 2 * ms(k))) + 0.00004 * sin(rad(2 * mp(k) - 2 * mf(k))) + 0.00004 * sin(rad(3 * ms(k))) + 0.00003 * sin(rad(mp(k) + ms(k) - 2 * mf(k))) + 0.00003 * sin(rad(2 * mp(k) + 2 * mf(k))) - 0.00003 * sin(rad(mp(k) + ms(k) + 2 * mf(k))) + 0.00003 * sin(rad(mp(k) - ms(k) + 2 * mf(k))) - 0.00002 * sin(rad(mp(k) - ms(k) - 2 * mf(k))) - 0.00002 * sin(rad(3 * mp(k) + ms(k))) + 0.00002 * sin(rad(4 * mp(k)))

// ---- planetary corrections in days, table 49.C --------------------------------
// A1's T^2 term is under a second and is omitted (Meeus, note to 49.C).
def a1(k) = 299.77 + 0.107408 * k
def a2(k) = 251.88 + 0.016321 * k
def a3(k) = 251.83 + 26.651886 * k
def a4(k) = 349.42 + 36.412478 * k
def a5(k) = 84.66 + 18.206239 * k
def a6(k) = 141.74 + 53.303771 * k
def a7(k) = 207.14 + 2.453732 * k
def a8(k) = 154.84 + 7.306860 * k
def a9(k) = 34.52 + 27.261239 * k
def a10(k) = 207.19 + 0.121824 * k
def a11(k) = 291.34 + 1.844379 * k
def a12(k) = 161.72 + 24.198154 * k
def a13(k) = 239.56 + 25.513099 * k
def a14(k) = 331.55 + 3.592518 * k
def corr_d(k) = 0.000325 * sin(rad(a1(k))) + 0.000165 * sin(rad(a2(k))) + 0.000164 * sin(rad(a3(k))) + 0.000126 * sin(rad(a4(k))) + 0.000110 * sin(rad(a5(k))) + 0.000062 * sin(rad(a6(k))) + 0.000060 * sin(rad(a7(k))) + 0.000056 * sin(rad(a8(k))) + 0.000047 * sin(rad(a9(k))) + 0.000042 * sin(rad(a10(k))) + 0.000040 * sin(rad(a11(k))) + 0.000037 * sin(rad(a12(k))) + 0.000035 * sin(rad(a13(k))) + 0.000023 * sin(rad(a14(k)))

// ---- the instant of full moon for lunation k ----------------------------------
def fullmoon(k) = base(k) + corr_a(k) + corr_b(k) + corr_c(k) + corr_d(k)

// ---- bucketing helpers --------------------------------------------------------
def kfirst(jd0) = ceil((jd0 - 2451550.09766) / 29.530588861 - 0.5) + 0.5  // first full moon on/after Jan 1
def mname(m) = if m == 1 then "January" else if m == 2 then "February" else if m == 3 then "March" else if m == 4 then "April" else if m == 5 then "May" else if m == 6 then "June" else if m == 7 then "July" else if m == 8 then "August" else if m == 9 then "September" else if m == 10 then "October" else if m == 11 then "November" else "December"
def mon(k) = date(fullmoon(k))[2]                          // calendar month of the lunation's full moon
def nfull(k0, q, c) = if q >= 13 then c else if fullmoon(k0 + q) < jd(year + 1, 1, 1) then nfull(k0, q + 1, c + 1) else c   // full moons of the year
def findb(k0, n, q) = if q >= n - 1 then -1 else if mon(k0 + q + 1) == mon(k0 + q) then q else findb(k0, n, q + 1)  // first doubled month's index
def restb(k0, n, q) = if q >= n - 1 then "" else if mon(k0 + q + 1) == mon(k0 + q) then ", " + mname(mon(k0 + q)) + restb(k0, n, q + 1) else restb(k0, n, q + 1)  // later doubled months
def allb(k0, n, q) = if q >= n - 1 then "" else if mon(k0 + q + 1) == mon(k0 + q) then mname(mon(k0 + q)) + restb(k0, n, q + 1) else allb(k0, n, q + 1)  // all doubled months, comma-joined

// ---- results ------------------------------------------------------------------
const k0 = kfirst(jd(year, 1, 1))
const count = nfull(k0, 0, 0)
const j = findb(k0, count, 0)
print("full moons in", year, ":", count)
print(if allb(k0, count, 0) == "" then "no month holds two full moons" else "month(s) with two full moons: " + allb(k0, count, 0))

/* The doubled month's two full moons, and the engine cross-check (the
built-in ephemeris knows nothing of the series above): the Moon's lit
face at both instants reads its full-moon ceiling. The ceiling is
0.9986, not 1, because the Moon runs up to 5 degrees off the ecliptic
(see full-moons.epher for the geometry). */
print("the pair:", iso(fullmoon(k0 + j)), "and", iso(fullmoon(k0 + j + 1)), "UT")
print("self-check, illum at them:", illum(11, fullmoon(k0 + j)), "and", illum(11, fullmoon(k0 + j + 1)))

/* ---- expected output ----
= full moons in 2026 : 13
= month(s) with two full moons: May
= the pair: 2026-05-01T17:24:25 and 2026-05-31T08:46:26 UT
= self-check, illum at them: 0.9984 and 0.9981
*/

scripts.name: full-moons
scripts.title: every full moon of one year, to about a minute
scripts.text:
/* ============================================================================
full-moons.epher -- every full moon of one year, to about a minute

Computes the instants of the full moons of `year` with the series of
chapter 49 of Jean Meeus, "Astronomical Algorithms" (2nd ed., Willmann-
Bell, 1998), full-moon column: the mean phase (eq. 49.1), the periodic
corrections of table 49.A and the planetary corrections of table 49.C.
Results are Julian Dates in Universal Time, good to about a minute for
the years 2000-2100 and within a few minutes a few centuries outside.

Modeled on "Phases of the Moon" by Sergio Filippini (ticalc.org archive,
the most-downloaded TI-83/84 BASIC astronomy program), whose README sets
"find the blue moon" as an exercise; the results answer it for any year
you plug in (thirteen full moons over twelve months means one month had
two).

This file is the reference example for the epher scripts folder (the
README at its root explains the format standard). It sits with the other
Moon scripts under astronomy/moon/. The file shows the language's
modern surface, one idea per line, with the guide chapter for each:
`for` loops (1.10), strings and `print` (1.7), `if` decisions (1.8),
and the astronomy accessors and constants (1.18).

Web/desktop:             paste the whole file into the entry, press Enter
Everything also works line by line in the TUI.

The one knob to edit is `year` below. Everything above the results
section is machinery you can leave alone.
============================================================================ */

// ---- the knob -----------------------------------------------------------------
const year = 2026

// ---- Meeus ch. 49: mean elements, angles in degrees (eq. 49.3-49.7) -----------
def e3(t) = 1 - 0.002516 * t - 0.0000074 * t ^ 2      // Earth's orbital eccentricity (no unit)
def mp(k) = 201.5643 + 385.81693528 * k               // Moon's mean anomaly, degrees
def ms(k) = 2.5534 + 29.10535670 * k                  // Sun's mean anomaly, degrees
def mf(k) = 160.7108 + 390.67050284 * k               // Moon's argument of latitude, degrees
def node(k) = 124.7746 - 1.56375588 * k               // Moon's ascending node, degrees

// ---- mean full-moon instant in JD: k counts lunations, full moons end in .5 --
def base(k) = 2451550.09766 + 29.530588861 * k + 0.00015437 * (k / 1236.85) ^ 2 - 0.000000150 * (k / 1236.85) ^ 3 + 0.00000000073 * (k / 1236.85) ^ 4  // 29.530588861 is the synodic month

// ---- periodic corrections in days, table 49.A full-moon column, by size -------
def corr_a(k) = -0.40614 * sin(rad(mp(k))) + 0.17302 * e3(k / 1236.85) * sin(rad(ms(k))) + 0.01614 * sin(rad(2 * mp(k))) + 0.01043 * sin(rad(2 * mf(k))) + 0.00734 * e3(k / 1236.85) * sin(rad(mp(k) - ms(k))) - 0.00515 * e3(k / 1236.85) * sin(rad(mp(k) + ms(k))) + 0.00209 * e3(k / 1236.85) ^ 2 * sin(rad(2 * ms(k))) - 0.00111 * sin(rad(mp(k) - 2 * mf(k)))
def corr_b(k) = -0.00057 * sin(rad(mp(k) + 2 * mf(k))) + 0.00056 * e3(k / 1236.85) * sin(rad(2 * mp(k) + ms(k))) - 0.00042 * sin(rad(3 * mp(k))) + 0.00042 * e3(k / 1236.85) * sin(rad(ms(k) + 2 * mf(k))) + 0.00038 * e3(k / 1236.85) * sin(rad(ms(k) - 2 * mf(k))) - 0.00024 * e3(k / 1236.85) * sin(rad(2 * mp(k) - ms(k)))
def corr_c(k) = -0.00017 * sin(rad(node(k))) - 0.00007 * sin(rad(mp(k) + 2 * ms(k))) + 0.00004 * sin(rad(2 * mp(k) - 2 * mf(k))) + 0.00004 * sin(rad(3 * ms(k))) + 0.00003 * sin(rad(mp(k) + ms(k) - 2 * mf(k))) + 0.00003 * sin(rad(2 * mp(k) + 2 * mf(k))) - 0.00003 * sin(rad(mp(k) + ms(k) + 2 * mf(k))) + 0.00003 * sin(rad(mp(k) - ms(k) + 2 * mf(k))) - 0.00002 * sin(rad(mp(k) - ms(k) - 2 * mf(k))) - 0.00002 * sin(rad(3 * mp(k) + ms(k))) + 0.00002 * sin(rad(4 * mp(k)))

// ---- planetary corrections in days, table 49.C --------------------------------
// A1's T^2 term is under a second and is omitted (Meeus, note to 49.C).
def a1(k) = 299.77 + 0.107408 * k
def a2(k) = 251.88 + 0.016321 * k
def a3(k) = 251.83 + 26.651886 * k
def a4(k) = 349.42 + 36.412478 * k
def a5(k) = 84.66 + 18.206239 * k
def a6(k) = 141.74 + 53.303771 * k
def a7(k) = 207.14 + 2.453732 * k
def a8(k) = 154.84 + 7.306860 * k
def a9(k) = 34.52 + 27.261239 * k
def a10(k) = 207.19 + 0.121824 * k
def a11(k) = 291.34 + 1.844379 * k
def a12(k) = 161.72 + 24.198154 * k
def a13(k) = 239.56 + 25.513099 * k
def a14(k) = 331.55 + 3.592518 * k
def corr_d(k) = 0.000325 * sin(rad(a1(k))) + 0.000165 * sin(rad(a2(k))) + 0.000164 * sin(rad(a3(k))) + 0.000126 * sin(rad(a4(k))) + 0.000110 * sin(rad(a5(k))) + 0.000062 * sin(rad(a6(k))) + 0.000060 * sin(rad(a7(k))) + 0.000056 * sin(rad(a8(k))) + 0.000047 * sin(rad(a9(k))) + 0.000042 * sin(rad(a10(k))) + 0.000040 * sin(rad(a11(k))) + 0.000037 * sin(rad(a12(k))) + 0.000035 * sin(rad(a13(k))) + 0.000023 * sin(rad(a14(k)))

// ---- the instant of full moon for lunation k ----------------------------------
def fullmoon(k) = base(k) + corr_a(k) + corr_b(k) + corr_c(k) + corr_d(k)

// ---- first lunation of the year: the first full moon at or after Jan 1 --------
def kfirst(jd0) = ceil((jd0 - 2451550.09766) / 29.530588861 - 0.5) + 0.5
// The lunation number of the year's first full moon, computed once and
// never changed: a `const` binds silently, so it stays out of the
// transcript (the knob convention, below, is the same statement).
const k = kfirst(jd(year, 1, 1))

// ---- results ------------------------------------------------------------------
/* The full moons of the year. A for loop (guide 1.10) stands in for
typing thirteen calls; n runs 0 to 12 inclusive. Each line names what
it shows and puts the readable instant first, the Julian Date second:
a label and a value, the shape every result line in this folder takes
(the README's output standard). Thirteen entries means the year holds
a blue moon, because one month held two. */
for n in 0 to 12 do print("full moon " + str(n + 1) + ":", iso(fullmoon(k + n)), "UT")

// The first full moon in everyday terms: how far into the year it falls,
// its clock time in UT, and the whole instant as an ISO 8601 date-time
// (iso, guide 1.18 - the readable form of a Julian Date). print (guide
// 1.7) joins its arguments with spaces into one readable line, and a
// unit conversion (`in hr`) keeps its unit label when a print argument
// carries it.
print("the first instant as a Julian Date (UT):", fullmoon(k))
print("first full moon:", fullmoon(k) - jd(year, 1, 1), "days into", year)
print("clock time in UT:", ((fullmoon(k) + 0.5) - floor(fullmoon(k) + 0.5)) * 24 in hr)  // the day's fraction past midnight
print("the instant as a date-time:", iso(fullmoon(k)), "UT")

/* How many full moons the year carries, which answers the blue-moon
exercise: thirteen moons over twelve months means one month held two
(a month can hold two only when the year has thirteen; the count is
the safe half of that fact). if (guide 1.8) picks between two strings,
which print then writes out. */
if fullmoon(k + 12) < jd(year + 1, 1, 1) then "13 full moons this year: one month holds two (a blue moon)" else "12 full moons this year"

/* The Moon's distance at that first instant: the built-in ephemeris
accessor dist (guide 1.18) gives AU, and the au and r_earth constants
convert the count to Earth radii, the number the eye can hold. */
print("Moon distance:", dist(11, fullmoon(k)) * au / r_earth, "Earth radii =", dist(11, fullmoon(k)), "AU")

/* Cross-check against the built-in ephemeris (the solar-ephemeris crate,
JPL-validated; guide 1.18), which knows nothing of Meeus: the Moon's
lit face at the first instant and half a day either side. Full moon
tops out at 0.9986, not 1: the Moon runs 5 degrees off the ecliptic,
so the instant of full illumination in longitude is not quite the
instant of maximum light, and the phase angle (the Sun-Moon-Earth
angle at the Moon) is 4.27 degrees, not 0. illum reports the fraction
to four decimals. */
print("lit fraction at the full-moon instant:", illum(11, fullmoon(k)))
print("lit fraction half a day before:", illum(11, fullmoon(k) - 0.5))
print("lit fraction half a day after:", illum(11, fullmoon(k) + 0.5))
print("phase angle at the instant, degrees:", phase(11, fullmoon(k)))
/* ---- expected output ----
= {full moon 1: 2026-01-03T10:04:05 UT, full moon 2: 2026-02-01T22:10:28 UT, full moon 3: 2026-03-03T11:39:07 UT, full moon 4: 2026-04-02T02:13:11 UT, full moon 5: 2026-05-01T17:24:25 UT, full moon 6: 2026-05-31T08:46:26 UT, full moon 7: 2026-06-29T23:57:53 UT, full moon 8: 2026-07-29T14:36:53 UT, full moon 9: 2026-08-28T04:19:41 UT, full moon 10: 2026-09-26T16:50:13 UT, full moon 11: 2026-10-26T04:12:59 UT, full moon 12: 2026-11-24T14:54:42 UT, full moon 13: 2026-12-24T01:29:24 UT}
= the first instant as a Julian Date (UT): 2461043.91951
= first full moon: 2.41950742295 days into 2026
= clock time in UT: 10.0681781508 hr
= the instant as a date-time: 2026-01-03T10:04:05 UT
= 13 full moons this year: one month holds two (a blue moon)
= Moon distance: 56.8693048187 Earth radii = 0.00242192177806 AU
= lit fraction at the full-moon instant: 0.9986
= lit fraction half a day before: 0.9948
= lit fraction half a day after: 0.9953
= phase angle at the instant, degrees: 4.27
*/

scripts.name: lunar-standstill-season
scripts.title: major and minor standstill years
scripts.text:
/* ============================================================================
lunar-standstill-season.epher -- major and minor standstill years

The Moon's monthly swing of declination breathes on the 18.6-year
cycle of its node: when the ascending node crosses 0 deg (the vernal
equinox) the extremes reach about +/-28.6 deg - a major standstill,
next around 2025 - and when the node crosses 180 deg they shrink to
about +/-18.3 deg - a minor standstill, last around 2015. This script
lists the standstill seasons that follow a knob year, from the mean
node's regression (Meeus ch. 49 elements: node 124.7746 - 1.56375588
per lunation, q.e. one full turn every 18.60 years), and sizes the
next major standstill for one place. Meeus discusses the cycle in
"Mathematical Astronomy Morsels" (the extreme declinations of the
Moon); the engine's own ephemeris (ELP-MPP02, JPL-validated; guide
1.16) supplies the sample check of the season's extremes.

The seasons are dated by the node's exact crossing, which the
literature rounds to a year or two: the extremes stay within a degree
of their peak for about a year on each side of the crossing. The
amplitude eps + 5.145 deg assumes the Moon reaches its full orbital
inclination at the lunistice; the true monthly extremes wobble by a
few tenths of a degree with the evection and the node's own
perturbations, so the amplitudes below are good to about +/-0.2 deg.
This is the mean-element approximation the mission statement asks
for; moon-max-declination.epher shows the engine's exact monthly
values instead.

Knobs: `after` (list the seasons that follow this year) and the
latitude of the place; the list covers four seasons (two major, two
minor) plus the next major standstill's amplitude and the engine
sample of its extremes.
============================================================================ */

// ---- the knobs ----------------------------------------------------------------
const after = 2000        // list the standstill seasons that follow this year
const lat = 51.4779       // the place whose view of the standstill is sized

// ---- mean elements (angles in degrees) ------------------------------------------
def w360(x) = x - 360 * floor(x / 360)
def T(j) = (j - 2451545) / 36525
def eps(j) = 23.4392911 - 46.8150 * T(j) / 3600 - 0.00059 * T(j) ^ 2 / 3600 + 0.001813 * T(j) ^ 3 / 3600   // mean obliquity of date
def jm(m) = 2451550.09766 + (124.7746 - 180 * m) * 29.530588861 / 1.56375588   // instant the node passes 180m deg
def yr(m) = date(jm(m))[1]
def isev(m) = m - 2 * floor(m / 2) == 0            // even m: node at 0 deg (major); odd: at 180 (minor)
def mfirst(m) = if yr(m) >= after then m else mfirst(m - 1)   // first crossing at/after the knob year

// ---- results ---------------------------------------------------------------------
const mf = mfirst(0)                          // first node crossing at/after the knob year
const mm = if isev(mf) then mf else mf - 1    // the next major standstill's m
print("standstill seasons after", after, ": node 0 deg major, 180 deg minor")

// The four seasons that follow the knob year (lines k = 0..3 below).
def sline(k) = (if isev(mf - k) then "major standstill" else "minor standstill") + " " + str(yr(mf - k)) + ": node " + str(w360(180 * (mf - k))) + " deg on " + iso(jm(mf - k)) + " UT"
print("first season:", sline(0))
print("second season:", sline(1))
print("third season:", sline(2))
print("fourth season:", sline(3))

/* The next major standstill's size, at the knob latitude: the Moon's
declination extremes of about +/-(eps + 5.145) deg, so its meridian
altitudes at this place swing through that band. */
print("next major standstill", yr(mm), ": declination extremes about +/-", eps(jm(mm)) + 5.145, "deg")
print("at lat", lat, "the Moon's transit altitude band at the standstill:")
print("  about", 90 - lat - eps(jm(mm)) - 5.145, "to", 90 - lat + eps(jm(mm)) + 5.145, "deg")

/* Engine sample: the built-in ephemeris scans the standstill months
(the crossing plus or minus six weeks, every 3 days) and reports the
largest |declination| it meets - the mean-element amplitude above,
checked against the engine's own Moon. */
const w0 = jm(mm) - 42        // scan window: 42 days before the crossing
def dv(q) = abs(decl(11, w0 + 3 * q))
def dmax(v, iv, q) = if q >= 29 then {v, iv} else if dv(q) > v then dmax(dv(q), q, q + 1) else dmax(v, iv, q + 1)
const r = dmax(dv(0), 0, 1)
print("engine sample: max |declination|", r[1], "deg on", iso(w0 + 3 * r[2]), "UT")
print("grade: mean-element seasons/amplitudes (+/-0.2 deg); engine sample")

/* ---- expected output ----
= standstill seasons after 2000 : node 0 deg major, 180 deg minor
= first season: major standstill 2006: node 0 deg on 2006-06-19T21:22:54 UT
= second season: minor standstill 2015: node 180 deg on 2015-10-10T01:58:56 UT
= third season: major standstill 2025: node 0 deg on 2025-01-29T06:34:58 UT
= fourth season: minor standstill 2034: node 180 deg on 2034-05-21T11:11:00 UT
= next major standstill 2006 : declination extremes about +/- 28.5834503624 deg
= at lat 51.4779 the Moon's transit altitude band at the standstill:
=   about 9.9386496376 to 67.1055503624 deg
= engine sample: max |declination| 28.452983014 deg on 2006-07-22T21:22:54 UT
= grade: mean-element seasons/amplitudes (+/-0.2 deg); engine sample
*/

scripts.name: moon-age
scripts.title: how old is the Moon: days since new moon
scripts.text:
/* ============================================================================
moon-age.epher -- how old is the Moon: days since new moon

Computes the Moon's age at an instant: the elapsed days since the
last new moon, plus the traditional phase name. The new-moon
instant comes from chapter 49 of Jean Meeus, "Astronomical
Algorithms" (2nd ed., Willmann-Bell, 1998): the mean phase (eq.
49.1), the new-moon column of table 49.A and the planetary
corrections of table 49.C - the same series full-moons.epher and
phases-of-the-month.epher carry, here only its new-moon column. The
community ancestor is hpcalc.org's "Moon Phase" (7975) and ticalc's
"moonecl"-style phase finders.

Accuracy: about a minute on the new-moon instant for 2000-2100, so
the age is honest to a few ten-thousandths of a day (a couple of
minutes of Moon).

Knobs: the two instants `t1` (mid-January, waxing) and `t2` (early
February, waning) below, in UT.
============================================================================ */

// ---- the knobs ----------------------------------------------------------------
const t1 = jd(2026, 1, 21)
const t2 = jd(2026, 2, 10)

// ---- Meeus ch. 49 mean elements and new-moon column ---------------------------
def e3(t) = 1 - 0.002516 * t - 0.0000074 * t ^ 2      // Earth's orbital eccentricity (no unit)
def mp(k) = 201.5643 + 385.81693528 * k               // Moon's mean anomaly, degrees
def ms(k) = 2.5534 + 29.10535670 * k                  // Sun's mean anomaly, degrees
def mf(k) = 160.7108 + 390.67050284 * k               // Moon's argument of latitude, degrees
def node(k) = 124.7746 - 1.56375588 * k               // Moon's ascending node, degrees
def base(k) = 2451550.09766 + 29.530588861 * k + 0.00015437 * (k / 1236.85) ^ 2 - 0.000000150 * (k / 1236.85) ^ 3 + 0.00000000073 * (k / 1236.85) ^ 4

def corr_new(k) = -0.40720 * sin(rad(mp(k))) + 0.17241 * e3(k / 1236.85) * sin(rad(ms(k))) + 0.01608 * sin(rad(2 * mp(k))) + 0.01039 * sin(rad(2 * mf(k))) + 0.00739 * e3(k / 1236.85) * sin(rad(mp(k) - ms(k))) - 0.00514 * e3(k / 1236.85) * sin(rad(mp(k) + ms(k))) + 0.00208 * e3(k / 1236.85) ^ 2 * sin(rad(2 * ms(k))) - 0.00111 * sin(rad(mp(k) - 2 * mf(k))) - 0.00057 * sin(rad(mp(k) + 2 * mf(k))) + 0.00056 * e3(k / 1236.85) * sin(rad(2 * mp(k) + ms(k))) - 0.00042 * sin(rad(3 * mp(k))) + 0.00042 * e3(k / 1236.85) * sin(rad(ms(k) + 2 * mf(k))) + 0.00038 * e3(k / 1236.85) * sin(rad(ms(k) - 2 * mf(k))) - 0.00024 * e3(k / 1236.85) * sin(rad(2 * mp(k) - ms(k))) - 0.00017 * sin(rad(node(k))) - 0.00007 * sin(rad(mp(k) + 2 * ms(k))) + 0.00004 * sin(rad(2 * mp(k) - 2 * mf(k))) + 0.00004 * sin(rad(3 * ms(k))) + 0.00003 * sin(rad(mp(k) + ms(k) - 2 * mf(k))) + 0.00003 * sin(rad(2 * mp(k) + 2 * mf(k))) - 0.00003 * sin(rad(mp(k) + ms(k) + 2 * mf(k))) + 0.00003 * sin(rad(mp(k) - ms(k) + 2 * mf(k))) - 0.00002 * sin(rad(mp(k) - ms(k) - 2 * mf(k))) - 0.00002 * sin(rad(3 * mp(k) + ms(k))) + 0.00002 * sin(rad(4 * mp(k)))

// ---- table 49.C planetary corrections in days ----------------------------------
def a1(k) = 299.77 + 0.107408 * k
def a2(k) = 251.88 + 0.016321 * k
def a3(k) = 251.83 + 26.651886 * k
def a4(k) = 349.42 + 36.412478 * k
def a5(k) = 84.66 + 18.206239 * k
def a6(k) = 141.74 + 53.303771 * k
def a7(k) = 207.14 + 2.453732 * k
def a8(k) = 154.84 + 7.306860 * k
def a9(k) = 34.52 + 27.261239 * k
def a10(k) = 207.19 + 0.121824 * k
def a11(k) = 291.34 + 1.844379 * k
def a12(k) = 161.72 + 24.198154 * k
def a13(k) = 239.56 + 25.513099 * k
def a14(k) = 331.55 + 3.592518 * k
def corr_d(k) = 0.000325 * sin(rad(a1(k))) + 0.000165 * sin(rad(a2(k))) + 0.000164 * sin(rad(a3(k))) + 0.000126 * sin(rad(a4(k))) + 0.000110 * sin(rad(a5(k))) + 0.000062 * sin(rad(a6(k))) + 0.000060 * sin(rad(a7(k))) + 0.000056 * sin(rad(a8(k))) + 0.000047 * sin(rad(a9(k))) + 0.000042 * sin(rad(a10(k))) + 0.000040 * sin(rad(a11(k))) + 0.000037 * sin(rad(a12(k))) + 0.000035 * sin(rad(a13(k))) + 0.000023 * sin(rad(a14(k)))

// ---- the new moon nearest (at or before) an instant, and the age --------------
def newmoon(k) = base(k) + corr_new(k) + corr_d(k)
def kb(j) = (j - 2451550.09766) / 29.530588861
def kn(j) = if newmoon(round(kb(j))) > j then round(kb(j)) - 1 else round(kb(j))
def age(j) = j - newmoon(kn(j))

// ---- the traditional name, by age in days (synodic month 29.53 d) -------------
def name(a) = if a < 0.75 then "new" else if a < 6.63 then "waxing crescent" else if a < 8.13 then "first quarter" else if a < 14.02 then "waxing gibbous" else if a < 15.52 then "full" else if a < 21.40 then "waning gibbous" else if a < 22.90 then "last quarter" else "waning crescent"

// ---- results ------------------------------------------------------------------
print("at", iso(t1), "the Moon is", age(t1), "days old -", name(age(t1)))
print("at", iso(t2), "the Moon is", age(t2), "days old -", name(age(t2)))

/* Self-check: the age through the phase law k = (1 - cos(360 x age
/ month)) / 2 against the built-in illum. Near new and full the two
agree to half a percent; near the quarters the slack can reach a
few percent, because the Moon runs up to 5 degrees off the ecliptic
(the same geometry that caps a full moon's illum at 0.9986 - see
full-moons.epher). */
print("illum from age at", "t1:", (1 - cos(rad(360 * age(t1) / 29.530588861))) / 2, "vs built-in:", illum(11, t1))
print("illum from age at", "t2:", (1 - cos(rad(360 * age(t2) / 29.530588861))) / 2, "vs built-in:", illum(11, t2))

/* ---- expected output ----
= at 2026-01-21T00:00:00 the Moon is 2.17134509422 days old - waxing crescent
= at 2026-02-10T00:00:00 the Moon is 22.1713450942 days old - last quarter
= illum from age at t1: 0.0524173237196 vs built-in: 0.0486
= illum from age at t2: 0.497510249515 vs built-in: 0.457
*/

scripts.name: moon-altitude-azimuth
scripts.title: where to look for the Moon one evening
scripts.text:
/* ============================================================================
moon-altitude-azimuth.epher -- where to look for the Moon one evening

Altitude and azimuth of the Moon at three times of one evening (19:00,
20:30, 22:00 UT) on 2026-06-22 at Greenwich (the Royal Observatory),
from the built-in accessors alt and az (the solar-ephemeris crate,
JPL-validated; guide 1.16). Altitude is degrees above the horizon
(negative means below); azimuth is degrees from north through east:
90 east, 180 south, 270 west. The Moon is near first quarter that
evening: it culminated at 18:28 UT (see moon-transit-time.epher) and
is descending in the south, so the altitude falls while the azimuth
swings from south toward southwest; it sets at 23:57 UT
(moonrise-moonset.epher).

Knobs: date, the three clock hours (UT), latitude and longitude.
============================================================================ */

// ---- the knobs --------------------------------------------------------------
const year = 2026
const month = 6
const day = 22
const h1 = 19          // three sample times of the evening, hours UT
const h2 = 20.5
const h3 = 22
const lat = 51.4779        // Greenwich, the Royal Observatory
const lon = 0

/* ---- results ----------------------------------------------------------------
Each line is one look at the sky: altitude and azimuth of the Moon.
At 19:00 UT the Moon is 29.8 deg up, an hour past culminating in the
south (azimuth 188); two hours later it is 15.4 deg up in the
southwest (azimuth 232), still climbing west. */
print("at", h1, "hr UT: alt", alt(11, jd(year, month, day, h1), lat, lon), "deg; az", az(11, jd(year, month, day, h1), lat, lon), "deg")
print("at", h2, "hr UT: alt", alt(11, jd(year, month, day, h2), lat, lon), "deg; az", az(11, jd(year, month, day, h2), lat, lon), "deg")
print("at", h3, "hr UT: alt", alt(11, jd(year, month, day, h3), lat, lon), "deg; az", az(11, jd(year, month, day, h3), lat, lon), "deg")

/* The azimuth runs 188 -> 212 -> 232 deg while the altitude falls from
29.8 to 15.4 deg: the Moon is moving west as the Earth turns, and its
path carries it below the horizon at 23:57 UT. All three altitudes are
positive, so the Moon is above the horizon through the whole sample. */
print("Moon still up at", h3, "hr:", alt(11, jd(year, month, day, h3), lat, lon) > 0)

/* ---- expected output ----
= at 19 hr UT: alt 29.8480081 deg; az 187.5518308 deg
= at 20.5 hr UT: alt 24.8969995 deg; az 211.5385071 deg
= at 22 hr UT: alt 15.4187962 deg; az 232.4553314 deg
= Moon still up at 22 hr: true
*/

scripts.name: moon-angular-diameter
scripts.title: the Moon's apparent size across a month
scripts.text:
/* ============================================================================
moon-angular-diameter.epher -- the Moon's apparent size across a month

Angular diameter of the Moon (built-in accessor diam, in degrees; the
solar-ephemeris crate, JPL-validated; guide 1.16) on the same five
dates of one month as the other moon scripts, printed in degrees and
in arcminutes (1 deg = 60 arcmin, so arcmin = diam * 60). The Moon's
disk spans about 0.49 deg (29.4 arcmin) at apogee to 0.56 deg
(33.5 arcmin) at perigee: it looks about 14 percent wider when close,
the same swing as the distance in moon-distance.epher, and the two
scripts share their sample days so the sizes and distances can be
compared line by line.

Knobs: year, month, and the sample days of the month.
============================================================================ */

// ---- the knobs --------------------------------------------------------------
const year = 2026
const month = 6
const days = {1, 8, 15, 22, 29}

/* ---- results ----------------------------------------------------------------
Diameter in degrees and arcminutes per sample day. Day 15 (new moon,
perigee) is the widest at 0.557 deg; days 1 and 29 (near full moon,
apogee) the narrowest at about 0.490 deg. For scale the Sun is about
the same apparent size, which is why total solar eclipses happen. */
print("day 1:", diam(11, jd(year, month, 1)), "deg =", diam(11, jd(year, month, 1)) * 60, "arcmin")
print("day 8:", diam(11, jd(year, month, 8)), "deg =", diam(11, jd(year, month, 8)) * 60, "arcmin")
print("day 15:", diam(11, jd(year, month, 15)), "deg =", diam(11, jd(year, month, 15)) * 60, "arcmin")
print("day 22:", diam(11, jd(year, month, 22)), "deg =", diam(11, jd(year, month, 22)) * 60, "arcmin")
print("day 29:", diam(11, jd(year, month, 29)), "deg =", diam(11, jd(year, month, 29)) * 60, "arcmin")

/* ---- expected output ----
= day 1: 0.4899475 deg = 29.39685 arcmin
= day 8: 0.513164611111 deg = 30.7898766667 arcmin
= day 15: 0.557373111111 deg = 33.4423866667 arcmin
= day 22: 0.511939277778 deg = 30.7163566667 arcmin
= day 29: 0.490269027778 deg = 29.4161416667 arcmin
*/

scripts.name: moon-distance
scripts.title: how far the Moon is, in Earth radii and km
scripts.text:
/* ============================================================================
moon-distance.epher -- how far the Moon is, in Earth radii and km

Geocentric distance of the Moon (built-in accessor dist, in AU; the
solar-ephemeris crate, JPL-validated; guide 1.16) on five dates of one
month, expressed two ways: Earth radii (dist * au / r_earth, with the
au and r_earth constants) and kilometres ((dist * (1 AU)) in km). The
Moon's orbit is eccentric (e about 0.055): the distance swings between
roughly 356500 km at perigee and 406700 km at apogee, about 4 Earth
radii (25000 km) either way of the mean 384400 km (60.3 Earth radii).
In June 2026 the new moon of the 15th falls near perigee and the full
moon near apogee, so the sample spans nearly the whole range.

Knobs: year, month, and the sample days of the month.
============================================================================ */

// ---- the knobs --------------------------------------------------------------
const year = 2026
const month = 6
const days = {1, 8, 15, 22, 29}

/* ---- results ----------------------------------------------------------------
Distance on each sample day. r_earth is 6371 km, so Earth radii here
run 56.1 (perigee near the new moon of day 15) to 63.8 (apogee near the
full moons of days 1 and 29); the whole sample sits inside the 356500
to 406700 km band of the real orbit. Compare day 15 (357197 km) with
day 1 (406354 km): the apogee distance is about 14 percent greater
than the perigee distance (perigee is about 12 percent closer). */
print("day 1:", dist(11, jd(year, month, 1)) * au / r_earth, "Earth radii;", (dist(11, jd(year, month, 1)) * (1 AU)) in km)
print("day 8:", dist(11, jd(year, month, 8)) * au / r_earth, "Earth radii;", (dist(11, jd(year, month, 8)) * (1 AU)) in km)
print("day 15:", dist(11, jd(year, month, 15)) * au / r_earth, "Earth radii;", (dist(11, jd(year, month, 15)) * (1 AU)) in km)
print("day 22:", dist(11, jd(year, month, 22)) * au / r_earth, "Earth radii;", (dist(11, jd(year, month, 22)) * (1 AU)) in km)
print("day 29:", dist(11, jd(year, month, 29)) * au / r_earth, "Earth radii;", (dist(11, jd(year, month, 29)) * (1 AU)) in km)

// A Moon distance in AU is a small number (0.0024 to 0.0027 here); the
// km and Earth-radii readings are the ones the eye can hold. The angular
// diameter swings the same way, see moon-angular-diameter.epher.
print("day 1, raw AU:", dist(11, jd(year, month, 1)))

/* ---- expected output ----
= day 1: 63.7817755454 Earth radii; 406353.692 km
= day 8: 60.8961169361 Earth radii; 387969.161 km
= day 15: 56.066125412 Earth radii; 357197.285 km
= day 22: 61.0418698791 Earth radii; 388897.753 km
= day 29: 63.7399491446 Earth radii; 406087.216 km
= day 1, raw AU: 0.00271630665663
*/

scripts.name: moon-ecliptic-position
scripts.title: the Moon's ecliptic longitude and latitude
scripts.text:
/* ============================================================================
moon-ecliptic-position.epher -- the Moon's ecliptic longitude and latitude

Converts the Moon's geocentric equatorial position (the built-in ra and
decl accessors; the solar-ephemeris crate, JPL-validated; guide 1.16)
into geocentric ecliptic longitude and latitude for one instant, with
the rotation of chapter 13 of Jean Meeus, "Astronomical Algorithms"
(2nd ed., Willmann-Bell, 1998):

  sin beta  = sin delta cos eps - cos delta sin eps sin alpha
  tan lambda = (sin alpha cos eps + tan delta sin eps) / cos alpha

using the mean obliquity of date (Meeus ch. 22):
  eps = 23.4392911 - 46.8150 T / 3600 - 0.00059 T^2 / 3600
        + 0.001813 T^3 / 3600 deg,  T in Julian centuries from J2000.

The ecliptic is the frame the classic lunar tables (and the eclipses
chapter's node geometry) work in, and it is what a planisphere's
zodiacal scale reads. The Sun's position goes through the same
rotation as the self-check: its ecliptic latitude must come out near
zero, because the Sun sits in the ecliptic by definition - the engine
reads a few hundredths of a degree of slack from the difference
between the mean obliquity used here and the apparent equator the
engine's ra and decl refer to (nutation swings the true obliquity by
up to about 9 arcseconds).

Accuracy: the conversion itself is exact given eps; the engine's
positions are arcsecond-class, so the result is honest to a few
arcseconds plus the ~10 arcsec mean-obliquity slack.

Knobs: the instant (below: 2026-03-25 19:18 UT, that month's first
quarter - the Sun-Moon longitude gap then reads about 90 deg).
============================================================================ */

// ---- the knobs ----------------------------------------------------------------
const year = 2026
const month = 3
const day = 25
const hr = 19.3       // hours UT (first quarter 2026-03-25T19:18:52, phases-of-the-month.epher)

// ---- mean obliquity and the ch. 13 rotation (angles in degrees) ---------------
def T(j) = (j - 2451545) / 36525                      // Julian centuries from J2000
def eps(j) = 23.4392911 - 46.8150 * T(j) / 3600 - 0.00059 * T(j) ^ 2 / 3600 + 0.001813 * T(j) ^ 3 / 3600   // mean obliquity of date, deg
def w360(x) = x - 360 * floor(x / 360)
def elon(j, b) = w360(deg(atan2(sin(rad(ra(b, j))) * cos(rad(eps(j))) + tan(rad(decl(b, j))) * sin(rad(eps(j))), cos(rad(ra(b, j))))))   // ecliptic longitude of body b, deg
def elat(j, b) = deg(asin(sin(rad(decl(b, j))) * cos(rad(eps(j))) - cos(rad(decl(b, j))) * sin(rad(eps(j))) * sin(rad(ra(b, j)))))   // ecliptic latitude of body b, deg

// ---- results ------------------------------------------------------------------
const t = jd(year, month, day, hr)
print("at", iso(t), "UT:")
print("mean obliquity of date:", eps(t), "deg")
print("Moon: ra", ra(11, t), "deg, declination", decl(11, t), "deg")
print("Moon's ecliptic longitude:", elon(t, 11), "deg")
print("Moon's ecliptic latitude:", elat(t, 11), "deg")
print("Sun: ecliptic longitude", elon(t, 10), "deg")
print("Sun's ecliptic latitude", elat(t, 10), "deg (self-check: near 0)")
print("Sun-Moon longitude gap:", w360(elon(t, 11) - elon(t, 10)), "deg (90 at first quarter)")

/* ---- expected output ----
= at 2026-03-25T19:18:00 UT:
= mean obliquity of date: 23.4358801773 deg
= Moon: ra 95.819056257 deg, declination 28.020648976 deg
= Moon's ecliptic longitude: 95.1522705654 deg
= Moon's ecliptic latitude: 4.68876913967 deg
= Sun: ecliptic longitude 5.14935635639 deg
= Sun's ecliptic latitude 0.00036572884576 deg (self-check: near 0)
= Sun-Moon longitude gap: 90.002914209 deg (90 at first quarter)
*/

scripts.name: moon-free-tonight
scripts.title: the Moon-free dark window of a night
scripts.text:
/* ============================================================================
moon-free-tonight.epher -- the Moon-free dark window of a night

For one place and one night (dusk of the knob date to the next dawn)
this finds the dark window: the stretch when the sky is fully dark -
the Sun below the -18 deg horizon of astronomical twilight - AND the
Moon is below the horizon. Two window shapes occur: when the Moon is
already down as the sky darkens the window runs from the end of
astronomical twilight to moonrise (or to dawn, if the Moon stays down
all night); when the Moon is up at dusk the window opens at moonset
and runs to dawn. When the Moon stays up through the whole dark night
there is no dark window at all.

The twilight ends come from the standard hour-angle method at the -18
deg horizon (USNO / NOAA notes, as in twilight-times.epher): cos H =
(sin h0 - sin lat sin dec) / (cos lat cos dec), with 4 minutes per
degree of hour angle around the solar transit. The solar transit is
recovered from lst and the Sun's right ascension at local noon (the
engine's transit() search is exact but slow), and the Sun's
declination is read at a fixed 0.27 d from it - where the -18 deg
crossing sits at temperate latitudes - so the twilight instants come
out accurate to a few seconds. The lunar events come from the built-in
rise/set accessors (the solar-ephemeris crate, JPL-validated; guide
1.16), which also tell whether the Moon is above the horizon at any
instant.

Accuracy: about ten seconds on every instant printed, and the window
length inherits that.

Knobs: the place and the date whose night is planned (below: Greenwich,
the night of 2026-02-05 - a waning gibbous Moon rises at 21:40 UT,
2h50m after full darkness falls). The consts A, B, R, S below echo the
worked instants as hours after the knob date's midnight.
============================================================================ */

// ---- the knobs ----------------------------------------------------------------
const lat = 51.4779            // Greenwich
const lon = 0
const day = {2026, 2, 5}       // the night of this date (dusk to next dawn)
const j0 = jd(day[1], day[2], day[3])   // 0h UT of the knob date
const j1 = j0 + 1                       // 0h UT of the next day

// ---- the astronomical-night bracket, hour-angle method at -18 deg -------------
// The solar transit comes from lst and the Sun's ra at local noon;
// the crossing sits about 0.27 d from it, where decl is read.
def w360(x) = x - 360 * floor(x / 360)
def ha(j) = w360(lst(j + 0.5, lon) * 15 - ra(10, j + 0.5))    // Sun's hour angle at local noon, deg
def ttrans(j) = j + 0.5 - (if ha(j) > 180 then ha(j) - 360 else ha(j)) / 360   // solar transit of local day j
def cx(dc) = (sin(rad(-18)) - sin(rad(lat)) * sin(rad(dc))) / (cos(rad(lat)) * cos(rad(dc)))   // cos of the -18 deg hour angle
def off(j, s) = if abs(cx(decl(10, ttrans(j) + s * 0.27))) > 1 then -1 else 4 * deg(acos(cx(decl(10, ttrans(j) + s * 0.27)))) / 1440   // -18 deg hour angle in days, s = +1 evening / -1 morning (-1 = never)
def aeve(j) = if off(j, 1) < 0 then 0 else ttrans(j) + off(j, 1)   // evening: Sun reaches -18 deg (0 = never)
def bdawn(j) = if off(j, -1) < 0 then 0 else ttrans(j) - off(j, -1)   // morning: Sun leaves -18 deg
const A = (aeve(j0) - j0) * 24    // dusk: astronomical twilight ends, hr after j0 (0 = never that dark)
const B = (bdawn(j1) - j0) * 24   // dawn: astronomical twilight resumes, hr after j0

// ---- lunar events of the night: the first rise and first set after dusk -------
def mrise(j) = rise(11, j, lat, lon)
def mset(j) = set(11, j, lat, lon)
def rnight(j) = if (mrise(j) - j0) * 24 > A then mrise(j) else mrise(j + 1)   // first moonrise after dusk
def snight(j) = if (mset(j) - j0) * 24 > A then mset(j) else mset(j + 1)      // first moonset after dusk
const R = (rnight(j0) - j0) * 24   // that moonrise, hr after j0
const S = (snight(j0) - j0) * 24   // that moonset, hr after j0
def moonup(j) = alt(11, j0 + A / 24, lat, lon) > -0.833   // is the Moon above the horizon at dusk?

// ---- results ------------------------------------------------------------------
print("night of", iso(j0), "at lat", lat, "lon", lon)

// The sky-darkness bracket (the -18 deg test can fail at high summer
// latitudes; A = 0 then, and the later lines stand down).
if A == 0 then "no astronomical night: the Sun never reaches -18 deg" else "astronomical night: " + iso(j0 + A / 24) + " to " + iso(j0 + B / 24) + " UT"

/* Where the Moon stands at dusk decides the window: down at dusk, it
runs from the end of twilight to moonrise (or to dawn when the Moon
stays down all night); up at dusk, it opens at moonset and runs to
dawn. The Moon up for the whole dark night leaves no window. */
if A == 0 then "no dark window to report" else if moonup(j0) then (if S < B then "dark window: " + iso(j0 + S / 24) + " to " + iso(j0 + B / 24) + " UT (moonset to dawn)" else "no dark window: the Moon is up the whole night") else (if R >= B then "dark window: the whole night (the Moon stays down)" else "dark window: " + iso(j0 + A / 24) + " to " + iso(j0 + R / 24) + " UT (dusk to moonrise)")

// The window length, from the same bracket as the line above.
if A == 0 then "window length: none" else if moonup(j0) then (if S < B then print("window length:", (B - S) in hr) else "window length: none") else (if R >= B then print("window length:", (B - A) in hr) else print("window length:", (R - A) in hr))

/* Self-check: at the computed end of twilight the engine's own Sun
altitude should read -18 deg (the hour-angle method rederived the
engine's geometry from lst, ra and a noon declination alone). */
if A == 0 then "self-check skipped (no astronomical night)" else "self-check: Sun altitude at that instant: " + str(alt(10, j0 + A / 24, lat, lon)) + " deg (target -18)"

/* ---- expected output ----
= night of 2026-02-05T00:00:00 at lat 51.4779 lon 0
= astronomical night: 2026-02-05T18:51:04 to 2026-02-06T05:36:12 UT
= dark window: 2026-02-05T18:51:04 to 2026-02-05T21:40:34 UT (dusk to moonrise)
= window length: 2.82473650575 hr
= self-check: Sun altitude at that instant: -17.9977183 deg (target -18)
*/

scripts.name: moon-illumination
scripts.title: the Moon's lit fraction across one month
scripts.text:
/* ============================================================================
moon-illumination.epher -- the Moon's lit fraction across one month

The illuminated fraction of the Moon's disk (0 = new moon, 1 = full) on
five dates of one month, from the built-in ephemeris accessor illum
(the solar-ephemeris crate, JPL-validated; guide 1.16). The accessor
rounds the fraction to four decimals. Full moon is the instant the
Sun-Moon-Earth angle at the Moon is smallest, and that angle never
reaches zero because the Moon's orbit is tilted about 5 deg to the
ecliptic: illum tops out near 0.9986-0.9988, not 1. In June 2026 the
full moon falls on the 29th at about 23:58 UT and the new moon on the
15th (see full-moons.epher in this folder for the full-moon series).

Knobs: year, month, and the sample days of the month.
============================================================================ */

// ---- the knobs --------------------------------------------------------------
const year = 2026
const month = 6
const days = {1, 8, 15, 22, 29}     // sample dates; 15 is new moon, 29 full

/* ---- results ----------------------------------------------------------------
One value per sample day, collected by the for loop (guide 1.30): the
month wanes from 0.9946 (just past full), through last quarter (day 8)
and new moon (day 15, near 0), then waxes through first quarter (day 22)
toward the full moon of June 29. The fraction is rounded to 4 decimals. */
for d in days do illum(11, jd(year, month, d))

/* The extremes, labelled. Near new moon the lit sliver is 0.0019, not 0:
alignment is never exact. At the full instant (23:58 UT on the 29th,
from the Meeus series of full-moons.epher) illum reads 0.9988: the 5 deg
tilt leaves a phase angle of a few degrees, so the face is not quite
all-lit. Moon-illumination and moon-phase-angle in this folder show the
same days; moon-phase-angle.epher relates illum to the phase angle. */
print("near new moon (day 15):", illum(11, jd(year, month, 15)))
print("full instant (day 29, 23.97 hr UT):", illum(11, jd(year, month, 29, 23.97)))

/* ---- expected output ----
= {0.9946, 0.5447, 0.0019, 0.5102, 0.9894}
= near new moon (day 15): 0.0019
= full instant (day 29, 23.97 hr UT): 0.9988
*/

scripts.name: moon-libration
scripts.title: optical libration and the terminator longitudes
scripts.text:
/* ============================================================================
moon-libration.epher -- optical libration and the terminator longitudes

The optical librations: the selenographic longitude and latitude of
the sub-Earth point (how far the Moon has "nodded" and "rolled"
relative to its mean face), plus the selenographic longitudes of the
sun and of the morning and evening terminators. The geometry follows
the treatment of Duffett-Smith & Zwart, "Practical Astronomy with
your Calculator or Spreadsheet", 4th ed., section "Selenographic
coordinates", worked here in vector form (the full physical ephemeris
of Meeus ch. 53 adds only ~0.02-0.04 deg of physical libration, which
is omitted).

The frame: the lunar equator is taken as the ecliptic tilted by
the inclination incl = 1.5424 deg about the mean node line; the prime meridian points at
the Moon's mean longitude L' (Meeus ch. 47 series), and the node
comes from the mean elements (Meeus ch. 49). Inputs at the chosen
instant: the Moon's and the Sun's geocentric ra and decl (the
solar-ephemeris crate, JPL-validated; guide 1.16), rotated to the
ecliptic with the mean obliquity (the ch. 13 rotation of
moon-ecliptic-position.epher). With lambda/beta the ecliptic
coordinates, Lbar the mean lunar longitude and O the node:

  sin b  = sin incl cos beta cos(O + lambda) - cos incl sin beta
  tan l  = (cos beta cos incl sin(lambda - Lbar)
            - sin beta sin incl sin(O + Lbar)) / (cos beta cos(lambda - Lbar))
  l_sun  = the same rotation applied to the Sun's direction
           (its longitude comes out near 0 at full moon, 180 at new)
  morning terminator at l_sun - 90, evening at l_sun + 90

Conventions printed below: l > 0 means the sub-Earth point lies east
of the mean meridian (a little of the Moon's east limb is visible);
b > 0 means the Earth is north of the lunar equator (the north polar
region tips into view). The small projection terms of order incl times
beta (up to 0.15 deg) are kept in l; terms of order incl squared are
dropped.

Accuracy: the librations come out to a few tenths of a degree (the
dropped incl-squared and physical terms together are under 0.05 deg, and
the engine's positions are arcsecond-class). The self-check below is
the geometry's own bound: the libration in latitude cannot leave the
+/-7 deg band (5.15 deg of orbital tilt plus 1.54 deg of equator
tilt), and the sub-solar longitude must read near 0 at the full
moon chosen.

Knobs: the instant (below: the full moon of 2026-05-31 08:46 UT, from
full-moons.epher - the sub-solar longitude must then read near 0).
============================================================================ */

// ---- the knobs ----------------------------------------------------------------
const year = 2026
const month = 5
const day = 31
const hr = 8.77       // hours UT (the full moon fell at 08:46)

// ---- mean elements and obliquity (angles in degrees) ----------------------------
def w360(x) = x - 360 * floor(x / 360)
def sym(x) = x - 360 * floor((x + 180) / 360)     // wrap into (-180, 180]
def T(j) = (j - 2451545) / 36525
const incl = 1.5424    // lunar equator's tilt to the ecliptic, deg - Meeus's i (ch. 53); named incl because i is reserved (guide 1.18)
def eps(j) = 23.4392911 - 46.8150 * T(j) / 3600 - 0.00059 * T(j) ^ 2 / 3600 + 0.001813 * T(j) ^ 3 / 3600   // mean obliquity of date
def Lbar(j) = w360(218.3164477 + 481267.88123421 * T(j) - 0.0015786 * T(j) ^ 2 + T(j) ^ 3 / 538841 - T(j) ^ 4 / 65194000)   // Moon's mean longitude, ch. 47
def node(j) = 124.7746 - 1.56375588 * (j - 2451550.09766) / 29.530588861   // Moon's mean ascending node, ch. 49

// ---- equatorial to ecliptic (the ch. 13 rotation) -------------------------------
def elon(j, b) = w360(deg(atan2(sin(rad(ra(b, j))) * cos(rad(eps(j))) + tan(rad(decl(b, j))) * sin(rad(eps(j))), cos(rad(ra(b, j))))))
def elat(j, b) = deg(asin(sin(rad(decl(b, j))) * cos(rad(eps(j))) - cos(rad(decl(b, j))) * sin(rad(eps(j))) * sin(rad(ra(b, j)))))

// ---- the sub-Earth and sub-solar selenographic coordinates -----------------------
/* b_E and l_E are the Earth's selenographic latitude and longitude (the
optical librations); l_s is the Sun's selenographic longitude; all
from the vector frame described above. The small frame-tilt terms of
order incl are kept in l. */
def bsub(j, lb, be) = deg(asin(sin(rad(incl)) * cos(rad(be)) * cos(rad(node(j) + lb)) - cos(rad(incl)) * sin(rad(be))))
def lsub(j, lb, be) = deg(atan2(cos(rad(be)) * cos(rad(incl)) * sin(rad(lb - Lbar(j))) - sin(rad(be)) * sin(rad(incl)) * sin(rad(node(j) + Lbar(j))), cos(rad(be)) * cos(rad(lb - Lbar(j)))))

// ---- results ---------------------------------------------------------------------
const t = jd(year, month, day, hr)
print("at", iso(t), "UT:")
const lm = elon(t, 11)
const bm = elat(t, 11)
const lsun = elon(t, 10)
print("Moon ecliptic lon/lat:", lm, "/", bm, "deg")
print("Sun ecliptic lon:", lsun, "deg")
print("mean lunar longitude L':", Lbar(t), "deg; mean node:", sym(node(t)), "deg")
print("libration in longitude (sub-Earth lon):", sym(lsub(t, lm, bm)), "deg")
print("libration in latitude (sub-Earth lat):", bsub(t, lm, bm), "deg")

/* Self-checks: the latitude libration must sit inside the +/-7 deg
band of the geometry, and the Sun's selenographic longitude must read
near 0 at this full-moon instant (the Sun stands behind the Earth, in
the direction of the mean meridian). The sub-solar longitude is the
anti-solar reading of the formula turned around by 180 deg. */
print("self-check: |libration in latitude| <= 7:", abs(bsub(t, lm, bm)) <= 7)
print("sub-solar longitude:", sym(lsub(t, lsun, 0) - 180), "deg (near 0 at full moon)")

// The terminators: the sunrise line sits 90 deg west of the sub-solar
// meridian, the sunset line 90 deg east of it (in selenographic lon).
print("morning terminator (sunrise) at longitude:", sym(lsub(t, lsun, 0) - 270), "deg")
print("evening terminator (sunset) at longitude:", sym(lsub(t, lsun, 0) - 90), "deg")

/* ---- expected output ----
= at 2026-05-31T08:46:12 UT:
= Moon ecliptic lon/lat: 249.93757467 / -4.96413066038 deg
= Sun ecliptic lon: 69.9297100558 deg
= mean lunar longitude L': 249.239804573 deg; mean node: -25.7933095683 deg
= libration in longitude (sub-Earth lon): 0.605405748088 deg
= libration in latitude (sub-Earth lat): 3.85651368997 deg
= self-check: |libration in latitude| <= 7: true
= sub-solar longitude: 0.689655540163 deg (near 0 at full moon)
= morning terminator (sunrise) at longitude: -89.3103444598 deg
= evening terminator (sunset) at longitude: 90.6896555402 deg
*/

scripts.name: moon-max-declination
scripts.title: the month's extreme declinations
scripts.text:
/* ============================================================================
moon-max-declination.epher -- the month's extreme declinations

Finds the month's maximum and minimum geocentric declination of the
Moon - when it stands highest and lowest against the stars - by
scanning the built-in decl accessor (the solar-ephemeris crate,
ELP-MPP02, JPL-validated; guide 1.16) in the same three cheap stages
as moon-perigee-apogee.epher: every 2 days across the month (the
Moon's draconic month is 27.2 days, so each declination extreme has a
sample within a day), every 6 hours over a 2-day window around each
coarse extreme, then a parabolic vertex through the best three
6-hour samples.

The monthly swing is the 18.6-year standstill cycle at work: the
declination extremes reach about 28.5 deg in a major-standstill year
and shrink to about 18.3 deg at the minor standstill (see
lunar-standstill-season.epher). Mid-2026 sits in the aftermath of the
2024-25 major standstill, so June 2026 swings between +27.9 and -28.0
deg. Meeus, "Astronomical Algorithms" ch. 52 treats the maximum
declinations of the Moon with mean elements; here the ephemeris
itself is scanned, which is why the values are exact to the engine
and the times carry only the sampling slack.

Accuracy: the declination values are engine-grade, and the 6-hour
parabolic refinement reads the extreme itself to well under 0.01 deg
(the curve is very nearly parabolic near its turning point); the
times are good to a few minutes. The coarse scan compares samples,
so when a month holds two extremes of one kind (June 2026's two
southern extremes) the finer one wins the reported value. There is
no independent builtin to cross-check against: the engine is its
own source here.

Knobs: `year` and `month` (below: June 2026, whose Moon reaches
+27.99 deg on the 15th and -27.99 deg on the 1st - the month carries
a second southern extreme, -27.99 deg again near the 29th, and the
scan reports the deepest).
============================================================================ */

// ---- the knobs ----------------------------------------------------------------
const year = 2026
const month = 6

// ---- the scan geometry ----------------------------------------------------------
const j0 = jd(year, month, 1)                     // 1st of the month, 0h UT
const d0 = j0 - 3                                 // coarse scan starts 3 days early
const num = 18                                      // coarse samples, one every 2 days

// ---- declination accessors, deg -------------------------------------------------
def dv(q) = decl(11, d0 + 2 * q)                  // coarse sample q
def fv(k, c) = decl(11, c - 1 + 0.25 * k)         // fine sample k, 6-hour steps in a 2-day window around day c
def cscan(lo, hi, ilo, ihi, q) = if q >= num then {lo, hi, ilo, ihi} else if dv(q) < lo then cscan(dv(q), hi, q, ihi, q + 1) else if dv(q) > hi then cscan(lo, dv(q), ilo, q, q + 1) else cscan(lo, hi, ilo, ihi, q + 1)   // {min, max, argmin, argmax} of the coarse declinations
def fmin(c, v, iv, k) = if k >= 9 then iv else if fv(k, c) < v then fmin(c, fv(k, c), k, k + 1) else fmin(c, v, iv, k + 1)   // fine scan: index of the smallest sample
def fmax(c, v, iv, k) = if k >= 9 then iv else if fv(k, c) > v then fmax(c, fv(k, c), k, k + 1) else fmax(c, v, iv, k + 1)   // fine scan: index of the largest sample
def vtx(c, m) = c - 1 + 0.25 * m + 0.125 * (fv(m - 1, c) - fv(m + 1, c)) / (fv(m - 1, c) - 2 * fv(m, c) + fv(m + 1, c))   // parabolic vertex through fine samples m-1, m, m+1 (JD)
def dcld(t) = decl(11, j0 + t / 24)               // declination at t hours after the 1st, deg

// ---- results ---------------------------------------------------------------------
const r = cscan(dv(0), dv(0), 0, 0, 1)
const cm = d0 + 2 * r[3]     // the coarse minimum day
const cM = d0 + 2 * r[4]     // the coarse maximum day
const tn = (vtx(cm, fmin(cm, fv(0, cm), 0, 1)) - j0) * 24   // minimum declination, hours after the 1st
const tx = (vtx(cM, fmax(cM, fv(0, cM), 0, 1)) - j0) * 24   // maximum declination, hours after the 1st
print("minimum declination of", month, "/", year, ":", iso(j0 + tn / 24), "UT:", dcld(tn), "deg")
print("  in degrees/minutes/seconds:", deg2dms(dcld(tn)))
print("maximum declination of", month, "/", year, ":", iso(j0 + tx / 24), "UT:", dcld(tx), "deg")
print("  in degrees/minutes/seconds:", deg2dms(dcld(tx)))
print("monthly swing:", dcld(tx) - dcld(tn), "deg (the standstill-cycle amplitude in 2026)")
print("grade: values engine-grade (vertex reading <0.01 deg); times a few minutes")

/* ---- expected output ----
= minimum declination of 6 / 2026 : 2026-06-01T16:47:50 UT: -27.992830996 deg
=   in degrees/minutes/seconds: -27° 59' 34"
= maximum declination of 6 / 2026 : 2026-06-15T05:17:37 UT: 27.990237301 deg
=   in degrees/minutes/seconds: 27° 59' 25"
= monthly swing: 55.983068297 deg (the standstill-cycle amplitude in 2026)
= grade: values engine-grade (vertex reading <0.01 deg); times a few minutes
*/

scripts.name: moon-parallax
scripts.title: the Moon's horizontal parallax at work
scripts.text:
/* ============================================================================
moon-parallax.epher -- the Moon's horizontal parallax at work

Two things: the Moon's horizontal parallax (HP) at one instant - the
angle the Earth's radius subtends at the Moon - from the built-in
distance (HP = asin(r_earth / dist), the relation of Duffett-Smith,
"Practical Astronomy", 4th ed., "The Moon's distance, angular size
and horizontal parallax", and of Meeus ch. 40, "Correction for
Parallax"), and then a live demonstration of what parallax does: the
Moon's geocentric altitude computed by plain trigonometry from ra,
decl and local sidereal time, versus the engine's topocentric
altitude for a place. Their difference is the parallax in altitude,
about HP cos(alt): the surface observer sees the Moon lower than the
geocentric sky - nothing at the zenith, nearly a full degree at the
horizon. Navigation almanacs add that same term back when reducing a
Moon sight: observed altitude plus the parallax correction gives the
geocentric altitude (Meeus ch. 40).

The distance accessor is geocentric (the solar-ephemeris crate,
JPL-validated; guide 1.16): HP reads the Moon's distance from the
Earth's centre. r_earth is the mean radius; the engine's topocentric
altitude uses the same spherical-Earth model, so the measured shift
and the HP cos(alt) prediction agree to a few thousandths of a degree
(the residual is the second order of the parallax, about HP^2 times
sine terms).

Accuracy: engine-grade throughout; the altitude shift is good to
about 0.01 deg.

Knobs: the place and the instant (below: Greenwich, 2026-06-22 22:00
UT - the Moon sits 15.4 deg up in the southwest, where the parallax
still shifts it nearly a full degree).
============================================================================ */

// ---- the knobs ----------------------------------------------------------------
const lat = 51.4779        // Greenwich - the Royal Observatory
const lon = 0
const year = 2026
const month = 6
const day = 22
const hr = 22          // hours UT

// ---- helpers ----------------------------------------------------------------
def w360(x) = x - 360 * floor(x / 360)
def hp(j) = deg(asin(r_earth / (dist(11, j) * au)))      // horizontal parallax, deg (r_earth and au in metres)
def altg(j, lat, lon) = deg(asin(sin(rad(lat)) * sin(rad(decl(11, j))) + cos(rad(lat)) * cos(rad(decl(11, j))) * cos(rad(w360(lst(j, lon) * 15 - ra(11, j))))))   // geocentric altitude from the hour angle

// ---- results ------------------------------------------------------------------
const t = jd(year, month, day, hr)
print("at", iso(t), "UT, from lat", lat, "lon", lon)
print("Moon distance:", dist(11, t), "AU")
print("horizontal parallax:", hp(t), "deg =", hp(t) * 60, "arcmin")

/* The demo: the geocentric altitude of the same instant (the sky as a
hypothetical observer at the Earth's centre would see it) versus the
engine's topocentric altitude for the place. Their difference is the
parallax in altitude: the Moon reads 0.89 deg lower for the surface
observer, and -HP cos(alt) predicts the shift. */
print("geocentric altitude (ra/dec/lst trig):", altg(t, lat, lon), "deg")
print("topocentric altitude (engine):", alt(11, t, lat, lon), "deg")
print("shift (topocentric minus geocentric):", alt(11, t, lat, lon) - altg(t, lat, lon), "deg")
print("shift predicted, -HP cos(alt):", -hp(t) * cos(rad(altg(t, lat, lon))), "deg")

/* ---- expected output ----
= at 2026-06-22T22:00:00 UT, from lat 51.4779 lon 0
= Moon distance: 0.00263138917792 AU
= horizontal parallax: 0.927339379581 deg = 55.6403627749 arcmin
= geocentric altitude (ra/dec/lst trig): 16.3114308383 deg
= topocentric altitude (engine): 15.4187962 deg
= shift (topocentric minus geocentric): -0.89263463826 deg
= shift predicted, -HP cos(alt): -0.890013300244 deg
*/

scripts.name: moon-perigee-apogee
scripts.title: this month's closest and farthest approach
scripts.text:
/* ============================================================================
moon-perigee-apogee.epher -- this month's closest and farthest approach

Finds the month's perigee and apogee - the instants of the Moon's
closest and farthest geocentric distance - by scanning the built-in
distance accessor (the solar-ephemeris crate, ELP-MPP02, JPL-validated;
guide 1.16) rather than by the mean-element series of Meeus ch. 50
("Perigee and Apogee of the Moon"), which is the classic shortcut for
the same instants; the distances themselves come straight from the
ephemeris. The scan works in three cheap stages: every 2 days across
the month (the Moon's anomalistic month is 27.55 days, so each
extremum has a sample within a day), then every 6 hours over a 3-day
window around each coarse extremum, then a parabolic vertex through
the best three 6-hour samples. Meeus discusses the extremes of the
Earth-Moon distance in "Mathematical Astronomy Morsels".

Accuracy: the distances are engine-grade (a few kilometres, the ELP's
own noise floor). The times carry the sampling slack: the coarse grid
cannot miss an extremum (they sit 13.8 days apart), the 6-hour
refinement brackets it to three hours, and the parabolic vertex on
those samples recovers the true instant to a few minutes (the
distance curve is very nearly parabolic near an extremum; the
residual asymmetry shifts the vertex by minutes at most).

Knobs: `year` and `month` (below: March 2026, whose perigee falls on
the 22nd at 366857 km and apogee on the 10th at 404384 km - a 38 Mm
swing, the eccentric orbit at work).
============================================================================ */

// ---- the knobs ----------------------------------------------------------------
const year = 2026
const month = 3

// ---- the scan geometry ----------------------------------------------------------
const j0 = jd(year, month, 1)                     // 1st of the month, 0h UT
const j1 = if month == 12 then jd(year + 1, 1, 1) else jd(year, month + 1, 1)   // 1st of the next month
const d0 = j0 - 3                                 // coarse scan starts 3 days early
const num = 18                                      // coarse samples, one every 2 days

// ---- distance accessors, km -----------------------------------------------------
def dv(q) = dist(11, d0 + 2 * q) * au / 1000      // coarse sample q (au is in metres)
def fv(k, c) = dist(11, c - 1 + 0.25 * k) * au / 1000      // fine sample k, 6-hour steps in a 2-day window around day c
def cscan(lo, hi, ilo, ihi, q) = if q >= num then {lo, hi, ilo, ihi} else if dv(q) < lo then cscan(dv(q), hi, q, ihi, q + 1) else if dv(q) > hi then cscan(lo, dv(q), ilo, q, q + 1) else cscan(lo, hi, ilo, ihi, q + 1)   // {min, max, argmin, argmax} of the coarse km
def fmin(c, v, iv, k) = if k >= 9 then iv else if fv(k, c) < v then fmin(c, fv(k, c), k, k + 1) else fmin(c, v, iv, k + 1)   // fine scan: index of the smallest sample
def fmax(c, v, iv, k) = if k >= 9 then iv else if fv(k, c) > v then fmax(c, fv(k, c), k, k + 1) else fmax(c, v, iv, k + 1)   // fine scan: index of the largest sample
def vtx(c, m) = c - 1 + 0.25 * m + 0.125 * (fv(m - 1, c) - fv(m + 1, c)) / (fv(m - 1, c) - 2 * fv(m, c) + fv(m + 1, c))   // parabolic vertex through fine samples m-1, m, m+1 (JD)
def dkm(t) = dist(11, j0 + t / 24) * au / 1000    // distance at t hours after the 1st, km

// ---- results ---------------------------------------------------------------------
const r = cscan(dv(0), dv(0), 0, 0, 1)
const cm = d0 + 2 * r[3]     // the coarse closest day
const cM = d0 + 2 * r[4]     // the coarse farthest day
const tp = (vtx(cm, fmin(cm, fv(0, cm), 0, 1)) - j0) * 24   // perigee, hours after the 1st
const ta = (vtx(cM, fmax(cM, fv(0, cM), 0, 1)) - j0) * 24   // apogee, hours after the 1st
print("perigee of", month, "/", year, ":", iso(j0 + tp / 24), "UT")
print("  distance:", dkm(tp), "km =", dkm(tp) * 1000 / au, "AU")
print("apogee of", month, "/", year, ":", iso(j0 + ta / 24), "UT")
print("  distance:", dkm(ta), "km =", dkm(ta) * 1000 / au, "AU")
print("swing:", dkm(ta) - dkm(tp), "km (mean distance 384400 km)")
print("grade: distances engine-grade; times a few minutes (6-h parabolic refine)")

/* ---- expected output ----
= perigee of 3 / 2026 : 2026-03-22T11:42:20 UT
=   distance: 366857.172 km = 0.00245228872766 AU
= apogee of 3 / 2026 : 2026-03-10T13:42:38 UT
=   distance: 404384.456 km = 0.00270314312702 AU
= swing: 37527.284 km (mean distance 384400 km)
= grade: distances engine-grade; times a few minutes (6-h parabolic refine)
*/
