scripts.name: moon-transit-time
scripts.title: when the Moon crosses the meridian
scripts.text:
/* ============================================================================
moon-transit-time.epher -- when the Moon crosses the meridian

Meridian transit (culmination) of the Moon at Greenwich (the Royal
Observatory) on three dates of June 2026, from the built-in accessor
transit (the solar-ephemeris crate, JPL-validated; guide 1.16).
Transit is the moment the Moon crosses the observer's meridian; on
the prime meridian it then stands due south, so the azimuth at that
instant should read about 180 deg, and the script prints it as a
check. The lunar day is about 24 h 50 min, so transit comes about
50 min later each day (the delay varies with the Moon's fast-changing
declination). Near new moon the Moon transits with the Sun around
noon; near full moon, around midnight. Hours are UT.

Knobs: year, month, latitude and longitude (Greenwich below).
============================================================================ */

// ---- the knobs --------------------------------------------------------------
const year = 2026
const month = 6
const lat = 51.4779        // Greenwich, the Royal Observatory
const lon = 0

// ---- helpers ----------------------------------------------------------------
// Transit hour of day d, and its azimuth at the transit instant.
def trh(y, m, d, lat, lon) = (transit(11, jd(y, m, d), lat, lon) - jd(y, m, d)) * 24
def trd(y, m, d, lat, lon) = trh(y, m, d, lat, lon) * 15    // hours as degrees
def azm(y, m, d, lat, lon) = az(11, transit(11, jd(y, m, d), lat, lon), lat, lon)

/* ---- results ----------------------------------------------------------------
June 15 is new moon: transit near local noon. June 29 is full moon:
transit near midnight. The clock column is deg2hms of the hour * 15
(guide 1.16), i.e. hour angle turned into hours-minutes-seconds. */
print("transit 2026-06-15:", trh(2026, 6, 15, lat, lon) in hr, "UT; clock", deg2hms(trd(2026, 6, 15, lat, lon)))
print("transit 2026-06-22:", trh(2026, 6, 22, lat, lon) in hr, "UT; clock", deg2hms(trd(2026, 6, 22, lat, lon)))
print("transit 2026-06-29:", trh(2026, 6, 29, lat, lon) in hr, "UT; clock", deg2hms(trd(2026, 6, 29, lat, lon)))

/* The culmination check: at transit the azimuth is due south, 180 deg.
The scatter of about 2 deg is the Moon's diurnal parallax (up to 1 deg)
and its fast motion; the Sun's own transit check in
local-sidereal-time.epher agrees to 0.001 deg. */
print("azimuth at transit 15:", azm(2026, 6, 15, lat, lon), "deg")
print("azimuth at transit 22:", azm(2026, 6, 22, lat, lon), "deg")
print("azimuth at transit 29:", azm(2026, 6, 29, lat, lon), "deg")

/* The daily delay between transits (mean about 50 min = 24.84 h lunar day
minus the 24 h solar day). On some dates the transit falls just before
0h UT and belongs to the previous civil evening: 31 May 2026 transited
at 23:32 UT on 30 May, so asking for May 31 would give a negative hour. */
print("delay, 22nd to 23rd:", (trh(2026, 6, 23, lat, lon) - trh(2026, 6, 22, lat, lon)) in hr)

/* ---- expected output ----
= transit 2026-06-15: 12.416457843 hr UT; clock 12h 24m 59s
= transit 2026-06-22: 18.4617175162 hr UT; clock 18h 27m 42s
= transit 2026-06-29: 24.1119554378 hr UT; clock 0h 6m 43s
= azimuth at transit 15: 179.8288718 deg
= azimuth at transit 22: 178.5016467 deg
= azimuth at transit 29: 180.3723853 deg
= delay, 22nd to 23rd: 0.710673842579 hr
*/

scripts.name: moonrise-azimuth
scripts.title: where the Moon rises and sets: azimuths
scripts.text:
/* ============================================================================
moonrise-azimuth.epher -- where the Moon rises and sets: azimuths

The azimuths of moonrise and moonset for one place and date, from the
built-in event accessors rise and set (the solar-ephemeris crate,
JPL-validated; guide 1.16): each returns the instant of the event of
the local solar day that starts at the Julian Date you pass, and the
engine's event instant IS the horizon crossing, so the azimuth right
then - az(body, event, lat, lon) - is the rise or set bearing. Azimuth
is degrees from north through east (90 east, 180 south, 270 west);
the compass name beside it is an 8-wind rounding of the same angle.

The engine finds the crossing of the standard -0.833-degree horizon
(the limb's centre, refraction and semidiameter included), so the
Moon's altitude at the reported instant reads about -0.83 deg - the
printed self-check. Rise and set can be absent on a given day (the
Moon is up all day, or down all day); both exist on the 2026-06-22
chosen below - the near-first-quarter Moon rises at 12:55 UT and sets
at 23:57 UT at Greenwich (see moonrise-moonset.epher) - and the Moon
is north of the celestial equator that day, so it rises and sets
north of the east and west points.

Accuracy: engine-grade event instants (about a minute); the azimuth
comes from the same engine at that instant.

Knobs: the place (Greenwich below) and the date (2026-06-22 carries
both events at that latitude; many dates do not - the Moon's events
drift about 50 minutes later each day).
============================================================================ */

// ---- the knobs ----------------------------------------------------------------
const lat = 51.4779        // Greenwich - the Royal Observatory
const lon = 0
const obs_date = {2026, 6, 22}   // a date with both a moonrise and a moonset

// ---- helpers ----------------------------------------------------------------
def tr(lat, lon, j0) = rise(11, j0, lat, lon)    // moonrise of the local day
def ts(lat, lon, j0) = set(11, j0, lat, lon)     // moonset of the local day
def comp(a) = if floor((a - 360 * floor(a / 360) + 22.5) / 45) == 0 then "north" else if floor((a - 360 * floor(a / 360) + 22.5) / 45) == 1 then "northeast" else if floor((a - 360 * floor(a / 360) + 22.5) / 45) == 2 then "east" else if floor((a - 360 * floor(a / 360) + 22.5) / 45) == 3 then "southeast" else if floor((a - 360 * floor(a / 360) + 22.5) / 45) == 4 then "south" else if floor((a - 360 * floor(a / 360) + 22.5) / 45) == 5 then "southwest" else if floor((a - 360 * floor(a / 360) + 22.5) / 45) == 6 then "west" else "northwest"

// ---- results ------------------------------------------------------------------
print("moon events at lat", lat, "lon", lon, "on", obs_date[3], "/", obs_date[2], "/", obs_date[1], "UT:")
print("moonrise:", iso(tr(lat, lon, jd(obs_date[1], obs_date[2], obs_date[3]))), "at azimuth", az(11, tr(lat, lon, jd(obs_date[1], obs_date[2], obs_date[3])), lat, lon), "deg -", comp(az(11, tr(lat, lon, jd(obs_date[1], obs_date[2], obs_date[3])), lat, lon)))
print("moonset:", iso(ts(lat, lon, jd(obs_date[1], obs_date[2], obs_date[3]))), "at azimuth", az(11, ts(lat, lon, jd(obs_date[1], obs_date[2], obs_date[3])), lat, lon), "deg -", comp(az(11, ts(lat, lon, jd(obs_date[1], obs_date[2], obs_date[3])), lat, lon)))

/* Self-check: the altitude the engine reports at the instant it found
for the event - the rise/set convention crosses the -0.833 deg horizon
(limb centre at the refracted horizon), so the printed altitude should
read about -0.83 deg at both events. */
print("altitude at moonrise:", alt(11, tr(lat, lon, jd(obs_date[1], obs_date[2], obs_date[3])), lat, lon), "deg")
print("altitude at moonset:", alt(11, ts(lat, lon, jd(obs_date[1], obs_date[2], obs_date[3])), lat, lon), "deg")

/* ---- expected output ----
= moon events at lat 51.4779 lon 0 on 22 / 6 / 2026 UT:
= moonrise: 2026-06-22T12:55:13 at azimuth 100.0353115 deg - east
= moonset: 2026-06-22T23:56:53 at azimuth 255.699662 deg - west
= altitude at moonrise: -0.8207621 deg
= altitude at moonset: -0.819297 deg
*/

scripts.name: moonrise-moonset
scripts.title: when the Moon rises and sets at Greenwich
scripts.text:
/* ============================================================================
moonrise-moonset.epher -- when the Moon rises and sets at Greenwich

Moonrise and moonset at Greenwich (the Royal Observatory) on three
dates of June 2026, from the built-in accessors rise and set (the
solar-ephemeris crate, JPL-validated; guide 1.16). Each returns the
event of the day that starts at j0 (0h UT) as a Julian Date;
subtracting j0 and multiplying by 24 gives the clock hour of the
day, which prints cleanly where the raw JD often prints as an exact
fraction. Hours below are UT - on the prime meridian that is Greenwich
Mean Time itself (London's summer clock adds one hour). The lunar day
(moonrise to moonrise) averages 24 h 50 min, so each event lands
about 50 min later than the previous day, and on many dates the
moonset precedes the moonrise.

Knobs: latitude and longitude (Greenwich below), and the three dates.
============================================================================ */

// ---- the knobs --------------------------------------------------------------
const lat = 51.4779        // Greenwich, the Royal Observatory
const lon = 0
const j22 = jd(2026, 6, 22)   // the three dates, 0h UT
const j23 = jd(2026, 6, 23)
const j29 = jd(2026, 6, 29)

// ---- helpers ----------------------------------------------------------------
// Clock hour of an event: hours past the 0h-UT start of the event's day.
def mrh(j0, lat, lon) = (rise(11, j0, lat, lon) - j0) * 24 in hr
def msh(j0, lat, lon) = (set(11, j0, lat, lon) - j0) * 24 in hr

// ---- results ----------------------------------------------------------------
// June 22: the Moon (near first quarter) is above the horizon from noon
// to late evening; rise before set, as the ordering check confirms.
print("moonrise 2026-06-22:", mrh(j22, lat, lon))
print("moonset  2026-06-22:", msh(j22, lat, lon))
print("rise before set:", mrh(j22, lat, lon) < msh(j22, lat, lon))

// One lunar day later the moonrise has slid 1.24 hr later (the mean is
// about 50 min; the exact delay varies with the Moon's declination).
print("moonrise 2026-06-23:", mrh(j23, lat, lon))
print("rise-to-rise delay:", mrh(j23, lat, lon) - mrh(j22, lat, lon))

/* June 29 is the full moon: moonset came in the small hours (2.54) and
the moonrise at dusk (20.69), so set precedes rise that day and the
Moon is up all night. The raw rise JD (same moment as the 20.69 hr
above) is also printed, with iso() (guide 1.18) reading it back as a
date-time: event JDs sometimes display as exact fractions, and
converting to hours or to the date-time keeps the reading clean. */
print("moonset  2026-06-29:", msh(j29, lat, lon))
print("moonrise 2026-06-29:", mrh(j29, lat, lon))
print("raw rise JD:", rise(11, j29, lat, lon), "=", iso(rise(11, j29, lat, lon)), "UT")

/* ---- expected output ----
= moonrise 2026-06-22: 12.9201933593 hr
= moonset  2026-06-22: 23.9481475241 hr
= rise before set: true
= moonrise 2026-06-23: 14.1554071158 hr
= rise-to-rise delay: 1.23521375656 hr
= moonset  2026-06-29: 2.53923911601 hr
= moonrise 2026-06-29: 20.6909887232 hr
= raw rise JD: 2461221.36212 = 2026-06-29T20:41:28 UT
*/

scripts.name: phases-of-the-month
scripts.title: the four principal moon phases of a month
scripts.text:
/* ============================================================================
phases-of-the-month.epher -- the four principal moon phases of a month

Computes the instants of the new moon, first quarter, full moon and
last quarter that fall in one calendar month, with the series of
chapter 49 of Jean Meeus, "Astronomical Algorithms" (2nd ed.,
Willmann-Bell, 1998): the mean phase (eq. 49.1), the periodic
corrections of table 49.A (its four columns: new, first quarter,
full, last quarter), the extra W correction of table 49.B for the
quarters, and the planetary corrections of table 49.C. Results are
Julian Dates in Universal Time, good to a minute or two for
2000-2100 (the dynamical-time slack that full-moons.epher discusses).

Modeled on the community pair: "Predicting Phases of the Moon"
(hpcalc.org 9389) and ticalc.org's "Phases of the Moon", which do the
same job on a TI-84. A month can hold five phases; when it does, the
fifth one sits at the edge and this panel shows it.

Knobs: `year` and `month` below.
============================================================================ */

// ---- the knobs ----------------------------------------------------------------
const year = 2026
const month = 3

// ---- Meeus ch. 49: mean elements, angles in degrees (eq. 49.3-49.7) -----------
def e3(t) = 1 - 0.002516 * t - 0.0000074 * t ^ 2      // Earth's orbital eccentricity (no unit)
def mp(k) = 201.5643 + 385.81693528 * k               // Moon's mean anomaly, degrees
def ms(k) = 2.5534 + 29.10535670 * k                  // Sun's mean anomaly, degrees
def mf(k) = 160.7108 + 390.67050284 * k               // Moon's argument of latitude, degrees
def node(k) = 124.7746 - 1.56375588 * k               // Moon's ascending node, degrees

// ---- mean phase in JD: k counts lunations, quarters at k + 0.25/0.5/0.75 ------
def base(k) = 2451550.09766 + 29.530588861 * k + 0.00015437 * (k / 1236.85) ^ 2 - 0.000000150 * (k / 1236.85) ^ 3 + 0.00000000073 * (k / 1236.85) ^ 4

// ---- table 49.A: new and full columns share all but the first two terms --------
def corr_nf(k, c1, c2) = c1 * sin(rad(mp(k))) + c2 * e3(k / 1236.85) * sin(rad(ms(k))) + 0.01611 * sin(rad(2 * mp(k))) + 0.01041 * sin(rad(2 * mf(k))) + 0.00736 * e3(k / 1236.85) * sin(rad(mp(k) - ms(k))) - 0.00515 * e3(k / 1236.85) * sin(rad(mp(k) + ms(k))) + 0.00208 * e3(k / 1236.85) ^ 2 * sin(rad(2 * ms(k))) - 0.00111 * sin(rad(mp(k) - 2 * mf(k))) - 0.00057 * sin(rad(mp(k) + 2 * mf(k))) + 0.00056 * e3(k / 1236.85) * sin(rad(2 * mp(k) + ms(k))) - 0.00042 * sin(rad(3 * mp(k))) + 0.00042 * e3(k / 1236.85) * sin(rad(ms(k) + 2 * mf(k))) + 0.00038 * e3(k / 1236.85) * sin(rad(ms(k) - 2 * mf(k))) - 0.00024 * e3(k / 1236.85) * sin(rad(2 * mp(k) - ms(k))) - 0.00017 * sin(rad(node(k))) - 0.00007 * sin(rad(mp(k) + 2 * ms(k))) + 0.00004 * sin(rad(2 * mp(k) - 2 * mf(k))) + 0.00004 * sin(rad(3 * ms(k))) + 0.00003 * sin(rad(mp(k) + ms(k) - 2 * mf(k))) + 0.00003 * sin(rad(2 * mp(k) + 2 * mf(k))) - 0.00003 * sin(rad(mp(k) + ms(k) + 2 * mf(k))) + 0.00003 * sin(rad(mp(k) - ms(k) + 2 * mf(k))) - 0.00002 * sin(rad(mp(k) - ms(k) - 2 * mf(k))) - 0.00002 * sin(rad(3 * mp(k) + ms(k))) + 0.00002 * sin(rad(4 * mp(k)))

// ---- table 49.A: the quarter columns (one column, first and last alike) --------
def corr_q(k) = -0.62801 * sin(rad(mp(k))) + 0.17172 * e3(k / 1236.85) * sin(rad(ms(k))) - 0.01183 * e3(k / 1236.85) * sin(rad(mp(k) + ms(k))) + 0.00862 * sin(rad(2 * mp(k))) + 0.00804 * sin(rad(2 * mf(k))) + 0.00454 * e3(k / 1236.85) * sin(rad(mp(k) - ms(k))) + 0.00204 * e3(k / 1236.85) ^ 2 * sin(rad(2 * ms(k))) - 0.00180 * sin(rad(mp(k) - 2 * mf(k))) - 0.00070 * sin(rad(mp(k) + 2 * mf(k))) - 0.00040 * sin(rad(3 * mp(k))) - 0.00034 * e3(k / 1236.85) * sin(rad(2 * mp(k) - ms(k))) + 0.00032 * e3(k / 1236.85) * sin(rad(ms(k) + 2 * mf(k))) + 0.00032 * e3(k / 1236.85) * sin(rad(ms(k) - 2 * mf(k))) - 0.00028 * e3(k / 1236.85) ^ 2 * sin(rad(mp(k) + 2 * ms(k))) + 0.00027 * e3(k / 1236.85) * sin(rad(2 * mp(k) + ms(k))) - 0.00017 * sin(rad(node(k))) - 0.00005 * sin(rad(mp(k) - ms(k) - 2 * mf(k))) + 0.00004 * sin(rad(2 * mp(k) + 2 * mf(k))) - 0.00004 * sin(rad(mp(k) + ms(k) + 2 * mf(k))) + 0.00004 * sin(rad(mp(k) - 2 * ms(k))) + 0.00003 * sin(rad(mp(k) + ms(k) - 2 * mf(k))) + 0.00003 * sin(rad(3 * ms(k))) + 0.00002 * sin(rad(2 * mp(k) - 2 * mf(k))) + 0.00002 * sin(rad(mp(k) - ms(k) + 2 * mf(k))) - 0.00002 * sin(rad(3 * mp(k) + ms(k)))

// ---- table 49.B: the extra W for the quarters (added first, subtracted last) ---
def w(k) = 0.00306 - 0.00038 * e3(k / 1236.85) * cos(rad(ms(k))) + 0.00026 * cos(rad(mp(k))) - 0.00002 * cos(rad(mp(k) - ms(k))) + 0.00002 * cos(rad(mp(k) + ms(k))) + 0.00002 * cos(rad(2 * mf(k)))

// ---- table 49.C: planetary corrections in days, shared by all phases -----------
// A1's T^2 term is under a second and is omitted (Meeus, note to 49.C).
def a1(k) = 299.77 + 0.107408 * k
def a2(k) = 251.88 + 0.016321 * k
def a3(k) = 251.83 + 26.651886 * k
def a4(k) = 349.42 + 36.412478 * k
def a5(k) = 84.66 + 18.206239 * k
def a6(k) = 141.74 + 53.303771 * k
def a7(k) = 207.14 + 2.453732 * k
def a8(k) = 154.84 + 7.306860 * k
def a9(k) = 34.52 + 27.261239 * k
def a10(k) = 207.19 + 0.121824 * k
def a11(k) = 291.34 + 1.844379 * k
def a12(k) = 161.72 + 24.198154 * k
def a13(k) = 239.56 + 25.513099 * k
def a14(k) = 331.55 + 3.592518 * k
def corr_d(k) = 0.000325 * sin(rad(a1(k))) + 0.000165 * sin(rad(a2(k))) + 0.000164 * sin(rad(a3(k))) + 0.000126 * sin(rad(a4(k))) + 0.000110 * sin(rad(a5(k))) + 0.000062 * sin(rad(a6(k))) + 0.000060 * sin(rad(a7(k))) + 0.000056 * sin(rad(a8(k))) + 0.000047 * sin(rad(a9(k))) + 0.000042 * sin(rad(a10(k))) + 0.000040 * sin(rad(a11(k))) + 0.000037 * sin(rad(a12(k))) + 0.000035 * sin(rad(a13(k))) + 0.000023 * sin(rad(a14(k)))

// ---- the instant of a phase: dispatch on the fraction of k --------------------
def fr(x) = x - floor(x)
def phase_jd(k) = base(k) + corr_d(k) + (if fr(k) == 0 then corr_nf(k, -0.40720, 0.17241) else if fr(k) == 0.5 then corr_nf(k, -0.40614, 0.17302) else corr_q(k) + (if fr(k) == 0.25 then w(k) else -w(k)))

// ---- the phase of fraction f nearest the start of the window, bumped forward --
def kb(j) = (j - 2451550.09766) / 29.530588861
def kf(j, f) = if phase_jd(round(kb(j)) + f) < j then round(kb(j)) + 1 + f else round(kb(j)) + f
def fmt(j0, j1, f) = if phase_jd(kf(j0, f)) < j1 then iso(phase_jd(kf(j0, f))) else "none this month"

// ---- results ------------------------------------------------------------------
const j0 = jd(year, month, 1)
const j1 = (if month == 12 then jd(year + 1, 1, 1) else jd(year, month + 1, 1))
print("principal phases of", month, "/", year, "UT:")
print("new moon:", fmt(j0, j1, 0))
print("first quarter:", fmt(j0, j1, 0.25))
print("full moon:", fmt(j0, j1, 0.5))
print("last quarter:", fmt(j0, j1, 0.75))

/* Self-checks against the built-in ephemeris (guide 1.29), which
knows nothing of the series above: the Moon's lit face at the
computed full moon must be at the maximum, and at the computed new
moon at the minimum. March 2026's full moon sits mid total lunar
 eclipse, where illum prints a flat 1; a non-eclipse month shows
the familiar 0.9986 ceiling (see full-moons.epher for why). */
print("illum at that full moon:", illum(11, phase_jd(kf(j0, 0.5))))
print("illum at that new moon:", illum(11, phase_jd(kf(j0, 0))))

/* ---- expected output ----
= principal phases of 3 / 2026 UT:
= new moon: 2026-03-19T01:24:41
= first quarter: 2026-03-25T19:18:52
= full moon: 2026-03-03T11:39:07
= last quarter: 2026-03-11T09:39:47
= illum at that full moon: 1
= illum at that new moon: 0.0002
*/

scripts.name: supermoon-check
scripts.title: how a named full moon measures up in its year
scripts.text:
/* ============================================================================
supermoon-check.epher -- how a named full moon measures up in its year

Picks the full moon that falls in one chosen month of a year (from the
chapter 49 series of Jean Meeus, "Astronomical Algorithms" 2nd ed. -
the same mean-phase machinery full-moons.epher carries) and checks it
against the year's other full moons: its geocentric distance and angular
diameter versus the closest, the farthest and the mean of that year's
full-moon distances, and the popular "supermoon" verdict.

Distance and diameter come from the built-in ephemeris (the
solar-ephemeris crate, JPL-validated; guide 1.16) evaluated only at the
full-moon instants, about thirteen dates a year. The supermoon test is
the common press rule (Espenak / timeanddate): a full moon counts as a
supermoon when it lies within 10% of the year's closest approach to
Earth; the exact rule scans every perigee of the year, and this script
approximates "closest approach" with the year's closest full moon, a
surrogate within a few thousand kilometres of the perigee figure.
Meeus discusses the range of extreme Earth-Moon distances in
"Mathematical Astronomy Morsels".

Accuracy: the instants are good to a minute (the series' grade for
2000-2100) and the distances are the engine's own (ELP-MPP02), so the
rankings below are trustworthy to their last printed kilometre; the
supermoon call itself depends on the convention, stated above.

Knobs: `year` and the `month` whose full moon is under test (2026's
December full moon, 2026-12-24, is the year's closest: a supermoon;
every month of the year must hold one full moon).
============================================================================ */

// ---- the knobs ----------------------------------------------------------------
const year = 2026
const month = 12

// ---- Meeus ch. 49: mean elements, angles in degrees (eq. 49.3-49.7) -----------
def e3(t) = 1 - 0.002516 * t - 0.0000074 * t ^ 2      // Earth's orbital eccentricity (no unit)
def mp(k) = 201.5643 + 385.81693528 * k               // Moon's mean anomaly, degrees
def ms(k) = 2.5534 + 29.10535670 * k                  // Sun's mean anomaly, degrees
def mf(k) = 160.7108 + 390.67050284 * k               // Moon's argument of latitude, degrees
def node(k) = 124.7746 - 1.56375588 * k               // Moon's ascending node, degrees

// ---- mean full-moon instant in JD: k counts lunations, full moons end in .5 --
def base(k) = 2451550.09766 + 29.530588861 * k + 0.00015437 * (k / 1236.85) ^ 2 - 0.000000150 * (k / 1236.85) ^ 3 + 0.00000000073 * (k / 1236.85) ^ 4

// ---- periodic corrections in days, table 49.A full-moon column, by size -------
def corr_a(k) = -0.40614 * sin(rad(mp(k))) + 0.17302 * e3(k / 1236.85) * sin(rad(ms(k))) + 0.01614 * sin(rad(2 * mp(k))) + 0.01043 * sin(rad(2 * mf(k))) + 0.00734 * e3(k / 1236.85) * sin(rad(mp(k) - ms(k))) - 0.00515 * e3(k / 1236.85) * sin(rad(mp(k) + ms(k))) + 0.00209 * e3(k / 1236.85) ^ 2 * sin(rad(2 * ms(k))) - 0.00111 * sin(rad(mp(k) - 2 * mf(k)))
def corr_b(k) = -0.00057 * sin(rad(mp(k) + 2 * mf(k))) + 0.00056 * e3(k / 1236.85) * sin(rad(2 * mp(k) + ms(k))) - 0.00042 * sin(rad(3 * mp(k))) + 0.00042 * e3(k / 1236.85) * sin(rad(ms(k) + 2 * mf(k))) + 0.00038 * e3(k / 1236.85) * sin(rad(ms(k) - 2 * mf(k))) - 0.00024 * e3(k / 1236.85) * sin(rad(2 * mp(k) - ms(k)))
def corr_c(k) = -0.00017 * sin(rad(node(k))) - 0.00007 * sin(rad(mp(k) + 2 * ms(k))) + 0.00004 * sin(rad(2 * mp(k) - 2 * mf(k))) + 0.00004 * sin(rad(3 * ms(k))) + 0.00003 * sin(rad(mp(k) + ms(k) - 2 * mf(k))) + 0.00003 * sin(rad(2 * mp(k) + 2 * mf(k))) - 0.00003 * sin(rad(mp(k) + ms(k) + 2 * mf(k))) + 0.00003 * sin(rad(mp(k) - ms(k) + 2 * mf(k))) - 0.00002 * sin(rad(mp(k) - ms(k) - 2 * mf(k))) - 0.00002 * sin(rad(3 * mp(k) + ms(k))) + 0.00002 * sin(rad(4 * mp(k)))

// ---- planetary corrections in days, table 49.C --------------------------------
// A1's T^2 term is under a second and is omitted (Meeus, note to 49.C).
def a1(k) = 299.77 + 0.107408 * k
def a2(k) = 251.88 + 0.016321 * k
def a3(k) = 251.83 + 26.651886 * k
def a4(k) = 349.42 + 36.412478 * k
def a5(k) = 84.66 + 18.206239 * k
def a6(k) = 141.74 + 53.303771 * k
def a7(k) = 207.14 + 2.453732 * k
def a8(k) = 154.84 + 7.306860 * k
def a9(k) = 34.52 + 27.261239 * k
def a10(k) = 207.19 + 0.121824 * k
def a11(k) = 291.34 + 1.844379 * k
def a12(k) = 161.72 + 24.198154 * k
def a13(k) = 239.56 + 25.513099 * k
def a14(k) = 331.55 + 3.592518 * k
def corr_d(k) = 0.000325 * sin(rad(a1(k))) + 0.000165 * sin(rad(a2(k))) + 0.000164 * sin(rad(a3(k))) + 0.000126 * sin(rad(a4(k))) + 0.000110 * sin(rad(a5(k))) + 0.000062 * sin(rad(a6(k))) + 0.000060 * sin(rad(a7(k))) + 0.000056 * sin(rad(a8(k))) + 0.000047 * sin(rad(a9(k))) + 0.000042 * sin(rad(a10(k))) + 0.000040 * sin(rad(a11(k))) + 0.000037 * sin(rad(a12(k))) + 0.000035 * sin(rad(a13(k))) + 0.000023 * sin(rad(a14(k)))

// ---- the instant of full moon for lunation k ----------------------------------
def fullmoon(k) = base(k) + corr_a(k) + corr_b(k) + corr_c(k) + corr_d(k)

// ---- the year's lunations, bucketing and engine distances ----------------------
def kfirst(jd0) = ceil((jd0 - 2451550.09766) / 29.530588861 - 0.5) + 0.5  // first full moon on/after Jan 1
const k0 = kfirst(jd(year, 1, 1))                 // first lunation of the year (its value echoes below)
def mon(k) = date(fullmoon(k))[2]                 // calendar month of the lunation's full moon
def nfull(q, c) = if q >= 13 then c else if fullmoon(k0 + q) < jd(year + 1, 1, 1) then nfull(q + 1, c + 1) else c   // full moons of the year
def dkm(q) = dist(11, fullmoon(k0 + q)) * au / 1000   // the lunation's full-moon distance, km (au is in metres)
def findm(n, q, m) = if q >= n then -1 else if mon(k0 + q) == m then q else findm(n, q + 1, m)   // first full moon of month m
def scan(n, q, lo, hi, sm, ilo, ihi) = if q >= n then {lo, hi, sm, ilo, ihi} else if dkm(q) < lo then scan(n, q + 1, dkm(q), hi, sm + dkm(q), q, ihi) else if dkm(q) > hi then scan(n, q + 1, lo, dkm(q), sm + dkm(q), ilo, q) else scan(n, q + 1, lo, hi, sm + dkm(q), ilo, ihi)  // {min, max, sum, argmin, argmax} in km
def ncloser(n, q, c, d) = if q >= n then c else if dkm(q) < d then ncloser(n, q + 1, c + 1, d) else ncloser(n, q + 1, c, d)   // how many full moons are closer than d km

// ---- results ------------------------------------------------------------------
const count = nfull(0, 0)
const i0 = findm(count, 0, month)
const rank = ncloser(count, 0, 0, dkm(i0)) + 1
print("the year's", count, "full moons are lunations", k0, "through", k0 + count - 1)

/* One scan over the year's full moons collects the closest, the
farthest and the summed distance (the echoed list {lo, hi, sum, index
of lo, index of hi}); the mean follows by division. */
const stats = scan(count, 1, dkm(0), dkm(0), dkm(0), 0, 0)
print("closest full moon:", iso(fullmoon(k0 + stats[4])), "UT,", stats[1], "km")
print("farthest full moon:", iso(fullmoon(k0 + stats[5])), "UT,", stats[2], "km")
print("mean full-moon distance:", stats[3] / count, "km")

/* The month's full moon under test: its instant, distance and angular
diameter (diam gives degrees; the eye reads arcminutes). */
print("full moon of month", month, ":", iso(fullmoon(k0 + i0)), "UT")
print("distance:", dkm(i0), "km; diameter:", diam(11, fullmoon(k0 + i0)) * 60, "arcmin")
print("rank among the year's full moons (1 = closest):", rank, "of", count)

// ---- the supermoon verdict: the 90% rule on the year's closest full moon ------
print(if dkm(i0) <= stats[1] + 0.1 * (stats[2] - stats[1]) then "supermoon by the 90% rule (within 10% of the year's closest full moon)" else "not a supermoon by the 90% rule")

/* Self-check: the built-in diameter read back from the distance - the
angular radius is asin of the Moon's radius over the distance, so
2*asin(r_moon / dist) must agree with the engine's diam at the same
instant (both geocentric). */
print("self-check: diam from dist:", 2 * deg(asin((r_moon / 1000) / dkm(i0))), "deg vs engine", diam(11, fullmoon(k0 + i0)), "deg")

/* ---- expected output ----
= the year's 13 full moons are lunations 321.5 through 333.5
= closest full moon: 2026-12-24T01:29:24 UT, 356737.601 km
= farthest full moon: 2026-05-31T08:46:26 UT, 406135.642 km
= mean full-moon distance: 383009.257154 km
= full moon of month 12 : 2026-12-24T01:29:24 UT
= distance: 356737.601 km; diameter: 33.48548 arcmin
= rank among the year's full moons (1 = closest): 1 of 13
= supermoon by the 90% rule (within 10% of the year's closest full moon)
= self-check: diam from dist: 0.558091328623 deg vs engine 0.558091333333 deg
*/

scripts.name: gha-sun
scripts.title: Greenwich hour angle and declination of the Sun
scripts.text:
/* ============================================================================
gha-sun.epher -- Greenwich hour angle and declination of the Sun

Prints the Sun's Greenwich hour angle and declination at a knob
instant, nautical-almanac style - the pair a navigator takes from
the daily pages to reduce a sight. GHA is the Sun's hour angle
measured west from Greenwich: with the engine's sidereal clock,

  GHA(sun) = Greenwich apparent sidereal time - right ascension

which this script reads as lst(jd, 0) (hours) and ra(10, jd), then
prints in the almanac's degrees-and-minutes form (the engine gives
positions about an arcsecond from JPL Horizons; the GHA is good to
a fraction of an arcminute of the almanac pages).

Knob: the instant below.
============================================================================ */

// ---- the knobs ----------------------------------------------------------------------
const tm = jd(2026, 9, 10, 12)

// ---- the almanac pair -------------------------------------------------------------------
const gha = 15 * lst(tm, 0) - ra(10, tm)
def wrap(x) = x - 360 * floor(x / 360)
const ghaw = wrap(gha)
print("at", iso(tm))
print("GHA:", deg2dms(ghaw), "(", ghaw, "deg )")
print("Dec:", deg2dms(decl(10, tm)))

/* Self-check: the Sun's GHA grows by about 15.041 degrees per
hour, and at Greenwich apparent noon it reads near zero (within
the equation of time). */
print("GHA one hour later minus now:", wrap(15 * lst(tm + 1 / 24, 0) - ra(10, tm + 1 / 24)) - ghaw, "deg")

/* ---- expected output ----
= at 2026-09-10T12:00:00
= GHA: 0° 45' 15" ( 0.75420171633 deg )
= Dec: 4° 49' 10"
= GHA one hour later minus now: 15.0036353123 deg
*/

scripts.name: great-circle
scripts.title: distance and bearing between two places
scripts.text:
/* ============================================================================
great-circle.epher -- distance and bearing between two places

Great-circle navigation: the shortest path between two points on a
sphere, in distance (km and nautical miles) and initial bearing
(degrees from north). The spherical law of cosines in haversine
form is stable at all distances:

  a = sin^2(dlat/2) + cos(lat1) cos(lat2) sin^2(dlon/2)
  c = 2 atan2(sqrt(a), sqrt(1 - a))     d = R c
  bearing = atan2(sin(dlon) cos(lat2),
                  cos(lat1) sin(lat2) - sin(lat1) cos(lat2) cos(dlon))

Accuracy: spherical-Earth (R = 6371 km) results are within about
0.3 percent of the WGS84 geodesic - the classic transatlantic
example prints near 5570 km against the geodesic 5586.

Knobs: the two places below (default: London to New York).
============================================================================ */

// ---- the knobs ---------------------------------------------------------------------
const la1 = 51.5074          // London
const lo1 = -0.1278
const la2 = 40.7128          // New York
const lo2 = -74.0060

// ---- helpers -------------------------------------------------------------------------
def wrap(x) = x - 360 * floor(x / 360)
def hav(a) = sin(a / 2) ^ 2
const a1 = hav(rad(la2 - la1)) + cos(rad(la1)) * cos(rad(la2)) * hav(rad(lo2 - lo1))
const c1 = 2 * atan2(sqrt(a1), sqrt(1 - a1))
const dkm = 6371 * c1
const brg = deg(atan2(sin(rad(wrap(lo2 - lo1))) * cos(rad(la2)), cos(rad(la1)) * sin(rad(la2)) - sin(rad(la1)) * cos(rad(la2)) * cos(rad(wrap(lo2 - lo1)))))
const brg2 = wrap(brg)

print("great circle from", la1, ",", lo1, "to", la2, ",", lo2)
print("distance:", dkm, "km =", dkm / 1.852, "nautical miles")
print("initial bearing:", brg2, "deg")

/* Self-checks: the route is symmetric and the transatlantic
distance sits near 5570 km on the sphere (the WGS84 geodesic is
5586 km - the spherical grade is about 0.3 percent). */
print("reverse distance equal:", 6371 * 2 * atan2(sqrt(hav(rad(la1 - la2)) + cos(rad(la2)) * cos(rad(la1)) * hav(rad(lo1 - lo2))), sqrt(1 - (hav(rad(la1 - la2)) + cos(rad(la2)) * cos(rad(la1)) * hav(rad(lo1 - lo2))))) == dkm)
print("London-New York in the classic 5570 km band:", dkm > 5500 and dkm < 5650)

/* ---- expected output ----
= great circle from 51.5074 , -0.1278 to 40.7128 , -74.006
= distance: 5570.22217974 km = 3007.67936271 nautical miles
= initial bearing: 288.329701594 deg
= reverse distance equal: true
= London-New York in the classic 5570 km band: true
*/

scripts.name: intercept-sight
scripts.title: one Sun sight reduced by the intercept method
scripts.text:
/* ============================================================================
intercept-sight.epher -- one Sun sight reduced by the intercept method

Takes one timed Sun sight and reduces it the way the navigators do
(Marcq Saint-Hilaire's intercept method, the technique behind the
hpcalc "Celestial Navigation" programs): from the assumed position
the sight's computed altitude Hc and azimuth Zn are worked, and
the observed altitude Ho is compared:

  intercept = (Ho - Hc) in minutes of arc = nautical miles,
  plotted from the assumed position toward (or away from) Zn.

Hc comes from the standard spherical relation with the engine's
geocentric Sun position and the assumed position; Zn is the
engine's azimuth (the same compass angle the almanac tables give).

Accuracy: Hc and Zn are engine-grade (arcsecond positions; the
printed check compares Hc with the engine's own topocentric
altitude - they agree to a few thousandths of a degree). The
result's worth is the observation's: Ho must be corrected for
index error, dip and refraction before it goes in.

Knobs: the observed (corrected) altitude Ho, the sight time tm and
the assumed position below.
============================================================================ */

// ---- the knobs ---------------------------------------------------------------------
const ho = 39.6              // observed (corrected) altitude, degrees
const tm = jd(2026, 9, 10, 14)
const alat = 50.0            // assumed latitude, degrees
const alon = -4.0            // assumed longitude, degrees east

// ---- the reduction -------------------------------------------------------------------
def wrap(x) = x - 360 * floor(x / 360)
def spread(x) = if wrap(x) > 180 then wrap(x) - 360 else wrap(x)
const sra = ra(10, tm)
const sde = decl(10, tm)
const lha = spread(15 * lst(tm, alon) - sra)
const hc = deg(asin(sin(rad(alat)) * sin(rad(sde)) + cos(rad(alat)) * cos(rad(sde)) * cos(rad(lha))))
const zn = az(10, tm, alat, alon)
const icpt = (ho - hc) * 60

print("at", iso(tm), "from assumed", alat, ",", alon)
print("Sun GHA-derived LHA:", lha, "deg")
print("computed altitude Hc:", hc, "deg")
print("azimuth Zn:", zn, "deg")
print("intercept:", icpt, "nautical miles", (if icpt > 0 then "toward" else "away from"), "the body")

/* Self-check: Hc is the same geometric altitude the engine's own
topocentric alt gives, to a few thousandths of a degree. */
print("Hc vs engine altitude:", hc, "vs", alt(10, tm, alat, alon))

/* ---- expected output ----
= at 2026-09-10T14:00:00 from assumed 50 , -4
= Sun GHA-derived LHA: 26.7614735961 deg
= computed altitude Hc: 39.4849560241 deg
= azimuth Zn: 215.5479187 deg
= intercept: 6.90263855521 nautical miles toward the body
= Hc vs engine altitude: 39.4849560241 vs 39.4830076
*/

scripts.name: noon-sight
scripts.title: latitude from the Sun's meridian altitude
scripts.text:
/* ============================================================================
noon-sight.epher -- latitude from the Sun's meridian altitude

Works the oldest navigation calculation there is: at local apparent
noon the Sun stands on the meridian, its altitude read off the
sextant gives the zenith distance z = 90 - Ho, and the latitude
follows as decl + or - z (add when the Sun bears south of you and
the declination has your same name, as here; subtract when it bears
north). The sight corrections run in the standard order: index
error, dip of the horizon (1.76 x sqrt(eye height in metres),
arcminutes), refraction (Bennett's formula, S. Y. van Altena ed.,
"Astronomical Almanac" refraction notes), the Sun's semidiameter
from the built-in diam accessor, and solar parallax (8.79 arcsec x
cos altitude). Declination and the LAN instant come from the
built-in transit and decl (guide 1.29), so the almanac table lookup
the old navigators performed is live.

This is the bread and butter of the HP community's celestial
navigation programs (hpcalc.org "Celestial Navigation 4.2", the
Sparcom Celestial Navigation Pac, "Almanac").

Accuracy: the recovered latitude is honest to about half a
kilometre (0.3 arcminutes) with a steady hand and a clear horizon;
the worked sight below was taken from a boat at 40.000 N and the
script recovers it.

Knobs: the date, the dead-reckoning position, the sextant altitude
Hs (degrees, Sun's lower limb), the index correction ic (arcminutes,
on-the-arc negative) and the eye height eye (metres).
============================================================================ */

// ---- the knobs ----------------------------------------------------------------
const day = {2026, 6, 21}
const drlat = 40               // dead-reckoning latitude, degrees N
const lon = 15                 // longitude, degrees E
const hs = 73.2464             // sextant altitude of the Sun's lower limb, deg
const ic = -1.0                // index correction, arcminutes
const eye = 3                  // height of eye, metres

// ---- the sight, step by step --------------------------------------------------
const lan = transit(10, jd(day[1], day[2], day[3]), drlat, lon)
const sun_dec = decl(10, lan)
const sd = diam(10, lan) / 2

// ---- corrections: dip and refraction in arcminutes ----------------------------
def dip(e) = 1.76 * sqrt(e)
def refr(h) = 0.97127 / tan(rad(h + 7.31 / (h + 4.4)))

// ---- observed altitude to true central altitude (Ho), then the latitude -------
const ha = hs + ic / 60 - dip(eye) / 60
const ho = ha - refr(ha) / 60 + sd + 8.79 * cos(rad(ha)) / 3600
z = 90 - ho
const lat = sun_dec + z

// ---- results ------------------------------------------------------------------
print("local apparent noon:", iso(lan))
print("Ho (true central altitude):", ho, "deg")
print("zenith distance:", z, "deg, declination:", sun_dec, "deg")
print("latitude from the noon sight:", lat, "N")

/* Self-check: the sight was taken from a boat whose DR latitude is
40 N; the noon sight must land on it - the printed difference is
the navigator's error bar for this sight. */
print("recovered minus DR:", lat - drlat, "deg")

/* ---- expected output ----
= 16.563026902
= local apparent noon: 2026-06-21T11:01:48
= Ho (true central altitude): 73.436973098 deg
= zenith distance: 16.563026902 deg, declination: 23.437886495 deg
= latitude from the noon sight: 40.000913397 N
= recovered minus DR: 0.000913396971313 deg
*/

scripts.name: polaris-sight
scripts.title: latitude from a Polaris sight
scripts.text:
/* ============================================================================
polaris-sight.epher -- latitude from a Polaris sight

The navigator's latitude shortcut: the altitude of Polaris equals
the latitude within about a degree, because the star sits less
than a degree from the north celestial pole. The correction comes from the spherical triangle pole-zenith-
star, solved exactly: with pd the polar distance of Polaris at the
date and H its local hour angle,

  sin(Ho) = sin(lat) cos(pd) + cos(lat) sin(pd) cos(H)

solved for lat (the closed form below). Polaris's position is an
in-script constant (J2000: RA 2h 31m 49.3s, Dec +89 15' 51"); its
declination increases by about 15 arcsec a year toward its ~2100
closest approach, applied here as a rate.

Accuracy: the geometry is exact - the residuals are the
observation's own (refraction and dip corrections assumed
already applied) plus the rate-model's share, under an arcminute.

Knobs: the observed altitude (Ho, degrees, corrected for
refraction and dip), the UT instant and the assumed longitude.
============================================================================ */

// ---- the knobs ---------------------------------------------------------------------
const ho = 51.28            // observed altitude, degrees
const tm = jd(2026, 9, 10, 22)
const lon = -5              // assumed longitude, degrees east

// ---- Polaris at the date ------------------------------------------------------------
const pra = 37.9554         // RA J2000 (2h 31m 49.3s), degrees
const pde = 89.2642         // Dec J2000 (+89 15' 51"), degrees
def wrap(x) = x - 360 * floor(x / 360)
def spread(x) = if wrap(x) > 180 then wrap(x) - 360 else wrap(x)
const dy = (jd(2026, 9, 10, 0) - 2451545) / 365.25
const pdec = pde + 15 / 3600 * dy      // the ~15 arcsec/yr increase
const pd = (90 - pdec)                  // polar distance, degrees
const h = spread(15 * lst(tm, lon) - pra)

// ---- the sight ------------------------------------------------------------------------
const sv = sin(rad(ho)) / sqrt(cos(rad(pd)) ^ 2 + (sin(rad(pd)) * cos(rad(h))) ^ 2)
const lat = deg(asin(sv)) - deg(atan2(sin(rad(pd)) * cos(rad(h)), cos(rad(pd))))
print("at", iso(tm), "lon", lon)
print("polar distance of Polaris:", pd * 60, "arcmin")
print("LHA of Polaris:", h, "deg")
print("latitude from the sight:", lat, "deg")

/* Self-check: on the meridian (H = 0) the correction must equal
the polar distance exactly - lat(H=0) = Ho - pd. */
const latz = deg(asin(sin(rad(ho)) / sqrt(cos(rad(pd)) ^ 2 + (sin(rad(pd))) ^ 2))) - deg(atan2(sin(rad(pd)), cos(rad(pd))))
print("H = 0 gives Ho - pd:", latz, "vs", ho - pd, "(equal:", latz == ho - pd, ")")

/* ---- expected output ----
= at 2026-09-10T22:00:00 lon -5
= polar distance of Polaris: 37.4755154004 arcmin
= LHA of Polaris: -83.0054371502 deg
= latitude from the sight: 51.2081210189 deg
= H = 0 gives Ho - pd: 50.6554080767 vs 50.6554080767 (equal: true )
*/

scripts.name: galilean-moons
scripts.title: Jupiter's four bright moons, positions and phenomena
scripts.text:
/* ============================================================================
galilean-moons.epher -- Jupiter's four bright moons, positions and phenomena

Where are Io, Europa, Ganymede, and Callisto right now, which side of
Jupiter is each on, and is any of them doing something worth getting up
for: crossing the disc (a transit), hidden behind it (an occultation),
in Jupiter's shadow (an eclipse), or casting its own tiny shadow onto
the clouds (a shadow transit) - the show Galileo watched in 1610.

The positions come from the E5 theory of the Galilean satellites
(Lieske; chapter 44 of Jean Meeus, "Astronomical Algorithms" 2nd ed.),
computed by the engine's satellite accessors (`satx saty satz satsep
satphen`, guide 1.18) and fed with the engine's real Earth-Jupiter
geometry. Earth's height above Jupiter's equatorial plane swings
between about plus and minus 3.4 degrees over Jupiter's 12-year orbit,
so the moons' apparent paths open and close: when the plane is edge-on
to us (the next time is in late 2026) transits and eclipses chain into
one another nearly every night. Distances are good to a few arcseconds
against JPL Horizons; treat event times from the scan below as good to
about ten minutes.

Web/desktop:             paste the whole file into the entry, press Enter

The one knob to edit is `when` below: the instant you want the table
for (and the anchor the scan searches forward from).
============================================================================ */

// ---- the knob ------------------------------------------------------------------
const when = jd(2026, 9, 17)

// ---- arcseconds per Jupiter radius at the observer, from the engine ------------
def sc(t) = 71492 / (dist(5, t) * au) * 206264.806247

// ---- which side of the disc: satx counts positive to the West ------------------
def side(t, s) = if satx(5, s, t) > 0 then "W" else "E"

// ---- the phenomenon code as a word --------------------------------------------
def word(p) = if p == 1 then "in transit" else if p == 2 then "occulted" else if p == 3 then "in eclipse" else if p == 4 then "shadow transit" else "visible"

// ---- one table line: name, separation from Jupiter's centre, side, phenomenon --
def line(s, name) = print(name, round(satsep(5, s, when)), "arcsec", side(when, s), "-", word(satphen(5, s, when)))

// ---- results -------------------------------------------------------------------
print("The Galilean moons at", iso(when), "UT")
print("(separation from Jupiter's centre, in arcseconds; W/E = which side)")
line(1, "Io:")
line(2, "Europa:")
line(3, "Ganymede:")
line(4, "Callisto:")

/* The next time Io is not plainly visible - a transit, an eclipse, or
a shadow pass - scanned in 30-minute steps for up to three days from
`when`. The scan answers the instant the moment it finds one (`return`
leaves the loop, guide 1.11), or 0 when all three days are plain
visible. */
def next_phenomenon(p, m, name, t0) do
  t = t0
  while t - t0 < 3 do if satphen(p, m, t + 1 / 48) != 0 then return print(name + "'s next phenomenon:", iso(t + 1 / 48), "UT -", word(satphen(p, m, t + 1 / 48))) else t = t + 1 / 48
  print(name + ": nothing but plain visible within 3 days")
end
next_phenomenon(5, 1, "Io", when)

/* Jupiter's distance right then, for scale: at opposition the whole
system is 44 arcseconds per Io-orbit wide and every moon fits in one
eyepiece field; near conjunction Jupiter is gone anyway. */
print("Jupiter distance:", round(dist(5, when) * 100) / 100, "AU")
/* ---- expected output ----
= The Galilean moons at 2026-09-17T00:00:00 UT
= (separation from Jupiter's centre, in arcseconds; W/E = which side)
= Io: 45 arcsec W - visible
= Europa: 138 arcsec E - visible
= Ganymede: 242 arcsec W - visible
= Callisto: 287 arcsec E - visible
= Io's next phenomenon: 2026-09-17T02:30:00 UT - in transit
= Jupiter distance: 6.07 AU
*/

scripts.name: jupiter-grs
scripts.title: Jupiter's System II central meridian and GRS transits
scripts.text:
/* ============================================================================
jupiter-grs.epher -- Jupiter's System II central meridian and GRS transits

Jupiter's central meridian in System II at a chosen instant, and the
next times the Great Red Spot crosses it - the moments to look for the
spot on the disk. System II is the rotation frame used for the Great Red
Spot and the other long-lived south-temperate features: its longitude
advances at 870.1869140 degrees per day (Meeus, "Astronomical
Algorithms" 2nd ed., ch. 43, physical ephemeris of Jupiter), which
corresponds to the System II rotation period of 9h 55m 40.6s as seen
from Earth. The zero point follows Meeus ch. 43: CM(II) = 181.62 +
870.1869140 d, with d the days from J2000.0 (dynamical time; the 69 s
of delta-T shift the meridian by two thirds of a degree and are worth
keeping).

The Great Red Spot is not fixed in System II: its own rotation period
differs from the system by a few seconds per turn, so its longitude
drifts. The knob below (255 deg, a working value for the mid-2020s) is
the first thing to refresh when the spot runs ahead of the predictions;
a fresh longitude from any current Jupiter observer's newsletter will
keep the transit times right to a few minutes.

Accuracy: the meridian itself is good to a few tenths of a degree (the
formula's own precision); transit times printed here are good to a few
minutes for a current spot longitude and degrade as the spot drifts
(roughly a degree a month at its present rate).

Knobs: the instant `tm` (UT) and the spot's System II longitude `grs`.
============================================================================ */

// ---- the knobs ---------------------------------------------------------------
const tm = jd(2026, 10, 15, 22)  // 2026-10-15 22:00 UT
const grs = 255                 // Great Red Spot longitude, System II (drifts)

// ---- System II (Meeus ch. 43; d in days from J2000.0, dynamical time) --------
def wrap360(x) = x - 360 * floor(x / 360)
def cm2(j) = wrap360(181.62 + 870.1869140 * (j + delta_t(j) / 86400 - jd(2000, 1, 1, 12)))
const cm = cm2(tm)
// The spot crosses the central meridian when cm2 = grs; solve for the
// first crossing at or after tm and step by one full turn.
const dt1 = wrap360(grs - cm) / 870.1869140
const tr1 = tm + dt1
const turn = 360 / 870.1869140

// ---- results ------------------------------------------------------------------
print("Jupiter System II central meridian at", iso(tm), "UT:", cm, "deg")
print("next GRS transits (spot longitude", grs, "deg System II):")
print("  1:", iso(tr1), "UT")
print("  2:", iso(tr1 + turn), "UT")
print("  3:", iso(tr1 + 2 * turn), "UT")
print("Jupiter magnitude", mag(5, tm), "; diameter", diam(5, tm) * 3600, "arcsec")

/* ---- expected output ----
= Jupiter System II central meridian at 2026-10-15T22:00:00 UT: 93.6604048703 deg
= next GRS transits (spot longitude 255 deg System II):
=   1: 2026-10-16T02:26:59 UT
=   2: 2026-10-16T12:22:43 UT
=   3: 2026-10-16T22:18:27 UT
= Jupiter magnitude -1.94 ; diameter 33.6349 arcsec
*/

scripts.name: planet-angular-diameters
scripts.title: apparent disk sizes of the planets
scripts.text:
/* ============================================================================
planet-angular-diameters.epher -- apparent disk sizes of the planets

Angular diameters of the planets on 2026-06-01, from the built-in
accessor diam, which returns degrees (the solar-ephemeris crate,
JPL-validated; guide 1.16). One degree is 3600 arcseconds, so the
arcsecond values below are diam * 3600. To the naked eye every planet
is a point; a telescope shows the disks. Jupiter's disk spans about
30-50 arcsec depending on its distance (here 32.4 arcsec at 5.95 AU);
Venus, closer at 1.26 AU, shows 13.3 arcsec as a gibbous phase; Pluto
is 0.09 arcsec, far below what any telescope can resolve as a disk.

Knob: the date tm.
============================================================================ */

// ---- the knob ---------------------------------------------------------------
const tm = jd(2026, 6, 1)     // 0h UT

/* ---- results ----------------------------------------------------------------
Arcseconds in body-number order (Mercury, Venus, Mars, Jupiter,
Saturn, Uranus, Neptune, Pluto). The Moon, for scale, spans about
1800 arcsec, and the Dawes limit of a 100 mm telescope is 1.16 arcsec
(see telescope-resolution.epher): only Jupiter (32.4), Venus (13.3)
and Saturn (16.1, ringless here) show real disks in a small scope. */
for b in {1, 2, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8, 9} do diam(b, tm) * 3600

// The same reading for the two classic showpieces, in degrees and
// arcseconds. Jupiter at 5.95 AU is near its smallest (about 50 arcsec
// at closest approach); Saturn at 9.97 AU is likewise on the small side.
print("Jupiter:", diam(5, tm), "deg =", diam(5, tm) * 3600, "arcsec")
print("Saturn:", diam(6, tm), "deg =", diam(6, tm) * 3600, "arcsec")

/* ---- expected output ----
= {6.1047, 13.2847, 4.2796, 32.377, 16.1143, 3.4174, 2.243, 0.0937926530789}
= Jupiter: 0.00899361111111 deg = 32.377 arcsec
= Saturn: 0.00447619444444 deg = 16.1143 arcsec
*/

scripts.name: planet-distances
scripts.title: how far the planets are on one date
scripts.text:
/* ============================================================================
planet-distances.epher -- how far the planets are on one date

Geocentric distances of the planets on 2026-06-01, from the built-in
accessor dist, in AU (the solar-ephemeris crate, JPL-validated; guide
1.16; body numbers: Mercury 1, Venus 2, Earth 3, Mars 4, Jupiter 5,
Saturn 6, Uranus 7, Neptune 8, Pluto 9). The AU is the mean
Earth-Sun distance, 149597870.7 km. Two distances are also converted
to kilometres with the (1 AU) quantity; light itself takes 8.3 min to
cross 1 AU and about 4.2 h to reach Neptune, which is 30 AU away.

Knob: the date tm.
============================================================================ */

// ---- the knob ---------------------------------------------------------------
const tm = jd(2026, 6, 1)     // 0h UT

/* ---- results ----------------------------------------------------------------
One AU per planet, in body-number order (Mercury, Venus, Mars, Jupiter,
Saturn, Uranus, Neptune, Pluto). The spread of the list is the scale
of the solar system: Mercury at 1.1 AU, Neptune at 30.3 AU, Pluto at
34.9 AU. A for loop over a list (guide 1.30) collects these values. */
for b in {1, 2, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8, 9} do dist(b, tm)

// Two of the eight in kilometres. Mars is on the far side of its orbit
// (2.18 AU, near its February 2027 opposition it will be near 0.65 AU);
// Neptune is 30 AU out, some 4.5 billion km away.
print("Mars, km:", (dist(4, tm) * (1 AU)) in km)
print("Neptune, km:", (dist(8, tm) * (1 AU)) in km)

/* Sanity by eye: every entry of the list above sits inside its orbit's
possible range - Mercury 0.3-1.7 AU, Venus 0.3-1.7, Mars 0.4-2.7,
Jupiter 4.0-6.5, Saturn 8.0-11.1, Uranus 18-21, Neptune 29-31,
Pluto 29-49 - so all eight are ordinary, unremarkable distances.
Light travel time to Neptune: au and c are plain numbers in m and
m/s, so dist * au / c is seconds. */
print("Neptune light travel:", dist(8, tm) * au / c / 3600, "hr")

/* ---- expected output ----
= {1.10205638799, 1.25621085414, 2.18405254195, 5.95439957981, 9.96506679977, 20.4654072206, 30.2709988554, 34.9371112782}
= Mars, km: 326729609.772 km
= Neptune, km: 4528476972.73 km
= Neptune light travel: 4.1959370112 hr
*/

scripts.name: planet-elements-table
scripts.title: mean Keplerian elements of the planets on a date
scripts.text:
/* ============================================================================
planet-elements-table.epher -- mean Keplerian elements of the planets on a date

The six mean Keplerian elements (semi-major axis a in AU, eccentricity e,
inclination i, mean longitude L, longitude of perihelion and longitude of
the ascending node in degrees) for the seven planets from Mercury to
Neptune, evaluated at a chosen date, each with its per-century rate.

The elements are the approximate Keplerian elements of Standish &
Williams (1992), mean ecliptic and equinox of J2000, valid 1800-2050;
Jean Meeus prints the same table as table 31.A of "Astronomical
Algorithms" (2nd ed., Willmann-Bell, 1998), chapter 31 ("the elements
of the planetary orbits"), and NASA JPL publishes it on its
approximate-positions page. Earth is not listed: the elements are
heliocentric, so Earth's orbit is the frame's reference plane only.

Accuracy: a display table of mean elements, exact to the digits
printed; the elements themselves reproduce the planets' heliocentric
positions to roughly 0.01 deg over 1800-2050 (Jupiter and Saturn need
the small periodic corrections of the same source for that grade; see
planet-by-hand.epher, which carries them).

The one knob to edit is `year` below (the table is evaluated at
January 1.5 of that year, the conventional epoch).
============================================================================ */

// ---- the knob -----------------------------------------------------------------
const year = 2026

// ---- table 31.A constants: value + per-century rate (T centuries from J2000) -
def T(j) = (j - jd(2000, 1, 1, 12)) / 36525
def tc(y) = (jd(y, 1, 1, 12) - jd(2000, 1, 1, 12)) / 36525
def wrap360(x) = x - 360 * floor(x / 360)

// ---- rows: (a, da, e, de, i, di, L, dL, peri, dperi, node, dnode) -------------
// Each row holds the printed table exactly: Mercury, Venus, Mars, Jupiter,
// Saturn, Uranus, Neptune (EM Bary, Earth's row, sits between Venus and
// Mars in the original; it is omitted here - see the header).
const me = {0.38709927, 0.00000037, 0.20563593, 0.00001906, 7.00497902, -0.00594749, 252.25032350, 149472.67411175, 77.45779628, 0.16047689, 48.33076593, -0.12534081}
const ve = {0.72333566, 0.00000390, 0.00677672, -0.00004107, 3.39467605, -0.00078890, 181.97909950, 58517.81538729, 131.60246718, 0.00268329, 76.67984255, -0.27769418}
const ma = {1.52371034, 0.00001847, 0.09339410, 0.00007882, 1.84969142, -0.00813131, -4.55343205, 19140.30268499, -23.94362959, 0.44441088, 49.55953891, -0.29257343}
const ju = {5.20288700, -0.00011607, 0.04838624, -0.00013253, 1.30439695, -0.00183714, 34.39644051, 3034.74612775, 14.72847983, 0.21252668, 100.47390909, 0.20469106}
const sa = {9.53667594, -0.00125060, 0.05386179, -0.00050991, 2.48599187, 0.00193609, 49.95424423, 1222.49362201, 92.59887831, -0.41897216, 113.66242448, -0.28867794}
const ur = {19.18916464, -0.00196176, 0.04725744, -0.00004397, 0.77263783, -0.00242939, 313.23810451, 428.48202785, 170.95427630, 0.40805281, 74.01692503, 0.04240589}
const ne = {30.06992276, 0.00026291, 0.00859048, 0.00005105, 1.77004347, 0.00035372, -55.12002969, 218.45945325, 44.96476227, -0.32241464, 131.78422574, -0.00508664}

// ---- helpers: value of element k of row r at the date ------------------------
def val(r, k) = r[k] + r[k + 1] * tc(year)     // element + rate * T

// ---- results: one row per planet, two lines of values and two of rates ------
const tt = tc(year)
print("mean Keplerian elements at", iso(jd(year, 1, 1, 12)))
print("T =", tt, "centuries from J2000.0; frame: mean ecliptic, equinox of J2000")
print("Mercury: a", val(me, 1), "AU  e", val(me, 3), "  i", val(me, 5), "deg")
print("         L", wrap360(val(me, 7)), "  peri", val(me, 9), "  node", val(me, 11), "deg")
print("Venus:   a", val(ve, 1), "AU  e", val(ve, 3), "  i", val(ve, 5), "deg")
print("         L", wrap360(val(ve, 7)), "  peri", val(ve, 9), "  node", val(ve, 11), "deg")
print("Mars:    a", val(ma, 1), "AU  e", val(ma, 3), "  i", val(ma, 5), "deg")
print("         L", wrap360(val(ma, 7)), "  peri", wrap360(val(ma, 9)), "  node", val(ma, 11), "deg")
print("Jupiter: a", val(ju, 1), "AU  e", val(ju, 3), "  i", val(ju, 5), "deg")
print("         L", wrap360(val(ju, 7)), "  peri", val(ju, 9), "  node", val(ju, 11), "deg")
print("Saturn:  a", val(sa, 1), "AU  e", val(sa, 3), "  i", val(sa, 5), "deg")
print("         L", wrap360(val(sa, 7)), "  peri", val(sa, 9), "  node", val(sa, 11), "deg")
print("Uranus:  a", val(ur, 1), "AU  e", val(ur, 3), "  i", val(ur, 5), "deg")
print("         L", wrap360(val(ur, 7)), "  peri", val(ur, 9), "  node", val(ur, 11), "deg")
print("Neptune: a", val(ne, 1), "AU  e", val(ne, 3), "  i", val(ne, 5), "deg")
print("         L", wrap360(val(ne, 7)), "  peri", wrap360(val(ne, 9)), "  node", val(ne, 11), "deg")
print("per-century rates (a in AU per century, the rest in deg per century):")
print("Mercury: da", me[2], "  de", me[4], "  di", me[6])
print("         dL", me[8], "  dperi", me[10], "  dnode", me[12])
print("Venus:   da", ve[2], "  de", ve[4], "  di", ve[6])
print("         dL", ve[8], "  dperi", ve[10], "  dnode", ve[12])
print("Mars:    da", ma[2], "  de", ma[4], "  di", ma[6])
print("         dL", ma[8], "  dperi", ma[10], "  dnode", ma[12])
print("Jupiter: da", ju[2], "  de", ju[4], "  di", ju[6])
print("         dL", ju[8], "  dperi", ju[10], "  dnode", ju[12])
print("Saturn:  da", sa[2], "  de", sa[4], "  di", sa[6])
print("         dL", sa[8], "  dperi", sa[10], "  dnode", sa[12])
print("Uranus:  da", ur[2], "  de", ur[4], "  di", ur[6])
print("         dL", ur[8], "  dperi", ur[10], "  dnode", ur[12])
print("Neptune: da", ne[2], "  de", ne[4], "  di", ne[6])
print("         dL", ne[8], "  dperi", ne[10], "  dnode", ne[12])

/* ---- expected output ----
= mean Keplerian elements at 2026-01-01T12:00:00
= T = 0.260013689254 centuries from J2000.0; frame: mean ecliptic, equinox of J2000
= Mercury: a 0.387099366205 AU  e 0.205640885861   i 7.00343259118 deg
=          L 237.191761947   peri 77.4995224682   node 48.2981756036 deg
