scripts.name: planet-illuminations
scripts.title: lit fraction of four planets
scripts.text:
/* ============================================================================
planet-illuminations.epher -- lit fraction of four planets

Illuminated fraction of the disk of Venus, Mars, Jupiter and Saturn on
2026-06-01, from the built-in accessor illum (the solar-ephemeris
crate, JPL-validated; guide 1.16; rounded to four decimals). The lit
fraction is (1 + cos(phase angle)) / 2 with the phase angle the
Sun-planet-Earth angle at the planet (see moon-phase-angle.epher).
Inner planets (Venus, Mercury) run through every phase, from a thin
crescent near inferior conjunction to a full disk near superior
conjunction, because Earth sees them at every elongation. Outer
planets never swing far from the Sun-Earth line as seen from the
planet: Jupiter's phase angle stays under about 11 deg and Saturn's
under 7 deg, so they always look nearly full (illum above 0.99).

Knob: the date tm.
============================================================================ */

// ---- the knob ---------------------------------------------------------------
const tm = jd(2026, 6, 1)     // 0h UT

// ---- model ------------------------------------------------------------------
// The lit fraction from the phase angle, radians trig (guide 1.13).
def lit(ph) = (1 + cos(rad(ph))) / 2

/* ---- results ----------------------------------------------------------------
Illumination and phase angle (degrees) for Venus, Mars, Jupiter,
Saturn. Venus is at 0.7953 with a 53.8 deg phase angle - a gibbous
disk heading toward the thin crescent of its October 2026 inferior
conjunction (see venus-illumination-cycle.epher). Mars, 2.18 AU out
near the far side of its orbit, shows 0.965. Jupiter and Saturn, seen
nearly Sun-on, are effectively full. */
for b in {2, 4, 5, 6} do illum(b, tm)
for b in {2, 4, 5, 6} do phase(b, tm)

/* Rebuild illum from phase and compare. Jupiter and Saturn agree to the
printed 4 decimals; the 1e-4 wobble everywhere is rounding (illum to
4 decimals, phase to 2). Venus is the one planet whose phase swings
widely over a year - the crescent-to-gibbous cycle of an inferior
planet, the same geometry that gives the Moon its phases. */
print("Jupiter rebuilt:", lit(phase(5, tm)), "vs", illum(5, tm))
print("Saturn rebuilt:", lit(phase(6, tm)), "vs", illum(6, tm))
print("Venus rebuilt:", lit(phase(2, tm)), "vs", illum(2, tm))

/* ---- expected output ----
= {0.7953, 0.965, 0.9956, 0.9979}
= {53.8, 21.56, 7.62, 5.23}
= Jupiter rebuilt: 0.995584656837 vs 0.9956
= Saturn rebuilt: 0.997918403498 vs 0.9979
= Venus rebuilt: 0.79530283381 vs 0.7953
*/

scripts.name: planet-magnitudes
scripts.title: how bright the planets look
scripts.text:
/* ============================================================================
planet-magnitudes.epher -- how bright the planets look

Apparent visual magnitudes of the planets on 2026-06-01, from the
built-in accessor mag (the solar-ephemeris crate, JPL-validated; guide
1.16). Magnitude is the logarithmic brightness scale: brighter means
smaller, and negative values are reserved for the brightest objects -
Sirius, the brightest star in the night sky, is -1.46. The magnitude
of a planet depends on its distance from Earth and from the Sun, and
on its phase.

Knob: the date tm.
============================================================================ */

// ---- the knob ---------------------------------------------------------------
const tm = jd(2026, 6, 1)     // 0h UT

/* ---- results ----------------------------------------------------------------
Magnitudes in body-number order (Mercury, Venus, Mars, Jupiter,
Saturn, Uranus, Neptune, Pluto). Reading the list, the brightest
planet of the eight is Venus at -3.98; Jupiter at -1.88 comes second.
For the eye's scale: Sirius is -1.46, so on this date Venus and
Jupiter both outshine every star in the sky, while Uranus (5.81) and
Neptune (7.91) need binoculars and Pluto (14.47) a large telescope.
(Mercury at -0.55 is an evening object low in the west; Mars at 1.27
is faint because it is 2.18 AU away near the far side of its orbit.) */
for b in {1, 2, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8, 9} do mag(b, tm)

// The two brightest, labelled, with the Sirius anchor for scale.
print("Venus:", mag(2, tm), "(brighter than Sirius at -1.46)")
print("Jupiter:", mag(5, tm))

/* ---- expected output ----
= {-0.55, -3.98, 1.27, -1.88, 0.65, 5.81, 7.91, 14.4693840929}
= Venus: -3.98 (brighter than Sirius at -1.46)
= Jupiter: -1.88
*/

scripts.name: planet-rise-set-transit
scripts.title: Mars through one day at Greenwich
scripts.text:
/* ============================================================================
planet-rise-set-transit.epher -- Mars through one day at Greenwich

Rise, meridian transit and set of Mars on 2026-06-01 at Greenwich
(the Royal Observatory), from the built-in accessors rise, transit
and set (the solar-ephemeris crate, JPL-validated; guide 1.16). Each
returns the event of the day that starts at j0 (0h UT) as a Julian
Date; subtracting j0 and multiplying by 24 gives the clock hour,
printed in hours and as a clock time (deg2hms of the hour times 15,
guide 1.16). Hours are UT - on the prime meridian that is Greenwich
Mean Time itself. Mars rises before the Sun (3.81 hr UT that day, see
sunrise-sunset.epher): about eight months before its February 2027
opposition the planet is a morning object.

Knobs: the date j0, latitude and longitude.
============================================================================ */

// ---- the knobs ---------------------------------------------------------------
const j0 = jd(2026, 6, 1)    // 0h UT
const lat = 51.4779        // Greenwich, the Royal Observatory
const lon = 0

// ---- helpers ----------------------------------------------------------------
// Clock hour of an event, and the clock-time display for it.
def evh(ev, j0) = (ev - j0) * 24
def evd(ev, j0) = (ev - j0) * 24 * 15

/* ---- results ----------------------------------------------------------------
The three events of the day, in order: rise at 2.57, transit at 9.87,
set at 17.17 hr UT. The ordering check below confirms rise comes
first: on this date Mars is up from 02:34 to 17:10 UT, crossing the
meridian just before 10:00 UT in the morning sky. */
print("Mars rise 2026-06-01:", evh(rise(4, j0, lat, lon), j0) in hr, "UT; clock", deg2hms(evd(rise(4, j0, lat, lon), j0)))
print("Mars transit 2026-06-01:", evh(transit(4, j0, lat, lon), j0) in hr, "UT; clock", deg2hms(evd(transit(4, j0, lat, lon), j0)))
print("Mars set 2026-06-01:", evh(set(4, j0, lat, lon), j0) in hr, "UT; clock", deg2hms(evd(set(4, j0, lat, lon), j0)))
print("rise before transit before set:", rise(4, j0, lat, lon) < transit(4, j0, lat, lon) and transit(4, j0, lat, lon) < set(4, j0, lat, lon))
print("transit instant as a date-time:", iso(transit(4, j0, lat, lon)), "UT")

// The Sun the same day transits at 11.97 hr UT (solar-noon-time.epher),
// so Mars culminates about 2.1 h earlier: the planet leads the Sun
// across the sky, the signature of a morning object.
print("Mars up at 4:00 UT:", alt(4, jd(2026, 6, 1, 4), lat, lon) > 0)

/* ---- expected output ----
= Mars rise 2026-06-01: 2.57032056525 hr UT; clock 2h 34m 13s
= Mars transit 2026-06-01: 9.86627928168 hr UT; clock 9h 51m 59s
= Mars set 2026-06-01: 17.1711040847 hr UT; clock 17h 10m 16s
= rise before transit before set: true
= transit instant as a date-time: 2026-06-01T09:51:59 UT
= Mars up at 4:00 UT: true
*/

scripts.name: planet-visibility-tonight
scripts.title: who is up in tonight's dark hours
scripts.text:
/* ============================================================================
planet-visibility-tonight.epher -- who is up in tonight's dark hours

For one night at one place, which of the five naked-eye planets can be
seen in the dark: each planet's rise and set (built-in events, upper
limb on the geometric horizon) are compared with the night itself, the
window between the end of astronomical twilight at dusk (Sun 18 degrees
below the horizon) and its start at dawn. A planet is reported visible
when it is above the horizon inside that window; the window's geometry
comes from the Sun's hour angle at -18 degrees.

The default night, 2026-10-15/16 from Greenwich, tells a real story:
Saturn rides the sky the whole dark window (its opposition fell on
2026-10-05), Mars climbs up after 23:27 and is well placed before dawn,
Jupiter joins it in the small hours, and Mercury and Venus - though both
lie east of the Sun - set before it at this latitude, running south of
the Sun's track (Venus a week and a half before its inferior
conjunction).

Accuracy: event times and altitudes follow the engine's conventions
(solar-ephemeris crate, JPL-Horizons-validated), so the windows are good
to about a minute; twilight uses the mean geometric -18 degree Sun
altitude, the standard astronomical definition.

Knobs: the night (the date `day` starts the local evening), the
observer's `lat` and `lon` (east positive). Times print in UT.
============================================================================ */

// ---- the knobs ---------------------------------------------------------------
const day = {2026, 10, 15}      // the evening of this date
const lat = 51.4779             // Greenwich
const lon = 0
const t15 = jd(day[1], day[2], day[3], 12)     // local day 1, noon
const t16 = jd(day[1], day[2], day[3] + 1, 12) // local day 2, noon

// ---- the astronomical night: Sun's hour angle at -18 degrees ----------------
def hms(x) = deg2hms(((x + 0.5) - floor(x + 0.5)) * 360)   // civil clock time of the instant
def sunh(j) = deg(acos((sin(rad(-18)) - sin(rad(lat)) * sin(rad(decl(10, j)))) / (cos(rad(lat)) * cos(rad(decl(10, j))))))   // hour angle, deg
const suntime = transit(10, t15, lat, lon)     // Sun's transit on the local day
const dusk = suntime + sunh(t15) / 360         // evening twilight ends (JD)
const dawn = transit(10, t16, lat, lon) - sunh(t16) / 360   // next morning's twilight starts (JD)

// ---- each planet's rise/set on the two local days ----------------------------
def r1(p) = rise(p, t15, lat, lon)
def s1(p) = set(p, t15, lat, lon)
def r2(p) = rise(p, t16, lat, lon)
def s2(p) = set(p, t16, lat, lon)
// The body is up at dusk when it rose before dusk and has not yet set.
def upatdusk(p) = if r1(p) < s1(p) then dusk < s1(p) else r1(p) < dusk
// Start and end of the body's time above the horizon inside the dark window.
def span(p) = {max(dusk, if upatdusk(p) then dusk else if r1(p) < s1(p) then r2(p) else r1(p)), min(dawn, if r1(p) < s1(p) then (if s1(p) > dusk then s1(p) else s2(p)) else s2(p))}

// ---- results ------------------------------------------------------------------
print("night of", iso(jd(day[1], day[2], day[3], 12)), "at lat", lat, "lon", lon)
print("dark window: dusk", hms(dusk), "to dawn", hms(dawn), "UT (", (dawn - dusk) * 24, "hours)")
print("Mercury:", if span(1)[2] - span(1)[1] > (dawn - dusk) * 0.98 then "up the whole dark window" else if span(1)[2] > span(1)[1] then "visible " + hms(span(1)[1]) + " to " + hms(span(1)[2]) else "not visible in the dark window")
print("Venus:  ", if span(2)[2] - span(2)[1] > (dawn - dusk) * 0.98 then "up the whole dark window" else if span(2)[2] > span(2)[1] then "visible " + hms(span(2)[1]) + " to " + hms(span(2)[2]) else "not visible in the dark window")
print("Mars:   ", if span(4)[2] - span(4)[1] > (dawn - dusk) * 0.98 then "up the whole dark window" else if span(4)[2] > span(4)[1] then "visible " + hms(span(4)[1]) + " to " + hms(span(4)[2]) else "not visible in the dark window")
print("Jupiter:", if span(5)[2] - span(5)[1] > (dawn - dusk) * 0.98 then "up the whole dark window" else if span(5)[2] > span(5)[1] then "visible " + hms(span(5)[1]) + " to " + hms(span(5)[2]) else "not visible in the dark window")
print("Saturn: ", if span(6)[2] - span(6)[1] > (dawn - dusk) * 0.98 then "up the whole dark window" else if span(6)[2] > span(6)[1] then "visible " + hms(span(6)[1]) + " to " + hms(span(6)[2]) else "not visible in the dark window")
print("Mercury and Venus set before dusk:", hms(s1(1)), hms(s1(2)))
print("their next rises:", hms(r2(1)), hms(r2(2)))
print("Saturn rises", hms(r1(6)), "and sets", hms(s2(6)), "the next morning")

/* ---- expected output ----
= night of 2026-10-15T12:00:00 at lat 51.4779 lon 0
= dark window: dusk 18h 58m 0s to dawn 4h 34m 34s UT ( 9.60945014656 hours)
= Mercury: not visible in the dark window
= Venus:   not visible in the dark window
= Mars:    visible 23h 27m 35s to 4h 34m 34s
= Jupiter: visible 0h 39m 18s to 4h 34m 34s
= Saturn:  up the whole dark window
= Mercury and Venus set before dusk: 17h 33m 45s 16h 38m 21s
= their next rises: 9h 2m 10s 8h 7m 41s
= Saturn rises 16h 53m 47s and sets 5h 15m 16s the next morning
*/

scripts.name: retrograde-stations
scripts.title: when a planet stands still, twice an apparition

scripts.name: saturn-ring-tilt
scripts.title: how wide open Saturn's rings look
scripts.text:
/* ============================================================================
saturn-ring-tilt.epher -- how wide open Saturn's rings look

The ring-plane aspect of Saturn for a chosen date: the angle B between
the line of sight and the plane of the rings (Meeus, "Astronomical
Algorithms" 2nd ed., ch. 45, physical ephemeris of Saturn). B is the
Saturnicentric latitude of the Earth measured from the ring plane:
positive when the rings' north face is presented, negative for the
south face, zero when the rings are exactly edge-on. The rings lie in
Saturn's equatorial plane, so B is the angle between the engine's
Saturn direction and the planet's rotation pole, whose direction comes
from the IAU 2000/2009 constants (as used in Meeus ch. 45 and the
Astronomical Almanac): pole RA 40.589 - 0.036 T deg, pole dec 83.537 -
0.004 T deg, referred to J2000 and here precessed to the equinox of
date to meet the engine's of-date position.

Accuracy: arcsecond-grade positions and the IAU pole give B good to a
few hundredths of a degree. Two independent checks ride in the output:
the Earth crossed the ring plane on 2025-03-23 and 2009-09-04 (famous
edge-on events), and the computed B is within 0.05 deg of zero on both
dates. On the default date, 2026-06-01, the rings present their south
face, open 8.3 degrees, still narrow after the 2025 edge-on.

The one knob is the instant `tm` (UT).
============================================================================ */

// ---- the knob ---------------------------------------------------------------
const tm = jd(2026, 6, 1)        // 2026-06-01 00:00 UT

// ---- precession (Meeus ch. 24): the IAU pole is J2000, the engine of date ---
def T(j) = (j - jd(2000, 1, 1, 12)) / 36525
def zeta(j) = (2306.2181 * T(j) + 0.30188 * T(j) ^ 2 + 0.017998 * T(j) ^ 3) / 3600
def zang(j) = (2306.2181 * T(j) + 1.09468 * T(j) ^ 2 + 0.018203 * T(j) ^ 3) / 3600
def theta(j) = (2004.3109 * T(j) - 0.42665 * T(j) ^ 2 - 0.041833 * T(j) ^ 3) / 3600
def rotz(a, v) = {v[1] * cos(rad(a)) - v[2] * sin(rad(a)), v[1] * sin(rad(a)) + v[2] * cos(rad(a)), v[3]}
def roty(a, v) = {v[1] * cos(rad(a)) + v[3] * sin(rad(a)), v[2], -v[1] * sin(rad(a)) + v[3] * cos(rad(a))}
def todate(j, v) = rotz(zeta(j), roty(-theta(j), rotz(zang(j), v)))   // J2000 -> of date
def dot(a, b) = a[1] * b[1] + a[2] * b[2] + a[3] * b[3]

// ---- the ring pole (IAU 2000/2009 constants, as in Meeus ch. 45) -------------
def pole_sat(j) = {cos(rad(83.537 - 0.004 * T(j))) * cos(rad(40.589 - 0.036 * T(j))), cos(rad(83.537 - 0.004 * T(j))) * sin(rad(40.589 - 0.036 * T(j))), sin(rad(83.537 - 0.004 * T(j)))}
// Unit vector toward Saturn (engine, of date) and the ring tilt B.
def usat(j) = {cos(rad(decl(6, j))) * cos(rad(ra(6, j))), cos(rad(decl(6, j))) * sin(rad(ra(6, j))), sin(rad(decl(6, j)))}
def bangle(j) = deg(asin(-dot(todate(j, pole_sat(j)), usat(j))))   // + = north face
def face(b) = if b > 1 then "north face of the rings presented" else if b < -1 then "south face of the rings presented" else "rings effectively edge-on"

// ---- results ------------------------------------------------------------------
print("Saturn ring-plane tilt B at", iso(tm), "UT:", bangle(tm), "deg")
print(face(bangle(tm)) + ";", "opening angle |B| =", abs(bangle(tm)), "deg")
print("cross-check at the known ring-plane crossings:")
print("  2025-03-23 (Earth crossing): B =", bangle(jd(2025, 3, 23)), "deg")
print("  2009-09-04 (Earth crossing): B =", bangle(jd(2009, 9, 4)), "deg")
print("context: after the 2025 edge-on the rings open to their southern")
print("maximum around 2032 and close again toward the next crossings,")
print("expected in the late 2030s (the cycle repeats every ~15 years).")

/* ---- expected output ----
= Saturn ring-plane tilt B at 2026-06-01T00:00:00 UT: -8.27226036509 deg
= south face of the rings presented; opening angle |B| = 8.27226036509 deg
= cross-check at the known ring-plane crossings:
=   2025-03-23 (Earth crossing): B = 0.0445223671135 deg
=   2009-09-04 (Earth crossing): B = -0.0336612984231 deg
= context: after the 2025 edge-on the rings open to their southern
= maximum around 2032 and close again toward the next crossings,
= expected in the late 2030s (the cycle repeats every ~15 years).
*/

scripts.name: saturn-satellites
scripts.title: Saturn's eight bright moons, positions and phenomena
scripts.text:
/* ============================================================================
saturn-satellites.epher -- Saturn's eight bright moons, positions and phenomena

Mimas, Enceladus, Tethys, Dione, Rhea, Titan, Hyperion, Iapetus: which
side of the rings each moon is on tonight, how far out it sits, and
whether any of them is transiting the disc, hiding behind it, or
slipping through Saturn's shadow. Titan is the prize - brighter than
most stars you can name - and Iapetus swings more than twice as far
out as Titan, dimming ten-fold as it crosses the dark side of its
orbit.

The positions come from chapter 46 of Jean Meeus, "Astronomical
Algorithms" (2nd ed.), computed by the engine's satellite accessors
(`satx saty satz satsep satphen`, guide 1.18) and fed with the engine's
real Earth-Saturn geometry. Saturn's equator is tilted about 27 degrees
to its orbit, so the moons' apparent paths open and close over
Saturn's 29-year orbit: the ring plane was edge-on to us in 2025 and
opens to nearly 14 degrees by 2028, when the moons spread north and
south of the rings again. Distances are good to a few arcseconds for
Titan and a few tenths of a Saturn radius for the inner moons against
JPL Horizons; treat event times from the scan below as approximate.

Web/desktop:             paste the whole file into the entry, press Enter

The one knob to edit is `when` below: the instant you want the table
for (and the anchor the scan searches forward from).
============================================================================ */

// ---- the knob ------------------------------------------------------------------
const when = jd(2026, 9, 17)

// ---- arcseconds per Saturn equatorial radius at the observer --------------------
def sc(t) = 60268 / (dist(6, t) * au) * 206264.806247

// ---- which side of the disc: satx counts positive to the West ------------------
def side(t, s) = if satx(6, s, t) > 0 then "W" else "E"

// ---- the phenomenon code as a word --------------------------------------------
def word(p) = if p == 1 then "in transit" else if p == 2 then "occulted" else if p == 3 then "in eclipse" else if p == 4 then "shadow transit" else "visible"

// ---- one table line: name, separation from Saturn's centre, side, phenomenon ---
def line(s, name) = print(name, round(satsep(6, s, when)), "arcsec", side(when, s), "-", word(satphen(6, s, when)))

// ---- results -------------------------------------------------------------------
print("Saturn's moons at", iso(when), "UT")
print("(separation from Saturn's centre, in arcseconds; W/E = which side)")
line(1, "Mimas:")
line(2, "Enceladus:")
line(3, "Tethys:")
line(4, "Dione:")
line(5, "Rhea:")
line(6, "Titan:")
line(7, "Hyperion:")
line(8, "Iapetus:")

/* The next time Titan is not plainly visible - a transit, an eclipse,
or a shadow pass - scanned in 30-minute steps for up to three days
from `when`. The scan answers the instant the moment it finds one
(`return` leaves the loop, guide 1.11), or 0 when all three days are
plain visible. Titan crosses the disc or its shadow about once a
fortnight. */
def next_phenomenon(p, m, name, t0) do
  t = t0
  while t - t0 < 3 do if satphen(p, m, t + 1 / 48) != 0 then return print(name + "'s next phenomenon:", iso(t + 1 / 48), "UT -", word(satphen(p, m, t + 1 / 48))) else t = t + 1 / 48
  print(name + ": nothing but plain visible within 3 days")
end
next_phenomenon(6, 6, "Titan", when)

/* Saturn's distance right then, for scale: the whole train of moons
spans about 4 degrees at Iapetus when the rings are wide open. */
print("Saturn distance:", round(dist(6, when) * 100) / 100, "AU")
/* ---- expected output ----
= Saturn's moons at 2026-09-17T00:00:00 UT
= (separation from Saturn's centre, in arcseconds; W/E = which side)
= Mimas: 22 arcsec E - visible
= Enceladus: 10 arcsec E - occulted
= Tethys: 9 arcsec E - occulted
= Dione: 59 arcsec E - visible
= Rhea: 27 arcsec W - shadow transit
= Titan: 166 arcsec E - visible
= Hyperion: 166 arcsec W - visible
= Iapetus: 198 arcsec W - visible
= Titan: nothing but plain visible within 3 days
= Saturn distance: 8.48 AU
*/

scripts.name: venus-illumination-cycle
scripts.title: Venus's phases across one year
scripts.text:
/* ============================================================================
venus-illumination-cycle.epher -- Venus's phases across one year

Illuminated fraction of Venus on the 15th of every month of 2026, from
the built-in accessor illum (the solar-ephemeris crate, JPL-validated;
guide 1.16; rounded to four decimals). Venus is an inferior planet:
its orbit lies inside Earth's, so Earth sees it at every elongation,
and it runs through the same crescent-to-gibbous cycle as the Moon -
full-looking near superior conjunction (far side of the Sun), a thin
crescent near inferior conjunction (between Earth and the Sun). The
cycle takes the synodic period of 584 days; one year of 2026 samples
shows the wane from 0.9993 in January to the 0.0372 sliver on
October 15 - days before the inferior conjunction of late October -
and the start of the waxing half in November.

Knob: the year.
============================================================================ */

// ---- the knob ---------------------------------------------------------------
const year = 2026

/* ---- results ----------------------------------------------------------------
Twelve values, one per month on the 15th: January through December.
The list runs 0.9993 (nearly full, Venus far on the far side of the
Sun) down to 0.0372 (October 15, a few days before the inferior
conjunction of late October, when the crescent thins to about 0.006)
and back up to 0.3835 in December. A for loop over the months
(guide 1.30) collects the values into the printed list. */
for m in 1 to 12 do illum(2, jd(year, m, 15))

/* The extremes of the twelve monthly samples, labelled. All twelve
entries sit in [0, 1] as an illuminated fraction must. Note the
counter-intuitive bit of the phase cycle: Venus is brightest in our
sky not when it looks full but around dichotomy (half lit), when it
is far closer to Earth. */
print("most lit of the monthly samples:", illum(2, jd(year, 1, 15)))
print("least lit of the monthly samples:", illum(2, jd(year, 10, 15)))

/* ---- expected output ----
= {0.9993, 0.9872, 0.9616, 0.9136, 0.8446, 0.7494, 0.635, 0.4884, 0.2875, 0.0372, 0.134, 0.3835}
= most lit of the monthly samples: 0.9993
= least lit of the monthly samples: 0.0372
*/

scripts.name: airmass-table
scripts.title: how much sky the light crosses
scripts.text:
/* ============================================================================
airmass-table.epher -- how much sky the light crosses

The airmass for a set of altitudes, from the built-in airmass(alt)
(guide 1.16): the length of the path through the atmosphere relative
to the zenith path, in the flat-atmosphere model airmass = sec of the
zenith distance = 1 / sin(alt). At 45 deg the path is sqrt(2) = 1.414
times the zenith path; at 10 deg it is 5.76 - the light of a star
low in the sky crosses nearly six times as much air as when the star
is overhead, which is why low stars twinkle and fade. The model
diverges toward the horizon (airmass would be infinite at 0 deg); the
real atmosphere is curved and finite, about 38 airmasses at the
horizon. The values below were checked in python against
1 / sin(altitude in radians), the oracle for the expected output.

Knob: none - the altitudes below are fixed.
============================================================================ */

/* ---- results ----------------------------------------------------------------
One airmass per altitude, zenith (90 deg) down to 5 deg above the
horizon. Notice the famous values in the middle: airmass(45) is
exactly sqrt(2), and airmass(30) = 2 is exactly twice the zenith
airmass, because 1 / sin(30 deg) = 2. */
print("airmass at 90 deg (zenith):", airmass(90))
print("airmass at 60 deg:", airmass(60))
print("airmass at 45 deg:", airmass(45), "(= sqrt(2))")
print("airmass at 30 deg:", airmass(30))
print("airmass at 20 deg:", airmass(20))
print("airmass at 10 deg:", airmass(10))
print("airmass at 5 deg:", airmass(5))

/* The jump from 10 deg to 5 deg doubles the airmass again (5.76 to
11.47): near the horizon the path length through the atmosphere
grows explosively, which is why the Sun flattens and reddens as it
sets. Photographers and observers use this table to plan exposures:
a star at 30 deg needs 2x the exposure time of one at the zenith. */
print("ratio 5 deg / 45 deg:", airmass(5) / airmass(45))

/* ---- expected output ----
= airmass at 90 deg (zenith): 1
= airmass at 60 deg: 1.15470053838
= airmass at 45 deg: 1.41421356237 (= sqrt(2))
= airmass at 30 deg: 2
= airmass at 20 deg: 2.92380440016
= airmass at 10 deg: 5.75877048314
= airmass at 5 deg: 11.4737132457
= ratio 5 deg / 45 deg: 8.1131404414
*/

scripts.name: altaz-hour-curve
scripts.title: a body's arc across one night, hour by hour
scripts.text:
/* ============================================================================
altaz-hour-curve.epher -- a body's arc across one night, hour by hour

The altitude and azimuth of one solar-system body at every full hour
of one night at one place: rows from 19:00 UT to 06:00 UT the next
morning, bracketing the body's rise and set, in the layout of the
altitude-vs-time planning curves that planetarium programs plot. The
row nearest the top of the arc (the sampled hour with the highest
altitude, i.e. the one straddling the meridian transit) is marked.
Every number is a built-in topocentric accessor reading (alt, az,
rise, set, transit; guide 1.16), so the curve carries the engine's
arcsecond-class accuracy; altitudes are geometric (no refraction).

The curve tells an observer when to look: for Saturn near its
opposition night of 2026-09-21 the arc runs from the east-north-east
horizon at dusk (alt 4 deg, az 91) through the meridian around 00:40
(alt 40 deg, az 180) down to the west at dawn.

A body that never leaves the horizon has no arc: for the polar-night
case below (the Sun at Svalbard in December) the script prints a note
instead of rows - the engine's rise/set calls would have no event to
return there.

Knobs: the body (guide 1.29 numbering), the night (the date whose dusk
opens it), the place, and the polar-night case used for the guard.
============================================================================ */

// ---- the knobs ---------------------------------------------------------------
const body = 6              // Saturn - near its 2026-10-04 opposition
const day = {2026, 9, 21}   // the night Sep 21-22, 2026
const lat = 51.4779         // Greenwich
const lon = 0
const latp = 78.2           // Svalbard: the polar-night guard case
const lonp = 15.6
const dpol = {2026, 12, 21} // December solstice: the Sun never rises there

// ---- the night's brackets ----------------------------------------------------
const j0 = jd(day[1], day[2], day[3])
const r1 = rise(body, j0, lat, lon)
const s2 = set(body, j0 + 1, lat, lon)
const tt = transit(body, j0 + 1, lat, lon)
def inst(h) = j0 + h / 24   // hour h of the night: 19-23 on day 1, 24-30 = 00-06 next day

// ---- the sampled altitudes (one engine call each) -----------------------------
const k19 = alt(body, j0 + 19 / 24, lat, lon)
const k20 = alt(body, j0 + 20 / 24, lat, lon)
const k21 = alt(body, j0 + 21 / 24, lat, lon)
const k22 = alt(body, j0 + 22 / 24, lat, lon)
const k23 = alt(body, j0 + 23 / 24, lat, lon)
const k24 = alt(body, j0 + 1, lat, lon)
const k25 = alt(body, j0 + 25 / 24, lat, lon)
const k26 = alt(body, j0 + 26 / 24, lat, lon)
const k27 = alt(body, j0 + 27 / 24, lat, lon)
const k28 = alt(body, j0 + 28 / 24, lat, lon)
const k29 = alt(body, j0 + 29 / 24, lat, lon)
const k30 = alt(body, j0 + 30 / 24, lat, lon)
const mx = max({k19, k20, k21, k22, k23, k24, k25, k26, k27, k28, k29, k30})
def tag(v) = if v == mx then "(highest)" else ""

/* ---- results ------------------------------------------------------------------
One row per full hour from 19:00 UT to 06:00 UT, altitude and azimuth
of Saturn as it climbs from the east, crosses the meridian near the
00:00-01:00 rows and sinks into the west. The azimuth shows the swing
the whole way: about 91 deg rising, 180 at the meridian, 250 setting. */
print("Saturn, night of 2026-09-21 at lat 51.4779 lon 0")
print("  above the horizon", iso(r1), "to", iso(s2))
print("  transits about", iso(tt))
print("19:00 UT: alt", k19, "deg, az", az(body, j0 + 19 / 24, lat, lon), "deg", tag(k19))
print("20:00 UT: alt", k20, "deg, az", az(body, j0 + 20 / 24, lat, lon), "deg", tag(k20))
print("21:00 UT: alt", k21, "deg, az", az(body, j0 + 21 / 24, lat, lon), "deg", tag(k21))
print("22:00 UT: alt", k22, "deg, az", az(body, j0 + 22 / 24, lat, lon), "deg", tag(k22))
print("23:00 UT: alt", k23, "deg, az", az(body, j0 + 23 / 24, lat, lon), "deg", tag(k23))
print("00:00 UT: alt", k24, "deg, az", az(body, j0 + 1, lat, lon), "deg", tag(k24))
print("01:00 UT: alt", k25, "deg, az", az(body, j0 + 25 / 24, lat, lon), "deg", tag(k25))
print("02:00 UT: alt", k26, "deg, az", az(body, j0 + 26 / 24, lat, lon), "deg", tag(k26))
print("03:00 UT: alt", k27, "deg, az", az(body, j0 + 27 / 24, lat, lon), "deg", tag(k27))
print("04:00 UT: alt", k28, "deg, az", az(body, j0 + 28 / 24, lat, lon), "deg", tag(k28))
print("05:00 UT: alt", k29, "deg, az", az(body, j0 + 29 / 24, lat, lon), "deg", tag(k29))
print("06:00 UT: alt", k30, "deg, az", az(body, j0 + 30 / 24, lat, lon), "deg", tag(k30))
print("all-night guard: above the horizon at some sampled hour:", mx > 0)

/* The guard case: the Sun at Svalbard on the December solstice never
rises at all - the hour-angle test on its noon declination says no
-0.833-deg crossing exists, so no arc is charted and the engine's
rise/set calls are never made. */
const t2 = transit(10, jd(dpol[1], dpol[2], dpol[3]), latp, lonp)
const d2 = decl(10, t2)
const cx2 = (sin(rad(-0.833)) - sin(rad(latp)) * sin(rad(d2))) / (cos(rad(latp)) * cos(rad(d2)))
if abs(cx2) > 1 then print("polar night at Svalbard (lat 78.2), 2026-12-21: the Sun never rises") else print("2026-12-21 at lat 78.2: the Sun does rise")
print("  solar declination at the day's transit:", d2, "deg")
/* ---- expected output ----
= Saturn, night of 2026-09-21 at lat 51.4779 lon 0
=   above the horizon 2026-09-21T18:31:16 to 2026-09-22T07:00:07
=   transits about 2026-09-22T00:45:43
= 19:00 UT: alt 3.9150281 deg, az 91.1169475 deg 
= 20:00 UT: alt 13.1956692 deg, az 103.0882568 deg 
= 21:00 UT: alt 22.0146995 deg, az 115.8772816 deg 
= 22:00 UT: alt 29.8631851 deg, az 130.158933 deg 
= 23:00 UT: alt 36.0929823 deg, az 146.5003794 deg 
= 00:00 UT: alt 39.9481638 deg, az 164.9827602 deg 
= 01:00 UT: alt 40.7899105 deg, az 184.7223776 deg (highest)
= 02:00 UT: alt 38.4555898 deg, az 204.0415582 deg 
= 03:00 UT: alt 33.3742617 deg, az 221.5468212 deg 
= 04:00 UT: alt 26.2827502 deg, az 236.854737 deg 
= 05:00 UT: alt 17.8995293 deg, az 250.3419856 deg 
= 06:00 UT: alt 8.8026656 deg, az 262.656729 deg 
= all-night guard: above the horizon at some sampled hour: true
= polar night at Svalbard (lat 78.2), 2026-12-21: the Sun never rises
=   solar declination at the day's transit: -23.436808724 deg
*/

scripts.name: circumpolar-check
scripts.title: which stars never set, never rise, or do both
scripts.text:
/* ============================================================================
circumpolar-check.epher -- which stars never set, never rise, or do both

At a given latitude a star of declination dec is circumpolar - it
never sets - when it clears the horizon even at lower culmination,
which happens when dec and the latitude share a sign and |dec| exceeds
90 - |lat|; at the mirror declination of the opposite sign it never
rises; everything between rises and sets daily (PyEphem's
circumpolar test is the same geometry). The classification below comes
from the hour-angle formula at the horizon, cos(H) = -tan(lat)
tan(dec): when |cos H| exceeds 1 no horizon crossing exists, and the
sign of cos H tells which kind - cos H < -1 means the object stays up
(circumpolar), cos H > 1 means it stays down (never rises). On the
boundary, |cos H| = 1, the object grazes the horizon once a day.

The same geometry gives the sky's shares: the cap of sky around each
celestial pole that never sets (or never rises) holds the fraction
(1 - cos(90 - |lat|)) / 2 = (1 - sin|lat|) / 2 of the celestial
sphere, and the rising-and-setting band between them holds the rest.
At Greenwich (51.48 N) that is about 10.9 percent of the sky that
never sets - Capella, declination +46, is inside it - and the equal
cap opposite that never rises.

Knobs: the latitude (Greenwich below) and the high-latitude place used
for the engine validation of the same geometry.
============================================================================ */

// ---- the knobs ---------------------------------------------------------------
const lat = 51.4779         // Greenwich
const latp = 78.2           // Longyearbyen, Svalbard - the engine check
const lonp = 15.6

// ---- model ------------------------------------------------------------------
def cosH(dec, phi) = -tan(rad(phi)) * tan(rad(dec))   // cos of the hour angle at the horizon
def cls(dec, phi) = if cosH(dec, phi) < -1 then "circumpolar: never sets" else if cosH(dec, phi) > 1 then "never rises" else "rises and sets daily"
def ccl(dec, phi) = if cosH(dec, phi) < -1 then 1 else if cosH(dec, phi) > 1 then -1 else 0
const fcirc = (1 - cos(rad(90 - abs(lat)))) / 2   // share of the sky in each polar cap

/* ---- results ------------------------------------------------------------------
Three declinations at Greenwich: +46 (Capella - circumpolar, the
textbook case), +20 (a normal rising-and-setting star) and -50 (below
the south cap, so never seen from 51 N). The fraction prints show the
size of the two caps and the band between them; they sum to 1. */
print("circumpolar check at lat 51.4779:")
print("  declination +46 deg:", cls(46, lat))
print("  declination +20 deg:", cls(20, lat))
print("  declination -50 deg:", cls(-50, lat))
print("share that never sets: (1 - cos(90 - |lat|)) / 2 =", fcirc)
print("share that never rises: the same by symmetry =", fcirc)
print("share that rises and sets daily:", 1 - 2 * fcirc)
print("  the three shares sum to:", fcirc + fcirc + (1 - 2 * fcirc))

/* Engine validation of the same rule on a real body: the Sun at
Svalbard on the 2026-06-21 solstice has declination +23.4 deg, beyond
90 - 78.2 = 11.8, so it must be circumpolar there that day - polar
day. The engine's altitude readings at 00:00 and 12:00 UT should both
be above the horizon. */
const d = decl(10, jd(2026, 6, 21))
const a0 = alt(10, jd(2026, 6, 21, 0), latp, lonp)
const a12 = alt(10, jd(2026, 6, 21, 12), latp, lonp)
print("Sun at Svalbard on 2026-06-21, declination", d, "deg")
print("  classified:", cls(d, latp))
print("engine check: altitudes at 00:00 and 12:00 UT:", a0, "and", a12, "deg")
print("  both above the horizon:", a0 > 0 and a12 > 0)
/* ---- expected output ----
= circumpolar check at lat 51.4779:
=   declination +46 deg: circumpolar: never sets
=   declination +20 deg: rises and sets daily
=   declination -50 deg: never rises
= share that never sets: (1 - cos(90 - |lat|)) / 2 = 0.108816008157
= share that never rises: the same by symmetry = 0.108816008157
= share that rises and sets daily: 0.782367983687
=   the three shares sum to: 1
= Sun at Svalbard on 2026-06-21, declination 23.437516214 deg
=   classified: circumpolar: never sets
= engine check: altitudes at 00:00 and 12:00 UT: 12.0180793 and 34.779948 deg
=   both above the horizon: true
*/

scripts.name: day-length-year
scripts.title: how daylight grows and shrinks through a year
scripts.text:
/* ============================================================================
day-length-year.epher -- how daylight grows and shrinks through a year

The length of daylight through the year at one latitude: twelve rows,
the 21st of each month with the equinoxes standing in for the 21sts
that bracket them (Mar 20 and Sep 23 in 2026; Jun 21 and Dec 21 are
the solstices themselves). Each row recomputes the day length from the
hour-angle formula at the standard sunrise horizon

  cos(H) = (sin(h0) - sin(lat) sin(dec)) / (cos(lat) cos(dec)),
  h0 = -0.833 deg (upper limb plus refraction), day length = 2H,
  time = 4 minutes per degree of hour angle

with the Sun's declination at 12:00 UT read from the built-in
accessor - the same machinery as twilight-times.epher and
sunrise-sunset.epher, good to about a minute. The row on the June
solstice is marked longest and the December one shortest (of the
sampled days; the true extremes fall within a day of the solstices).

The script assumes the Sun rises and sets daily at the place: within
the polar circles the machinery would find no H, and midnight-sun.epher
is the right tool there.

Knobs: the year and the latitude and longitude (Greenwich below).
============================================================================ */

// ---- the knobs ---------------------------------------------------------------
const year = 2026
const lat = 51.4779         // Greenwich
const lon = 0

// ---- model: day length from the Sun's declination at 12:00 UT ----------------
def cx(h0, dec, phi) = (sin(rad(h0)) - sin(rad(phi)) * sin(rad(dec))) / (cos(rad(phi)) * cos(rad(dec)))
def hours(dec) = deg(acos(cx(-0.833, dec, lat))) / 7.5   // H deg, 4 min per deg, both halves: 2H*4/60 = H/7.5 h
def dld(y, m, d) = if abs(cx(-0.833, decl(10, jd(y, m, d, 12)), lat)) > 1 then -1 else hours(decl(10, jd(y, m, d, 12)))
def tag(v, mx, mn) = if v == mx then "(longest)" else if v == mn then "(shortest)" else ""

// ---- the twelve rows, each one declination reading ----------------------------
const djan = dld(year, 1, 21)
const dfeb = dld(year, 2, 21)
const dmar = dld(year, 3, 20)
const dapr = dld(year, 4, 21)
const dmay = dld(year, 5, 21)
const djun = dld(year, 6, 21)
const djul = dld(year, 7, 21)
const daug = dld(year, 8, 21)
const dsep = dld(year, 9, 23)
const doct = dld(year, 10, 21)
const dnov = dld(year, 11, 21)
const ddec = dld(year, 12, 21)

/* ---- results ------------------------------------------------------------------
The year's swing at Greenwich: 16.6 hours of daylight at the June
solstice against 7.8 at the December one, with the equinox rows near
12.2 (not 12: the -0.833 horizon adds the upper limb and refraction).
The longest and shortest marks fall on the two solstice rows. */
const mx = max({djan, dfeb, dmar, dapr, dmay, djun, djul, daug, dsep, doct, dnov, ddec})
const mn = min({djan, dfeb, dmar, dapr, dmay, djun, djul, daug, dsep, doct, dnov, ddec})

print("day length through", year, "at lat", lat, "lon", lon, "(h0 = -0.833 deg)")
print("Jan 21:", if djan < 0 then "polar: no sunrise" else djan in hr, tag(djan, mx, mn))
print("Feb 21:", if dfeb < 0 then "polar: no sunrise" else dfeb in hr, tag(dfeb, mx, mn))
print("Mar 20 (equinox):", if dmar < 0 then "polar: no sunrise" else dmar in hr, tag(dmar, mx, mn))
print("Apr 21:", if dapr < 0 then "polar: no sunrise" else dapr in hr, tag(dapr, mx, mn))
print("May 21:", if dmay < 0 then "polar: no sunrise" else dmay in hr, tag(dmay, mx, mn))
print("Jun 21 (solstice):", if djun < 0 then "polar: no sunrise" else djun in hr, tag(djun, mx, mn))
print("Jul 21:", if djul < 0 then "polar: no sunrise" else djul in hr, tag(djul, mx, mn))
print("Aug 21:", if daug < 0 then "polar: no sunrise" else daug in hr, tag(daug, mx, mn))
print("Sep 23 (equinox):", if dsep < 0 then "polar: no sunrise" else dsep in hr, tag(dsep, mx, mn))
print("Oct 21:", if doct < 0 then "polar: no sunrise" else doct in hr, tag(doct, mx, mn))
print("Nov 21:", if dnov < 0 then "polar: no sunrise" else dnov in hr, tag(dnov, mx, mn))
print("Dec 21 (solstice):", if ddec < 0 then "polar: no sunrise" else ddec in hr, tag(ddec, mx, mn))

/* Self-check against the engine's own rise/set events (upper limb,
same -0.833 horizon, but the events iterate the true geometry while
the rows freeze the declination at noon): the June 21 span below
should match the row within a minute or two. */
const es = (set(10, jd(year, 6, 21), lat, lon) - rise(10, jd(year, 6, 21), lat, lon)) * 24
print("self-check: engine rise/set span 2026-06-21:", es in hr)
print("  vs the formula row:", djun in hr)
/* ---- expected output ----
= day length through 2026 at lat 51.4779 lon 0 (h0 = -0.833 deg)
= Jan 21: 8.61861756848 hr 
= Feb 21: 10.3992119049 hr 
= Mar 20 (equinox): 12.170706945 hr 
= Apr 21: 14.2472960702 hr 
= May 21: 15.8962603087 hr 
= Jun 21 (solstice): 16.6335832338 hr (longest)
= Jul 21: 15.9319249971 hr 
= Aug 21: 14.2561815313 hr 
= Sep 23 (equinox): 12.1459917739 hr 
= Oct 21: 10.3376060179 hr 
= Nov 21: 8.58963943771 hr 
= Dec 21 (solstice): 7.83026100458 hr (shortest)
= self-check: engine rise/set span 2026-06-21: 16.6341501698 hr
=   vs the formula row: 16.6335832338 hr
*/

scripts.name: day-length
scripts.title: how long the daylight lasts through the year
scripts.text:
/* ============================================================================
day-length.epher -- how long the daylight lasts through the year

Length of daylight at Greenwich (the Royal Observatory) on three
dates of 2026 (the March equinox and the two solstices), as the span
between the built-in set and rise events of the Sun, body 10 (the
solar-ephemeris crate, JPL-validated; guide 1.16): (set - rise) * 24
hours. The two events both fall inside the same UT day at this
latitude, so the difference is the day length. The swing is the tilt
of the Earth's axis: about 16.63 h at the June solstice, 7.83 h at
the December solstice. The equinox day is 12.17 h, not 12: sunrise
and sunset are taken at the moment the Sun's upper limb touches the
horizon and refraction lifts it, so daylight outlasts the geometric
half-day by some minutes.

Knobs: latitude and longitude (Greenwich below); the three dates below.
============================================================================ */

// ---- the knobs ---------------------------------------------------------------
const lat = 51.4779        // Greenwich, the Royal Observatory
const lon = 0
const d_mar = {2026, 3, 20}    // March equinox
const d_jun = {2026, 6, 21}    // June solstice
const d_dec = {2026, 12, 21}   // December solstice

// ---- helpers ----------------------------------------------------------------
// Length of daylight on the day of the given date, in hours.
def dl(ds, lat, lon) = (set(10, jd(ds[1], ds[2], ds[3]), lat, lon) - rise(10, jd(ds[1], ds[2], ds[3]), lat, lon)) * 24 in hr

/* ---- results ----------------------------------------------------------------
The June solstice carries Greenwich's longest day (16.63 h) and the
December solstice the shortest (7.83 h); the equinox splits the
difference at 12.17 h. Each reading is positive and less than 24 h. */
print("day length 2026-03-20:", dl(d_mar, lat, lon))
print("day length 2026-06-21:", dl(d_jun, lat, lon))
print("day length 2026-12-21:", dl(d_dec, lat, lon))

/* The two solstice readings add to about 24.5 h, not 24: each daylight
reading carries the upper-limb and refraction extras of its season,
and the Sun's declination is still moving on both dates, so the pair
is only roughly complementary. */
print("June plus December:", (dl(d_jun, lat, lon) + dl(d_dec, lat, lon)) in hr)

/* ---- expected output ----
= day length 2026-03-20: 12.1683208868 hr
= day length 2026-06-21: 16.6341501698 hr
= day length 2026-12-21: 7.8335351944 hr
= June plus December: 24.4676853642 hr
*/

scripts.name: extinction-limiting-magnitude
scripts.title: how faint you can see, altitude by altitude
scripts.text:
/* ============================================================================
extinction-limiting-magnitude.epher -- how faint you can see, altitude by altitude

Atmospheric extinction dims every object by an amount that grows with
the airmass it is seen through: a star at altitude h loses k airmasses'
worth of light, where the airmass is the built-in airmass(h) (the
secant model, see airmass-table.epher) and k is the extinction in
magnitudes per airmass at the zenith - about 0.2 mag at a typical
dark site, more through haze or at sea level (Duffett-Smith,
"Practical Astronomy", "Atmospheric extinction"). The script tabulates
extinction and the resulting limiting magnitude at altitudes 90 to 5
degrees for one telescope aperture and one naked-eye limit.

The limiting magnitude at the zenith follows the crude aperture law
  m = NELM + 5 log(D / d_eye)
with D the aperture and d_eye the dark-adapted pupil, about 7 mm
(B. Schaefer, "Telescopic Limiting Magnitudes", PASP 102, 1990; the
same rule fills the telescope pages of Sky & Telescope). At altitude h
the limit drops by the extinction k * airmass(h). Honest grade: about
0.5 magnitude either way - the law ignores seeing, optics quality,
magnification and sky brightness, and extinction varies with the night.

Knobs: the extinction k per airmass, the aperture D (mm), the naked-eye
limit NELM at the zenith and the eye-pupil diameter d_eye (mm).
============================================================================ */

// ---- the knobs ---------------------------------------------------------------
const k = 0.2               // extinction, magnitudes per airmass at the zenith
const D = 200               // telescope aperture, mm
const NELM = 6              // naked-eye limiting magnitude at the zenith
const d_eye = 7             // dark-adapted pupil, mm

// ---- model ------------------------------------------------------------------
const m0 = NELM + 5 * log(D / d_eye)   // telescope limit at the zenith, mag
def X(h) = airmass(h)                     // built-in airmass at altitude h
def ext(h) = k * X(h)                     // extinction in magnitudes at h
def mlim(h) = m0 - ext(h)                 // limiting magnitude at h

/* ---- results ----------------------------------------------------------------
One row per altitude. The story is in the last two columns: at 30 deg
the object's light crosses twice the zenith air, costing 0.4 mag, and
at 5 deg the same telescope sees barely a magnitude fainter than the
naked eye does overhead - which is why observers wait for objects to
climb. */
print("extinction", k, "mag per airmass; telescope", D, "mm; naked-eye limit NELM", NELM)
print("limiting magnitude at the zenith:", m0, "mag")
print("at 90 deg (zenith): airmass", X(90))
print("  extinction", ext(90), "mag; limiting", mlim(90), "mag")
print("at 60 deg: airmass", X(60))
print("  extinction", ext(60), "mag; limiting", mlim(60), "mag")
print("at 45 deg: airmass", X(45))
print("  extinction", ext(45), "mag; limiting", mlim(45), "mag")
print("at 30 deg: airmass", X(30))
print("  extinction", ext(30), "mag; limiting", mlim(30), "mag")
print("at 20 deg: airmass", X(20))
print("  extinction", ext(20), "mag; limiting", mlim(20), "mag")
print("at 10 deg: airmass", X(10))
print("  extinction", ext(10), "mag; limiting", mlim(10), "mag")
print("at 5 deg: airmass", X(5))
print("  extinction", ext(5), "mag; limiting", mlim(5), "mag")

// The aperture gain over the eye alone, from the same law.
print("aperture gain 5 log(D / d_eye):", m0 - NELM, "mag")

/* Self-check: the built-in airmass is the secant model 1/sin(h); the
two agree by construction at every altitude (one row, at 60 deg). */
print("check: airmass(60) vs 1/sin(60 deg):", X(60), 1 / sin(rad(60)))
/* ---- expected output ----
= extinction 0.2 mag per airmass; telescope 200 mm; naked-eye limit NELM 6
= limiting magnitude at the zenith: 13.2796597782 mag
= at 90 deg (zenith): airmass 1
=   extinction 0.2 mag; limiting 13.0796597782 mag
= at 60 deg: airmass 1.15470053838
=   extinction 0.230940107676 mag; limiting 13.0487196706 mag
= at 45 deg: airmass 1.41421356237
=   extinction 0.282842712475 mag; limiting 12.9968170658 mag
= at 30 deg: airmass 2
=   extinction 0.4 mag; limiting 12.8796597782 mag
= at 20 deg: airmass 2.92380440016
=   extinction 0.584760880033 mag; limiting 12.6948988982 mag
= at 10 deg: airmass 5.75877048314
=   extinction 1.15175409663 mag; limiting 12.1279056816 mag
= at 5 deg: airmass 11.4737132457
=   extinction 2.29474264913 mag; limiting 10.9849171291 mag
= aperture gain 5 log(D / d_eye): 7.27965977825 mag
= check: airmass(60) vs 1/sin(60 deg): 1.15470053838 1.15470053838
*/

scripts.name: eyepiece-planner
scripts.title: what each eyepiece does to the view
scripts.text:
/* ============================================================================
eyepiece-planner.epher -- what each eyepiece does to the view

For one telescope (aperture and focal-ratio knobs) and a set of
eyepieces, the three numbers that decide the view: magnification =
telescope focal length / eyepiece focal length; exit pupil = eyepiece
focal length / focal ratio (equivalently aperture / magnification) -
the little disc of light at the eye, which should not exceed the
dark-adapted pupil of about 7 mm; and true field = apparent field /
magnification, the degrees of sky the eyepiece shows (the standard
approximation; real eyepieces add a few percent of distortion).

Each row carries a one-word role from the exit pupil, the observer's
rule of thumb: 2-4 mm exit pupil for deep-sky sweeping (the sky
background stays dark and the eye's own pupil is fully used), 0.5-1 mm
for planets and double stars (the highest power the seeing usually
permits), 1-2 mm the high-power middle ground, and below 0.5 mm an
empty, over-magnified image. Complements telescope-resolution.epher,
which answers how fine the same scope can split detail; this file
stays with the eyepiece side and prints no Dawes values.

Knobs: aperture (mm) and focal ratio of the telescope, the apparent
field of the eyepieces (a 50-degree Plossl below) and the list of
eyepiece focal lengths in mm.
============================================================================ */

// ---- the knobs ---------------------------------------------------------------
const aperture = 200        // telescope aperture, mm
const fr = 10               // focal ratio f/10: focal length 2000 mm
const afov = 50             // apparent field of the eyepieces, degrees
const eps = {4, 5, 8, 12.5, 20, 32}   // eyepiece focal lengths, mm

// ---- model ------------------------------------------------------------------
const fl = aperture * fr    // telescope focal length, mm
def magnification(ep) = fl / ep       // magnification
def xp(ep) = ep / fr        // exit pupil, mm (also aperture / mag)
def tf(ep) = afov / magnification(ep) // true field on the sky, degrees
def role(ep) = if xp(ep) > 4 then "sweeps" else if xp(ep) >= 2 then "deep-sky" else if xp(ep) >= 1 then "high-power" else if xp(ep) >= 0.5 then "planets" else "over"

/* ---- results ----------------------------------------------------------------
One row per eyepiece, shortest to longest. The 4 mm row magnifies the
2000 mm focal length 500 times into an exit pupil of 0.4 mm - beyond
the useful ceiling - while the 20 and 32 mm eyepieces deliver the
2-4 mm exit pupils that suit nebulae and clusters. */
print("telescope", aperture, "mm f/", fr, "; eyepieces, Plossl-type, afov", afov, "deg")
print("4 mm:", magnification(4), "x; exit pupil", xp(4), "mm; true field", tf(4), "deg; role:", role(4))
print("5 mm:", magnification(5), "x; exit pupil", xp(5), "mm; true field", tf(5), "deg; role:", role(5))
print("8 mm:", magnification(8), "x; exit pupil", xp(8), "mm; true field", tf(8), "deg; role:", role(8))
print("12.5 mm:", magnification(12.5), "x; exit pupil", xp(12.5), "mm; true field", tf(12.5), "deg; role:", role(12.5))
print("20 mm:", magnification(20), "x; exit pupil", xp(20), "mm; true field", tf(20), "deg; role:", role(20))
print("32 mm:", magnification(32), "x; exit pupil", xp(32), "mm; true field", tf(32), "deg; role:", role(32))

/* The useful ceiling: about 2x per mm of aperture (the seeing-limited
rule that pairs with the Dawes limit in telescope-resolution.epher).
The exit pupil identity - aperture / magnification - is the same
number the ep / fr row shows, checked here on the 20 mm row. */
print("useful ceiling 2x per mm:", 2 * aperture, "x - the 4 mm row exceeds it")
print("check: aperture / mag vs exit pupil on the 20 mm row:", aperture / magnification(20), "mm =", xp(20), "mm")

/* An eyepiece longer than about 7 mm exit pupil would throw away
light: the eye's dark-adapted pupil cannot open wider than that. */
print("longest eyepiece that uses all the light: f/", fr, "* 7 mm =", fr * 7, "mm")

/* ---- expected output ----
= telescope 200 mm f/ 10 ; eyepieces, Plossl-type, afov 50 deg
= 4 mm: 500 x; exit pupil 0.4 mm; true field 0.1 deg; role: over
= 5 mm: 400 x; exit pupil 0.5 mm; true field 0.125 deg; role: planets
= 8 mm: 250 x; exit pupil 0.8 mm; true field 0.2 deg; role: planets
= 12.5 mm: 160 x; exit pupil 1.25 mm; true field 0.3125 deg; role: high-power
= 20 mm: 100 x; exit pupil 2 mm; true field 0.5 deg; role: deep-sky
= 32 mm: 62.5 x; exit pupil 3.2 mm; true field 0.8 deg; role: deep-sky
= useful ceiling 2x per mm: 400 x - the 4 mm row exceeds it
= check: aperture / mag vs exit pupil on the 20 mm row: 2 mm = 2 mm
= longest eyepiece that uses all the light: f/ 10 * 7 mm = 70 mm
*/

scripts.name: golden-blue-hour
scripts.title: the photography golden/blue hour for a place
scripts.text:
/* ============================================================================
golden-blue-hour.epher -- the photography golden/blue hour for a place

When the warm light happens: the morning and evening spans in which the
Sun's altitude lies between 6 degrees above the horizon and 4 degrees
below it - the band the photography apps call the golden hour (with
the pre-sunrise -4-to-0-degree slice carrying the blue hour tones).
The script reports the Sun's crossings of -4 deg and +6 deg, morning
and evening, as ISO date-times in UT, and the length of each band.

The hour-angle machinery is the same as twilight-times.epher: the
events come from cos(H) = (sin(h0) - sin(lat) sin(dec)) / (cos(lat)
cos(dec)) at the custom horizons h0 = -4 and +6, with the Sun's
declination at the day's transit from the built-in accessors, and each
event time = transit -/+ 4 minutes per degree of hour angle, as UT.

Sources: the USNO/NOAA hour-angle method (see twilight-times.epher)
and the photography convention used by PhotoPills and timeanddate's
golden-hour pages: the golden hour window runs from the Sun at -4 deg
to +6 deg, morning and evening.

Accuracy: about a minute, as in twilight-times.epher. Where a band
cannot form - the Sun never climbs to +6 deg in a high-latitude winter,
or never drops below it in summer - the script says so rather than
printing an event.

Knobs: the place (lat, lon), the polar-test place (latp, lonp) and the
three dates below.
============================================================================ */

// ---- the knobs ----------------------------------------------------------------
const lat = 51.4779            // Greenwich
const lon = 0
const latp = 78.2              // Longyearbyen, Svalbard - the polar test
const lonp = 15.6
const day1 = {2026, 6, 21}     // June solstice: the long light
const day2 = {2026, 12, 21}    // December solstice: the short light
const day3 = {2026, 12, 21}    // polar night at the polar-test place

// ---- one transit and one declination per date ---------------------------------
const t1 = transit(10, jd(day1[1], day1[2], day1[3]), lat, lon)
const t2 = transit(10, jd(day2[1], day2[2], day2[3]), lat, lon)
const t3 = transit(10, jd(day3[1], day3[2], day3[3]), latp, lonp)
const d1 = decl(10, t1)
const d2 = decl(10, t2)
const d3 = decl(10, t3)

// ---- the hour-angle machinery at a custom horizon h0 --------------------------
def cx(h0, dec, phi) = (sin(rad(h0)) - sin(rad(phi)) * sin(rad(dec))) / (cos(rad(phi)) * cos(rad(dec)))
def nom(h0) = if h0 == -4 then "no -4 deg crossing today" else "no +6 deg crossing today"
def evm(h0, dec, tt, phi) = if abs(cx(h0, dec, phi)) > 1 then nom(h0) else iso(tt - 4 * deg(acos(cx(h0, dec, phi))) / 1440)
def eve(h0, dec, tt, phi) = if abs(cx(h0, dec, phi)) > 1 then nom(h0) else iso(tt + 4 * deg(acos(cx(h0, dec, phi))) / 1440)
def dur(h0a, h0b, dec, phi) = (deg(acos(cx(h0a, dec, phi))) - deg(acos(cx(h0b, dec, phi)))) * 4 / 60
def both(h0a, h0b, dec, phi) = abs(cx(h0a, dec, phi)) <= 1 and abs(cx(h0b, dec, phi)) <= 1

/* ---- results ------------------------------------------------------------------
Each band starts when the Sun crosses -4 deg (blue tones while it is
still below the horizon, golden after it clears it) and ends when it
reaches +6 deg; in the evening the order reverses. The two bands of a
day last the same length, because the crossings are symmetric about
the transit instant. */
print("golden/blue hour band: Sun between -4 deg and +6 deg")
print("2026-06-21 at lat 51.4779 lon 0:")
print("  morning:", evm(-4, d1, t1, lat), "to", evm(6, d1, t1, lat))
print("  evening:", eve(6, d1, t1, lat), "to", eve(-4, d1, t1, lat))
if both(-4, 6, d1, lat) then print("  each band lasts:", dur(-4, 6, d1, lat) in hr) else print("  no band forms today")
print("2026-12-21 at lat 51.4779 lon 0:")
print("  morning:", evm(-4, d2, t2, lat), "to", evm(6, d2, t2, lat))
print("  evening:", eve(6, d2, t2, lat), "to", eve(-4, d2, t2, lat))
if both(-4, 6, d2, lat) then print("  each band lasts:", dur(-4, 6, d2, lat) in hr) else print("  no band forms today")

// The polar test: in the December polar night the Sun never climbs to
// -4 deg, so no band exists; the honest print shows why. This whole
// choice is one statement, so it sits on one line.
print("polar test, 2026-12-21 at lat 78.2 lon 15.6:")
if cx(-4, d3, latp) > 1 then print("  the Sun never reaches -4 deg: no golden/blue hour - polar night") else if cx(6, d3, latp) < -1 then print("  the Sun never drops below +6 deg: no golden/blue hour - midnight sun") else print("  morning:", evm(-4, d3, t3, latp), "to", evm(6, d3, t3, latp), "; evening:", eve(6, d3, t3, latp), "to", eve(-4, d3, t3, latp))
print("  (highest the Sun gets:", 90 - abs(latp - d3), "deg)")
/* ---- expected output ----
= golden/blue hour band: Sun between -4 deg and +6 deg
= 2026-06-21 at lat 51.4779 lon 0:
=   morning: 2026-06-21T03:14:34 to 2026-06-21T04:37:00
=   evening: 2026-06-21T19:26:37 to 2026-06-21T20:49:03
=   each band lasts: 1.37383037215 hr
= 2026-12-21 at lat 51.4779 lon 0:
=   morning: 2026-12-21T07:38:02 to 2026-12-21T09:04:46
=   evening: 2026-12-21T14:51:21 to 2026-12-21T16:18:06
=   each band lasts: 1.44560565835 hr
= polar test, 2026-12-21 at lat 78.2 lon 15.6:
=   the Sun never reaches -4 deg: no golden/blue hour - polar night
=   (highest the Sun gets: -11.636808724 deg)
*/

scripts.name: kepler-equation
scripts.title: Kepler's equation, solved
scripts.text:
/* ============================================================================
kepler-equation.epher -- Kepler's equation, solved

Kepler's equation M = E - e sin E ties the mean anomaly M of a body
on an elliptic orbit (the time since perihelion, as an angle) to its
eccentric anomaly E, with e the orbit's eccentricity. It is a
transcendental equation - E appears inside the sine - so it is solved
numerically; epher's builtin kepler(M, e) does that (guide 1.16).
The builtin is unit-consistent: feed M in degrees and it returns E in
degrees (the equation is homogeneous, so radians work the same way).
Each line below solves the equation for one orbit, then the script
evaluates E - e sin E from its own answer and checks it reproduces
M. The first pair is the Earth (e = 0.0167); the last two are
comet-like eccentricities. Values were checked in python by solving
E - e sin E = M in radians with Newton's method, the oracle.

Knob: none - the (M, e) pairs below are fixed.
============================================================================ */

// ---- model ------------------------------------------------------------------
// Residual of the solved equation, all in radians.
def kres(M, e) = rad(kepler(M, e)) - e * sin(rad(kepler(M, e))) - rad(M)

/* ---- results ----------------------------------------------------------------
Earth-like (e = 0.0167) at two mean anomalies, and two high-eccentric
orbits (e = 0.5 and 0.9, the latter close to a comet's). The solution
E runs ahead of M by e sin E, up to about 57 e degrees at M = 90. */
print("M = 1 deg, e = 0.0167: E =", kepler(1, 0.0167), "deg")
print("solved, |residual| < 1e-9 rad:", abs(kres(1, 0.0167)) < 1e-9)
print("M = 60 deg, e = 0.0167: E =", kepler(60, 0.0167), "deg")
print("solved, |residual| < 1e-9 rad:", abs(kres(60, 0.0167)) < 1e-9)
print("M = 200 deg, e = 0.5: E =", kepler(200, 0.5), "deg")
print("solved, |residual| < 1e-9 rad:", abs(kres(200, 0.5)) < 1e-9)
print("M = 10 deg, e = 0.9: E =", kepler(10, 0.9), "deg")
print("solved, |residual| < 1e-9 rad:", abs(kres(10, 0.9)) < 1e-9)

// The raw residual for the first pair, printed to show the scale: the
// solver converges to machine precision (about 1e-16 rad), so the
// boolean checks above are all true.
print("raw residual (rad):", kres(60, 0.0167))

/* ---- expected output ----
= M = 1 deg, e = 0.0167: E = 1.01698271965 deg
= solved, |residual| < 1e-9 rad: true
= M = 60 deg, e = 0.0167: E = 60.8355356973 deg
= solved, |residual| < 1e-9 rad: true
= M = 200 deg, e = 0.5: E = 193.3737029 deg
= solved, |residual| < 1e-9 rad: true
= M = 10 deg, e = 0.9: E = 48.7979832632 deg
= solved, |residual| < 1e-9 rad: true
= raw residual (rad): 0.000000000000000222044604925
*/

scripts.name: magnitude-flux-conversions
scripts.title: magnitudes and Janskys
scripts.text:
/* ============================================================================
magnitude-flux-conversions.epher -- magnitudes and Janskys

Conversions between apparent magnitude and flux density in Janskys
with the built-ins mag2jy and jy2mag (guide 1.16). The magnitude
scale is logarithmic: five magnitudes are a factor of 100 in flux, so
one magnitude is 100^(1/5) = 2.512, and the zero point is 3631 Jy
(the builtin's convention): mag2jy(m) = 3631 * 10^(-m / 2.5). A
Jansky is 1e-26 W per square metre per hertz; modern radio
telescopes work in millijanskys, optical surveys in microjanskys.
For scale: Sirius at -1.46 mag is about 13900 Jy in this convention,
and a magnitude 20 source, 0.00003631 Jy, is near the limit of a
large survey telescope. Values were checked in python, the oracle.

Knob: none - the magnitudes below are fixed.
============================================================================ */

/* ---- results ----------------------------------------------------------------
The same zero-point chain every five magnitudes: 3631 Jy at mag 0,
36.31 Jy at mag 5, 0.3631 Jy at mag 10, and so on down to 3.631e-5 Jy
at mag 20 - each step of five divides the flux by exactly 100. */
print("mag 0:", mag2jy(0), "Jy")
print("mag 5:", mag2jy(5), "Jy")
print("mag 10:", mag2jy(10), "Jy")
print("mag 15:", mag2jy(15), "Jy")
print("mag 20:", mag2jy(20), "Jy")

// Round trips: converting back must recover the magnitude. The list is
// a for loop (guide 1.30) collecting jy2mag(mag2jy(m)) for each m.
for m in {5, 10, 15, 20, 25} do jy2mag(mag2jy(m))

// The scale checks: five magnitudes are 100x in flux, and the reverse
// conversion of 1 Jy lands at mag 8.9. Sirius at -1.46 comes out at
// about 13900 Jy, 3.8x the 3631 Jy of a mag 0 star.
print("flux ratio over 5 mags:", mag2jy(15) / mag2jy(20))
print("1 Jy is mag:", jy2mag(1))
print("Sirius, -1.46 mag:", mag2jy(-1.46), "Jy")

/* ---- expected output ----
= mag 0: 3631 Jy
= mag 5: 36.31 Jy
= mag 10: 0.3631 Jy
= mag 15: 0.003631 Jy
= mag 20: 0.00003631 Jy
= {5, 10, 15, 20, 25}
= flux ratio over 5 mags: 100
= 1 Jy is mag: 8.90006562228
= Sirius, -1.46 mag: 13932.4100838 Jy
*/

scripts.name: midnight-sun
scripts.title: polar day and polar night for a latitude
scripts.text:
/* ============================================================================
midnight-sun.epher -- polar day and polar night for a latitude

Whether a date at a latitude is polar day (the Sun never sets), polar
night (it never rises) or a normal day-night cycle, plus how many days
until the next polar transition. The test is the geometry of the
meridian: on a day when the Sun's declination stays beyond 90 - |lat|
the Sun cannot dip below the horizon even at lower culmination, so

  sign(lat) * declination >  90 - |lat|  -> polar day
  sign(lat) * declination < -(90 - |lat|) -> polar night

with the declination read from the engine's solar ephemeris. The day
count comes from scanning the declination forward (two-day steps,
then a one-day refinement) until it crosses the threshold. timeanddate
counts the same spells by "no sunrise / no sunset" on the -0.833-deg
sunrise horizon, so their 2026 dates for Longyearbyen (polar day Apr
20 - Aug 22, polar night until Feb 16) lead the geometric crossings
below by up to about two days; the clean geometric test here is the
deduction from the declination alone. Latitudes inside the polar
circles (|lat| < 66.56 deg) never reach the threshold: the Sun's
declination tops out at 23.44 deg.

Accuracy: the geometry is exact and the declination is the engine's
arcsecond-class value; the transition day is found to about a day (the
Sun moves up to 0.4 deg per day, and the scan steps two days before
refining).

Knobs: the polar place (lat, lon - Longyearbyen below), the two dates
tested there, and the mid-latitude place used to show the normal case.
============================================================================ */

// ---- the knobs ---------------------------------------------------------------
const lat = 78.2            // Longyearbyen, Svalbard
const lon = 15.6
const day1 = {2026, 6, 21}  // June solstice: polar day expected
const day2 = {2026, 12, 21} // December solstice: polar night expected
const lat2 = 51.4779        // Greenwich - the normal-cycle comparison
const lon2 = 0

// ---- model ------------------------------------------------------------------
def sgnp(phi) = if phi >= 0 then 1 else -1
def rgh(j, phi) = if sgnp(phi) * decl(10, j) > 90 - abs(phi) then 1 else if sgnp(phi) * decl(10, j) < -(90 - abs(phi)) then -1 else 0
def cl(j, phi) = if rgh(j, phi) == 1 then "polar day: the Sun never sets" else if rgh(j, phi) == -1 then "polar night: the Sun never rises" else "normal day-night cycle"
def lab(r) = if r == 1 then "polar day begins" else if r == -1 then "polar night begins" else "normal cycle returns"
def nxt(j, j0, phi, r0) = if j - j0 >= 220 then -1 else if rgh(j, phi) != r0 then (if rgh(j - 1, phi) != r0 then j - 1 - j0 else j - j0) else nxt(j + 2, j0, phi, r0)

/* ---- results ------------------------------------------------------------------
Both spells tested at Longyearbyen: the June solstice sits inside the
polar day, the December one inside the polar night. The scans then
count the days to the spell's end - the declination falling back below
90 - 78.2 = 11.8 deg in late August, and climbing back above -11.8 deg
in mid-February. */
const j0 = jd(day1[1], day1[2], day1[3])
const j2 = jd(day2[1], day2[2], day2[3])
const n1 = nxt(j0 + 2, j0, lat, rgh(j0, lat))
const n2 = nxt(j2 + 2, j2, lat, rgh(j2, lat))

print("polar day/night test, lat", lat, "lon", lon, ": threshold |decl| >", 90 - abs(lat), "deg")
print("2026-06-21:", cl(j0, lat), "(declination", decl(10, j0), "deg)")
if n1 >= 0 then print("  next transition in about", n1, "days:", lab(rgh(j0 + n1, lat))) else print("  no polar transition within 220 days")
if n1 >= 0 then print("  transition around", iso(j0 + n1)) else print("  (the scan reached 220 days ahead)")
print("2026-12-21:", cl(j2, lat), "(declination", decl(10, j2), "deg)")
if n2 >= 0 then print("  next transition in about", n2, "days:", lab(rgh(j2 + n2, lat))) else print("  no polar transition within 220 days")
if n2 >= 0 then print("  transition around", iso(j2 + n2)) else print("  (the scan reached 220 days ahead)")

// The mid-latitude comparison: Greenwich never crosses the threshold,
// and the scan says so instead of inventing a transition.
print("2026-06-21 at lat 51.4779 lon 0:", cl(jd(day1[1], day1[2], day1[3]), lat2))
print("  |lat| below the polar circle (66.56 deg): polar day and night never occur")

/* Self-check against a published case: timeanddate lists Longyearbyen
2026-06-21 as polar day, with the polar day ending Aug 22 and the
polar night lifting around Feb 16 (their -0.833-deg sunrise horizon
leads the geometric crossing by up to two days, as the header says). */
print("known case check (timeanddate): 2026-06-21 polar day at Longyearbyen:", rgh(j0, lat) == 1)
/* ---- expected output ----
= polar day/night test, lat 78.2 lon 15.6 : threshold |decl| > 11.8 deg
= 2026-06-21: polar day: the Sun never sets (declination 23.437516214 deg)
=   next transition in about 63 days: normal cycle returns
=   transition around 2026-08-23T00:00:00
= 2026-12-21: polar night: the Sun never rises (declination -23.43452839 deg)
=   next transition in about 59 days: normal cycle returns
=   transition around 2027-02-18T00:00:00
= 2026-06-21 at lat 51.4779 lon 0: normal day-night cycle
=   |lat| below the polar circle (66.56 deg): polar day and night never occur
= known case check (timeanddate): 2026-06-21 polar day at Longyearbyen: true
*/

scripts.name: prayer-times
scripts.title: the five daily prayer windows from the Sun
scripts.text:
/* ============================================================================
prayer-times.epher -- the five daily prayer windows from the Sun

The daylight prayer times for a place and date, from the Sun's hour
angle: Fajr and Isha at a fixed solar depression (the Muslim World
League convention, 18 degrees below the horizon - the astronomical
twilight depth), Maghrib at sunset, and Asr when a vertical object's
shadow reaches its own length plus the noon shadow (shadow factor 1,
the majority/Shafi'i rule; the Hanafi school uses factor 2). The Asr
altitude follows from cot(alt) = tan|lat - dec| + factor, and every
event time comes from the standard hour-angle formula

  cos(H) = (sin(h0) - sin(lat) sin(dec)) / (cos(lat) cos(dec)),
  time = transit -/+ 4 minutes per degree of hour angle,

with the Sun's declination at the day's transit read from the built-in
accessor - the same machinery as twilight-times.epher, good to about a
minute. The conventions vary by region and school (Fajr/Isha angles of
17 to 19.5 degrees, shadow factors 1 or 2), so every angle is a knob;
this script states its convention rather than claiming a religious
authority.

Knobs: the place (Mecca below), the date, the Fajr/Isha depression
angle and the Asr shadow factor.
============================================================================ */

// ---- the knobs ---------------------------------------------------------------
const lat = 21.42           // Mecca
const lon = 39.83
const day = {2026, 6, 21}   // near the June solstice
const fajr_ang = 18         // Fajr and Isha: Sun this far below the horizon, deg
const asr_f = 1             // Asr shadow factor (1 majority rule, 2 Hanafi)

// ---- model ------------------------------------------------------------------
def cx(h0, dec, phi) = (sin(rad(h0)) - sin(rad(phi)) * sin(rad(dec))) / (cos(rad(phi)) * cos(rad(dec)))
def evm(h0, dec, tt, phi) = if abs(cx(h0, dec, phi)) > 1 then "does not occur (sky never that dark)" else iso(tt - 4 * deg(acos(cx(h0, dec, phi))) / 1440)
def eve(h0, dec, tt, phi) = if abs(cx(h0, dec, phi)) > 1 then "does not occur (sky never that dark)" else iso(tt + 4 * deg(acos(cx(h0, dec, phi))) / 1440)
def asr_alt(dec, phi) = deg(atan(1 / (asr_f + tan(rad(abs(phi - dec))))))   // Sun's altitude at Asr
def evasr(dec, tt, phi) = if abs(cx(asr_alt(dec, phi), dec, phi)) > 1 then "does not occur (sun too low all day)" else iso(tt + 4 * deg(acos(cx(asr_alt(dec, phi), dec, phi))) / 1440)

// ---- the day's transit and declination ----------------------------------------
const t0 = transit(10, jd(day[1], day[2], day[3]), lat, lon)
const d0 = decl(10, t0)

/* ---- results ------------------------------------------------------------------
The five times in chronological order (the Dhuhr window opens at the
solar transit itself). Times are UT; Mecca local time is UT + 3 h.
Plausibility: Fajr leads sunrise by about 1.4 h at this latitude in
June - the expected 1-1.5 h for an 18-degree depression - and Asr
falls late in the afternoon as the shadow stretches to factor 1. */
print("prayer times 2026-06-21 at Mecca, lat 21.42 lon 39.83 (times UT)")
print("  convention: Fajr/Isha at", fajr_ang, "deg depression (MWL)")
print("  Maghrib at sunset; Asr at shadow factor", asr_f, "(Hanafi schools use 2)")
print("Fajr:", evm(-fajr_ang, d0, t0, lat))
print("Sunrise:", evm(-0.833, d0, t0, lat))
print("Dhuhr (solar transit):", iso(t0))
print("Asr:", evasr(d0, t0, lat), "(Sun at", asr_alt(d0, lat), "deg)")
print("Maghrib:", eve(-0.833, d0, t0, lat))
print("Isha:", eve(-fajr_ang, d0, t0, lat))
print("  local time is UT + 3 h at Mecca; angles are knobs above, and")
print("  conventions (17-19.5 deg, Hanafi factor 2) shift the times")

/* Plausibility check: the Fajr-to-sunrise gap is the signature of the
18-degree convention - about 1-1.5 h at mid-latitudes. The gap below
is computed between the two hour-angle events above. */
const tsr = t0 - 4 * deg(acos(cx(-0.833, d0, lat))) / 1440
const tfajr = t0 - 4 * deg(acos(cx(-fajr_ang, d0, lat))) / 1440
print("plausibility: Fajr leads sunrise by", (tsr - tfajr) * 24 in hr)
print("  (about 1-1.5 h is the mid-latitude span for an 18 deg depression)")
/* ---- expected output ----
= prayer times 2026-06-21 at Mecca, lat 21.42 lon 39.83 (times UT)
=   convention: Fajr/Isha at 18 deg depression (MWL)
=   Maghrib at sunset; Asr at shadow factor 1 (Hanafi schools use 2)
= Fajr: 2026-06-21T01:13:41
= Sunrise: 2026-06-21T02:39:04
= Dhuhr (solar transit): 2026-06-21T09:22:12
= Asr: 2026-06-21T12:42:02 (Sun at 44.0081941458 deg)
= Maghrib: 2026-06-21T16:05:20
= Isha: 2026-06-21T17:30:44
=   local time is UT + 3 h at Mecca; angles are knobs above, and
=   conventions (17-19.5 deg, Hanafi factor 2) shift the times
= plausibility: Fajr leads sunrise by 1.42323792726 hr
=   (about 1-1.5 h is the mid-latitude span for an 18 deg depression)
*/

scripts.name: refraction-correction
scripts.title: how refraction lifts the stars
scripts.text:
/* ============================================================================
refraction-correction.epher -- how refraction lifts the stars

The refraction correction that raises every celestial body as seen
through the air: a table of correction and true altitude for apparent
altitudes 0 to 60 degrees, from Bennett's formula (1982), as quoted in
Jean Meeus, "Astronomical Algorithms", 2nd ed., ch. 16:

  R = 1 / tan(h + 7.31 / (h + 4.4))  arcminutes, h the apparent
  altitude in degrees.

The formula is calibrated for the standard atmosphere (about 10 C,
1010 hPa); under those conditions it is good to about 0.1 arcminute
above 15 degrees, and below 15 degrees real refraction depends on the
temperature gradient of the day and the formula is only approximate.
At the horizon it gives 34.5 arcminutes - the textbook half-degree
lift that makes the Sun set minutes late (the -0.833 degree horizon of
the rise/set scripts is 34 arcmin of refraction plus the Sun's radius).
Bennett's formula takes the apparent altitude; for the reverse
direction the companion Saeundsson variant (1986), R = 1.02 / tan(h +
10.3 / (h + 5.11)) arcminutes with h the true altitude, is used below
for a round-trip check. See Duffett-Smith, "Practical Astronomy",
chapter on refraction, for the same pair. No engine calls: the
formulas are the point.

Knob: the altitude at which the single correction below is printed.
============================================================================ */

// ---- the knob ---------------------------------------------------------------
const h_knob = 15           // degrees apparent; the correction at this altitude

// ---- the two formulas -------------------------------------------------------
def r(h) = 1 / tan(rad(h + 7.31 / (h + 4.4)))       // Bennett: h apparent, result arcmin
def rs(h) = 1.02 / tan(rad(h + 10.3 / (h + 5.11)))  // Saeundsson: h true, result arcmin

/* ---- results ----------------------------------------------------------------
One row per apparent altitude: the correction in arcminutes and the
true altitude that follows (true = apparent - R/60). Notice the sweep:
a body seen on the horizon is really 0.57 degrees below it, while at
60 degrees the correction is barely half an arcminute. */
print("Bennett refraction, standard atmosphere (about 10 C, 1010 hPa)")
print("at apparent 0 deg -> R", r(0), "arcmin, true", -r(0) / 60, "deg")
print("at apparent 5 deg -> R", r(5), "arcmin, true", 5 - r(5) / 60, "deg")
print("at apparent 10 deg -> R", r(10), "arcmin, true", 10 - r(10) / 60, "deg")
print("at apparent 20 deg -> R", r(20), "arcmin, true", 20 - r(20) / 60, "deg")
print("at apparent 30 deg -> R", r(30), "arcmin, true", 30 - r(30) / 60, "deg")
print("at apparent 60 deg -> R", r(60), "arcmin, true", 60 - r(60) / 60, "deg")

// The single correction at the knob altitude.
print("correction at", h_knob, "deg apparent:", r(h_knob), "arcmin")

/* Round-trip self-check of the two directions: Saeundsson's variant
turns a true altitude of 0.5 deg into an apparent one, and Bennett's
formula read back at that apparent altitude must return the same
correction. The pair agree to a few hundredths of an arcminute. */
print("Saeundsson round trip at true 0.5 deg:", rs(0.5), "arcmin")
print("Bennett read back at the apparent altitude:", r(0.5 + rs(0.5) / 60), "arcmin")

/* ---- expected output ----
= Bennett refraction, standard atmosphere (about 10 C, 1010 hPa)
= at apparent 0 deg -> R 34.4775337433 arcmin, true -0.574625562388 deg
= at apparent 5 deg -> R 9.88314423418 arcmin, true 4.83528092943 deg
= at apparent 10 deg -> R 5.39150546757 arcmin, true 9.91014157554 deg
= at apparent 20 deg -> R 2.70341069988 arcmin, true 19.954943155 deg
= at apparent 30 deg -> R 1.71731013355 arcmin, true 29.9713781644 deg
= at apparent 60 deg -> R 0.574711801858 arcmin, true 59.99042147 deg
= correction at 15 deg apparent: 3.63622639517 arcmin
= Saeundsson round trip at true 0.5 deg: 25.0039088882 arcmin
= Bennett read back at the apparent altitude: 24.9887891294 arcmin
*/

scripts.name: season-boundaries
scripts.title: the equinoxes and solstices of a year
scripts.text:
