/* ============================================================================
season-boundaries.epher -- the equinoxes and solstices of a year

The four season boundaries of 2026 - March equinox, June solstice,
September equinox, December solstice - from the built-ins
march_equinox, june_solstice, september_equinox and december_solstice,
which return the instant as a Julian Date (the solar-ephemeris
crate, JPL-validated; guide 1.16). Each boundary is printed as days
into the year, ((event - jd(year, 1, 1)) days), which reads cleanly
where the raw JD may print as an exact fraction. The Sun's declination
at each instant is printed as a structural check: about 0 at the
equinoxes, about +23.44 deg at the June solstice and -23.44 deg at
the December solstice. The boundaries fall on March 20, June 21,
September 23 and December 21 in 2026, and the year's four seasons
are not equal in length: the Sun runs fastest near perihelion in
early January, so northern winter is the shortest season.

Knob: the year.
============================================================================ */

// ---- the knob ---------------------------------------------------------------
const year = 2026

/* ---- results ----------------------------------------------------------------
Days into the year of each boundary. Read as calendar dates: March 20
at about 14:46 UT, June 21 at 08:25, September 23 at 00:05, December
21 at 20:50. The autumn equinox lands on the 23rd because the leap
day of 2024 pushed the equinoxes later in the calendar (in 2025 the
autumn equinox fell on September 22). The four gaps are the
seasons' lengths: spring 92.7 days, summer 93.7, autumn 89.9,
winter 89.0 (to the next March equinox) - the winter half of the
year is about a week shorter than the summer half because the Earth
is nearest the Sun in January. */
print("spring equinox:", march_equinox(year) - jd(year, 1, 1), "days into", year)
print("summer solstice:", june_solstice(year) - jd(year, 1, 1), "days into", year)
print("autumn equinox:", september_equinox(year) - jd(year, 1, 1), "days into", year)
print("winter solstice:", december_solstice(year) - jd(year, 1, 1), "days into", year)

/* The raw JDs of two boundaries: an event JD is a moment in time like
any other JD. The June solstice displays as a plain decimal; the
March equinox's decimal would repeat, so it shows as the exact
fraction 1129654133/459 - same moment, different display. */
print("raw JD of the March equinox:", march_equinox(year))
print("raw JD of the June solstice:", june_solstice(year))

/* The same four instants in the readable form: iso() (guide 1.18)
reads a Julian Date as the ISO 8601 calendar date and UT clock, and
time() picks out the {hour, minute, second} of it. These are the
clock readings the prose above spelled out by hand. */
print("spring equinox at:", iso(march_equinox(year)), "UT")
print("summer solstice at:", iso(june_solstice(year)), "UT")
print("autumn equinox at:", iso(september_equinox(year)), "UT")
print("winter solstice at:", iso(december_solstice(year)), "UT")
print("the June instant's clock:", time(june_solstice(year)))

/* The structural check: the Sun's declination at each boundary. The
equinox is defined by declination 0, and the solstices by the
extremes of about +23.44 and -23.44 deg (the axial tilt); all four
readings land where they must, to well under 0.001 deg. */
print("sun decl at spring equinox:", decl(10, march_equinox(year)), "deg")
print("sun decl at summer solstice:", decl(10, june_solstice(year)), "deg")
print("sun decl at autumn equinox:", decl(10, september_equinox(year)), "deg")
print("sun decl at winter solstice:", decl(10, december_solstice(year)), "deg")

/* The tropical year, measured solstice to solstice: about 365.24 days
(the classical tropical year, equinox to equinox, is 365.2422 days;
the solstice-to-solstice span wobbles by minutes). The Gregorian
calendar averages 365.2425 days a year, so the boundaries drift
slowly - hours per century - and the leap-year rhythm makes the
day-of-year readings jump by a few hours each year. */
print("June solstice to June solstice:", june_solstice(year + 1) - june_solstice(year), "days")

/* ---- expected output ----
= spring equinox: 78.6154679945 days into 2026
= summer solstice: 171.350897795 days into 2026
= autumn equinox: 265.00382519 days into 2026
= winter solstice: 354.868221609 days into 2026
= raw JD of the March equinox: 1129654133/459
= raw JD of the June solstice: 2461212.8509
= spring equinox at: 2026-03-20T14:46:16 UT
= summer solstice at: 2026-06-21T08:25:18 UT
= autumn equinox at: 2026-09-23T00:05:30 UT
= winter solstice at: 2026-12-21T20:50:14 UT
= the June instant's clock: {8, 25, 18}
= sun decl at spring equinox: 0.000098383 deg
= sun decl at summer solstice: 23.437930402 deg
= sun decl at autumn equinox: -0.000039286 deg
= sun decl at winter solstice: -23.43747375 deg
= June solstice to June solstice: 365.240008163 days
*/

scripts.name: shadow-length
scripts.title: the gnomon's shadow, length and bearing
scripts.text:
/* ============================================================================
shadow-length.epher -- the gnomon's shadow, length and bearing

Where a vertical gnomon's shadow falls at a given place and time: the
Sun's altitude and azimuth from the built-in accessors (topocentric,
geometric - no refraction; guide 1.16) give the shadow of a gnomon of
height h as
  length = h / tan(altitude),   bearing = solar azimuth + 180 degrees
because the shadow points exactly away from the Sun. Azimuth runs from
north through east, 0-360 degrees, so at Greenwich the 15:00-UT June
Sun sits in the south-west (azimuth about 248 deg) and the shadow
falls toward the north-east (about 68 deg). At solar noon the shadow
is shortest and points north (bearing near 0 deg), the moment a
sundial or a compass-and-string can find.

Sources: the geometry is elementary (any surveying or sundial text;
Duffett-Smith, "Practical Astronomy", the Sun's altitude and azimuth
chapter); the Sun's position itself comes from the engine's
solar-ephemeris accessors.

Accuracy: the shadow geometry is exact; the reading inherits the
engine's arcsecond-class solar position, and no refraction is applied,
so the printed length fits the geometric Sun. The usual caveat: a real
shadow's edge is softened by the solar disc (about half a degree).

Knobs: gnomon height (m), the place, the sample date and hour (UT), and
the night date used to show the Sun-down guard.
============================================================================ */

// ---- the knobs ---------------------------------------------------------------
const hgt = 1               // gnomon height, m
const lat = 51.4779         // Greenwich
const lon = 0
const day = {2026, 6, 21}   // sample date
const hr = 15               // sample hour, UT
const day2 = {2026, 12, 21} // night date for the Sun-down guard
const hr2 = 0               // 00:00 UT: the Sun is far below

// ---- model ------------------------------------------------------------------
def wb(a) = a + 180 - 360 * floor((a + 180) / 360)   // shadow bearing, 0-360 deg from north
def shadow_len(a) = hgt / tan(rad(a))                        // shadow length for solar altitude a

// ---- the sample instant -----------------------------------------------------
const a1 = alt(10, jd(day[1], day[2], day[3], hr), lat, lon)
const z1 = az(10, jd(day[1], day[2], day[3], hr), lat, lon)

/* ---- results ------------------------------------------------------------------
The 15:00-UT sample: the Sun is past the meridian, in the south-west,
so the shadow lies north-east. The length is close to the gnomon's own
height - the Sun at 45.9 deg makes tan(45.9) near 1 - and a one-metre
stick throws a shadow of about 0.97 m. */
print("gnomon height", hgt, "m at lat", lat, "lon", lon)
print("2026-06-21 15:00 UT: Sun alt", a1, "deg, az", z1, "deg")
print("  shadow length:", shadow_len(a1), "m; shadow bearing:", wb(z1), "deg from north")

// ---- the noon cross-check ----------------------------------------------------
const t0 = transit(10, jd(day[1], day[2], day[3]), lat, lon)
const a0 = alt(10, t0, lat, lon)
const z0 = az(10, t0, lat, lon)
const d0 = decl(10, t0)
print("at solar noon", iso(t0), ": Sun alt", a0, "deg, az", z0, "deg")
print("  shortest shadow:", shadow_len(a0), "m; bearing", wb(z0), "deg (north)")

/* Self-check: at the transit instant the measured altitude and the
meridian formula 90 - |lat - decl| meet (they differ by the Sun's
parallax, arcseconds, as in sun-altitude-at-noon.epher), and the
azimuth reads due south, 180 deg. */
print("alt at transit vs 90 - |lat - decl|:", a0, "vs", 90 - abs(lat - d0), "deg")
print("azimuth at transit: due south reads 180 deg - measured", z0, "deg")

// ---- the Sun-down guard ------------------------------------------------------
const a2 = alt(10, jd(day2[1], day2[2], day2[3], hr2), lat, lon)
const z2 = az(10, jd(day2[1], day2[2], day2[3], hr2), lat, lon)
if a2 <= 0 then print("2026-12-21 00:00 UT: the Sun is down (alt", a2, "deg): no shadow") else print("2026-12-21 00:00 UT: shadow length", shadow_len(a2), "m, bearing", wb(z2), "deg")

/* ---- expected output ----
= gnomon height 1 m at lat 51.4779 lon 0
= 2026-06-21 15:00 UT: Sun alt 45.9278503 deg, az 247.7014893 deg
=   shadow length: 0.968125308321 m; shadow bearing: 67.7014893 deg from north
= at solar noon 2026-06-21T12:01:49 : Sun alt 61.9588272 deg, az 179.9987742 deg
=   shortest shadow: 0.532631544272 m; bearing 359.9987742 deg (north)
= alt at transit vs 90 - |lat - decl|: 61.9588272 vs 61.959948058 deg
= azimuth at transit: due south reads 180 deg - measured 179.9987742 deg
= 2026-12-21 00:00 UT: the Sun is down (alt -61.9546138 deg): no shadow
*/

scripts.name: solar-irradiance
scripts.title: clear-sky direct sun on a tilted panel
scripts.text:
/* ============================================================================
solar-irradiance.epher -- clear-sky direct sun on a tilted panel

The direct-beam solar irradiance on a tilted plane at a knob place,
date and hour, under a clear sky. The beam is attenuated by the air it
crosses, and the airmass comes from the built-in airmass(altitude)
(the secant model - fine above about 20 deg, which is when a panel
collects anyway):

  I = 1.353 kW/m2 * 0.7^(airmass^0.678)

with 1.353 kW/m2 the solar constant (Thekaekara's value, the basis of
the standard spectra) and 0.7^(X^0.678) the classic clear-sky beam
transmission parameterization quoted after F. Kasten in the
solar-engineering texts (Kreith, "Principles of Solar Engineering";
Meinel & Meinel, "Applied Solar Energy", use the same form). That is
the beam on a surface facing the Sun; the panel gets the beam times
the cosine of the angle between the panel normal and the Sun:

  cos i = cos(tilt) sin(alt) + sin(tilt) cos(alt) cos(az - panel az),

the standard tilted-surface geometry. Honest grade: the model is a
clear-sky direct-beam estimate, good to about 10 percent near noon -
it omits the diffuse sky component (10-20 percent of the total on
clear days), aerosols and clouds. The direct beam on the horizontal is
printed too, and the sanity check at the end asks whether a summer
noon lands in the familiar 0.8-1.0 kW/m2 band.

The day's optimal fixed tilt follows the installer rule of thumb
(SEI-style handbook): latitude minus 15 degrees in the summer half,
latitude plus 15 in the winter half, about latitude at the equinoxes.
The panel below is set near the summer optimum, facing due south.

Knobs: the place, date and hour (UT), the panel tilt (deg from
horizontal) and azimuth (deg from north) - 180 is due south in the
northern hemisphere.
============================================================================ */

// ---- the knobs ---------------------------------------------------------------
const lat = 51.4779         // Greenwich
const lon = 0
const day = {2026, 6, 21}   // June solstice: summer sun
const hr = 12               // sample hour, UT (solar noon is 12:01:49)
const tilt = 35             // panel tilt from the horizontal, deg
const azp = 180             // panel azimuth: due south

// ---- model ------------------------------------------------------------------
def dni(x) = 1.353 * 0.7 ^ (x ^ 0.678)   // clear-sky direct normal beam, kW/m2
def cosi(a, z) = cos(rad(tilt)) * sin(rad(a)) + sin(rad(tilt)) * cos(rad(a)) * cos(rad(z - azp))
def tiltopt(m, phi) = if m >= 4 and m <= 9 then phi - 15 else if m == 3 or m == 9 then phi else phi + 15

/* ---- results ------------------------------------------------------------------
The readings at the knob hour: the Sun at 62 deg (airmass 1.13) sends
a direct beam of about 0.92 kW/m2, of which the horizontal surface
catches sin(alt) = 0.81 kW/m2 and the 35-deg south-facing panel, whose
normal lies within a degree of the Sun, catches nearly the whole beam.
The guard lines cover a knob hour after sunset. */
const a = alt(10, jd(day[1], day[2], day[3], hr), lat, lon)
const z = az(10, jd(day[1], day[2], day[3], hr), lat, lon)
print("clear-sky direct beam,", iso(jd(day[1], day[2], day[3], hr)), "at lat", lat, "lon", lon)
print("Sun: alt", a, "deg, az", z, "deg; airmass", airmass(a))
if a > 0 then print("direct normal beam:", dni(airmass(a)), "kW/m2") else print("the Sun is below the horizon: no direct beam")
if a > 0 then print("on the horizontal:", dni(airmass(a)) * sin(rad(a)), "kW/m2") else print("(horizontal reading skipped)")
if a > 0 and cosi(a, z) > 0 then print("panel tilted", tilt, "deg toward az", azp, ": cos(incidence)", cosi(a, z)) else print("the panel faces away from the Sun: no direct beam on it")
if a > 0 and cosi(a, z) > 0 then print("beam on the panel:", dni(airmass(a)) * cosi(a, z), "kW/m2") else print("(panel reading skipped)")

/* The sanity check and the seasonal rule. The noon horizontal reading
should sit in the familiar 0.8-1.0 kW/m2 summer band, and the optimal
tilt for the knob month (June: the summer branch of the rule of thumb)
should sit near the panel's 35 deg. */
print("sanity: noon horizontal direct beam in the 0.8-1.0 kW/m2 band:", 0.8 <= dni(airmass(a)) * sin(rad(a)) and dni(airmass(a)) * sin(rad(a)) <= 1)
print("optimal fixed tilt this month (latitude +-15 deg rule):", tiltopt(day[2], lat), "deg")

/* Self-check at the true transit: the meridian formula 90 - |lat -
dec| predicts the Sun's noon altitude, and the engine agrees within
its parallax arcseconds (see sun-altitude-at-noon.epher). */
const t0 = transit(10, jd(day[1], day[2], day[3]), lat, lon)
print("alt at solar transit", iso(t0), ":", alt(10, t0, lat, lon), "deg")
print("  meridian formula 90 - |lat - dec|:", 90 - abs(lat - decl(10, t0)), "deg")
/* ---- expected output ----
= clear-sky direct beam, 2026-06-21T12:00:00 at lat 51.4779 lon 0
= Sun: alt 61.9566445 deg, az 179.114422 deg; airmass 1.13302623966
= direct normal beam: 0.91771509252 kW/m2
= on the horizontal: 0.809968084056 kW/m2
= panel tilted 35 deg toward az 180 : cos(incidence) 0.992605875759
= beam on the panel: 0.910929393108 kW/m2
= sanity: noon horizontal direct beam in the 0.8-1.0 kW/m2 band: true
= optimal fixed tilt this month (latitude +-15 deg rule): 36.4779 deg
= alt at solar transit 2026-06-21T12:01:49 : 61.9588272 deg
=   meridian formula 90 - |lat - dec|: 61.959948058 deg
*/

scripts.name: solar-noon-time
scripts.title: when the Sun crosses the meridian
scripts.text:
/* ============================================================================
solar-noon-time.epher -- when the Sun crosses the meridian

Solar noon (the Sun's meridian transit) at Greenwich (the Royal
Observatory) on three dates of 2026, from the built-in transit
accessor for the Sun, body 10 (the solar-ephemeris crate, JPL-
validated; guide 1.16), converted to clock hours and to a clock
display (deg2hms of the hour times 15). Two things set solar noon's
clock time. First the longitude: the mean Sun crosses the meridian
at 12 - lon/15 in UT, hours west of Greenwich later, east earlier --
set `lon` below to your own site and every line follows. Greenwich
sits 0 deg from the prime meridian, so there the mean Sun crosses at
12 - 0/15 = 12 UT: UT is mean solar time on the prime meridian.
Second the equation of time: the real Sun runs ahead of or behind
the mean Sun by up to about 16 min over the year (the orbit is
elliptical and the ecliptic is tilted), so the actual noon wanders
around the mean transit.

Knobs: latitude and longitude (Greenwich below); the three dates below.
============================================================================ */

// ---- the knobs ---------------------------------------------------------------
const lat = 51.4779        // Greenwich, the Royal Observatory
const lon = 0
const d_mar = {2026, 3, 20}    // March equinox
const d_jun = {2026, 6, 21}    // June solstice
const d_dec = {2026, 12, 21}   // December solstice

// ---- helpers ----------------------------------------------------------------
// Clock hour of solar noon, and its clock-time display.
def nh(ds, lat, lon) = (transit(10, jd(ds[1], ds[2], ds[3]), lat, lon) - jd(ds[1], ds[2], ds[3])) * 24 in hr
def nd(ds, lat, lon) = (transit(10, jd(ds[1], ds[2], ds[3]), lat, lon) - jd(ds[1], ds[2], ds[3])) * 24 * 15

/* ---- results ----------------------------------------------------------------
The three noons, hours UT, compared with the mean 12 UT: the March
equinox noon runs 7.8 min late (equation of time about -8 min), the
June solstice noon 1.8 min late, the December solstice noon 1.9 min
early - in mid-February or early November the swing reaches about
14-16 min. The clock column shows the same hours as a civil reading. */
print("solar noon 2026-03-20:", nh(d_mar, lat, lon), "UT; clock", deg2hms(nd(d_mar, lat, lon)))
print("solar noon 2026-06-21:", nh(d_jun, lat, lon), "UT; clock", deg2hms(nd(d_jun, lat, lon)))
print("solar noon 2026-12-21:", nh(d_dec, lat, lon), "UT; clock", deg2hms(nd(d_dec, lat, lon)))

// The reference the noons wander around: the mean Sun's transit hour
// for the longitude (no equation of time): 12 - lon/15. At Greenwich
// the longitude term is 0/15 and the reference is 12 UT exactly; at
// another site it moves by the site's longitude. All three readings
// sit within about 8 min of it, and every one of them is within 0-24.
print("mean solar noon (12 - lon/15):", (12 - lon / 15) in hr)

/* ---- expected output ----
= solar noon 2026-03-20: 12.1291872002 hr UT; clock 12h 7m 45s
= solar noon 2026-06-21: 12.0302131176 hr UT; clock 12h 1m 49s
= solar noon 2026-12-21: 11.9676772803 hr UT; clock 11h 58m 4s
= mean solar noon (12 - lon/15): 12 hr
*/

scripts.name: spring-neap-tides
scripts.title: the Moon's and Sun's tides, and the month's dates
scripts.text:
/* ============================================================================
spring-neap-tides.epher -- the Moon's and Sun's tides, and the month's dates

Two tidal numbers for a knob month. First the ratio of the Moon's tidal
pull to the Sun's at a knob date, from the inverse-cube law of tides:
tidal force goes as the body's mass over the cube of its distance, so
  F_moon / F_sun = (m_moon / m_sun) * (dist_sun / dist_moon)^3
with the masses from the built-in constants and the distances from the
engine's dist accessor. The mean ratio is about 2.2 (Meeus-style
essays give 2.18); at the dates below the Moon's distance swings it
between about 2 and 2.6. The ratio is why the Moon rules the tides,
and why spring tides (Sun and Moon pulling along the same line, at new
and full moon) are higher than neaps (at first and last quarter, the
Sun's tide pulls at right angles and subtracts).

Second, the spring and neap dates of the lunation that follows the
knob date, found by scanning the Moon's phase angle day by day (the
phase angle is 0 deg at full moon and 180 deg at new): a local minimum
is a full moon, a local maximum a new moon - the springs - and a
crossing of 90 deg is a quarter - the neaps, distinguished by the
direction of the crossing. The instants are refined by interpolation
between the daily samples, good to about half a day; the exact times
are the business of full-moons.epher and its sister scripts.

Sources: Newton's inverse-cube tidal law (Principia, Book III), as
worked through in Jean Meeus, "Mathematical Astronomy Morsels" (the
spring/neap cycle essays).

Knobs: the start date (the lunation is followed from there) and how
many days of window the scans may use.
============================================================================ */

// ---- the knobs ---------------------------------------------------------------
const day = {2026, 6, 1}     // start date: ratio here, lunation followed from here
const window = 37            // scan days (a lunation is 29.53)

// ---- model ------------------------------------------------------------------
def p(j) = phase(11, j)      // the Moon's phase angle, deg: 0 at full, 180 at new
def fu(j, end, pp, cp) = if j > end then -1 else if pp < 90 and cp >= 90 then j else fu(j + 1, end, cp, p(j + 1))
def fd(j, end, pp, cp) = if j > end then -1 else if pp > 90 and cp <= 90 then j else fd(j + 1, end, cp, p(j + 1))
def fmax(j, end, pp, cp, np) = if j > end then -1 else if cp >= pp and cp >= np then j else fmax(j + 1, end, cp, np, p(j + 2))
def fmin(j, end, pp, cp, np) = if j > end then -1 else if cp <= pp and cp <= np then j else fmin(j + 1, end, cp, np, p(j + 2))
def xt(j) = (j - 1) + (90 - p(j - 1)) / (p(j) - p(j - 1))   // quarter instant by linear interpolation
def xa(j) = j + 0.5 * (p(j - 1) - p(j + 1)) / (p(j - 1) - 2 * p(j) + p(j + 1))  // extremum by parabola

// ---- the ratio at the knob date -------------------------------------------------
const j0 = jd(day[1], day[2], day[3])
const jend = j0 + window
const r = (m_moon / m_sun) * (dist(10, j0) / dist(11, j0)) ^ 3
print("Moon:Sun tidal-force ratio at", iso(j0), ":", r)
print("  (mean ratio about 2.2; the Sun's tide is", 1 / r, "of the Moon's)")

/* ---- the month's spring and neap dates ------------------------------------------
The lunation's four events in order: last quarter (a neap, the phase
angle crossing 90 deg upward), new moon (a spring, the maximum), first
quarter (a neap, crossing downward), full moon (a spring, the
minimum). Each line carries the event's role. */
const c1 = fu(j0 + 1, jend, p(j0), p(j0 + 1))
const m1 = fmax(c1 + 1, jend, p(c1), p(c1 + 1), p(c1 + 2))
const c2 = fd(m1 + 1, jend, p(m1), p(m1 + 1))
const m2 = fmin(c2 + 1, jend, p(c2), p(c2 + 1), p(c2 + 2))
const t1 = xt(c1)
const t2 = xa(m1)
const t3 = xt(c2)
const t4 = xa(m2)
print("lunation events from", iso(j0), "(instants to about half a day):")
print("  neap, last quarter:", iso(t1))
print("  spring, new moon:", iso(t2))
print("  neap, first quarter:", iso(t3))
print("  spring, full moon:", iso(t4))

// Plausibility check against the engine's own illuminated fraction:
// the lit fraction must be near 0 at the new moon and near 1 at the full.
print("illuminated fraction at the new moon above:", illum(11, t2))
print("illuminated fraction at the full moon above:", illum(11, t4))

/* ---- expected output ----
= Moon:Sun tidal-force ratio at 2026-06-01T00:00:00 : 1.92011165835
=   (mean ratio about 2.2; the Sun's tide is 0.520803045828 of the Moon's)
= lunation events from 2026-06-01T00:00:00 (instants to about half a day):
=   neap, last quarter: 2026-06-08T10:12:22
=   spring, new moon: 2026-06-15T02:10:19
=   neap, first quarter: 2026-06-21T21:40:41
=   spring, full moon: 2026-06-30T00:16:06
= illuminated fraction at the new moon above: 0.0017
= illuminated fraction at the full moon above: 0.9988
*/

scripts.name: sun-altitude-at-noon
scripts.title: how high the Sun gets, season by season
scripts.text:
/* ============================================================================
sun-altitude-at-noon.epher -- how high the Sun gets, season by season

The Sun's altitude at Greenwich (the Royal Observatory) around local
noon on the March equinox and the two solstices of 2026, from the
built-in accessor alt for the Sun, body 10 (the solar-ephemeris
crate, JPL-validated; guide 1.16). The script prints two readings
per date: the altitude at 12:00 UT (the noon-hour knob; on the prime
meridian the mean Sun crosses at 12:00 UT exactly, and the true noon
stays within about 8 min of it on these dates, see
solar-noon-time.epher), and the altitude at the true transit
instant, which the meridian formula 90 - |lat - decl| predicts: the
Sun's maximum altitude follows from the observer's latitude and the
Sun's declination, read here from the built-in decl accessor. The
measured and the formula agree to about 0.003 deg on each date: that
residual is the Sun's parallax, a few arcseconds, and the altitudes
are geometric (no refraction).

Knobs: latitude and longitude (Greenwich below), the noon hour, dates.
============================================================================ */

// ---- the knobs ---------------------------------------------------------------
const lat = 51.4779        // Greenwich, the Royal Observatory
const lon = 0
const hr = 12              // noon sample, hours UT
const d_mar = {2026, 3, 20}    // March equinox
const d_jun = {2026, 6, 21}    // June solstice
const d_dec = {2026, 12, 21}   // December solstice

// ---- model ------------------------------------------------------------------
// The meridian formula and the Sun's culmination data at a date.
def mer(lat, dec) = 90 - abs(lat - dec)
def culm(ds, lat, lon) = alt(10, transit(10, jd(ds[1], ds[2], ds[3]), lat, lon), lat, lon)
def cdec(ds, lat, lon) = decl(10, transit(10, jd(ds[1], ds[2], ds[3]), lat, lon))

/* ---- results ----------------------------------------------------------------
The noon sample at 12:00 UT: 38.5 deg in March, 62.0 deg in June,
15.1 deg in December. The formula 90 - |lat - decl| shows why: at the
solstices the Sun's declination is about +23.44 and -23.44 deg, so
the maximum altitude is 90 - (51.48 - 23.44) = 61.96 deg in summer
and 90 - (51.48 + 23.44) = 15.08 deg in winter. At Greenwich the
true noon falls within about 8 min of 12:00 UT on these dates, so
the 12:00-UT sample sits within a few hundredths of a degree of the
maximum. */
print("alt at 12:00 UT, 2026-03-20:", alt(10, jd(d_mar[1], d_mar[2], d_mar[3], hr), lat, lon), "deg")
print("alt at 12:00 UT, 2026-06-21:", alt(10, jd(d_jun[1], d_jun[2], d_jun[3], hr), lat, lon), "deg")
print("alt at 12:00 UT, 2026-12-21:", alt(10, jd(d_dec[1], d_dec[2], d_dec[3], hr), lat, lon), "deg")

// At the true transit instant the measured altitude and the meridian
// formula meet: culmination altitude on the left, 90 - |lat - decl| on
// the right, declination read from the builtin at the same instant.
print("culmination 2026-03-20:", culm(d_mar, lat, lon), "deg; formula:", mer(lat, cdec(d_mar, lat, lon)), "deg")
print("culmination 2026-06-21:", culm(d_jun, lat, lon), "deg; formula:", mer(lat, cdec(d_jun, lat, lon)), "deg")
print("culmination 2026-12-21:", culm(d_dec, lat, lon), "deg; formula:", mer(lat, cdec(d_dec, lat, lon)), "deg")

/* ---- expected output ----
= alt at 12:00 UT, 2026-03-20: 38.450645 deg
= alt at 12:00 UT, 2026-06-21: 61.9566445 deg
= alt at 12:00 UT, 2026-12-21: 15.0815426 deg
= culmination 2026-03-20: 38.4767143 deg; formula: 38.478669299 deg
= culmination 2026-06-21: 61.9588272 deg; formula: 61.959948058 deg
= culmination 2026-12-21: 15.0827563 deg; formula: 15.085158744 deg
*/

scripts.name: sunrise-sunset
scripts.title: when the Sun rises and sets at Greenwich
scripts.text:
/* ============================================================================
sunrise-sunset.epher -- when the Sun rises and sets at Greenwich

Sunrise and sunset at Greenwich (the Royal Observatory, on the prime
meridian) on three dates of 2026 - the March equinox (Mar 20) and the
June and December solstices (Jun 21, Dec 21) - from the built-in
accessors rise and set for the Sun, body 10 (the solar-ephemeris
crate, JPL-validated; guide 1.16). Each returns the event of the day
that starts at j0 (0h UT) as a Julian Date; the clock hour below is
(event - j0) * 24 in hours UT, which on the prime meridian is mean
time itself (London's summer clock adds one hour). The seasonal
spread is the point: Greenwich's sunrise swings from 3.71 hr UT on
the June solstice to 8.05 hr on the December solstice, more than
four hours.

Knobs: latitude and longitude (Greenwich below); the three dates below.
============================================================================ */

// ---- the knobs ---------------------------------------------------------------
const lat = 51.4779        // Greenwich, the Royal Observatory
const lon = 0
const d_mar = {2026, 3, 20}    // March equinox
const d_jun = {2026, 6, 21}    // June solstice
const d_dec = {2026, 12, 21}   // December solstice

// ---- helpers ----------------------------------------------------------------
// Clock hour of the Sun's rise or set on the day of the given date.
def rh(ds, lat, lon) = (rise(10, jd(ds[1], ds[2], ds[3]), lat, lon) - jd(ds[1], ds[2], ds[3])) * 24 in hr
def sh(ds, lat, lon) = (set(10, jd(ds[1], ds[2], ds[3]), lat, lon) - jd(ds[1], ds[2], ds[3])) * 24 in hr

/* ---- results ----------------------------------------------------------------
On the equinox the Sun rises about 6.05 UT and sets about 18.22 UT;
on the June solstice it is up from 3.71 (4:43 BST) to 20.35 UT, and
on the December solstice from 8.05 to 15.88 UT. All six hours lie in
0-24 as events of their day must. */
print("sunrise 2026-03-20:", rh(d_mar, lat, lon))
print("sunset  2026-03-20:", sh(d_mar, lat, lon))
print("sunrise 2026-06-21:", rh(d_jun, lat, lon))
print("sunset  2026-06-21:", sh(d_jun, lat, lon))
print("sunrise 2026-12-21:", rh(d_dec, lat, lon))
print("sunset  2026-12-21:", sh(d_dec, lat, lon))

/* The equinox day is close to 12 h long but not exactly: the Sun's
upper limb and atmospheric refraction make daylight a little longer
than the geometric half-day (see day-length.epher for the numbers).
The longest and shortest days of the year sit within a day of the
solstices, which fall on 2026-06-21 and 2026-12-21. */

/* ---- expected output ----
= sunrise 2026-03-20: 6.0481319949 hr
= sunset  2026-03-20: 18.2164528817 hr
= sunrise 2026-06-21: 3.71313311532 hr
= sunset  2026-06-21: 20.3472832851 hr
= sunrise 2026-12-21: 8.05090104416 hr
= sunset  2026-12-21: 15.8844362386 hr
*/

scripts.name: telescope-resolution
scripts.title: what a telescope can split apart
scripts.text:
/* ============================================================================
telescope-resolution.epher -- what a telescope can split apart

The Dawes resolution limit for four telescope apertures, from the
built-in dawes(d) with d in millimetres, which returns arcseconds
(guide 1.16). The Dawes limit, 116 / d arcseconds, is the empirical
rule for splitting an equal pair of close stars of medium brightness;
the Rayleigh criterion, 138 / d arcseconds, is the physical one for
two point images of a perfect aperture (1.22 * wavelength / diameter
at 550 nm gives 138.4, rounded to 138 in the usual rule of thumb). Dawes is the easier test, so its
spacing is about 116/138 = 0.84 of Rayleigh's. A 100 mm refractor
reaches 1.16 arcsec; the 254 mm (10 inch) telescope reaches 0.46
arcsec. Values were checked in python (116 / d and 138 / d), the
oracle for the expected output.

Knob: none - the apertures below are fixed.
============================================================================ */

// ---- model ------------------------------------------------------------------
// Rayleigh criterion for wavelength 550 nm, arcseconds (classroom
// formula; there is no builtin for it, so the script defines it).
def rayleigh(d) = 138 / d

/* ---- results ----------------------------------------------------------------
Dawes limit for a 60 mm finder scope, the classic 100 mm refractor,
a 200 mm reflector and a 254 mm (10 inch) telescope, in arcseconds.
Two of the values print as exact fractions (29/15 and 58/127): the
decimals repeat, and epher shows the exact value instead. */
print("Dawes, 60 mm:", dawes(60), "arcsec")
print("Dawes, 100 mm:", dawes(100), "arcsec")
print("Dawes, 200 mm:", dawes(200), "arcsec")
print("Dawes, 254 mm:", dawes(254), "arcsec")

// The Rayleigh criterion for the same apertures, for comparison: it is
// the spacing at which two equal stars are just separated by the
// diffraction physics, always a little wider than the Dawes limit.
print("Rayleigh, 60 mm:", rayleigh(60), "arcsec")
print("Rayleigh, 100 mm:", rayleigh(100), "arcsec")
print("Rayleigh, 200 mm:", rayleigh(200), "arcsec")
print("Rayleigh, 254 mm:", rayleigh(254), "arcsec")

// For scale: the Moon spans about 1800 arcsec, Jupiter 30-50 arcsec
// (planet-angular-diameters.epher), and Pluto's disk 0.09 arcsec - a
// pair 0.46 arcsec apart is at the edge of what the 254 mm can split.
print("Dawes / Rayleigh:", dawes(100) / rayleigh(100))

/* ---- expected output ----
= Dawes, 60 mm: 29/15 arcsec
= Dawes, 100 mm: 1.16 arcsec
= Dawes, 200 mm: 0.58 arcsec
= Dawes, 254 mm: 58/127 arcsec
= Rayleigh, 60 mm: 2.3 arcsec
= Rayleigh, 100 mm: 1.38 arcsec
= Rayleigh, 200 mm: 0.69 arcsec
= Rayleigh, 254 mm: 69/127 arcsec
= Dawes / Rayleigh: 58/69
*/

scripts.name: twilight-times
scripts.title: when the sky darkens: twilight for a place
scripts.text:
/* ============================================================================
twilight-times.epher -- when the sky darkens: twilight for a place

Computes sunrise/sunset and the three twilight bands for a place and
date: civil (Sun 6 degrees below the horizon), nautical (12 degrees)
and astronomical (18 degrees). The engine's rise/set events use the
standard -0.833-degree horizon, so the bands come from the hour-angle
formula at custom horizons: cos(H) = (sin(h0) - sin(lat) sin(dec)) /
(cos(lat) cos(dec)), with the Sun's declination at the day's transit
from the built-in accessors (decl, transit; guide 1.29) and each
event time = transit -/+ 4 minutes per degree of hour angle, as UT.

Method and source: the standard hour-angle method of the USNO
(Explanatory Supplement ch. 12 notes, aa.usno.navy.mil/faq/rs_algor)
and NOAA's solar calculator (gml.noaa.gov/grad/solcalc/calcdetails.html);
the same bands timeanddate lists per day. Duffett-Smith, "Practical
Astronomy", 4th ed., chapter "Twilight" walks the same formula.

Accuracy: about a minute. Against NOAA's independent calculator,
Greenwich 2026-06-21 civil band 02:55-21:08 UT and 2026-02-12
astronomical band 05:26-19:02 agree within a minute.

Knobs: the place and the two dates below.
============================================================================ */

// ---- the knobs ----------------------------------------------------------------
const lat = 51.4779            // Greenwich
const lon = 0
const day1 = {2026, 6, 21}     // June solstice: the short night
const day2 = {2026, 2, 12}     // a winter date with a full dark night

// ---- one transit and one declination per date (each is real work) --------------
const j1 = jd(day1[1], day1[2], day1[3])
const j2 = jd(day2[1], day2[2], day2[3])
const t1 = transit(10, j1, lat, lon)
const t2 = transit(10, j2, lat, lon)
const d1 = decl(10, t1)
const d2 = decl(10, t2)

// ---- hour-angle formula at a custom horizon h0, events as ISO date-times -------
def cx(h0, dec) = (sin(rad(h0)) - sin(rad(lat)) * sin(rad(dec))) / (cos(rad(lat)) * cos(rad(dec)))
def ev(h0, dec, tt) = if abs(cx(h0, dec)) > 1 then "never that dark" else iso(tt - 4 * deg(acos(cx(h0, dec))) / 1440)
def ev2(h0, dec, tt) = if abs(cx(h0, dec)) > 1 then "never that dark" else iso(tt + 4 * deg(acos(cx(h0, dec))) / 1440)

// ---- results: the night of the June solstice ----------------------------------
print("twilight at lat", lat, "lon", lon)
print("night of 2026-06-21:")
print("  sunrise / sunset:", ev(-0.833, d1, t1), "/", ev2(-0.833, d1, t1))
print("  civil:", ev(-6, d1, t1), "/", ev2(-6, d1, t1))
print("  nautical:", ev(-12, d1, t1), "/", ev2(-12, d1, t1))
print("  astronomical:", ev(-18, d1, t1), "/", ev2(-18, d1, t1))

// ---- results: the February night, which goes properly dark --------------------
print("night of 2026-02-12:")
print("  sunrise / sunset:", ev(-0.833, d2, t2), "/", ev2(-0.833, d2, t2))
print("  civil:", ev(-6, d2, t2), "/", ev2(-6, d2, t2))
print("  nautical:", ev(-12, d2, t2), "/", ev2(-12, d2, t2))
print("  astronomical:", ev(-18, d2, t2), "/", ev2(-18, d2, t2))

/* ---- expected output ----
= twilight at lat 51.4779 lon 0
= night of 2026-06-21:
=   sunrise / sunset: 2026-06-21T03:42:48 / 2026-06-21T20:20:49
=   civil: 2026-06-21T02:55:06 / 2026-06-21T21:08:31
=   nautical: 2026-06-21T01:40:39 / 2026-06-21T22:22:58
=   astronomical: never that dark / never that dark
= night of 2026-02-12:
=   sunrise / sunset: 2026-02-12T07:19:27 / 2026-02-12T17:09:31
=   civil: 2026-02-12T06:44:36 / 2026-02-12T17:44:22
=   nautical: 2026-02-12T06:05:23 / 2026-02-12T18:23:36
=   astronomical: 2026-02-12T05:26:46 / 2026-02-12T19:02:13
*/

scripts.name: binary-orbit
scripts.title: a visual binary's position angle and separation
scripts.text:
/* ============================================================================
binary-orbit.epher -- a visual binary's position angle and separation
from its orbital elements

Projects a circular-element double-star orbit onto the sky (Meeus
ch. 57, "Binary stars"; Duffett-Smith, "Practical Astronomy", the
chapter on binary-star orbits): the mean anomaly M = 360 (t - T) / P
drives Kepler's equation (the builtin kepler(M, e), degrees in and
out), the true anomaly follows from tan(v/2) = sqrt((1+e)/(1-e))
tan(E/2), the radius from r = (1 - e cos E) / (1 - e^2) in units of
the semimajor axis, and the sky-plane projection of Meeus eq. 57.1
gives the apparent separation rho and position angle theta from the
elements a, e, i, Omega, omega.

The worked pair is Sirius A and B with the elements of the WDS Sixth
Catalog orbit of Benest and Duvent (A&A 299, 101, 1995) as commonly
tabulated: P = 50.128 yr, periastron 1894.6, a = 7.50 arcsec,
const e = 0.5923, i = 136.53 deg, Omega = 44.57 deg, omega = 146.33 deg
(digits vary slightly between catalogues; demonstration grade).

Accuracy: the projection is exact for the given elements. The check
that needs no external data: the separation at periastron must not
exceed a(1 - e) - equality only if periastron lies in the sky plane -
and the pair must be widest near apastron around 2019-2020, as
observed (~11 arcsec).

Knobs: the orbital elements and the four epochs below.
============================================================================ */

// ---- the knobs: elements of the Sirius A-B orbit (Benest & Duvent 1995) --------
const orbp = 50.128        // period, years
const orbt = 1894.6        // epoch of periastron, year
const orbe = 0.5923        // eccentricity
const orba = 7.5           // semimajor axis, arcsec
const orbi = 136.53        // inclination, deg
const orbo = 44.57         // position angle of the node, deg
const orbw = 146.33        // longitude of periastron, deg
const y0 = 2026.5          // the epoch to compute

// ---- Meeus ch. 57: the anomaly chain -------------------------------------------
def mod360(x) = x - 360 * floor(x / 360)
def nanom(y) = mod360(360 * (y - orbt) / orbp)          // mean anomaly, deg
def eanom(y) = kepler(nanom(y), orbe)                   // eccentric anomaly, deg
def tanom(y) = 2 * deg(atan2(sqrt(1 + orbe) * sin(rad(eanom(y) / 2)), sqrt(1 - orbe) * cos(rad(eanom(y) / 2))))
def rnorm(y) = 1 - orbe * cos(rad(eanom(y)))            // r / a

// ---- the sky-plane projection: x, then rho and theta ---------------------------
def xp(y) = rnorm(y) * cos(rad(tanom(y) + orbw))
def yp(y) = rnorm(y) * sin(rad(tanom(y) + orbw)) * cos(rad(orbi))
def sep(y) = orba * sqrt(xp(y) ^ 2 + yp(y) ^ 2)         // apparent separation
def pa(y) = mod360(deg(atan2(yp(y), xp(y))) + orbo)     // position angle, deg

// ---- results ------------------------------------------------------------------
print("Sirius B at", y0, ": PA", pa(y0), "deg, separation", sep(y0), "arcsec")
print("periastron 1894.6: PA", pa(1894.6), "deg, separation", sep(1894.6), "arcsec")
print("apastron 2019.9: PA", pa(2019.9), "deg, separation", sep(2019.9), "arcsec")
print("one period on, 2076.6: PA", pa(2076.6), "deg, separation", sep(2076.6), "arcsec")

/* Self-checks: the periastron separation must be at most a(1 - e)
(equality only if periastron lies in the sky plane), and one full
period later the pair must return to the same place on the sky. */
print("periastron vs a(1-e) =", orba * (1 - orbe), "arcsec (must be >=)")
print("repeat after one period:", sep(y0 + orbp) - sep(y0), "arcsec (must be ~0)")

/* ---- expected output
= Sirius B at 2026.5 : PA 57.9342883939 deg, separation 11.0769344215 arcsec
= periastron 1894.6: PA 250.371726288 deg, separation 2.82659080413 arcsec
= apastron 2019.9: PA 70.4104993118 deg, separation 11.0371884471 arcsec
= one period on, 2076.6: PA 57.9881779747 deg, separation 11.0799751269 arcsec
= periastron vs a(1-e) = 3.05775 arcsec (must be >=)
= repeat after one period: -0.000000000000017763568394 arcsec (must be ~0)
*/

scripts.name: bv-temperature
scripts.title: a star's B-V colour index into its effective
scripts.text:
/* ============================================================================
bv-temperature.epher -- a star's B-V colour index into its effective
temperature

The B-V colour index measures how much brighter a star is in blue
than in visual light, which tracks its surface temperature. The
interpolation law used here is the closed fit of F. J. Ballesteros,
"New insights into black bodies" (EPL 97, 34008, 2012):

  T = 4600 * (1 / (0.92 (B-V) + 1.7) + 1 / (0.92 (B-V) + 0.62))

a two-term rational (Pade) approximation to the Planck curve that needs no
tables - the reason the Z-Routines community programs carry it.
The table runs from a hot white A-star to a red supergiant.

Accuracy and domain, stated honestly: the fit claims validity from
about 3700 K to 50000 K (B-V from about -0.33 to 1.5), and inside
that it is within a few per cent of measured temperatures for normal
stars (the Sun lands at 5778 K against the accepted 5772 K). It runs
hot for cool M dwarfs and it is a colour-mean: variable and dust-
reddened stars like Betelgeuse scatter about the fit.

Knobs: the B-V values below (SIMBAD, mostly Johnson et al. photometry).
============================================================================ */

// ---- the knobs ----------------------------------------------------------------
const bv_sir = 0       // Sirius A, B-V (the zero point of the scale)
const bv_proc = 0.42   // Procyon
const bv_sun = 0.65    // the Sun
const bv_arc = 1.23    // Arcturus
const bv_barnard = 1.57  // Barnard's Star, an M dwarf
const bv_bet = 1.85    // Betelgeuse, a red supergiant, B-V variable

// ---- Ballesteros 2012, EPL 97, 34008 ------------------------------------------
def bvt(bv) = 4600 * (1 / (0.92 * bv + 1.7) + 1 / (0.92 * bv + 0.62))

// ---- results: the famous-star table -------------------------------------------
print("Sirius A: B-V", bv_sir, "->", bvt(bv_sir), "K")
print("Procyon: B-V", bv_proc, "->", bvt(bv_proc), "K")
print("Sun: B-V", bv_sun, "->", bvt(bv_sun), "K")
print("Arcturus: B-V", bv_arc, "->", bvt(bv_arc), "K")
print("Barnard's Star: B-V", bv_barnard, "->", bvt(bv_barnard), "K")
print("Betelgeuse: B-V", bv_bet, "->", bvt(bv_bet), "K")

/* Cross-checks the reader can carry out: the Sun's 5778 K here sits
against the accepted 5772 K (within 0.1 per cent), Arcturus lands near
its measured 4300 K, and Sirius's ~10100 K is high against its 9940 K
- the fit's zero-point stretch at B-V = 0. wien-peak.epher turns any
of these temperatures into a peak wavelength. */

// The fit's domain, flagged in the output as the header promises:
print("domain: the fit claims 3700-50000 K; cool M dwarfs read hot")

/* ---- expected output
= Sirius A: B-V 0 -> 5336000/527 K
= Procyon: B-V 0.42 -> 6775.50181903 K
= Sun: B-V 0.65 -> 5778.42373107 K
= Arcturus: B-V 1.23 -> 4250.69359627 K
= Barnard's Star: B-V 1.57 -> 3691.16854287 K
= Betelgeuse: B-V 1.85 -> 3333.19661485 K
= domain: the fit claims 3700-50000 K; cool M dwarfs read hot
*/

scripts.name: combined-magnitude
scripts.title: the magnitude two or more stars add up to
scripts.text:
/* ============================================================================
combined-magnitude.epher -- the magnitude two or more stars add up to

Two stars close together (a visual double, or a pair seen as one) show
the combined flux of both, and fluxes add while magnitudes do not: the
combined magnitude of m1 and m2 is -2.5 log10(10^(-0.4 m1) +
10^(-0.4 m2)), and an n-component list works the same way with the
sum over all components (the Pogson law of Meeus ch. 56, "Double
stars"). The builtin dist_mod or mag2jy do not do this one, so the
script defines the two-line law itself.

Accuracy: exact arithmetic on whatever magnitudes you feed it.
Telescopic component magnitudes carry visual-estimate scatter of a
few tenths, which is why the eps Lyrae values below are labelled
approximate.

Knobs: the pair magnitudes below (Mizar and Alcor, then the four
components of the Double-Double, eps Lyrae, approximate).
============================================================================ */

// ---- the knobs ----------------------------------------------------------------
const mizar = 2.2    // Mizar, mag (SIMBAD visual)
const alcor = 4.0    // Alcor, the naked-eye companion, mag
const eps1a = 5.2    // epsilon Lyrae 1 A, mag (approximate)
const eps1b = 5.5    // epsilon Lyrae 1 B, mag (approximate)
const eps2a = 5.1    // epsilon Lyrae 2 A, mag (approximate)
const eps2b = 5.4    // epsilon Lyrae 2 B, mag (approximate)

// ---- Meeus ch. 56: fluxes add, magnitudes compress ----------------------------
def flux(m) = 10 ^ (-0.4 * m)                    // linear flux, m = 0 star as unit
def comb2(m1, m2) = -2.5 * log(flux(m1) + flux(m2))
def combn(ms) = -2.5 * log(sum(flux(ms)))        // any number of components

// ---- results ------------------------------------------------------------------
print("Mizar + Alcor:", comb2(mizar, alcor))
print("eps Lyr 1 pair:", comb2(eps1a, eps1b))
print("eps Lyr 2 pair:", comb2(eps2a, eps2b))
print("all four eps Lyr stars together:", combn({eps1a, eps1b, eps2a, eps2b}))

/* Self-check: two equal stars must gain exactly 2.5 log10(2) =
0.752575 magnitudes over either one (Meeus's own check case), so the
last lines pair the m = 4 + 4 combination against that number. */
print("two m-4 stars together:", comb2(4, 4))
print("their gain over m 4:", 4 - comb2(4, 4), "mag (2.5 log10 2)")

/* ---- expected output
= Mizar + Alcor: 2.01063448397
= eps Lyr 1 pair: 4.58709617291
= eps Lyr 2 pair: 4.48709617291
= all four eps Lyr stars together: 3.78337029791
= two m-4 stars together: 3.24742501084
= their gain over m 4: 0.75257498916 mag (2.5 log10 2)
*/

scripts.name: flux-ratio
scripts.title: magnitude difference into flux ratio, and back
scripts.text:
/* ============================================================================
flux-ratio.epher -- magnitude difference into flux ratio, and back

The Pogson magnitude law: a step of m magnitudes multiplies the light
ratio by 100^(m/5), so the flux ratio is 10^(0.4 m) and the inverse is
const m = 2.5 log10(ratio). This is the arithmetic of Meeus ch. 56, "Double
stars" / magnitudes, the same 2.512 table every field guide carries.
Both directions are given: magnitude difference -> flux ratio, and
flux ratio -> magnitude difference.

Accuracy: exact arithmetic. One honesty note: the classroom factor
2.512 is the rounded 100^(1/5); the exact value is 2.51188643151, and
the script uses the exact 10^(0.4 m) throughout, so 5 magnitudes give
a clean factor of 100 (2.512^5 would give 100.0226).

Knobs: the magnitude difference `dm` and the flux ratio `ratio`.
============================================================================ */

// ---- the knobs ----------------------------------------------------------------
const dm = 1        // magnitude difference to convert
const ratio = 100   // flux ratio to convert back

// ---- Meeus ch. 56: the Pogson law, both directions ----------------------------
def fratio(m) = 10 ^ (0.4 * m)     // flux ratio for a magnitude difference
def fdmag(r) = 2.5 * log(r)        // magnitude difference for a flux ratio

// ---- results: difference -> ratio ---------------------------------------------
print(dm, "mag dimmer means", fratio(dm), "times fainter")
print("5 mag dimmer:", fratio(5), "times (the definition of the scale)")
print("the classroom 2.512 is really 100^(1/5):", 100 ^ (1 / 5))

// A famous worked pair: the Sun (-26.74) against the full Moon
// (-12.74) is 14 magnitudes, the ratio that lights a landscape at
// night yet cannot be looked at safely by day.
print("Sun over full Moon, 14 mag:", fratio(14), "times")
print("Venus (-4.6) over Sirius (-1.46), 3.14 mag:", fratio(3.14), "times")

// ---- results: ratio -> difference ---------------------------------------------
print(ratio, "times brighter is", fdmag(ratio), "mag")
print("2 times brighter:", fdmag(2), "mag (the equal-pair correction)")

/* ---- expected output
= 1 mag dimmer means 2.51188643151 times fainter
= 5 mag dimmer: 100 times (the definition of the scale)
= the classroom 2.512 is really 100^(1/5): 2.51188643151
= Sun over full Moon, 14 mag: 398107.170553 times
= Venus (-4.6) over Sirius (-1.46), 3.14 mag: 18.0301774086 times
= 100 times brighter is 5 mag
= 2 times brighter: 0.75257498916 mag (the equal-pair correction)
*/

scripts.name: messier-tonight
scripts.title: which famous Messier objects transit in
scripts.text:
/* ============================================================================
messier-tonight.epher -- which famous Messier objects transit in
tonight's dark window

Takes eight of the sky's showpieces (the Andromeda Galaxy, the Orion
Nebula, the Hercules Cluster, the Pleiades, the Ring, the Dumbbell,
the Whirlpool and the Sombrero) by their J2000 catalogue coordinates
and magnitudes (SIMBAD values, cited catalogue: the Messier catalog
as given in H. G. Corwin's and SIMBAD's modern positions), precesses
them to the date with the rigorous method of Meeus ch. 21 (the same
recipe star-tonight.epher carries), and answers the observer's
question: which of them come to the meridian between the end of
evening astronomical twilight (Sun 18 degrees down) and the start of
morning astronomical twilight? The window comes from the hour-angle
formula at the -18-degree horizon (the method of
twilight-times.epher, USNO/NOAA); transit times from the sidereal
rate 1.002737909. Objects whose transit altitude is zero or less are
guarded as never rising - from southern sites the guard fires on the
northern objects.

Accuracy: the same as star-tonight.epher - IAU-1976 precession,
exact horizon arithmetic, about an arcsecond of omitted aberration;
twilight instants good to a couple of minutes (refraction
approximated).

Knobs: the place, the observing night, and the eight objects below.
============================================================================ */

// ---- the knobs ----------------------------------------------------------------
const lat = 51.4779           // Greenwich
const lon = 0
const night = {2026, 2, 25}   // the observing night (evening of this date)
const dep = -18               // astronomical twilight: the Sun this far down

// ---- J2000 catalogue positions and visual magnitudes (SIMBAD) ------------------
const m31_ra = hms2deg(0, 42, 44.3)     // M31 Andromeda Galaxy
const m31_dec = dms2deg(41, 16, 9)
const m31_mag = 3.4
const m42_ra = hms2deg(5, 35, 17.3)     // M42 Orion Nebula
const m42_dec = dms2deg(-5, 23, 28)
const m42_mag = 4.0
const m13_ra = hms2deg(16, 41, 41.4)    // M13 Hercules Cluster
const m13_dec = dms2deg(36, 27, 37)
const m13_mag = 5.8
const m45_ra = hms2deg(3, 47, 0)        // M45 Pleiades
const m45_dec = dms2deg(24, 7, 0)
const m45_mag = 1.6
const m57_ra = hms2deg(18, 53, 35.9)    // M57 Ring Nebula
const m57_dec = dms2deg(33, 1, 45)
const m57_mag = 8.8
const m27_ra = hms2deg(19, 59, 36.3)    // M27 Dumbbell Nebula
const m27_dec = dms2deg(22, 43, 16)
const m27_mag = 7.4
const m51_ra = hms2deg(13, 29, 52.7)    // M51 Whirlpool Galaxy
const m51_dec = dms2deg(47, 11, 43)
const m51_mag = 8.4
const m104_ra = hms2deg(12, 40, 2.4)    // M104 Sombrero Galaxy
const m104_dec = dms2deg(-11, 37, 23)
const m104_mag = 8.0

// ---- Meeus ch. 21: of-date right ascension and declination --------------------
def cent0(j) = (j - jd(2000, 1, 1, 12)) / 36525
def sig(tt, T) = ((2306.2181 + 1.39656 * T - 0.000139 * T ^ 2) * tt + (0.30188 - 0.000344 * T) * tt ^ 2 + 0.017988 * tt ^ 3) / 3600
def zeta(tt, T) = ((2306.2181 + 1.39656 * T - 0.000139 * T ^ 2) * tt + (1.09468 + 0.000066 * T) * tt ^ 2 + 0.018203 * tt ^ 3) / 3600
def phi(tt, T) = ((2004.3109 - 0.8533 * T - 0.000217 * T ^ 2) * tt - (0.42665 + 0.000217 * T) * tt ^ 2 - 0.041833 * tt ^ 3) / 3600
def mod360(x) = x - 360 * floor(x / 360)
def mod24(x) = x - 24 * floor(x / 24)
def ra_of(ra, dec, j) = mod360(deg(atan2(cos(rad(dec)) * sin(rad(ra + sig((j - jd(2000, 1, 1, 12)) / 36525, cent0(j)))), cos(rad(phi((j - jd(2000, 1, 1, 12)) / 36525, cent0(j)))) * cos(rad(dec)) * cos(rad(ra + sig((j - jd(2000, 1, 1, 12)) / 36525, cent0(j)))) - sin(rad(phi((j - jd(2000, 1, 1, 12)) / 36525, cent0(j)))) * sin(rad(dec)))) + zeta((j - jd(2000, 1, 1, 12)) / 36525, cent0(j)))
def dec_of(ra, dec, j) = deg(asin(sin(rad(phi((j - jd(2000, 1, 1, 12)) / 36525, cent0(j)))) * cos(rad(dec)) * cos(rad(ra + sig((j - jd(2000, 1, 1, 12)) / 36525, cent0(j)))) + cos(rad(phi((j - jd(2000, 1, 1, 12)) / 36525, cent0(j)))) * sin(rad(dec))))

// ---- horizon arithmetic: hour angle, altitude, meridian transit ----------------
def hangle(ra, dec, j) = lst(j, lon) * 15 - ra_of(ra, dec, j)
def alt_of(ra, dec, j) = deg(asin(sin(rad(lat)) * sin(rad(dec_of(ra, dec, j))) + cos(rad(lat)) * cos(rad(dec_of(ra, dec, j))) * cos(rad(hangle(ra, dec, j)))))
def trans(ra, dec, j) = j + mod24(ra_of(ra, dec, j) / 15 - lst(j, lon)) / 1.002737909 / 24

// ---- tonight: the observing instant and each object's transit ------------------
const j0 = jd(night[1], night[2], night[3], 12)   // noon: each next transit is tonight's
def trj(ra, dec) = trans(ra, dec, j0)
def talt(ra, dec) = alt_of(ra, dec, trj(ra, dec))

// ---- the dark window: Sun 18 deg down, evening side to morning side ------------
def cx(h0, dec) = (sin(rad(h0)) - sin(rad(lat)) * sin(rad(dec))) / (cos(rad(lat)) * cos(rad(dec)))
const sun_t1 = transit(10, jd(night[1], night[2], night[3], 8), lat, lon)
const sun_t2 = transit(10, jd(night[1], night[2], night[3], 8) + 1, lat, lon)
const wbegin = sun_t1 + deg(acos(cx(dep, decl(10, sun_t1)))) / 360
const wend = sun_t2 - deg(acos(cx(dep, decl(10, sun_t2)))) / 360
def vis(ra, dec) = if talt(ra, dec) <= 0 then "never rises here" else if trj(ra, dec) >= wbegin and trj(ra, dec) <= wend then "in the dark window" else "transits outside the window"

// ---- results ------------------------------------------------------------------
print("dark window:", iso(wbegin), "to", iso(wend))
print("M31 Andromeda Galaxy: m", m31_mag, "transit", iso(trj(m31_ra, m31_dec)), "alt", talt(m31_ra, m31_dec))
print("M31:", vis(m31_ra, m31_dec))
print("M42 Orion Nebula: m", m42_mag, "transit", iso(trj(m42_ra, m42_dec)), "alt", talt(m42_ra, m42_dec))
print("M42:", vis(m42_ra, m42_dec))
print("M13 Hercules Cluster: m", m13_mag, "transit", iso(trj(m13_ra, m13_dec)), "alt", talt(m13_ra, m13_dec))
print("M13:", vis(m13_ra, m13_dec))
print("M45 Pleiades: m", m45_mag, "transit", iso(trj(m45_ra, m45_dec)), "alt", talt(m45_ra, m45_dec))
print("M45:", vis(m45_ra, m45_dec))
print("M57 Ring Nebula: m", m57_mag, "transit", iso(trj(m57_ra, m57_dec)), "alt", talt(m57_ra, m57_dec))
print("M57:", vis(m57_ra, m57_dec))
print("M27 Dumbbell Nebula: m", m27_mag, "transit", iso(trj(m27_ra, m27_dec)), "alt", talt(m27_ra, m27_dec))
print("M27:", vis(m27_ra, m27_dec))
print("M51 Whirlpool Galaxy: m", m51_mag, "transit", iso(trj(m51_ra, m51_dec)), "alt", talt(m51_ra, m51_dec))
print("M51:", vis(m51_ra, m51_dec))
print("M104 Sombrero Galaxy: m", m104_mag, "transit", iso(trj(m104_ra, m104_dec)), "alt", talt(m104_ra, m104_dec))
print("M104:", vis(m104_ra, m104_dec))

/* Self-check: the transit altitude of M13 must equal the meridian
formula 90 - |lat - dec| (the same check body-almanac.epher runs on
Mars). The verdicts also carry the season's lesson: this winter night
belongs to the spring galaxies (M104 and M51 transit near mid-window)
while Orion's nebula is a near-miss, on the meridian minutes before
the sky is properly dark - its night comes a month earlier. */
print("M13 alt check:", talt(m13_ra, m13_dec), "vs", 90 - abs(lat - dec_of(m13_ra, m13_dec, trj(m13_ra, m13_dec))))

/* ---- expected output
= dark window: 2026-02-25T19:24:06 to 2026-02-26T05:00:31
= M31 Andromeda Galaxy: m 3.4 transit 2026-02-25T14:22:19 alt 79.9342361639
= M31: transits outside the window
= M42 Orion Nebula: m 4 transit 2026-02-25T19:13:55 alt 33.1462497237
= M42: transits outside the window
= M13 Hercules Cluster: m 5.8 transit 2026-02-26T06:18:09 alt 74.9338735803
= M13: transits outside the window
= M45 Pleiades: m 1.6 transit 2026-02-25T17:26:12 alt 62.7181729482
= M45: transits outside the window
= M57 Ring Nebula: m 8.8 transit 2026-02-26T08:29:44 alt 71.5853062477
= M57: transits outside the window
= M27 Dumbbell Nebula: m 7.4 transit 2026-02-26T09:35:43 alt 61.3160999091
= M27: transits outside the window
= M51 Whirlpool Galaxy: m 8.4 transit 2026-02-26T03:07:02 alt 85.5829773359
= M51: in the dark window
= M104 Sombrero Galaxy: m 8 transit 2026-02-26T02:17:35 alt 26.7557501363
= M104: in the dark window
= M13 alt check: 74.9338735803 vs 74.9338735803
*/

scripts.name: parallax-distance
scripts.title: a star's distance from its annual parallax
scripts.text:
/* ============================================================================
parallax-distance.epher -- a star's distance from its annual parallax

The annual parallax p is the half-angle the Earth's orbit subtends at
the star, so the distance follows from simple trigonometry: at one
parsec the parallax is one arcsecond, hence d = 1/p parsecs (d in pc,
p in arcseconds, the classroom formula Meeus ch. 56 recalls). The pc
and ly constants (guide 1.18) convert to light-years. This is the
oldest geometric rung of the cosmic distance ladder (Bessel, 61 Cygni,
1838) and the whole reason the parsec exists.

Accuracy: exact within the model; real error is the parallax error
itself, and the table's three stars carry very different ones.

The vintage of each value, stated honestly:
  Proxima Centauri  0.7687"  CTIO/RECONS trigonometric program,
                             consistent with Gaia DR2's 0.76851" - good
                             to about 0.0001", so the distance is solid.
  Sirius A          0.379"   Hipparcos (van Leeuwen 2007); Sirius is
                             too bright for Gaia, so Hipparcos still
                             stands - good to about 0.001".
  Betelgeuse        0.005"   an order-of-magnitude figure: Hipparcos
                             gave 6.55 +/- 0.83 mas, interferometric
                             and HST estimates scatter from about 4.5
                             to 6.5 mas, so the distance here is
                             uncertain by roughly half its value.

Knobs: the three parallaxes below, in arcseconds.
============================================================================ */

// ---- the knobs ----------------------------------------------------------------
const prox_par = 0.7687   // Proxima Centauri, arcsec (CTIO/RECONS, Gaia-consistent)
const sir_par = 0.379     // Sirius A, arcsec (Hipparcos, van Leeuwen 2007)
const bet_par = 0.005     // Betelgeuse, arcsec (order-of-magnitude; see header)

// ---- model: d = 1/p with the pc and ly constants -------------------------------
def dpc(p) = 1 / p                   // parsecs from parallax in arcsec
def dly(p) = dpc(p) * pc / ly        // light-years (pc, ly are metres, guide 1.18)

// ---- results ------------------------------------------------------------------
print("Proxima Centauri:", dpc(prox_par), "pc =", dly(prox_par), "ly")
print("Sirius A:", dpc(sir_par), "pc =", dly(sir_par), "ly")
print("Betelgeuse (uncertain):", dpc(bet_par), "pc =", dly(bet_par), "ly")

// The rule of thumb the law gives: a parallax of 0.1 arcsec is always
// 10 parsecs, whatever the star. Doubling the parallax halves the
// distance, which the last line shows on Proxima.
print("rule of thumb: p = 0.1 arcsec means", dpc(0.1), "pc")
print("halve Proxima's parallax, distance doubles:", dpc(prox_par / 2), "pc")

/* Self-check: Proxima must land near the 4.24 ly of the almanacs
(it is the nearest known star) and Sirius near its 8.6 ly; both do,
which is the whole table cross-checked against the literature. The
Betelgeuse line cannot be checked that way - its distance is the
disputed one - hence the uncertainty carried in the header. */

/* ---- expected output
= Proxima Centauri: 1.30089761936 pc = 4.2429605531 ly
= Sirius A: 1000/379 pc = 8.60570917458 ly
= Betelgeuse (uncertain): 200 pc = 652.312755433 ly
= rule of thumb: p = 0.1 arcsec means 10 pc
= halve Proxima's parallax, distance doubles: 2.60179523871 pc
*/

scripts.name: star-luminosity
scripts.title: a star's luminosity from its apparent
scripts.text:
/* ============================================================================
star-luminosity.epher -- a star's luminosity from its apparent
magnitude and distance

Two steps of the classic chain (Meeus ch. 56 carries the magnitude
law; the distance modulus is standard photometry): the distance
modulus m - M = 5 log10(d / 10 pc) turns apparent magnitude and
distance into absolute magnitude M, and the Pogson law against the
Sun turns M into luminosity, L/Lsun = 10^(0.4 (4.83 - M)), with
4.83 the Sun's absolute visual magnitude (the knob here) and the
builtin dist_mod(dm) = 10^(1 + dm/5) pc used as the independent
cross-check of the first step (its convention: modulus in,
parsecs out). l_sun converts the final ratio to watts.

Accuracy: exact arithmetic on the inputs; the honest caveat is the
band. These are VISUAL magnitudes, so the result is visual
luminosity. Bolometric corrections shift it: the Sun barely (+0.07
mag), but Betelgeuse radiates most of its power in the infrared (its
true bolometric output is several times the number below) and M
dwarfs similarly; hot stars lose ultraviolet flux to the V band too.

Knobs: the Sun's absolute magnitude and each star's apparent
magnitude and distance (parsecs) below. Sirius/Vega/Proxima
distances are Hipparcos; Betelgeuse's distance and magnitude are
both uncertain (see parallax-distance.epher).
============================================================================ */

// ---- the knobs ----------------------------------------------------------------
const msun_mag = 4.83     // Sun's absolute visual magnitude
const sir_m = -1.46       // Sirius A, apparent mag
const sir_d = 2.637       // Sirius A, pc (Hipparcos parallax 0.379")
const veg_m = 0.03        // Vega, apparent mag (the V=0 definition star)
const veg_d = 7.68        // Vega, pc (Hipparcos 130.2 mas)
const bet_m = 0.5         // Betelgeuse, apparent mag (varies 0.0-1.6)
const bet_d = 168         // Betelgeuse, pc (~548 ly, interferometric; uncertain)
const prox_m = 11.13      // Proxima Centauri, apparent mag
const prox_d = 1.301      // Proxima Centauri, pc (0.7687")

// ---- the two-step chain --------------------------------------------------------
def dabsm(m, d) = m - 5 * log(d / 10)          // absolute magnitude, d in pc
def lum(M) = 10 ^ (0.4 * (msun_mag - M))       // luminosity in Lsun
def lumw(M) = l_sun * lum(M)                   // the same in watts (l_sun, 1.18)

// ---- results ------------------------------------------------------------------
print("Sirius A: M", dabsm(sir_m, sir_d), "L", lum(dabsm(sir_m, sir_d)), "Lsun")
print("Vega: M", dabsm(veg_m, veg_d), "L", lum(dabsm(veg_m, veg_d)), "Lsun")
print("Betelgeuse: M", dabsm(bet_m, bet_d), "L", lum(dabsm(bet_m, bet_d)), "Lsun")
print("Proxima: M", dabsm(prox_m, prox_d), "L", lum(dabsm(prox_m, prox_d)), "Lsun")
print("Sirius in watts:", lumw(dabsm(sir_m, sir_d)), "W")

/* Independent cross-check of the distance-modulus step with the
builtin dist_mod (modulus in, parsecs out): fed Sirius's modulus it
must return the 2.637 pc we started from. The M values also match
the literature (Sirius 1.43, Vega 0.58, Proxima 15.6). */
print("dist_mod check, Sirius:", dist_mod(sir_m - dabsm(sir_m, sir_d)), "pc")

// The band honesty, in the output as in the header:
print("note: visual band; bolometric adds the IR and UV")

/* ---- expected output
= Sirius A: M 1.43444935103 L 22.814988783 Lsun
= Vega: M 0.603193899842 L 49.0594234527 Lsun
= Betelgeuse: M -5.62654640863 L 15227.1478099 Lsun
= Proxima: M 15.5586135172 L 0.000051115733019 Lsun
= Sirius in watts: 8733577706116784000000000000 W
= dist_mod check, Sirius: 2.637 pc
= note: visual band; bolometric adds the IR and UV
*/

scripts.name: wien-peak
scripts.title: the wavelength where a radiator peaks
scripts.text:
/* ============================================================================
wien-peak.epher -- the wavelength where a radiator peaks

Wien's displacement law: a blackbody of temperature T radiates most
strongly at lambda_max = w / T, with w = 2.897771955e-3 m*K the Wien
constant - built into epher as the constant `wien` (physics group,
guide 1.18), which this script uses instead of retyping the digits.
The table covers the Sun, Sirius, Betelgeuse and an M dwarf, so the
same law spans green light to the near infrared; bv-temperature.epher
is its colour-index partner and feeds it temperatures.

Accuracy: exact arithmetic for a perfect blackbody. A stellar spectrum
is only approximately black (absorption lines, molecular bands in cool
stars), so treat the peaks as model peaks: honest to a few per cent
for the Sun, rougher for the M dwarf, whose "peak" sits in the TiO
band forest.

Knobs: the temperature `temp` below, in kelvin; edit it for your own
radiator. The named stars keep their accepted temperatures.
============================================================================ */

// ---- the knobs ----------------------------------------------------------------
const temp = 5772         // your radiator, K (default: the Sun's effective T)
const sir_t = 9940        // Sirius A, K
const bet_t = 3400        // Betelgeuse, K (interferometric estimates ~3300-3660)
const prox_t = 3042       // Proxima Centauri, K (an M5.5 dwarf)

// ---- Wien's displacement law, peak in nanometres ------------------------------
def peaknm(t) = wien / t * 10 ^ 9    // wien is m*K; 1e9 nm per m

// ---- results ------------------------------------------------------------------
print("Wien's constant built in:", wien, "m K")
print("a", temp, "K radiator peaks at", peaknm(temp), "nm")
print("Sun, 5772 K:", peaknm(5772), "nm")
print("Sirius A, 9940 K:", peaknm(sir_t), "nm")
print("Betelgeuse, 3400 K:", peaknm(bet_t), "nm")
print("Proxima, 3042 K:", peaknm(prox_t), "nm")

/* Cross-checks: the Sun's peak lands at 502 nm, the green it would
look if we saw it in isolation (it looks white from space because it
fills the visible band); Betelgeuse peaks at ~850 nm, the near-
infrared value usually quoted; Sirius, hotter, peaks in the
ultraviolet at 291 nm - which is why it sparkles blue-white. */

/* ---- expected output
= Wien's constant built in: 0.002897771955 m K
= a 5772 K radiator peaks at 502.039493243 nm
= Sun, 5772 K: 502.039493243 nm
= Sirius A, 9940 K: 291.526353622 nm
= Betelgeuse, 3400 K: 852.285869118 nm
= Proxima, 3042 K: 952.58775641 nm
*/
