scripts.name: carrington-number
scripts.title: the Carrington rotation number of a date
scripts.text:
/* ============================================================================
carrington-number.epher -- the Carrington rotation number of a date

The Sun rotates on its axis in about 25.4 days, and since 1853 the
rotations have been numbered. This script computes the Carrington
rotation number of a knob date from the mean-rate convention of
Duffett-Smith and Zwart, "Practical Astronomy with your Calculator
or Spreadsheet" (4th ed., Cambridge, 2017), their section on
Carrington rotation numbers: rotation 1 began on 1853 November 9 and
the mean synodic rotation is 27.2753 days, so

  rotation number = 1 + floor((JD - 2398167.0) / 27.2753)

The epoch instant used here is JD 2398167.0, noon of 1853 Nov 9 (the
JD of that date is sometimes quoted loosely as 2398220.0, which is in
fact 1854 Jan 1; the astronomically consistent choice is the JD the
engine gives for 1853 Nov 9, and it keeps the count aligned with the
almanac numbering). The date's rotation starts at the epoch plus
(rotation - 1) times 27.2753 days; the script prints that start, the
following rotation's start, and how far into the rotation the knob
date falls.

The mean grid drifts against the corrected boundaries: Meeus,
"Astronomical Algorithms" 2nd ed. ch. 29, eqs. 29.1-29.2 gives the
corrected start JDE = 2398140.227 + 27.2752316 N plus a periodic
term of amplitude 0.15 day, and the two agree within the +/-1 day
convention caveat stated for this script - the printed corrected
boundary of the knob date's rotation is the cross-check.

Accuracy: the rotation NUMBER of a date more than a day inside a
rotation is exact; dates within about a day of a boundary can be
assigned to the neighbouring rotation by tables that use the
corrected or observed (sunspot-based) boundaries, and the historical
rotation count itself carries an uncertainty of the same size.

Knob: the date. No ephemeris accessors are used - pure calendar
arithmetic (jd and iso), as the mean convention deserves.
============================================================================ */

// ---- the knobs ----------------------------------------------------------------
const day = {2026, 6, 21}    // the date to number
const epoch = 2398167.0      // JD of 1853 Nov 9 12:00, start of rotation 1
const period = 27.2753       // mean synodic rotation, days (DS)

// ---- helpers ------------------------------------------------------------------
def num(j) = floor((j - epoch) / period) + 1          // rotation containing JD j
def rstart(n) = epoch + (n - 1) * period              // grid start of rotation n
def mcorr(n) = 281.96 + 26.882476 * n                 // Meeus ch. 29, eq. 29.2 angle
def corr(n) = 0.1454 * sin(rad(mcorr(n))) - 0.0085 * sin(rad(2 * mcorr(n))) - 0.0141 * cos(rad(2 * mcorr(n)))
def rcorr(n) = 2398140.227 + 27.2752316 * n + corr(n) // corrected start, eq. 29.1-29.2 (TD)

// ---- results ------------------------------------------------------------------
const n = num(jd(day[1], day[2], day[3]))
print("Carrington rotation number of", iso(jd(day[1], day[2], day[3])), ":", n)
print("rotation", n, "start (mean grid):", iso(rstart(n)))
print("rotation", n + 1, "start:", iso(rstart(n + 1)))
print("days into rotation", n, ":", jd(day[1], day[2], day[3]) - rstart(n))

/* Cross-check against the corrected almanac boundary (Meeus ch. 29,
eqs. 29.1-29.2), evaluated at this rotation's own number: the grid
sits within about half a day of it, and never more than about a day
away for dates between 1853 and now - the +/- 1 day convention
caveat. The corrected instant comes out in TD, converted to UT. */
print("corrected start of rotation", n, ":", iso(rcorr(n) - delta_t(rcorr(n)) / 86400), "UT")
print("difference grid - corrected:", rstart(n) - (rcorr(n) - delta_t(rcorr(n)) / 86400), "days (negative = grid early)")

/* Epoch self-check: the grid must number the days right after the
epoch as rotation 1 and the days after the first mean rotation as
rotation 2 (checked a day inside each boundary, away from the
floating-point edge at the exact boundary instant). */
print("epoch check: rotation on 1853-11-10:", num(jd(1853, 11, 10)), "and on 1853-12-07:", num(jd(1853, 12, 7)))

/* Caveat: the real rotation boundaries wobble by up to about a day
around this mean grid (the Sun's rotation is not perfectly uniform
and the grid's fixed 27.2753-day period is a mean), so a date within
about one day of a printed boundary can belong to the neighbouring
rotation in tables built on observed boundaries. */

/* ---- expected output ----
= Carrington rotation number of 2026-06-21T00:00:00 : 2312
= rotation 2312 start (mean grid): 2026-06-08T17:14:21
= rotation 2313 start: 2026-07-05T23:50:47
= days into rotation 2312 : 12.2817000002
= corrected start of rotation 2312 : 2026-06-09T02:56:43 UT
= difference grid - corrected: -0.404418156482 days (negative = grid early)
= epoch check: rotation on 1853-11-10: 1 and on 1853-12-07: 2
*/

scripts.name: solar-physical
scripts.title: the Sun's disk orientation: P, B0, L0
scripts.text:
/* ============================================================================
solar-physical.epher -- the Sun's disk orientation: P, B0, L0

The physical ephemeris of the Sun for one date: P, the position angle
of the Sun's rotation axis measured eastward from the celestial north
pole; B0, the heliographic latitude of the center of the disk; and L0,
the heliographic longitude of the disk's center (the Carrington
longitude of the central meridian). All three come from chapter 29 of
Jean Meeus, "Astronomical Algorithms" (2nd ed., Willmann-Bell, 1998),
the closed-form physical-ephemeris section: the Sun's apparent
geocentric position here comes from the engine's built-in ra/decl
accessors (the solar-ephemeris crate, arcsecond-class, JPL-validated;
guide 1.18) instead of Meeus's own solar theory, and the chapter's
transformation then applies the standard solar rotation elements: the
solar equator's inclination i = 7.25 deg to the ecliptic, its
ascending node at 73.6667 + 1.3958333 T deg (T in Julian centuries
from 1850.0, the Carrington node epoch JD 2396758.0), the Carrington
frame phase theta = (JD - 2398220.0) x 360 / 25.38 deg of the
25.38-day sidereal rotation (2398220.0 is the modern convention's
frame constant; the combination puts L0 = 0 at the start of rotation
1, 1853 Nov 9), and the mean obliquity of date for the ecliptic-to-
equatorial reduction. The three outputs are the ones solar observers
read from the almanac's daily Sun table to orient images and place
sunspot latitudes.

Accuracy: the engine position is arcsecond-class, so the residual
error is the closed-form transformation itself; against the worked
example of Meeus ch. 29 (1992 Oct 13, 0h TD: P = 26.27, B0 = 5.99,
L0 = 238.63 deg) the script below prints its own values and the
differences - a few hundredths of a degree, dominated by nutation
handling at the 0.005 deg level. Almanac tables agree within their
0.01-deg rounding.

Knob: the sample date (the instant is 0h UT of that date).
============================================================================ */

// ---- the knobs ----------------------------------------------------------------
const day = {2026, 6, 21}    // sample date; the instant is 0h TD of it
const incl = 7.25            // inclination of the solar equator to the ecliptic, deg

// ---- ch. 29 machinery, angles in degrees -------------------------------------
def mod360(x) = x - 360 * floor(x / 360)
def dyn(j0) = j0 + delta_t(j0) / 86400  // the 0h-TD instant, on the engine's UT-referenced JD scale
def cent(j) = (j - jd(2000, 1, 1, 12)) / 36525
/* The engine's accessors and the calendar JD are UT-based, while the
ch. 29 series want the dynamical instant; feeding the TD offset to
both keeps them on the same instant to well under a tenth of a
minute (the engine adds delta_t internally for its positions). j
below is the dynamical JD returned by dyn(). */
def eps0(t) = 23.4392911 - 0.0130042 * t - 0.000000164 * t ^ 2 + 0.000000504 * t ^ 3  // mean obliquity, eq. 22.2
/* The standard solar rotation elements (Meeus ch. 29): inclination
incl, the ascending node of the solar equator on the ecliptic of
date (anchor 1850.0, JD 2396758.0), and the Carrington frame
phase from the 25.38-day sidereal rotation (frame constant JD
2398220.0; L0 = 0 falls at the start of rotation 1, 1853 Nov 9). */
def node(j) = 73.6667 + 1.3958333 * (j - 2396758.0) / 36525
def theta(j) = (j - 2398220.0) * 360 / 25.38
def sunlon(j) = deg(atan2(sin(rad(ra(10, j))) * cos(rad(eps0(cent(j)))) + tan(rad(decl(10, j))) * sin(rad(eps0(cent(j)))), cos(rad(ra(10, j)))))  // the Sun's geocentric apparent longitude, from the built-in ra/decl
def b0(j) = deg(asin(sin(rad(sunlon(j) - node(j))) * sin(rad(incl))))
def eta(j) = deg(atan2(-sin(rad(sunlon(j) - node(j))) * cos(rad(incl)), -cos(rad(sunlon(j) - node(j)))))
def l0(j) = mod360(eta(j) - theta(j))
def px(j) = deg(atan(-cos(rad(sunlon(j))) * tan(rad(eps0(cent(j))))))
def py(j) = deg(atan(-cos(rad(sunlon(j) - node(j))) * tan(rad(incl))))
def p(j) = px(j) + py(j)

// ---- results ------------------------------------------------------------------
const j0 = dyn(jd(day[1], day[2], day[3]))
print("solar physical ephemeris at", iso(jd(day[1], day[2], day[3])), "0h TD")
print("P  (axis position angle):", p(j0), "deg")
print("B0 (disk-center latitude):", b0(j0), "deg")
print("L0 (disk-center longitude):", l0(j0), "deg")

/* Structure notes: B0 stays within +-7.25 deg (the inclination) and
is zero when the Sun's longitude meets the node, early June and early
December; L0 runs 0..360 and wraps at each Carrington rotation start.
The knobs' values change slowly through the day - L0 moves about
13.2 deg per day - so the printed instant matters for L0. */

/* Self-check against the worked example of Meeus ch. 29: 1992 Oct 13,
0h TD gives P = 26.27, B0 = 5.99, L0 = 238.63 deg (rounded to 0.01).
The same dyn() offset puts the example on its dynamical instant. */
const je = dyn(jd(1992, 10, 13))
print("example, 1992-10-13 0h TD: P", p(je), "B0", b0(je), "L0", l0(je))

/* ---- expected output ----
= solar physical ephemeris at 2026-06-21T00:00:00 0h TD
= P  (axis position angle): -7.19552175864 deg
= B0 (disk-center latitude): 1.69262509614 deg
= L0 (disk-center longitude): 202.782037871 deg
= example, 1992-10-13 0h TD: P 26.2739814267 B0 5.98784870686 L0 238.636752275
*/

scripts.name: solstice-noon-table
scripts.title: noon Sun altitude at the four season points
scripts.text:
/* ============================================================================
solstice-noon-table.epher -- noon Sun altitude at the four season points

The Sun's maximum (meridian) altitude on the days of the four season
boundaries - 90 - |lat - declination| - tabulated across a ladder of
latitudes, from the equator to inside the Arctic Circle. The season
instants come from the built-ins march_equinox, june_solstice,
september_equinox and december_solstice of `year` (the solar-ephemeris
crate, JPL-validated; the same accessors season-boundaries.epher
uses), and the declination at each instant from the built-in decl for
the Sun (body 10). The table extends sun-altitude-at-noon.epher,
which measured the same formula at Greenwich on three of the four
dates, across the latitudes where the daylight story changes:
23.44 deg is the Tropic of Cancer, where the June Sun passes through
the zenith; 66.56 deg is the Arctic Circle, the midnight-sun line -
above it the June Sun never sets and the December Sun never rises.

Accuracy: the meridian formula is exact for a geometric (refraction-
free) Sun; the residual against the engine's measured transit
altitude is printed below and runs about 0.003 deg (the Sun's
parallax, a few arcseconds). The columns use the declination at the
season instant: near an equinox the declination changes about 0.4
deg per day, so the actual noon altitude at a longitude far from the
event's meridian can differ from the table by up to about 0.2 deg on
equinox days; near the solstices the declination is stationary and
the table is good to 0.01 deg.

Knobs: the year and the ladder of latitudes.
============================================================================ */

// ---- the knobs ----------------------------------------------------------------
const year = 2026
const lats = {0, 23.44, 40, 51.48, 66.56, 70}    // latitude ladder, deg

// ---- the season instants (computed once) --------------------------------------
const jmar = march_equinox(year)
const jjun = june_solstice(year)
const jsep = september_equinox(year)
const jdec = december_solstice(year)

// ---- model --------------------------------------------------------------------
def mer(la, j) = 90 - abs(la - decl(10, j))      // meridian noon altitude from the declination at j
def mdtag(j) = iso(j)[6] + iso(j)[7] + iso(j)[8] + iso(j)[9] + iso(j)[10]   // the date's month-day from the ISO string

// ---- results ------------------------------------------------------------------
print("noon altitude of the Sun (deg, geometric) at the season instants of", year)
print("lat | spring", mdtag(jmar), "| summer", mdtag(jjun), "| autumn", mdtag(jsep), "| winter", mdtag(jdec))
print("lat", lats[1], ":", mer(lats[1], jmar), mer(lats[1], jjun), mer(lats[1], jsep), mer(lats[1], jdec))
print("lat", lats[2], ":", mer(lats[2], jmar), mer(lats[2], jjun), "(overhead)", mer(lats[2], jsep), mer(lats[2], jdec))
print("lat", lats[3], ":", mer(lats[3], jmar), mer(lats[3], jjun), mer(lats[3], jsep), mer(lats[3], jdec))
print("lat", lats[4], ":", mer(lats[4], jmar), mer(lats[4], jjun), mer(lats[4], jsep), mer(lats[4], jdec))
print("-- midnight-sun line: above lat 66.56 the June Sun never sets --")
print("lat", lats[5], ":", mer(lats[5], jmar), mer(lats[5], jjun), mer(lats[5], jsep), mer(lats[5], jdec), "*")
print("lat", lats[6], ":", mer(lats[6], jmar), mer(lats[6], jjun), "(midnight sun)", mer(lats[6], jsep), mer(lats[6], jdec))

/* Reading the table: the summer column is the classic "how high does
the Sun get" number - 66.56 deg at the equator's summer, 61.96 at
Greenwich's, 46.88 at the Arctic Circle's. The winter column goes
negative above 66.56: the Sun never rises there in December. The
Tropic row (23.44) shows the June Sun at the zenith (89.998 deg),
and the row below the midnight-sun line shows the winter Sun still
climbing to 15 deg at noon. The star marks the rows at or inside
the midnight-sun line: from the Arctic Circle (66.56) northward
the June Sun never sets - at 66.56 itself it only grazes the
horizon at midnight, and the winter Sun's noon altitude there is
about 0 deg, both visible in the row. */
print("declinations:", decl(10, jmar), decl(10, jjun), decl(10, jsep), decl(10, jdec), "deg")
print("midnight-sun line this year: 90 -", decl(10, jjun), "=", 90 - decl(10, jjun), "deg")

/* Self-check: the meridian formula against the engine's measured
altitude at the true transit, Greenwich, on the June solstice day
(the day's transit declination, not the instant's, is the right
comparison here - see the equinox-day caveat above). */
const j = transit(10, jd(year, 6, 21), 51.48, 0)
print("self-check, lat 51.48: formula", 90 - abs(51.48 - decl(10, j)), "vs engine", alt(10, j, 51.48, 0), "deg (transit)")

/* ---- expected output ----
= noon altitude of the Sun (deg, geometric) at the season instants of 2026
= lat | spring 03-20 | summer 06-21 | autumn 09-23 | winter 12-21
= lat 0 : 89.999901617 66.562069598 89.999960714 66.56252625
= lat 23.44 : 66.560098383 89.997930402 (overhead) 66.559960714 43.12252625
= lat 40 : 50.000098383 73.437930402 49.999960714 26.56252625
= lat 51.48 : 38.520098383 61.957930402 38.519960714 15.08252625
= -- midnight-sun line: above lat 66.56 the June Sun never sets --
= lat 66.56 : 23.440098383 46.877930402 23.439960714 0.00252625 *
= lat 70 : 20.000098383 43.437930402 (midnight sun) 19.999960714 -3.43747375
= declinations: 0.000098383 23.437930402 -0.000039286 -23.43747375 deg
= midnight-sun line this year: 90 - 23.437930402 = 66.562069598 deg
= self-check, lat 51.48: formula 61.957848058 vs engine 61.9567272 deg (transit)
*/

scripts.name: sun-position-noaa
scripts.title: the NOAA solar-position chain, step by step
scripts.text:
/* ============================================================================
sun-position-noaa.epher -- the NOAA solar-position chain, step by step

The solar-position decomposition published with the NOAA Global
Monitoring Laboratory's online Solar Calculator (gml.noaa.gov/grad/
solcalc; its "calculation details" page states each equation): the
geometric mean longitude and mean anomaly of the Sun, the Earth's
eccentricity and the equation of center, the Sun's true and
apparent longitude, the mean and corrected obliquity, the Sun's
declination, the equation of time, and then the observer's hour
angle, altitude and azimuth. The equations are the standard
low-precision solar theory - the same series as Jean Meeus,
"Astronomical Algorithms" (2nd ed., Willmann-Bell, 1998) chs. 25
and 28 - evaluated exactly as NOAA prints them, so each printed
line is the value the NOAA calculator shows on its details page
for the same input (its declination column and equation-of-time
column, for example).

Accuracy: this series is good to about 0.01 deg in the solar
declination and a fraction of a minute in the equation of time
(NOAA's own grade is +/- 1 minute of rise/set time, which needs
about 0.25 deg of altitude). Refraction is omitted, as in the
NOAA equations. The script then prints its altitude and azimuth
against the engine's own alt and az accessors (the solar-ephemeris
crate, JPL-validated): the engine integrates a fuller VSOP2013
model with nutation, and at this sample the two sit within a few
thousandths of a degree of each other; through the year the
low-precision series drifts up to about 0.01 deg in declination
against the full theory, and refraction (omitted here, though
NOAA's calculator display adds it) is the largest near-horizon
term - the engine remains the fuller model.

Knobs: the instant (date plus hours UT) and the place.
============================================================================ */

// ---- the knobs ----------------------------------------------------------------
const day = {2026, 6, 21}    // sample date
const hr = 12.5              // hours UT (12.5 = 12:30)
const lat = 51.4779          // Greenwich
const lon = 0                // degrees east

// ---- NOAA's equations: each def is one printed step ---------------------------
def t(j) = (j - 2451545.0) / 36525                      // Julian centuries from J2000
def mod360(x) = x - 360 * floor(x / 360)
def l0(j) = mod360(280.46646 + t(j) * (36000.76983 + t(j) * 0.0003032))   // geometric mean longitude of the Sun, deg
def manom(j) = mod360(357.52911 + t(j) * (35999.05029 - 0.0001537 * t(j)))  // geometric mean anomaly, deg
def eccen(j) = 0.016708634 - t(j) * (0.000042037 + 0.0000001267 * t(j))   // Earth's orbital eccentricity
def eqcen(j) = sin(rad(manom(j))) * (1.914602 - t(j) * (0.004817 + 0.000014 * t(j))) + sin(rad(2 * manom(j))) * (0.019993 - 0.000101 * t(j)) + 0.000289 * sin(rad(3 * manom(j)))  // equation of center, deg
def trlon(j) = l0(j) + eqcen(j)                         // true longitude, deg
def omega(j) = 125.04 - 1934.136 * t(j)                 // argument for the corrections, deg
def applon(j) = trlon(j) - 0.00569 - 0.00478 * sin(rad(omega(j)))   // apparent longitude, deg
def mobliq(j) = 23 + 26 / 60 + 21.448 / 3600 - t(j) * (46.815 + t(j) * (0.00059 - 0.001813 * t(j))) / 3600  // mean obliquity, deg
def cobliq(j) = mobliq(j) + 0.00256 * cos(rad(omega(j)))  // corrected obliquity, deg
def declin(j) = deg(asin(sin(rad(cobliq(j))) * sin(rad(applon(j)))))  // solar declination, deg
def vy(j) = tan(rad(cobliq(j)) / 2) ^ 2                 // auxiliary y for the equation of time
def eot(j) = 4 * deg(vy(j) * sin(rad(2 * l0(j))) - 2 * eccen(j) * sin(rad(manom(j))) + 4 * eccen(j) * vy(j) * sin(rad(manom(j))) * cos(rad(2 * l0(j))) - 0.5 * vy(j) ^ 2 * sin(rad(4 * l0(j))) - 1.25 * eccen(j) ^ 2 * sin(rad(2 * manom(j))))  // equation of time, minutes
def ha(j) = 15 * (hr + lon / 15 - 12) + eot(j) / 4      // hour angle, deg (west positive)
def altv(j) = deg(asin(sin(rad(lat)) * sin(rad(declin(j))) + cos(rad(lat)) * cos(rad(declin(j))) * cos(rad(ha(j)))))  // altitude, deg
def zen(j) = 90 - altv(j)
def azv(j) = deg(acos((sin(rad(declin(j))) * cos(rad(lat)) - cos(rad(declin(j))) * sin(rad(lat)) * cos(rad(ha(j)))) / sin(rad(zen(j)))))  // azimuth from north, deg
def aznoaa(j) = if ha(j) > 0 then 360 - azv(j) else azv(j)

// ---- results: the NOAA chain, printed step by step -----------------------------
const j = jd(day[1], day[2], day[3], hr)
print("NOAA solar position for", iso(j), "UT at lat", lat, "lon", lon)
print("step 1  Julian centuries n:", t(j))
print("step 2  geometric mean longitude L0:", l0(j), "deg")
print("step 3  geometric mean anomaly M:", manom(j), "deg")
print("step 4  eccentricity e:", eccen(j))
print("step 5  equation of center C:", eqcen(j), "deg")
print("step 6  true longitude:", trlon(j), "deg")
print("step 7  omega:", omega(j), "deg")
print("step 8  apparent longitude:", applon(j), "deg")
print("step 9  mean obliquity:", mobliq(j), "deg; corrected:", cobliq(j), "deg")
print("step 10 declination:", declin(j), "deg")
print("step 11 equation of time:", eot(j), "min")
print("step 12 hour angle:", ha(j), "deg")
print("step 13 altitude:", altv(j), "deg; zenith distance:", zen(j), "deg")
print("step 14 azimuth:", aznoaa(j), "deg from north")

/* Cross-check against the engine's built-in alt and az (the same
instant, same place): the engine runs a fuller VSOP2013-based model
with nutation. On this sample date the NOAA series stays within a
few thousandths of a degree of it; the gap is not constant (the
low-precision declination series drifts up to about 0.01 deg over
the year, and refraction would add more near the horizon), so this
print is the honest per-run comparison and the engine is the
reference side. */
print("cross-check: NOAA altitude", altv(j), "deg vs engine", alt(10, j, lat, lon), "deg")
print("cross-check: NOAA azimuth", aznoaa(j), "deg vs engine", az(10, j, lat, lon), "deg")

/* ---- expected output ----
= NOAA solar position for 2026-06-21T12:30:00 UT at lat 51.4779 lon 0
= step 1  Julian centuries n: 0.264695984486
= step 2  geometric mean longitude L0: 89.7256936317 deg
= step 3  geometric mean anomaly M: 166.333156286 deg
= step 4  eccentricity e: 0.0166974980978
= step 5  equation of center C: 0.443094441422 deg
= step 6  true longitude: 90.1687880731 deg
= step 7  omega: -386.918032649 deg
= step 8  apparent longitude: 90.1652620526 deg
= step 9  mean obliquity: 23.4358489583 deg; corrected: 23.4381315953 deg
= step 10 declination: 23.4380282689 deg
= step 11 equation of time: -1.82881005973 min
= step 12 hour angle: 7.04279748507 deg
= step 13 altitude: 61.4390663151 deg; zenith distance: 28.5609336849 deg
= step 14 azimuth: 193.609169747 deg from north
= cross-check: NOAA altitude 61.4390663151 deg vs engine 61.4373877 deg
= cross-check: NOAA azimuth 193.609169747 deg vs engine 193.6134812 deg
*/

scripts.name: sundial-lines
scripts.title: hour-line angles for a vertical declining dial
scripts.text:
/* ============================================================================
sundial-lines.epher -- hour-line angles for a vertical declining dial

The hour lines of a planar sundial are where the Sun's hour planes
meet the dial plane. An hour plane contains the Earth's axis and the
Sun at that hour angle, so it is the meridian plane rotated around
the axis by the hour angle H (15 deg per hour, positive after noon),
and its intersection with a vertical wall whose outward normal
declines D degrees west of south gives the hour line. The angle v of
that line from the wall's vertical noon line is, for a wall at
latitude phi (Meeus, "Astronomical Algorithms" 2nd ed., ch. 58,
planar sundials, declining vertical wall; the same result as Waugh,
"Sundials: Their Theory and Construction"):

  tan v = cos(phi) sin(H) / (cos(D) cos(H) + sin(phi) sin(H) sin(D))

For a due-south wall (D = 0) this reduces to the classic vertical
south dial tan v = cos(phi) tan(H); for a wall facing due west or
east (D = +-90) the lines become parallel, the polar dial, making
the angle 90 - phi with the noon line - the two limits printed as
checks below. The gnomon is a rod parallel to the Earth's axis
sticking out of the wall; the hour lines do not depend on its
length. Solar (apparent) time is meant: a clock reads mean time, so
the equation of time (a quarter hour at most) must be added to the
clock before reading the dial, and the wall's longitude fixes local
noon.

Accuracy: the geometry is exact for an ideal wall and a point gnomon;
real dials add gnomon thickness, wall tilt and refraction at the
1-2 arcmin level and above, which are not modeled.

Knobs: the latitude and the wall's declination (orientation).
============================================================================ */

// ---- the knobs ----------------------------------------------------------------
const lat = 51.4779          // dial latitude, deg (Greenwich)
const wdecl = 25             // wall declination, deg: the wall faces 25 deg west of south

// ---- the dial geometry --------------------------------------------------------
def v(h) = deg(atan2(cos(rad(lat)) * sin(rad(h)), cos(rad(wdecl)) * cos(rad(h)) + sin(rad(lat)) * sin(rad(h)) * sin(rad(wdecl))))  // hour-line angle from the noon line, deg
def ha(hh) = (hh - 12) * 15  // hour angle H of a solar-time hour

// ---- results ------------------------------------------------------------------
print("vertical declining dial at lat", lat, "facing", wdecl, "deg west of south")
print("hour-line angle v from the vertical noon line (positive toward the east end):")

/* One labelled row per hour, 6:00 to 18:00 solar time. Positive v
leans toward the wall's east end, where the afternoon shadow falls;
the morning lines mirror on the west side but not symmetrically -
the declining wall's hour fan is asymmetric, its signature. Angles
past +-90 deg mean the ray climbs above the style's foot (that hour
the Sun stands behind the wall's facing); the paired rays h and
h + 12 lie on one straight line, as on every planar dial. */
print("6:00  H", ha(6), ": line at", v(ha(6)), "deg")
print("7:00  H", ha(7), ": line at", v(ha(7)), "deg")
print("8:00  H", ha(8), ": line at", v(ha(8)), "deg")
print("9:00  H", ha(9), ": line at", v(ha(9)), "deg")
print("10:00 H", ha(10), ": line at", v(ha(10)), "deg")
print("11:00 H", ha(11), ": line at", v(ha(11)), "deg")
print("12:00 H", ha(12), ": line at", v(ha(12)), "deg (the noon line)")
print("13:00 H", ha(13), ": line at", v(ha(13)), "deg")
print("14:00 H", ha(14), ": line at", v(ha(14)), "deg")
print("15:00 H", ha(15), ": line at", v(ha(15)), "deg")
print("16:00 H", ha(16), ": line at", v(ha(16)), "deg")
print("17:00 H", ha(17), ": line at", v(ha(17)), "deg")
print("18:00 H", ha(18), ": line at", v(ha(18)), "deg")

/* Checks against the two textbook limits of the same formula. A
due-south wall (D = 0) at this latitude puts the 1 pm line at
atan(cos(phi) tan 15) = 9.48 deg, the classic vertical south dial
value; a wall facing due west (D = 90) degenerates into the polar
dial whose lines are all parallel at 90 - phi from the noon line. */
print("check, due-south wall (D = 0), 1 pm line:", deg(atan(cos(rad(lat)) * tan(rad(15)))), "deg")
print("check, polar-dial limit (D = 90): lines parallel at", 90 - lat, "deg")

/* ---- expected output ----
= vertical declining dial at lat 51.4779 facing 25 deg west of south
= hour-line angle v from the vertical noon line (positive toward the east end):
= 6:00  H -90 : line at -117.96309623 deg
= 7:00  H -75 : line at -98.0241226486 deg
= 8:00  H -60 : line at -72.8150998009 deg
= 9:00  H -45 : line at -47.2530172188 deg
= 10:00 H -30 : line at -26.6852339829 deg
= 11:00 H -15 : line at -11.5348300422 deg
= 12:00 H 0 : line at 0 deg (the noon line)
= 13:00 H 15 : line at 9.5220398875 deg
= 14:00 H 30 : line at 18.1453515136 deg
= 15:00 H 45 : line at 26.7256883376 deg
= 16:00 H 60 : line at 36.1062126729 deg
= 17:00 H 75 : line at 47.3612264364 deg
= 18:00 H 90 : line at 62.0369037702 deg
= check, due-south wall (D = 0), 1 pm line: 9.47439105165 deg
= check, polar-dial limit (D = 90): lines parallel at 38.5221 deg
*/

scripts.name: besselian-epoch
scripts.title: Besselian years and Julian dates
scripts.text:
/* ============================================================================
besselian-epoch.epher -- Besselian years and Julian dates

Converts between the Besselian epochs that old catalogues use
(B1875, B1900, B1950 - the 1950 positions of the Palomar Sky Atlas
and of a generation of atlases) and Julian dates. A Besselian year
is a tropical year of 365.242198781 days, counted from the
Besselian epoch of 1900.0 at JD 2415020.31352:

  B = 1900 + (jd - 2415020.31352) / 365.242198781

so B1950.0 falls on JD 2433282.4235. Compare the Julian EPOCHS
(J2000.0 = JD 2451545.0 exactly, the modern frame): J2000.0 reads
Besselian 2000.001278, because a Besselian year is the tropical
year, 0.001278 years (about 11 hours) shorter than the Julian year
the modern epochs count - mix the two epoch types up and old and
new catalogues disagree by the precession of that span.

Knobs: the date below.
============================================================================ */

// ---- the knobs -------------------------------------------------------------------------
const tm = jd(2026, 9, 10, 0)

// ---- the conversions ---------------------------------------------------------------------
const b = 1900 + (tm - 2415020.31352) / 365.242198781
const tb = 2415020.31352 + 365.242198781 * (b - 1900)

print("JD", tm, "is Besselian year", b)
print("back to JD:", tb, " (difference", tb - tm, "d)")

/* Self-checks: the B1950.0 anchor sits at JD 2433282.4235, and
J2000.0 (the Julian epoch, JD 2451545.0) reads Besselian
2000.001278 - the 0.001278-year offset between the two epoch
types. */
print("B1950.0 anchor residual (d):", 2415020.31352 + 365.242198781 * 50 - 2433282.4235)
print("J2000.0 in Besselian years:", 1900 + (2451545 - 2415020.31352) / 365.242198781)

/* ---- expected output ----
= JD 2461293.5 is Besselian year 2026.69178598
= back to JD: 2461293.5  (difference 0 d)
= B1950.0 anchor residual (d): -0.0000409502536058
= J2000.0 in Besselian years: 2000.00127751
*/

scripts.name: date-from-julian-day
scripts.title: Julian Date back to a calendar date
scripts.text:
/* ============================================================================
date-from-julian-day.epher -- Julian Date back to a calendar date

The inverse of jd(y, m, d): the built-ins date(), time() and iso()
turn a Julian Date into the calendar date and clock time. The
algorithm is the one from chapter 7 of Jean Meeus, "Astronomical
Algorithms" (2nd ed., Willmann-Bell, 1998), built in (guide 1.18):
floor arithmetic on the day number, with the Gregorian/Julian
calendar switch of 1582-10-15 handled. date(jd) gives the
{year, month, day}; time(jd) gives the {hour, minute, second} clock
in UT, rounded to the second; iso(jd) spells the same moment as the
ISO 8601 date-time (YYYY-MM-DDTHH:MM:SS), the notation the JPL
Horizons tables print. Every bare date below is checked by a round
trip back through jd(), which prints true when the pair agrees.

Knob: none - the dates below are fixed, famous ones, plus one
fractional instant that shows the clock half of the conversion.
============================================================================ */

/* ---- results ----------------------------------------------------------------
Round trips: the date of a JD that jd() produced, and the check that
converting back yields the original JD (true on every line). The
famous bare JD 2451545 is J2000.0, noon on 2000-01-01; iso() reads
it back as the full date-time, and the time part carries the 12:00
that the date alone cannot. The Gregorian/Julian switch sits between
the two 1582 lines: jd(1582, 10, 4, 12) is the last Julian-calendar
day and jd(1582, 10, 15) the first Gregorian one, ten days later. */
print("jd(2026, 3, 15) ->", iso(jd(2026, 3, 15)))
print("round trip:", jd(date(jd(2026, 3, 15))[1], date(jd(2026, 3, 15))[2], date(jd(2026, 3, 15))[3]) == jd(2026, 3, 15))
print("J2000.0, JD 2451545 ->", iso(2451545))
print("its clock:", time(2451545))
print("leap day, jd(2000, 2, 29) ->", iso(jd(2000, 2, 29)))
print("round trip:", jd(date(jd(2000, 2, 29))[1], date(jd(2000, 2, 29))[2], date(jd(2000, 2, 29))[3]) == jd(2000, 2, 29))
print("Gregorian start, jd(1582, 10, 15) ->", iso(jd(1582, 10, 15)))
print("round trip:", jd(date(jd(1582, 10, 15))[1], date(jd(1582, 10, 15))[2], date(jd(1582, 10, 15))[3]) == jd(1582, 10, 15))
print("last Julian day, jd(1582, 10, 4, 12) ->", iso(jd(1582, 10, 4, 12)))
print("round trip:", jd(date(jd(1582, 10, 4, 12))[1], date(jd(1582, 10, 4, 12))[2], date(jd(1582, 10, 4, 12))[3], 12) == jd(1582, 10, 4, 12))
print("century non-leap, jd(2100, 2, 28) ->", iso(jd(2100, 2, 28)))
print("round trip:", jd(date(jd(2100, 2, 28))[1], date(jd(2100, 2, 28))[2], date(jd(2100, 2, 28))[3]) == jd(2100, 2, 28))
print("year end, jd(2026, 12, 31) ->", iso(jd(2026, 12, 31)))
print("round trip:", jd(date(jd(2026, 12, 31))[1], date(jd(2026, 12, 31))[2], date(jd(2026, 12, 31))[3]) == jd(2026, 12, 31))
print("half past noon, jd(2026, 3, 20, 12.5) ->", iso(jd(2026, 3, 20, 12.5)))
print("date and clock of that instant:", date(jd(2026, 3, 20, 12.5)), time(jd(2026, 3, 20, 12.5)))

/* ---- expected output ----
= jd(2026, 3, 15) -> 2026-03-15T00:00:00
= round trip: true
= J2000.0, JD 2451545 -> 2000-01-01T12:00:00
= its clock: {12, 0, 0}
= leap day, jd(2000, 2, 29) -> 2000-02-29T00:00:00
= round trip: true
= Gregorian start, jd(1582, 10, 15) -> 1582-10-15T00:00:00
= round trip: true
= last Julian day, jd(1582, 10, 4, 12) -> 1582-10-04T12:00:00
= round trip: true
= century non-leap, jd(2100, 2, 28) -> 2100-02-28T00:00:00
= round trip: true
= year end, jd(2026, 12, 31) -> 2026-12-31T00:00:00
= round trip: true
= half past noon, jd(2026, 3, 20, 12.5) -> 2026-03-20T12:30:00
= date and clock of that instant: {2026, 3, 20} {12, 30, 0}
*/

scripts.name: day-of-week-from-date
scripts.title: what weekday a date falls on
scripts.text:
/* ============================================================================
day-of-week-from-date.epher -- what weekday a date falls on

The weekday of a calendar date from its Julian Date: the day number
is floor(jd + 1.5), and its remainder mod 7 names the weekday with
0 = Sunday (the convention of Meeus, "Astronomical Algorithms",
ch. 7; the +1.5 moves the count from the noon-based JD to civil
days). The dates below are famous or fixed, and their weekdays were
verified with python's datetime module, which is the oracle for the
expected output. Two of them are history: 1582-10-15 was a Friday,
the day after the Thursday of 1582-10-04 in the Julian calendar -
the Gregorian reform skipped ten days.

Knob: none - the dates below are fixed.
============================================================================ */

// ---- helpers ----------------------------------------------------------------
def wd(jd0) = mod(floor(jd0 + 1.5), 7)   // 0 = Sunday ... 6 = Saturday
def dayname(h) = if h == 0 then "Sunday" else if h == 1 then "Monday" else if h == 2 then "Tuesday" else if h == 3 then "Wednesday" else if h == 4 then "Thursday" else if h == 5 then "Friday" else "Saturday"

/* ---- results ----------------------------------------------------------------
The anchors the guide gives: 2000-01-01 was a Saturday, 2026-01-01 a
Thursday. The raw weekday number for the first one shows the 0 =
Sunday convention at work (h = 6 for Saturday). */
print("2000-01-01:", dayname(wd(jd(2000, 1, 1))))
print("h for that date:", wd(jd(2000, 1, 1)), "(0 = Sunday)")
print("1582-10-15:", dayname(wd(jd(1582, 10, 15))))
print("2026-01-01:", dayname(wd(jd(2026, 1, 1))))
print("2026-03-15:", dayname(wd(jd(2026, 3, 15))))
print("2026-06-21:", dayname(wd(jd(2026, 6, 21))))
print("2026-12-25:", dayname(wd(jd(2026, 12, 25))))

/* ---- expected output ----
= 2000-01-01: Saturday
= h for that date: 6 (0 = Sunday)
= 1582-10-15: Friday
= 2026-01-01: Thursday
= 2026-03-15: Sunday
= 2026-06-21: Sunday
= 2026-12-25: Friday
*/

scripts.name: days-between-dates
scripts.title: the day count between two dates
scripts.text:
/* ============================================================================
days-between-dates.epher -- the day count between two dates

The number of days between two calendar dates, as the difference of
their Julian Dates (guide 1.16). Because jd(y, m, d) counts from the
same 0h-UT instant for every date, the difference is exactly the day
count of the civil calendar, leap days included - no month lengths
need summing by hand. The spans below were verified with python's
datetime module, which is the oracle for the expected output. The
sign of the difference follows the order of the subtraction, so the
same two dates give +9497 one way and -9497 the other.

Knob: none - the spans below are fixed.
============================================================================ */

/* ---- results ----------------------------------------------------------------
26 years from 2000-01-01 to 2026-01-01: 26 * 365 + 7 leap days (2000,
2004, ..., 2024) = 9497. Then the leap-year contrast around 2024:
365 days across an ordinary year, 366 across one that holds a
February 29, and the shorter span from mid-March to the solstice. */
print("2000-01-01 to 2026-01-01:", jd(2026, 1, 1) - jd(2000, 1, 1), "days")
print("2023-01-01 to 2024-01-01:", jd(2024, 1, 1) - jd(2023, 1, 1), "days")
print("2024-01-01 to 2025-01-01:", jd(2025, 1, 1) - jd(2024, 1, 1), "days (2024 is a leap year)")
print("2026-03-15 to 2026-06-21:", jd(2026, 6, 21) - jd(2026, 3, 15), "days")
print("signed the other way:", jd(2000, 1, 1) - jd(2026, 1, 1), "days")
print("1582-10-15 to 2000-01-01:", jd(2000, 1, 1) - jd(1582, 10, 15), "days")

/* ---- expected output ----
= 2000-01-01 to 2026-01-01: 9497 days
= 2023-01-01 to 2024-01-01: 365 days
= 2024-01-01 to 2025-01-01: 366 days (2024 is a leap year)
= 2026-03-15 to 2026-06-21: 98 days
= signed the other way: -9497 days
= 1582-10-15 to 2000-01-01: 152384 days
*/

scripts.name: delta-t-history
scripts.title: Delta T across the centuries
scripts.text:
/* ============================================================================
delta-t-history.epher -- Delta T across the centuries

Prints the engine's Delta T (TT - UT, the accumulated drift of the
rotating Earth against atomic time; guide 1.29, built on the
Espenak-Meeus polynomial set of Meeus ch. 10) for a spread of years.
The table is the story of the Earth's slowing spin: Delta T fell
from about 120 seconds in 1600 to a few seconds around 1700-1800,
went negative near 1900, and has climbed steadily since - by 2100
the extrapolation passes 4 minutes, which is why leap seconds
disappeared from the UTC definition and why historic eclipse paths
shift west by about 1500 km per hour of Delta T.

Accuracy: the engine's own (Espenak-Meeus; a few seconds in the
modern era, growing for the extrapolated 2200/2500 rows, stated in
the polynomial notes).

Knob: none - the table is fixed.
============================================================================ */

// ---- the table ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
print("Delta T (TT - UT) on 1 January of each listed year")
print("1600:", delta_t(jd(1600, 1, 1)), "s")
print("1650:", delta_t(jd(1650, 1, 1)), "s")
print("1700:", delta_t(jd(1700, 1, 1)), "s")
print("1750:", delta_t(jd(1750, 1, 1)), "s")
print("1800:", delta_t(jd(1800, 1, 1)), "s")
print("1850:", delta_t(jd(1850, 1, 1)), "s")
print("1900:", delta_t(jd(1900, 1, 1)), "s")
print("1950:", delta_t(jd(1950, 1, 1)), "s")
print("2000:", delta_t(jd(2000, 1, 1)), "s")
print("2025:", delta_t(jd(2025, 1, 1)), "s")
print("2050:", delta_t(jd(2050, 1, 1)), "s")
print("2100:", delta_t(jd(2100, 1, 1)), "s")
print("2200:", delta_t(jd(2200, 1, 1)), "s")
print("2500:", delta_t(jd(2500, 1, 1)), "s")

/* Self-check: the famous landmarks - Delta T was about 120 s in
1600 and it dips negative near 1900 (the observed minimum, about
-3 s around 1902); the 2000.0 row above reads about 64 s. */
print("negative near 1900:", delta_t(jd(1900, 1, 1)) < 0)
print("about 64 s at 2000.0:", abs(delta_t(jd(2000, 1, 1)) - 64) < 1)

/* ---- expected output ----
= Delta T (TT - UT) on 1 January of each listed year
= 1600: 119.993286072 s
= 1650: 50.1820183562 s
= 1700: 8.831096916 s
= 1750: 13.370846523 s
= 1800: 13.7186348306 s
= 1850: 7.10724564462 s
= 1900: -2.78795477478 s
= 1950: 29.07 s
= 2000: 63.8595419813 s
= 2025: 69.1333105179 s
= 2050: 93 s
= 2100: 202.73677646 s
= 2200: 442.070012374 s
= 2500: 1459.63829735 s
= negative near 1900: true
= about 64 s at 2000.0: true
*/
