scripts.name: equation-of-time
scripts.title: how far the sundial runs fast or slow
scripts.text:
/* ============================================================================
equation-of-time.epher -- how far the sundial runs fast or slow

Computes the equation of time E for several dates: the minutes by
which a sundial leads (positive) or trails (negative) a clock read
in local mean time. The engine's own alpha-style accessors do not
expose E, so the script carries Meeus's chapter 28 recipe: E (deg) =
L0 - 0.0057183 - alpha + Delta-psi x cos(eps), where L0 is the Sun's
mean longitude, alpha its apparent right ascension, Delta-psi the
nutation in longitude (largest terms) and eps the obliquity. Times
are TD via the built-in delta_t; 1 degree of longitude = 4 minutes.

Method and source: Jean Meeus, "Astronomical Algorithms" 2nd ed.
ch. 28 (with the apparent-longitude step of ch. 25); the largest
nutation terms of ch. 22 (truncating the rest costs about 0.03 s).
The same quantity is the classic calculator "EQT" program (hpcalc
7618, HP-48 "Analemma") and NOAA's solar-calculator `eqtime`.

Accuracy: about +/- 0.1 minute of time. The values below were
cross-checked against NOAA's independent Fourier series (their
solareqns.PDF): 2026-02-12 -14.25 vs -14.2 here, 2026-11-03 +16.34
vs +16.4 - agreement to a few tenths of a minute, which is what the
Fourier series itself guarantees.

Knobs: the four dates below (any 2026 date can be swapped in).
============================================================================ */

// ---- the knobs ----------------------------------------------------------------
const d_feb = {2026, 2, 12}    // near the mid-February minimum
const d_apr = {2026, 4, 15}    // near a zero crossing
const d_jun = {2026, 6, 21}    // June solstice
const d_nov = {2026, 11, 3}    // near the early-November maximum

// ---- Meeus ch. 28: mean elements in T (Julian centuries from J2000, TD) -------
def mod360(x) = x - 360 * floor(x / 360)
def cent(j) = (j + delta_t(j) / 86400 - jd(2000, 1, 1, 12)) / 36525
def l0(t) = mod360(280.46061837 + 36000.77005360 * t + 0.000387933 * t ^ 2 - t ^ 3 / 38710000)
def m(t) = mod360(357.5291092 + 35999.0502909 * t - 0.0001536 * t ^ 2)
def omega(t) = mod360(125.04 - 1934.136 * t)
def eps(t) = 23.4392911 - 0.0130042 * t - 0.000000164 * t ^ 2 + 0.000000504 * t ^ 3

// ---- equation of center (ch. 25), apparent longitude and right ascension ------
def cen(t) = (1.914602 - 0.004817 * t - 0.000014 * t ^ 2) * sin(rad(m(t))) + (0.019993 - 0.000101 * t) * sin(rad(2 * m(t))) + 0.000289 * sin(rad(3 * m(t)))
def applon(t) = l0(t) + cen(t) - 0.0057183 - 0.0047833 * sin(rad(omega(t)))
def alpha(t) = deg(atan2(cos(rad(eps(t))) * sin(rad(applon(t))), cos(rad(applon(t)))))

// ---- nutation in longitude, degrees: the three largest terms (ch. 22) ---------
def psi(t) = (-17.20 * sin(rad(omega(t))) - 1.32 * sin(rad(2 * l0(t))) + 0.21 * sin(rad(2 * omega(t)))) / 3600

// ---- the equation of time in minutes of time ----------------------------------
def signed360(x) = if x > 180 then x - 360 else x
def eot(j) = signed360(l0(cent(j)) - 0.0057183 - alpha(cent(j)) + psi(cent(j)) * cos(rad(eps(cent(j))))) * 4

// ---- results ------------------------------------------------------------------
print("equation of time, minutes (sundial fast +):")
print("2026-02-12:", eot(jd(d_feb[1], d_feb[2], d_feb[3])))
print("2026-04-15:", eot(jd(d_apr[1], d_apr[2], d_apr[3])))
print("2026-06-21:", eot(jd(d_jun[1], d_jun[2], d_jun[3])))
print("2026-11-03:", eot(jd(d_nov[1], d_nov[2], d_nov[3])))

/* Reading the numbers: in mid-February the sundial runs about 14
minutes slow, and a clock set to the November sun would run 16
minutes fast - the extremes of the year. The four zero crossings
fall near April 15, June 13, September 1 and December 25. */
print("year's spread (Nov max minus Feb min):", eot(jd(d_nov[1], d_nov[2], d_nov[3])) - eot(jd(d_feb[1], d_feb[2], d_feb[3])), "min")

/* ---- expected output ----
= equation of time, minutes (sundial fast +):
= 2026-02-12: -14.1935995278
= 2026-04-15: -0.158945038735
= 2026-06-21: -1.71739350749
= 2026-11-03: 16.4392227149
= year's spread (Nov max minus Feb min): 30.6328222427 min
*/

scripts.name: hebrew-calendar
scripts.title: Gregorian date to the Hebrew calendar

scripts.name: hijri-date
scripts.title: Gregorian date to the Islamic (Hijri) calendar
scripts.text:
/* ============================================================================
hijri-date.epher -- Gregorian date to the Islamic (Hijri) calendar

Converts a Gregorian date into the Islamic calendar: Hijri year,
month and day. The calendar is purely lunar: 12 months of 29 or 30
days, with 11 leap years (355 days) in each 30-year cycle. The
script uses the arithmetic "tabular" calendar - the fixed civil
variant whose epoch is 1 Muharram 1 AH = 19 July 622 (Julian), day
number 1948440, with the classic leap test (11 yr + 14) mod 30 < 11
(the calendar of Meeus ch. 9 and the "Kuwaiti algorithm" of the
Calendar FAQ). The tabular calendar agrees with the crescent-based
calendars and with the Umm al-Qura calendar of Saudi Arabia to
within a day at month starts - that one-day spread is inherent to
the several Islamic calendars, not an error.

Accuracy: exact arithmetic for the tabular calendar.

Knobs: the date below.
============================================================================ */

// ---- the knobs ---------------------------------------------------------------------
const yr = 2026
const m = 9
const dcal = 7

// ---- the Kuwaiti tabular algorithm (integer arithmetic on the day number) ------------
def mname(k) = if k == 1 then "Muharram" else if k == 2 then "Safar" else if k == 3 then "Rabi al-awwal" else if k == 4 then "Rabi al-thani" else if k == 5 then "Jumada al-ula" else if k == 6 then "Jumada al-akhirah" else if k == 7 then "Rajab" else if k == 8 then "Shaban" else if k == 9 then "Ramadan" else if k == 10 then "Shawwal" else if k == 11 then "Dhu al-Qidah" else "Dhu al-Hijjah"
def al0(j) = j - 1948440 + 10632
def anv(j) = floor(al0(j) / 10631)
def al1(j) = al0(j) - 10631 * anv(j) + 354
def ajv(j) = floor((10985 - al1(j)) / 5316) * floor(50 * al1(j) / 17719) + floor(al1(j) / 5670) * floor(43 * al1(j) / 15238)
def al2(j) = al1(j) - floor((30 - ajv(j)) / 15) * floor(17719 * ajv(j) / 50) - floor(ajv(j) / 16) * floor(15238 * ajv(j) / 43) + 29
def amv(j) = floor(24 * al2(j) / 709)
def adv(j) = al2(j) - floor(709 * amv(j) / 24)
def ayv(j) = 30 * anv(j) + ajv(j) - 30

print("Hijri year leap test of the epoch: 1 Muharram 1 AH = JDN 1948440:", floor(jd(622, 7, 16) + 0.5) == 1948440)

print("Gregorian", yr, "-", m, "-", dcal, "is Hijri", adv(floor(jd(yr, m, dcal) + 0.5)), mname(amv(floor(jd(yr, m, dcal) + 0.5))), ayv(floor(jd(yr, m, dcal) + 0.5)), "AH")
print("2026-06-26 is tabular Hijri", adv(floor(jd(2026, 6, 26) + 0.5)), mname(amv(floor(jd(2026, 6, 26) + 0.5))), ayv(floor(jd(2026, 6, 26) + 0.5)), "(Umm al-Qura: 11 Muharram 1448 - the 1-day spread)")
/* ---- expected output ----
= Hijri year leap test of the epoch: 1 Muharram 1 AH = JDN 1948440: true
= Gregorian 2026 - 9 - 7 is Hijri 24 Rabi al-awwal 1448 AH
= 2026-06-26 is tabular Hijri 10 Muharram 1448 (Umm al-Qura: 11 Muharram 1448 - the 1-day spread)
*/

scripts.name: julian-calendar-date
scripts.title: Gregorian and Julian calendar dates
scripts.text:
/* ============================================================================
julian-calendar-date.epher -- Gregorian and Julian calendar dates

Reads a date in both Western calendars, split by the 1582 reform:
the Julian calendar (in force until Thursday 4 October 1582) and
the Gregorian calendar (Friday 15 October 1582 onward). The
conversions use the classic integer algorithms - Meeus,
"Astronomical Algorithms" 2nd ed. ch. 7 with B = 0 for the Julian
calendar. The engine's own jd() follows the historical calendar
too: dates before the reform are Julian dates, from the reform day
on they are Gregorian - so jd(1582, 10, 4) and jd(1582, 10, 15)
are consecutive days.

Accuracy: exact for all dates. The two calendars differ by 10 days
at the reform and gain 3 more days per 400 years (13 today).

Knobs: the date below (default: a modern date).
============================================================================ */

// ---- the knobs --------------------------------------------------------------------
const yr = 2026
const m = 9
const dcal = 7

// ---- helper: day number -> Julian-calendar date (reverse of the B = 0 formulas) -----
def rday(j) = j + 32082 - floor(1461 * floor((4 * (j + 32082) + 3) / 1461) / 4) - floor((153 * floor((5 * (j + 32082 - floor(1461 * floor((4 * (j + 32082) + 3) / 1461) / 4)) + 2) / 153) + 2) / 5) + 1
def rmon(j) = floor((5 * (j + 32082 - floor(1461 * floor((4 * (j + 32082) + 3) / 1461) / 4)) + 2) / 153) + 3 - 12 * floor(floor((5 * (j + 32082 - floor(1461 * floor((4 * (j + 32082) + 3) / 1461) / 4)) + 2) / 153) / 10)
def ryer(j) = floor((4 * (j + 32082) + 3) / 1461) - 4800 + floor(floor((5 * (j + 32082 - floor(1461 * floor((4 * (j + 32082) + 3) / 1461) / 4)) + 2) / 153) / 10)

// ---- the reading ----------------------------------------------------------------------
const jdn = floor(jd(yr, m, dcal) + 0.5)
print("Gregorian", yr, "-", m, "-", dcal, " is the same day as Julian", ryer(jdn), "-", rmon(jdn), "-", rday(jdn))

// ---- the reform --------------------------------------------------------------------------
const jr = floor(jd(1582, 10, 15) + 0.5)
print("Gregorian 1582-10-15 was Julian", ryer(jr), "-", rmon(jr), "-", rday(jr), "(the reform skipped 1582-10-05..14)")

/* Self-checks: the engine's jd() reads pre-reform dates as Julian
(so jd(1582,10,4) is the Julian day number minus a half), and the
reform made the two JDs consecutive. */
print("engine reads 1582-10-04 as Julian:", jd(1582, 10, 4) == 2299159.5)
print("reform days are consecutive:", jd(1582, 10, 15) - jd(1582, 10, 4) == 1)
print("2026-09-07 reads Julian 2026-08-25:", rday(jdn) == 25 and rmon(jdn) == 8 and ryer(jdn) == 2026)

/* ---- expected output ----
= Gregorian 2026 - 9 - 7  is the same day as Julian 2026 - 8 - 25
= Gregorian 1582-10-15 was Julian 1582 - 10 - 5 (the reform skipped 1582-10-05..14)
= engine reads 1582-10-04 as Julian: true
= reform days are consecutive: true
= 2026-09-07 reads Julian 2026-08-25: true
*/

scripts.name: julian-centuries-since-j2000
scripts.title: the T of astronomy formulas
scripts.text:
/* ============================================================================
julian-centuries-since-j2000.epher -- the T of astronomy formulas

The time variable T = (jd - 2451545) / 36525: Julian centuries of
36525 days (100 Julian years of 365.25 days) since the J2000.0 epoch,
2000-01-01 12:00 UT (guide 1.16). Nearly every series in practical
astronomy - the VSOP87 planetary theory, the lunar theories, the
precession and nutation polynomials - is a polynomial in T, so one
script's first line is usually the one below. The examples were
verified against plain arithmetic in python, the oracle for the
expected output.

Knob: none - the epochs below are fixed.
============================================================================ */

// ---- model ------------------------------------------------------------------
def T(j) = (j - 2451545) / 36525

/* ---- results ----------------------------------------------------------------
The anchor epochs: J2000.0 itself is T = 0 by definition; 1950-01-01
is exactly half a Julian century before it, and 2050-01-01 exactly
half a century after. 2026-01-01 is 26 Julian years after 2000, and
26 * 365.25 = 9496.5 days is exactly 0.26 of a Julian century, so T
prints 0.26 exactly rather than a repeating decimal. The last line
is a mid-year epoch whose decimal repeats and so displays as the
exact fraction 9668/36525. */
print("J2000.0 (2000-01-01 12:00 UT):", T(jd(2000, 1, 1, 12)))
print("1950-01-01:", T(jd(1950, 1, 1)))
print("2026-01-01:", T(jd(2026, 1, 1)))
print("2050-01-01:", T(jd(2050, 1, 1)))
print("2026-06-21 12:00 UT:", T(jd(2026, 6, 21, 12)))

/* For a sense of scale: T reaches 1 exactly 36525 days (100 Julian
years) after J2000.0, but the Gregorian century is one day short
because 2100 is not a leap year, so 2100-01-01 sits at T = 0.999986.
(The March equinox of 2026 prints as the exact fraction 1129654133/459
in season-boundaries.epher - event JDs with repeating decimals show
as fractions, while 9668/36525 here happens to display as the
decimal 0.2646954141.) The solar-ephemeris crate that backs the
astronomy accessors stays arcsecond-class over roughly T = -50 to
+50, about 5000 years around the present (guide 1.16). */
print("2100-01-01:", T(jd(2100, 1, 1)))

/* ---- expected output ----
= J2000.0 (2000-01-01 12:00 UT): 0
= 1950-01-01: -0.5
= 2026-01-01: 0.26
= 2050-01-01: 0.5
= 2026-06-21 12:00 UT: 0.2646954141
= 2100-01-01: 0.999986310746
*/

scripts.name: julian-day-from-date
scripts.title: calendar dates as Julian Dates
scripts.text:
/* ============================================================================
julian-day-from-date.epher -- calendar dates as Julian Dates

Converts a few famous calendar dates to Julian Dates with the built-in
jd(y, m, d [, hr]) (guide 1.16), the count of days since 4713 BC
January 1, 12:00 UT (the epoch of the Julian Period). A JD is noon-
based: the .5 that ends so many values below is midnight, and
jd(2000, 1, 1, 12) = 2451545 defines the J2000.0 epoch that most
astronomy formulas count from. The inverse conversion, JD to calendar
date, is date-from-julian-day.epher in this folder, and the
difference of two JDs is the day count that days-between-dates.epher
prints. The dates here
are proleptic Gregorian (the calendar the Gregorian reform of 1582
defines for all years), matching the datetime module of python, which
is the oracle the expected output was checked against.

Knob: none - the dates below are fixed, famous ones.
============================================================================ */

/* ---- results ----------------------------------------------------------------
The J2000.0 epoch, the Unix epoch (1970-01-01 00:00 UT, whose JD
2440587.5 every POSIX clock counts seconds from), and the start of
the Gregorian calendar. Then two dates of 2026 and one with an hour
of day: jd(2026, 6, 21, 18) is 18:00 UT on the summer solstice date. */
print("J2000.0, 2000-01-01 12:00 UT:", jd(2000, 1, 1, 12))
print("Unix epoch, 1970-01-01:", jd(1970, 1, 1))
print("Gregorian adoption, 1582-10-15:", jd(1582, 10, 15))
print("2026-01-01:", jd(2026, 1, 1))
print("2026-12-31:", jd(2026, 12, 31))
print("2026-06-21 18:00 UT:", jd(2026, 6, 21, 18))

// Reading them back (guide 1.18): iso() prints a Julian Date as the
// ISO 8601 date-time in UT - the human-readable form of the number -
// and date() and time() give the same instant as a {year, month, day}
// and an {hour, minute, second}. The round trip closes: jd() of the
// date and clock is the JD again.
print("J2000.0 as a date-time:", iso(2451545))
print("J2000.0 date and clock:", date(2451545), time(2451545))
print("round trip:", jd(date(2451545)[1], date(2451545)[2], date(2451545)[3], (time(2451545)[1] + time(2451545)[2] / 60 + time(2451545)[3] / 3600)) == 2451545)
print("Unix epoch as a date-time:", iso(2440587.5))
print("Gregorian adoption as a date-time:", iso(2299160.5))
print("summer solstice 18:00 as a date-time:", iso(2461213.25))

// The Modified Julian Date shifts the zero point to 1858-11-17 and
// starts each day at midnight, so the .5 endings disappear: MJD = JD
// - 2400000.5. mjd takes the same year, month, day, hour arguments.
print("MJD of J2000.0:", mjd(2000, 1, 1, 12))
print("MJD of 2026-01-01:", mjd(2026, 1, 1))

/* ---- expected output ----
= J2000.0, 2000-01-01 12:00 UT: 2451545
= Unix epoch, 1970-01-01: 2440587.5
= Gregorian adoption, 1582-10-15: 2299160.5
= 2026-01-01: 2461041.5
= 2026-12-31: 2461405.5
= 2026-06-21 18:00 UT: 2461213.25
= J2000.0 as a date-time: 2000-01-01T12:00:00
= J2000.0 date and clock: {2000, 1, 1} {12, 0, 0}
= round trip: true
= Unix epoch as a date-time: 1970-01-01T00:00:00
= Gregorian adoption as a date-time: 1582-10-15T00:00:00
= summer solstice 18:00 as a date-time: 2026-06-21T18:00:00
= MJD of J2000.0: 51544.5
= MJD of 2026-01-01: 61041
*/

scripts.name: local-mean-time
scripts.title: clock time against the local sun
scripts.text:
/* ============================================================================
local-mean-time.epher -- clock time against the local sun

Shows the standing difference between zone (clock) time and local
mean time - the time a sundial keeps before the equation-of-time
correction - caused by longitude alone: the Sun crosses the local
meridian 4 minutes later for every degree of longitude west of the
zone's central meridian.  clock - LMT = zone - lon / 15  (hours).

Local mean time matters for the old solar observations and for
anyone comparing a sundial with a watch; the equation of time
(e.g. equation-of-time.epher) rides on top of this geometric
offset.

Accuracy: exact arithmetic; the zone offsets below are the standard
legal ones (no daylight saving - state that when quoting).

Knobs: the longitude and zone below (default: Greenwich).
============================================================================ */

// ---- the knobs -------------------------------------------------------------------------
const lon = -0.1278           // Greenwich, degrees east
const zone = 0                // UTC in winter

// ---- the offset ------------------------------------------------------------------------
const off = zone - lon / 15         // hours, clock minus LMT
print("longitude", lon, "deg east, zone UTC", zone)
print("clock - local mean time:", off, "hours =", off * 60, "minutes")

/* Self-check: a city on the zone's central meridian (lon = 15 *
zone) has zero offset by construction; the Beijing case below is
the classic: clock runs ~14 minutes ahead of the local sun. */
print("central meridian offset zero:", zone - (15 * zone) / 15 == 0)
print("Beijing (lon 116.4, zone +8) offset:", 8 - 116.4 / 15, "hours =", (8 - 116.4 / 15) * 60, "minutes")

/* ---- expected output ----
= longitude -0.1278 deg east, zone UTC 0
= clock - local mean time: 0.00852 hours = 0.5112 minutes
= central meridian offset zero: true
= Beijing (lon 116.4, zone +8) offset: 0.24 hours = 14.4 minutes
*/

scripts.name: local-sidereal-time
scripts.title: the hour angle of the stars
scripts.text:
/* ============================================================================
local-sidereal-time.epher -- the hour angle of the stars

Local sidereal time (LST) for one instant at two longitudes, from the
built-in lst(jd, lon), which returns hours east of the meridian
(guide 1.16; the solar-ephemeris crate, JPL-validated). LST is the
hour angle of the vernal equinox: the Earth-fixed sky coordinate that
says which stars are up. It gains 360 deg per sidereal day, and the
sidereal day (23.9345 h) is shorter than the solar day because the
Earth must turn a little extra each day to face the Sun again - so a
given star rises about 3.94 min earlier every night, and LST at a
fixed clock hour gains the same amount. Two built-in checks close the
script: LST grows eastward by exactly lon / 15 hours, and at the
Sun's meridian transit the LST equals the Sun's right ascension (the
gap of about 2 arcsec is the equation of equinoxes, mean versus
apparent sidereal time).

Knobs: the instant, the two longitudes, latitude for the transit.
============================================================================ */

// ---- the knobs ---------------------------------------------------------------
const t0 = jd(2026, 6, 21, 12)     // 12:00 UT on the solstice date
const lon_b = 13.405               // Berlin
const lon_g = 0                    // Greenwich
const lat = 52.52                  // Berlin, for the Sun transit check

/* ---- results ----------------------------------------------------------------
The same physical instant, read at Greenwich (lon 0) and at Berlin,
13.405 deg east: Berlin's sky is ahead by 13.405 / 15 = 0.8937 hours.
As a clock reading, deg2hms of the hours times 15 (guide 1.16). */
print("LST at Greenwich:", lst(t0, lon_g) in hr)
print("LST at Berlin:", lst(t0, lon_b) in hr)
print("eastward gain:", (lst(t0, lon_b) - lst(t0, lon_g)) in hr, "= lon / 15:", (lon_b / 15) in hr)
print("Berlin, as a clock:", deg2hms(lst(t0, lon_b) * 15))

/* The sidereal drift: 24 solar hours later, at 0h UT on June 22, LST at
Greenwich has gained 0.0657 h = 3.94 min - the stars rise 3.94 min
earlier each night, because a solar day holds 24 * 366.25 / 365.25 =
24.0657 sidereal hours (the Earth spins 366.25 times per year). */
print("LST gain over 24 h:", (lst(jd(2026, 6, 22), lon_g) - lst(jd(2026, 6, 21), lon_g)) in hr)

// The Sun check: at solar transit the Sun stands on the meridian, so
// its hour angle is zero and LST must equal the Sun's right ascension.
// The residual, about 2 arcsec, is the equation of equinoxes.
print("LST * 15 at solar transit:", lst(transit(10, jd(2026, 6, 21), lat, lon_b), lon_b) * 15, "deg")
print("Sun RA at that instant:", ra(10, transit(10, jd(2026, 6, 21), lat, lon_b)), "deg")
print("gap:", (ra(10, transit(10, jd(2026, 6, 21), lat, lon_b)) - lst(transit(10, jd(2026, 6, 21), lat, lon_b), lon_b) * 15) * 3600, "arcsec")

/* ---- expected output ----
= LST at Greenwich: 5.98008964453 hr
= LST at Berlin: 6.8737563112 hr
= eastward gain: 0.893666666667 hr = lon / 15: 0.893666666667 hr
= Berlin, as a clock: 6h 52m 26s
= LST gain over 24 h: 0.0657092126912 hr
= LST * 15 at solar transit: 90.1171104235 deg
= Sun RA at that instant: 90.117670936 deg
= gap: 2.01784510509 arcsec
*/

scripts.name: unix-time
scripts.title: Unix seconds and Julian dates
scripts.text:
/* ============================================================================
unix-time.epher -- Unix seconds and Julian dates

Converts between the Unix time scale (seconds since 1970-01-01
00:00:00 UTC, the clock of every computer) and the Julian Date used
throughout this script collection. The anchor is the epoch

  JD(1970-01-01 00:00:00 UTC) = 2440587.5

so unix = (jd - 2440587.5) * 86400 and back. The engine's jd()
accepts fractional hours, so the round trip below goes through
12:34:56.64 without loss.

Accuracy: exact for any instant (pure arithmetic on the engine's
JD); before 1970 the seconds simply read negative.

Knobs: the instant below.
============================================================================ */

// ---- the knobs -------------------------------------------------------------------------
const tm = jd(2026, 9, 10, 12.5824)   // 12:34:56.64 UT

// ---- the conversions ----------------------------------------------------------------------
const ux = (tm - 2440587.5) * 86400
const t2 = 2440587.5 + ux / 86400

print("instant:", iso(tm))
print("unix seconds:", ux)
print("back-converted unix seconds:", (t2 - 2440587.5) * 86400)
print("round-trip JD difference:", t2 - tm, "d")

/* Self-checks: the epoch identity and a full round trip must both
be exact. */
print("epoch JD is 2440587.5:", jd(1970, 1, 1) == 2440587.5)
print("round trip exact:", t2 == tm)
print("unix seconds of the epoch:", (jd(1970, 1, 1) - 2440587.5) * 86400)

/* ---- expected output ----
= instant: 2026-09-10T12:34:57
= unix seconds: 1789043696.64
= back-converted unix seconds: 1789043696.64
= round-trip JD difference: 0 d
= epoch JD is 2440587.5: true
= round trip exact: true
= unix seconds of the epoch: 0
*/

scripts.name: chain-rule-check
scripts.title: derivative of exp(x^2), first and second
scripts.text:
/* ============================================================================
chain-rule-check.epher -- derivative of exp(x^2), first and second

For g(x) = exp(x^2) the chain rule gives g'(x) = 2x exp(x^2) and,
differentiating once more, g''(x) = (2 + 4x^2) exp(x^2) (Stewart,
"Calculus", 8th ed., sec. 3.4). The builtin derivative is numeric, so
the checks compare with the rules applied by hand at three points.

The builtin also nests: derivative(derivative(h(x), x), p) numerically
differentiates twice. It works, but each numeric pass costs about
1e-9 of relative accuracy, so the second-derivative residuals below
are checked at 1e-7 and 1e-6 rather than 1e-9.

Accuracy: first-derivative residuals are under 1e-9; the nested
second derivative of x^3 at 2 lands within 1.2e-8 of 12, and of
exp(x^2) at 0.5 within 6.2e-8 of (2 + 4x^2) exp(x^2) = 3 exp(0.25).

No knobs: the points are the demonstration.
============================================================================ */

// ---- helpers ----------------------------------------------------------------
def g(x) = exp(x^2)
def gp(x) = 2*x*exp(x^2)              // chain rule: g' = 2x exp(x^2)
def gpp(x) = (2 + 4*x^2)*exp(x^2)     // g'' by the product rule on g'

// ---- first derivative at p = 0.5, 1 and 1.5 ---------------------------------
print("from the builtin:", derivative(g(x), 0.5))
print("by hand:", gp(0.5))
print("they agree:", abs(derivative(g(x), 0.5) - gp(0.5)) < 1e-9)
print("from the builtin:", derivative(g(x), 1))
print("by hand:", gp(1))
print("they agree:", abs(derivative(g(x), 1) - gp(1)) < 1e-9)
print("from the builtin:", derivative(g(x), 1.5))
print("by hand:", gp(1.5))
print("they agree:", abs(derivative(g(x), 1.5) - gp(1.5)) < 1e-9)

// ---- nested second derivative: d^2/dx^2 x^3 = 6x, checked at x = 2 ----------
print("from the builtin:", derivative(derivative(x^3, x), 2))
print("exact:", 12)
print("they agree:", abs(derivative(derivative(x^3, x), 2) - 12) < 1e-7)

// ---- nested second derivative of exp(x^2) at x = 0.5 ------------------------
print("from the builtin:", derivative(derivative(g(x), x), 0.5))
print("by hand:", gpp(0.5))
print("they agree:", abs(derivative(derivative(g(x), x), 0.5) - gpp(0.5)) < 1e-6)

/* ---- expected output ---------------------------------------------------------
= from the builtin: 1.28402541669
= by hand: 1.28402541669
= they agree: true
= from the builtin: 5.43656365692
= by hand: 5.43656365692
= they agree: true
= from the builtin: 28.4632075091
= by hand: 28.4632075091
= they agree: true
= from the builtin: 12.0000000114
= exact: 12
= they agree: true
= from the builtin: 3.85207625
= by hand: 3.85207625006
= they agree: true
*/

scripts.name: derivative-of-sin-check
scripts.title: derivative(sin x) against cos x
scripts.text:
/* ============================================================================
derivative-of-sin-check.epher -- derivative(sin x) against cos x

If the builtin derivative does its job, derivative(sin(x), p) should
match cos(p) at every point p: that is the identity d/dx sin x = cos x
(Stewart, "Calculus", 8th ed., sec. 3.3). The builtin derivative is a
numeric central difference, so the comparison is the honest one: each
line pairs the computed slope with cos(p) and prints a boolean
residual check at 1e-9.

The four sample points (0.3, 1, 2 and pi/2) are ordinary arguments,
including one where cos(p) itself is nearly zero (at pi/2 the exact
slope of sin x is 0, and the numeric value is about 7e-14).

Accuracy: every residual below is well under 1e-9; at p = pi/2 the
absolute residual is about 7.2e-14.

No knobs: the four points are the demonstration.
============================================================================ */

// ---- at p = 0.3 -------------------------------------------------------------
print("from the builtin:", derivative(sin(x), 0.3))
print("cos of the same point:", cos(0.3))
print("they agree:", abs(derivative(sin(x), 0.3) - cos(0.3)) < 1e-9)

// ---- at p = 1 ---------------------------------------------------------------
print("from the builtin:", derivative(sin(x), 1))
print("cos of the same point:", cos(1))
print("they agree:", abs(derivative(sin(x), 1) - cos(1)) < 1e-9)

// ---- at p = 2 ---------------------------------------------------------------
print("from the builtin:", derivative(sin(x), 2))
print("cos of the same point:", cos(2))
print("they agree:", abs(derivative(sin(x), 2) - cos(2)) < 1e-9)

// ---- at p = pi/2, where the exact slope is 0 --------------------------------
print("from the builtin:", derivative(sin(x), pi/2))
print("cos of the same point:", cos(pi/2))
print("they agree:", abs(derivative(sin(x), pi/2) - cos(pi/2)) < 1e-9)

/* ---- expected output ---------------------------------------------------------
= from the builtin: 0.955336489126
= cos of the same point: 0.955336489126
= they agree: true
= from the builtin: 0.540302305868
= cos of the same point: 0.540302305868
= they agree: true
= from the builtin: -0.416146836547
= cos of the same point: -0.416146836547
= they agree: true
= from the builtin: -0.0000000000000719765968398
= cos of the same point: 0.0000000000000000612323399574
= they agree: true
*/

scripts.name: extrema-of-a-cubic
scripts.title: classify the extrema of x^3 - 3x
scripts.text:
/* ============================================================================
extrema-of-a-cubic.epher -- classify the extrema of x^3 - 3x

Standard calculus routine (Stewart, "Calculus", 8th ed., sec. 4.3):
find the critical points where f'(x) = 0, then classify each with the
second derivative. For f(x) = x^3 - 3x:

  f'(x) = 3x^2 - 3, so the critical points solve 3x^2 - 3 = 0.
  f''(x) = 6x: negative at x = -1 (local maximum), positive at
  x = 1 (local minimum).

The builtin solve finds the roots of the polynomial equation (the
equation is the analytic derivative, written by hand); the factored
form 3(x - 1)(x + 1) gives the same two roots for the checks below.
The builtin numeric derivative confirms that the slope really is 0
at both critical points.

Accuracy: f values and second derivatives at the roots are exact;
the numeric slope at the roots is about 1e-12, checked at 1e-9.

No knobs: the cubic is the demonstration.
============================================================================ */

// ---- helpers ----------------------------------------------------------------
def f(x) = x^3 - 3*x
def fpp(x) = 6*x                    // second derivative, by hand

// ---- critical points: solve the analytic derivative 3x^2 - 3 = 0 ------------
solve 3*x^2 - 3 == 0

// ---- classification by the second derivative at each root -------------------
print("f'' at -1:", fpp(-1), "negative, so a local maximum")
print("f'' at 1:", fpp(1), "positive, so a local minimum")
print("local maximum f(-1):", f(-1))
print("local minimum f(1):", f(1))

// ---- confirm: the numeric slope is 0 at both critical points ----------------
print("slope is 0 at the maximum:", abs(derivative(f(x), -1)) < 1e-9)
print("slope is 0 at the minimum:", abs(derivative(f(x), 1)) < 1e-9)

/* ---- expected output ---------------------------------------------------------
= x = -1, x = 1
= f'' at -1: -6 negative, so a local maximum
= f'' at 1: 6 positive, so a local minimum
= local maximum f(-1): 2
= local minimum f(1): -2
= slope is 0 at the maximum: true
= slope is 0 at the minimum: true
*/

scripts.name: product-rule-check
scripts.title: derivative of x^2 sin(x) vs the product rule
scripts.text:
/* ============================================================================
product-rule-check.epher -- derivative of x^2 sin(x) vs the product rule

For f(x) = x^2 sin(x) the product rule gives f'(x) = 2x sin(x) +
x^2 cos(x) (Stewart, "Calculus", 8th ed., sec. 3.2). The builtin
derivative works on one expression in one free variable, so the check
writes the product directly inside derivative(f(x), p) and compares
with the rule applied by hand at three points.

The three points (0.7, 1.5, 2.5) exercise the rule away from the
origin, where neither term of the product dominates.

Accuracy: the boolean residuals are checked at 1e-9; the largest of
the three is about 2e-12.

No knobs: the three points are the demonstration.
============================================================================ */

// ---- helpers ----------------------------------------------------------------
def f(x) = x^2*sin(x)
def fp(x) = 2*x*sin(x) + x^2*cos(x)   // product rule: f' = u'v + uv'

// ---- at p = 0.7 -------------------------------------------------------------
print("from the builtin:", derivative(f(x), 0.7))
print("by hand:", fp(0.7))
print("they agree:", abs(derivative(f(x), 0.7) - fp(0.7)) < 1e-9)

// ---- at p = 1.5 -------------------------------------------------------------
print("from the builtin:", derivative(f(x), 1.5))
print("by hand:", fp(1.5))
print("they agree:", abs(derivative(f(x), 1.5) - fp(1.5)) < 1e-9)

// ---- at p = 2.5 -------------------------------------------------------------
print("from the builtin:", derivative(f(x), 2.5))
print("by hand:", fp(2.5))
print("they agree:", abs(derivative(f(x), 2.5) - fp(2.5)) < 1e-9)

/* ---- expected output ---------------------------------------------------------
= from the builtin: 1.2766774339
= by hand: 1.2766774339
= they agree: true
= from the builtin: 3.15164366357
= by hand: 3.15164366356
= they agree: true
= from the builtin: -2.01478687665
= by hand: -2.01478687665
= they agree: true
*/

scripts.name: slope-at-a-point
scripts.title: the builtin derivative vs textbook rules
scripts.text:
/* ============================================================================
slope-at-a-point.epher -- the builtin derivative vs textbook rules

derivative(f(x), p) evaluates the numeric derivative of an expression
at a point p (a central difference, not a symbolic rule: the variable
is the free variable of the expression, here x). This script checks
five power, root, log and exponential slopes against their textbook
derivatives, written out by hand next to each result.

The derivative rules checked are the power rule (x^2 -> 2x, x^3 ->
3x^2), the root rule (sqrt(x) -> 1/(2 sqrt(x))), the logarithm rule
(ln x -> 1/x) and the exponential rule (e^x -> e^x), all in Stewart,
"Calculus", 8th ed., ch. 3.

Accuracy: each boolean asks for agreement to 1e-9; at these points
the numeric derivative agrees to about 1e-12 or better (it is exact
at the displayed precision for polynomials at integer points).

No knobs: the five (function, point) pairs are the demonstration.
============================================================================ */

// ---- helpers: the analytic derivatives, for comparison ----------------------
def fp_sq(x) = 2*x
def fp_cb(x) = 3*x^2
def fp_rt(x) = 1/(2*sqrt(x))
def fp_ln(x) = 1/x
def fp_ex(x) = e^x

// ---- power rule: d/dx x^2 at x = 3 is 2x = 6 --------------------------------
print("from the builtin:", derivative(x^2, 3))
print("by hand:", fp_sq(3))
print("they agree:", abs(derivative(x^2, 3) - fp_sq(3)) < 1e-9)

// ---- power rule: d/dx x^3 at x = 2 is 3x^2 = 12 -----------------------------
print("from the builtin:", derivative(x^3, 2))
print("by hand:", fp_cb(2))
print("they agree:", abs(derivative(x^3, 2) - fp_cb(2)) < 1e-9)

// ---- root rule: d/dx sqrt(x) at x = 4 is 1/(2 sqrt(4)) = 1/4 ----------------
print("from the builtin:", derivative(sqrt(x), 4))
print("by hand:", fp_rt(4))
print("they agree:", abs(derivative(sqrt(x), 4) - fp_rt(4)) < 1e-9)

// ---- log rule: d/dx ln(x) at x = 5 is 1/5 -----------------------------------
print("from the builtin:", derivative(ln(x), 5))
print("by hand:", fp_ln(5))
print("they agree:", abs(derivative(ln(x), 5) - fp_ln(5)) < 1e-9)

// ---- exponential rule: d/dx e^x at x = 1 is e -------------------------------
print("from the builtin:", derivative(e^x, 1))
print("by hand:", fp_ex(1))
print("they agree:", abs(derivative(e^x, 1) - fp_ex(1)) < 1e-9)

/* ---- expected output ---------------------------------------------------------
= from the builtin: 6
= by hand: 6
= they agree: true
= from the builtin: 12
= by hand: 12
= they agree: true
= from the builtin: 0.25
= by hand: 0.25
= they agree: true
= from the builtin: 0.2
= by hand: 0.2
= they agree: true
= from the builtin: 2.71828182846
= by hand: 2.71828182846
= they agree: true
*/

scripts.name: tangent-line
scripts.title: the tangent line to y = x^2 at x = 2
scripts.text:
/* ============================================================================
tangent-line.epher -- the tangent line to y = x^2 at x = 2

The tangent line to y = f(x) at x = a is y = f(a) + f'(a)(x - a)
(Stewart, "Calculus", 8th ed., sec. 2.7). For f(x) = x^2 at a = 2 the
slope f'(2) = 4 comes from the builtin numeric derivative, and the
line is y = 4x - 4. The script checks the line where it must hold
exactly (at x = 2) and where it only approximates: 0.5 away, at
x = 2.5, the parabola has risen 6.25 while the tangent says 6. The
gap is the square of the offset: f(2 + d) - L(2 + d) = d^2 = 0.25.

Accuracy: the slope prints exactly 4; all checks are exact decimal
arithmetic at the displayed precision.

The knob to edit is `a`, the point of tangency.
============================================================================ */

// ---- the knob ---------------------------------------------------------------
const a = 2

// ---- helpers ----------------------------------------------------------------
def f(x) = x^2
def fp(x) = 2*x
def tangent(x) = f(a) + fp(a)*(x - a)   // tangent line at x = a

// ---- the slope at x = 2, from the builtin derivative and by hand ------------
print("slope at x = 2:", derivative(x^2, a), "by the power rule:", fp(a))
print("they agree:", abs(derivative(x^2, a) - fp(a)) < 1e-9)

// ---- the line y = 4x - 4, evaluated at x = 2 and x = 2.5 --------------------
print("tangent at x = 2:", tangent(a), "parabola there:", f(a))
print("tangent at x = 2.5:", tangent(2.5), "line formula:", 4*2.5 - 4)
print("parabola at x = 2.5:", f(2.5))
print("gap f - tangent at 2.5:", f(2.5) - tangent(2.5))
print("tangent and curve meet at the point of tangency:", abs(tangent(a) - f(a)) < 1e-12)

/* ---- expected output ---------------------------------------------------------
= slope at x = 2: 4 by the power rule: 4
= they agree: true
= tangent at x = 2: 4 parabola there: 4
= tangent at x = 2.5: 6 line formula: 6
= parabola at x = 2.5: 6.25
= gap f - tangent at 2.5: 0.25
= tangent and curve meet at the point of tangency: true
*/

scripts.name: arc-length-of-parabola
scripts.title: length of y = x^2 from x = 0 to 1
scripts.text:
/* ============================================================================
arc-length-of-parabola.epher -- length of y = x^2 from x = 0 to 1

The arc length formula (Stewart, "Calculus", 8th ed., sec. 8.1) for
y = f(x) on [a, b] is integral(sqrt(1 + (dy/dx)^2), a, b). Here
y = x^2, so dy/dx = 2x and the integrand is sqrt(1 + 4x^2):

  length = integral(sqrt(1 + (2*x)^2), 0, 1)

which the adaptive Simpson builtin evaluates numerically. The closed
form, from the integral of sqrt(1 + 4x^2) with the substitution
x = (1/2) sinh(u), is [ x sqrt(1 + 4x^2)/2 + asinh(2x)/4 ] from 0 to
1 = sqrt(5)/2 + asinh(2)/4, printed underneath for comparison.

Accuracy: the builtin value and the closed form agree to about
5e-12; both are checked at 1e-9.

No knobs: the arc from x = 0 to x = 1 is the demonstration.
============================================================================ */

// ---- the arc length by the builtin integral ---------------------------------
print("arc length by the builtin:", integral(sqrt(1 + (2*x)^2), 0, 1))

// ---- the closed form sqrt(5)/2 + asinh(2)/4, for comparison -----------------
print("closed form:", sqrt(5)/2 + asinh(2)/4)
print("they agree:", abs(integral(sqrt(1 + (2*x)^2), 0, 1) - (sqrt(5)/2 + asinh(2)/4)) < 1e-9)

/* ---- expected output ---------------------------------------------------------
= arc length by the builtin: 1.47894285754
= closed form: 1.47894285754
= they agree: true
*/

scripts.name: area-between-curves
scripts.title: the area between y = x and y = x^2
scripts.text:
/* ============================================================================
area-between-curves.epher -- the area between y = x and y = x^2

The area between two curves is the integral of (top curve minus
bottom curve) over the interval where the top stays on top (Stewart,
"Calculus", 8th ed., sec. 6.1). On [0, 1] the line y = x lies above
the parabola y = x^2 (they meet at x = 0 and x = 1), so:

  area = integral(x - x^2, 0, 1) = 1/2 - 1/3 = 1/6

The adaptive Simpson builtin is exact on this quadratic integrand,
and 1/6 is a repeating decimal, so epher prints the exact fraction
1/6. The same area built from the two separate integrals agrees:
integral(x, 0, 1) - integral(x^2, 0, 1).

Accuracy: exact at the displayed precision.

No knobs: the interval [0, 1] is the demonstration.
============================================================================ */

// ---- the area as one integral of top minus bottom ---------------------------
print("area as one integral:", integral(x - x^2, 0, 1))
print("exactly 1/6:", abs(integral(x - x^2, 0, 1) - 1/6) < 1e-12)

// ---- the same area as two integrals, 1/2 - 1/3 ------------------------------
print("the same area as two integrals:", integral(x, 0, 1) - integral(x^2, 0, 1))

/* ---- expected output ---------------------------------------------------------
= area as one integral: 1/6
= exactly 1/6: true
= the same area as two integrals: 1/6
*/

scripts.name: average-value-of-function
scripts.title: mean value of a function on [a, b]
scripts.text:
/* ============================================================================
average-value-of-function.epher -- mean value of a function on [a, b]

The average value of f on [a, b] is integral(f, a, b)/(b - a)
(Stewart, "Calculus", 8th ed., sec. 6.5). The mean value theorem then
guarantees some c in (a, b) with f(c) equal to that average; for
f(x) = x^2 on [0, 3] the average is 9/3 = 3 and the point is
const c = sqrt(3), where x^2 = 3 again.

A second check uses sin on [0, pi]: the average is 2/pi, about
0.63662, since one arch of sine encloses area 2.

Accuracy: exact at the displayed precision (the average of x^2 on
[0, 3] prints exactly 3).

No knobs: the two examples are the demonstration.
============================================================================ */

// ---- helpers: average values, by the textbook formula -----------------------
def avg_sq(a, b) = integral(x^2, a, b)/(b - a)
def avg_sin(a, b) = integral(sin(x), a, b)/(b - a)

// ---- f(x) = x^2 on [0, 3]: average 3, attained at c = sqrt(3) ---------------
print("average of x^2 on [0, 3]:", avg_sq(0, 3))
print("point c with f(c) = average:", sqrt(3))
print("f(sqrt(3)):", (sqrt(3))^2)
print("f(c) equals the average:", abs((sqrt(3))^2 - avg_sq(0, 3)) < 1e-9)

// ---- sin on [0, pi]: average 2/pi -------------------------------------------
print("average of sin on [0, pi]:", avg_sin(0, pi))
print("2/pi for comparison:", 2/pi)
print("they agree:", abs(avg_sin(0, pi) - 2/pi) < 1e-9)

/* ---- expected output ---------------------------------------------------------
= average of x^2 on [0, 3]: 3
= point c with f(c) = average: 1.73205080757
= f(sqrt(3)): 3
= f(c) equals the average: true
= average of sin on [0, pi]: 0.636619772368
= 2/pi for comparison: 0.636619772368
= they agree: true
*/

scripts.name: definite-integral-demo
scripts.title: the builtin integral vs exact values
scripts.text:
/* ============================================================================
definite-integral-demo.epher -- the builtin integral vs exact values

integral(expr, a, b) is the adaptive Simpson definite integral of an
expression in its free variable, from a to b. Adaptive Simpson is
exact (up to rounding) on polynomials of degree 3 or less, which is
why the polynomial results print as exact numbers and fractions:

  integral(x^2, 0, 3) = 3^3/3 = 9        (power rule)
  integral(x^3, 0, 2) = 2^4/4 = 4        (power rule)
  integral(x^2, 1, 2) = 8/3 - 1/3 = 7/3  (prints as the fraction 7/3)

and sin is handled by Simpson's own refinement:

  integral(sin(x), 0, pi) = 2            (one full arch of sine)

The interval direction follows the convention of the fundamental
theorem: integral(x^2, 3, 0) = -9, reversing the limits.

Accuracy: each value below is exact at the displayed precision; the
endpoints are the standard Stewart, "Calculus", 8th ed., ch. 5
examples.

No knobs: the five integrals are the demonstration.
============================================================================ */

// ---- polynomial integrands: exact by the power rule -------------------------
print("integral of x^2 on [0, 3]:", integral(x^2, 0, 3))
print("integral of x^3 on [0, 2]:", integral(x^3, 0, 2))
print("integral of x^2 on [1, 2]:", integral(x^2, 1, 2))

// ---- trigonometric integrand: one arch of sine ------------------------------
print("one arch of sine:", integral(sin(x), 0, pi))

// ---- reversed limits change the sign ----------------------------------------
print("reversed limits:", integral(x^2, 3, 0))

/* ---- expected output ---------------------------------------------------------
= integral of x^2 on [0, 3]: 9
= integral of x^3 on [0, 2]: 4
= integral of x^2 on [1, 2]: 7/3
= one arch of sine: 2
= reversed limits: -9
*/

scripts.name: integral-of-sine-over-full-period
scripts.title: orthogonality on [0, 2 pi]
scripts.text:
/* ============================================================================
integral-of-sine-over-full-period.epher -- orthogonality on [0, 2 pi]

Over one full period the arch of sine above the axis balances the
arch below it, so integral(sin(x), 0, 2*pi) = 0; the builtin returns
about -1.7e-17, which is zero to its precision. The deeper statement
is orthogonality (Fourier series groundwork, Stewart, "Calculus",
8th ed., sec. 7.2):

  integral(sin(x)^2, 0, 2*pi) = pi        (mean of sin^2 is 1/2)
  integral(sin(x)*cos(x), 0, 2*pi) = 0    (sin and cos are orthogonal)

Accuracy: sin(x) integrates to about 1.7e-17 and sin(x)*cos(x) to
about 3.2e-16 (both checked at 1e-9); sin(x)^2 prints as pi to the
displayed digits.

No knobs: one full period is the demonstration.
============================================================================ */

// ---- sine over a full period is 0, to the builtin's precision ---------------
print("sine over a full period:", integral(sin(x), 0, 2*pi))
print("zero to the builtin's precision:", abs(integral(sin(x), 0, 2*pi)) < 1e-9)

// ---- sin^2 over a full period is pi -----------------------------------------
print("sin^2 over a full period:", integral(sin(x)^2, 0, 2*pi))
print("it is pi:", abs(integral(sin(x)^2, 0, 2*pi) - pi) < 1e-9)

// ---- sin times cos over a full period is 0: orthogonality -------------------
print("sin times cos over a full period:", integral(sin(x)*cos(x), 0, 2*pi))
print("orthogonal, so zero:", abs(integral(sin(x)*cos(x), 0, 2*pi)) < 1e-9)

/* ---- expected output ---------------------------------------------------------
= sine over a full period: -0.0000000000000000170992950553
= zero to the builtin's precision: true
= sin^2 over a full period: 3.14159265359
= it is pi: true
= sin times cos over a full period: 0.000000000000000324886606051
= orthogonal, so zero: true
*/

scripts.name: substitution-check
scripts.title: integral of 2x exp(x^2) equals e - 1
scripts.text:
/* ============================================================================
substitution-check.epher -- integral of 2x exp(x^2) equals e - 1

The substitution u = x^2 (du = 2x dx) turns the integral into a
one-liner (Stewart, "Calculus", 8th ed., sec. 5.5):

  integral(2*x*exp(x^2), 0, 1) = integral(e^u, 0, 1) = e - 1

because 2x exp(x^2) is exactly the derivative of exp(x^2): the
integrand is already in the form f'(x) e^(f(x)) with f(x) = x^2.
The builtin integral is numeric (it does not substitute symbolically),
so the check is: evaluate the substituted integral integral(e^x, 0, 1)
and the original one, and compare both with e - 1.

Accuracy: all three values agree to about 1e-15 at the displayed
precision; the boolean residual is checked at 1e-6.

No knobs: the interval [0, 1] is the demonstration.
============================================================================ */

// ---- the original integral: integrand 2x exp(x^2) on [0, 1] -----------------
print("the original integral:", integral(2*x*exp(x^2), 0, 1))

// ---- after u = x^2 the same integral is integral(e^x, 0, 1) = e - 1 ---------
print("after the substitution:", integral(e^x, 0, 1))
print("the closed form:", e - 1)
print("they agree:", abs(integral(2*x*exp(x^2), 0, 1) - (e - 1)) < 1e-6)

/* ---- expected output ---------------------------------------------------------
= the original integral: 1.71828182846
= after the substitution: 1.71828182846
= the closed form: 1.71828182846
= they agree: true
*/

scripts.name: volume-of-revolution
scripts.title: y = x^2 spun around the x-axis, [0, 2]
scripts.text:
/* ============================================================================
volume-of-revolution.epher -- y = x^2 spun around the x-axis, [0, 2]

The disc method (Stewart, "Calculus", 8th ed., sec. 6.2): rotating
y = f(x) about the x-axis on [a, b] sweeps discs of radius f(x), so

  volume = pi * integral(f(x)^2, a, b).

For f(x) = x^2 on [0, 2] the integrand is (x^2)^2 = x^4 and the
volume is pi * integral(x^4, 0, 2) = pi * 2^5/5 = 32 pi / 5, about
20.106193. The exact value 32*pi/5 is printed beneath it for
comparison.

Accuracy: Simpson is exact on the polynomial x^4; the two printed
values agree to about 1e-15.

The knobs to edit are `a` and `b`, the ends of the interval.
============================================================================ */

// ---- the knobs --------------------------------------------------------------
const a = 0
const b = 2

// ---- volume by the disc method: pi times the integral of the radius^2 ------
print("volume by the disc method:", pi * integral(x^4, a, b))

// ---- the exact value 32 pi / 5, for comparison ------------------------------
print("exact:", 32*pi/5)
print("they agree:", abs(pi*integral(x^4, a, b) - 32*pi/5) < 1e-9)

/* ---- expected output ---------------------------------------------------------
= volume by the disc method: 20.106192983
= exact: 20.106192983
= they agree: true
*/

scripts.name: limit-of-ln1plusx-over-x
scripts.title: ln(1 + xv)/xv tends to 1 at xv = 0
scripts.text:
/* ============================================================================
limit-of-ln1plusx-over-x.epher -- ln(1 + xv)/xv tends to 1 at xv = 0

The standard limit ln(1 + xv)/xv -> 1 as xv -> 0 (Stewart, "Calculus",
8th ed., sec. 3.8 exercises): it is the derivative of ln xv at xv = 1.
Probed at xv = 1e-2, 1e-4 and 1e-8; the last sample trails 1 by about
1.1e-8 because adding xv to 1 rounds at the 16th decimal digit, which
then divides back out only approximately.

The builtin derivative of ln at 1 is the same limit, so it is printed
as a cross-check.

Accuracy: samples print at about the 12th digit; the deficit at
xv = 1e-8 is an artifact of rounding 1 + xv, not of the limit.

The knob to edit is `xv` below.
============================================================================ */

// ---- the knob ---------------------------------------------------------------
const xv = 1e-8

// ---- ln(1 + xv)/xv at the three sample sizes ----------------------------------
print("the ratio at the knob:", ln(1 + xv)/xv)
for t in {1e-2, 1e-4, xv} do ln(1 + t)/t
print("within 1e-6 of 1:", abs(ln(1 + xv)/xv - 1) < 1e-6)

// ---- cross-check: derivative of ln at 1, on a fresh variable t -------------
// (xv is bound by the knob above; t is free).
print("the same limit, as a derivative:", derivative(ln(t), 1))

/* ---- expected output ---------------------------------------------------------
= the ratio at the knob: 0.999999988923
= {0.995033085317, 0.999950003333, 0.999999988923}
= within 1e-6 of 1: true
= the same limit, as a derivative: 1
*/

scripts.name: limit-of-one-minus-cosx-over-x2
scripts.title: (1 - cos xv)/xv^2 tends to 1/2
scripts.text:
/* ============================================================================
limit-of-one-minus-cosx-over-x2.epher -- (1 - cos xv)/xv^2 tends to 1/2

The classic limit behind the derivative of cos xv (Stewart, "Calculus",
8th ed., sec. 2.6): (1 - cos xv)/xv^2 -> 1/2 as xv -> 0. Direct numeric
evaluation is treacherous: below xv ~ 1e-7 the subtraction 1 - cos xv
cancels completely (at xv = 1e-8 it prints 0). At xv = 1e-2 to 1e-4 the
ratio approaches 1/2 with a truncation error of order xv^2/24.

The double-angle identity 1 - cos xv = 2 sin^2(xv/2) rewrites the ratio
as 2 sin^2(xv/2)/xv^2, a form that survives down to xv = 1e-8 and prints
1/2 exactly; that stable form is what any careful code should use.

Accuracy: values print at about the 12th digit; the identity form at
xv = 1e-8 is 1/2 to machine precision.

The knob to edit is `xv` below.
============================================================================ */

// ---- the knob ---------------------------------------------------------------
const xv = 1e-8

// ---- direct form at xv = 1e-8: 1 - cos(xv) cancels to 0 -----------------------
print("the direct form:", (1 - cos(xv))/xv^2)

// ---- larger xv: the ratio closes in on 1/2 -----------------------------------
for t in {1e-2, 1e-3, 1e-4} do (1 - cos(t))/t^2
print("closes in on 1/2:", abs((1 - cos(1e-4))/(1e-4)^2 - 1/2) < 1e-8)

// ---- stable double-angle form 2 sin^2(xv/2)/xv^2 at xv = 1e-8 ------------------
print("the stable double-angle form:", 2*sin(xv/2)^2/xv^2)

/* ---- expected output ---------------------------------------------------------
= the direct form: 0
= {0.499995833347, 0.499999958326, 0.499999996961}
= closes in on 1/2: true
= the stable double-angle form: 0.5
*/

scripts.name: limit-of-one-plus-one-over-n
scripts.title: the sequence that defines e
scripts.text:
/* ============================================================================
limit-of-one-plus-one-over-n.epher -- the sequence that defines e

(1 + 1/n)^n approaches e as n grows (Stewart, "Calculus", 8th ed.,
sec. 6.2, where e is defined by this very limit). The sequence creeps
up toward e from below: 2.59 at n = 10, 2.718268... at n = 100000,
still about 1.4e-4 short of e = 2.718281828459...

A for loop over the n values collects the terms into one printed
list, and the last term is compared with the builtin constant e.

Accuracy: each term is printed as the calculator shows it; the gap
to e falls like e/(2n), so it is 1.4e-4 at n = 100000.

The knob to edit is `ns`, the sample sizes below.
============================================================================ */

// ---- the knob ---------------------------------------------------------------
const ns = {10, 100, 1000, 100000}

// ---- the terms (1 + 1/n)^n, one per n, as a collected list ------------------
for n in ns do (1 + 1/n)^n

// ---- e for comparison, and how far the last term still is from it -----------
print("the limit, e:", e)
print("the last term is within 1e-3 of it:", abs((1 + 1/100000)^100000 - e) < 1e-3)

/* ---- expected output ---------------------------------------------------------
= {2.5937424601, 2.70481382942, 2.71692393224, 2.71826823719}
= the limit, e: 2.71828182846
= the last term is within 1e-3 of it: true
*/

scripts.name: carbon-dating
scripts.title: age of a sample from its carbon-14 fraction
scripts.text:
/* ============================================================================
carbon-dating.epher -- age of a sample from its carbon-14 fraction

Radiocarbon dating (Libby, 1949; any archaeology text) reads the age
of a sample off the fraction of carbon-14 still in it. With decay
constant lambda = ln(2)/5730 per year (half-life 5730 years), the
fraction left after t years is e^(-lambda t), so the age is

  age = -ln(fraction) * 5730/ln(2)

The script ages three samples (50%, 25% and 90% of the original
carbon-14), checks the two textbook anchors (half left means 5730
years, a quarter left means 11460 years) and runs a round trip: a
sample that has decayed for 10000 years holds fraction 0.29829..., a
value the age formula sends back to 10000 years.

Assumptions, stated honestly: the decay constant is unchanged over
time, the sample's initial carbon-14 matched the atmosphere of its
day, and nothing was added or removed since (no contamination).

Accuracy: the anchors print exactly 5730 and 11460; the round trip
agrees to better than 1e-6 years.

The knob to edit is `thalf` (or the sample fractions in `fs`).
============================================================================ */

// ---- the knobs --------------------------------------------------------------
const thalf = 5730               // half-life of carbon-14, years
const fs = {0.5, 0.25, 0.9}      // fractions of carbon-14 left

// ---- helpers ----------------------------------------------------------------
def age(f) = -thalf*ln(f)/ln(2)          // sample age in years
def leftover(t) = e^(-ln(2)*t/thalf)     // fraction left after t years

// ---- ages of the three samples, as a collected list -------------------------
for f in fs do age(f)

// ---- the anchors: 50% left is 5730 years, 25% left is 11460 years -----------
print("anchor, half left:", abs(age(0.5) - 5730) < 1e-6)
print("anchor, a quarter left:", abs(age(0.25) - 2*thalf) < 1e-6)

// ---- round trip: 10000 years of decay, then back to 10000 years -------------
print("fraction left after 10000 years:", leftover(10000))
print("age of that fraction, years:", age(leftover(10000)))
print("the round trip closes:", abs(age(leftover(10000)) - 10000) < 1e-6)

/* ---- expected output ---------------------------------------------------------
= {5730, 11460, 870.97772544}
= anchor, half left: true
= anchor, a quarter left: true
= fraction left after 10000 years: 0.298292436424
= age of that fraction, years: 10000
= the round trip closes: true
*/

scripts.name: euler-method
scripts.title: Euler's method for y' = y on [0, 1]
scripts.text:
/* ============================================================================
euler-method.epher -- Euler's method for y' = y on [0, 1]

epher has no builtin ODE solver (derivative and integral work on
expressions, not initial-value problems), so the method is the
point. Euler's method steps along the slope field: from (t, y) with
y' = f(t, y), the next point is (t + h, y + h f(t, y)) (Stewart,
"Calculus", 8th ed., sec. 9.2; Burden and Faires, "Numerical
Analysis", ch. 5).

The packed while loop carries the state {t, y, step} in one list and
takes one Euler step per iteration; with h = 0.1 and y(0) = 1 the
value at t = 1 is (1.1)^10 = 2.5937424601, short of e = 2.71828...
Euler is a first-order method: halving h roughly halves the error
(0.12454 at h = 0.1, 0.06498 at h = 0.05).

Accuracy: the h = 0.1 result is exact to the printed digits; its
error against e is 0.124539368359, about (e/2) h as the theory of
the method predicts.

The knobs to edit are `h` and `steps` below.
============================================================================ */

// ---- the knobs --------------------------------------------------------------
const h = 0.1                  // step size
const steps = 10               // steps to reach t = 1

// ---- helpers ----------------------------------------------------------------
def slope(t, y) = y            // the equation: y' = y

// ---- one Euler run from t = 0 to t = 1, state {t, y, step} ------------------
v = {0, 1, 0}
while v[3] < steps do v = {v[1] + h, v[2] + h*slope(v[1], v[2]), v[3] + 1}
print("the state after the run:", v)
print("y(1) by Euler with h = 0.1:", v[2])
print("true value e:", e)
print("error:", e - v[2])

// ---- the same run at h = 0.05: the error nearly halves ----------------------
w = {0, 1, 0}
while w[3] < 20 do w = {w[1] + 0.05, w[2] + 0.05*slope(w[1], w[2]), w[3] + 1}
print("y(1) by Euler with h = 0.05:", w[2])
print("error:", e - w[2])
print("halving h halves the error:", e - w[2] < (e - v[2])/1.9)

/* ---- expected output ---------------------------------------------------------
= {0, 1, 0}
= the state after the run: {1, 2.5937424601, 10}
= y(1) by Euler with h = 0.1: 2.5937424601
= true value e: 2.71828182846
= error: 0.124539368359
= {0, 1, 0}
= y(1) by Euler with h = 0.05: 2.65329770514
= error: 0.0649841233146
= halving h halves the error: true
*/

scripts.name: exponential-growth
scripts.title: population with a constant growth rate
scripts.text:
/* ============================================================================
exponential-growth.epher -- population with a constant growth rate

The exponential model N(t) = N0 e^(r t) (Stewart, "Calculus", 8th
ed., sec. 3.8) describes a population whose rate of change is
proportional to its size, with N0 the initial size and r the growth
rate per year. The script tabulates N(t) for t = 0, 10, 25 and 50
years at r = 0.02 per year (2% per year) and recovers the doubling
time t2 = ln(2)/r: after t2 years the population has exactly
doubled, which the closing boolean checks.

Accuracy: values are printed as the calculator shows them; the
doubling-time check agrees with 2 N0 to about 1e-12.

The knobs to edit are `n0`, `r` and `ts` below.
============================================================================ */

// ---- the knobs --------------------------------------------------------------
const n0 = 1000
const r = 0.02                    // growth rate, per year
const ts = {0, 10, 25, 50}        // sample times, years

// ---- the model --------------------------------------------------------------
def grow(t) = n0*e^(r*t)

// ---- the population at each sample time, as a collected list ----------------
for t in ts do grow(t)

// ---- doubling time ln(2)/r, and the population there ------------------------
print("doubling time, years:", ln(2)/r)
print("population at the doubling time:", grow(ln(2)/r))
print("exactly doubled there:", abs(grow(ln(2)/r) - 2*n0) < 1e-6)

/* ---- expected output ---------------------------------------------------------
= {1000, 1221.40275816, 1648.7212707, 2718.28182846}
= doubling time, years: 34.657359028
= population at the doubling time: 2000
= exactly doubled there: true
*/

scripts.name: logistic-growth-model
scripts.title: growth with a carrying capacity
scripts.text:
/* ============================================================================
logistic-growth-model.epher -- growth with a carrying capacity

The logistic model (Verhulst, 1838; Stewart, "Calculus", 8th ed.,
sec. 9.4) describes a population that levels off at a carrying
capacity K instead of growing without bound:

  P(t) = K/(1 + A e^(-r t)),  with A = (K - P0)/P0

The knobs below model a population of 100 that grows at rate r =
0.1 per year toward capacity K = 1000, so A = 9. The script tabs
P(t), notes that P tends to K (after 100 years it is within 0.5 of
the capacity), and locates the half-capacity time ln(A)/r = 21.97
years, where P = K/2 = 500.

Accuracy: values print as the calculator shows them; the boolean
checks agree to better than 1e-9 at half capacity.

The knobs to edit are `K`, `p0`, `r` and `ts` below.
============================================================================ */

// ---- the knobs --------------------------------------------------------------
const K = 1000                 // carrying capacity
const p0 = 100                 // initial population
const r = 0.1                  // intrinsic growth rate, per year
const ts = {0, 20, 50, 100}    // sample times, years

// ---- the model --------------------------------------------------------------
const A = (K - p0)/p0          // shape constant, 9 with the knobs above
def pop(t) = K/(1 + A*e^(-r*t))

// ---- the population at each sample time, as a collected list ----------------
for t in ts do pop(t)

// ---- toward the carrying capacity, and the half-capacity time ---------------
print("gap to K after 100 years:", K - pop(100))
print("settled on the capacity:", abs(K - pop(100)) < 0.5)
print("half-capacity time ln(A)/r, years:", ln(A)/r)
print("population there:", pop(ln(A)/r))
print("half the capacity there:", abs(pop(ln(A)/r) - K/2) < 1e-6)

/* ---- expected output ---------------------------------------------------------
= {100, 450.853060379, 942.825618574, 999.591567517}
= gap to K after 100 years: 0.408432482608
= settled on the capacity: true
= half-capacity time ln(A)/r, years: 21.9722457734
= population there: 500
= half the capacity there: true
*/

scripts.name: newton-law-of-cooling
scripts.title: a cooling cup of coffee
scripts.text:
/* ============================================================================
newton-law-of-cooling.epher -- a cooling cup of coffee

Newton's law of cooling: the temperature gap to the room shrinks
exponentially, T(t) = Tenv + (T0 - Tenv) e^(-k t) (Stewart,
"Calculus", 8th ed., sec. 9.1 example). The script solves a small
puzzle: coffee brewed at 95 C cools to 70 C in 5 minutes in a 20 C
room.

  1. The rate constant k comes from that one observation:
     k = ln((T0 - Tenv)/(70 - Tenv))/5 = ln(1.5)/5 per minute.
  2. The temperature at 10 minutes follows from the model: 20 C +
     75 C e^(-10k) = 53.333... C (printed as the fraction 160/3).
  3. The time to reach a target temperature uses the closed form
     t = -ln((T - Tenv)/(T0 - Tenv))/k, inverted from the model by
     hand. No root finder is needed; solve() would only be required
     if the model could not be inverted.

The closing check feeds the computed time back into the model and
asks for the target temperature back.

Accuracy: k is good to about 1e-14 per minute; the closed-form time
to 40 C is 16.2992550228 minutes and the round trip agrees to
better than 1e-9.

The knobs to edit are `t0`, `tenv`, `obs_t` and `obs_temp` below.
============================================================================ */

// ---- the knobs --------------------------------------------------------------
const t0 = 95                  // coffee temperature at t = 0, C
const tenv = 20                // room temperature, C
const obs_t = 5                // the observation time, minutes
const obs_temp = 70            // temperature observed at obs_t, C

// ---- the rate constant from the one observation -----------------------------
const k = ln((t0 - tenv)/(obs_temp - tenv))/obs_t   // per minute

// ---- the model --------------------------------------------------------------
def cool(t) = tenv + (t0 - tenv)*e^(-k*t)

// ---- the observation reproduces, and 10 minutes is 160/3 C ------------------
print("rate constant k, per minute:", k)
print("temperature at 5 minutes:", cool(obs_t))
print("the observation is reproduced:", abs(cool(obs_t) - obs_temp) < 1e-9)
print("temperature at 10 minutes:", cool(10))

// ---- time to reach 40 C, from the inverted closed form ----------------------
def treach(target) = -ln((target - tenv)/(t0 - tenv))/k
print("time to reach 40 C, minutes:", treach(40))
print("temperature there, by the model:", cool(treach(40)))
print("the round trip lands on the target:", abs(cool(treach(40)) - 40) < 1e-6)

/* ---- expected output ---------------------------------------------------------
= rate constant k, per minute: 0.0810930216216
= temperature at 5 minutes: 70
= the observation is reproduced: true
= temperature at 10 minutes: 160/3
= time to reach 40 C, minutes: 16.2992550228
= temperature there, by the model: 40
= the round trip lands on the target: true
*/

scripts.name: radioactive-half-life
scripts.title: carbon-14 decay and its half-life
scripts.text:
/* ============================================================================
radioactive-half-life.epher -- carbon-14 decay and its half-life

Radioactive decay is exponential: the fraction left after time t is
e^(-lambda t), where lambda is the decay constant, and the half-life
is T = ln(2)/lambda, the time after which half remains (Stewart,
"Calculus", 8th ed., sec. 3.8; any nuclear physics text). Carbon-14
has the well-known half-life of 5730 years, so its decay constant is
const lambda = ln(2)/5730 per year.

The script builds lambda from the half-life knob, checks that the
fraction left after one and two half-lives is 1/2 and 1/4, computes
the fraction left after 10000 years (about 0.2983, or 29.83%), and
recovers the half-life from the decay constant by the formula above.

Accuracy: the recovered half-life prints as 5730 exactly; fractions
at 1, 2 and 10000 half-lives agree to better than 1e-12.

The knob to edit is `thalf` (use any isotope's half-life, same units).
============================================================================ */

// ---- the knob ---------------------------------------------------------------
const thalf = 5730                  // half-life of carbon-14, years

// ---- decay constant from the half-life -------------------------------------
const lam = ln(2)/thalf             // lambda = ln(2)/T, per year

// ---- helpers ----------------------------------------------------------------
def frac_left(t) = e^(-lam*t)            // fraction of nuclei left after t years

// ---- one and two half-lives: 1/2 and 1/4 remain -----------------------------
print("fraction after one half-life:", frac_left(thalf))
print("fraction after two half-lives:", frac_left(2*thalf))
print("one half-life checks out:", abs(frac_left(thalf) - 1/2) < 1e-9)

// ---- after 10000 years ------------------------------------------------------
print("fraction after 10000 years:", frac_left(10000))

// ---- the half-life recovered from the decay constant ------------------------
print("half-life from lambda, years:", ln(2)/lam)
print("it matches the knob:", abs(ln(2)/lam - thalf) < 1e-6)

/* ---- expected output ---------------------------------------------------------
= fraction after one half-life: 0.5
= fraction after two half-lives: 0.25
= one half-life checks out: true
= fraction after 10000 years: 0.298292436424
= half-life from lambda, years: 5730
= it matches the knob: true
*/

scripts.title: the classic RK4 method for y' = y on [0, 1]

scripts.name: dc-motor-speed-step
scripts.title: a motor's spin-up, predicted from its nameplate
scripts.text:
/* ============================================================================
dc-motor-speed-step.epher -- a motor's spin-up, predicted from its nameplate

A small DC motor obeys the first-order speed response
omega(t) = omega_ss (1 - e^(-t/tau)) with the mechanical time constant
tau = J R / (Kt Ke) -- rotor inertia times winding resistance over the
motor-constant square -- and no-load speed omega_ss = V / Ke. The
script predicts the spin-up for a 12 V step on a Kt = Ke = 0.05 motor.

Source: Franklin, Powell and Emami-Naeini, Feedback Control of Dynamic
Systems, ch. 2 (dynamic models: DC-motor transfer function, Kt, Ke,
J and R combining into a first-order lag); the same model in Ogata,
Modern Control Engineering, ch. 2.

Web/desktop: paste the whole file into the entry, press Enter.
============================================================================ */

// ---- knobs ------------------------------------------------------------------
const k_t = 0.05            // torque constant, N m / A
const k_e = 0.05            // back-EMF constant, V s / rad
const resistance = 1.0      // winding resistance, ohm
const rotor_j = 2.0e-4      // rotor inertia, kg m^2
const volts = 12            // the applied step, 12 V

// ---- model ------------------------------------------------------------------
const tau = rotor_j * resistance / (k_t * k_e)      // the motor's time constant, s
const omega_ss = volts / k_e                        // no-load speed, rad/s
def speed(t) = omega_ss * (1 - exp(-t / tau))       // the spin-up curve
for mark in {0.08, 0.16, 0.32} do print("at " + str(mark) + " s:", speed(mark), "rad/s")
const rpm_ss = omega_ss * 60 / (2 * pi)

// ---- results -----------------------------------------------------------------
print("time constant J R / (Kt Ke):", tau, "s")
print("no-load speed at 12 V:", omega_ss, "rad/s")
print("the same speed in rpm:", rpm_ss)
print("63% of speed at one tau:", speed(tau) / omega_ss)
print("settled (2% band) at:", 4 * tau, "s")
print("stall current at the instant of the step:", volts / resistance, "A")

/* The rotor reaches 63 percent of its 2291 rpm in 80 milliseconds and
calls itself spun-up by a third of a second -- numbers a designer
reads straight off four nameplate constants. The last line is the
ugly truth of the step: at standstill the motor is a 1-ohm wire, and
the controller must choke 12 amperes until the back-EMF builds.
Speed control is easy; current inrush is the design problem. */

/* ---- expected output ----
= {at 0.08 s: 151.708934119 rad/s, at 0.16 s: 207.519532023 rad/s, at 0.32 s: 235.604246667 rad/s}
= time constant J R / (Kt Ke): 0.08 s
= no-load speed at 12 V: 240 rad/s
= the same speed in rpm: 2291.83118052
= 63% of speed at one tau: 0.632120558829
= settled (2% band) at: 0.32 s
= stall current at the instant of the step: 12 A
*/

scripts.name: first-order-step-response
scripts.title: how a system settles into its answer
scripts.text:
/* ============================================================================
first-order-step-response.epher -- how a system settles into its answer

A first-order system (a thermometer, a small motor, an RC filter) obeys
y(t) = K (1 - e^(-t/tau)). The landmarks: 63.2 percent of the change
after one time constant tau, 95 percent after three, and the 2 percent
engineering "settled" line at 4 tau. The loop walks the curve and the
checks recover tau from the curve itself.

Source: Ogata, Modern Control Engineering, 5th ed., ch. 5 (transient
response of first-order systems: the exponential response and its
time-constant landmarks, section 5-2).

Web/desktop: paste the whole file into the entry, press Enter.
============================================================================ */

// ---- knobs ------------------------------------------------------------------
const gain = 2.0            // steady-state gain K
const tau = 0.5             // the time constant, 0.5 s
for mark in {0.25, 0.5, 1, 2} do print("at t = " + str(mark) + " s:", gain * (1 - exp(-mark / tau)))

// ---- results -----------------------------------------------------------------
print("value at one tau (63.2% rule):", gain * (1 - exp(-1)))
print("value at three tau:", gain * (1 - exp(-3)))
print("settled (2% band) at:", 4 * tau, "s")
print("settled value:", gain)
print("one-tau lands 63.2% of the way:", abs((gain * (1 - exp(-1))) / gain - 0.632) < 0.0005)
print("speed up the system by halving tau:", gain * (1 - exp(-1 / (tau / 2))) == gain * (1 - exp(-2)))

/* The curve is always the same exponential wearing different units:
at half a tau it has covered 63 percent, at four it calls itself
settled. Halving tau doubles every landmark's speed but changes
nothing else -- which is why control engineers speak of a system by
its tau and K alone, and why the first measurement to make on any
slow process is exactly this one: how long is the constant? */

/* ---- expected output ----
= {at t = 0.25 s: 0.786938680575, at t = 0.5 s: 1.26424111766, at t = 1 s: 1.72932943353, at t = 2 s: 1.96336872222}
= value at one tau (63.2% rule): 1.26424111766
= value at three tau: 1.90042586326
= settled (2% band) at: 2 s
= settled value: 2
= one-tau lands 63.2% of the way: true
= speed up the system by halving tau: false
*/

scripts.name: pid-walkthrough
scripts.title: P, I and D acting on one error history
scripts.text:
/* ============================================================================
pid-walkthrough.epher -- P, I and D acting on one error history

A controller sees an error sequence -- 10, 8, 5, 2, 0 -- as a process
settles. Proportional reacts to the now, integral sums the past (the
steady droop killer), derivative damps the trend. The script walks the
five steps with Kp = 2, Ki = 0.5, Kd = 0.1 and shows the three terms'
parts shrink, build and vanish in turn.

Source: Ogata, Modern Control Engineering, 5th ed., ch. 8 (PID
controllers: u = Kp e + Ki integral e dt + Kd de/dt and each term's
role); the digital sum-difference form per Franklin, Powell and
Workman, Digital Control of Dynamic Systems, ch. 3.

Web/desktop: paste the whole file into the entry, press Enter.
============================================================================ */

// ---- knobs ------------------------------------------------------------------
const errors = {10, 8, 5, 2, 0}     // the error the controller sees
const kp = 2                        // proportional gain
const ki = 0.5                      // integral gain, per step
const kd = 0.1                      // derivative gain, per step

// ---- model ------------------------------------------------------------------
const p_term = kp * errors[1]
const p_last = kp * errors[5]
const error_sum = sum(errors)                 // the I term's memory
const i_contribution = ki * error_sum
const d_first = kd * (errors[2] - errors[1]) // the trend, negative and calming

// ---- results -----------------------------------------------------------------
print("P term at the first (worst) error:", p_term)
print("P term once the error is gone:", p_last)
print("integral of the whole history:", error_sum)
print("I term's contribution by the end:", i_contribution)
print("D term on the first move (damping):", d_first)
print("final output U at the last step:", kp * errors[5] + i_contribution + kd * (errors[5] - errors[4]))
print("I holds when P forgets:", i_contribution > 0 and p_last == 0)

/* Proportional does the heavy lifting and leaves: at zero error it
outputs nothing, which is precisely the droop the integral exists to
cure -- by the last step P is 0 and I is holding 12.5 of output, the
memory of every past error. Derivative only speaks when the error is
moving, braking the first lunge by 0.2. Tune Kp for speed, Ki for
accuracy, Kd for manners. */

/* ---- expected output ----
= P term at the first (worst) error: 20
= P term once the error is gone: 0
= integral of the whole history: 25
= I term's contribution by the end: 12.5
= D term on the first move (damping): -0.2
= final output U at the last step: 12.3
= I holds when P forgets: true
*/

scripts.name: second-order-step-response
scripts.title: overshoot, set by damping alone
scripts.text:
/* ============================================================================
second-order-step-response.epher -- overshoot, set by damping alone

An underdamped second-order system (a mass on a spring with damping,
a position servo) rises past its target and rings before settling.
With natural frequency omega_n and damping ratio zeta, the overshoot
is Mp = e^(-pi zeta / sqrt(1 - zeta^2)), the peak time pi/omega_d, and
the 2 percent settling time about 4/(zeta omega_n) -- all three set by
zeta and omega_n alone.

Source: Ogata, Modern Control Engineering, 5th ed., ch. 5 (transient
response of second-order systems: maximum overshoot eq. 5-21, peak
time eq. 5-19, settling time eq. 5-23).

Web/desktop: paste the whole file into the entry, press Enter.
============================================================================ */

// ---- knobs ------------------------------------------------------------------
const omega_n = 10          // natural frequency, 10 rad/s
const zeta = 0.3            // damping ratio, 0.3 (underdamped)
const target = 1.0          // the step the system must reach

// ---- model ------------------------------------------------------------------
const omega_d = omega_n * sqrt(1 - zeta ^ 2)         // damped frequency
const overshoot = exp(-pi * zeta / sqrt(1 - zeta ^ 2))   // fraction
const peak_time = pi / omega_d                       // s
const settle_time = 4 / (zeta * omega_n)             // 2 percent band, s
const peak_value = target * (1 + overshoot)          // the first hump

// ---- results -----------------------------------------------------------------
print("damped frequency omega_d:", omega_d, "rad/s")
print("overshoot Mp:", overshoot)
print("peak value after a unit step:", peak_value)
print("peak time:", peak_time, "s")
