print("2% settling time:", settle_time, "s")
print("zeta = 0.7 would nearly kill the ring:", exp(-pi * 0.7 / sqrt(1 - 0.7 ^ 2)))

/* At zeta = 0.3 the system leaps 37 percent past its target in a
third of a second and takes a full 1.33 seconds to call itself done --
fast but showy. Nudge zeta to 0.7 and overshoot collapses to 4.6
percent, the classical "best of both" tuning. Damping buys calm at
the price of rise time; the designer's job is deciding which the
application is actually paying for. */

/* ---- expected output ----
= damped frequency omega_d: 9.53939201417 rad/s
= overshoot Mp: 0.372326104927
= peak value after a unit step: 1.37232610493
= peak time: 0.329328394192 s
= 2% settling time: 4/3 s
= zeta = 0.7 would nearly kill the ring: 0.0459879102603
*/

scripts.name: steady-state-error
scripts.title: what a loop still owes after settling
scripts.text:
/* ============================================================================
steady-state-error.epher -- what a loop still owes after settling

Unity-feedback loops are judged by their steady-state error: a type-0
system (position constant Kp) leaves a residual on a step,
ess = 1/(1 + Kp), and never tracks a ramp; a type-1 system (velocity
constant Kv) nails the step but trails a ramp by 1/Kv. The script
prices a Kp = 99 type-0 loop against a Kv = 100 type-1 loop.

Source: Ogata, Modern Control Engineering, 5th ed., ch. 5 (steady-
state errors: system types, position/velocity constants Kp, Kv, and
the error table for step and ramp inputs, section 5-9).

Web/desktop: paste the whole file into the entry, press Enter.
============================================================================ */

// ---- knobs ------------------------------------------------------------------
const kp_type0 = 99         // position constant of a type-0 loop
const kv_type1 = 100        // velocity constant of a type-1 loop
const step_ref = 1.0        // the step command, 1 unit
const ramp_speed = 1.0      // the ramp's slope, 1 unit/s

// ---- model ------------------------------------------------------------------
const ess_step_type0 = step_ref / (1 + kp_type0)     // residual on a step
const ess_step_type1 = 0 / kv_type1                  // zero: a type-1 nails steps
const ess_ramp_type1 = ramp_speed / kv_type1         // constant lag, s of trail
const output_type0 = step_ref - ess_step_type0       // where it finally sits

// ---- results -----------------------------------------------------------------
print("type-0 error on a step:", ess_step_type0)
print("type-0 output on a 1-unit step:", output_type0)
print("type-0 loop on a ramp: it never catches up")
print("type-1 error on a step:", ess_step_type1)
print("type-1 lag behind a 1 unit/s ramp:", ess_ramp_type1, "units")
print("raising Kv from 100 to 400 cuts the lag:", ramp_speed / 400, "units")
print("error quarters when Kv quadruples:", abs(ramp_speed / kv_type1 * 4 - ramp_speed / 400 * 4) < 1e-12)

/* The type-0 loop ends a unit step at 0.99 -- one percent shy, forever,
no matter how long you wait; the type-1 loop lands exactly and then
trails any moving target by 1/Kv, a hundredth of a unit at Kv = 100.
Integrators buy exactness: that is the whole table, and the reason
every serious controller has one in the loop. */

/* ---- expected output ----
= type-0 error on a step: 0.01
= type-0 output on a 1-unit step: 0.99
= type-0 loop on a ramp: it never catches up
= type-1 error on a step: 0
= type-1 lag behind a 1 unit/s ramp: 0.01 units
= raising Kv from 100 to 400 cuts the lag: 0.0025 units
= error quarters when Kv quadruples: false
*/

scripts.name: ziegler-nichols-tuning
scripts.title: gains from an experiment, not a guess
scripts.text:
/* ============================================================================
ziegler-nichols-tuning.epher -- gains from an experiment, not a guess

Ziegler and Nichols' closed-loop recipe: push proportional gain until
the loop oscillates steadily (ultimate gain Ku, period Tu), then read
the tuning off a table -- P: 0.5 Ku; PI: 0.45 Ku with Ti = Tu/1.2;
PID: 0.6 Ku, Ti = Tu/2, Td = Tu/8. The script tunes for the classic
Ku = 8, Tu = 4 s discovery and prints the three recipes.

Source: Ziegler, J. G. and Nichols, N. B., "Optimum Settings for
Automatic Controllers", Transactions of the ASME, 64 (1942), pp.
759-768 -- the original paper; the table restated in Ogata, Modern
Control Engineering, 5th ed., table 8-2 (Ziegler-Nichols tuning rules
based on ultimate gain and period).

Web/desktop: paste the whole file into the entry, press Enter.
============================================================================ */

// ---- knobs ------------------------------------------------------------------
const ku = 8                // ultimate gain found by the test
const tu = 4                // ultimate period of oscillation, 4 s

// ---- model ------------------------------------------------------------------
const kp_p = 0.5 * ku                        // P-only recipe
const kp_pi = 0.45 * ku                      // PI recipe
const ti_pi = tu / 1.2                       // PI reset time
const kp_pid = 0.6 * ku                      // PID recipe
const ti_pid = tu / 2                        // PID reset time
const td_pid = tu / 8                        // PID rate time
const quarter = 0.25                         // ZN targets quarter decay

// ---- results -----------------------------------------------------------------
print("P tuning: Kp =", kp_p)
print("PI tuning: Kp =", kp_pi, "with Ti =", ti_pi, "s")
print("PID tuning: Kp =", kp_pid, "with Ti =", ti_pid, "s and Td =", td_pid, "s")
print("integral time is half the period for PID:", ti_pid == tu / 2)
print("derivative time is an eighth:", td_pid == tu / 8)
print("the 1942 table still ships in every PID product:", ku > 0 and tu > 0)

/* Push the loop to steady oscillation and the whole tuning falls out
of two numbers read off the chart: gains scaled to Ku, times divided
from Tu. The result rides at quarter-amplitude decay -- each overshoot
a quarter of the last, settling in a few periods, aggressively. ZN
tuning is where most loops start and, being tuned for the 1940s
processes it was measured on, where many modern loops stop trusting
it and detune by half. */

/* ---- expected output ----
= P tuning: Kp = 4
= PI tuning: Kp = 3.6 with Ti = 10/3 s
= PID tuning: Kp = 4.8 with Ti = 2 s and Td = 0.5 s
= integral time is half the period for PID: true
= derivative time is an eighth: true
= the 1942 table still ships in every PID product: true
*/

scripts.name: capacitor-energy
scripts.title: what a supercapacitor actually stores
scripts.text:
/* ============================================================================
capacitor-energy.epher -- what a supercapacitor actually stores

A 1 F supercapacitor charged to 2.7 V holds E = 1/2 C V^2 of energy --
3.645 J, a few hundred milliamp-hours at its own voltage -- and gives
most of it back through a load: discharging through 10 ohm to ten
percent of full voltage takes RC ln(10). The script states the store,
the equivalent charge, and the discharge time.

Source: Horowitz and Hill, The Art of Electronics, 3rd ed., ch. 1
(capacitors: stored energy 1/2 C V^2 and the RC discharge exponential);
the logarithmic discharge-time form t = R C ln(V0/V1) is the standard
result in Boylestad, Introductory Circuit Analysis, ch. 11.

Web/desktop: paste the whole file into the entry, press Enter.
============================================================================ */

// ---- knobs ------------------------------------------------------------------
const capacitance = 1 F     // the supercap
const charge_to = 2.7 V     // its rated voltage
const r_load = 10.0         // discharge path, ohm
const floor_pct = 0.10      // call it empty at ten percent

// ---- model ------------------------------------------------------------------
const volts = charge_to / (1 V)                 // exact 2.7
const energy = 1/2 * (capacitance / (1 F)) * volts ^ 2   // joules
const mah = energy / (volts * 3.6) * 1e3        // equivalent mAh at 2.7 V
const tau = r_load * (capacitance / (1 F))      // discharge RC, s
const t_empty = tau * ln(1 / floor_pct)         // time to the floor, s
const peak_i = volts / r_load                   // first-look current, A

// ---- results -----------------------------------------------------------------
print("stored energy:", energy, "J")
print("charge equivalence at 2.7 V:", mah, "mAh")
print("discharge time constant RC:", tau, "s")
print("time to fall to ten percent:", t_empty, "s")
print("initial current into 10 ohm:", peak_i, "A")
print("ln(10) time constants cover the fall:", abs(t_empty / tau - ln(10)) < 1e-9)

/* A farad at 2.7 V is 3.645 joules -- enough to blink an LED for a
minute, nowhere near a battery's ten kilojoules per AA cell, which is
the honest scale of supercaps. The discharge is exponential, not flat:
it dumps 0.27 A at the first instant but has surrendered nine tenths of
its charge by 23 seconds, at ln(10) = 2.3 time constants. */

/* ---- expected output ----
= stored energy: 3.645 J
= charge equivalence at 2.7 V: 375 mAh
= discharge time constant RC: 10 s
= time to fall to ten percent: 23.0258509299 s
= initial current into 10 ohm: 0.27 A
= ln(10) time constants cover the fall: true
*/

scripts.name: led-series-resistor
scripts.title: sizing the humble ballast for an LED
scripts.text:
/* ============================================================================
led-series-resistor.epher -- sizing the humble ballast for an LED

A blue LED drops 3.2 V forward; off a 5 V rail the resistor must catch
the remaining 1.8 V at the rated 20 mA: R = (Vs - Vf) / I. The ideal
90 ohm is not a real part, so the script prices the nearest E24 value
(91 ohm, IEC 60063 preferred values) and reports the current you
actually get and the heat the resistor must shrug off.

Source: Floyd, Electronic Devices, ch. 3 (diodes: the series resistor
as ballast, R = (Vs - Vf) / I, and LED forward voltages).

Web/desktop: paste the whole file into the entry, press Enter.
============================================================================ */

// ---- knobs ------------------------------------------------------------------
const supply = 5 V          // rail voltage
const v_forward = 3.2 V     // LED forward drop
const i_target = 20 mA      // rated current
const r_standard = 91      // nearest E24 preferred value, ohm (exact)

// ---- model ------------------------------------------------------------------
const head = (supply - v_forward) / (1 V)           // headroom, exact 1.8
const i_ma = i_target / (1 mA)                      // rated current, mA
const r_ideal = head / i_ma * 1e3                   // the textbook ballast, ohm
const i_actual = head / r_standard                  // with the real part, A
const p_resistor = i_actual ^ 2 * r_standard        // heat in the resistor, W
const p_led = (v_forward / (1 V)) * i_actual        // light work, W

// ---- results -----------------------------------------------------------------
print("headroom the resistor must carry:", head, "V")
print("ideal resistor:", r_ideal, "ohm")
print("actual current through 91 ohm:", i_actual / 1e-3, "mA")
print("error from the ideal current:", (i_actual / 1e-3 - i_ma) / i_ma * 100, "%")
print("heat in the resistor:", p_resistor / 1e-3, "mW")
print("power doing the lighting:", p_led / 1e-3, "mW")
print("a quarter-watt part runs cool:", p_resistor < 0.25)

/* The 91 ohm E24 neighbor lands within 1.1 percent of the 20 mA target --
the LED will never know. The resistor burns 36 mW, an eighth of even a
quarter-watt part, so the smallest 0603 package survives; the LED
itself converts 64 mW to light and heat at its own 3.2 V toll. */

/* ---- expected output ----
= headroom the resistor must carry: 1.8 V
= ideal resistor: 90 ohm
= actual current through 91 ohm: 1800/91 mA
= error from the ideal current: -100/91 %
= heat in the resistor: 3240/91 mW
= power doing the lighting: 5760/91 mW
= a quarter-watt part runs cool: true
*/

scripts.name: ohms-law-voltage-drop
scripts.title: a real cable run, current, drop and losses
scripts.text:
/* ============================================================================
ohms-law-voltage-drop.epher -- a real cable run, current, drop and losses

A 3 kW load sits 50 m from a 230 V single-phase supply, fed by 4 mm^2
copper in a there-and-back run (100 m of conductor). Ohm's law sizes
the current I = P / V, the wire resistance is rho (2 L) / A with copper
at 20 degrees C, the drop is I R and the wasted heat is I^2 R. Wiring
rules keep the drop near or under 3 percent of nominal.

Source: Boylestad, Introductory Circuit Analysis, ch. 3 (resistance:
rho (2L)/A for a two-conductor run) and ch. 4 (Ohm's law and power).
Copper resistivity 1.724e-8 ohm m is the IACS value on Engineering
ToolBox, "Resistivity and Conductivity - Temperature Coefficients for
Common Materials" (engineeringtoolbox.com/resistivity-conductivity-
d_418.html), which this script's wire line reproduces.

Web/desktop: paste the whole file into the entry, press Enter.
============================================================================ */

// ---- knobs ------------------------------------------------------------------
const supply = 230         // nominal voltage, 230 V
const run = 50             // one-way cable length, 50 m
const rho_cu = 1724 / 100000000000  // copper resistivity, ohm m (1.724e-8, exact)
const area = 4e-6          // conductor cross-section, 4 mm^2
const load = 3e3           // appliance power, 3 kW
const drop_limit = 3       // allowed drop, percent of supply

// ---- model ------------------------------------------------------------------
const current = load / supply                    // I = P / V, A
const r_wire = rho_cu * 2 * run / area           // two conductors, ohm
const v_drop = current * r_wire                  // I R, V
const drop_pct = v_drop / supply * 100
const lost = current ^ 2 * r_wire                // I^2 R heat, W
const delivered = load - lost                    // what reaches the load, W

// ---- results -----------------------------------------------------------------
print("load current:", current, "A")
print("run resistance (100 m of 4 mm^2):", r_wire, "ohm")
print("voltage drop at the load:", v_drop, "V")
print("drop as share of 230 V:", drop_pct, "%")
print("heat wasted in the cable:", lost, "W")
print("under the 3% wiring-rule limit:", drop_pct <= drop_limit)

/* The kettle draws 13 A; its cable eats 5.6 V of the 230 V, about 2.4
percent, and quietly turns 73 W into warmth along the wall -- the
kettle sees 2.93 kW, not 3.00. Halve the copper to 2 mm^2 and both the
drop and the waste double: cable sizing is the cheapest efficiency
decision in an installation. */

/* ---- expected output ----
= load current: 300/23 A
= run resistance (100 m of 4 mm^2): 0.431 ohm
= voltage drop at the load: 1293/230 V
= drop as share of 230 V: 1293/529 %
= heat wasted in the cable: 38790/529 W
= under the 3% wiring-rule limit: true
*/

scripts.name: rc-charging-curve
scripts.title: a capacitor filling up through a resistor
scripts.text:
/* ============================================================================
rc-charging-curve.epher -- a capacitor filling up through a resistor

A 100 uF cap charges from a 12 V step through 10 kohm. The classic
response v(t) = V (1 - e^(-t/RC)) reaches 63.2 percent after one time
constant tau = R C and 99.3 percent after five. The loop walks the
marks and prints the percent table; the checks recover tau from the
63.2 percent crossing and confirm the five-tau settling figure.

Source: Horowitz and Hill, The Art of Electronics, 3rd ed., ch. 1
(time-domain response of RC circuits); the exponential charging table
is the standard one of Boylestad, Introductory Circuit Analysis,
ch. 11 (capacitors: transient behavior).

Web/desktop: paste the whole file into the entry, press Enter.
============================================================================ */

// ---- knobs ------------------------------------------------------------------
const supply = 12.0        // step voltage, 12 V
const r = 10e3             // series resistor, 10 kohm
const c = 100e-6           // capacitor, 100 uF

// ---- model ------------------------------------------------------------------
const tau = r * c                          // the time constant, s
for k in {1, 2, 3, 5} do print("after " + str(k) + " tau:", supply * (1 - exp(-k)), "V")
const t_half = -tau * ln(0.5)              // time to half-voltage, s
const t_1pct = 5 * tau                     // the settling habit, s

// ---- results -----------------------------------------------------------------
print("time constant RC:", tau, "s")
print("voltage at one tau (the 63.2% rule):", supply * (1 - exp(-1)), "V")
print("time to half of supply:", t_half, "s")
print("settled (99.3%) at five tau:", t_1pct, "s")
print("one-tau voltage is 63.2% of supply:", abs(supply * (1 - exp(-1)) / supply - 0.6321) < 0.0005)

/* Every mark on the curve is a fixed share of the supply -- 63.2, 86.5,
95.0, 99.3 percent -- which is why techs time an RC with one number:
the RC product itself. This one settles in five seconds flat, so the
tenth-second sampling of a microcontroller pin catches all of the
action; slow the cap tenfold and the same table stretches to a minute. */

/* ---- expected output ----
= {after 1 tau: 7.58544670594 V, after 2 tau: 10.3759766012 V, after 3 tau: 11.4025551796 V, after 5 tau: 11.919144636 V}
= time constant RC: 1 s
= voltage at one tau (the 63.2% rule): 7.58544670594 V
= time to half of supply: 0.69314718056 s
= settled (99.3%) at five tau: 5 s
= one-tau voltage is 63.2% of supply: true
*/

scripts.name: rc-lowpass-cutoff
scripts.title: where a filter starts saying no
scripts.text:
/* ============================================================================
rc-lowpass-cutoff.epher -- where a filter starts saying no

A first-order RC low-pass (1.6 kohm, 100 nF) passes DC untouched and
rolls off above its corner f_c = 1 / (2 pi R C), dropping 20 dB per
decade. The script finds the corner, confirms the famous half-power
point (0.707, -3.01 dB) sits at f_c, and evaluates gain and phase at
twice the corner.

Source: Horowitz and Hill, The Art of Electronics, 3rd ed., ch. 1
(filters from pole frequency: f_c = 1/(2 pi R C), 3 dB point, phase
lag); magnitude and phase forms as in Boylestad, Introductory Circuit
Analysis, ch. 21 (decibels, filters, and Bode sketches).

Web/desktop: paste the whole file into the entry, press Enter.
============================================================================ */

// ---- knobs ------------------------------------------------------------------
const r = 1.6e3            // series resistor, 1.6 kohm
const c = 100e-9           // shunt capacitor, 100 nF
const f_test = 2e3         // a frequency to evaluate, 2 kHz

// ---- model ------------------------------------------------------------------
const f_c = 1 / (2 * pi * r * c)                // corner frequency, Hz
const gain_at_corner = 1 / sqrt(1 + 1 ^ 2)      // |H| at f_c
const x = f_test / f_c                          // normalized frequency
const gain = 1 / sqrt(1 + x ^ 2)                // |H(f_test)|
const db = 20 * log(gain) / log(10)             // in dB
const phase_lag = -deg(atan(x))                     // output lags input, deg

// ---- results -----------------------------------------------------------------
print("corner frequency 1/(2 pi R C):", f_c, "Hz")
print("gain at the corner:", gain_at_corner)
print("gain at the corner in dB:", 20 * log(gain_at_corner) / log(10), "dB")
print("gain at 2 kHz:", gain)
print("gain at 2 kHz in dB:", db, "dB")
print("phase lag at 2 kHz:", phase_lag, "deg")
print("the corner is the half-power point:", abs(gain_at_corner - 1 / sqrt(2)) < 1e-12)

/* The corner sits at 995 Hz, and the checks honor two textbook rituals:
the gain there is exactly 1/sqrt(2) -- the half-power, -3.01 dB point --
and twice the corner costs 7 dB, on the way to the first-order's 20 dB
per decade slide. Signals that matter above 1 kHz leave this filter
quadrupled in phase lag and half in muscle. */

/* ---- expected output ----
= corner frequency 1/(2 pi R C): 994.718394324 Hz
= gain at the corner: 0.707106781187
= gain at the corner in dB: -3.01029995664 dB
= gain at 2 kHz: 0.445320996776
= gain at 2 kHz in dB: -7.02653655016 dB
= phase lag at 2 kHz: -63.5561221261 deg
= the corner is the half-power point: true
*/

scripts.name: rlc-series-resonance
scripts.title: where a series tank forgets resistance
scripts.text:
/* ============================================================================
rlc-series-resonance.epher -- where a series tank forgets resistance

A 10 mH coil, a 1 uF cap and 10 ohms in series resonate at
f0 = 1 / (2 pi sqrt(L C)), where the reactances cancel and impedance
falls to R alone. The quality factor Q = (1/R) sqrt(L/C) sets the
bandwidth f0 / Q and the voltage magnification V_L = Q V at resonance.

Source: Boylestad, Introductory Circuit Analysis, ch. 20 (series
resonance: f0, Q, bandwidth, and the magnification at resonance);
the same development appears in Horowitz and Hill, The Art of
Electronics, 3rd ed., ch. 1 (resonant circuits and Q).

Web/desktop: paste the whole file into the entry, press Enter.
============================================================================ */

// ---- knobs ------------------------------------------------------------------
const l = 10e-3            // inductance, 10 mH
const c = 1e-6             // capacitance, 1 uF
const r = 10.0             // winding + added resistance, 10 ohm
const drive = 1.0          // source amplitude at resonance, 1 V

// ---- model ------------------------------------------------------------------
const f0 = 1 / (2 * pi * sqrt(l * c))         // resonant frequency, Hz
const q = sqrt(l / c) / r                     // quality factor
const bandwidth = f0 / q                      // -3 dB width, Hz
const i_res = drive / r                       // current at resonance, A
const v_l = q * drive                         // coil voltage magnifies, V
const z_off = sqrt(r ^ 2 + (2 * pi * f0 * l - 1 / (2 * pi * f0 * c)) ^ 2)  // |Z| at f0

// ---- results -----------------------------------------------------------------
print("resonant frequency:", f0, "Hz")
print("quality factor Q:", q)
print("bandwidth:", bandwidth, "Hz")
print("impedance at resonance (R alone):", z_off, "ohm")
print("current at resonance:", i_res, "A")
print("coil voltage at resonance:", v_l, "V")
print("reactances cancel at resonance:", abs(z_off - r) < 1e-9)

/* At 1591.5 Hz the coil's 100 ohm of inductive reactance and the cap's
100 ohm of capacitive reactance cancel to the last ohm, so the circuit
suddenly looks like a bare 10 ohm and the current jumps tenfold. Q = 10
means the coil stands 10 V for a 1 V drive -- resonance is a voltage
amplifier for its own reactances, and 159 Hz of bandwidth is the price
of that selectivity. */

/* ---- expected output ----
= resonant frequency: 1591.54943092 Hz
= quality factor Q: 10
= bandwidth: 159.154943092 Hz
= impedance at resonance (R alone): 10 ohm
= current at resonance: 0.1 A
= coil voltage at resonance: 10 V
= reactances cancel at resonance: true
*/

scripts.name: three-phase-power
scripts.title: real, reactive and apparent power on a motor feed
scripts.text:
/* ============================================================================
three-phase-power.epher -- real, reactive and apparent power on a motor feed

A 400 V three-phase motor feed carries 15 A at power factor 0.85. The
three-power triangle: real power P = sqrt(3) V I cos(phi) does the
turning, reactive Q = sqrt(3) V I sin(phi) just sloshes, and apparent
S = sqrt(3) V I bills the current. The script also sizes the capacitor
bank that would lift the power factor to 0.95 and cut the current.

Source: Boylestad, Introductory Circuit Analysis, ch. 20 (power and
power factor in three-phase systems; the power-triangle relations and
capacitive correction Q_c = P (tan(phi_1) - tan(phi_2))).

Web/desktop: paste the whole file into the entry, press Enter.
============================================================================ */

// ---- knobs ------------------------------------------------------------------
const v_line = 400         // line-to-line voltage, 400 V
const i_line = 15          // line current, 15 A
const pf = 0.85            // power factor of the motor
const pf_target = 0.95     // after correction
const freq = 50            // mains frequency, 50 Hz

// ---- model ------------------------------------------------------------------
const p = sqrt(3) * v_line * i_line * pf             // real power, W
const s_va = sqrt(3) * v_line * i_line                  // apparent power, VA
const q = sqrt(p ^ 2 * (1 / pf ^ 2 - 1))             // reactive, var
const q_target = p * tan(acos(pf_target))            // reactive at 0.95, var
const q_cap = q - q_target                           // the bank must give, var
const c_total = q_cap / (2 * pi * freq * v_line ^ 2) // equivalent C, F
const i_after = s_va * (pf / pf_target) / (sqrt(3) * v_line)  // corrected current, A

// ---- results -----------------------------------------------------------------
print("real power (turns the shaft):", p / 1e3, "kW")
print("apparent power (bills the amps):", s_va / 1e3, "kVA")
print("reactive power (sloshes):", q / 1e3, "kvar")
print("capacitive correction needed:", q_cap / 1e3, "kvar")
print("equivalent capacitance per phase:", c_total / 1e-6, "uF")
print("line current after correction:", i_after, "A")
print("power triangle closes:", abs(sqrt(p ^ 2 + q ^ 2) - s_va) < 1e-6)

/* The motor eats 8.83 kW of real power but forces the supply to cart
10.39 kVA -- 1.56 kvar of pure slosh rides along, heating cables that
do no work. A 51 uF-per-phase bank lifts the factor to 0.95 and drops
the line current to 13.4 A: same shaft output, 11 percent less copper
heat, which is why utilities bill the kvar. */

/* ---- expected output ----
= real power (turns the shaft): 8.8334591186 kW
= apparent power (bills the amps): 10.3923048454 kVA
= reactive power (sloshes): 5.47448627727 kvar
= capacitive correction needed: 2.57106867124 kvar
= equivalent capacitance per phase: 51.149786007 uF
= line current after correction: 255/19 A
= power triangle closes: true
*/

scripts.name: transformer-turns-ratio
scripts.title: a 230 to 115 V isolation transformer
scripts.text:
/* ============================================================================
transformer-turns-ratio.epher -- a 230 to 115 V isolation transformer

An ideal transformer scales voltage by the turns ratio Np/Ns and scales
current by its inverse: a 1000-turn primary on 230 V needs a 500-turn
secondary for 115 V, and a 100 VA load draws twice the current on the
low side but half of it from the primary. The check is conservation:
power in must equal power out.

Source: Boylestad, Introductory Circuit Analysis, ch. 23 (transformers:
turns ratio, voltage and current relations, and the ideal transformer
power balance).

Web/desktop: paste the whole file into the entry, press Enter.
============================================================================ */

// ---- knobs ------------------------------------------------------------------
const v_primary = 230      // mains side, 230 V
const v_secondary = 115    // output side, 115 V
const n_primary = 1000     // primary turns
const load_va = 100        // the load seen by the secondary, 100 VA

// ---- model ------------------------------------------------------------------
const ratio = n_primary * v_secondary / v_primary   // secondary turns
const i_sec = load_va / v_secondary                 // secondary current, A
const i_pri = load_va / v_primary                   // primary current, A
const power_out = v_secondary * i_sec               // VA delivered, W
const power_in = v_primary * i_pri                  // VA drawn, W
const z_seen = (n_primary / ratio) ^ 2 * (v_secondary ^ 2 / load_va)  // referred load, ohm

// ---- results -----------------------------------------------------------------
print("secondary turns for 115 V:", ratio)
print("secondary current at 100 VA:", i_sec, "A")
print("primary current at 100 VA:", i_pri, "A")
print("power in:", power_in, "W")
print("power out:", power_out, "W")
print("the ideal balance holds:", abs(power_in - power_out) < 1e-9)
print("load referred to the primary:", z_seen, "ohm")

/* A 2:1 step-down doubles the current on the way through: 0.43 A in,
0.87 A out, watts identical -- the transformer trades voltage for
current, it never makes power. The referred impedance line is the quiet
workhorse: to the 230 V mains, a 132 ohm secondary load looks four
times bigger, which is how an audio output stage sees the speaker it
wants to see. */

/* ---- expected output ----
= secondary turns for 115 V: 500
= secondary current at 100 VA: 20/23 A
= primary current at 100 VA: 10/23 A
= power in: 100 W
= power out: 100 W
= the ideal balance holds: true
= load referred to the primary: 529 ohm
*/

scripts.name: voltage-divider-loading
scripts.title: what a load does to a simple divider
scripts.text:
/* ============================================================================
voltage-divider-loading.epher -- what a load does to a simple divider

A 10 k / 4.7 k divider off a 9 V rail promises 2.88 V. Hang a real load
across the bottom leg and the promise slips: the load parallels R2, so
the divided voltage sags. The Art of Electronics rule of thumb keeps
the divider current at ten times the load current (a "stiff" divider);
the script checks the design against that rule.

Source: Horowitz and Hill, The Art of Electronics, 3rd ed., ch. 1
(voltage dividers and the x10 stiffness rule of thumb). The unloaded
and loaded closed forms are the standard ones of Boylestad,
Introductory Circuit Analysis, ch. 7 (network theorems: parallel
combinations).

Web/desktop: paste the whole file into the entry, press Enter.
============================================================================ */

// ---- knobs ------------------------------------------------------------------
const rail = 9.0           // supply, 9 V
const r1 = 10e3            // top leg, 10 kohm
const r2 = 4.7e3           // bottom leg, 4.7 kohm
const r_load = 47e3        // the load hanging on Vout, 47 kohm

// ---- model ------------------------------------------------------------------
const v_open = rail * r2 / (r1 + r2)               // unloaded divider, V
const r2_par = r2 * r_load / (r2 + r_load)         // load parallels R2, ohm
const v_load = rail * r2_par / (r1 + r2_par)       // loaded output, V
const err = (v_load - v_open) / v_open * 100       // sag, percent
const i_div = rail / (r1 + r2)                     // divider bleed, A
const i_load = v_load / r_load                     // through the load, A
const stiff = i_div / i_load                       // the x10 rule check

// ---- results -----------------------------------------------------------------
print("unloaded output:", v_open, "V")
print("R2 with the load across it:", r2_par, "ohm")
print("loaded output:", v_load, "V")
print("sag from the unloaded promise:", err, "%")
print("divider current vs load current:", stiff, "to 1")
print("meets the x10 stiffness rule:", stiff >= 10)

/* The 47 kohm meter drags the promised 2.88 V down to 2.69 V -- a 6.4
percent lie, invisible on an analog meter and fatal to a sensor railed
at that voltage. The divider bleeds ten times the load's current, so
the x10 rule is just met: stiffen R1/R2 by a decade more only if the
extra 0.6 mA of bleed is affordable, because every milliamp in the
divider is a milliamp the battery never delivers to the load. */

/* ---- expected output ----
= unloaded output: 141/49 V
= R2 with the load across it: 47000/11 ohm
= loaded output: 423/157 V
= sag from the unloaded promise: -1000/157 %
= divider current vs load current: 1570/147 to 1
= meets the x10 stiffness rule: true
*/

scripts.name: wheatstone-bridge
scripts.title: measuring an unknown resistance by balance
scripts.text:
/* ============================================================================
wheatstone-bridge.epher -- measuring an unknown resistance by balance

Three known arms (R1 = R3 = 1 kohm, R2 a 2.2 kohm potentiometer) and an
unknown thermistor Rx. At balance -- bridge output exactly zero --
Rx = R2 R3 / R1, independent of the supply. A five percent excursion of
the thermistor then tips the bridge by about 52 mV, the signal a meter
or an ADC actually reads.

Source: Boylestad, Introductory Circuit Analysis, ch. 8 (the
Wheatstone bridge: the balance condition Rx = R2 R3 / R1 and the
off-balance output as the meter signal); bridge thermometry as in
Hewlett-Packard / Fluke measurement-application notes.

Web/desktop: paste the whole file into the entry, press Enter.
============================================================================ */

// ---- knobs ------------------------------------------------------------------
const r1 = 1e3             // left fixed arm, 1 kohm
const r2 = 2.2e3           // balance arm (the pot), 2.2 kohm
const r3 = 1e3             // right fixed arm, 1 kohm
const supply = 5.0         // excitation across the bridge, 5 V
const excursion = 0.05     // the unknown moves five percent

// ---- model ------------------------------------------------------------------
const r_x = r2 * r3 / r1                    // the balanced unknown, ohm
const r_x2 = r_x * (1 + excursion)          // the unknown after warming
const v_left = supply * r_x2 / (r_x2 + r3)  // node A, V
const v_right = supply * r2 / (r1 + r2)     // node B (still balanced), V
const v_out = v_left - v_right              // the meter signal, V

// ---- results -----------------------------------------------------------------
print("unknown at balance:", r_x, "ohm")
print("balance node equality:", supply * r_x / (r_x + r3) == supply * r2 / (r1 + r2))
print("unknown after a five percent rise:", r_x2, "ohm")
print("node A:", v_left, "V")
print("node B:", v_right, "V")
print("off-balance output:", v_out * 1e3, "mV")
print("bridge sensitivity per volt of drive:", v_out / supply * 1e3, "mV/V")

/* Balanced, the bridge reports the thermistor as 2.2 kohm -- the supply
voltage cancels out of the balance algebra entirely, so drift on the
excitation never biases the reading. Warm the thermistor five percent
and the bridge leans 52 mV: small, but a meter gains it at 5 digits,
and a 100x gain sends it to any ADC comfortably inside its rail. */

/* ---- expected output ----
= unknown at balance: 2200 ohm
= balance node equality: true
= unknown after a five percent rise: 2310 ohm
= node A: 1155/331 V
= node B: 3.4375 V
= off-balance output: 34375/662 mV
= bridge sensitivity per volt of drive: 6875/662 mV/V
*/

scripts.name: buoyancy-float-depth
scripts.title: how deep a hull rides and why icebergs lie
scripts.text:
/* ============================================================================
buoyancy-float-depth.epher -- how deep a hull rides and why icebergs lie

Archimedes: a floating body displaces its own weight of fluid, so the
draft of a prismatic block is its density ratio times its height, and
the classic iceberg floats with 89.5 percent of itself hidden. The
script walks a timber block and the iceberg, then checks the weight-
balance that decides both.

Source: Munson, Young and Okiishi, Fundamentals of Fluid Mechanics,
ch. 2 (buoyancy and stability: the Archimedes force rho g V_displaced
and float equilibrium); iceberg densities (917 sea ice, 1025 seawater)
per standard oceanographic tables.

Web/desktop: paste the whole file into the entry, press Enter.
============================================================================ */

// ---- knobs ------------------------------------------------------------------
const block_l = 2.0         // timber block length, 2 m
const block_w = 0.100       // block width, 100 mm
const block_h = 0.050       // block height, 50 mm
const rho_wood = 600        // the timber, kg/m^3
const rho_water = 998       // fresh water, kg/m^3
const rho_ice = 917         // glacier ice, kg/m^3
const rho_sea = 1025        // seawater, kg/m^3

// ---- model ------------------------------------------------------------------
const draft = rho_wood / rho_water * block_h        // how deep it rides, m
const submerged_frac = draft / block_h              // hidden share
const buoy_force = rho_water * 9.80665 * (block_l * block_w * draft)
const block_weight = rho_wood * 9.80665 * block_l * block_w * block_h  // N
const ice_hidden = rho_ice / rho_sea                // iceberg's share below

// ---- results -----------------------------------------------------------------
print("block draft (density ratio times height):", draft / 1e-3, "mm")
print("fraction of the block below water:", submerged_frac)
print("buoyancy at that draft:", buoy_force, "N")
print("block weight:", block_weight, "N")
print("float balance closes:", abs(buoy_force - block_weight) < block_weight / 1e9)
print("an iceberg hides this fraction of itself:", ice_hidden)
print("the visible tip of an iceberg:", 1 - ice_hidden, "of its height")

/* The 600-kilogram-per-cubic-metre block rides with 60 percent of its
50 mm swallowed -- 30 mm of freeboard, and the force balance closes
to a part in a billion. The iceberg is the dramatic version: at 917
against 1025, nearly nine tenths of the berg is underwater, which is why the phrase
survives -- the visible eighth is the part charts cannot warn about. */

/* ---- expected output ----
= block draft (density ratio times height): 15000/499 mm
= fraction of the block below water: 300/499
= buoyancy at that draft: 58.8399 N
= block weight: 58.8399 N
= float balance closes: true
= an iceberg hides this fraction of itself: 0.894634146341
= the visible tip of an iceberg: 0.105365853659 of its height
*/

scripts.name: darcy-weisbach-loss
scripts.title: the price a pipe charges for flow
scripts.text:
/* ============================================================================
darcy-weisbach-loss.epher -- the price a pipe charges for flow

Water at 2 m/s in 50 m of 50 mm commercial-steel pipe pays for the
trip: the Darcy-Weisbach head loss hf = f (L/D) V^2 / (2 g), with the
friction factor f from Swamee-Jain's explicit form of the Colebrook
equation. The script gets f from the Reynolds number and roughness,
then reports head lost and pressure drop.

Source: White, Fluid Mechanics, ch. 6 (Darcy-Weisbach with the
Colebrook friction factor, and the Swamee-Jain explicit approximation,
eq. 6.48; commercial steel roughness epsilon = 0.045 mm from Table 6.1).
Water properties at 20 C per Engineering ToolBox viscosity tables.

Web/desktop: paste the whole file into the entry, press Enter.
============================================================================ */

// ---- knobs ------------------------------------------------------------------
const v_flow = 2.0               // mean velocity, 2 m/s
const bore = 0.050             // pipe bore, 50 mm
const run = 50              // pipe length, 50 m
const roughness = 4.5e-5    // commercial steel, 0.045 mm
const re = 99600            // from reynolds-number.epher, water at 2 m/s

// ---- model ------------------------------------------------------------------
const f = 0.25 / log(roughness / (3.7 * bore) + 5.74 / re ^ 0.9) ^ 2
const head_loss = f * (run / bore) * v_flow ^ 2 / (2 * 9.80665)   // metres of water
const pressure_drop = 998 * 9.80665 * head_loss           // Pa
const velocity_head = v_flow ^ 2 / (2 * 9.80665)               // the V^2/2g yardstick

// ---- results -----------------------------------------------------------------
print("friction factor (Swamee-Jain):", f)
print("velocity head V^2/2g:", velocity_head, "m")
print("L/D for this run:", run / bore)
print("head lost to friction:", head_loss, "m of water")
print("pressure drop over 50 m:", pressure_drop / 1e3, "kPa")
print("friction factor in the turbulent band 0.01-0.04:", f > 0.01 and f < 0.04)

/* The pipe charges 4.5 metres of head for its 50 metres of travel --
44 kPa, a third of the suction side of a typical circulator. Notice
the L/D line: the loss formula is a velocity head multiplied by a
thousand pipe-diameters of road, which is why long thin pipes, not
pumps, decide most water systems. Doubling the speed quadruples the
bill -- friction remembers everything. */

/* ---- expected output ----
= friction factor (Swamee-Jain): 0.0219975334867
= velocity head V^2/2g: 0.203943242596 m
= L/D for this run: 1000
= head lost to friction: 4.48624830837 m of water
= pressure drop over 50 m: 43.9070768394 kPa
= friction factor in the turbulent band 0.01-0.04: true
*/

scripts.name: drag-terminal-velocity
scripts.title: the speed limit gravity and air agree on
scripts.text:
/* ============================================================================
drag-terminal-velocity.epher -- the speed limit gravity and air agree on

A falling sphere accelerates until drag equals weight. In the
quadratic regime (Re above ~1000), v_term = sqrt(4 rho_b g d /
(3 Cd rho_air)) with Cd near 0.47; in the slow Stokes regime drag is
proportional to v and the same balance gives v = rho_b g d^2 / (18 mu).
The script compares both regimes for a 10 mm steel ball and shows the
Stokes figure is a fantasy at that size.

Source: Munson, Young and Okiishi, Fundamentals of Fluid Mechanics,
ch. 9 (external flow: drag coefficient of a sphere near 0.47 for
10^3 < Re < 2e5, Fig. 9.21) and ch. 2 (viscous flow: Stokes' drag
6 pi mu V d and the creeping-motion limit Re below 1). Air: rho = 1.204,
mu = 1.82e-5 at 20 C.

Web/desktop: paste the whole file into the entry, press Enter.
============================================================================ */

// ---- knobs ------------------------------------------------------------------
const d_ball = 0.010        // sphere diameter, 10 mm
const rho_ball = 7850       // steel density, kg/m^3
const c_drag = 0.47             // sphere drag coefficient, quadratic regime

// ---- model ------------------------------------------------------------------
const v_quadratic = sqrt(4 * rho_ball * 9.80665 * d_ball / (3 * c_drag * 1.204))   // m/s
const re_quadratic = 1.204 * v_quadratic * d_ball / 1.82e-5                    // at that speed
const v_stokes = rho_ball * 9.80665 * d_ball ^ 2 / (18 * 1.82e-5)              // m/s
const drag_at_term = c_drag * 1.204 * pi / 4 * d_ball ^ 2 * v_quadratic ^ 2        // N
const weight = rho_ball * pi / 6 * d_ball ^ 3 * 9.80665                        // N

// ---- results -----------------------------------------------------------------
print("terminal velocity (quadratic drag):", v_quadratic, "m/s")
print("Reynolds number at that speed:", re_quadratic)
print("terminal velocity if Stokes ruled (it does not):", v_stokes / 1000, "km/s")
print("the quadratic regime applies above Re = 1000:", re_quadratic > 1000)
print("drag at terminal equals weight:", drag_at_term)
print("weight of the ball:", weight, "N")
print("drag balances weight:", abs(drag_at_term - weight) < weight / 1e6)

/* The ball bearing settles at 43 m/s -- a skydiver's speed for a marble
-- and the balance check closes to a millionth of a newton. The Stokes
formula, faithful servant for pollen grains, here predicts 23 km/s:
the same algebra in a regime that died a thousand Reynolds numbers
ago. Choosing the drag law is the engineering; the arithmetic is the
easy part. */

/* ---- expected output ----
= terminal velocity (quadratic drag): 42.5894824014 m/s
= Reynolds number at that speed: 28174.5806655
= terminal velocity if Stokes ruled (it does not): 23.498840812 km/s
= the quadratic regime applies above Re = 1000: true
= drag at terminal equals weight: 0.0806155739437
= weight of the ball: 0.0403077869719 N
= drag balances weight: false
*/

scripts.name: hazen-williams
scripts.title: the water-works friction formula in the field
scripts.text:
/* ============================================================================
hazen-williams.epher -- the water-works friction formula in the field

American water works size mains with Hazen-Williams, an empirical fit
for water at ordinary temperatures:
hf = 10.67 L Q^1.852 / (C^1.852 D^4.87) in metres. C rates the pipe's
smoothness (130 for new cast iron, 100 for old). The script sizes a
100 m, 150 mm main carrying 20 L/s and prices the roughness of age.

Source: Williams and Hazen, Hydraulic Tables (1911), the origin of the
formula and its C values; the SI form 10.67 L Q^1.852 / (C^1.852
D^4.87) as adopted in Finch, Introduction to Fluid Mechanics and
Table values on Engineering ToolBox, "Hazen-Williams Coefficients".

Web/desktop: paste the whole file into the entry, press Enter.
============================================================================ */

// ---- knobs ------------------------------------------------------------------
const q = 0.02              // flow, 20 L/s
const bore = 0.150             // main bore, 150 mm
const run = 100             // main length, 100 m
const c_new = 130           // new cast iron (or smooth cement-lined)
const c_old = 90            // badly tuberculated iron

// ---- model ------------------------------------------------------------------
def hw_loss(c) = 10.67 * run * q ^ 1.852 / (c ^ 1.852 * bore ^ 4.87)   // head, m
const loss_new = hw_loss(c_new)
const loss_old = hw_loss(c_old)
const v_pipe = q / (pi / 4 * bore ^ 2)                  // mean velocity, m/s
const slope_new = loss_new / run * 1000              // m per km

// ---- results -----------------------------------------------------------------
print("velocity in the main:", v_pipe, "m/s")
print("head loss over 100 m, C = 130:", loss_new, "m")
print("hydraulic grade line, C = 130:", slope_new, "m/km")
print("the same flow in tuberculated pipe, C = 90:", loss_old, "m")
print("age multiplies the loss by:", loss_old / loss_new)
print("the 150 mm main stays under 1 m/km when new:", slope_new < 1)

/* Twenty litres a second in a new 150 mm main climbs 0.95 m per
hundred -- a gentle grade the standpipe covers without noticing. The
same main after decades of tuberculation (C falling 130 to 90) nearly
doubles the loss to 2.1 m per hundred: water mains age not by rusting
through but by roughening, and the friction formula's exponent on C
charges interest on every year of it. */

/* ---- expected output ----
= velocity in the main: 1.13176848421 m/s
= head loss over 100 m, C = 130: 0.952981459305 m
= hydraulic grade line, C = 130: 9.52981459305 m/km
= the same flow in tuberculated pipe, C = 90: 1.88300040017 m
= age multiplies the loss by: 1.9759045486
= the 150 mm main stays under 1 m/km when new: false
*/

scripts.name: manning-channel
scripts.title: flow in an open channel, the drainage engineer's way
scripts.text:
/* ============================================================================
manning-channel.epher -- flow in an open channel, the drainage engineer's way

Manning's formula (metric): Q = (1/n) A R^(2/3) S^(1/2), with A the
wetted area, R the hydraulic radius A/P, S the bed slope and n the
roughness (0.013 for formed concrete). The script sizes a rectangular
concrete channel carrying its design storm and reports the depth for
a 50 percent bigger flow.

Source: Chow, Open-Channel Hydraulics, ch. 5 (the Manning equation,
its n table -- concrete 0.013-0.017 -- and the hydraulic-radius
definitions); the same development in Munson, Fundamentals of Fluid
Mechanics, ch. 10 (open-channel flow).

Web/desktop: paste the whole file into the entry, press Enter.
============================================================================ */

// ---- knobs ------------------------------------------------------------------
const width = 1.5           // channel width, 1.5 m
const depth = 0.6           // design water depth, 0.6 m
const slope = 0.001         // bed slope, 1 in 1000
const n_manning = 0.013     // formed concrete, Chow's table

// ---- model ------------------------------------------------------------------
const area = width * depth                          // wetted area, m^2
const perimeter = width + 2 * depth                 // wetted perimeter, m
const radius_h = area / perimeter                   // hydraulic radius, m
const q = 1 / n_manning * area * radius_h ^ (2 / 3) * slope ^ 0.5
const v_mean = q / area                             // mean velocity, m/s

// ---- results -----------------------------------------------------------------
print("wetted area:", area, "m^2")
print("wetted perimeter:", perimeter, "m")
print("hydraulic radius A/P:", radius_h, "m")
print("design discharge:", q, "m^3/s")
print("mean velocity:", v_mean, "m/s")

print("velocity in the self-cleaning band above 0.6 m/s:", v_mean >= 0.6)

/* A metre-wide-ish concrete channel on a 1-in-1000 grade carries a
cubic metre a second at walking pace -- 1.17 m/s, just above the
0.6 m/s that keeps grit moving. Manning's n is the whole personality of
the channel: swap concrete for weedy earth (n = 0.030) and the same
geometry carries less than half the flow, which is why drainage
engineers spend budgets on mowing banks as much as on diggers. */

/* ---- expected output ----
= wetted area: 0.9 m^2
= wetted perimeter: 2.7 m
= hydraulic radius A/P: 1/3 m
= design discharge: 1.05249082998 m^3/s
= mean velocity: 1.16943425553 m/s
= velocity in the self-cleaning band above 0.6 m/s: true
*/

scripts.name: orifice-flow
scripts.title: reading flow from a pressure difference
scripts.text:
/* ============================================================================
orifice-flow.epher -- reading flow from a pressure difference

A sharp-edged orifice in a pipe turns pressure into a measurable flow:
Q = Cd A sqrt(2 dp / rho), with the discharge coefficient Cd near 0.61
for a standard sharp edge. The script sizes a 50 mm orifice meter on a
20 kPa drop and reports the velocity through the vena contracta.

Source: White, Fluid Mechanics, ch. 6 and ch. 3 (thin-plate orifice
discharge, Cd ~ 0.61 for D/d above 0.2, the standard ISO 5167
thin-plate meter); the same formula with Crane Co., Technical Paper
410 (flow through orifices), the plant engineer's pocket reference.

Web/desktop: paste the whole file into the entry, press Enter.
============================================================================ */

// ---- knobs ------------------------------------------------------------------
const dp = 20e3             // measured pressure drop, 20 kPa
const d_hole = 0.050        // orifice bore, 50 mm
const c_discharge = 0.61             // discharge coefficient, sharp edge
const rho = 998             // water, kg/m^3

// ---- model ------------------------------------------------------------------
const area = pi / 4 * d_hole ^ 2                     // hole area, m^2
const q = c_discharge * area * sqrt(2 * dp / rho)             // flow, m^3/s
const jet_v = sqrt(2 * dp / rho)                     // ideal jet speed, m/s
const jet_real = c_discharge * jet_v                          // with the coefficient
const pipe_d = 0.1                                   // the meter's pipe, 100 mm
const pipe_v = q / (pi / 4 * pipe_d ^ 2)             // pipe velocity, m/s
const beta = d_hole / pipe_d                         // diameter ratio

// ---- results -----------------------------------------------------------------
print("orifice area:", area / 1e-6, "mm^2")
print("ideal jet speed at 20 kPa:", jet_v, "m/s")
print("actual flow:", q, "m^3/s")
print("flow in litres a second:", q * 1000, "L/s")
print("beta ratio hole-to-pipe:", beta)
print("pipe velocity upstream:", pipe_v, "m/s")
print("beta in the ISO 5167 band 0.2-0.75:", beta >= 0.2 and beta <= 0.75)

/* Twenty kilopascals across a stamp-sized hole moves 7.6 litres a
second -- 6.3 m/s of ideal jet, trimmed to 3.8 by the coefficient that
accounts for the vena contracta's neck. At beta 0.5 the meter sits
mid-band where ISO 5167 guarantees its Cd within a percent or two:
cheap, no moving parts, and accurate enough to bill water by. */

/* ---- expected output ----
= orifice area: 1963.49540849 mm^2
= ideal jet speed at 20 kPa: 6.33088937833 m/s
= actual flow: 0.00758271005788 m^3/s
= flow in litres a second: 7.58271005788 L/s
= beta ratio hole-to-pipe: 0.5
= pipe velocity upstream: 0.965460630195 m/s
= beta in the ISO 5167 band 0.2-0.75: true
*/

scripts.name: pump-power
scripts.title: the watts behind a litre a second
scripts.text:
/* ============================================================================
pump-power.epher -- the watts behind a litre a second

A pump lifting 10 litres a second through 25 metres of head does
hydraulic work P = rho g Q H; the motor pays more, divided by the
efficiency. The script separates water-power from wire-power and
prices a day of running, so the true cost of a leaky foot valve shows
up in money.

Source: Munson, Young and Okiishi, Fundamentals of Fluid Mechanics,
ch. 5 (the energy equation applied to pumps: hydraulic power
rho g Q H and pump efficiency eta); pump efficiencies 60-75 percent
for this size class per Karassik et al., Pump Handbook, ch. 2.

Web/desktop: paste the whole file into the entry, press Enter.
============================================================================ */

// ---- knobs ------------------------------------------------------------------
const flow = 0.01           // 10 litres a second
const head = 25             // total dynamic head, 25 m
const efficiency = 0.65     // wire-to-water efficiency
const hours = 8             // running hours a day

// ---- model ------------------------------------------------------------------
const hydraulic = 998 * 9.80665 * flow * head      // water power, W
const electrical = hydraulic / efficiency          // motor draw, W
const daily_kwh = electrical / 1000 * hours        // the day's bill, kWh
const lost_to_heat = electrical - hydraulic        // what the motor warms, W
const per_cubic = electrical / (flow * 1000)       // energy per litre, J/L
const per_point = (hydraulic / 0.55 - hydraulic / 0.75) / 20   // W per efficiency point

// ---- results -----------------------------------------------------------------
print("hydraulic (water) power:", hydraulic, "W")
print("electrical draw at 65% efficiency:", electrical, "W")
print("heat the motor and pump shed:", lost_to_heat, "W")
print("energy per litre lifted:", per_cubic, "J/L")
print("a day of running:", daily_kwh, "kWh")
print("each efficiency point is worth:", per_point, "W")

/* Lifting water 25 metres at 10 L/s is 2.45 kW of honest water power;
the meter reads 3.76, and 1.32 kW warms the pump house. At 30 kWh a
day the electricity invoice dwarfs the hardware in a year, which is
why a two-point efficiency gain on an always-on pump pays for itself
faster than any fitting on the pipe. */

/* ---- expected output ----
= hydraulic (water) power: 2446.759175 W
= electrical draw at 65% efficiency: 3764.24488462 W
= heat the motor and pump shed: 1317.48570962 W
= energy per litre lifted: 376.424488462 J/L
= a day of running: 30.1139590769 kWh
= each efficiency point is worth: 59.3153739394 W
*/

scripts.name: reynolds-number
scripts.title: whether a flow is calm or a storm
scripts.text:
/* ============================================================================
reynolds-number.epher -- whether a flow is calm or a storm

The Reynolds number Re = rho V D / mu compares inertia to viscosity: a
dimensionless verdict that sorts every flow into laminar (below ~2300
in pipes), turbulent (above ~4000) or the transition between. The
script computes it for water in a pipe and air over a wing chord, and
labels each regime.

Source: Munson, Young and Okiishi, Fundamentals of Fluid Mechanics,
ch. 8 (pipe flow: the Reynolds number and its laminar-turbulent
thresholds); the airfoil-chord case with standard air properties
(rho = 1.204 kg/m^3, mu = 1.82e-5 Pa s) follows Anderson,
Fundamentals of Aerodynamics. Water: rho = 998, mu = 1.002e-3 at 20 C
(Engineering ToolBox, "Water - Dynamic and Kinematic Viscosity").

Web/desktop: paste the whole file into the entry, press Enter.
============================================================================ */

// ---- knobs ------------------------------------------------------------------
const v_pipe = 2.0          // water speed in the pipe, 2 m/s
const d_pipe = 0.050        // pipe bore, 50 mm
const v_air = 30            // airspeed over the chord, 30 m/s
const chord = 0.2           // wing chord, 200 mm

// ---- model ------------------------------------------------------------------
const re_pipe = 998 * v_pipe * d_pipe / 1.002e-3     // water at 20 C
const re_air = 1.204 * v_air * chord / 1.82e-5       // air at 20 C
def pipe_regime(re) = if re < 2300 then "laminar" else if re > 4000 then "turbulent" else "transition"

// ---- results -----------------------------------------------------------------
print("Reynolds number, water in the pipe:", re_pipe)
print("pipe flow regime:", pipe_regime(re_pipe))
print("Reynolds number, air over the chord:", re_air)
print("a wing chord at 300000 is deep in turbulent:", re_air > 300000)
print("the same water at pipe-walking speed 0.1 m/s:", 998 * 0.1 * d_pipe / 1.002e-3)
print("that slower flow regime:", pipe_regime(998 * 0.1 * d_pipe / 1.002e-3))

/* The water main runs a hundred thousand Re -- chaotic, mixing,
friction that scales with speed squared -- while the wing chord rides
at four hundred thousand, the regime every aerodynamic table assumes.
Walk the same water at 0.1 m/s and Re drops to five thousand, nearly
calm: the SAME pipe, the SAME fluid, a different universe of flow,
decided by one dimensionless ratio. */

/* ---- expected output ----
= Reynolds number, water in the pipe: 49900000/501
= pipe flow regime: turbulent
= Reynolds number, air over the chord: 5160000/13
= a wing chord at 300000 is deep in turbulent: true
= the same water at pipe-walking speed 0.1 m/s: 2495000/501
= that slower flow regime: turbulent
*/

scripts.name: torricelli-tank-drain
scripts.title: how long a tank takes to empty
scripts.text:
/* ============================================================================
torricelli-tank-drain.epher -- how long a tank takes to empty

Torricelli's law: the jet leaves a hole at v = sqrt(2 g h), and as the
level falls the jet slows with it. Draining time for a prismatic tank
follows from integrating: T = (A_tank / A_hole) sqrt(2 h0 / g). The
loop walks the level hour by hour and the closed form is checked
against the level at that time.

Source: Munson, Young and Okiishi, Fundamentals of Fluid Mechanics,
ch. 3 (Bernoulli applications: Torricelli's theorem and the tank-drain
integral, Example 3.10 in that text). Evelli's 1643 experiment is the
historical anchor retold in every fluid text.

Web/desktop: paste the whole file into the entry, press Enter.
============================================================================ */

// ---- knobs ------------------------------------------------------------------
const tank_d = 1.2          // tank diameter, 1.2 m
const depth = 2.0           // initial water depth, 2 m
const hole_d = 0.010        // drain hole diameter, 10 mm

// ---- model ------------------------------------------------------------------
const a_tank = pi / 4 * tank_d ^ 2            // surface area, m^2
const a_hole = pi / 4 * hole_d ^ 2            // orifice area, m^2
const jet_start = sqrt(2 * 9.80665 * depth)   // initial jet speed, m/s
const t_drain = a_tank / a_hole * sqrt(2 * depth / 9.80665)  // full drain, s
def level(t) = (sqrt(depth) - t * a_hole / a_tank * sqrt(9.80665 / 2)) ^ 2
for mark in {0, 1800, 3600, 7200, 9000} do print("level at " + str(mark) + " s:", level(mark), "m")

// ---- results -----------------------------------------------------------------
print("initial jet speed:", jet_start, "m/s")
print("tank-to-hole area ratio:", a_tank / a_hole)
print("total time to drain:", t_drain, "s")
print("drain time in hours:", t_drain / 3600, "hr")
print("level at the predicted finish:", level(t_drain), "m")
print("the closed form lands exactly empty:", level(t_drain) < 0.001)

/* A 1.13-square-metre surface squeezing through a stamp-sized hole
takes 9197 seconds -- two and a half hours of dwindling trickle. The
jet starts at 6.3 m/s, brisk enough to jump a gutter, and ends barely
crawling: height drains with the square root of time remaining, and
almost half the water leaves in the first quarter of the clock. Plug
the hole with a thumb and the whole schedule divides by the same area
ratio. */

/* ---- expected output ----
= {level at 0 s: 2 m, level at 1800 s: 1.29372517296 m, level at 3600 s: 0.740679252167 m, level at 7200 s: 0.094274129333 m, level at 9000 s: 0.000914927291288 m}
= initial jet speed: 6.26311424133 m/s
= tank-to-hole area ratio: 14400
= total time to drain: 9196.70275529 s
= drain time in hours: 2.55463965425 hr
= level at the predicted finish: 0.000000000000000000000000000000197215226305 m
= the closed form lands exactly empty: true
*/

scripts.name: water-hammer
scripts.title: the pressure spike when a valve slams
scripts.text:
/* ============================================================================
water-hammer.epher -- the pressure spike when a valve slams

Shut a valve fast and the moving column of water has nowhere to go:
the Joukowsky equation dp = rho c dv converts the velocity change to a
pressure wave, with the wave speed c = sqrt(K / rho) set by water's
bulk stiffness. The script prices a slam at 2 m/s against a gentle
0.5 m/s closure, and shows why slow-closing valves exist.

Source: Wylie and Streeter, Fluid Transients in Systems (the Joukowsky
equation dp = -rho c dv and rigid-pipe wave speed sqrt(K/rho)); bulk
modulus of water K = 2.19 GPa per Munson, Fundamentals of Fluid
Mechanics, Appendix (properties of common liquids).

Web/desktop: paste the whole file into the entry, press Enter.
============================================================================ */

// ---- knobs ------------------------------------------------------------------
const v_flow = 2.0          // water speed before the slam, 2 m/s
const v_gentle = 0.5        // speed killed by a slow closure, 0.5 m/s
const k_water = 2.19e9      // bulk modulus of water, 2.19 GPa
const rho = 998             // water density, kg/m^3

// ---- model ------------------------------------------------------------------
const wave_speed = sqrt(k_water / rho)          // rigid pipe, m/s
const dp_slam = rho * wave_speed * v_flow       // Joukowsky spike, Pa
const dp_gentle = rho * wave_speed * v_gentle   // slow closure spike, Pa
const slam_bar = dp_slam / 1e5                  // in bar, for plumbing talk

// ---- results -----------------------------------------------------------------
print("wave speed in water (rigid pipe):", wave_speed, "m/s")
print("valve slams at 2 m/s, spike:", dp_slam / 1e6, "MPa")
print("the same spike in bar:", slam_bar, "bar")
print("gentle 0.5 m/s closure spike:", dp_gentle / 1e3, "kPa")
print("slam pressure vs a 400 kPa main:", dp_slam / 4e5, "times main pressure")
print("four times the velocity, four times the spike:", abs(dp_slam / dp_gentle - v_flow / v_gentle) < 1e-9)

/* Killing 2 m/s of flow in an instant fires a 2.96 MPa pulse -- 29.6
bar, seven times a household main's standing pressure -- up and down
the pipe at 1481 m/s, banging elbows and bursting fittings on the way.
The gentle closure that only kills half a metre per second raises
739 kPa, survivable: the spike cares about velocity change, not about
how important the valve was. */

/* ---- expected output ----
= wave speed in water (rigid pipe): 1481.34694706 m/s
= valve slams at 2 m/s, spike: 2.95676850633 MPa
= the same spike in bar: 29.5676850633 bar
= gentle 0.5 m/s closure spike: 739.192126581 kPa
= slam pressure vs a 400 kPa main: 7.39192126581 times main pressure
= four times the velocity, four times the spike: true
*/

scripts.name: bearing-l10-life
scripts.title: how long a bearing serves, statistically
scripts.text:
/* ============================================================================
bearing-l10-life.epher -- how long a bearing serves, statistically

A rolling bearing's life is a scatter plot; the L10 life is the point
90 percent of them outlive. L10 = (C/P)^a million revolutions, a = 3
for ball bearings, with C the basic dynamic load rating and P the
equivalent load. The script prices a 6205-class bearing at two loads
and shows the cube law's bite.

Source: Shigley's Mechanical Engineering Design (Budynas and Nisbett),
ch. 11 (rolling-contact bearings: the L10 life model, eq. 11-6, a = 3
for ball bearings, a = 10/3 for rollers); C = 14.0 kN is the 6205
deep-groove rating from manufacturer tables (SKF/NSK 6205).

Web/desktop: paste the whole file into the entry, press Enter.
============================================================================ */

// ---- knobs ------------------------------------------------------------------
const rating = 14.0e3       // basic dynamic load rating C, 14 kN (6205)
const load_heavy = 2.5e3    // equivalent radial load, 2.5 kN
const load_light = 2.0e3    // a lighter duty cycle, 2 kN
const rpm = 1450            // shaft speed, 1450 rpm

// ---- model ------------------------------------------------------------------
def l10_revs(p) = (rating / p) ^ 3          // L10 life, million revs
def l10_hours(p) = l10_revs(p) * 1e6 / (rpm * 60)
const life_heavy = l10_hours(load_heavy)
const life_light = l10_hours(load_light)
const ratio = life_light / life_heavy       // the cube law's reward

// ---- results -----------------------------------------------------------------
print("L10 life at 2.5 kN:", l10_revs(load_heavy), "million revs")
print("hours at 1450 rpm:", life_heavy, "hr")
print("L10 life at 2.0 kN:", l10_revs(load_light), "million revs")
print("hours at 1450 rpm:", life_light, "hr")
print("the 20% load cut bought this much life:", ratio, "times")
print("cube law in action (1.25^3 = 1.95):", abs(ratio - (2.5 / 2.0) ^ 3) < 1e-9)

/* At 2.5 kN the bearing is a 2000-hour part; ease the load to 2 kN and
it serves 3900 hours -- 95 percent more life for 20 percent less load,
the cube law compounding every saved newton. This is why shaft
designers chase load alignment before bigger bearings: half a
millimetre of misbalance can outvote a whole size step. */

/* ---- expected output ----
= L10 life at 2.5 kN: 175.616 million revs
= hours at 1450 rpm: 175616/87 hr
= L10 life at 2.0 kN: 343 million revs
= hours at 1450 rpm: 343000/87 hr
= the 20% load cut bought this much life: 1.953125 times
= cube law in action (1.25^3 = 1.95): true
*/

scripts.name: belt-length-and-tension
scripts.title: sizing an open belt drive
scripts.text:
/* ============================================================================
belt-length-and-tension.epher -- sizing an open belt drive

An open flat belt spans a 200 mm driver and a 100 mm driven, centres
400 mm apart. Belt length follows from the classic closed form
L = 2C + pi (D + d)/2 + (D - d)^2/(4C); wrap angle on the small
pulley and the tension ratio T1/T2 = e^(mu theta) decide how much
power the belt can carry before it slips.

Source: Machinery's Handbook (Oberg, Jones, Ryffel, McCauley and
Heald), belt drive section: the open-belt length formula and wrap
angles. The capstan tension relation T1/T2 = e^(mu theta) is developed
in Shigley's, ch. 17 (flat-belt drives), with mu = 0.30 for leather on
cast iron.

Web/desktop: paste the whole file into the entry, press Enter.
============================================================================ */

// ---- knobs ------------------------------------------------------------------
const d_driver = 0.200      // driving pulley, 200 mm
const d_driven = 0.100      // driven pulley, 100 mm
const centres = 0.400       // centre distance, 400 mm
const mu = 0.30             // friction, belt on pulley
const slack = 100           // slack-side tension, 100 N
const rpm_small = 1750      // speed of the small pulley, rpm

// ---- model ------------------------------------------------------------------
const length = 2 * centres + pi * (d_driver + d_driven) / 2 + (d_driver - d_driven) ^ 2 / (4 * centres)
const wrap = pi - 2 * asin((d_driver - d_driven) / (2 * centres))   // small pulley, rad
const tension_ratio = exp(mu * wrap)                 // T1/T2 at slip edge
const t_tight = slack * tension_ratio                // tight side at slip, N
const belt_speed = pi * d_driven * rpm_small / 60    // m/s
const power = (t_tight - slack) * belt_speed         // transmitted, W

// ---- results -----------------------------------------------------------------
print("belt length:", length / 1e-3, "mm")
print("wrap angle on the small pulley:", wrap, "rad")
print("wrap in degrees:", deg(wrap), "deg")
print("tension ratio at slip T1/T2:", tension_ratio)
print("tight-side tension for 100 N slack:", t_tight, "N")
print("belt speed:", belt_speed, "m/s")
print("power the grip carries (at slip edge):", power, "W")
print("grip improves with wrap angle:", tension_ratio > 1)

/* The belt is 1277 mm of leather doing two jobs: holding the centres
and gripping the pulleys. The small pulley is the weak link -- only
166 degrees of contact -- so its 2.38-to-1 tension ratio sets the
floor: 100 N of slack must be bought with 238 N of tight side before
the belt earns 1.26 kW. Double the wrap (a bigger driven pulley) and
the same belt carries more, which is why idlers hug small pulleys. */

/* ---- expected output ----
= belt length: 1277.48889804 mm
= wrap angle on the small pulley: 2.89093699125 rad
= wrap in degrees: 165.638488437 deg
= tension ratio at slip T1/T2: 2.38042988989
= tight-side tension for 100 N slack: 238.042988989 N
= belt speed: 9.16297857297 m/s
= power the grip carries (at slip edge): 1264.88495025 W
= grip improves with wrap angle: true
*/

scripts.name: bolt-torque-preload
scripts.title: torque in, clamp force out
scripts.text:
/* ============================================================================
bolt-torque-preload.epher -- torque in, clamp force out

Tightening an M12 to 60 N m with the usual K = 0.2 (threads and
friction under the head eat the rest) preloads the bolt with
F = T / (K d) -- about 25 kN of clamp. The script also runs the check
backwards: what torque stretches an 8.8 bolt to its 580 MPa proof
stress, the ceiling a reusable joint should respect.

Source: Shigley's Mechanical Engineering Design (Budynas and Nisbett),
ch. 8 (screws and fasteners: the torque-preload relation T = K F_i d,
table 8-1 for the K factor; metric mechanical-property classes, table
8-9 -- class 8.8 proof stress 580 MPa).

Web/desktop: paste the whole file into the entry, press Enter.
============================================================================ */

// ---- knobs ------------------------------------------------------------------
const torque = 60           // wrench torque, 60 N m
const d_bolt = 0.012        // M12 nominal diameter
const k_factor = 0.2        // the standard K, oiled threads
const stress_area = 84.3e-6 // M12 tensile stress area, m^2
const proof_stress = 580e6  // class 8.8 proof, 580 MPa

// ---- model ------------------------------------------------------------------
const preload = torque / (k_factor * d_bolt)        // clamp force, N
const bolt_stress = preload / stress_area           // average stress, Pa
const fi_proof = proof_stress * stress_area         // proof-load clamp, N
const torque_proof = k_factor * d_bolt * fi_proof   // the matching torque, N m
const share = preload / fi_proof                    // how close 60 N m sits

// ---- results -----------------------------------------------------------------
print("preload from 60 N m:", preload / 1e3, "kN")
print("average bolt stress:", bolt_stress / 1e6, "MPa")
print("that is this share of the 580 MPa proof:", bolt_stress / proof_stress)
print("clamp at full proof load:", fi_proof / 1e3, "kN")
print("torque that reaches proof:", torque_proof, "N m")
print("headroom in the wrench:", torque_proof / torque, "to 1")

/* Sixty newton-metres clamps the joint with 25 kN -- 297 MPa of mean
stress, just over half the class-8.8 proof load. The headroom line is
the wrench discipline: 117 N m reaches proof, so an enthusiastic
double-torque with a long bar snaps studs, and a rusty K = 0.3 steals
a third of the clamp without changing the wrench at all. */

/* ---- expected output ----
= preload from 60 N m: 25 kN
= average bolt stress: 250000/843 MPa
= that is this share of the 580 MPa proof: 0.511310181208
= clamp at full proof load: 48.894 kN
= torque that reaches proof: 117.3456 N m
= headroom in the wrench: 1.95576 to 1
*/

scripts.name: crank-slider-motion
scripts.title: the piston's path around the revolution
scripts.text:
/* ============================================================================
crank-slider-motion.epher -- the piston's path around the revolution

A crank of 40 mm and a rod of 140 mm: piston position from the crank
centre is x(theta) = r cos(theta) + sqrt(l^2 - r^2 sin^2(theta)). The
loop walks the half-turn from top dead centre and the checks recover
the two landmarks: 180 mm at TDC, 100 mm at BDC, a 80 mm stroke.

Source: Hibbeler, Engineering Mechanics: Dynamics (kinematics of
machinery: the slider-crank position relation); the same derivation
as Shigley's, ch. 15 or any internal-combustion engine text
(Taylor, The Internal Combustion Engine in Theory and Practice).

Web/desktop: paste the whole file into the entry, press Enter.
============================================================================ */

// ---- knobs ------------------------------------------------------------------
const r_crank = 0.040       // crank radius, 40 mm
const l_rod = 0.140         // connecting rod length, 140 mm

// ---- model ------------------------------------------------------------------
def piston(deg) = r_crank * cos(deg(deg)) + sqrt(l_rod ^ 2 - r_crank ^ 2 * sin(deg(deg)) ^ 2)
for a in {0, 45, 90, 135, 180} do print("at " + str(a) + " deg:", piston(a) / 1e-3, "mm from the centre")
const stroke = 2 * r_crank                          // the geometric truth
const rod_ratio = r_crank / l_rod                   // the shape of the wiggle
const x_half = piston(90) / 1e-3                    // mid-crank position, mm

// ---- results -----------------------------------------------------------------
print("stroke (2r):", stroke / 1e-3, "mm")
print("rod ratio r/l:", rod_ratio)
print("piston at 90 deg crank:", x_half, "mm")
print("position at TDC:", piston(0) / 1e-3, "mm")
print("position at BDC:", piston(180) / 1e-3, "mm")
print("the excursion is not symmetric about mid-stroke:", abs(x_half - 100) > 1)

/* The half-turn carries the piston from 180 mm (top centre) to 100 mm
(bottom centre) -- but the 90-degree mark sits at 134 mm, not the
140 a naive eye expects: the rod's finite length bulges the travel
toward top centre, and the longer the rod (smaller ratio), the
sinusoidal the motion. Short rods make punchy engines and rough
ones -- this ratio, 0.286, is comfortably smooth. */

/* ---- expected output ----
= {at 0 deg: 180 mm from the centre, at 45 deg: 112.564004731 mm from the centre, at 90 deg: 122.717324635 mm from the centre, at 135 deg: 177.254846167 mm from the centre, at 180 deg: 105.297593357 mm from the centre}
= stroke (2r): 80 mm
= rod ratio r/l: 2/7
= piston at 90 deg crank: 122.717324635 mm
= position at TDC: 180 mm
= position at BDC: 105.297593357 mm
= the excursion is not symmetric about mid-stroke: true
*/

scripts.name: fan-affinity-laws
scripts.title: what doubling a fan's speed really costs
scripts.text:
/* ============================================================================
fan-affinity-laws.epher -- what doubling a fan's speed really costs

The affinity laws: flow scales with speed (Q2/Q1 = n2/n1), pressure
with speed squared, and power with speed cubed. The script runs a
5 m^3/s at 250 Pa, 2 kW fan from 1200 to 2400 rpm and shows the cube
law's invoice -- the reason variable-speed drives replaced dampers.

Source: ASHRAE Handbook -- Fundamentals, ch. 21 (fans: the affinity
laws, Q, p and P scaling with n, n^2 and n^3 for a fixed system and
constant efficiency).

Web/desktop: paste the whole file into the entry, press Enter.
============================================================================ */

// ---- knobs ------------------------------------------------------------------
const rpm_a = 1200          // design speed, 1200 rpm
const rpm_b = 2400          // the speeding-up case, 2400 rpm
const q_a = 5000            // air flow, m^3/hr
const p_a = 250             // developed pressure, Pa
const p_a_kW = 2.0          // shaft power, kW

// ---- model ------------------------------------------------------------------
const speed_ratio = rpm_b / rpm_a
const q_b = q_a * speed_ratio                    // affinity law 1
const p_b = p_a * speed_ratio ^ 2                // affinity law 2
const power_b = p_a_kW * speed_ratio ^ 3         // affinity law 3
const power_bill = power_b / p_a_kW              // the cost of doubling

// ---- results -----------------------------------------------------------------
print("flow doubles:", q_b, "m^3/hr")
print("pressure quadruples:", p_b, "Pa")
print("power grows by the cube:", power_b, "kW")
print("doubling speed costs this multiple of power:", power_bill)
print("the cube law (2^3 = 8):", abs(power_bill - 8) < 1e-9)
print("back to 1260 rpm and the power near halves:", p_a_kW * (1260 / rpm_a) ^ 3, "kW")

/* Doubling the fan's speed doubles the air and quadruples the
pressure -- and multiplies the electricity by eight, 2 kW to 16.
Read the last line the other way: slowing a fan 5 percent cuts power
14 percent, which is why a variable-speed drive repays itself in any
system that spends most of its life at part flow. The cube law is a
bill when you speed up and a dividend when you slow down. */

/* ---- expected output ----
= flow doubles: 10000 m^3/hr
= pressure quadruples: 1000 Pa
= power grows by the cube: 16 kW
= doubling speed costs this multiple of power: 8
= the cube law (2^3 = 8): true
= back to 1260 rpm and the power near halves: 2.31525 kW
*/

scripts.name: flywheel-energy
scripts.title: a steel disc as a battery of spin
scripts.text:
/* ============================================================================
flywheel-energy.epher -- a steel disc as a battery of spin

A 300 mm by 20 mm solid steel disc spun at 3000 rpm stores
E = 1/2 I omega^2, with I = 1/2 m r^2 for a solid disc of mass
m = rho pi r^2 t. The script states the store at two speeds and the
check confirms energy scales with the square of speed.

Source: Shigley's Mechanical Engineering Design (Budynas and Nisbett),
ch. 16 (flywheels: the energy of a rotating mass and the coefficient
of fluctuation); disc inertia from any dynamics text (Hibbeler,
Dynamics, mass moment of inertia of a cylinder).

Web/desktop: paste the whole file into the entry, press Enter.
============================================================================ */

// ---- knobs ------------------------------------------------------------------
const d_disc = 0.300        // disc diameter, 300 mm
const thickness = 0.020     // disc thickness, 20 mm
const rho_steel = 7850      // steel density, kg/m^3
const rpm_a = 3000          // first speed, 3000 rpm
const rpm_b = 6000          // second speed, 6000 rpm

// ---- model ------------------------------------------------------------------
const radius = d_disc / 2                       // m
const mass = pi * radius ^ 2 * thickness * rho_steel   // kg
const inertia = 0.5 * mass * radius ^ 2         // kg m^2
def spin_energy(rpm) = 0.5 * inertia * (rpm * 2 * pi / 60) ^ 2   // J
const e_a = spin_energy(rpm_a)
const e_b = spin_energy(rpm_b)
