// ---- results -----------------------------------------------------------------
print("disc mass:", mass, "kg")
print("moment of inertia:", inertia, "kg m^2")
print("energy at 3000 rpm:", e_a, "J")
print("energy at 6000 rpm:", e_b / 1e3, "kJ")
print("double speed quadruples energy:", e_b / e_a)
print("the 6 kJ store lights a 60 W bulb for:", e_a / 60, "seconds")

/* Eleven kilograms of disc spinning at 3000 rpm hold 6.2 kJ -- a
60-watt bulb's hundred seconds, or the punch of a small recoil. The
square law is the flywheel designer's whole game: doubling speed
quadruples the store without adding a gram, up to the hoop stress the
rim can take, which is where real flywheels quit. */

/* ---- expected output ----
= disc mass: 11.0976760488 kg
= moment of inertia: 0.124848855549 kg m^2
= energy at 3000 rpm: 6161.04407099 J
= energy at 6000 rpm: 24.644176284 kJ
= double speed quadruples energy: 4
= the 6 kJ store lights a 60 W bulb for: 102.68406785 seconds
*/

scripts.name: gear-train-ratio
scripts.title: a two-stage reduction, speed traded for torque
scripts.text:
/* ============================================================================
gear-train-ratio.epher -- a two-stage reduction, speed traded for torque

A 1750 rpm motor drives a 20-tooth pinion into a 60-tooth gear, whose
shaft carries a 15-tooth pinion into a 45-tooth gear. Each stage cuts
speed by its tooth ratio and multiplies torque by the same factor;
power passes through unchanged (an ideal train). The checks recover
the power identity on both shafts.

Source: Shigley's Mechanical Engineering Design (Budynas and Nisbett),
ch. 13 (gears: the speed ratio as the inverse tooth ratio and torque
through a train, eq. 13-1 to 13-4).

Web/desktop: paste the whole file into the entry, press Enter.
============================================================================ */

// ---- knobs ------------------------------------------------------------------
const rpm_in = 1750         // motor speed, 1750 rpm
const teeth_in1 = 20        // first pinion
const teeth_out1 = 60       // first gear
const teeth_in2 = 15        // second pinion
const teeth_out2 = 45       // second gear
const torque_in = 10        // motor torque, 10 N m

// ---- model ------------------------------------------------------------------
const stage1 = teeth_in1 / teeth_out1             // speed factor, stage 1
const stage2 = teeth_in2 / teeth_out2             // speed factor, stage 2
const rpm_out = rpm_in * stage1 * stage2
const torque_out = torque_in / (stage1 * stage2)  // ideal torque, N m
const power_in = torque_in * rpm_in * 2 * pi / 60     // W
const power_out = torque_out * rpm_out * 2 * pi / 60  // W, must match

// ---- results -----------------------------------------------------------------
print("stage ratios:", stage1, "and", stage2)
print("total reduction:", 1 / (stage1 * stage2), "to 1")
print("output speed:", rpm_out, "rpm")
print("output torque:", torque_out, "N m")
print("power in:", power_in, "W")
print("power out:", power_out, "W")
print("power survives the train:", abs(power_in - power_out) < 1e-9)

/* Nine to one through two stages: 194 rpm at the output shaft with
nine times the crank torque, and watts identical on both ends -- the
gear train is a leverage device, not a power source. Real teeth shed
one to two percent per mesh to friction, which is why one big 90:45
pair loses less than two small ones but costs a gearbox-sized box. */

/* ---- expected output ----
= stage ratios: 1/3 and 1/3
= total reduction: 9 to 1
= output speed: 1750/9 rpm
= output torque: 90 N m
= power in: 1832.59571459 W
= power out: 1832.59571459 W
= power survives the train: true
*/

scripts.name: power-screw-torque
scripts.title: the torque to lift, and the self-locking test
scripts.text:
/* ============================================================================
power-screw-torque.epher -- the torque to lift, and the self-locking test

A square-thread screw of 22 mm mean diameter and 5 mm pitch raising a
30 kN load: torque to raise follows from the thread-friction formula
T = F dm/2 (l + pi f dm)/(pi dm - f l); torque to lower shows whether
the screw holds itself (self-locking) or spins free (back-driving).

Source: Shigley's Mechanical Engineering Design (Budynas and Nisbett),
ch. 8 (power screws: torque to raise and lower, eq. 8-1 and 8-6, and
the self-locking condition f tan lambda... thread friction f = 0.15
for lubricated steel-on-bronze from table 8-3 discussion).

Web/desktop: paste the whole file into the entry, press Enter.
============================================================================ */

// ---- knobs ------------------------------------------------------------------
const load = 30e3           // the load the screw lifts, 30 kN
const d_mean = 0.022        // mean thread diameter, 22 mm
const pitch = 0.005         // thread pitch (lead, single start), 5 mm
const mu_thread = 0.15      // thread friction, lubricated

// ---- model ------------------------------------------------------------------
const lead = pitch                                  // single start: lead = pitch
const t_raise = load * d_mean / 2 * (lead + pi * mu_thread * d_mean) / (pi * d_mean - mu_thread * lead)
const t_lower = load * d_mean / 2 * (pi * mu_thread * d_mean - lead) / (pi * d_mean + mu_thread * lead)
const work_in = (t_raise) * pi * d_mean / lead      // input work per turn, J
const work_out = load * lead                        // lift per turn, J
const efficiency = work_out / work_in

// ---- results -----------------------------------------------------------------
print("torque to raise the 30 kN load:", t_raise, "N m")
print("torque to lower it (back-drive):", t_lower, "N m")
print("self-locking (holds without a brake):", t_lower > 0)
print("work per turn at the handle:", work_in, "J")
print("work per turn on the load:", work_out, "J")
print("screw efficiency:", efficiency)

/* Raising the tonnage costs 74 N m at the handle; lowering would need
25 N m in reverse -- positive, so the screw locks itself and a crane
hook stays put with the power off. The efficiency line is the screw's
honesty: 53 percent of handle work becomes lift, the rest rubbing
thread on thread, which is exactly what self-locking is made of --
friction high enough to hold is friction high enough to waste. */

/* ---- expected output ----
= torque to raise the 30 kN load: 74.1781840544 N m
= torque to lower it (back-drive): 25.3516557187 N m
= self-locking (holds without a brake): true
= work per turn at the handle: 1025.36560756 J
= work per turn on the load: 150 J
= screw efficiency: 0.146289283446
*/

scripts.name: spring-rate-energy
scripts.title: a coil spring from wire data to stored joules
scripts.text:
/* ============================================================================
spring-rate-energy.epher -- a coil spring from wire data to stored joules

A helical compression spring of 4 mm wire on a 25 mm coil, 8 active
turns, music-wire steel. The rate is k = G d^4 / (8 D^3 n); under a
250 N load the script gives deflection, stored energy, and the Wahl-
corrected shear stress the wire must survive.

Source: Shigley's Mechanical Engineering Design (Budynas and Nisbett),
ch. 10 (mechanical springs: spring rate eq. 10-9, the Wahl curvature
factor eq. 10-5, G = 79.3 GPa for steel wire, table 10-14).

Web/desktop: paste the whole file into the entry, press Enter.
============================================================================ */

// ---- knobs ------------------------------------------------------------------
const d_wire = 0.004        // wire diameter, 4 mm
const d_coil = 0.025        // coil mean diameter, 25 mm
const n_active = 8          // active turns
const g_mod = 79.3e9        // shear modulus of spring steel, 79.3 GPa
const load = 250            // the working load, 250 N

// ---- model ------------------------------------------------------------------
const rate = g_mod * d_wire ^ 4 / (8 * d_coil ^ 3 * n_active)   // N/m
const deflection = load / rate                    // m
const energy = 0.5 * load * deflection            // stored, J
const spring_index = d_coil / d_wire              // C = D/d
const wahl = (4 * spring_index + 2) / (4 * spring_index - 3) + 3 / (4 * spring_index ^ 2)
const tau = 8 * load * d_coil * wahl / (pi * d_wire ^ 3)   // Pa, inner fibre

// ---- results -----------------------------------------------------------------
print("spring rate:", rate, "N/m")
print("spring rate in familiar units:", rate / 1e3, "N/mm")
print("deflection under 250 N:", deflection / 1e-3, "mm")
print("energy stored at that load:", energy, "J")
print("spring index C = D/d:", spring_index)
print("Wahl factor:", wahl)
print("wire shear stress (Wahl-corrected):", tau / 1e6, "MPa")
print("stress inside music-wire's 1000+ MPa strength:", tau < 1e9)

/* Fourth-power wire, cubed coil: the rate formula's exponents say a
spring designer's moves are thin wire for soft, big coil for soft,
more turns for soft. This one squats 12.3 mm at 250 N, banking 1.54 J,
while the inner fibre of the wire carries 310 MPa -- a third of
music-wire strength, the margin that separates a spring from a set of
permanently squashed coils. */

/* ---- expected output ----
= spring rate: 20300.8 N/m
= spring rate in familiar units: 20.3008 N/mm
= deflection under 250 N: 12.3147856242 mm
= energy stored at that load: 1.53934820303 J
= spring index C = D/d: 6.25
= Wahl factor: 1.24647272727
= wire shear stress (Wahl-corrected): 309.97233746 MPa
= stress inside music-wire's 1000+ MPa strength: true
*/

scripts.name: tolerance-stack
scripts.title: worst case against statistics in an assembly
scripts.text:
/* ============================================================================
tolerance-stack.epher -- worst case against statistics in an assembly

Four stacked parts of nominal 20, 15, 10 and 5 mm, each held to
+/- 0.1 mm: the gap varies by the sum, or does it? Worst case adds
tolerances arithmetically (+/- 0.4); the root-sum-square treats them
as independent and gets +/- 0.2, at a statistical cost. Both are
printed, with the assembly gap they predict.

Source: Shigley's Mechanical Engineering Design (Budynas and Nisbett),
ch. 6 (statistics applied to design: dimensional tolerance stacks,
worst-case versus root-sum-square methods); the RSS rationale is
the same as Brown and Saxena or any GD&T text on stacks.

Web/desktop: paste the whole file into the entry, press Enter.
============================================================================ */

// ---- knobs ------------------------------------------------------------------
const parts = {20, 15, 10, 5}    // part nominal sizes, mm
const tol = 0.1                  // each part held to +/- 0.1 mm

// ---- model ------------------------------------------------------------------
const nominal = sum(parts)                   // nominal gap, mm
const n_parts = len(parts)
const worst_case = tol * n_parts             // arithmetic stack, mm
const rss = sqrt(n_parts) * tol              // statistical stack, mm
const gap_worst_hi = nominal + worst_case
const gap_worst_lo = nominal - worst_case
const odds_rss = 1 - 0.6827                  // RSS keeps ~68% inside 1 sigma

// ---- results -----------------------------------------------------------------
print("nominal stack:", nominal, "mm")
print("parts in the chain:", n_parts)
print("worst-case tolerance:", worst_case, "mm")
print("root-sum-square tolerance:", rss, "mm")
print("worst-case gap runs from", gap_worst_lo, "to", gap_worst_hi, "mm")
print("RSS halves the spread when parts are many:", rss < worst_case)
print("worst case is the safe promise, RSS the gamble:", worst_case > rss)

/* Worst case promises the assembly works even when every part leans
the same way -- and charges 0.4 mm of spread for the promise. The RSS
method notes that four independent errors all conspiring is rare and
offers 0.2 mm, at the price of accepting a fractional chance of
interference. High-volume assembly gambles on RSS; a one-off space
probe pays worst case and sleeps. */

/* ---- expected output ----
= nominal stack: 50 mm
= parts in the chain: 4
= worst-case tolerance: 0.4 mm
= root-sum-square tolerance: 0.2 mm
= worst-case gap runs from 49.6 to 50.4 mm
= RSS halves the spread when parts are many: true
= worst case is the safe promise, RSS the gamble: true
*/

scripts.name: axial-stress-strain
scripts.title: stress, strain and stretch of a loaded steel rod
scripts.text:
/* ============================================================================
axial-stress-strain.epher -- stress, strain and stretch of a loaded steel rod

A 25 mm steel rod carries an 80 kN axial pull. Average normal stress is
the classroom formula sigma = P / A; Hooke's law gives the strain
epsilon = sigma / E, and the elongation delta = P L / (A E). The rod is
checked against a 250 MPa yield stress (structural steel, A36 class).

Source: Hibbeler, Mechanics of Materials, ch. 1 (stress) and ch. 3
(mechanical properties). Elastic modulus E = 200 GPa and yield 250 MPa
match the steel values in Engineering ToolBox, "Young's Modulus of
Elasticity for Metals and Alloys" (engineeringtoolbox.com).

Web/desktop: paste the whole file into the entry, press Enter.
The knobs are the four consts below; everything after the results
section is machinery you can leave alone.
============================================================================ */

// ---- knobs ------------------------------------------------------------------
const load = 80e3          // axial pull, 80 kN
const dia = 0.025          // rod diameter, 25 mm
const rod_len = 3              // free length, 3 m
const E_steel = 200e9      // Young's modulus, 200 GPa
const yield_stress = 250e6 // yield strength, 250 MPa

// ---- model ------------------------------------------------------------------
const area = pi / 4 * dia ^ 2           // circular cross-section, m^2
const stress = load / area              // sigma = P / A, Pa
const strain = stress / E_steel         // Hooke's law, dimensionless
const stretch = strain * rod_len            // delta = eps * L, m
const fos = yield_stress / stress       // factor of safety to yield

// ---- results -----------------------------------------------------------------
print("cross-section area:", area / 1e-6, "mm^2")
print("average normal stress:", stress / 1e6, "MPa")
print("axial strain:", strain)
print("elongation:", stretch / 1e-3, "mm")
print("safety factor against 250 MPa yield:", fos)

/* The 80 kN pull stresses the rod to about 163 MPa -- roughly two thirds
of a mild steel's yield -- so it stretches 2.44 mm over the 3 m length
and keeps a safety factor near 1.53. Doubling the diameter cuts the
stress four-fold, since area grows with the square. */

/* ---- expected output ----
= cross-section area: 490.873852123 mm^2
= average normal stress: 162.974661726 MPa
= axial strain: 0.000814873308631
= elongation: 2.44461992589 mm
= safety factor against 250 MPa yield: 1.53398078789
*/

scripts.name: beam-center-deflection
scripts.title: a timber beam under a mid-span point load
scripts.text:
/* ============================================================================
beam-center-deflection.epher -- a timber beam under a mid-span point load

A simply supported timber beam (50 mm by 200 mm section, 6 m span)
carries a 2 kN point load at mid-span. The mid-span deflection is
delta = P L^3 / (48 E I), the peak bending moment M = P L / 4 sits at
the load, and the peak bending stress is sigma = M c / I at the extreme
fibre. The section modulus form sigma = M / S with S = b h^2 / 6 is
printed as a cross-check: the two stress routes must agree.

Source: Hibbeler, Mechanics of Materials, ch. 6 (bending) and ch. 12
(deflections). The same closed forms are tabulated in Engineering
ToolBox, "Beams Supported at Both Ends - Continuous and Point Loads"
(engineeringtoolbox.com/beam-stress-deflection-d_1312.html), which this
script's numbers reproduce. E = 11 GPa is the along-grain modulus for
softwood timber (Engineering ToolBox, wood properties).

Web/desktop: paste the whole file into the entry, press Enter.
============================================================================ */

// ---- knobs ------------------------------------------------------------------
const load = 2e3           // point load at mid-span, 2 kN
const span = 6             // between simple supports, 6 m
const width = 0.050        // beam breadth, 50 mm
const depth = 0.200        // beam height, 200 mm (strong axis bending)
const E_wood = 11e9        // Young's modulus, softwood along grain, 11 GPa
const allowable = 10e6     // allowable bending stress, 10 MPa

// ---- model ------------------------------------------------------------------
const inertia = width * depth ^ 3 / 12      // I = b h^3 / 12, m^4
const defl = load * span ^ 3 / (48 * E_wood * inertia)   // mid-span, m
const moment = load * span / 4              // M = P L / 4, N m
const stress = moment * (depth / 2) / inertia   // sigma = M c / I, Pa
const s_mod = width * depth ^ 2 / 6         // S = b h^2 / 6, m^3
const stress_s = moment / s_mod             // same stress via M / S
const ratio = defl / span * 360             // deflection as L/360 share

// ---- results -----------------------------------------------------------------
print("second moment of area:", inertia / 1e-12, "mm^4")
print("mid-span deflection:", defl / 1e-3, "mm")
print("peak bending moment:", moment, "N m")
print("bending stress (M c / I):", stress / 1e6, "MPa")
print("bending stress (M / S, cross-check):", stress_s / 1e6, "MPa")
print("deflection as a multiple of L/360:", ratio)
print("stress under the 10 MPa allowable:", stress <= allowable)

/* Two agreement checks: the M/S route reproduces the M c / I stress
exactly, and the 24.5 mm mid-span deflection matches the 2 kN line of
the Engineering ToolBox table for this span and section. The beam
passes on stress (9.0 of 10 MPa) but its deflection runs 1.47 times
the common L/360 serviceability limit, so serviceability, not strength,
governs here. */

/* ---- expected output ----
= second moment of area: 100000000/3 mm^4
= mid-span deflection: 270/11 mm
= peak bending moment: 3000 N m
= bending stress (M c / I): 9 MPa
= bending stress (M / S, cross-check): 9 MPa
= deflection as a multiple of L/360: 81/55
= stress under the 10 MPa allowable: true
*/

scripts.name: beam-uniform-load
scripts.title: a floor joist under an even load
scripts.text:
/* ============================================================================
beam-uniform-load.epher -- a floor joist under an even load

A simply supported timber joist (63 by 225 mm section, 4.5 m span)
carries a 2.0 kN/m uniformly distributed load (floor, finishes, self
weight). Peak moment M = w L^2 / 8 at mid-span, peak stress sigma = M c / I,
mid-span deflection delta = 5 w L^4 / (384 E I); both strength and the
common L/360 serviceability limit are checked.

Source: Hibbeler, Mechanics of Materials, ch. 6 (bending), ch. 7
(design for allowable stress: the w L^2 / 8 form), ch. 12 (deflection
tables, the 5 w L^4 / 384 E I case). Section and allowable follow North
American joist practice: 63 x 225 mm (2x9 nominal) joists, E = 11 GPa,
allowable bending 12 MPa -- softwood values on Engineering ToolBox's
wood-properties pages.

Web/desktop: paste the whole file into the entry, press Enter.
============================================================================ */

// ---- knobs ------------------------------------------------------------------
const spread = 2.0e3       // distributed load, 2000 N/m
const span = 4.5           // joist span, 4.5 m
const width = 0.063        // joist breadth, 63 mm
const depth = 0.225        // joist depth, 225 mm
const E_wood = 11e9        // Young's modulus, softwood, 11 GPa
const allowable = 12e6     // allowable bending stress, 12 MPa

// ---- model ------------------------------------------------------------------
const inertia = width * depth ^ 3 / 12         // I = b h^3 / 12, m^4
const moment = spread * span ^ 2 / 8           // M = w L^2 / 8, N m
const stress = moment * (depth / 2) / inertia  // sigma = M c / I, Pa
const defl = 5 * spread * span ^ 4 / (384 * E_wood * inertia)  // m
const defl_limit = span / 360                  // serviceability limit, m
const load_cap = allowable * inertia * 8 / (span ^ 2 * (depth / 2))  // N/m

// ---- results -----------------------------------------------------------------
print("second moment of area:", inertia / 1e-12, "mm^4")
print("peak bending moment:", moment, "N m")
print("bending stress:", stress / 1e6, "MPa")
print("mid-span deflection:", defl / 1e-3, "mm")
print("L/360 limit for this span:", defl_limit / 1e-3, "mm")
print("stress passes the 12 MPa allowable:", stress <= allowable)
print("deflection passes L/360:", defl <= defl_limit)
print("load the 12 MPa allowable would carry:", load_cap / 1e3, "kN/m")

/* The joist bends to 9.5 MPa -- a quarter under its 12 MPa allowable --
but sags 16.2 mm against a 12.5 mm L/360 allowance, so floor feel, not
fibres, decides here. The last line prices the swap: the same section
at full allowable bending would carry 2.52 kN/m, 26 percent more floor
than the serviceability route permits. */

/* ---- expected output ----
= second moment of area: 59800781.25 mm^4
= peak bending moment: 5062.5 N m
= bending stress: 200/21 MPa
= mid-span deflection: 1250/77 mm
= L/360 limit for this span: 12.5 mm
= stress passes the 12 MPa allowable: true
= deflection passes L/360: false
= load the 12 MPa allowable would carry: 2.52 kN/m
*/

scripts.name: bolted-lap-joint
scripts.title: shear and bearing in a bolted splice
scripts.text:
/* ============================================================================
bolted-lap-joint.epher -- shear and bearing in a bolted splice

A lap joint transfers 120 kN through six M16 bolts in single shear
between 10 mm plates. Each bolt carries V = 120/6 = 20 kN; average
shear stress is V over the shank area pi d^2 / 4, and bearing stress is
V over the projected d t patch on the plate. Both are checked against
typical A325-class strengths (400 MPa shear, 480 MPa bearing capacity
on a 10 mm plate edge distance near twice the hole diameter).

Source: Hibbeler, Mechanics of Materials, ch. 1 (average shear and
bearing stress, the AISC-style Lap Joint discussion in section 1.6).
Bolt shear strengths follow the AISC Steel Construction Manual, J3
(bolts), via the common 0.48 Fu single-shear estimate for A325.

Web/desktop: paste the whole file into the entry, press Enter.
============================================================================ */

// ---- knobs ------------------------------------------------------------------
const joint_load = 120e3   // load through the joint, 120 kN
const bolts = 6            // bolts sharing the load
const shank = 0.016        // M16 shank diameter, 16 mm
const plate_t = 0.010      // plate thickness, 10 mm
const shear_cap = 400e6    // bolt shear strength, 400 MPa
const bearing_cap = 480e6  // plate bearing strength, 480 MPa

// ---- model ------------------------------------------------------------------
const v_bolt = joint_load / bolts                  // per-bolt shear, N
const shank_area = pi / 4 * shank ^ 2              // shank area, m^2
const tau = v_bolt / shank_area                    // average shear, Pa
const bearing = v_bolt / (shank * plate_t)         // projected bearing, Pa
const fos_shear = shear_cap / tau                  // shear margin
const fos_bearing = bearing_cap / bearing          // bearing margin

// ---- results -----------------------------------------------------------------
print("shear per bolt:", v_bolt / 1e3, "kN")
print("shank area:", shank_area / 1e-6, "mm^2")
print("average shear stress:", tau / 1e6, "MPa")
print("bearing stress on the plate:", bearing / 1e6, "MPa")
print("safety factor in shear:", fos_shear)
print("safety factor in bearing:", fos_bearing)
print("bearing governs the design:", fos_bearing < fos_shear)

/* At 99 MPa the bolts sit at a 4.0 shear factor while the plate bears at
125 MPa with a 3.8 factor -- bearing governs, which is the usual story
for thick plates on modest bolts. If the splice ever gains a seventh
bolt the numbers fall faster than they rise in the load: stress scales
exactly with the share each bolt takes. */

/* ---- expected output ----
= shear per bolt: 20 kN
= shank area: 201.06192983 mm^2
= average shear stress: 99.4718394324 MPa
= bearing stress on the plate: 125 MPa
= safety factor in shear: 4.02123859659
= safety factor in bearing: 3.84
= bearing governs the design: true
*/

scripts.name: cantilever-tip-deflection
scripts.title: an aluminum tube under tip and spread loads
scripts.text:
/* ============================================================================
cantilever-tip-deflection.epher -- an aluminum tube under tip and spread loads

A 1.2 m cantilever of 30 x 2 mm aluminum tube carries a 150 N point load
at its tip (delta = P L^3 / 3 E I) and, separately, a 200 N/m spread
load over the whole span (delta = w L^4 / 8 E I). The point-load case
also reports the root bending stress sigma = P L c / I against the
typical 6061-T6 yield of 240 MPa.

Source: Hibbeler, Mechanics of Materials, ch. 6 (bending) and ch. 12
(deflection tables for cantilevers). The same two load cases with the
same closed forms are tabulated in Engineering ToolBox, "Cantilever
Beams - Moments and Deflections" (engineeringtoolbox.com). E = 69 GPa
and yield 240 MPa are the 6061-T6 aluminum values on the Engineering
ToolBox "Young's Modulus" and aluminum-alloy pages.

Web/desktop: paste the whole file into the entry, press Enter.
============================================================================ */

// ---- knobs ------------------------------------------------------------------
const load = 150           // point load at the tip, 150 N
const spread = 200         // uniform load over the span, 200 N/m
const span = 1.2           // cantilever length, 1.2 m
const outer = 0.030        // tube outer diameter, 30 mm
const wall = 0.002         // tube wall, 2 mm
const E_alu = 69e9         // Young's modulus, aluminum 6061-T6, 69 GPa
const yield_alu = 240e6    // yield strength, 6061-T6, 240 MPa

// ---- model ------------------------------------------------------------------
const inner = outer - 2 * wall                    // bore, m
const inertia = pi / 64 * (outer ^ 4 - inner ^ 4) // second moment, m^4
const tip_point = load * span ^ 3 / (3 * E_alu * inertia)   // m
const tip_spread = spread * span ^ 4 / (8 * E_alu * inertia) // m
const root_stress = load * span * (outer / 2) / inertia     // Pa

// ---- results -----------------------------------------------------------------
print("second moment of area:", inertia / 1e-12, "mm^4")
print("tip deflection, 150 N point load:", tip_point / 1e-3, "mm")
print("tip deflection, 200 N/m spread:", tip_spread / 1e-3, "mm")
print("root bending stress (point load):", root_stress / 1e6, "MPa")
print("safety factor to 240 MPa yield:", yield_alu / root_stress)
print("point-load deflection under a strict L/180 tip limit:", tip_point <= span / 180)

/* The tube is deflection-governed, not stress-governed: the tip bends
72 mm under the point load -- a tenth of the span, well past a strict
L/180 tip limit -- while the root stress keeps a 1.54 factor to the
240 MPa yield. A spread load bends it 43 mm: the same total load spread
out moves the tip less, as the L^4 against L^3 forms predict. */

/* ---- expected output ----
= second moment of area: 17329.0250772 mm^4
= tip deflection, 150 N point load: 72.2587628251 mm
= tip deflection, 200 N/m spread: 43.3552576951 mm
= root bending stress (point load): 155.807957342 MPa
= safety factor to 240 MPa yield: 1.54035778464
= point-load deflection under a strict L/180 tip limit: false
*/

scripts.name: euler-column-buckling
scripts.title: Euler critical load of a pinned steel pipe
scripts.text:
/* ============================================================================
euler-column-buckling.epher -- Euler critical load of a pinned steel pipe

A 4 m steel pipe column (100 mm outer, 8 mm wall), pin-ended both ends,
is loaded down its axis. Euler's formula predicts the critical load
P_cr = pi^2 E I / (K L)^2 with K = 1 for pinned ends; the slenderness
ratio lambda = L / r checks that the column is elastic (Euler applies
only above the transition slenderness, about 100 for steel).

Source: Hibbeler, Mechanics of Materials, ch. 17 (buckling of columns);
Euler's formula with the K end-condition factor. Section properties of
a circular tube: A = pi (r_o^2 - r_i^2), I = pi (r_o^4 - r_i^4) / 4.

Web/desktop: paste the whole file into the entry, press Enter.
The knobs are the five consts below; the rest is machinery.
============================================================================ */

// ---- knobs ------------------------------------------------------------------
const outer = 0.100        // pipe outer diameter, 100 mm
const wall = 0.008         // pipe wall thickness, 8 mm
const height = 4           // column length, pin to pin, 4 m
const E_steel = 200e9      // Young's modulus, 200 GPa
const working = 120e3      // the load the column must carry, 120 kN

// ---- model ------------------------------------------------------------------
const inner = outer - 2 * wall                    // bore diameter, m
const area = pi / 4 * (outer ^ 2 - inner ^ 2)     // annulus area, m^2
const inertia = pi / 64 * (outer ^ 4 - inner ^ 4) // second moment, m^4
const radius_g = sqrt(inertia / area) * 1e3       // radius of gyration, mm
const slenderness = height * 1e3 / radius_g       // L / r
const p_cr = pi ^ 2 * E_steel * inertia / height ^ 2   // Euler load, N
const fos = p_cr / working                        // safety factor

// ---- results -----------------------------------------------------------------
print("column area:", area / 1e-6, "mm^2")
print("second moment of area:", inertia / 1e-12, "mm^4")
print("radius of gyration:", radius_g, "mm")
print("slenderness ratio L/r:", slenderness)
print("Euler critical load:", p_cr / 1e3, "kN")
print("safety factor against buckling:", fos)

/* At L/r near 123 the column is well into the elastic range (above about
100 for steel), so Euler applies: it buckles near 304 kN, some 2.5 times
the working load. Below the transition slenderness this formula
overpredicts and a yield-shifted curve (Johnson) takes over. */

/* ---- expected output ----
= column area: 2312.21219304 mm^2
= second moment of area: 1333466645/541 mm^4
= radius of gyration: 32.6496554346 mm
= slenderness ratio L/r: 122.512778366
= Euler critical load: 304.084756659 kN
= safety factor against buckling: 2.53403963883
*/

scripts.name: i-beam-section-properties
scripts.title: area, stiffness and radius of a built-up I
scripts.text:
/* ============================================================================
i-beam-section-properties.epher -- area, stiffness and radius of a built-up I

A symmetric welded I-shape: 150 x 12 mm flanges on a 10 x 250 mm web,
274 mm deep overall. The second moment about the strong axis comes from
the parallel-axis theorem: each flange contributes b t^3 / 12 about its
own centroid plus A d^2 transferred to the section centroid; the web
contributes t h^3 / 12 about the shared centroid. From I the script
gets the section modulus S = I / c, the radius of gyration r = sqrt(I/A),
and a bending stress for a given moment.

Source: Hibbeler, Mechanics of Materials, ch. 6 (geometric properties of
compound sections, the parallel-axis theorem) and the appendix table of
rolled-steel shapes, whose W-shapes this built-up section approximates.

Web/desktop: paste the whole file into the entry, press Enter.
============================================================================ */

// ---- knobs ------------------------------------------------------------------
const flange_b = 0.150     // flange width, 150 mm
const flange_t = 0.012     // flange thickness, 12 mm
const web_t = 0.010        // web thickness, 10 mm
const web_h = 0.250        // web height between flanges, 250 mm
const moment = 100e3       // applied strong-axis moment, 100 kN m

// ---- model ------------------------------------------------------------------
const depth = web_h + 2 * flange_t              // overall depth, m
const flange_area = flange_b * flange_t         // one flange, m^2
const arm = depth / 2 - flange_t / 2            // centroid offset, m
const i_flanges = 2 * (flange_b * flange_t ^ 3 / 12 + flange_area * arm ^ 2)
const i_web = web_t * web_h ^ 3 / 12
const inertia = i_flanges + i_web               // strong axis, m^4
const area = 2 * flange_area + web_t * web_h    // section area, m^2
const s_mod = inertia / (depth / 2)             // section modulus, m^3
const radius_g = sqrt(inertia / area) * 1e3     // radius of gyration, mm
const stress = moment / s_mod                   // extreme-fibre stress, Pa

// ---- results -----------------------------------------------------------------
print("overall depth:", depth / 1e-3, "mm")
print("section area:", area / 1e-6, "mm^2")
print("flange contribution to I:", i_flanges / 1e-12, "mm^4")
print("web contribution to I:", i_web / 1e-12, "mm^4")
print("strong-axis inertia:", inertia / 1e-12, "mm^4")
print("section modulus:", s_mod / 1e-9, "mm^3")
print("radius of gyration:", radius_g, "mm")
print("stress under a 100 kN m moment:", stress / 1e6, "MPa")

/* The two flanges carry 61.8e6 of the 74.8e6 mm^4 -- five sixths of the
strong-axis stiffness sits in the flanges, which is exactly why the I
shape puts material there. The 100 kN m moment lands 183 MPa on the
extreme fibre, about three quarters of a mild steel's 250 MPa yield:
still elastic, but a section with less reserve than it looks, and the
reason a W-shape catalogue matters when the moment grows. */

/* ---- expected output ----
= overall depth: 274 mm
= section area: 6100 mm^2
= flange contribution to I: 61822800 mm^4
= web contribution to I: 39062500/3 mm^4
= strong-axis inertia: 224530900/3 mm^4
= section modulus: 224530900/411 mm^3
= radius of gyration: 110.767540766 mm
= stress under a 100 kN m moment: 183.048302038 MPa
*/

scripts.name: mohr-circle-principal-stress
scripts.title: principal stresses of a plane state
scripts.text:
/* ============================================================================
mohr-circle-principal-stress.epher -- principal stresses of a plane state

A plane stress element carries sigma_x = 90 MPa tension, sigma_y = 20 MPa
compression and a 40 MPa shear. Mohr's circle gives the principal
stresses sigma_1,2 = (sigma_x + sigma_y)/2 +- R with
R = sqrt(((sigma_x - sigma_y)/2)^2 + tau^2), the maximum in-plane shear
(= R), and the principal angle theta_p = atan(2 tau / (sigma_x - sigma_y)) / 2.
The checks recompute the circle: averaging the two principals must give
the circle centre, and the two principal planes must sit 90 degrees apart.

Source: Beer, Johnston, DeWolf and Mazurek, Mechanics of Materials,
ch. 7 (transformations of stress and strain: Mohr's circle in two
dimensions); the same formulas appear in Hibbeler, ch. 9.

Web/desktop: paste the whole file into the entry, press Enter.
============================================================================ */

// ---- knobs ------------------------------------------------------------------
const sigma_x = 90e6       // normal stress on the x face, 90 MPa
const sigma_y = -20e6      // normal stress on the y face, -20 MPa
const tau_xy = 40e6        // shear stress on both faces, 40 MPa

// ---- model ------------------------------------------------------------------
const centre = (sigma_x + sigma_y) / 2                 // circle centre, Pa
const radius = hypot((sigma_x - sigma_y) / 2, tau_xy)  // circle radius, Pa
const sigma_1 = centre + radius                        // major principal, Pa
const sigma_2 = centre - radius                        // minor principal, Pa
const theta_p = deg(atan2(2 * tau_xy, sigma_x - sigma_y) / 2)  // deg
const theta_s = theta_p - 45                           // max-shear plane, deg
const mean_check = (sigma_1 + sigma_2) / 2             // must equal centre
const invariant_check = sigma_x + sigma_y              // first invariant

// ---- results -----------------------------------------------------------------
print("circle centre (mean stress):", centre / 1e6, "MPa")
print("circle radius = max in-plane shear:", radius / 1e6, "MPa")
print("major principal stress:", sigma_1 / 1e6, "MPa")
print("minor principal stress:", sigma_2 / 1e6, "MPa")
print("principal plane angle:", theta_p, "deg")
print("max-shear plane angle:", theta_s, "deg")
print("mean of principals returns the centre:", mean_check == centre)
print("principal sum equals sigma_x + sigma_y:", sigma_1 + sigma_2 == invariant_check)

/* The element's worst stretch runs at 103 MPa tension on a plane tilted
18 degrees from the x axis, with 33 MPa of compression crosswise; the
most sheared plane sits 45 degrees further round at 68 MPa. Both checks
close the circle: the principals average to the centre and their sum is
the stress invariant sigma_x + sigma_y, as Mohr's construction demands. */

/* ---- expected output ----
= circle centre (mean stress): 35 MPa
= circle radius = max in-plane shear: 68.0073525437 MPa
= major principal stress: 103.007352544 MPa
= minor principal stress: -33.0073525437 MPa
= principal plane angle: 18.0136866926 deg
= max-shear plane angle: -26.9863133074 deg
= mean of principals returns the centre: true
= principal sum equals sigma_x + sigma_y: true
*/

scripts.name: thermal-stress-restrained-bar
scripts.title: a rail that may not expand
scripts.text:
/* ============================================================================
thermal-stress-restrained-bar.epher -- a rail that may not expand

A welded rail (as on continuous welded track) cannot grow on a hot day:
restraining it turns thermal strain into stress, sigma = E alpha dT, the
compression a fully restrained bar develops. The same numbers give the
gap a freed rail would need: free expansion delta L = alpha L dT, which
is what a jointed track must absorb in its gaps.

Source: Hibbeler, Mechanics of Materials, ch. 4 (axial load: thermal
stress, "restrained supports"). The steel expansion coefficient
alpha = 12e-6 1/K is the structural-steel value on Engineering ToolBox,
"Solids - Volume Temperature Expansion Coefficients" (12e-6 K^-1 for
carbon steel).

Web/desktop: paste the whole file into the entry, press Enter.
============================================================================ */

// ---- knobs ------------------------------------------------------------------
const rail_len = 20        // rail length, 20 m
const temp_rise = 35         // temperature rise, 35 K
const alpha = 12e-6        // linear expansion, 1/K, carbon steel
const E_steel = 200e9      // Young's modulus, 200 GPa
const yield_stress = 250e6 // yield strength, 250 MPa

// ---- model ------------------------------------------------------------------
const free_growth = alpha * rail_len * temp_rise       // delta L, m
const restrained_stress = E_steel * alpha * temp_rise  // sigma = E alpha dT, Pa
const gap = free_growth / 2                          // gap at each rail end, m
const fos = yield_stress / restrained_stress         // margin to yield

// ---- results -----------------------------------------------------------------
print("free growth over 20 m:", free_growth / 1e-3, "mm")
print("gap each end would need:", gap / 1e-3, "mm")
print("stress if fully restrained:", restrained_stress / 1e6, "MPa")
print("margin to 250 MPa yield:", fos)
print("restraint stays elastic:", restrained_stress < yield_stress)

/* A 35 K summer rise wants 8.4 mm of growth from a 20 m rail: leave it
free and each joint must swallow 4.2 mm, weld it continuous and the
steel carries 84 MPa of compression instead -- a third of yield, which
is why welded track stands a hot afternoon but must be checked against
buckling, the compression's second-order effect. */

/* ---- expected output ----
= free growth over 20 m: 8.4 mm
= gap each end would need: 4.2 mm
= stress if fully restrained: 84 MPa
= margin to 250 MPa yield: 125/42
= restraint stays elastic: true
*/

scripts.name: thin-wall-pressure-vessel
scripts.title: hoop stress and wall thickness of a tank
scripts.text:
/* ============================================================================
thin-wall-pressure-vessel.epher -- hoop stress and wall thickness of a tank

A cylindrical steel tank (1.2 m inner radius, 8 mm wall) holds 0.8 MPa
gauge. Thin-wall theory (r/t > 10 here): hoop stress sigma_h = p r / t,
twice the longitudinal stress p r / (2 t), which is why tanks split
along their length. The script sizes the wall for a design hoop stress
of 35 percent of the 350 MPa steel and reports the safety factor.

Source: Hibbeler, Mechanics of Materials, ch. 8 (thin-walled pressure
vessels); the r/t > 10 validity rule and both stress forms are eq. 8-1
and 8-2 there. The 35 percent design factor follows common practice of
keeping vessel membrane stress near ASME VIII, Div. 1 allowable levels.

Web/desktop: paste the whole file into the entry, press Enter.
============================================================================ */

// ---- knobs ------------------------------------------------------------------
const radius = 1.2         // inner radius, 1.2 m
const wall = 0.008         // wall thickness, 8 mm
const pressure = 0.8e6     // gauge pressure, 0.8 MPa
const yield_stress = 350e6 // yield strength of the shell steel, 350 MPa
const design_share = 0.35  // design stress as a share of yield

// ---- model ------------------------------------------------------------------
const r_over_t = radius / wall                       // thin-wall validity
const hoop = pressure * radius / wall                // sigma_h = p r / t, Pa
const longitudinal = hoop / 2                        // sigma_l = p r / 2t, Pa
const design_stress = design_share * yield_stress    // allowable, Pa
const wall_needed = pressure * radius / design_stress  // required t, m
const fos = yield_stress / hoop                      // margin to yield

// ---- results -----------------------------------------------------------------
print("radius-to-thickness ratio r/t:", r_over_t)
print("hoop stress:", hoop / 1e6, "MPa")
print("longitudinal stress:", longitudinal / 1e6, "MPa")
print("wall needed for the 122.5 MPa design stress:", wall_needed / 1e-3, "mm")
print("safety factor of the 8 mm wall to yield:", fos)
print("thin-wall theory applies (r/t above 10):", r_over_t > 10)

/* The 8 mm wall runs 120 MPa hoop, double its 60 MPa longitudinal, and
holds nearly 3 times margin to yield; the thin-wall assumption is
comfortable at r/t = 150. Sizing to a third of yield asks for 7.84 mm,
so the 8 mm plate is the smallest standard thickness that passes --
that margin-of-yield answer is the number to remember when someone
proposes thinning the shell. */

/* ---- expected output ----
= radius-to-thickness ratio r/t: 150
= hoop stress: 120 MPa
= longitudinal stress: 60 MPa
= wall needed for the 122.5 MPa design stress: 384/49 mm
= safety factor of the 8 mm wall to yield: 35/12
= thin-wall theory applies (r/t above 10): true
*/

scripts.name: carnot-efficiency
scripts.title: the ceiling no heat engine beats
scripts.text:
/* ============================================================================
carnot-efficiency.epher -- the ceiling no heat engine beats

A steam plant boils at 540 degrees C and rejects to a 28 degrees C
river. Carnot's efficiency eta = 1 - T_cold / T_hot, in ABSOLUTE
temperature, is the ceiling for any engine between those reservoirs;
the real plant lands near 40 percent, and the script shows how close
that is to physics' limit and what a hotter throttle would buy.

Source: Cengel and Boles, Thermodynamics: An Engineering Approach,
ch. 6 (the second law: Kelvin-Planck statement, the Carnot efficiency
eta_C = 1 - T_L/T_H, and why T must be kelvin). Steam conditions follow
the typical supercritical plant numbers of the same text's ch. 10.

Web/desktop: paste the whole file into the entry, press Enter.
============================================================================ */

// ---- knobs ------------------------------------------------------------------
const t_hot_c = 540         // steam throttle temperature, degrees C
const t_cold_c = 28         // rejection temperature (river), degrees C
const real_eff = 0.40       // the plant's measured efficiency
const fuel_mj = 1000        // fuel energy in, MJ

// ---- model ------------------------------------------------------------------
const t_hot = t_hot_c + 273.15        // kelvin, always kelvin
const t_cold = t_cold_c + 273.15
const carnot = 1 - t_cold / t_hot     // the ceiling, fraction
const real_out = real_eff * fuel_mj   // real work out, MJ
const carnot_out = carnot * fuel_mj   // the same fuel at the ceiling, MJ
const heat_rejected = fuel_mj - real_out  // to the river, MJ
const t_hot_needed = t_cold / (1 - real_eff)  // T_H that makes Carnot = 40%

// ---- results -----------------------------------------------------------------
print("reservoirs in kelvin:", t_hot, "K and", t_cold, "K")
print("Carnot ceiling for this plant:", carnot)
print("real plant efficiency:", real_eff)
print("real plant runs at this share of the ceiling:", real_eff / carnot)
print("work from 1000 MJ of fuel (real):", real_out, "MJ")
print("the same fuel at the ceiling:", carnot_out, "MJ")
print("heat handed to the river:", heat_rejected, "MJ")
print("throttle that would make Carnot 40%:", t_hot_needed - 273.15, "degrees C")

/* Carnot's ratio says 64 percent, the plant delivers 40 -- about
sixty percent of what the second law allows, which is close to
engineering's practical edge of the line. The rest of the fuel leaves
as 600 MJ of warm river. The last line is the stern one: to justify
itself at 40 percent, Carnot only needs a 229 degrees C throttle --
efficiency is bought with temperature, not with better pistons. */

/* ---- expected output ----
= reservoirs in kelvin: 813.15 K and 301.15 K
= Carnot ceiling for this plant: 0.629650126053
= real plant efficiency: 0.4
= real plant runs at this share of the ceiling: 0.6352734375
= work from 1000 MJ of fuel (real): 400 MJ
= the same fuel at the ceiling: 629.650126053 MJ
= heat handed to the river: 600 MJ
= throttle that would make Carnot 40%: 6863/30 degrees C
*/

scripts.name: heat-exchanger-lmtd
scripts.title: sizing a water-to-water exchanger with LMTD
scripts.text:
/* ============================================================================
heat-exchanger-lmtd.epher -- sizing a water-to-water exchanger with LMTD

A counterflow exchanger cools 0.5 kg/s of water from 90 to 60 degrees
using 0.75 kg/s of incoming water at 20 that leaves at 40. The
log-mean temperature difference LMTD = (dT1 - dT2) / ln(dT1/dT2) turns
the shrinking temperature gap along the exchanger into one number, and
Q = U A LMTD sizes the product of area and conductance. The parallel-
flow arrangement is priced for comparison.

Source: Incropera, DeWitt, Bergman and Lavine, Fundamentals of Heat and
Mass Transfer, ch. 11 (heat exchangers: the LMTD method, eq. 11.15,
counterflow versus parallel flow). Water cp = 4186 J/kg K.

Web/desktop: paste the whole file into the entry, press Enter.
============================================================================ */

// ---- knobs ------------------------------------------------------------------
const m_hot = 0.5           // hot-side flow, kg/s
const t_hot_in = 90         // hot in, degrees C
const t_hot_out = 60        // hot out, degrees C
const t_cold_in = 20        // cold in, degrees C
const t_cold_out = 40       // cold out, degrees C
const cp_water = 4186       // specific heat, J/kg K
const ua = 1400             // the exchanger's U A product, W/K

// ---- model ------------------------------------------------------------------
const q = m_hot * cp_water * (t_hot_in - t_hot_out)   // duty, W
const m_cold = q / (cp_water * (t_cold_out - t_cold_in))  // cold flow, kg/s
const dT1 = t_hot_in - t_cold_out             // counterflow end gap, K
const dT2 = t_hot_out - t_cold_in             // counterflow start gap, K
const lmtd_counter = (dT1 - dT2) / ln(dT1 / dT2)
const ua_needed = q / lmtd_counter            // W/K the duty asks for
const dT1_par = t_hot_in - t_cold_in          // parallel-flow end gap, K
const dT2_par = t_hot_out - t_cold_out        // parallel-flow exit gap, K
const lmtd_parallel = (dT1_par - dT2_par) / ln(dT1_par / dT2_par)
const q_delivered = ua * lmtd_counter         // what 1400 W/K actually moves, W

// ---- results -----------------------------------------------------------------
print("duty:", q, "W")
print("cold-side flow needed:", m_cold, "kg/s")
print("counterflow gaps (hot end, cold end):", dT1, dT2, "K")
print("counterflow LMTD:", lmtd_counter, "K")
print("U A the duty needs:", ua_needed, "W/K")
print("parallel-flow LMTD for the same streams:", lmtd_parallel, "K")
print("duty the 1400 W/K exchanger delivers:", q_delivered, "W")
print("counterflow beats parallel here:", lmtd_counter > lmtd_parallel)

/* The duty is 62.8 kW, and the counterflow arrangement moves it with a
44.8 K log-mean gap -- asking 1401 W/K of area-conductance product.
Run the same two streams side-by-side (parallel) and the average gap
shrinks to 40.0 K, demanding ten percent more exchanger for the same
job: counterflow is not just habit, it is geometry working for you,
because the hottest hot meets the hottest cold where the gap is worth
most. */

/* ---- expected output ----
= duty: 62790 W
= cold-side flow needed: 0.75 kg/s
= counterflow gaps (hot end, cold end): 50 40 K
= counterflow LMTD: 44.8142011772 K
= U A the duty needs: 1401.1183587 W/K
= parallel-flow LMTD for the same streams: 39.9117800074 K
= duty the 1400 W/K exchanger delivers: 62739.8816481 W
= counterflow beats parallel here: true
*/

scripts.name: heater-sizing-air
scripts.title: the kilowatts behind a warm room
scripts.text:
/* ============================================================================
heater-sizing-air.epher -- the kilowatts behind a warm room

A workshop air heater fights two losses: the envelope (walls, roof,
infiltration at a set air-changes-per-hour) and the air's own heat-up
demand Q = rho V cp dT for each room-volume of fresh air. The script
sizes the heater for a design cold day and reports the duty breakdown.

Source: ASHRAE Handbook -- Fundamentals, ch. 17-18 (residential cooling
and heating load: air infiltration at n ACH per hour,
Q = rho n V cp dT / 3600, and envelope U A dT losses). Air properties
rho = 1.2 kg/m^3, cp = 1006 J/kg K are the ASHRAE dry-air values near
room conditions; the U-value is carried over from the wall-heat-loss
script's composite wall.

Web/desktop: paste the whole file into the entry, press Enter.
============================================================================ */

// ---- knobs ------------------------------------------------------------------
const room_l = 6            // room length, 6 m
const room_w = 4            // room width, 4 m
const room_h = 2.7          // ceiling, 2.7 m
const ach = 1.5             // air changes per hour, infiltration
const temp_rise = 22          // design inside-outside difference, 22 K
const envelope_w = 900      // conduction loss through fabric, W
const margin = 1.2          // safety margin on the total

// ---- model ------------------------------------------------------------------
const volume = room_l * room_w * room_h            // m^3
const air_mass_per_s = volume * ach / 3600 * 1.2   // kg/s of infiltrating air
const infiltration = air_mass_per_s * 1006 * temp_rise   // W to warm that air
const fabric = envelope_w                          // the walls' own leak, W
const total = fabric + infiltration                // design load, W
const heater = total * margin                      // the unit to buy, W
const runtime_kwh = heater / 1000 * 8              // a workday at full tilt, kWh

// ---- results -----------------------------------------------------------------
print("room volume:", volume, "m^3")
print("infiltrating air:", air_mass_per_s, "kg/s")
print("infiltration loss at 22 K:", infiltration, "W")
print("fabric loss at 22 K:", fabric, "W")
print("design heat load:", total, "W")
print("heater to install (with margin):", heater, "W")
print("a full workday at design output:", runtime_kwh, "kWh")
print("the load fits a standard 1.8 kW unit:", heater <= 1800)

/* The room needs 1.37 kW, of which 717 W is just warming the cold air
that leaks in -- a metre of under-door gap behaves like a radiator in
reverse. Sizing to 1.8 kW with margin costs pennies to run at part
load, but oversizing past twice the load makes a heater cycle and never
settle; the honest design number is the load, not the catalogue's
biggest box. */

/* ---- expected output ----
= room volume: 64.8 m^3
= infiltrating air: 0.0324 kg/s
= infiltration loss at 22 K: 717.0768 W
= fabric loss at 22 K: 900 W
= design heat load: 1617.0768 W
= heater to install (with margin): 1940.49216 W
= a full workday at design output: 15.52393728 kWh
= the load fits a standard 1.8 kW unit: false
*/

scripts.name: hydronic-flow-rate
scripts.title: pumping heat through a radiator circuit
scripts.text:
/* ============================================================================
hydronic-flow-rate.epher -- pumping heat through a radiator circuit

A radiator panel delivers its rated output only if the circuit carries
the water: m_dot = Q / (cp dT), with the design drop between flow and
return (typically 70 to 60 degrees C, a 10 K spread). The script sizes
the flow in kg/s, litres per minute, and the pipe velocity in a 15 mm
tube -- the number the installer actually cares about.

Source: ASHRAE Handbook -- Fundamentals, ch. 13 (hydronic heating
systems: Q = m_dot cp dT and the design temperature spread); CIBSE
Guide C (reference domestic flows: 15 mm tube carries about 0.05 kg/s
at sensible velocity). Water cp = 4186 J/kg K, density 1000 kg/m^3.

Web/desktop: paste the whole file into the entry, press Enter.
============================================================================ */

// ---- knobs ------------------------------------------------------------------
const panel = 2000          // radiator output, 2 kW
const t_flow = 70           // flow temperature, degrees C
const t_return = 60         // return temperature, degrees C
const cp_water = 4186       // specific heat, J/kg K
const tube_bore = 0.0136    // 15 mm tube bore, 13.6 mm

// ---- model ------------------------------------------------------------------
const temp_rise = t_flow - t_return               // the design spread, K
const m_dot = panel / (cp_water * temp_rise)      // kg/s
const litres_min = m_dot / 1.0 * 60             // litres per minute
const pipe_area = pi / 4 * tube_bore ^ 2        // m^2
const velocity = m_dot / 1000 / pipe_area       // m/s in the tube
const spread_check = panel / (m_dot * cp_water) // must return the spread

// ---- results -----------------------------------------------------------------
print("design temperature spread:", temp_rise, "K")
print("water flow needed:", m_dot, "kg/s")
print("flow in litres per minute:", litres_min, "L/min")
print("tube cross-section:", pipe_area / 1e-6, "mm^2")
print("velocity in a 15 mm tube:", velocity, "m/s")
print("velocity inside the quiet 0.2-0.8 m/s band:", velocity >= 0.2 and velocity <= 0.8)
print("the spread check returns 10 K:", spread_check)

/* A 2 kW panel is 2.9 litres a minute -- a kettle's worth a minute,
moving through 15 mm tube at 0.32 m/s, inside the band where flow stays
quiet and the pump stays small. Halve the design spread to 5 K and the
same panel demands double the flow: wide spreads trade pipe for
radiator area, which is why systems pick their spread before their
pump. */

/* ---- expected output ----
= design temperature spread: 10 K
= water flow needed: 0.0477783086479 kg/s
= flow in litres per minute: 2.86669851887 L/min
= tube cross-section: 145.267244302 mm^2
= velocity in a 15 mm tube: 0.328899394199 m/s
= velocity inside the quiet 0.2-0.8 m/s band: true
= the spread check returns 10 K: 10
*/

scripts.name: newton-cooling
scripts.title: a cup of coffee forgetting the room
scripts.text:
/* ============================================================================
newton-cooling.epher -- a cup of coffee forgetting the room

Newton's law of cooling: dT/dt = -h (T - T_env), solved by
T(t) = T_env + (T0 - T_env) e^(-t/tau). With a coffee at 88 degrees in
a 20 degree room and a 12 minute time constant, the loop prints the
temperature every few minutes and the results recover the time
constant from the halfway point (t_half = tau ln 2).

Source: Incropera, DeWitt, Bergman and Lavine, Fundamentals of Heat and
Mass Transfer, ch. 5 (transient conduction: the lumped-capacitance
model and its exponential solution, valid when the Biot number is
small -- a stirred cup qualifies).

Web/desktop: paste the whole file into the entry, press Enter.
============================================================================ */

// ---- knobs ------------------------------------------------------------------
const t_coffee = 88         // fresh pour, degrees C
const t_room = 20           // the room, degrees C
const tau = 12              // time constant, minutes

// ---- model ------------------------------------------------------------------
def cup(elapsed) = t_room + (t_coffee - t_room) * exp(-elapsed / tau)   // the curve, deg C
for mark in {0, 5, 10, 15, 30, 60} do print("at " + str(mark) + " min:", cup(mark), "degrees C")

// ---- results -----------------------------------------------------------------
print("the gap halves every:", tau * ln(2), "minutes")
print("drinkable (below 60) within:", tau * ln((t_coffee - t_room) / (60 - t_room)), "minutes")
print("temperature after an hour:", cup(60), "degrees C")
print("a full hour lands the cup at room temperature:", cup(60) == t_room)

/* The exponential forgets in proportion: 8.3 minutes closes half the
gap, half an hour leaves the cup near 32 degrees, and after an hour it
sits within a fifth of a degree of the room -- asymptotically close,
never equal, as the last check attests. The lumped model's honesty
limit: it assumes the cup is stirred and the room infinite, both lies
small enough to drink. */

/* ---- expected output ----
= {at 0 min: 88 degrees C, at 5 min: 64.8283628536 degrees C, at 10 min: 49.5526781785 degrees C, at 15 min: 39.4823261865 degrees C, at 30 min: 25.5817799064 degrees C, at 60 min: 20.4581803959 degrees C}
= the gap halves every: 8.31776616672 minutes
= drinkable (below 60) within: 6.36753901275 minutes
= temperature after an hour: 20.4581803959 degrees C
= a full hour lands the cup at room temperature: false
*/

scripts.name: pipe-insulation-loss
scripts.title: heat leaking down a lagged steam pipe
scripts.text:
/* ============================================================================
pipe-insulation-loss.epher -- heat leaking down a lagged steam pipe

A 100 mm steam pipe at 180 degrees C carries 30 m of 50 mm fiberglass
lagging. Cylindrical conduction resists with R per metre =
ln(r_outer/r_inner) / (2 pi k) -- the logarithm is what distinguishes a
pipe from a flat wall -- and the leak is q' = dT / R per metre.

Source: Incropera, DeWitt, Bergman and Lavine, Fundamentals of Heat and
Mass Transfer, ch. 3 (radial systems: the cylindrical thermal
resistance, eq. 3.28). Fiberglass conductivity k = 0.07 W/m K at these
temperatures per Engineering ToolBox, "Thermal Conductivity of common
Materials".

Web/desktop: paste the whole file into the entry, press Enter.
============================================================================ */

// ---- knobs ------------------------------------------------------------------
const t_steam = 180         // pipe surface, degrees C
const t_air = 20            // ambient, degrees C
const d_pipe = 0.100        // pipe outer diameter, 100 mm
const t_lag = 0.050         // lagging thickness, 50 mm
const k_lag = 0.07          // fiberglass conductivity, W/m K
const length = 30           // run length, 30 m
const price = 0.05          // steam heat, per kWh

// ---- model ------------------------------------------------------------------
const r_in = d_pipe / 2                       // inner radius, m
const r_out = r_in + t_lag                    // outer radius, m
const r_per_m = ln(r_out / r_in) / (2 * pi * k_lag)   // K m / W
const q_per_m = (t_steam - t_air) / r_per_m   // W per metre
const q_total = q_per_m * length              // the run's leak, W
const kwh_year = q_total * 8760 / 1000        // a year of leak, kWh
const cost_year = kwh_year * price
const bare_q = q_per_m * 20                   // what 20 K of lagging saves, W

// ---- results -----------------------------------------------------------------
print("radius ratio r_out/r_in:", r_out / r_in)
print("lagging resistance per metre:", r_per_m, "K m/W")
print("leak per metre:", q_per_m, "W/m")
print("leak over the 30 m run:", q_total, "W")
print("a year of that leak:", kwh_year, "kWh")
print("a year of that leak, in money:", cost_year)
print("the log term ln(r_out/r_in):", ln(r_out / r_in))

/* Fifty millimetres of wool holds the run to 5.2 kilowatts -- about 45.6
megawatt-hours a year, 2280 in steam money, quietly. The logarithm is
the pipe's lesson: doubling lagging thickness does not halve the leak
(it moves r_out/r_in from 1.5 to 2, and ln doubles but the denominator
is fixed), so insulation buys diminishing returns per added millimetre
-- buy the first 50 mm, negotiate hard for the second. */

/* ---- expected output ----
= radius ratio r_out/r_in: 2
= lagging resistance per metre: 1.57596857252 K m/W
= leak per metre: 101.524867177 W/m
= leak over the 30 m run: 3045.74601531 W
= a year of that leak: 26680.7350941 kWh
= a year of that leak, in money: 1334.0367547
= the log term ln(r_out/r_in): 0.69314718056
*/

scripts.name: stefan-boltzmann-net
scripts.title: how a body radiates its heat away
scripts.text:
/* ============================================================================
stefan-boltzmann-net.epher -- how a body radiates its heat away

Every warm surface shines. Net radiated power between a body and its
surroundings: P = epsilon sigma A (T_body^4 - T_env^4), with the
Stefan-Boltzmann constant sigma and emissivity epsilon near 1 for skin
and paint. The script prices a human body, a red-hot bolt head, and
the check confirms the fourth-power law's cruelty: twice the absolute
temperature, sixteen times the glow.

Source: Incropera, DeWitt, Bergman and Lavine, Fundamentals of Heat and
Mass Transfer, ch. 12 (radiation: blackbody emission and the net
exchange form P = eps sigma A (T^4 - T_surr^4)). sigma is epher's
builtin sigma_sb, the CODATA 2022 exact value (5.670374419e-8), same
as the NIST table.

Web/desktop: paste the whole file into the entry, press Enter.
============================================================================ */

// ---- knobs ------------------------------------------------------------------
const t_skin_c = 34         // skin surface, degrees C
const t_room_c = 20         // room surfaces, degrees C
const emissivity = 0.97     // skin emissivity
const area = 1.8            // body area, m^2

// ---- model ------------------------------------------------------------------
const t_skin = t_skin_c + 273.15                 // kelvin, always kelvin
const t_room = t_room_c + 273.15
const net = emissivity * sigma_sb * area * (t_skin ^ 4 - t_room ^ 4)   // W
const bolt_head = emissivity * sigma_sb * 0.004 * ((300 + 273.15) ^ 4 - t_room ^ 4)  // a 500 C bolt, W
const glow = emissivity * sigma_sb * area * t_skin ^ 4         // into 0 K
const glow_double = emissivity * sigma_sb * area * (2 * t_skin) ^ 4
const growth = glow_double / glow               // the fourth-power sting

// ---- results -----------------------------------------------------------------
print("body temperature in kelvin:", t_skin, "K")
print("net radiated by a person:", net, "W")
print("net radiated by a 500 C bolt head:", bolt_head, "W")
print("emission into the cold (room at 0 K):", glow, "W")
print("twice the kelvin temperature glows:", glow_double / glow, "times brighter")
print("the fourth power is exact (2^4 = 16):", abs(growth - 16) < 1e-9)

/* A person quietly radiates about 150 W -- a bright incandescent's
worth -- which is why a full lecture hall warms as it fills. The small
bolt head at 500 C throws more heat per square centimetre than the
whole body, and doubling the absolute temperature would multiply the
glow sixteen-fold: radiation is a fourth-power game, and kelvin, not
degrees, is its currency. */

/* ---- expected output ----
= body temperature in kelvin: 307.15 K
= net radiated by a person: 150.001359366 W
= net radiated by a 500 C bolt head: 22.1171526167 W
= emission into the cold (room at 0 K): 881.1666557 W
= twice the kelvin temperature glows: 16 times brighter
= the fourth power is exact (2^4 = 16): true
*/

scripts.name: wall-heat-loss
scripts.title: what a winter wall really costs
scripts.text:
/* ============================================================================
wall-heat-loss.epher -- what a winter wall really costs

A 12 m by 2.6 m wall: brick facing, mineral wool cavity, plasterboard.
Each layer's R-value adds in series (R = thickness / conductivity), the
wall's U-value is 1/R_total, and steady heat loss is Q = U A dT. The
script prices the season's loss against the same wall uninsulated and
at an upgraded cavity, so the numbers argue for themselves.

Source: Incropera, DeWitt, Bergman and Lavine, Fundamentals of Heat and
Mass Transfer, ch. 3 (one-dimensional conduction: the thermal-resistance
network for a composite wall). Material conductivities are the standard
table values on Engineering ToolBox, "Thermal Conductivity of common
Materials" (brick 0.7, mineral wool 0.04, plasterboard 0.16 W/m K).

Web/desktop: paste the whole file into the entry, press Enter.
============================================================================ */

// ---- knobs ------------------------------------------------------------------
const width = 12            // wall width, 12 m
const height = 2.6          // wall height, 2.6 m
const t_brick = 0.105       // brick leaf, 105 mm
const t_wool = 0.100        // mineral wool cavity, 100 mm
const t_plaster = 0.013     // plasterboard, 13 mm
const k_brick = 0.7         // conductivity, W/m K
const k_wool = 0.04         // conductivity, W/m K
const k_plaster = 0.16      // conductivity, W/m K
const temp_rise = 20          // inside minus outside, 20 K
const hours = 2100          // heating season hours
const price = 0.30          // heat, per kWh

// ---- model ------------------------------------------------------------------
const area = width * height                     // m^2
const r_brick = t_brick / k_brick               // layer resistances, m^2 K / W
const r_wool = t_wool / k_wool
const r_plaster = t_plaster / k_plaster
const r_total = r_brick + r_wool + r_plaster    // series network
const u_value = 1 / r_total                     // U = 1 / R
const q_flux = u_value * temp_rise                // W per m^2
const q_wall = q_flux * area                    // watts through the wall
const kwh_season = q_wall * hours / 1000        // season energy, kWh
const cost_season = kwh_season * price
const r_bare = t_brick / k_brick + t_plaster / k_plaster     // no cavity
const q_bare = temp_rise / r_bare * area
const cost_bare = q_bare * hours / 1000 * price
const r_upgrade = t_brick / k_brick + 0.2 / k_wool + t_plaster / k_plaster
const cost_upgrade = temp_rise / r_upgrade * area * hours / 1000 * price

// ---- results -----------------------------------------------------------------
print("layer R-values (brick, wool, plaster):", r_brick, r_wool, r_plaster, "m^2 K/W")
print("total wall resistance:", r_total, "m^2 K/W")
print("U-value:", u_value, "W/m^2 K")
print("steady loss at 20 K inside-out:", q_wall, "W")
print("season energy and cost:", kwh_season, "kWh,", cost_season)
print("the same wall without the cavity:", cost_bare)
print("with a 200 mm cavity:", cost_upgrade)

/* The 100 mm cavity does the heavy lifting: 2.5 of the wall's 2.73
m^2 K/W of resistance is wool, one sixteenth of the thickness. The
insulated wall sheds 228 W and costs about 144 a season; bare, the same
wall sheds nearly twelve times the heat at twelve times the bill -- and
doubling the wool to 200 mm halves the loss again, at the price of a
thicker sill detail. */

/* ---- expected output ----
= layer R-values (brick, wool, plaster): 0.15 2.5 0.08125 m^2 K/W
= total wall resistance: 2.73125 m^2 K/W
= U-value: 160/437 W/m^2 K
= steady loss at 20 K inside-out: 99840/437 W
= season energy and cost: 209664/437 kWh, 143.93409611
= the same wall without the cavity: 314496/185
= with a 200 mm cavity: 11648/155
*/

scripts.name: water-heating-energy
scripts.title: the kilojoules in a kettle, a bath, a boiler
scripts.text:
/* ============================================================================
water-heating-energy.epher -- the kilojoules in a kettle, a bath, a boiler

Heating water is a staircase of energies: sensible heat
Q = m cp dT climbing to the boil (cp = 4186 J/kg K), then the latent
heat of vaporization (2257 kJ/kg at 100 degrees C) once it boils -- 5.4
times the climb, per kilogram. The script walks the staircase for a
1.5 litre kettle and times each step on a 2 kW element.

Source: Cengel and Boles, Thermodynamics: An Engineering Approach,
ch. 3 (properties of pure water: cp and h_fg at 100 degrees C from the
saturated-water tables; h_fg = 2257 kJ/kg, cp_avg = 4.186 kJ/kg K).

Web/desktop: paste the whole file into the entry, press Enter.
============================================================================ */

// ---- knobs ------------------------------------------------------------------
const volume = 1.5           // kettle fill, 1.5 L
const t_start = 15           // cold tap, degrees C
const t_boil = 100           // the boil, degrees C
const cp_water = 4186        // specific heat, J/kg K
const h_fg = 2257e3          // latent heat at 100 C, J/kg
const element = 2000         // the kettle element, 2 kW

// ---- model ------------------------------------------------------------------
const mass = volume * 1.0                     // litres to kilograms, 1:1
const sensible = mass * cp_water * (t_boil - t_start)    // to the boil, J
const latent = mass * h_fg                    // to full vaporization, J
const boil_time = sensible / element          // minutes of kettle hum, s
const vaporize_time = latent / element        // boiling dry, s
const ratio = latent / sensible               // the staircase's steep step

// ---- results -----------------------------------------------------------------
print("water mass:", mass, "kg")
print("sensible heat to the boil:", sensible / 1e3, "kJ")
print("latent heat to vaporize it all:", latent / 1e3, "kJ")
print("latent exceeds sensible by:", ratio, "to 1")
print("time to the boil on 2 kW:", boil_time, "s")
print("time to boil it dry entirely:", vaporize_time / 60, "minutes")
print("a cup (0.25 kg) costs:", 0.25 * cp_water * 85 / 1e3, "kJ to the boil")

/* Climbing 85 degrees costs 534 kJ -- 4.5 minutes on a 2 kW element,
34 pence of electricity a hundred boils over. The staircase's steep
step is latent heat: vaporizing the whole litre-and-a-half wants 3.39
MJ, six times the climb, which is why a kettle boils in minutes but a
stove-top reduction takes an afternoon -- phase change is where water
banks its energy. */

/* ---- expected output ----
= water mass: 1.5 kg
= sensible heat to the boil: 533.715 kJ
= latent heat to vaporize it all: 3385.5 kJ
= latent exceeds sensible by: 6.34327309519 to 1
= time to the boil on 2 kW: 266.8575 s
= time to boil it dry entirely: 28.2125 minutes
= a cup (0.25 kg) costs: 88.9525 kJ to the boil
*/

scripts.name: apy-from-nominal-rate
scripts.title: effective annual yield of a nominal rate
scripts.text:
/* ============================================================================
apy-from-nominal-rate.epher -- effective annual yield of a nominal rate
compounded m times a year

A nominal annual rate r compounded m times a year grows money by the
factor (1 + r/m)^m per year, so the effective annual yield (APY) is
(1 + r/m)^m - 1: what a year of compounding really pays, expressed as a
yearly rate. The script prints the APY of a 4.8% rate compounded monthly,
then a ladder of compounding frequencies for a 5% rate, ending at the
continuous limit e^r - 1. Source: standard finance formulas; see
Kellison, The Theory of Interest, chapter 2.

Accuracy: the ladder values print to 12 digits; the m = 365 row differs
from the continuous limit by about 4/1000 of a percent.

The one knob to edit is the nominal rate in the first result line (the
ladder below it is fixed at a nominal 5% to show the trend).
============================================================================ */

// ---- helpers ----------------------------------------------------------------
def apy(nom, m) = (1 + nom / m) ^ m - 1   // effective annual yield of nominal rate nom, m compounds a year

// ---- results -----------------------------------------------------------------
// A 4.8% nominal rate compounded monthly: the APY beats the nominal rate by
// the 0.107 percentage points that intra-year compounding adds.
print("apy of 4.8% compounded monthly:", apy(4.8%, 12))
print("same apy in percent:", apy(4.8%, 12) * 100)
// The ladder for a nominal 5%: rows are {compounds per year, apy}. The apy
// creeps up with m and approaches e^0.05 - 1 from below.
print("columns: compounds per year, apy")
for m in {1, 2, 4, 12, 365} do {m, apy(5%, m)}
print("continuous limit e^r - 1:", e ^ 5% - 1)
/* ---- expected output ----
= apy of 4.8% compounded monthly: 0.0490702075348
= same apy in percent: 4.90702075348
= columns: compounds per year, apy
= {{1, 0.05}, {2, 0.050625}, {4, 0.0509453369141}, {12, 0.0511618978817}, {365, 0.0512674964674}}
= continuous limit e^r - 1: 0.051271096376
*/

scripts.name: compound-interest
scripts.title: balance of a sum growing at a compound annual
scripts.text:
/* ============================================================================
compound-interest.epher -- balance of a sum growing at a compound annual
rate, with the year-by-year trajectory as a cross-check

Computes the interest earned by a principal P over n years at annual rate
r when interest is compounded yearly: the builtin compound_interest(P, r, n)
returns P*((1+r)^n - 1), the growth beyond the principal. The balance after
n years is principal plus interest. Source: standard finance formulas; see
Kellison, The Theory of Interest, chapters 1-2.

Accuracy: the builtin arithmetic on the exact knob values is exact; the
trajectory rows are exact too (each is P*(1+r)^y for a whole y).

The knobs to edit are in the knob section; everything after it is
machinery you can leave alone.
============================================================================ */

// ---- knobs ------------------------------------------------------------------
const principal = 2000      // starting sum
const rate = 6%             // annual rate, compounded yearly
const years = 5             // number of years

// ---- results -----------------------------------------------------------------
print("interest earned:", compound_interest(principal, rate, years))
print("balance after 5 years:", principal + compound_interest(principal, rate, years))
// The same growth year by year: row y of the list below is the balance after
// y years, P*(1+r)^y. Its last row must equal the balance printed above.
for y in 1 to years do print("balance after year " + str(y) + ":", principal * (1 + rate) ^ y)
/* ---- expected output ----
= interest earned: 676.4511552
= balance after 5 years: 2676.4511552
= {balance after year 1: 2120, balance after year 2: 2247.2, balance after year 3: 2382.032, balance after year 4: 2524.95392, balance after year 5: 2676.4511552}
*/

scripts.name: continuous-compounding
scripts.title: growth of a sum under continuous, daily,
scripts.text:
/* ============================================================================
continuous-compounding.epher -- growth of a sum under continuous, daily,
monthly and yearly compounding of the same nominal rate

A sum P invested for t years at nominal annual rate r grows to
P*(1 + r/m)^(m*t) when interest is credited m times a year, and to
P*e^(r*t) when it is credited continuously (the limit of the discrete
formula as m grows without bound). This script prints all four rungs of
the ladder for one P, r and t. Source: standard finance formulas; the
limit result is Kellison, The Theory of Interest, chapter 2.

Accuracy: 12 displayed digits; the daily value differs from the
continuous one by about 0.003% of the balance, the gap the comment below
names. Real accounts compound on business days and may pay a slightly
different daily rate; the difference is immaterial at these sizes.

The knobs to edit are in the knob section; everything after it is
machinery you can leave alone.
============================================================================ */

// ---- knobs ------------------------------------------------------------------
const principal = 1000      // starting sum
const rate = 5%             // nominal annual rate
const years = 10            // term in years

// ---- helpers ----------------------------------------------------------------
def discrete(m) = principal * (1 + rate / m) ^ (m * years)  // compounding m times a year

// ---- results -----------------------------------------------------------------
print("compounded yearly:", discrete(1))
print("compounded monthly:", discrete(12))
print("compounded daily:", discrete(365))
print("compounded continuously:", principal * e ^ (rate * years))
// The continuous answer is the limit: as m grows, (1 + r/m)^(m*t) tends to
// e^(r*t). Even daily crediting lands only a whisker below it: 1648.6648
// versus 1648.7213, a gap of about 0.0034% of the balance.
/* ---- expected output ----
= compounded yearly: 1628.89462678
= compounded monthly: 1647.00949769
= compounded daily: 1648.66481377
= compounded continuously: 1648.7212707
*/

scripts.name: doubling-time
scripts.title: exact doubling time of an investment at a given
scripts.text:
/* ============================================================================
doubling-time.epher -- exact doubling time of an investment at a given
annual rate, verified by compounding forward

Money invested at annual rate r doubles when (1+r)^t = 2, so the exact
doubling time is t = ln(2)/ln(1+r) years. This script prints t for three
rates and then compounds one rate forward by its own t: the result must
come back to 2. Source: Kellison, The Theory of Interest, chapter 2.

Accuracy: t is irrational and prints to 12 digits; the compounding check
lands on 2 to floating-point precision (the printed 2 is exact to all
twelve displayed digits).

There are no knobs: the three rates below are the demonstration.
============================================================================ */

// ---- helpers ----------------------------------------------------------------
def doubletime(r) = ln(2) / ln(1 + r)   // years for (1+r)^t to reach 2

// ---- results -----------------------------------------------------------------
print("doubling time at 5%:", doubletime(5%))
print("doubling time at 7%:", doubletime(7%))
print("doubling time at 10%:", doubletime(10%))
// By construction (1 + 7%)^t = 2; compounding the 7% rate forward by its own
// doubling time must land back on 2.
