print("check: (1 + 7%) ^ t =", (1 + 7%) ^ doubletime(7%))
/* ---- expected output ----
= doubling time at 5%: 14.2066990829
= doubling time at 7%: 10.2447683511
= doubling time at 10%: 7.27254089734
= check: (1 + 7%) ^ t = 2
*/

scripts.name: future-value
scripts.title: what a lump sum grows to at a compound rate, three
scripts.text:
/* ============================================================================
future-value.epher -- what a lump sum grows to at a compound rate, three
ways that must agree

A sum P invested for n years at annual rate r grows to P*(1+r)^n. This
script computes that future value with the finance builtin tvm_fv and
cross-checks it against the plain compound formula and against the
compound_interest builtin (interest plus the original principal).
Source: standard finance formulas; see Kellison, The Theory of Interest,
chapters 1-2.

Accuracy: all three routes agree to all twelve displayed digits.

The knobs to edit are in the knob section; everything after it is
machinery you can leave alone.
============================================================================ */

// ---- knobs ------------------------------------------------------------------
const principal = 10000     // the lump sum
const rate = 5%             // annual rate
const years = 20            // years invested

/* ---- results -----------------------------------------------------------------
The builtin tvm_fv(n, r, pv, pmt) with no periodic payments: the principal
is entered negative (money out today), the future value comes back
positive. With pmt = 0 the builtin is exactly the compound formula. */
print("future value, builtin tvm_fv:", tvm_fv(years, rate, -principal, 0))
print("future value, compound formula:", principal * (1 + rate) ^ years)
print("compound_interest plus principal:", compound_interest(principal, rate, years) + principal)
/* ---- expected output ----
= future value, builtin tvm_fv: 26532.9770514
= future value, compound formula: 26532.9770514
= compound_interest plus principal: 26532.9770514
*/

scripts.name: inflation-adjusted-value
scripts.title: translating sums of money across years
scripts.text:
/* ============================================================================
inflation-adjusted-value.epher -- translating sums of money across years
at a steady inflation rate

At the yearly inflation rate, prices multiply by (1 + inflation)^years
over the years. So a sum of money today buys, years from now, what
1/(1 + inflation)^years of it buys today; and a sum quoted in future
money is worth only 1/(1 + inflation)^years as much in today's money.
This script prints both directions for one sum.
Source: standard finance formulas; the same deflation appears in
Kellison, The Theory of Interest, chapter 1.

Accuracy: the values print to 12 digits and are exact rationals of the
knob values (the division 1000/1.03^10 does not repeat in a way the
display keeps as a fraction, so it shows as a decimal).

The knobs to edit are in the knob section; everything after it is
machinery you can leave alone.
============================================================================ */

// ---- knobs ------------------------------------------------------------------
const amount = 1000         // the sum of money
const inflation = 3%        // yearly inflation rate
const years = 10            // how many years the money moves

// ---- helpers ----------------------------------------------------------------
def inflate(a, r, n) = a * (1 + r) ^ n      // today's a, grown n years

def deflate(a, r, n) = a / (1 + r) ^ n      // a in n years, valued in today's money

// ---- results -----------------------------------------------------------------
// 1000 today keeps its buying power as 1343.92 of ten-years-from-now money:
// the price level rises 34.4% over the decade.
print("1000 today, after 10 years of inflation:", inflate(amount, inflation, years))
// 1000 promised in 10 years is only 744.09 in today's money: divide by
// 1.03^10 (equivalently, multiply by 1.03^-10).
print("1000 in 10 years, in today's money:", deflate(amount, inflation, years))
print("price level multiplier:", (1 + inflation) ^ years)
/* ---- expected output ----
= 1000 today, after 10 years of inflation: 1343.91637934
= 1000 in 10 years, in today's money: 744.093914897
= price level multiplier: 1.34391637934
*/

scripts.name: present-value
scripts.title: what a future sum is worth today at a discount rate
scripts.text:
/* ============================================================================
present-value.epher -- what a future sum is worth today at a discount rate

A sum F received n years from now is worth F/(1+r)^n today when money can
grow at rate r: that is the present value. The script computes it two
ways that must agree: the bare formula, and the finance builtin tvm_pv,
which solves the same equation from the other end. Source: standard
finance formulas; see Kellison, The Theory of Interest, chapter 1.

Accuracy: the two routes agree to all twelve displayed digits. The builtin
signs its answer negative (money out today, in the builtin's sign
convention); the sum itself is 20863.25.

The knobs to edit are in the knob section; everything after it is
machinery you can leave alone.
============================================================================ */

// ---- knobs ------------------------------------------------------------------
const goal = 50000          // the future sum
const rate = 6%             // annual discount rate
const years = 15            // years until the sum arrives

// ---- results -----------------------------------------------------------------
// The bare classroom formula, fv/(1+r)^n.
print("present value, formula fv/(1+r)^n:", goal / (1 + rate) ^ years)
// The builtin tvm_pv(n, r, pmt, fv) with no payments in between: same
// number, negative because buying that future 50000 means paying today.
print("present value, builtin tvm_pv:", tvm_pv(years, rate, 0, goal))
// Round trip: invest the present value at 6% and the goal comes back.
print("compounding the pv forward returns:", tvm_fv(years, rate, tvm_pv(years, rate, 0, goal), 0))
/* ---- expected output ----
= present value, formula fv/(1+r)^n: 20863.2530368
= present value, builtin tvm_pv: -20863.2530368
= compounding the pv forward returns: 50000
*/

scripts.name: real-rate-of-return
scripts.title: the Fisher equation: real return after
scripts.text:
/* ============================================================================
real-rate-of-return.epher -- the Fisher equation: real return after
inflation

If an investment earns the nominal rate while prices rise at the
inflation rate, the real (inflation-adjusted) rate of return is the rate
r that solves 1 + r = (1 + nominal)/(1 + inflation), so
r = (1 + nominal)/(1 + inflation) - 1. The popular approximation
r ~ nominal - inflation is printed underneath for comparison. Source: Irving Fisher,
"The Theory of Interest" (1930); the multiplicative form is standard.

Accuracy: exact. The exact rate 9/205 prints as a fraction because its
decimal 0.0439024390... repeats forever; it is the same number as
4.3902%. The approximation overshoots by about 0.11 percentage points.

The knobs to edit are in the knob section; everything after it is
machinery you can leave alone.
============================================================================ */

// ---- knobs ------------------------------------------------------------------
const nominal = 7%          // return the investment pays, per year
const inflation = 2.5%      // yearly price inflation over the same period

// ---- results -----------------------------------------------------------------
// Exact: 1 + real = (1 + nominal)/(1 + inflation).
print("exact real rate (Fisher):", (1 + nominal) / (1 + inflation) - 1)
// Approximation: subtract the rates directly. At 7% and 2.5% it says 4.5%
// where the exact answer is 4.3902%; the gap grows with the rates.
print("approximation, nominal - inflation:", nominal - inflation)
/* ---- expected output ----
= exact real rate (Fisher): 9/205
= approximation, nominal - inflation: 0.045
*/

scripts.title: the Rule of 72 estimate of doubling time versus the

scripts.name: simple-interest
scripts.title: interest earned on a principal at a simple rate
scripts.text:
/* ============================================================================
simple-interest.epher -- interest earned on a principal at a simple rate

Computes the interest I = P*r*t on a principal P at annual rate r over t
years, and the total (principal plus interest) due at maturity. Simple
interest pays no interest on interest: every year earns rate times the
original principal. The script calls the builtin simple_interest(P, r, t),
which implements exactly that formula (see the finance builtins in
"epher scripts/README.md"). Source: standard finance formulas; see
Kellison, The Theory of Interest, chapter 1.

Accuracy: the builtin multiplies the exact knob values, so the numbers
printed below are exact.

The knobs to edit are in the knob section; everything after it is
machinery you can leave alone.
============================================================================ */

// ---- knobs ------------------------------------------------------------------
const principal = 5000      // amount lent or deposited
const rate = 4%             // annual simple rate, 4% is 0.04
const years = 6             // term in years

// ---- results -----------------------------------------------------------------
// Interest is P*r*t. The builtin returns the interest alone, so the total at
// maturity is principal plus interest.
print("interest earned:", simple_interest(principal, rate, years))
print("total at maturity:", principal + simple_interest(principal, rate, years))
/* ---- expected output ----
= interest earned: 1200
= total at maturity: 6200
*/

scripts.name: breakeven-quantity
scripts.title: units that must sell to cover fixed costs,
scripts.text:
/* ============================================================================
breakeven-quantity.epher -- units that must sell to cover fixed costs,
and the profit at a planned volume

Each unit sold brings in the price and costs the variable cost, leaving a
contribution of price - variable toward the fixed costs. The breakeven
quantity is fixed/(price - variable): the volume at which contribution
exactly covers the fixed costs and profit is zero. Above that volume each
extra unit adds the full contribution to profit. Source: standard cost
accounting; see any managerial accounting text (e.g. Horngren), the
cost-volume-profit chapter.

Assumptions: fixed costs (rent, salaries) do not change with volume;
variable costs (materials) are proportional to units; everything produced
sells at one price. The plan volume below is the seller's target.

Accuracy: exact arithmetic on the knobs.

The knobs to edit are in the knob section; everything after it is
machinery you can leave alone.
============================================================================ */

// ---- knobs ------------------------------------------------------------------
const fixed_cost = 12000    // monthly fixed costs
const price = 8             // selling price per unit
const variable = 5          // variable cost per unit
const planned = 6000        // units the seller plans to sell in a month

// ---- results -----------------------------------------------------------------
print("contribution per unit:", price - variable)
print("breakeven quantity:", fixed_cost / (price - variable))
print("revenue at breakeven:", fixed_cost / (price - variable) * price)
print("profit at 6000 units:", planned * (price - variable) - fixed_cost)
print("contribution margin ratio:", (price - variable) / price)
/* Selling 4000 units breaks even at 32000 of revenue; every unit beyond
4000 adds 3 of profit, so 6000 units profit 6000. The contribution
margin ratio 0.375 says each unit of revenue leaves 0.375 toward
fixed costs and profit. */
/* ---- expected output ----
= contribution per unit: 3
= breakeven quantity: 4000
= revenue at breakeven: 32000
= profit at 6000 units: 6000
= contribution margin ratio: 0.375
*/

scripts.name: cagr
scripts.title: compound annual growth rate of an investment over several
scripts.text:
/* ============================================================================
cagr.epher -- compound annual growth rate of an investment over several
years

An investment that grows from start to end over n years has the compound
annual growth rate cagr = (end/start)^(1/n) - 1: the single yearly rate
that would produce the same final value when compounded. The script also
compounds the rate back over the n years, which must recover the end
value. Source: standard finance formulas; see Kellison, The Theory of
Interest, chapter 2.

Accuracy: the rate is irrational and prints to 12 digits; the check line
recovers 35000 to all twelve displayed digits.

The knobs to edit are in the knob section; everything after it is
machinery you can leave alone.
============================================================================ */

// ---- knobs ------------------------------------------------------------------
const start = 10000         // value at the beginning
const end = 35000           // value n years later
const years = 8             // years between the two values

// ---- helpers ----------------------------------------------------------------
def cagr(s, e, n) = (e / s) ^ (1 / n) - 1   // compound annual growth rate

// ---- results -----------------------------------------------------------------
print("cagr:", cagr(start, end, years))
print("cagr in percent:", cagr(start, end, years) * 100)
print("compounding check, start*(1+cagr)^8:", start * (1 + cagr(start, end, years)) ^ years)
// The 10000 grew to 35000 in 8 years: a smooth 16.952% a year, even if the
// year-by-year returns actually swung around that average.
/* ---- expected output ----
= cagr: 0.169522295584
= cagr in percent: 16.9522295584
= compounding check, start*(1+cagr)^8: 35000
*/

scripts.name: internal-rate-of-return
scripts.title: the rate that makes the project's npv
scripts.text:
/* ============================================================================
internal-rate-of-return.epher -- the rate that makes the project's npv
zero

The internal rate of return is the discount rate at which the project's
cash flows exactly pay back their cost: npv(irr, flows) = 0. The finance
builtin irr(flows) solves that equation. If the irr beats the cost of
capital, the project is worth doing; here the same flows as
net-present-value.epher carry an 8% hurdle. Source: standard
capital-budgeting formulas; see Brealey and Myers, Principles of
Corporate Finance, chapter 5.

Accuracy: 12 displayed digits. At the printed rate the npv is about
-2.9e-11 in floating point, i.e. zero to float precision (verified
against the builtin npv in the sibling scripts).

The flows knob below is the only value to edit.
============================================================================ */

// ---- knobs ------------------------------------------------------------------
const flows = {-100000, 30000, 40000, 40000, 30000}   // year 0 outflow, then four yearly inflows

// ---- results -----------------------------------------------------------------
print("internal rate of return:", irr(flows))
// 14.895% against the 8% cost of capital: the project clears its hurdle
// with room to spare, which is the same verdict the positive npv gave.
/* ---- expected output ----
= internal rate of return: 0.148950281274
*/

scripts.name: irr-vs-hurdle-rate
scripts.title: judging a project by comparing its irr with
scripts.text:
/* ============================================================================
irr-vs-hurdle-rate.epher -- judging a project by comparing its irr with
the required return, with an if/else verdict at two hurdle rates

The irr decision rule: accept the project when its internal rate of
return (the builtin irr, the rate that zeroes the npv) beats the required
return, reject it when it does not. The verdict is printed by an if/else
expression for each hurdle. The npv at the hurdle is printed underneath
because it must carry the same sign as the verdict: npv above zero means
accept. Source: standard capital-budgeting formulas; see Brealey and
Myers, Principles of Corporate Finance, chapters 2 and 5.

Accuracy: 12 displayed digits.

The knobs to edit are in the knob section; everything after it is
machinery you can leave alone.
============================================================================ */

// ---- knobs ------------------------------------------------------------------
const hurdle_low = 8%       // a lenient required return
const hurdle_high = 20%     // a demanding required return
const flows = {-100000, 30000, 40000, 40000, 30000}   // the project's cash flows

// ---- results -----------------------------------------------------------------
const r = irr(flows)              // the project's internal rate of return
print("project irr:", r)
print("at an 8% hurdle:", if r > hurdle_low then "accept: the irr beats the required return" else "reject: the irr misses the required return")
print("at a 20% hurdle:", if r > hurdle_high then "accept: the irr beats the required return" else "reject: the irr misses the required return")
print("npv at the 8% hurdle:", npv(hurdle_low, flows))
print("npv at the 20% hurdle:", npv(hurdle_high, flows))
/* The npv signs agree with the verdicts: positive npv at 8% (accept),
negative npv at 20% (reject). The two rules never contradict each other
for a project whose cash flows change sign once. The 20% line prints as
the exact fraction -259375/27 because its decimal -9606.48148148...
repeats (epher keeps the fraction when the decimal repeats). */
/* ---- expected output ----
= project irr: 0.148950281274
= at an 8% hurdle: accept: the irr beats the required return
= at a 20% hurdle: reject: the irr misses the required return
= npv at the 8% hurdle: 15875.5158145
= npv at the 20% hurdle: -259375/27
*/

scripts.name: margin-vs-markup
scripts.title: profit margin (profit over price) versus markup
scripts.text:
/* ============================================================================
margin-vs-markup.epher -- profit margin (profit over price) versus markup
(profit over cost), and the conversion between them

A product bought for `cost` and sold for `price` earns the same profit
either way it is quoted, but the two quotings differ: margin = profit/
price, markup = profit/cost. The classic confusion is forgetting which is
which: a 25% markup is only a 20% margin. The conversions are
markup = margin/(1 - margin) and margin = markup/(1 + markup). Source:
standard retail accounting practice.

Accuracy: exact arithmetic, so every number below is exact.

The knobs to edit are in the knob section; everything after it is
machinery you can leave alone.
============================================================================ */

// ---- knobs ------------------------------------------------------------------
const cost = 80             // what the seller pays
const price = 100           // what the buyer pays

// ---- helpers ----------------------------------------------------------------
def margin(c, p) = (p - c) / p        // profit as a share of the selling price
def markup(c, p) = (p - c) / c        // profit as a share of the cost

// ---- results -----------------------------------------------------------------
print("profit:", price - cost)
print("margin (profit / price):", margin(cost, price))
print("markup (profit / cost):", markup(cost, price))
print("markup in percent:", markup(cost, price) * 100)
// The conversions: a 20% margin is a 25% markup, and back again.
print("markup implied by a 20% margin:", margin(cost, price) / (1 - margin(cost, price)))
print("margin implied by a 25% markup:", markup(cost, price) / (1 + markup(cost, price)))
// The same 20 of profit reads as 20% margin but 25% markup. Margins can
// never reach 100% (that would need a free product); markups can exceed
// it freely. Pricing from cost at a 25% markup: 80*(1 + 25%) = 100.
/* ---- expected output ----
= profit: 20
= margin (profit / price): 0.2
= markup (profit / cost): 0.25
= markup in percent: 25
= markup implied by a 20% margin: 0.25
= margin implied by a 25% markup: 0.2
*/

scripts.name: net-present-value
scripts.title: npv of a small project at an 8% cost of
scripts.text:
/* ============================================================================
net-present-value.epher -- npv of a small project at an 8% cost of
capital, and the accept/reject decision it implies

The net present value discounts every cash flow back to today at the cost
of capital r: npv = sum of flow_k/(1+r)^k, with year 0's outflow counted
at k = 0. The finance builtin npv(r, flows) computes the sum. A positive
npv means the project earns more than the 8% the money could earn
elsewhere, so it adds value; a negative one destroys value. Source:
standard capital-budgeting formulas; see Brealey and Myers, Principles of
Corporate Finance, chapter 2 (the classic reference for npv).

Cash flows: the project costs 100000 today and returns 30000, 40000,
40000 and 30000 over the next four years.

Accuracy: 12 displayed digits.

The knobs to edit are in the knob section; everything after it is
machinery you can leave alone.
============================================================================ */

// ---- knobs ------------------------------------------------------------------
const rate = 8%             // the cost of capital (hurdle rate)
const flows = {-100000, 30000, 40000, 40000, 30000}   // year 0 outflow, then four yearly inflows

// ---- results -----------------------------------------------------------------
print("net present value at 8%:", npv(rate, flows))
print("decision:", if npv(rate, flows) > 0 then "accept: the project earns more than the 8% cost of capital" else "reject: the project destroys value at an 8% cost of capital")
// The npv of 15875.52 is the value the project adds, in today's money,
// after paying for the capital it uses. The sibling script
// internal-rate-of-return.epher asks the same question as a rate.
/* ---- expected output ----
= net present value at 8%: 15875.5158145
= decision: accept: the project earns more than the 8% cost of capital
*/

scripts.name: payback-period
scripts.title: how many years until a project's cash flows

scripts.name: price-earnings-valuation
scripts.title: fair price of a share from earnings
scripts.text:
/* ============================================================================
price-earnings-valuation.epher -- fair price of a share from earnings
per share and a target P/E, with an over/under-valued verdict

The P/E approach prices a share as eps * target_pe: what the market
typically pays per unit of earnings for comparable firms. Comparing the
fair price with the market price gives the verdict (an if/else prints it)
and the gap in percent. Source: standard equity-valuation practice; see
Brealey and Myers, Principles of Corporate Finance, chapter 4.

Assumptions: the target P/E comes from comparable companies or the
industry and is a rule of thumb, not a law; the verdict is about price,
not quality. Earnings are the trailing twelve months.

Accuracy: exact arithmetic, so the fair prices and gaps are exact.

The knobs to edit are in the knob section; everything after it is
machinery you can leave alone.
============================================================================ */

// ---- knobs ------------------------------------------------------------------
const eps_a = 2.40          // earnings per share, scenario A
const pe_a = 18             // target P/E, scenario A
const market_a = 40         // market price, scenario A
const eps_b = 3.10          // earnings per share, scenario B
const pe_b = 15             // target P/E, scenario B
const market_b = 50         // market price, scenario B

// ---- helpers ----------------------------------------------------------------
def fair(eps, pe) = eps * pe   // fair price = earnings per share times target P/E

// ---- results -----------------------------------------------------------------
print("fair value A:", fair(eps_a, pe_a))
print("verdict A:", if fair(eps_a, pe_a) > market_a then "undervalued: fair value sits above the market price" else "overvalued: fair value sits below the market price")
print("gap A in percent:", (fair(eps_a, pe_a) - market_a) / market_a * 100)
print("fair value B:", fair(eps_b, pe_b))
print("verdict B:", if fair(eps_b, pe_b) > market_b then "undervalued: fair value sits above the market price" else "overvalued: fair value sits below the market price")
print("gap B in percent:", (fair(eps_b, pe_b) - market_b) / market_b * 100)
/* Scenario A: 2.40 of earnings at a P/E of 18 prices the share at 43.20
against a 40 market price, an 8% upside if the target P/E is right.
Scenario B: 3.10 at a P/E of 15 prices it at 46.50 against a 50 market
price, 7% downside. Same method, opposite verdicts. */
/* ---- expected output ----
= fair value A: 43.2
= verdict A: undervalued: fair value sits above the market price
= gap A in percent: 8
= fair value B: 46.5
= verdict B: overvalued: fair value sits below the market price
= gap B in percent: -7
*/

scripts.name: roi
scripts.title: return on investment of a small business venture
scripts.text:
/* ============================================================================
roi.epher -- return on investment of a small business venture

The return on investment of a venture is its net profit divided by what
was put in: roi = (money back - money in)/money in. Here a 25000 venture
returns 8000, 12000 and 15000 over three years. Source: standard
accounting practice (the simple, cash-based roi taught in every
introductory finance course; see Brealey and Myers, Principles of
Corporate Finance, chapter 1).

Assumptions: the flows are the venture's net cash flows (revenue minus
running costs), and the 25000 is the whole investment. This simple roi
ignores WHEN the profits arrive; the sibling scripts npv and irr value
the timing, and a venture paying early is worth more than one paying
late at the same roi.

Accuracy: exact arithmetic, so the printed roi is exact.

The knobs to edit are in the knob section; everything after it is
machinery you can leave alone.
============================================================================ */

// ---- knobs ------------------------------------------------------------------
const invested = 25000      // money put into the venture
const flows = {8000, 12000, 15000}   // net cash flows returned, years 1 to 3

// ---- results -----------------------------------------------------------------
print("total returned over the three years:", sum(flows))
print("net profit:", sum(flows) - invested)
print("roi:", (sum(flows) - invested) / invested)
print("roi in percent:", (sum(flows) - invested) / invested * 100)
// 40000 came back on 25000 put in: a 40% roi over the life of the venture,
// which averages to about 13% a year before timing is considered.
/* ---- expected output ----
= total returned over the three years: 35000
= net profit: 10000
= roi: 0.4
= roi in percent: 40
*/

scripts.name: total-return
scripts.title: return on a shareholding, including the dividends
scripts.text:
/* ============================================================================
total-return.epher -- return on a shareholding, including the dividends
collected along the way

The total return of an investment is everything it returned, divided by
what it cost: (price gain + dividends)/cost. The script splits the return
of a 100-share holding into the price part and the dividend part, then
adds them. Source: standard investment-measurement practice; see
Brealey and Myers, Principles of Corporate Finance, chapter 8 (total
return on common stock).

Assumptions: 100 shares bought at 45 and sold at 61.20, with 3.60 per
share of dividends collected over the holding period. Taxes, commissions
and the timing of the dividends are ignored, and the return is not
annualized (the sibling script cagr.epher does that).

Accuracy: exact arithmetic, so the three returns print exactly.

The knobs to edit are in the knob section; everything after it is
machinery you can leave alone.
============================================================================ */

// ---- knobs ------------------------------------------------------------------
const shares = 100          // shares bought
const buy = 45              // price paid per share
const sell = 61.20          // price per share at the sale
const dividends = 3.60      // dividends collected per share over the holding period

// ---- results -----------------------------------------------------------------
print("cost of the position:", shares * buy)
print("price gain:", shares * (sell - buy))
print("dividends collected:", shares * dividends)
print("total return:", (shares * (sell - buy) + shares * dividends) / (shares * buy))
print("price part of the return:", shares * (sell - buy) / (shares * buy))
print("dividend part of the return:", shares * dividends / (shares * buy))
print("total return in percent:", (shares * (sell - buy) + shares * dividends) / (shares * buy) * 100)
// The price rose 36% and the dividends added 8%, so the total return is
// 44% over the holding period. A quote of "the stock returned 44%" counts
// the dividends; a quote of "36%" counts only the price.
/* ---- expected output ----
= cost of the position: 4500
= price gain: 1620
= dividends collected: 360
= total return: 0.44
= price part of the return: 0.36
= dividend part of the return: 0.08
= total return in percent: 44
*/

scripts.name: amortization-schedule
scripts.title: the first twelve months of a small loan,
scripts.text:
/* ============================================================================
amortization-schedule.epher -- the first twelve months of a small loan,
month by month: interest, principal and balance

For a loan of P at monthly rate r paid off in n equal payments pmt, the
amortization recurrence is, for month k:
  interest_k = balance_(k-1) * r
  principal_k = pmt - interest_k
  balance_k = balance_(k-1) - principal_k = balance_(k-1)*(1+r) - pmt
The helper bal(k) below answers each balance with the finance
builtin amort(P, r, n, k), which runs that recurrence; the payment
comes from the finance builtin tvm_pmt. Source: standard amortization
formulas; see Kellison, The Theory of Interest, chapter 3.

Accuracy: the schedule rows are rounded to the cent for display; the
underlying math runs on the full-precision values, and the check at
the end confirms the balance after the full term is 0.

The knobs to edit are in the knob section; everything after it is
machinery you can leave alone.
============================================================================ */

// ---- knobs ------------------------------------------------------------------
const principal = 1000      // amount borrowed
const mrate = 1%            // rate per month (a 12% nominal annual rate)
const months = 12           // term in months
const sched_payment = tvm_pmt(months, mrate, -principal, 0)   // constant monthly payment

// ---- helpers ----------------------------------------------------------------
def bal(k) = amort(principal, mrate, months, k)   // balance after k payments, from the finance builtin amort
def interest(k) = bal(k - 1) * mrate       // interest in month k: previous balance times the rate
def cents(x) = floor(x * 100 + 0.5) / 100  // rounds to the cent, for the display rows
def row(k) = {k, cents(interest(k)), cents(sched_payment - interest(k)), cents(bal(k))}

/* ---- results -----------------------------------------------------------------
The payment is the same every month; each row below is
{month, interest, principal, balance}, rounded to the cent. Notice the
interest column shrinking while the principal column grows. */
print("columns: month, interest, principal, balance")
for k in 1 to months do row(k)
print("balance after the full term (must be 0):", amort(principal, mrate, months, months))
print("total interest over the year, rounded:", cents(sched_payment * months - principal))
/* ---- expected output ----
= columns: month, interest, principal, balance
= {{1, 10, 78.85, 921.15}, {2, 9.21, 79.64, 841.51}, {3, 8.42, 80.43, 761.08}, {4, 7.61, 81.24, 679.84}, {5, 6.8, 82.05, 597.79}, {6, 5.98, 82.87, 514.92}, {7, 5.15, 83.7, 431.22}, {8, 4.31, 84.54, 346.68}, {9, 3.47, 85.38, 261.3}, {10, 2.61, 86.24, 175.07}, {11, 1.75, 87.1, 87.97}, {12, 0.88, 87.97, 0}}
= balance after the full term (must be 0): 0
= total interest over the year, rounded: 66.19
*/

scripts.name: balloon-loan
scripts.title: payments on a note that still owes a balloon sum at
scripts.text:
/* ============================================================================
balloon-loan.epher -- payments on a note that still owes a balloon sum at
maturity

A balloon loan amortizes only part of the principal: the finance builtin
tvm_pmt takes the future value argument fv, the balance still owed at the
end, so tvm_pmt(n, r, -P, balloon) is the payment that leaves exactly the
balloon unpaid after n months. Source: standard TVM formulas; see
Kellison, The Theory of Interest, chapter 3.

Sign convention: principal negative, payment positive, balloon positive,
as in the builtin example tvm_pmt(360, 0.08/12, -100000, 0).

Accuracy: 12 displayed digits. The balloon is typically refinanced or
paid from savings at maturity; if it cannot be, the borrower may face a
forced sale, which is the risk this structure carries.

The knobs to edit are in the knob section; everything after it is
machinery you can leave alone.
============================================================================ */

// ---- knobs ------------------------------------------------------------------
const principal = 50000     // amount borrowed
const rate = 5.4%           // quoted annual rate
const years = 5             // term in years
const balloon = 20000       // balance still owed at maturity

// ---- results -----------------------------------------------------------------
const balloon_payment = tvm_pmt(years * 12, rate / 12, -principal, balloon)   // monthly payment
print("monthly payment with the 20000 balloon:", balloon_payment)
print("payment to amortize the whole principal:", tvm_pmt(years * 12, rate / 12, -principal, 0))
print("monthly saving vs full amortization:", tvm_pmt(years * 12, rate / 12, -principal, 0) - balloon_payment)
print("total paid with the balloon (payments plus balloon):", balloon_payment * (years * 12) + balloon)
print("interest paid with the balloon:", balloon_payment * (years * 12) + balloon - principal)
// The lower payment buys a cheaper month but a dearer loan: interest runs
// about 9699.07 with the balloon versus 7165.12 on a fully amortized note.
/* ---- expected output ----
= monthly payment with the 20000 balloon: 661.651184744
= payment to amortize the whole principal: 952.751974573
= monthly saving vs full amortization: 291.100789829
= total paid with the balloon (payments plus balloon): 59699.0710846
= interest paid with the balloon: 9699.07108462
*/

scripts.name: car-loan-payment
scripts.title: monthly payment of a 5-year auto loan with a
scripts.text:
/* ============================================================================
car-loan-payment.epher -- monthly payment of a 5-year auto loan with a
down payment

The buyer puts a down payment on the price and finances the rest with a
fixed-rate loan: the financed amount is price*(1 - down), and the monthly
payment over n months at rate r comes from the finance builtin tvm_pmt,
the annuity formula pmt = P*r/(1 - (1+r)^-n). Source: standard
amortization formulas; see Kellison, The Theory of Interest, chapter 3.

Sign convention: principal negative, payment positive, as in the builtin
example tvm_pmt(360, 0.08/12, -100000, 0).

Accuracy: 12 displayed digits. Dealers quote "6.9% APR" for the monthly
rate 6.9%/12; fees and sales tax are not part of this price.

The knobs to edit are in the knob section; everything after it is
machinery you can leave alone.
============================================================================ */

// ---- knobs ------------------------------------------------------------------
const price = 32000         // the car's price
const down = 15%            // down payment as a share of the price
const rate = 6.9%           // quoted annual rate on the loan
const years = 5             // loan term in years

// ---- results -----------------------------------------------------------------
print("down payment:", price * down)
print("amount financed:", price * (1 - down))
const car_payment = tvm_pmt(years * 12, rate / 12, -(price * (1 - down)), 0)   // monthly payment
print("monthly payment:", car_payment)
print("total of 60 payments:", car_payment * (years * 12))
print("interest over the term:", car_payment * (years * 12) - price * (1 - down))
/* ---- expected output ----
= down payment: 4800
= amount financed: 27200
= monthly payment: 537.310224456
= total of 60 payments: 32238.6134674
= interest over the term: 5038.61346738
*/

scripts.name: extra-payment-savings
scripts.title: how an extra 100 a month shortens a 30-year
scripts.text:
/* ============================================================================
extra-payment-savings.epher -- how an extra 100 a month shortens a 30-year
mortgage and cuts its interest

The borrower pays the regular monthly payment plus a fixed extra amount.
The finance builtins answer the payoff questions directly: tvm_n solves
the annuity equation for the fractional term on the boosted payment, and
the closed form of the amortization recurrence,
  balance_k = balance_(k-1) * (1 + r) - boosted,
gives the balance before the last payment, whose true final payment is
smaller. The baseline is the same loan at its minimum payment over the
full 360 months. Source: standard TVM and amortization formulas; see
Kellison, The Theory of Interest, chapter 3.

Accuracy: 12 displayed digits. tvm_n's term is fractional; the schedule
takes ceil of it full payments, the last one smaller, and the interest
figures below account for that smaller payment. (The sibling script
amortization-schedule.epher walks the same recurrence month by month.)

The knobs to edit are in the knob section; everything after it is
machinery you can leave alone.
============================================================================ */

// ---- knobs ------------------------------------------------------------------
const principal = 200000    // loan amount at closing
const rate = 6%             // quoted annual rate
const years = 30            // term in years
const extra = 100           // extra paid every month on top of the minimum
const loan_payment = tvm_pmt(years * 12, rate / 12, -principal, 0)   // minimum monthly payment
const boosted = loan_payment + extra                                 // payment with the extra 100

// ---- results -----------------------------------------------------------------
const payoff_months = ceil(tvm_n(rate / 12, -principal, boosted, 0))   // full payments to reach zero
def bal(k) = principal * (1 + rate / 12) ^ k - boosted * ((1 + rate / 12) ^ k - 1) / (rate / 12)   // balance after k payments, closed form of the recurrence
const last_payment = bal(payoff_months - 1) * (1 + rate / 12)          // the true final payment is smaller
print("minimum payment:", loan_payment)
print("months to pay off with the extra 100:", payoff_months)
print("true last payment (smaller):", last_payment)
print("interest paid with the extra 100:", (payoff_months - 1) * boosted + last_payment - principal)
print("interest paid on the baseline plan:", years * 12 * loan_payment - principal)
print("interest saved:", (years * 12 * loan_payment - principal) - ((payoff_months - 1) * boosted + last_payment - principal))
/* The extra 100 cuts the term from 360 months to 295 (24.6 years) and saves
about 49138.41 of interest. tvm_n's fractional term on the boosted payment is
294.46 months on the same numbers, consistent with 295 full payments and a
smaller last one. */
/* ---- expected output ----
= minimum payment: 1199.10105031
= months to pay off with the extra 100: 295
= true last payment (smaller): 602.261007745
= interest paid with the extra 100: 182537.969798
= interest paid on the baseline plan: 231676.37811
= interest saved: 49138.4083124
*/

scripts.name: mortgage-affordability
scripts.title: how large a mortgage a target payment
scripts.text:
/* ============================================================================
mortgage-affordability.epher -- how large a mortgage a target payment
supports, using the 28% income rule

The 28% rule of thumb keeps housing costs at or under 28% of gross
income, so a borrower earning `income` can pay about income/12*28% per
month. The finance builtin tvm_pv answers how large a loan that payment
buys at a given rate and term: it solves the same annuity equation as
tvm_pmt, but for the principal. Source: standard TVM formulas and the
common lender rule; the formula is Kellison, The Theory of Interest,
chapter 3.

Sign convention: the payment is entered negative (money leaves the pocket
each month) and the answer comes back positive. Property tax, insurance
and other debts are not part of this 28% slice.

Accuracy: 12 displayed digits.

The knobs to edit are in the knob section; everything after it is
machinery you can leave alone.
============================================================================ */

// ---- knobs ------------------------------------------------------------------
const income = 90000        // gross yearly income
const share = 28%           // the 28% rule: housing budget share of income
const rate = 6.5%           // quoted annual rate
const years = 30            // term in years

// ---- results -----------------------------------------------------------------
print("monthly budget at the 28% rule:", income / 12 * share)
// tvm_pv(360, 6.5%/12, -2100, 0): the loan whose 360 payments of 2100 at
// 6.5% exactly repay it.
print("largest loan at 6.5% for 30 years:", tvm_pv(years * 12, rate / 12, -(income / 12 * share), 0))
// With the usual 20% down payment the loan covers 80% of the price.
print("largest home price with 20% down:", tvm_pv(years * 12, rate / 12, -(income / 12 * share), 0) / 80%)
/* ---- expected output ----
= monthly budget at the 28% rule: 2100
= largest loan at 6.5% for 30 years: 332242.721028
= largest home price with 20% down: 415303.401285
*/

scripts.name: mortgage-balance-after-years
scripts.title: what is still owed on a 30-year
scripts.text:
/* ============================================================================
mortgage-balance-after-years.epher -- what is still owed on a 30-year
mortgage after 5 and 10 years

Each payment on an amortizing loan splits into interest on the remaining
balance and principal that reduces it. The balance after k of n payments
is computed by the finance builtin amort(P, r, n, k), which runs the
recurrence balance_k = balance_(k-1)*(1+r) - pmt for k months. Source:
standard amortization formulas; see Kellison, The Theory of Interest,
chapter 3.

Accuracy: 12 displayed digits; rounding to the cent is omitted.

The knobs to edit are in the knob section; everything after it is
machinery you can leave alone.
============================================================================ */

// ---- knobs ------------------------------------------------------------------
const principal = 250000    // loan amount at closing
const rate = 6.5%           // quoted annual rate
const years = 30            // term in years

// ---- results -----------------------------------------------------------------
const mbal_payment = tvm_pmt(years * 12, rate / 12, -principal, 0)   // monthly payment
print("monthly payment:", mbal_payment)
// Balances after 60 and 120 payments of the 360-month loan.
print("balance after 5 years:", amort(principal, rate / 12, years * 12, 5 * 12))
print("balance after 10 years:", amort(principal, rate / 12, years * 12, 10 * 12))
print("principal paid off in the first 5 years:", principal - amort(principal, rate / 12, years * 12, 5 * 12))
print("principal paid off in the first 10 years:", principal - amort(principal, rate / 12, years * 12, 10 * 12))
print("payments made in the first 10 years:", mbal_payment * (10 * 12))
// After 10 years the borrower has paid 189620.41 but only about 38059.68 of
// it (one fifth) has reduced the debt; the other four fifths went to
// interest. The balance is what a refinance would have to cover.
/* ---- expected output ----
= monthly payment: 1580.17005873
= balance after 5 years: 234027.443604
= balance after 10 years: 211940.315908
= principal paid off in the first 5 years: 15972.5563961
= principal paid off in the first 10 years: 38059.6840925
= payments made in the first 10 years: 189620.407048
*/

scripts.name: mortgage-payment
scripts.title: monthly payment of a 30-year fixed-rate mortgage
scripts.text:
/* ============================================================================
mortgage-payment.epher -- monthly payment of a 30-year fixed-rate mortgage

A mortgage of P at annual rate r over n months is an annuity: each month
the borrower pays the same amount, and the payment formula is
const pmt = P*r/(1 - (1+r)^-n) with r = rate/12, solved here by the finance
builtin tvm_pmt (see the finance builtins in "epher scripts/README.md").
Source: standard amortization formulas; see Kellison, The Theory of
Interest, chapter 3.

Sign convention: the principal is entered negative and the payment comes
back positive, exactly as in the builtin's own example
tvm_pmt(360, 0.08/12, -100000, 0) = 733.764573879. Only the size of the
payment matters below.

Accuracy: 12 displayed digits. Real lenders round the payment to the
cent, and escrow for tax and insurance is separate; both are omitted.

The knobs to edit are in the knob section; everything after it is
machinery you can leave alone.
============================================================================ */

// ---- knobs ------------------------------------------------------------------
const principal = 250000    // loan amount at closing
const rate = 6.5%           // quoted annual rate (APR-style, monthly compounding)
const years = 30            // term in years

// ---- results -----------------------------------------------------------------
// n = 30*12 = 360 months, r = 6.5%/12 per month. The payment is constant
// over the whole term (end of each month, the builtin's default timing).
print("monthly payment:", tvm_pmt(years * 12, rate / 12, -principal, 0))
print("annual total (12 payments):", 12 * tvm_pmt(years * 12, rate / 12, -principal, 0))
/* ---- expected output ----
= monthly payment: 1580.17005873
= annual total (12 payments): 18962.0407048
*/

scripts.name: mortgage-rate
scripts.title: the interest rate a given payment implies, and the

scripts.name: mortgage-term
scripts.title: how long a fixed monthly payment takes to clear a
scripts.text:
/* ============================================================================
mortgage-term.epher -- how long a fixed monthly payment takes to clear a
mortgage

The finance builtin tvm_n solves the annuity equation for the number of
periods: given the rate, the principal (negative) and a fixed payment, it
returns the months until the balance is zero. Source: standard TVM
formulas; see Kellison, The Theory of Interest, chapter 3.

Sign convention: principal negative, payment positive, as in the builtin
example tvm_pmt(360, 0.08/12, -100000, 0).

Accuracy: 12 displayed digits. The answer 209.25 months is fractional;
a real lender takes 210 payments, the last one smaller.

The knobs to edit are in the knob section; everything after it is
machinery you can leave alone.
============================================================================ */

// ---- knobs ------------------------------------------------------------------
const principal = 250000    // loan amount at closing
const rate = 6.5%           // quoted annual rate
const term_payment = 2000   // fixed monthly payment the borrower can afford

// ---- results -----------------------------------------------------------------
const months = tvm_n(rate / 12, -principal, term_payment, 0)   // months to pay off, from the builtin
print("paying 2000 per month clears the loan in:", months, "months")
print("that is", months / 12, "years")
/* The minimum payment on this loan is 1580.17 (see mortgage-payment.epher),
which runs the full 360 months. The extra 419.83 per month shortens the
term by about 150.75 months (12.6 years) and saves roughly 150,000 of
interest. */
/* ---- expected output ----
= paying 2000 per month clears the loan in: 209.246700004 months
= that is 17.4372250004 years
*/

scripts.name: mortgage-total-interest
scripts.title: interest paid over the full life of a
scripts.text:
/* ============================================================================
mortgage-total-interest.epher -- interest paid over the full life of a
30-year fixed-rate mortgage

Over n months of payment pmt on a principal P, the borrower pays n*pmt
in total, of which n*pmt - P is interest (the principal is repaid exactly
once). The payment comes from the finance builtin tvm_pmt, the same
annuity formula as the sibling script mortgage-payment.epher. Source:
standard amortization formulas; see Kellison, The Theory of Interest,
chapter 3.

Sign convention: principal negative, payment positive, as in the builtin
example tvm_pmt(360, 0.08/12, -100000, 0).

Accuracy: 12 displayed digits; rounding to the cent is omitted.

The knobs to edit are in the knob section; everything after it is
machinery you can leave alone.
============================================================================ */

// ---- knobs ------------------------------------------------------------------
const principal = 250000    // loan amount at closing
const rate = 6.5%           // quoted annual rate
const years = 30            // term in years

// ---- helpers ----------------------------------------------------------------
def cents(x) = floor(x * 100 + 0.5) / 100   // rounds to the cent, for display

// ---- results -----------------------------------------------------------------
const ti_payment = tvm_pmt(years * 12, rate / 12, -principal, 0)   // monthly payment
print("monthly payment:", ti_payment)
print("total paid over the term:", cents(ti_payment * (years * 12)))
print("total interest over the term:", cents(ti_payment * (years * 12) - principal))
/* The totals round the 360 full-precision payments to the cent, the way real
mortgages are paid; the unrounded total is 568861.2211436688. Interest
dominates early: the first month's interest alone is principal*rate/12 =
1354.17 of the 1580.17 payment, about 86%. */
/* ---- expected output ----
= monthly payment: 1580.17005873
= total paid over the term: 568861.22
= total interest over the term: 318861.22
*/

scripts.name: refinance-breakeven
scripts.title: when a refinance pays for its closing costs
scripts.text:
/* ============================================================================
refinance-breakeven.epher -- when a refinance pays for its closing costs

Refinancing the same principal from an old rate to a new one lowers the
monthly payment; the closing costs spent up front are recovered once the
accumulated savings equal them, so the break-even point in months is
costs / (old payment - new payment). Both payments come from the finance
builtin tvm_pmt. Source: standard amortization formulas; the break-even
arithmetic is common lender practice, see Kellison, The Theory of
Interest, chapter 3.

Assumptions: the same 300000 principal and a fresh 30-year term at the
new rate, which is what most refinances do (the clock restarts). A real
refinance starts from the remaining balance and may roll costs into the
loan, which shifts the break-even a little.

Accuracy: 12 displayed digits.

The knobs to edit are in the knob section; everything after it is
machinery you can leave alone.
============================================================================ */

// ---- knobs ------------------------------------------------------------------
const principal = 300000    // loan amount at closing
const rate_old = 7%         // rate of the current loan
const rate_new = 5.5%       // rate offered by the refinance
const years = 30            // term in years, restarted at the new rate
const costs = 6000          // closing costs paid up front

// ---- results -----------------------------------------------------------------
print("current payment at 7%:", tvm_pmt(years * 12, rate_old / 12, -principal, 0))
print("new payment at 5.5%:", tvm_pmt(years * 12, rate_new / 12, -principal, 0))
print("monthly saving:", tvm_pmt(years * 12, rate_old / 12, -principal, 0) - tvm_pmt(years * 12, rate_new / 12, -principal, 0))
print("break-even in months:", costs / (tvm_pmt(years * 12, rate_old / 12, -principal, 0) - tvm_pmt(years * 12, rate_new / 12, -principal, 0)))
/* The 6000 in costs is recovered after about 20.5 months (1.7 years); every
month after that saves 292.54. Two cautions: the term restarts at 30
years, and if the loan is sold or refinanced again before the break-even,
the costs are lost. */
/* ---- expected output ----
= current payment at 7%: 1995.90748554
= new payment at 5.5%: 1703.36700404
= monthly saving: 292.540481497
= break-even in months: 20.5099819666
*/

scripts.name: annuity-due-value
scripts.title: retirement balance when deposits are made at
scripts.text:
/* ============================================================================
annuity-due-value.epher -- retirement balance when deposits are made at
the START of each month, compared with end-of-month deposits

The finance builtin tvm_fv takes an optional last argument, the payment
timing: 0 (the default) means the payment lands at the END of each
period, 1 means the BEGINNING (an annuity due). A deposit made at the
start of the month earns that month's interest, so the annuity-due
balance is the end-of-period balance times (1+r). Source: standard
annuity formulas; see Kellison, The Theory of Interest, chapter 3.

Sign convention: deposit negative, balance positive.

Accuracy: 12 displayed digits; the difference printed below is exactly
one month of interest on the end-of-period balance.

The knobs to edit are in the knob section; everything after it is
machinery you can leave alone.
============================================================================ */

// ---- knobs ------------------------------------------------------------------
const deposit = 300         // monthly deposit
const rate = 7%             // annual rate of return
const years = 30            // years of saving

// ---- results -----------------------------------------------------------------
print("deposits at month end (timing 0):", tvm_fv(years * 12, rate / 12, 0, -deposit, 0))
print("deposits at month start (timing 1):", tvm_fv(years * 12, rate / 12, 0, -deposit, 1))
print("difference:", tvm_fv(years * 12, rate / 12, 0, -deposit, 1) - tvm_fv(years * 12, rate / 12, 0, -deposit, 0))
// The difference is one month of interest on the end-of-period balance:
// 365991.30 * 7%/12 = 2134.95. Moving the deposits one month earlier, once,
// is worth that much after 30 years.
/* ---- expected output ----
= deposits at month end (timing 0): 365991.298733
= deposits at month start (timing 1): 368126.247975
= difference: 2134.94924261
*/

scripts.name: college-fund-payment
scripts.title: monthly deposit that grows to a college
scripts.text:
/* ============================================================================
college-fund-payment.epher -- monthly deposit that grows to a college
fund over 18 years

Saving for a child born today means a monthly deposit for 18 years (216
months) that must reach the goal by then. The finance builtin tvm_pmt
solves the deposit: tvm_pmt(n, r, 0, goal), present value 0, the goal as
the future value. Source: standard annuity formulas; see Kellison, The
Theory of Interest, chapter 3.

Sign convention: the builtin returns the deposit negative (money out);
the size is printed positive.

Accuracy: 12 displayed digits; the round-trip line below compounds the
exact deposit back to the goal.

The knobs to edit are in the knob section; everything after it is
machinery you can leave alone.
============================================================================ */

// ---- knobs ------------------------------------------------------------------
const goal = 80000          // college fund needed in 18 years
const rate = 5%             // annual rate of return
const years = 18            // years until college starts

// ---- results -----------------------------------------------------------------
print("monthly deposit needed:", 0 - tvm_pmt(years * 12, rate / 12, 0, goal))
print("round trip: the deposits grow to:", tvm_fv(years * 12, rate / 12, 0, tvm_pmt(years * 12, rate / 12, 0, goal)))
print("total deposited out of pocket:", (0 - tvm_pmt(years * 12, rate / 12, 0, goal)) * (years * 12))
print("growth supplies:", goal - (0 - tvm_pmt(years * 12, rate / 12, 0, goal)) * (years * 12))
// 216 deposits of about 229.09 put in 49484.25; the remaining 30515.75 of
// the goal (38%) comes from growth.
/* ---- expected output ----
= monthly deposit needed: 229.093748265
= round trip: the deposits grow to: 80000
= total deposited out of pocket: 49484.2496252
= growth supplies: 30515.7503748
*/

scripts.name: dollar-cost-averaging
scripts.title: 500 a month into an index fund versus the
scripts.text:
/* ============================================================================
dollar-cost-averaging.epher -- 500 a month into an index fund versus the
same money invested as a lump sum at the start

Dollar-cost averaging feeds a fixed amount into the market every month.
Its balance after n months at monthly rate r is the annuity future value
(finance builtin tvm_fv). The comparison invests the same total money,
all of it, at the start and lets it compound for the whole term. Source:
standard annuity and compound formulas, Kellison, The Theory of Interest,
chapters 2-3.

Sign convention: money in negative, balance positive.

Accuracy: 12 displayed digits. The comparison assumes the market simply
earns its average rate every month, with no ups and downs; real markets
swing, which is exactly where dollar-cost averaging earns its keep.

The knobs to edit are in the knob section; everything after it is
machinery you can leave alone.
============================================================================ */

// ---- knobs ------------------------------------------------------------------
const deposit = 500         // monthly deposit
const rate = 8%             // average annual return of the fund
const years = 20            // years of investing

// ---- results -----------------------------------------------------------------
print("balance after 20 years of monthly deposits:", tvm_fv(years * 12, rate / 12, 0, -deposit))
print("lump sum equal to all the deposits, invested at the start:", deposit * (years * 12) * (1 + rate / 12) ^ (years * 12))
print("difference:", deposit * (years * 12) * (1 + rate / 12) ^ (years * 12) - tvm_fv(years * 12, rate / 12, 0, -deposit))
/* The 120000 total invested up front beats the monthly plan by 296706.12
at the same average return: every lump-sum unit earns the full 20 years
while the monthly deposits earn less and less. Dollar-cost averaging does
not raise the expected return; it smooths the risk of buying at one
unlucky moment, and it is the only option for money that arrives monthly. */
/* ---- expected output ----
= balance after 20 years of monthly deposits: 294510.207811
= lump sum equal to all the deposits, invested at the start: 591216.332497
= difference: 296706.124686
*/

scripts.name: employer-match-growth
scripts.title: a 401k with a full 5% employer match:
scripts.text:
/* ============================================================================
employer-match-growth.epher -- a 401k with a full 5% employer match:
final balance and how much of it the match built

The saver contributes 5% of salary and the employer matches it 100%, so
every month two equal deposits land in the account. The final balance is
the annuity future value of their sum (finance builtin tvm_fv), and the
employer's share is the future value of the employer's deposits alone.
Source: standard annuity formulas, Kellison, The Theory of Interest,
chapter 3; the 5% match is the common plan design.

Sign convention: deposits negative, balance positive.

Accuracy: 12 displayed digits; matches usually cap at a share of salary,
which here is the full 5%.

The knobs to edit are in the knob section; everything after it is
machinery you can leave alone.
============================================================================ */

// ---- knobs ------------------------------------------------------------------
const salary = 60000        // yearly salary
const own_share = 5%        // share of salary the saver deposits
const match_share = 5%      // share of salary the employer matches (100% match)
const rate = 7%             // annual rate of return
const years = 30            // years of saving

// ---- results -----------------------------------------------------------------
print("your monthly deposit (5% of salary):", salary / 12 * own_share)
print("employer monthly deposit:", salary / 12 * match_share)
print("balance after 30 years:", tvm_fv(years * 12, rate / 12, 0, -(salary / 12 * (own_share + match_share))))
print("the employer's half of the pot:", tvm_fv(years * 12, rate / 12, 0, -(salary / 12 * match_share)))
print("your own deposits over 30 years:", salary / 12 * own_share * (years * 12))
// Your deposits match the employer's one for one, so half the 609985.50 pot
// is the match's doing. Your own 90000 out of pocket would have grown to
// 304992.75 alone; the match adds another 304992.75 on top.
/* ---- expected output ----
= your monthly deposit (5% of salary): 250
= employer monthly deposit: 250
= balance after 30 years: 609985.497888
= the employer's half of the pot: 304992.748944
= your own deposits over 30 years: 90000
*/

scripts.name: future-value-of-annuity
scripts.title: retirement balance of regular monthly
scripts.text:
/* ============================================================================
future-value-of-annuity.epher -- retirement balance of regular monthly
deposits at the end of each month

Depositing the same amount at the end of every month for n months at
monthly rate r builds the annuity future value
  fv = pmt * ((1+r)^n - 1) / r
computed here by the finance builtin tvm_fv (see the finance builtins in
"epher scripts/README.md"). Source: standard annuity formulas; see
Kellison, The Theory of Interest, chapter 3.

Sign convention: the deposit is entered negative (money out each month)
and the balance comes back positive. Deposits at the START of the month
are the sibling script annuity-due-value.epher.

Accuracy: 12 displayed digits; the last deposit (end of month n) earns
no interest.

The knobs to edit are in the knob section; everything after it is
machinery you can leave alone.
============================================================================ */

// ---- knobs ------------------------------------------------------------------
const deposit = 300         // monthly deposit
const rate = 7%             // annual rate of return
const years = 30            // years of saving

// ---- results -----------------------------------------------------------------
// tvm_fv(n, r, pv, pmt): 360 monthly deposits at 7%/12, nothing saved yet.
print("balance after 30 years:", tvm_fv(years * 12, rate / 12, 0, -deposit))
print("total deposited out of pocket:", deposit * (years * 12))
print("interest earned:", tvm_fv(years * 12, rate / 12, 0, -deposit) - deposit * (years * 12))
// Of the 365991.30 balance, 108000 came from the deposits themselves and
// 257991.30 (about 70%) from compounding.
/* ---- expected output ----
= balance after 30 years: 365991.298733
= total deposited out of pocket: 108000
= interest earned: 257991.298733
*/

scripts.name: lump-sum-vs-annuity
scripts.title: take 500000 now, or 3000 a month for 30
scripts.text:
/* ============================================================================
lump-sum-vs-annuity.epher -- take 500000 now, or 3000 a month for 30
years? Compare at one rate, then find the rate that ties them

The annuity's present value is what a 30-year stream of 3000/month is
worth today at the given rate, from the finance builtin tvm_pv. If that
value beats the lump sum, the annuity is the better deal at this rate;
otherwise the lump sum is. The tie rate comes from tvm_i, the rate that
makes a 500000 account exactly fund 360 withdrawals of 3000. Source:
standard TVM formulas; see Kellison, The Theory of Interest, chapters
3-4.

Sign convention: the stream is entered as its monthly payment (positive,
money in), so tvm_pv answers negative; the value is printed positive.

Accuracy: 12 displayed digits.

The knobs to edit are in the knob section; everything after it is
machinery you can leave alone.
============================================================================ */

// ---- knobs ------------------------------------------------------------------
const lump = 500000         // the lump sum offered today
const monthly = 3000        // the annuity's monthly payment
const years = 30            // years the annuity pays
const rate = 5%             // the rate of return assumed available

// ---- helpers ----------------------------------------------------------------
def cents(x) = floor(x * 100 + 0.5) / 100   // rounds to the cent, for display

// ---- results -----------------------------------------------------------------
// The present value is rounded to the cent for display (the exact value
// 558844.8511382258 is what the if below compares with the lump sum).
print("annuity present value at 5%:", cents(0 - tvm_pv(years * 12, rate / 12, monthly, 0)))
print("the stream beats the lump sum by:", cents(0 - tvm_pv(years * 12, rate / 12, monthly, 0) - lump))
print("better deal at 5%:", if 0 - tvm_pv(years * 12, rate / 12, monthly, 0) > lump then "the 3000/month annuity (worth more today)" else "the lump sum")
print("the lump alone at 5% funds 3000/month for:", tvm_n(rate / 12, -lump, monthly, 0), "months")
print("rate that ties the two (nominal, 12 x monthly):", 12 * tvm_i(years * 12, -lump, monthly, 0))
/* At 5% the stream is worth 558844.85 today, more than the 500000 lump, so
the annuity wins; invested at 5% the lump runs dry after 285.14 months
(23.8 years) of 3000/month withdrawals. Above about 6.0% nominal (6.18%
effective) the lump sum overtakes the annuity: then investing it yourself
is the better deal. */
/* ---- expected output ----
= annuity present value at 5%: 558844.85
= the stream beats the lump sum by: 58844.85
= better deal at 5%: the 3000/month annuity (worth more today)
= the lump alone at 5% funds 3000/month for: 285.142080771 months
= rate that ties the two (nominal, 12 x monthly): 0.0600699000811
*/

scripts.name: regular-deposit-growth
scripts.title: year-by-year table of a monthly savings
scripts.text:
/* ============================================================================
regular-deposit-growth.epher -- year-by-year table of a monthly savings
plan, cross-checked against the annuity builtin

Depositing `deposit` at the end of every month at annual rate `rate`, the
balance after y years is the annuity future value of 12*y monthly
deposits (finance builtin tvm_fv). The table below lists that balance for
every year of the plan; the final line recomputes year 10 directly.
Source: standard annuity formulas; see Kellison, The Theory of Interest,
chapter 3.

Sign convention: deposit negative, balance positive.

Accuracy: 12 displayed digits on every row; the last row and the final
check line are the same number.

The knobs to edit are in the knob section; everything after it is
machinery you can leave alone.

// ---- knobs ------------------------------------------------------------------

// ---- results -----------------------------------------------------------------
// Rows are {year, balance at its end}; each row is tvm_fv(12*y, 6%/12, 0,
// -250), the balance after y years of deposits.
print("columns: year, balance")
for y in 1 to years do {y, tvm_fv(y * 12, rate / 12, 0, -deposit)}
print("10-year balance, direct tvm_fv call:", tvm_fv(years * 12, rate / 12, 0, -deposit))

// 30000 was deposited and 10969.84 was interest.
/* ---- expected output ----
= columns: year, balance
= {{1, 3083.89059322}, {2, 6357.98881027}, {3, 9834.02624117}, {4, 13524.4580548}, {5, 17442.5076275}, {6, 21602.2139246}, {7, 26018.4818041}, {8, 30707.135423}, {9, 35684.9749378}, {10, 40969.8367016}}

scripts.name: retirement-goal

/* ============================================================================
retirement-goal.epher -- how long monthly deposits take to reach a
million, at 6%

The finance builtin tvm_n solves the annuity equation for the number of
periods: tvm_n(r, pv, pmt, fv) returns the months of deposit pmt (money
out, negative) that grow an empty account to the goal fv. Source:
standard annuity formulas; see Kellison, The Theory of Interest,
chapter 3.

Sign convention: deposit negative, goal positive.

Accuracy: 12 displayed digits. The answer is fractional (359.25 months);
in practice the last month's deposit is smaller.

The knobs to edit are in the knob section; everything after it is
machinery you can leave alone.
============================================================================ */

// ---- knobs ------------------------------------------------------------------

print("reaching 1,000,000 takes:", months, "months, or", months / 12, "years")
print("deposited out of pocket in that time:", months * deposit)
print("interest earned:", goal - months * deposit)
// Almost 30 years of 1000/month deposits put in 359247.03; compounding
// supplies the other 640752.97, about 64% of the goal. At 8% the same
// deposits reach the goal in about 306 months instead of 359.

= reaching 1,000,000 takes: 359.247028874 months, or 29.9372524062 years
= deposited out of pocket in that time: 359247.028874
= interest earned: 640752.971126
*/

to reach a vacation fund

The finance builtin tvm_n solves the annuity equation for the term:
