scripts.name: sinking-fund-payment
scripts.title: monthly deposit that grows to a target sum
scripts.text:
/* ============================================================================
sinking-fund-payment.epher -- monthly deposit that grows to a target sum

A sinking fund is the saver's mirror of a loan: regular deposits that
accumulate to a known target at the end. The finance builtin tvm_pmt
solves the deposit: tvm_pmt(n, r, 0, target) with present value 0 and the
target as the future value. Source: standard annuity formulas; see
Kellison, The Theory of Interest, chapter 3.

Sign convention: the builtin returns the deposit negative (money out each
month); the size is printed positive.

Accuracy: 12 displayed digits; the round-trip line below compounds the
exact deposit back to the target.

The knobs to edit are in the knob section; everything after it is
machinery you can leave alone.
============================================================================ */

// ---- knobs ------------------------------------------------------------------
const target = 50000        // the sum needed at the end
const rate = 4%             // annual rate of return
const years = 5             // years to save

// ---- results -----------------------------------------------------------------
print("monthly deposit needed:", 0 - tvm_pmt(years * 12, rate / 12, 0, target))
print("round trip: the deposits grow to:", tvm_fv(years * 12, rate / 12, 0, tvm_pmt(years * 12, rate / 12, 0, target)))
// Over 60 months the deposits themselves total 45249.57; the account's
// interest supplies the remaining 4750.43 of the 50000 target.
/* ---- expected output ----
= monthly deposit needed: 754.159436097
= round trip: the deposits grow to: 50000
*/

scripts.name: annulus-area
scripts.title: area of a ring between two circles
scripts.text:
/* ============================================================================
annulus-area.epher -- area of a ring between two circles

The annulus between the circles of radius R and r (R > r) has area
A = pi R^2 - pi r^2 = pi (R^2 - r^2), the disk minus its hole
(standard formula). The results check the difference form against the
separate disk areas, and the r = 0 case reduces to the whole circle.

Web/desktop:             paste the whole file into the entry, press Enter

The knobs to edit are `R` (outer radius) and `r` (inner radius).
Everything above the results section is machinery you can leave alone.
============================================================================ */

// ---- the knobs ----------------------------------------------------------------
const R = 8
const r = 3

// ---- the model ----------------------------------------------------------------
def annulus(R, r) = pi * (R ^ 2 - r ^ 2)   // A = pi (R^2 - r^2)
def minus(R, r) = pi * R ^ 2 - pi * r ^ 2   // the disk areas taken separately

// ---- results ------------------------------------------------------------------
print("annulus area:", annulus(R, r))
print("difference form agrees:", abs(annulus(R, r) - minus(R, r)) < 1e-9)
print("radius 5 with no hole is the circle:", annulus(5, 0))
/* ---- expected output ----
= annulus area: 172.787595947
= difference form agrees: true
= radius 5 with no hole is the circle: 78.5398163397
*/

scripts.name: arc-length
scripts.title: length of a circular arc
scripts.text:
/* ============================================================================
arc-length.epher -- length of a circular arc

An arc of radius r and central angle ang (degrees) is the fraction
ang / 360 of the circumference, length L = ang / 360 * 2 pi r. Written
with the angle in radians, theta = rad(ang), this is the standard form
L = r theta. The results compute both forms and check they agree; the
semicircle case, ang = 180, is half of 2 pi r, that is, pi r.

Web/desktop:             paste the whole file into the entry, press Enter

The knobs to edit are `r` (radius) and `ang` (central angle in degrees).
Everything above the results section is machinery you can leave alone.
============================================================================ */

// ---- the knobs ----------------------------------------------------------------
const r = 5
const ang = 60

// ---- the model ----------------------------------------------------------------
def arc(r, ang) = rad(ang) * r   // L = r theta, theta in radians

// ---- results ------------------------------------------------------------------
print("arc length:", arc(r, ang))
print("ang / 360 form agrees:", abs(arc(r, ang) - ang / 360 * 2 * pi * r) < 1e-9)
print("semicircle of radius 5:", arc(5, 180))
/* ---- expected output ----
= arc length: 5.23598775598
= ang / 360 form agrees: true
= semicircle of radius 5: 15.7079632679
*/

scripts.name: chord-length
scripts.title: chord of a circle from radius and central angle
scripts.text:
/* ============================================================================
chord-length.epher -- chord of a circle from radius and central angle

A chord spans the central angle ang; the radius to either endpoint and
the chord form an isosceles triangle, so the chord is
L = 2 r sin(ang / 2) (standard formula; drop the perpendicular from the
center, which bisects the chord). Angles go in radians, so ang is
converted with rad() before halving. A 60 degree chord of radius 5 is
10 sin(30 deg) = 5, and 180 degrees spans the full diameter.

Web/desktop:             paste the whole file into the entry, press Enter

The knobs to edit are `r` (radius) and `ang` (central angle in degrees).
Everything above the results section is machinery you can leave alone.
============================================================================ */

// ---- the knobs ----------------------------------------------------------------
const r = 5
const ang = 60

// ---- the model ----------------------------------------------------------------
def chord(r, ang) = 2 * r * sin(rad(ang / 2))   // L = 2 r sin(ang/2), ang in degrees

// ---- results ------------------------------------------------------------------
print("chord of 60 degrees:", chord(r, ang))
print("chord of 90 degrees:", chord(5, 90))
print("180 degrees spans the diameter:", chord(5, 180))
print("diameter check:", abs(chord(5, 180) - 2 * r) < 1e-9)
/* ---- expected output ----
= chord of 60 degrees: 5
= chord of 90 degrees: 7.07106781187
= 180 degrees spans the diameter: 10
= diameter check: true
*/

scripts.name: circle-area
scripts.title: area from the radius
scripts.text:
/* ============================================================================
circle-area.epher -- area from the radius

The area of a circle of radius r is A = pi r^2 (standard formula;
Archimedes' "Measurement of a Circle", about 250 BC). For radius 5 the
area is 25 pi. The last result recovers the same area from the
circumference with A = C^2 / (4 pi), which is the same formula in
disguise, and checks the two computations agree.

Web/desktop:             paste the whole file into the entry, press Enter

The knob to edit is `r`, the radius. Everything above the results
section is machinery you can leave alone.
============================================================================ */

// ---- the knob -----------------------------------------------------------------
const r = 5

// ---- the model ----------------------------------------------------------------
def area(r) = pi * r ^ 2    // A = pi r^2
def circ(r) = 2 * pi * r    // for the cross-check below

// ---- results ------------------------------------------------------------------
print("area:", area(r))
print("radius 1 area is pi:", area(1))
print("A = C^2 / (4 pi) agrees:", abs(area(r) - circ(r) ^ 2 / (4 * pi)) < 1e-9)
/* ---- expected output ----
= area: 78.5398163397
= radius 1 area is pi: 3.14159265359
= A = C^2 / (4 pi) agrees: true
*/

scripts.name: circle-circumference
scripts.title: circumference from the radius
scripts.text:
/* ============================================================================
circle-circumference.epher -- circumference from the radius

The circumference of a circle of radius r is C = 2 pi r (standard
formula; the ratio of circumference to diameter is the constant pi).
For radius 5 the circumference is 10 pi, and for radius 1 it is tau,
the builtin constant for one full turn, 2 pi.

Web/desktop:             paste the whole file into the entry, press Enter

The knob to edit is `r`, the radius. Everything above the results
section is machinery you can leave alone.
============================================================================ */

// ---- the knob -----------------------------------------------------------------
const r = 5

// ---- the model ----------------------------------------------------------------
def circ(r) = 2 * pi * r   // C = 2 pi r

// ---- results ------------------------------------------------------------------
print("circumference:", circ(r))
print("radius 1 is one tau:", circ(1))
print("tau agrees:", abs(circ(1) - tau) < 1e-9)
/* ---- expected output ----
= circumference: 31.4159265359
= radius 1 is one tau: 6.28318530718
= tau agrees: true
*/

scripts.name: radius-from-area
scripts.title: radius of the circle with a given area
scripts.text:
/* ============================================================================
radius-from-area.epher -- radius of the circle with a given area

The area formula A = pi r^2 solved for the radius: r = sqrt(A / pi)
(standard formula). The knob is a symbolic area, pi * 25, so the first
result is exactly 5 and is hand-checkable; the second example takes a
plain area of 100. The round-trip check squares the radius again and
compares with the starting area.

Web/desktop:             paste the whole file into the entry, press Enter

The knob to edit is `area`. Everything above the results section is
machinery you can leave alone.
============================================================================ */

// ---- the knob -----------------------------------------------------------------
const area = pi * 25

// ---- the model ----------------------------------------------------------------
def radius(a) = sqrt(a / pi)   // r = sqrt(A / pi)

// ---- results ------------------------------------------------------------------
print("radius of the 25 pi circle:", radius(area))
print("radius of an area-100 circle:", radius(100))
print("round trip:", abs(pi * radius(100) ^ 2 - 100) < 1e-9)
/* ---- expected output ----
= radius of the 25 pi circle: 5
= radius of an area-100 circle: 5.64189583548
= round trip: true
*/

scripts.name: radius-from-circumference
scripts.title: radius from the circumference
scripts.text:
/* ============================================================================
radius-from-circumference.epher -- radius from the circumference

The circumference formula C = 2 pi r solved for the radius:
const r = C / (2 pi) (standard formula). The knob is a symbolic
circumference, pi * 10, so the first result is exactly 5; the second
example takes a plain circumference of 100. The round-trip check
multiplies the radius back up and compares with the starting value.

Web/desktop:             paste the whole file into the entry, press Enter

The knob to edit is `circ`. Everything above the results section is
machinery you can leave alone.
============================================================================ */

// ---- the knob -----------------------------------------------------------------
const circ = pi * 10

// ---- the model ----------------------------------------------------------------
def radius(c) = c / (2 * pi)   // r = C / (2 pi)

// ---- results ------------------------------------------------------------------
print("radius of the 10 pi circle:", radius(circ))
print("radius of a circumference-100 circle:", radius(100))
print("round trip:", abs(2 * pi * radius(100) - 100) < 1e-9)
/* ---- expected output ----
= radius of the 10 pi circle: 5
= radius of a circumference-100 circle: 15.9154943092
= round trip: true
*/

scripts.name: sector-area
scripts.title: area of a circular sector
scripts.text:
/* ============================================================================
sector-area.epher -- area of a circular sector

A sector of radius r and central angle ang (degrees) holds the fraction
ang / 360 of the disk, so its area is A = ang / 360 * pi r^2. Written with
the angle in radians, theta = rad(ang), this is the standard form
A = theta r^2 / 2 (two lines cancel: pi r^2 * theta / (2 pi)). The
results compute both forms and check they agree.

Web/desktop:             paste the whole file into the entry, press Enter

The knobs to edit are `r` (radius) and `ang` (central angle in degrees).
Everything above the results section is machinery you can leave alone.
============================================================================ */

// ---- the knobs ----------------------------------------------------------------
const r = 6
const ang = 60

// ---- the model ----------------------------------------------------------------
def sector(r, ang) = rad(ang) * r ^ 2 / 2   // A = theta r^2 / 2, theta in radians

// ---- results ------------------------------------------------------------------
print("sector area:", sector(r, ang))
print("ang / 360 form agrees:", abs(sector(r, ang) - ang / 360 * pi * r ^ 2) < 1e-9)
print("quarter circle, radius 4:", sector(4, 90))
/* ---- expected output ----
= sector area: 18.8495559215
= ang / 360 form agrees: true
= quarter circle, radius 4: 12.5663706144
*/

scripts.name: distance-between-points-2d
scripts.title: distance between two points
scripts.text:
/* ============================================================================
distance-between-points-2d.epher -- distance between two points

The distance between (x1, y1) and (x2, y2) is the hypotenuse of the
right triangle they span, d = sqrt((x2 - x1)^2 + (y2 - y1)^2)
(Pythagorean theorem; standard formula). Points are held as two-number
lists {x, y}. The builtin hypot(dx, dy) computes the same distance and
the last result cross-checks the formula against it.

Web/desktop:             paste the whole file into the entry, press Enter

The point pairs to try are in the results section below; edit them
there.
============================================================================ */

// ---- the model ----------------------------------------------------------------
def dist2d(p, q) = sqrt((p[1] - q[1]) ^ 2 + (p[2] - q[2]) ^ 2)

// ---- results ------------------------------------------------------------------
print("(0, 0) to (3, 4):", dist2d({0, 0}, {3, 4}))
print("(1, 1) to (4, 5):", dist2d({1, 1}, {4, 5}))
print("(0, 0) to (1, 1):", dist2d({0, 0}, {1, 1}))
print("hypot agrees:", dist2d({0, 0}, {3, 4}) == hypot(3, 4))
/* ---- expected output ----
= (0, 0) to (3, 4): 5
= (1, 1) to (4, 5): 5
= (0, 0) to (1, 1): 1.41421356237
= hypot agrees: true
*/

scripts.name: distance-between-points-3d
scripts.title: distance between two points in space
scripts.text:
/* ============================================================================
distance-between-points-3d.epher -- distance between two points in space

The distance between (x1, y1, z1) and (x2, y2, z2) extends Pythagoras
by one dimension: d = sqrt((x2 - x1)^2 + (y2 - y1)^2 + (z2 - z1)^2)
(standard formula; apply the 2-D distance to the face diagonal, then
one more right triangle with the height). Points are three-number
lists {x, y, z}. The examples land on exact integers, and the last
one, sqrt(61), is checked against the builtin directly.

Web/desktop:             paste the whole file into the entry, press Enter

The point pairs to try are in the results section below; edit them
there.
============================================================================ */

// ---- the model ----------------------------------------------------------------
def dist3d(p, q) = sqrt((p[1] - q[1]) ^ 2 + (p[2] - q[2]) ^ 2 + (p[3] - q[3]) ^ 2)

// ---- results ------------------------------------------------------------------
print("(0, 0, 0) to (1, 2, 2):", dist3d({0, 0, 0}, {1, 2, 2}))
print("(0, 0, 0) to (2, 3, 6):", dist3d({0, 0, 0}, {2, 3, 6}))
print("(1, 2, 3) to (4, 6, 9):", dist3d({1, 2, 3}, {4, 6, 9}))
print("sqrt(61) check:", abs(dist3d({1, 2, 3}, {4, 6, 9}) - sqrt(61)) < 1e-9)
/* ---- expected output ----
= (0, 0, 0) to (1, 2, 2): 3
= (0, 0, 0) to (2, 3, 6): 7
= (1, 2, 3) to (4, 6, 9): 7.81024967591
= sqrt(61) check: true
*/

scripts.name: line-equation-two-points
scripts.title: y = m x + b through two points
scripts.text:
/* ============================================================================
line-equation-two-points.epher -- y = m x + b through two points

The line through two points has slope m = (y2 - y1) / (x2 - x1) and
intercept b = y1 - m x1, so the equation is y = m x + b (standard
formula; b solves the line through (x1, y1)). Points are two-number
lists. The example line has slope 2/3, shown as an exact fraction,
and the checks plug both points back into the equation.

Web/desktop:             paste the whole file into the entry, press Enter

The knobs to edit are `P` and `Q`, the two points on the line.
Everything above the results section is machinery you can leave alone.
============================================================================ */

// ---- the knobs ----------------------------------------------------------------
const P = {0, 2}
const Q = {3, 4}

// ---- the model ----------------------------------------------------------------
def mof(p, q) = (q[2] - p[2]) / (q[1] - p[1])   // slope m
def bof(p, q) = p[2] - mof(p, q) * p[1]         // intercept b

// ---- results ------------------------------------------------------------------
print("slope:", mof(P, Q))
print("intercept:", bof(P, Q))
print("equation: y =", mof(P, Q), "x +", bof(P, Q))
print("P lies on the line:", mof(P, Q) * P[1] + bof(P, Q) == P[2])
print("Q lies on the line:", mof(P, Q) * Q[1] + bof(P, Q) == Q[2])
/* ---- expected output ----
= slope: 2/3
= intercept: 2
= equation: y = 2/3 x + 2
= P lies on the line: true
= Q lies on the line: true
*/

scripts.name: midpoint-of-segment
scripts.title: midpoint of a segment

scripts.name: point-to-line-distance
scripts.title: distance from a point to a line
scripts.text:
/* ============================================================================
point-to-line-distance.epher -- distance from a point to a line

The distance from (x0, y0) to the line a x + b y + c = 0 is
const d = |a x0 + b y0 + c| / sqrt(a^2 + b^2) (standard formula; drop the
perpendicular and solve, or project the point onto the normal). The
line 3 x + 4 y - 5 = 0 has normal length 5, so the origin is 1 unit
away and (1, 2) is 6/5 = 1.2, exact. A point on the line gives 0.

Web/desktop:             paste the whole file into the entry, press Enter

The knobs to edit are `a`, `b`, `c` (the line a x + b y + c = 0).
Everything above the results section is machinery you can leave alone.
============================================================================ */

// ---- the knobs ----------------------------------------------------------------
const a = 3
const b = 4
const c = -5

// ---- the model ----------------------------------------------------------------
def line_dist(a, b, c, p) = abs(a * p[1] + b * p[2] + c) / sqrt(a ^ 2 + b ^ 2)

// ---- results ------------------------------------------------------------------
print("origin to the line:", line_dist(a, b, c, {0, 0}))
print("(1, 2) to the line:", line_dist(a, b, c, {1, 2}))
print("(-1, 1) to the line:", line_dist(a, b, c, {-1, 1}))
print("a point on the line:", line_dist(a, b, c, {1, 0.5}))
/* ---- expected output ----
= origin to the line: 1
= (1, 2) to the line: 1.2
= (-1, 1) to the line: 0.8
= a point on the line: 0
*/

scripts.name: polygon-area-shoelace
scripts.title: area of a polygon, shoelace formula
scripts.text:
/* ============================================================================
polygon-area-shoelace.epher -- area of a polygon, shoelace formula

For vertices taken in order around a polygon, twice the area is the
absolute value of the alternating sum x_p y_q - y_p x_q over
consecutive pairs, with the last vertex paired back to the first
(the shoelace, or surveyor's, formula; Gauss, 1794; standard
formula). The helper pair(p, q) is one shoelace term, and the helper
sums the terms around the polygon. The pentagon example has area 9
and the rectangle cross-check, 12, matches width times height; the
signed sum before halving is also exact.

Web/desktop:             paste the whole file into the entry, press Enter

The vertices to try are in the results section below; edit them
there. List them in order around the polygon.
============================================================================ */

// ---- the model ----------------------------------------------------------------
// pair(p, q) is one shoelace term; the raw helpers sum the terms around
// the polygon and area5/area4 halve the absolute value.
def pair(p, q) = p[1] * q[2] - p[2] * q[1]
def raw5(a, b, c, d, e) = pair(a, b) + pair(b, c) + pair(c, d) + pair(d, e) + pair(e, a)
def raw4(a, b, c, d) = pair(a, b) + pair(b, c) + pair(c, d) + pair(d, a)
def area5(a, b, c, d, e) = abs(raw5(a, b, c, d, e)) / 2
def area4(a, b, c, d) = abs(raw4(a, b, c, d)) / 2

// ---- results ------------------------------------------------------------------
print("pentagon:", area5({0, 0}, {2, 0}, {3, 2}, {2, 4}, {0, 3}))
print("rectangle:", area4({0, 0}, {4, 0}, {4, 3}, {0, 3}))
print("rectangle by width times height:", 4 * 3)
print("signed sum, pentagon:", raw5({0, 0}, {2, 0}, {3, 2}, {2, 4}, {0, 3}))
/* ---- expected output ----
= pentagon: 9
= rectangle: 12
= rectangle by width times height: 12
= signed sum, pentagon: 18
*/

scripts.name: slope-of-line
scripts.title: slope of the line through two points
scripts.text:
/* ============================================================================
slope-of-line.epher -- slope of the line through two points

The slope is rise over run, m = (y2 - y1) / (x2 - x1) (standard
formula). A vertical line has x1 = x2, so its slope is undefined;
the helper returns a string for that case instead of dividing by
zero. A horizontal line has slope 0. Reversing the two points leaves
the slope unchanged: both numerator and denominator change sign.

Web/desktop:             paste the whole file into the entry, press Enter

The point pairs to try are in the results section below; edit them
there.
============================================================================ */

// ---- the model ----------------------------------------------------------------
def slope(p, q) = if p[1] == q[1] then "vertical, undefined" else (q[2] - p[2]) / (q[1] - p[1])

// ---- results ------------------------------------------------------------------
print("(1, 2) to (4, 8):", slope({1, 2}, {4, 8}))
print("(0, 0) to (2, 3):", slope({0, 0}, {2, 3}))
print("(1, 3) to (3, 3) is horizontal:", slope({1, 3}, {3, 3}))
print("(2, 1) to (2, 5) is vertical:", slope({2, 1}, {2, 5}))
print("reversed direction:", slope({4, 8}, {1, 2}))
/* ---- expected output ----
= (1, 2) to (4, 8): 2
= (0, 0) to (2, 3): 1.5
= (1, 3) to (3, 3) is horizontal: 0
= (2, 1) to (2, 5) is vertical: vertical, undefined
= reversed direction: 2
*/

scripts.name: diagonals-of-polygon
scripts.title: diagonals of a convex n-gon
scripts.text:
/* ============================================================================
diagonals-of-polygon.epher -- diagonals of a convex n-gon

Each of the n vertices connects to n - 3 others (everyone but itself
and its two neighbors), and each diagonal is counted twice that way,
so the number of diagonals is n (n - 3) / 2 (standard formula). The
results are exact: 5 * 2 / 2 = 5 for the pentagon and 6 * 3 / 2 = 9
for the hexagon.

Web/desktop:             paste the whole file into the entry, press Enter

The values of n to try are in the results section below; edit them
there.
============================================================================ */

// ---- the model ----------------------------------------------------------------
def diag(n) = n * (n - 3) / 2   // diagonals of a convex n-gon

// ---- results ------------------------------------------------------------------
print("quadrilateral:", diag(4))
print("pentagon:", diag(5))
print("hexagon:", diag(6))
print("octagon:", diag(8))
print("decagon:", diag(10))
print("pentagon and hexagon checks:", diag(5) == 5, diag(6) == 9)
/* ---- expected output ----
= quadrilateral: 2
= pentagon: 5
= hexagon: 9
= octagon: 20
= decagon: 35
= pentagon and hexagon checks: true true
*/

scripts.name: exterior-angle-regular
scripts.title: one exterior angle of a regular n-gon
scripts.text:
/* ============================================================================
exterior-angle-regular.epher -- one exterior angle of a regular n-gon

Turning one full corner of a regular n-gon sweeps 360 / n degrees, and
the exterior angles of any convex polygon sum to 360 degrees (standard
formula; walk once around the polygon and you turn a full circle). The
last result checks that six hexagon corners indeed sum to 360.

Web/desktop:             paste the whole file into the entry, press Enter

The values of n to try are in the results section below; edit them
there.
============================================================================ */

// ---- the model ----------------------------------------------------------------
def angext(n) = 360 / n   // degrees, one exterior angle of a regular n-gon

// ---- results ------------------------------------------------------------------
print("equilateral triangle:", angext(3))
print("square:", angext(4))
print("pentagon:", angext(5))
print("hexagon:", angext(6))
print("octagon:", angext(8))
print("six hexagon corners sum to 360:", 6 * angext(6) == 360)
/* ---- expected output ----
= equilateral triangle: 120
= square: 90
= pentagon: 72
= hexagon: 60
= octagon: 45
= six hexagon corners sum to 360: true
*/

scripts.name: interior-angle-regular
scripts.title: one interior angle of a regular n-gon
scripts.text:
/* ============================================================================
interior-angle-regular.epher -- one interior angle of a regular n-gon

A regular n-gon has equal interior angles, so each is the angle sum
(n - 2) * 180 divided by n (standard formula). The results are exact:
540 / 5 = 108 for the pentagon, 1080 / 8 = 135 for the octagon, and so
on, all hand-checkable. The 3-gon case, 60 degrees, is the equilateral
triangle.

Web/desktop:             paste the whole file into the entry, press Enter

The values of n to try are in the results section below; edit them
there.
============================================================================ */

// ---- the model ----------------------------------------------------------------
def angreg(n) = (n - 2) * 180 / n   // degrees, one angle of a regular n-gon

// ---- results ------------------------------------------------------------------
print("equilateral triangle:", angreg(3))
print("square:", angreg(4))
print("pentagon:", angreg(5))
print("hexagon:", angreg(6))
print("octagon:", angreg(8))
print("the pentagon angle is exact:", angreg(5) == 108)
/* ---- expected output ----
= equilateral triangle: 60
= square: 90
= pentagon: 108
= hexagon: 120
= octagon: 135
= the pentagon angle is exact: true
*/

scripts.name: interior-angle-sum
scripts.title: sum of the interior angles of an n-gon
scripts.text:
/* ============================================================================
interior-angle-sum.epher -- sum of the interior angles of an n-gon

Any n-gon triangulates into n - 2 triangles, so its interior angles
sum to (n - 2) * 180 degrees (Euclid's Elements, book I, proposition
32 applied by triangulation; standard formula). All results are exact
integers, easy to check by hand: a hexagon holds four triangles.

Web/desktop:             paste the whole file into the entry, press Enter

The values of n to try are in the results section below; edit them
there.
============================================================================ */

// ---- the model ----------------------------------------------------------------
def angsum(n) = (n - 2) * 180   // degrees; n - 2 triangles of 180 degrees

// ---- results ------------------------------------------------------------------
print("triangle:", angsum(3))
print("quadrilateral:", angsum(4))
print("pentagon:", angsum(5))
print("hexagon:", angsum(6))
print("octagon:", angsum(8))
print("a hexagon is four triangles:", angsum(6) == 4 * 180)
/* ---- expected output ----
= triangle: 180
= quadrilateral: 360
= pentagon: 540
= hexagon: 720
= octagon: 1080
= a hexagon is four triangles: true
*/

scripts.name: kite-area
scripts.title: area of a kite from its diagonals
scripts.text:
/* ============================================================================
kite-area.epher -- area of a kite from its diagonals

The diagonals of a kite (a quadrilateral with two pairs of adjacent
equal sides) are perpendicular, so the long diagonal splits the kite
into two triangles and the area is A = d1 d2 / 2, the same rule that
holds for the rhombus (standard formula). With diagonals 6 and 4 the
area is 12, exactly.

Web/desktop:             paste the whole file into the entry, press Enter

The knobs to edit are `d1` and `d2`, the two diagonals.
Everything above the results section is machinery you can leave alone.
============================================================================ */

// ---- the knobs ----------------------------------------------------------------
const d1 = 6
const d2 = 4

// ---- the model ----------------------------------------------------------------
def area(d1, d2) = d1 * d2 / 2   // A = d1 d2 / 2 for perpendicular diagonals

// ---- results ------------------------------------------------------------------
print("area:", area(d1, d2))
print("two triangles of area d1 d2 / 4 each:", 2 * (d1 / 2 * d2 / 2))
print("matches d1 d2 / 2:", area(d1, d2) == 6 * 4 / 2)
/* ---- expected output ----
= area: 12
= two triangles of area d1 d2 / 4 each: 12
= matches d1 d2 / 2: true
*/

scripts.name: parallelogram-area
scripts.title: area from a base and its height
scripts.text:
/* ============================================================================
parallelogram-area.epher -- area from a base and its height

A parallelogram of base b and height h (perpendicular distance between
the parallel sides) has area A = b h, because shearing along the base
preserves area and turns it into a rectangle (Euclid's Elements,
book I, proposition 35; standard formula). All results are exact.

Web/desktop:             paste the whole file into the entry, press Enter

The knobs to edit are `b` (the base) and `h` (the height to it).
Everything above the results section is machinery you can leave alone.
============================================================================ */

// ---- the knobs ----------------------------------------------------------------
const b = 9
const h = 5

// ---- the model ----------------------------------------------------------------
def area(b, h) = b * h   // A = b h

// ---- results ------------------------------------------------------------------
print("area:", area(b, h))
print("base 6, height 3.5:", area(6, 3.5))
print("rectangle with the same base and height:", area(b, h) == 9 * 5)
/* ---- expected output ----
= area: 45
= base 6, height 3.5: 21
= rectangle with the same base and height: true
*/

scripts.name: regular-polygon-area
scripts.title: area of a regular num-gon from its side
scripts.text:
/* ============================================================================
regular-polygon-area.epher -- area of a regular num-gon from its side

A regular num-gon of side s is num congruent isosceles triangles with apex
angle 2 pi / num at the center, each of area s^2 / (4 tan(pi / num)), so
A = num s^2 / (4 tan(pi / num)) (standard formula; tangent in radians).
The num = 6 case is six equilateral triangles: 6 * 2^2 * sqrt(3) / 4,
about 10.392. The square case recovers side times side, and the num = 3
case matches the equilateral formula s^2 sqrt(3) / 4.

Web/desktop:             paste the whole file into the entry, press Enter

The knobs to edit are `num` (number of sides) and `s` (side length).
Everything above the results section is machinery you can leave alone.
============================================================================ */

// ---- the knobs ----------------------------------------------------------------
const num = 6
const s = 2

// ---- the model ----------------------------------------------------------------
def area(num, s) = num * s ^ 2 / (4 * tan(pi / num))   // A = num s^2 / (4 tan(pi / num))

// ---- results ------------------------------------------------------------------
print("hexagon, side 2:", area(num, s))
print("square, side 4:", area(4, 4))
print("triangle, side 6:", area(3, 6))
print("the square is exactly 16:", abs(area(4, 4) - 16) < 1e-9)
// the side-6 triangle, 15.5884572681 above, matches the equilateral
// formula s^2 sqrt(3) / 4 used in equilateral-area-height.epher.
/* ---- expected output ----
= hexagon, side 2: 10.3923048454
= square, side 4: 16
= triangle, side 6: 15.5884572681
= the square is exactly 16: true
*/

scripts.name: rhombus-area
scripts.title: area from the diagonals
scripts.text:
/* ============================================================================
rhombus-area.epher -- area from the diagonals

The diagonals of a rhombus cross at right angles and bisect each other
(Euclid's Elements, book I, proposition 46 corollary; standard fact),
so they split it into four right triangles and the area is
A = d1 d2 / 2. The side is the hypotenuse of half-diagonals, so with
diagonals 4 and 3 the side is sqrt(2^2 + 1.5^2) = 2.5 and the perimeter
is 10, all exact.

Web/desktop:             paste the whole file into the entry, press Enter

The knobs to edit are `d1` and `d2`, the two diagonals.
Everything above the results section is machinery you can leave alone.
============================================================================ */

// ---- the knobs ----------------------------------------------------------------
const d1 = 4
const d2 = 3

// ---- the model ----------------------------------------------------------------
def area(d1, d2) = d1 * d2 / 2                        // A = d1 d2 / 2
def side(d1, d2) = sqrt((d1 / 2) ^ 2 + (d2 / 2) ^ 2)

// ---- results ------------------------------------------------------------------
print("area:", area(d1, d2))
print("side from the diagonals:", side(d1, d2))
print("perimeter:", 4 * side(d1, d2))
print("area is the 3-4 rectangle halved:", area(d1, d2) == 4 * 3 / 2)
/* ---- expected output ----
= area: 6
= side from the diagonals: 2.5
= perimeter: 10
= area is the 3-4 rectangle halved: true
*/

scripts.name: trapezoid-area
scripts.title: area of a trapezoid from its bases and height
scripts.text:
/* ============================================================================
trapezoid-area.epher -- area of a trapezoid from its bases and height

A trapezoid with parallel bases a and b and height h (the distance
between them) has area A = (a + b) h / 2, the average base times the
height (standard formula; two congruent trapezoids tile a parallelogram
of base a + b). The 5 and 7 by 4 example gives 6 * 4 = 24, exactly.

Web/desktop:             paste the whole file into the entry, press Enter

The knobs to edit are `a` and `b` (the parallel bases) and `h` (the
height). Everything above the results section is machinery you can
leave alone.
============================================================================ */

// ---- the knobs ----------------------------------------------------------------
const a = 5
const b = 7
const h = 4

// ---- the model ----------------------------------------------------------------
def area(a, b, h) = (a + b) / 2 * h   // A = (a + b) h / 2

// ---- results ------------------------------------------------------------------
print("area:", area(a, b, h))
print("bases 10 and 6, height 5:", area(10, 6, 5))
print("average base times height:", area(a, b, h) == (5 + 7) / 2 * 4)
/* ---- expected output ----
= area: 24
= bases 10 and 6, height 5: 40
= average base times height: true
*/

scripts.name: box-space-diagonal
scripts.title: space diagonal of a rectangular box
scripts.text:
/* ============================================================================
box-space-diagonal.epher -- space diagonal of a rectangular box

The space diagonal of a box of sides l, w, h is the hypotenuse of the
right triangle made of the height and the face diagonal, so
const d = sqrt(l^2 + w^2 + h^2), Pythagoras applied twice (standard
formula). The 3 by 4 by 12 box has diagonal sqrt(9 + 16 + 144) = 13,
exact, and the unit cube gives sqrt(3). The last result walks the
face-diagonal route and checks it agrees.

Web/desktop:             paste the whole file into the entry, press Enter

The boxes to try are in the results section below; edit them there.
============================================================================ */

// ---- the model ----------------------------------------------------------------
def diag(l, w, h) = sqrt(l ^ 2 + w ^ 2 + h ^ 2)   // d = sqrt(l^2 + w^2 + h^2)
def face(l, w) = sqrt(l ^ 2 + w ^ 2)   // the face diagonal, for the check
def diag2(l, w, h) = sqrt(face(l, w) ^ 2 + h ^ 2)   // Pythagoras twice

// ---- results ------------------------------------------------------------------
print("3 by 4 by 12 box:", diag(3, 4, 12))
print("2 by 3 by 6 box:", diag(2, 3, 6))
print("unit cube:", diag(1, 1, 1))
print("face-diagonal route:", abs(diag(3, 4, 12) - diag2(3, 4, 12)) < 1e-9)
/* ---- expected output ----
= 3 by 4 by 12 box: 13
= 2 by 3 by 6 box: 7
= unit cube: 1.73205080757
= face-diagonal route: true
*/

scripts.name: box-volume-surface
scripts.title: volume and surface area of a box
scripts.text:
/* ============================================================================
box-volume-surface.epher -- volume and surface area of a box

A rectangular box of sides l, w, h has volume V = l w h and surface
area S = 2 (l w + l h + w h), three pairs of congruent faces (standard
formula). The 6 by 4 by 3 box has volume 72 and surface 108, both
exact, and the last result checks the surface against its unfolded
net, the six faces laid flat.

Web/desktop:             paste the whole file into the entry, press Enter

The knobs to edit are `l`, `w`, `h`, the three edge lengths.
Everything above the results section is machinery you can leave alone.
============================================================================ */

// ---- the knobs ----------------------------------------------------------------
const l = 6
const w = 4
const h = 3

// ---- the model ----------------------------------------------------------------
def vol(l, w, h) = l * w * h                            // V = l w h
def surf(l, w, h) = 2 * (l * w + l * h + w * h)          // S = 2(lw + lh + wh)

// ---- results ------------------------------------------------------------------
print("volume:", vol(l, w, h))
print("surface area:", surf(l, w, h))
print("unfolded net:", surf(l, w, h) == 2 * (6 * 4 + 6 * 3 + 4 * 3))
/* ---- expected output ----
= volume: 72
= surface area: 108
= unfolded net: true
*/

scripts.name: cone-volume
scripts.title: volume of a cone from radius and height
scripts.text:
/* ============================================================================
cone-volume.epher -- volume of a cone from radius and height

A cone is one third of the cylinder on the same base and height,
V = pi r^2 h / 3 (Archimedes and Eudoxus, by the method of
exhaustion; standard formula). For radius 3 and height 5 the volume is
15 pi. The results check the one-third relation against the cylinder
volume and confirm a cone of radius 1 and height 3 holds exactly pi.

Web/desktop:             paste the whole file into the entry, press Enter

The knobs to edit are `r` (radius) and `h` (height).
Everything above the results section is machinery you can leave alone.
============================================================================ */

// ---- the knobs ----------------------------------------------------------------
const r = 3
const h = 5

// ---- the model ----------------------------------------------------------------
def vol(r, h) = pi * r ^ 2 * h / 3   // V = pi r^2 h / 3
def cyl(r, h) = pi * r ^ 2 * h       // the surrounding cylinder, for the check

// ---- results ------------------------------------------------------------------
print("volume:", vol(r, h))
print("third of the cylinder:", abs(vol(r, h) - cyl(r, h) / 3) < 1e-9)
print("cone of radius 1, height 3:", vol(1, 3))
/* ---- expected output ----
= volume: 47.1238898038
= third of the cylinder: true
= cone of radius 1, height 3: 3.14159265359
*/

scripts.name: cube-volume-surface
scripts.title: volume and surface area of a cube
scripts.text:
/* ============================================================================
cube-volume-surface.epher -- volume and surface area of a cube

A cube of edge a has volume V = a^3 and surface area S = 6 a^2 (six
square faces; standard formula). This script works in meters: lengths
carry the m unit, volumes print as m^3 and areas as m^2, and the
conversions to centimeters show the `in` operator at work. With edge
2 m the volume is 8 m^3 and the surface 24 m^2, exact.

Web/desktop:             paste the whole file into the entry, press Enter

The knob to edit is `a`, the edge length, unit included (try 3 cm).
Everything above the results section is machinery you can leave alone.
============================================================================ */

// ---- the knob -----------------------------------------------------------------
const a = 2 m

// ---- results ------------------------------------------------------------------
print("volume:", a ^ 3)
print("surface area:", 6 * a ^ 2)
print("edge in cm:", a in cm)
print("volume in cm^3:", (a ^ 3) in cm ^ 3)
print("1 m^3 in cm^3:", (1 m ^ 3) in cm ^ 3)
/* ---- expected output ----
= volume: 8 m^3
= surface area: 24 m^2
= edge in cm: 200 cm
= volume in cm^3: 8000000 cm^3
= 1 m^3 in cm^3: 1000000 cm^3
*/

scripts.name: cylinder-surface-area
scripts.title: surface area of a cylinder
scripts.text:
/* ============================================================================
cylinder-surface-area.epher -- surface area of a cylinder

A cylinder of radius r and height h has a curved side that unrolls
into a 2 pi r by h rectangle, plus two end disks, so
S = 2 pi r h + 2 pi r^2 (standard formula). The factorized form
2 pi r (r + h) is checked against it, and the lateral part alone is
printed too.

Web/desktop:             paste the whole file into the entry, press Enter

The knobs to edit are `r` (radius) and `h` (height).
Everything above the results section is machinery you can leave alone.
============================================================================ */

// ---- the knobs ----------------------------------------------------------------
const r = 3
const h = 5

// ---- the model ----------------------------------------------------------------
def surf(r, h) = 2 * pi * r * h + 2 * pi * r ^ 2   // S = 2 pi r h + 2 pi r^2

// ---- results ------------------------------------------------------------------
print("surface area:", surf(r, h))
print("lateral part, 2 pi r h:", 2 * pi * r * h)
print("factorized form agrees:", abs(surf(r, h) - 2 * pi * r * (r + h)) < 1e-9)
/* ---- expected output ----
= surface area: 150.796447372
= lateral part, 2 pi r h: 94.2477796077
= factorized form agrees: true
*/

scripts.name: cylinder-volume
scripts.title: volume of a cylinder from radius and height
scripts.text:
/* ============================================================================
cylinder-volume.epher -- volume of a cylinder from radius and height

A cylinder is a prism, so its volume is the base area times the
height, V = pi r^2 h (standard formula; a disk of area pi r^2 stacked
h times). For radius 3 and height 5 the volume is 45 pi. The unit
cylinder holds exactly pi.

Web/desktop:             paste the whole file into the entry, press Enter

The knobs to edit are `r` (radius) and `h` (height).
Everything above the results section is machinery you can leave alone.
============================================================================ */

// ---- the knobs ----------------------------------------------------------------
const r = 3
const h = 5

// ---- the model ----------------------------------------------------------------
def vol(r, h) = pi * r ^ 2 * h   // V = pi r^2 h

// ---- results ------------------------------------------------------------------
print("volume:", vol(r, h))
print("unit cylinder:", vol(1, 1))
print("doubling the height doubles the volume:", vol(3, 10) == 2 * vol(3, 5))
/* ---- expected output ----
= volume: 141.371669412
= unit cylinder: 3.14159265359
= doubling the height doubles the volume: true
*/

scripts.name: frustum-volume
scripts.title: volume of a conical frustum
scripts.text:
/* ============================================================================
frustum-volume.epher -- volume of a conical frustum

A conical frustum is a cone with its top cut off: with base radius R,
top radius r and height h, its volume is V = pi h (R^2 + R r + r^2) / 3
(standard formula; the average of the two disk areas and their
geometric mean times the height). For R = 4, r = 2, h = 6 the volume
is 56 pi. The checks: R = r reduces the frustum to a cylinder, and the
frustum equals the full cone of height 12 minus its tip (similar
cones, h R / (R - r) = 12).

Web/desktop:             paste the whole file into the entry, press Enter

The knobs to edit are `R` (base radius), `r` (top radius) and `h`
(height). Everything above the results section is machinery you can
leave alone.
============================================================================ */

// ---- the knobs ----------------------------------------------------------------
const R = 4
const r = 2
const h = 6

// ---- the model ----------------------------------------------------------------
def vol(R, r, h) = pi * h * (R ^ 2 + R * r + r ^ 2) / 3
// The frustum is the full cone of height h R / (R - r) = 12 minus the
// tip cone of height 6, which the last result checks.
def fullcone(R) = pi * R ^ 2 * 12 / 3

def tipcone(r) = pi * r ^ 2 * 6 / 3

// ---- results ------------------------------------------------------------------
print("frustum volume:", vol(R, r, h))
print("R = r is a cylinder:", abs(vol(2, 2, 6) - pi * 2 ^ 2 * 6) < 1e-9)
print("cone minus tip:", abs(vol(R, r, h) - (fullcone(R) - tipcone(r))) < 1e-9)
/* ---- expected output ----
= frustum volume: 175.929188601
= R = r is a cylinder: true
= cone minus tip: true
*/

scripts.name: sphere-surface-area
scripts.title: surface area of a sphere from its radius
scripts.text:
/* ============================================================================
sphere-surface-area.epher -- surface area of a sphere from its radius

The surface area of a sphere of radius r is S = 4 pi r^2 (Archimedes,
"On the Sphere and Cylinder", about 225 BC: the sphere's surface is
exactly the area of its circumscribed cylinder's curved side; standard
formula). For radius 3 it is 36 pi, the same number as the volume of
the radius-3 sphere: the volume is V = r S / 3, checked below.

Web/desktop:             paste the whole file into the entry, press Enter

The knob to edit is `r`, the radius. Everything above the results
section is machinery you can leave alone.
============================================================================ */

// ---- the knob -----------------------------------------------------------------
const r = 3

// ---- the model ----------------------------------------------------------------
def surf(r) = 4 * pi * r ^ 2   // S = 4 pi r^2
def vol(r) = 4 / 3 * pi * r ^ 3   // V = 4 pi r^3 / 3, for the cross-check

// ---- results ------------------------------------------------------------------
print("surface area:", surf(r))
print("unit sphere:", surf(1))
print("V = r S / 3 holds:", abs(vol(r) - r * surf(r) / 3) < 1e-9)
/* ---- expected output ----
= surface area: 113.097335529
= unit sphere: 12.5663706144
= V = r S / 3 holds: true
*/

scripts.name: sphere-volume
scripts.title: volume of a sphere from its radius
scripts.text:
/* ============================================================================
sphere-volume.epher -- volume of a sphere from its radius

The volume of a sphere of radius r is V = 4 pi r^3 / 3, which
Archimedes proved by comparing the sphere with the cylinder around it
("On the Sphere and Cylinder", about 225 BC; standard formula). For
radius 3 the volume is 36 pi, about 113.097. The last result checks
the relation V = r S / 3 with the surface area S = 4 pi r^2, the
sphere seen as a cone with base S and apex at the center.

Web/desktop:             paste the whole file into the entry, press Enter

The knob to edit is `r`, the radius. Everything above the results
section is machinery you can leave alone.
============================================================================ */

// ---- the knob -----------------------------------------------------------------
const r = 3

// ---- the model ----------------------------------------------------------------
def vol(r) = 4 / 3 * pi * r ^ 3   // V = 4 pi r^3 / 3
def surf(r) = 4 * pi * r ^ 2      // S = 4 pi r^2, for the cross-check

// ---- results ------------------------------------------------------------------
print("volume:", vol(r))
print("unit sphere:", vol(1))
print("V = r S / 3 holds:", abs(vol(r) - r * surf(r) / 3) < 1e-9)
/* ---- expected output ----
= volume: 113.097335529
= unit sphere: 4.18879020479
= V = r S / 3 holds: true
*/

scripts.name: square-pyramid-volume
scripts.title: volume of a square pyramid
scripts.text:
/* ============================================================================
square-pyramid-volume.epher -- volume of a square pyramid

A pyramid is one third of the prism on the same base and height,
V = b^2 h / 3 for a square base of side b (standard formula; the cube
splits into three congruent pyramids). The 6 by 6 base with height 10
gives V = 360 / 3 = 120, exact. The results check that the pyramid
with a 3 by 3 base and height 4 holds exactly 12.

Web/desktop:             paste the whole file into the entry, press Enter

The knobs to edit are `b` (base side) and `h` (height).
Everything above the results section is machinery you can leave alone.
============================================================================ */

// ---- the knobs ----------------------------------------------------------------
const b = 6
const h = 10

// ---- the model ----------------------------------------------------------------
def vol(b, h) = b ^ 2 * h / 3   // V = b^2 h / 3

// ---- results ------------------------------------------------------------------
print("volume:", vol(b, h))
print("base 3, height 4:", vol(3, 4))
print("third of the surrounding box:", vol(b, h) == 6 * 6 * 10 / 3)
/* ---- expected output ----
= volume: 120
= base 3, height 4: 12
= third of the surrounding box: true
*/

scripts.name: tetrahedron-volume
scripts.title: volume of a regular tetrahedron
scripts.text:
/* ============================================================================
tetrahedron-volume.epher -- volume of a regular tetrahedron

A regular tetrahedron of edge a has volume V = a^3 / (6 sqrt(2)), a
classic exercise (standard formula; place two vertices on an axis and
integrate, or slice the cube). The results give the textbook form
V = a^3 sqrt(2) / 12 as a cross-check and the a = 2 case, whose
volume is 8 / (6 sqrt(2)).

Web/desktop:             paste the whole file into the entry, press Enter

The knob to edit is `a`, the edge length. Everything above the results
section is machinery you can leave alone.
============================================================================ */

// ---- the knob -----------------------------------------------------------------
const a = 6

// ---- the model ----------------------------------------------------------------
def vol(a) = a ^ 3 / (6 * sqrt(2))   // V = a^3 / (6 sqrt(2))

// ---- results ------------------------------------------------------------------
print("volume:", vol(a))
print("other textbook form agrees:", abs(vol(a) - a ^ 3 * sqrt(2) / 12) < 1e-9)
print("edge 2:", vol(2))
/* ---- expected output ----
= volume: 25.4558441227
= other textbook form agrees: true
= edge 2: 0.942809041582
*/

scripts.name: equilateral-area-height
scripts.title: height and area from the side
scripts.text:
/* ============================================================================
equilateral-area-height.epher -- height and area from the side

An equilateral triangle of side s splits into two 30-60-90 triangles,
so the height is h = s sqrt(3) / 2 and the area is A = s^2 sqrt(3) / 4
(standard formula; Pythagoras applied to the half triangle). For s = 6
the height is 3 sqrt(3) and the area 9 sqrt(3). The last result checks
that the area also comes out of base times height.

Web/desktop:             paste the whole file into the entry, press Enter

The knob to edit is `s`, the side length. Everything above the results
section is machinery you can leave alone.
============================================================================ */

// ---- the knob -----------------------------------------------------------------
const s = 6

// ---- the model ----------------------------------------------------------------
def height(s) = s * sqrt(3) / 2    // h = s sqrt(3) / 2
def area(s) = s ^ 2 * sqrt(3) / 4  // A = s^2 sqrt(3) / 4

// ---- results ------------------------------------------------------------------
print("height:", height(s))
print("area:", area(s))
print("area from base times height:", abs(area(s) - s * height(s) / 2) < 1e-9)
/* ---- expected output ----
= height: 5.19615242271
= area: 15.5884572681
= area from base times height: true
*/

scripts.name: heron-area
scripts.title: triangle area from three sides (Heron's formula)
scripts.text:
/* ============================================================================
heron-area.epher -- triangle area from three sides (Heron's formula)

With the semiperimeter s = (a + b + c) / 2, the area of a triangle is
sqrt(s (s - a) (s - b) (s - c)), Heron's formula (Heron of Alexandria,
Metrica, about 60 AD; standard formula). The 13-14-15 triangle has
semiperimeter 21 and area sqrt(21 * 8 * 7 * 6) = sqrt(7056) = 84,
exactly, and the 3-4-5 triangle lands on 6, matching base times height.

Web/desktop:             paste the whole file into the entry, press Enter

The knobs to edit are `a`, `b`, `c`, the three side lengths.
Everything above the results section is machinery you can leave alone.
============================================================================ */

// ---- the knobs ----------------------------------------------------------------
const a = 13
const b = 14
const c = 15

// ---- the model ----------------------------------------------------------------
def semi(a, b, c) = (a + b + c) / 2                 // the semiperimeter
def heron(s, a, b, c) = sqrt(s * (s - a) * (s - b) * (s - c))

// ---- results ------------------------------------------------------------------
print("semiperimeter:", semi(a, b, c))
print("area of the 13-14-15 triangle:", heron(semi(a, b, c), a, b, c))
print("area of the 3-4-5 triangle:", heron(semi(3, 4, 5), 3, 4, 5))
print("3-4-5 by base times height:", 3 * 4 / 2)
print("Heron matches base-height:", heron(semi(3, 4, 5), 3, 4, 5) == 3 * 4 / 2)
/* ---- expected output ----
= semiperimeter: 21
= area of the 13-14-15 triangle: 84
= area of the 3-4-5 triangle: 6
= 3-4-5 by base times height: 6
= Heron matches base-height: true
*/

scripts.name: pythagorean-hypotenuse
scripts.title: hypotenuse c from the legs a and b
scripts.text:
/* ============================================================================
pythagorean-hypotenuse.epher -- hypotenuse c from the legs a and b

Computes the hypotenuse of a right triangle from its two legs with the
Pythagorean theorem, c = sqrt(a^2 + b^2) (Euclid's Elements, book I,
proposition 47). The builtin hypot(a, b) returns the same length in one
call, and the last result cross-checks the formula against it; the
formula is written out because the method is the point of the script.

Web/desktop:             paste the whole file into the entry, press Enter

The knobs to edit are `a` and `b`, the two legs. Everything above the
results section is machinery you can leave alone.
============================================================================ */

// ---- the knobs ----------------------------------------------------------------
const a = 3
const b = 4

// ---- the model ----------------------------------------------------------------
// c = sqrt(a^2 + b^2), the Pythagorean theorem.
def hyp(a, b) = sqrt(a ^ 2 + b ^ 2)

// ---- results ------------------------------------------------------------------
print("hypotenuse of the 3-4-5 triangle:", hyp(a, b))
print("hypotenuse of a 5-12-13 triangle:", hyp(5, 12))
print("the builtin hypot agrees:", hyp(a, b) == hypot(a, b))
/* ---- expected output ----
= hypotenuse of the 3-4-5 triangle: 5
= hypotenuse of a 5-12-13 triangle: 13
= the builtin hypot agrees: true
*/

scripts.name: pythagorean-leg
scripts.title: a leg a from the hypotenuse c and the other leg b
scripts.text:
/* ============================================================================
pythagorean-leg.epher -- a leg a from the hypotenuse c and the other leg b

The Pythagorean theorem solved for a leg of a right triangle:
const a = sqrt(c^2 - b^2) (Euclid's Elements, book I, proposition 47). The
5-12-13 example lands exactly on 12: 13^2 - 5^2 = 169 - 25 = 144, a
perfect square, so the results are exact.

Web/desktop:             paste the whole file into the entry, press Enter

The knobs to edit are `c` (the hypotenuse) and `b` (the known leg).
Everything above the results section is machinery you can leave alone.
============================================================================ */

// ---- the knobs ----------------------------------------------------------------
const c = 13
const b = 5

// ---- the model ----------------------------------------------------------------
// a = sqrt(c^2 - b^2), the Pythagorean theorem solved for a leg.
def leg(c, b) = sqrt(c ^ 2 - b ^ 2)

// ---- results ------------------------------------------------------------------
print("leg of the 5-12-13 triangle:", leg(c, b))
print("3-4-5 check: the missing leg is", leg(5, 4))
print("7-24-25 check: the missing leg is", leg(25, 7))
print("exact integer result:", leg(c, b) == 12)
/* ---- expected output ----
= leg of the 5-12-13 triangle: 12
= 3-4-5 check: the missing leg is 3
= 7-24-25 check: the missing leg is 24
= exact integer result: true
*/

scripts.name: right-triangle-angles
scripts.title: the acute angles of a right triangle
scripts.text:
/* ============================================================================
right-triangle-angles.epher -- the acute angles of a right triangle

From the side lengths, the angle opposite a side is
atan(opposite / adjacent), the SOH-CAH-TOA tangent rule (standard
formula). epher's trig functions take radians, and deg() converts each
angle to degrees for the results. The two acute angles of a right
triangle must sum to 90 degrees, and the results verify that.

Web/desktop:             paste the whole file into the entry, press Enter

The knobs to edit are `a` and `b`, the two legs. Everything above the
results section is machinery you can leave alone.
============================================================================ */

// ---- the knobs ----------------------------------------------------------------
const a = 3
const b = 4

// ---- the model ----------------------------------------------------------------
def cside(a, b) = sqrt(a ^ 2 + b ^ 2)   // the hypotenuse (Pythagoras)
def angle_a(a, b) = deg(atan(a / b))    // degrees; opposite the leg a
def angle_b(a, b) = deg(atan(b / a))    // degrees; opposite the leg b

// ---- results ------------------------------------------------------------------
print("angle opposite the side of length", a, ":", angle_a(a, b), "degrees")
print("angle opposite the side of length", b, ":", angle_b(a, b), "degrees")
print("sum is 90:", abs(angle_a(a, b) + angle_b(a, b) - 90) < 1e-9)
print("asin cross-check:", abs(deg(asin(a / cside(a, b))) - angle_a(a, b)) < 1e-9)
/* ---- expected output ----
= angle opposite the side of length 3 : 36.8698976458 degrees
= angle opposite the side of length 4 : 53.1301023542 degrees
= sum is 90: true
= asin cross-check: true
*/

scripts.name: special-triangle-ratios
scripts.title: 30-60-90 and 45-45-90 side ratios
scripts.text:
/* ============================================================================
special-triangle-ratios.epher -- 30-60-90 and 45-45-90 side ratios

The 30-60-90 triangle has sides in the ratio 1 : sqrt(3) : 2 (short
leg, long leg, hypotenuse) and the 45-45-90 triangle in the ratio
1 : 1 : sqrt(2), both from Pythagoras on the half equilateral triangle
and the half square (standard formula). The results scale the ratios,
then verify them against the builtin sin: the opposite side over the
hypotenuse must equal sin of the opposite angle. Angles are written
with the deg unit, which epher converts to radians for trig.

Web/desktop:             paste the whole file into the entry, press Enter

The scales to try are in the results section (5 and 4 below).
============================================================================ */

// ---- the model ----------------------------------------------------------------
def long30(s) = s * sqrt(3)   // long leg of a 30-60-90, short leg s
def hyp30(s) = 2 * s          // hypotenuse of a 30-60-90, short leg s
def hyp45(s) = s * sqrt(2)    // hypotenuse of a 45-45-90, legs s

// ---- results ------------------------------------------------------------------
print("30-60-90, short leg 5:", 5, long30(5), hyp30(5))
print("45-45-90, legs 4:", 4, 4, hyp45(4))
print("short over hyp = sin(30 deg):", 5 / hyp30(5))
print("long over hyp = sin(60 deg):", long30(5) / hyp30(5))
print("leg over hyp = sin(45 deg):", 4 / hyp45(4))
print("sin(30 deg) matches:", abs(5 / hyp30(5) - sin(30 deg)) < 1e-9)
print("sin(60 deg) matches:", abs(long30(5) / hyp30(5) - sin(60 deg)) < 1e-9)
print("sin(45 deg) matches:", abs(4 / hyp45(4) - sin(45 deg)) < 1e-9)
/* ---- expected output ----
= 30-60-90, short leg 5: 5 8.66025403784 10
= 45-45-90, legs 4: 4 4 5.65685424949
= short over hyp = sin(30 deg): 0.5
= long over hyp = sin(60 deg): 0.866025403784
= leg over hyp = sin(45 deg): 0.707106781187
= sin(30 deg) matches: true
= sin(60 deg) matches: true
= sin(45 deg) matches: true
*/

scripts.name: triangle-angle-sum-check
scripts.title: two angles give the third
scripts.text:
/* ============================================================================
triangle-angle-sum-check.epher -- two angles give the third

The three angles of a triangle sum to 180 degrees (Euclid's Elements,
book I, proposition 32), so two known angles determine the third:
C = 180 - A - B. Angles add linearly, so the whole script works in
degrees as plain numbers, no radian conversion needed. The known
30-60-90 and isosceles cases confirm the rule.

Web/desktop:             paste the whole file into the entry, press Enter

The knobs to edit are `a` and `b`, two angles in degrees.
Everything above the results section is machinery you can leave alone.
============================================================================ */

// ---- the knobs ----------------------------------------------------------------
const a = 35
const b = 65

// ---- the model ----------------------------------------------------------------
// C = 180 - A - B, degrees, from the angle sum of a triangle.
def third(x, y) = 180 - x - y

// ---- results ------------------------------------------------------------------
print("third angle:", third(a, b), "degrees")
print("the three sum to 180:", a + b + third(a, b) == 180)
print("30-60-90 triangle:", third(30, 60), "degrees")
print("70-70 isosceles:", third(70, 70), "degrees")
print("a right triangle needs", third(90, 47), "degrees more")
/* ---- expected output ----
= third angle: 80 degrees
= the three sum to 180: true
= 30-60-90 triangle: 90 degrees
= 70-70 isosceles: 40 degrees
= a right triangle needs 43 degrees more
*/

scripts.name: triangle-area-base-height
scripts.title: area from a base and its height
scripts.text:
/* ============================================================================
triangle-area-base-height.epher -- area from a base and its height

The area of a triangle is half the product of any side (the base) and
the perpendicular distance to the opposite vertex (the height),
A = b h / 2 (Euclid's Elements, book I, proposition 41; standard
formula). The 10 by 6 example gives 30, exactly.

Web/desktop:             paste the whole file into the entry, press Enter

The knobs to edit are `b` (the base) and `h` (the height to that
base). Everything above the results section is machinery you can leave
alone.
============================================================================ */

// ---- the knobs ----------------------------------------------------------------
const b = 10
const h = 6

// ---- the model ----------------------------------------------------------------
// A = b h / 2, half the base times the height.
def area(b, h) = b * h / 2

// ---- results ------------------------------------------------------------------
print("area of the 10 by 6 triangle:", area(b, h))
print("area of a 7 by 4 triangle:", area(7, 4))
print("half of the rectangle:", area(b, h) == 10 * 6 / 2)
/* ---- expected output ----
= area of the 10 by 6 triangle: 30
= area of a 7 by 4 triangle: 14
= half of the rectangle: true
*/

scripts.name: triangle-inequality
scripts.title: do three lengths make a triangle?
scripts.text:
/* ============================================================================
triangle-inequality.epher -- do three lengths make a triangle?

Three lengths a, b, c bound a triangle exactly when every side is
shorter than the sum of the other two: a + b > c and a + c > b and
b + c > a (Euclid's Elements, book I, proposition 20; standard
formula). The comparison is strict: a + b = c means the three points
are collinear, a degenerate triangle, so those triples report false.

Web/desktop:             paste the whole file into the entry, press Enter

The triples to test are in the results section below; edit them there.
============================================================================ */

// ---- the model ----------------------------------------------------------------
// Strict triangle inequality on all three pairs of sides.
def valid(a, b, c) = a + b > c and a + c > b and b + c > a

// ---- results ------------------------------------------------------------------
print("2, 3, 4:", valid(2, 3, 4))
print("5, 12, 13:", valid(5, 12, 13))
print("1, 1, 1:", valid(1, 1, 1))
print("1, 2, 3 (collinear):", valid(1, 2, 3))
print("1, 1, 2 (collinear):", valid(1, 1, 2))
print("3, 4, 8 (too long):", valid(3, 4, 8))
/* ---- expected output ----
= 2, 3, 4: true
= 5, 12, 13: true
= 1, 1, 1: true
= 1, 2, 3 (collinear): false
= 1, 1, 2 (collinear): false
= 3, 4, 8 (too long): false
*/

scripts.name: boxplot-two-classes
scripts.title: two class tests, side by side in boxes
scripts.text:
/* ============================================================================
boxplot-two-classes.epher -- two class tests, side by side in boxes

The box-and-whisker plot (Tukey, 1977) shows a distribution in five
numbers - min, Q1, median, Q3, max - and makes two classes comparable
at a glance: same median, different spread, one stray top score. The
class scores below are small enough to check by hand; the quartiles
are TI-style, the median of each half (quartile(d, k), e.g. Moore
and McCabe, "Introduction to the Practice of Statistics", ch. 1).
The script graphs one boxplot and prints both classes' five numbers.

Web/desktop:             paste the whole file into the entry, press Enter
The graph lines open the plot pane in the desktop, web and TUI apps;
the CLI transcript records them as "graph:" lines.
============================================================================ */

// ---- the data ------------------------------------------------------------------
const classA = {62, 67, 71, 74, 76, 79, 81, 84, 87, 91}
const classB = {55, 58, 64, 70, 73, 75, 78, 82, 88, 96}

// ---- results -------------------------------------------------------------------
print("class A median and quartiles:", median(classA), quartile(classA, 1), quartile(classA, 3))
print("class B median and quartiles:", median(classB), quartile(classB, 1), quartile(classB, 3))
print("means, A", mean(classA), "vs B", mean(classB))
print("spread, A", range(classA), "vs B", range(classB))

// ---- the picture ---------------------------------------------------------------
graph boxplot(classA)

/* ---- expected output ----
= class A median and quartiles: 77.5 71 84
= class B median and quartiles: 74 64 82
= means, A 77.2 vs B 73.9
= spread, A 29 vs B 41
graph: boxplot(classA)
*/

scripts.name: expreg-culture-growth
scripts.title: exponential growth from a culture count
scripts.text:
/* ============================================================================
expreg-culture-growth.epher -- exponential growth from a culture count

A bacterial culture multiplies by the same factor each hour, so its
counts N = 100*e^(0.35*t) lie on an exponential; the fit is done on
log counts, which is what expreg reports (the standard growth model,
e.g. Murray, "Mathematical Biology", ch. 1; the TI-style expreg
matches any calculator). Eight hourly counts with small frozen noise
(sigma 0.35, randseed(14)) are fitted; the doubling time follows as
ln(2)/0.35 hours. The script graphs the points with the fitted
exponential and prints the doubling time twice over.

Web/desktop:             paste the whole file into the entry, press Enter
The graph lines open the plot pane in the desktop, web and TUI apps;
the CLI transcript records them as "graph:" lines.
============================================================================ */

// ---- the model -----------------------------------------------------------------
const r = 0.35    // growth rate per hour

// ---- the data ------------------------------------------------------------------
const ts = {1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8}
const noise = {0.417428189714, -0.542802197271, -0.0783123440943, 0.387685831055, -0.0789349992734, 0.0327153409827, -0.673316592615, 0.175714392028}
const ns = 100 * e^(r * ts) + noise

// ---- results -------------------------------------------------------------------
print("doubling time, ln(2)/r:", ln(2) / r)
print("counts at hour 1 and 8:", ns[1], ns[8])
print("the fitted exponential and its r:", expreg(ts, ns))

// ---- the picture ---------------------------------------------------------------
graph scatter(ts, ns, expreg)

/* ---- expected output ----
= doubling time, ln(2)/r: 1.98042051589
= counts at hour 1 and 8: 142.324183049 1644.6403915
= the fitted exponential and its r: y = 100.0546*e^(0.3499*x) (r = 1)
graph: scatter(ts, ns, expreg)
*/

scripts.name: histogram-two-dice
scripts.title: sixty throws of a pair of dice
scripts.text:
/* ============================================================================
histogram-two-dice.epher -- sixty throws of a pair of dice

Two dice summed give 2 to 12, with 7 the likeliest: six of the
thirty-six combinations. The sixty sums here were drawn once with
randseed(3) from the real randint generator and frozen, so the
transcript is stable; the empirical mean should sit near 7 and the
standard deviation near sqrt(35/6) = 2.415 (the variance of one die
is 35/12, and variances add - any probability text, e.g. Blitzstein
and Hwang, "Introduction to Probability", ch. 2). The script graphs
the histogram and prints the comparison.

Web/desktop:             paste the whole file into the entry, press Enter
The graph lines open the plot pane in the desktop, web and TUI apps;
the CLI transcript records them as "graph:" lines.
============================================================================ */

// ---- the data (60 real throws, frozen) -----------------------------------------
const sums = {6, 5, 6, 7, 9, 10, 6, 10, 3, 6, 11, 7, 10, 3, 10, 10, 8, 5, 8, 6, 5, 11, 6, 7, 5, 10, 8, 6, 6, 7, 5, 9, 7, 10, 8, 3, 7, 3, 6, 8, 7, 4, 11, 7, 5, 12, 8, 7, 9, 9, 5, 8, 5, 8, 8, 6, 6, 6, 4, 8}

// ---- results -------------------------------------------------------------------
print("throws:", len(sums))
print("mean, theory 7:", mean(sums))
print("stdev, theory sqrt(35/6) =", sqrt(35 / 6), ":", stdev(sums))
print("lowest and highest seen:", min(sums), max(sums))

// ---- the picture ---------------------------------------------------------------
graph histogram(sums, 11)

/* ---- expected output ----
= throws: 60
= mean, theory 7: 7.1
= stdev, theory sqrt(35/6) = 2.4152294577 : 2.18860686282
= lowest and highest seen: 3 12
graph: histogram(sums, 11)
*/

scripts.name: quadreg-projectile
scripts.title: fitting the parabola of a thrown ball
scripts.text:
/* ============================================================================
quadreg-projectile.epher -- fitting the parabola of a thrown ball

A ball thrown at 20 m/s from 1.8 m height rides y = 1.8 + x*(20*cos(40 deg))/... in
the usual no-drag model y = h + t*v*sin(th) - g*t^2/2. Nine samples of
its height, taken at 0.25 s steps and jittered once with
randseed(12) (sigma 0.3, frozen), are fitted with a quadratic. The
fit recovers the flight numbers within the noise (least squares
again; TI-style quadreg, Stewart, "Precalculus", ch. 2.7 on
modelling with quadratic functions). The script graphs the points
with the fitted parabola and prints the vertex the model implies.

Web/desktop:             paste the whole file into the entry, press Enter
The graph lines open the plot pane in the desktop, web and TUI apps;
the CLI transcript records them as "graph:" lines.
============================================================================ */

// ---- the model -----------------------------------------------------------------
const v0 = 20       // launch speed, m/s
const th = 40       // launch angle, degrees
const h = 1.8       // release height, m
def ty(t) = h + t * v0 * sin(rad(th)) - 4.905 * t ^ 2

// ---- the data ------------------------------------------------------------------
const ts = {0, 0.25, 0.5, 0.75, 1, 1.25, 1.5, 1.75, 2}
const noise = {0.291164844291, 0.422145022342, -0.0464449403208, 0.00196629019192, 0.289739771157, -0.0488004201598, 0.264718486232, 0.120942636075, -0.0972088430788}
const ys = ty(ts) + noise

// ---- results -------------------------------------------------------------------
print("true flight time to the ground:")
solve h + t * v0 * sin(rad(40)) - 4.905 * t ^ 2 == 0
print("true vertex time, v*sin(th)/g:", v0 * sin(rad(th)) / 9.81)
print("the fitted quadratic and its r:", quadreg(ts, ys))

// ---- the picture ---------------------------------------------------------------
graph scatter(ts, ys, quadreg)

/* ---- expected output ----
= true flight time to the ground:
= x = -0.13324152617505275, x = 2.7541899856512577
= true vertex time, v*sin(th)/g: 1.31047422974
= the fitted quadratic and its r: y = -4.8619*x^2 + 12.6439*x + 2.084 (r = 0.9981)
graph: scatter(ts, ys, quadreg)
*/

scripts.name: scatter-noisy-line
scripts.title: a straight line hiding in noisy data

scripts.name: catenary-vs-parabola
scripts.title: the hanging chain is not a parabola
scripts.text:
/* ============================================================================
catenary-vs-parabola.epher -- the hanging chain is not a parabola

A uniform chain hangs in a catenary, y = cosh(x) - 1 after scaling;
a parabola y = x^2/2 matches it in height and slope at the vertex.
Galileo guessed the parabola; Jacques Bernoulli derived the catenary
in 1691 (see Lockwood, "A Book of Curves", ch. 6). The two agree to
within a few percent out to x = 1 and then part company: the catenary
grows like e^x/2, the parabola like x^2/2. The script graphs both
together and prints the comparison numbers.

Web/desktop:             paste the whole file into the entry, press Enter
The graph lines open the plot pane in the desktop, web and TUI apps;
the CLI transcript records them as "graph:" lines.
============================================================================ */

// ---- the two curves ------------------------------------------------------------
def cat(x) = cosh(x) - 1
def par(x) = x ^ 2 / 2

// ---- results -------------------------------------------------------------------
print("height at x = 1: catenary", cat(1), "parabola", par(1))
print("height at x = 2: catenary", cat(2), "parabola", par(2))
print("height at x = 3: catenary", cat(3), "parabola", par(3))
print("slope at x = 1: catenary", sinh(1), "parabola", 1)
print("both slope 0 at the vertex:", sinh(0) == 0)

// ---- the picture ---------------------------------------------------------------
graph cosh(x) - 1 from -2 to 2
graph x ^ 2 / 2 from -2 to 2

/* ---- expected output ----
= height at x = 1: catenary 0.543080634815 parabola 0.5
= height at x = 2: catenary 2.76219569108 parabola 2
= height at x = 3: catenary 9.06766199578 parabola 4.5
= slope at x = 1: catenary 1.17520119364 parabola 1
= both slope 0 at the vertex: true
graph: cosh(x) - 1 from -2 to 2
graph: x ^ 2 / 2 from -2 to 2
*/

scripts.name: damped-oscillation
scripts.title: a decaying sine and its exponential envelope
scripts.text:
/* ============================================================================
damped-oscillation.epher -- a decaying sine and its exponential envelope

A damped oscillation y = e^(-x/3) * sin(2*x) swings between the two
exponential envelopes +-e^(-x/3), touching them where the sine peaks.
The zeros sit at x = n*pi/2, one every quarter period, and the ratio
of successive peaks is e^(-period/3), the logarithmic decrement of the
damping (standard second-order dynamics, e.g. Rayleigh, "The Theory
of Sound", ch. 4a). The script graphs the curve with its envelopes
and prints the landmarks.

Web/desktop:             paste the whole file into the entry, press Enter
The graph lines open the plot pane in the desktop, web and TUI apps;
the CLI transcript records them as "graph:" lines.
============================================================================ */

// ---- the model -----------------------------------------------------------------
def f(x) = e^(0 - x / 3) * sin(2 * x)
def env(x) = e^(0 - x / 3)

// ---- results -------------------------------------------------------------------
print("envelope touch at pi/4:", f(pi / 4))
print("envelope there:", env(pi / 4))
print("envelope touch at 5*pi/4:", f(5 * pi / 4))
print("peak ratio per period, e^(-pi*2/3):", env(5 * pi / 4) / env(pi / 4))
print("first zero at pi/2:", f(pi / 2))

// ---- the picture ---------------------------------------------------------------
graph e^(0 - x / 3) * sin(2 * x) from 0 to 12
graph e^(0 - x / 3) from 0 to 12
graph 0 - e^(0 - x / 3) from 0 to 12

/* ---- expected output ----
= envelope touch at pi/4: 0.769665412493
= envelope there: 0.769665412493
= envelope touch at 5*pi/4: 0.270090838144
= peak ratio per period, e^(-pi*2/3): 0.350919807178
= first zero at pi/2: 0.0000000000000000725462206973
graph: e^(0 - x / 3) * sin(2 * x) from 0 to 12
graph: e^(0 - x / 3) from 0 to 12
graph: 0 - e^(0 - x / 3) from 0 to 12
*/
