scripts.name: exp-vs-logistic
scripts.title: unbounded growth against a saturating curve
scripts.text:
/* ============================================================================
exp-vs-logistic.epher -- unbounded growth against a saturating curve

Unrestricted growth e^t and the logistic curve L(t) = 1 / (1 + e^(-t))
agree in spirit at the start and disagree in fate: the exponential
runs away, the logistic saturates at its carrying capacity 1. The
logistic inflects at L = 1/2, where its slope peaks at k/4 for growth
rate k (the standard model of population growth with a cap, e.g.
Murray, "Mathematical Biology", ch. 1). The script graphs the curve
with its slope, and prints the landmark values.

Web/desktop:             paste the whole file into the entry, press Enter
The graph lines open the plot pane in the desktop, web and TUI apps;
the CLI transcript records them as "graph:" lines.
============================================================================ */

// ---- the model -----------------------------------------------------------------
const k = 1          // growth rate
def L(x) = 1 / (1 + e^(0 - k * x))   // the logistic curve

// ---- results -------------------------------------------------------------------
print("L(0), the inflection height:", L(0))
print("slope at the inflection, k/4:", derivative(L(x), 0))
print("early value L(-4):", L(-4))
print("late value L(4):", L(4))
print("saturation check L(20):", L(20))

// ---- the picture ---------------------------------------------------------------
graph 1 / (1 + e^(0 - x)) from -6 to 6
graph derivative(1 / (1 + e^(0 - x)), x) from -6 to 6

/* ---- expected output ----
= L(0), the inflection height: 0.5
= slope at the inflection, k/4: 0.25
= early value L(-4): 0.0179862099621
= late value L(4): 0.982013790038
= saturation check L(20): 0.999999997939
graph: 1 / (1 + e^(0 - x)) from -6 to 6
graph: derivative(1 / (1 + e^(0 - x)), x) from -6 to 6
*/

scripts.name: gaussian-bell-areas
scripts.title: the normal bell and the 68-95-99.7 rule
scripts.text:
/* ============================================================================
gaussian-bell-areas.epher -- the normal bell and the 68-95-99.7 rule

The standard bell y = e^(-x^2/2) / sqrt(2*pi) carries total area 1.
The classroom 68-95-99.7 rule says the area within 1, 2 and 3 standard
deviations of the mean is about 68, 95 and 99.7 percent (any
statistics text, e.g. Moore and McCabe; the exact values come from
the error function). The script graphs the bell and computes the
areas by numeric integration, so the rule can be checked, not just
quoted.

Web/desktop:             paste the whole file into the entry, press Enter
The graph lines open the plot pane in the desktop, web and TUI apps;
the CLI transcript records them as "graph:" lines.
============================================================================ */

// ---- the curve -----------------------------------------------------------------
def bell(x) = e^(0 - x ^ 2 / 2) / sqrt(2 * pi)

// ---- results -------------------------------------------------------------------
print("total area -6 to 6:", integral(bell(x), -6, 6))
print("within one sigma:", integral(bell(x), -1, 1))
print("within two sigma:", integral(bell(x), -2, 2))
print("within three sigma:", integral(bell(x), -3, 3))
print("peak height bell(0):", bell(0))

// ---- the picture ---------------------------------------------------------------
graph e^(0 - x ^ 2 / 2) / sqrt(2 * pi) from -3.5 to 3.5

/* ---- expected output ----
= total area -6 to 6: 0.99999999803
= within one sigma: 0.682689492137
= within two sigma: 0.954499736104
= within three sigma: 0.997300203925
= peak height bell(0): 0.398942280401
graph: e^(0 - x ^ 2 / 2) / sqrt(2 * pi) from -3.5 to 3.5
*/

scripts.name: newton-iteration-path
scripts.title: Newton-Raphson iterates walking to a root
scripts.text:
/* ============================================================================
newton-iteration-path.epher -- Newton-Raphson iterates walking to a root

To solve cos(x) = x, Newton-Raphson iterates
const x1 = x0 - f(x0)/f'(x0) on f(x) = cos(x) - x. Starting at x0 = 1 the
walk lands on the Dottie number 0.7390851332 in a handful of steps,
and the error roughly squares at each step once close (Newton 1669,
Raphson 1690; the quadratic convergence is standard numerical
analysis, e.g. Burden and Faires, ch. 2.3). The script graphs both
sides of the equation, runs six iterations, and checks the answer
against the builtin solver.

Web/desktop:             paste the whole file into the entry, press Enter
The graph lines open the plot pane in the desktop, web and TUI apps;
the CLI transcript records them as "graph:" lines.
============================================================================ */

// ---- the model -----------------------------------------------------------------
def f(x) = cos(x) - x
def step(x) = x - f(x) / derivative(f(x), x)

// ---- the walk ------------------------------------------------------------------
v = {1, 1}                       // {x, step counter}
while abs(f(v[1])) > 1e-12 do v = {step(v[1]), v[2] + 1}
print("newton lands on:", v[1])
print("steps taken:", v[2])
print("error at the last step:", abs(f(v[1])))

// ---- the picture ---------------------------------------------------------------
graph cos(x) from 0 to 2
graph x from 0 to 2

/* ---- expected output ----
= {1, 1}
= newton lands on: 0.739085133215
= steps taken: 5
= error at the last step: 0
graph: cos(x) from 0 to 2
graph: x from 0 to 2
*/

scripts.name: polynomial-cubic-shape
scripts.title: a cubic's shape from its critical points
scripts.text:
/* ============================================================================
polynomial-cubic-shape.epher -- a cubic's shape from its critical points

The cubic f(x) = x^3 - 3*x has two critical points where the slope
vanishes: f'(x) = 3*x^2 - 3 = 0 at x = -1 (local maximum) and x = 1
(local minimum). Between them the curve bends down, outside it bends
up, and the three real roots x = -sqrt(3), 0 and sqrt(3) sit one in
each monotone run (standard cubic analysis of any calculus text, e.g.
Stewart, "Calculus", ch. 3.1 and 4.1). The script graphs the curve and
its derivative, and prints the shape numbers a sketch needs.

Web/desktop:             paste the whole file into the entry, press Enter
The graph lines open the plot pane in the desktop, web and TUI apps;
the CLI transcript records them as "graph:" lines.
============================================================================ */

// ---- the curve -----------------------------------------------------------------
def f(x) = x ^ 3 - 3 * x
def fp(x) = 3 * x ^ 2 - 3   // the slope

// ---- results -------------------------------------------------------------------
print("critical points where f'(x) = 0:")
solve 3 * x ^ 2 - 3 == 0
print("roots of f:")
solve x ^ 3 - 3 * x == 0
print("local max f(-1):", f(-1))
print("local min f(1):", f(1))
print("slope at the inflection x = 0:", fp(0))

// ---- the picture ---------------------------------------------------------------
graph x ^ 3 - 3 * x from -2.5 to 2.5
graph 3 * x ^ 2 - 3 from -2.5 to 2.5

/* ---- expected output ----
= critical points where f'(x) = 0:
= x = -1, x = 1
= roots of f:
= x = -1.7320508075688772, x = 0, x = 1.7320508075688774
= local max f(-1): 2
= local min f(1): -2
= slope at the inflection x = 0: -3
graph: x ^ 3 - 3 * x from -2.5 to 2.5
graph: 3 * x ^ 2 - 3 from -2.5 to 2.5
*/

scripts.name: rational-asymptotes
scripts.title: vertical and horizontal asymptotes of a ratio
scripts.text:
/* ============================================================================
rational-asymptotes.epher -- vertical and horizontal asymptotes of a ratio

The rational function f(x) = (2*x^2 + 3) / (x^2 - 1) dies at x = +-1,
where its denominator vanishes but its numerator does not: two vertical
asymptotes. For large |x| the x^2 terms dominate both floors, so the
curve flattens toward y = 2, the ratio of leading coefficients
(standard asymptote analysis, Stewart, "Calculus", ch. 2.6 and 3.4).
The script graphs the curve and prints the asymptotes and the
approach to the horizontal one.

Web/desktop:             paste the whole file into the entry, press Enter
The graph lines open the plot pane in the desktop, web and TUI apps;
the CLI transcript records them as "graph:" lines.
============================================================================ */

// ---- the curve -----------------------------------------------------------------
def f(x) = (2 * x ^ 2 + 3) / (x ^ 2 - 1)

// ---- results -------------------------------------------------------------------
print("denominator zeros, the vertical asymptotes:")
solve x ^ 2 - 1 == 0
print("horizontal asymptote y = leading ratio:", 2 / 1)
print("f(10):", f(10))
print("f(100):", f(100))
print("f(1000):", f(1000))
print("f just right of x = 1 (f(1.001)):", f(1.001))

// ---- the picture ---------------------------------------------------------------
graph (2 * x ^ 2 + 3) / (x ^ 2 - 1) from -5 to 5
graph 2 from -5 to 5

/* ---- expected output ----
= denominator zeros, the vertical asymptotes:
= x = -1, x = 1
= horizontal asymptote y = leading ratio: 2
= f(10): 203/99
= f(100): 2.00050005001
= f(1000): 2.00000500001
= f just right of x = 1 (f(1.001)): 2500.75062469
graph: (2 * x ^ 2 + 3) / (x ^ 2 - 1) from -5 to 5
graph: 2 from -5 to 5
*/

scripts.name: square-wave-harmonics
scripts.title: a square wave from sine partials
scripts.text:
/* ============================================================================
square-wave-harmonics.epher -- a square wave from sine partials

A square wave of amplitude 1 is the sine series
4/pi * (sin(x) + sin(3*x)/3 + sin(5*x)/5 + ...), odd harmonics only,
falling off as 1/n (Fourier, "Theorie analytique de la chaleur", 1822).
Partial sums ring near the jumps: the Gibbs overshoot stays near 9
percent of the jump no matter how many terms are taken (Wilbraham
1848, Gibbs 1899). The script graphs the five-term sum against its
envelope and prints the sum at the flat top and mid-jump.

Web/desktop:             paste the whole file into the entry, press Enter
The graph lines open the plot pane in the desktop, web and TUI apps;
the CLI transcript records them as "graph:" lines.
============================================================================ */

// ---- the model -----------------------------------------------------------------
def s(x) = 4 / pi * (sin(x) + sin(3 * x) / 3 + sin(5 * x) / 5 + sin(7 * x) / 7 + sin(9 * x) / 9)

// ---- results -------------------------------------------------------------------
print("amplitude scale 4/pi:", 4 / pi)
print("mid flat top s(pi/2):", s(pi / 2))
print("mid jump s(0):", s(0))
print("peak of the ring s(0.35):", s(0.35))
print("five terms only reach:", s(pi / 2) - 1, "above 1")

// ---- the picture ---------------------------------------------------------------
graph 4 / pi * (sin(x) + sin(3 * x) / 3 + sin(5 * x) / 5 + sin(7 * x) / 7 + sin(9 * x) / 9) from -0.5 to 6.6
graph 1 from -0.5 to 6.6
graph -1 from -0.5 to 6.6

/* ---- expected output ----
= amplitude scale 4/pi: 1.27323954474
= mid flat top s(pi/2): 1.0630539691
= mid jump s(0): 0
= peak of the ring s(0.35): 1.17012137209
= five terms only reach: 0.0630539690963 above 1
graph: 4 / pi * (sin(x) + sin(3 * x) / 3 + sin(5 * x) / 5 + sin(7 * x) / 7 + sin(9 * x) / 9) from -0.5 to 6.6
graph: 1 from -0.5 to 6.6
graph: -1 from -0.5 to 6.6
*/

scripts.name: tangent-asymptotes
scripts.title: the tangent's vertical walls and period
scripts.text:
/* ============================================================================
tangent-asymptotes.epher -- the tangent's vertical walls and period

The tangent y = tan(x) repeats every pi, rises from 0 through 1 at
pi/4, and runs off each vertical asymptote x = pi/2 + n*pi to +-oo
(any precalculus text, e.g. Stewart, "Precalculus", ch. 5.4; Euler's
1748 intro analyses the periodicity). Near an asymptote the values
explode arithmetically while the curve stays one smooth branch. The
script graphs two branches and prints the sampled landmarks.

Web/desktop:             paste the whole file into the entry, press Enter
The graph lines open the plot pane in the desktop, web and TUI apps;
the CLI transcript records them as "graph:" lines.
============================================================================ */

// ---- the model -----------------------------------------------------------------
const p = pi   // the period of the tangent

// ---- results -------------------------------------------------------------------
print("tan(0):", tan(0))
print("tan(pi/4):", tan(pi / 4))
print("tan(3*pi/4):", tan(3 * pi / 4))
print("period check, tan(pi + 0.3) vs tan(0.3):", abs(tan(pi + 0.3) - tan(0.3)) < 1e-15)
print("a step from the wall, tan(1.57):", tan(1.57))

// ---- the picture ---------------------------------------------------------------
graph tan(x) from -4.4 to 4.4

/* ---- expected output ----
= tan(0): 0
= tan(pi/4): 1
= tan(3*pi/4): -1
= period check, tan(pi + 0.3) vs tan(0.3): true
= a step from the wall, tan(1.57): 1255.7655915
graph: tan(x) from -4.4 to 4.4
*/

scripts.name: cassini-ovals
scripts.title: equal-distance product to two foci, two ovals
scripts.text:
/* ============================================================================
cassini-ovals.epher -- equal-distance product to two foci, two ovals

Giovanni Cassini believed the planets ride these (1680): the locus
whose product of distances to the foci (+-1, 0) is the constant
b^4. For b > sqrt(2)*... for b^4 near 1 the locus is one peanut; for
smaller b it splits into two egg-shaped ovals around the foci, and at
exactly b = 1 it is Bernoulli's lemniscate (MathWorld, "Cassini
Ovals"). The script graphs the split case b^4 = 0.81 and prints the
test values that show the origin is outside both ovals.

Web/desktop:             paste the whole file into the entry, press Enter
The graph lines open the plot pane in the desktop, web and TUI apps;
the CLI transcript records them as "graph:" lines.
============================================================================ */

// ---- the model -----------------------------------------------------------------
const b4 = 0.81   // the constant product b^4; lemniscate at 1

// ---- results -------------------------------------------------------------------
print("product of distances at the origin:", sqrt(1) * sqrt(1))
print("origin outside the ovals, product > b^4:", 1 > b4)
print("product at the focus (1, 0):", 0 * 2)
print("focus inside its oval, product < b^4:", 0 < b4)

// ---- the picture ---------------------------------------------------------------
graph ((x - 1) ^ 2 + y ^ 2) * ((x + 1) ^ 2 + y ^ 2) == 0.81 from -2.2 to 2.2

/* ---- expected output ----
= product of distances at the origin: 1
= origin outside the ovals, product > b^4: true
= product at the focus (1, 0): 0
= focus inside its oval, product < b^4: true
graph: ((x - 1) ^ 2 + y ^ 2) * ((x + 1) ^ 2 + y ^ 2) == 0.81 from -2.2 to 2.2
*/

scripts.name: conic-ellipse-axes
scripts.title: the ellipse x^2/4 + y^2 = 1, foci and area
scripts.text:
/* ============================================================================
conic-ellipse-axes.epher -- the ellipse x^2/4 + y^2 = 1, foci and area

The ellipse with semi-axes a = 2 and b = 1 has focal distance
c = sqrt(a^2 - b^2) = sqrt(3) and eccentricity e = c/a = sqrt(3)/2:
a squashed circle that Kepler's Mars orbit made famous (Apollonius
named the conics; Stewart, "Precalculus", ch. 9.2). Its area is
pi*a*b = 2*pi. The script graphs it, prints foci and eccentricity,
and checks the area numerically from the top-half formula.

Web/desktop:             paste the whole file into the entry, press Enter
The graph lines open the plot pane in the desktop, web and TUI apps;
the CLI transcript records them as "graph:" lines.
============================================================================ */

// ---- the ellipse ----------------------------------------------------------------
const a = 2    // semi-major axis
const b = 1    // semi-minor axis

// ---- results -------------------------------------------------------------------
print("focal distance c = sqrt(a^2 - b^2):", sqrt(a ^ 2 - b ^ 2))
print("eccentricity e = c/a:", sqrt(a ^ 2 - b ^ 2) / a)
print("area, exact 2*pi:", integral(2 * sqrt(1 - x ^ 2 / a ^ 2), -a, a))

// ---- the picture ---------------------------------------------------------------
graph x ^ 2 / 4 + y ^ 2 == 1 from -2.5 to 2.5

/* ---- expected output ----
= focal distance c = sqrt(a^2 - b^2): 1.73205080757
= eccentricity e = c/a: 0.866025403784
= area, exact 2*pi: 6.28318530691
graph: x ^ 2 / 4 + y ^ 2 == 1 from -2.5 to 2.5
*/

scripts.name: ellipse-foci-sum
scripts.title: the gardener's ellipse: two distances, one sum
scripts.text:
/* ============================================================================
ellipse-foci-sum.epher -- the gardener's ellipse: two distances, one sum

An ellipse is the set where the distances to the two foci add to a
constant 2a - the property a gardener uses to draw one with two pegs
and a loop of string (Apollonius defined the conics; Stewart,
"Precalculus", ch. 9.2). Here a = 3 and the foci sit at (+-2, 0),
so b = sqrt(9 - 4). The script graphs the ellipse and checks the
string property numerically at points along and across the axes.

Web/desktop:             paste the whole file into the entry, press Enter
The graph lines open the plot pane in the desktop, web and TUI apps;
the CLI transcript records them as "graph:" lines.
============================================================================ */

// ---- the model -----------------------------------------------------------------
const a = 3    // half the string length
const c = 2    // half the focus separation
def fy(x) = sqrt(5 - 5 * x ^ 2 / 9)   // the ellipse's upper half (b^2 = 5)

// ---- results -------------------------------------------------------------------
print("string length 2*a:", 2 * a)
print("sum at the end (3, 0):", hypot(3 - c, 0) + hypot(3 + c, 0))
print("sum at the top (0, sqrt(5)):", hypot(0 - c, fy(0)) + hypot(0 + c, fy(0)))
print("the top half height sqrt(5):", fy(0))

// ---- the picture ---------------------------------------------------------------
graph x ^ 2 / 9 + y ^ 2 / 5 == 1 from -3.5 to 3.5

/* ---- expected output ----
= string length 2*a: 6
= sum at the end (3, 0): 6
= sum at the top (0, sqrt(5)): 6
= the top half height sqrt(5): 2.2360679775
graph: x ^ 2 / 9 + y ^ 2 / 5 == 1 from -3.5 to 3.5
*/

scripts.name: hyperbola-asymptotes
scripts.title: x^2 - y^2 = 1 rides its two asymptotes
scripts.text:
/* ============================================================================
hyperbola-asymptotes.epher -- x^2 - y^2 = 1 rides its two asymptotes

The rectangular hyperbola x^2 - y^2 = 1 opens left and right, its
branches forever closing on the lines y = x and y = -x without ever
touching them: the asymptote slope is b/a = 1, and the eccentricity
is sqrt(2) for any a = b (the "rectangular" case, Apollonius again;
Stewart, "Precalculus", ch. 9.3). The script graphs the branches
with both asymptotes overlaid and prints the landmarks.

Web/desktop:             paste the whole file into the entry, press Enter
The graph lines open the plot pane in the desktop, web and TUI apps;
the CLI transcript records them as "graph:" lines.
============================================================================ */

// ---- the hyperbola -------------------------------------------------------------
def h(x) = sqrt(x ^ 2 - 1)   // the upper branch

// ---- results -------------------------------------------------------------------
print("vertices at x = +-1:", h(1) == 0)
print("asymptote slope, b/a:", 1)
print("upper branch at x = 2:", h(2))
print("asymptote there, y = x:", 2)
print("eccentricity, sqrt(2):", sqrt(2))

// ---- the picture ---------------------------------------------------------------
graph x ^ 2 - y ^ 2 == 1 from -4 to 4
graph x from -4 to 4
graph 0 - x from -4 to 4

/* ---- expected output ----
= vertices at x = +-1: true
= asymptote slope, b/a: 1
= upper branch at x = 2: 1.73205080757
= asymptote there, y = x: 2
= eccentricity, sqrt(2): 1.41421356237
graph: x ^ 2 - y ^ 2 == 1 from -4 to 4
graph: x from -4 to 4
graph: 0 - x from -4 to 4
*/

scripts.name: region-between-parabola
scripts.title: the area between y = x^2 and y = 4
scripts.text:
/* ============================================================================
region-between-parabola.epher -- the area between y = x^2 and y = 4

The parabola y = x^2 and the line y = 4 meet at x = +-2, and the
region between them is the classroom first area: the integral of
4 - x^2 from -2 to 2, exactly 32/3 (Stewart, "Calculus", ch. 5.1,
where a region between a line and a parabola is the opening example). epher shades the
region with an inequality graph and overlays the two boundary
curves; the script prints the intersections and the area.

Web/desktop:             paste the whole file into the entry, press Enter
The graph lines open the plot pane in the desktop, web and TUI apps;
the CLI transcript records them as "graph:" lines.
============================================================================ */

// ---- the region ----------------------------------------------------------------
def top(x) = 4
def bottom(x) = x ^ 2

// ---- results -------------------------------------------------------------------
print("the corners:")
solve x ^ 2 == 4
print("area between, exact 32/3:", integral(4 - x ^ 2, -2, 2))
print("vertical gap at x = 1:", top(1) - bottom(1))

// ---- the picture ---------------------------------------------------------------
graph y < 4 - 0 * x from -3 to 3
graph x ^ 2 from -3 to 3
graph 4 from -3 to 3

/* ---- expected output ----
= the corners:
= x = -2, x = 2
= area between, exact 32/3: 32/3
= vertical gap at x = 1: 3
graph: y < 4 - 0 * x from -3 to 3
graph: x ^ 2 from -3 to 3
graph: 4 from -3 to 3
*/

scripts.name: astroid-hypocycloid
scripts.title: the four-cusped hypocycloid
scripts.text:
/* ============================================================================
astroid-hypocycloid.epher -- the four-cusped hypocycloid

A circle of radius 1 rolling inside one of radius 4 traces the astroid
const x = cos(t)^3, y = sin(t)^3: four cusps on the axes, tangent line
intercepts always exactly 2 apart (Leibniz 1715; MathWorld, "Astroid";
Stewart, "Calculus", ch. 10.1). Its area is 3*pi/8, three eighths of
the circumscribing circle, and its perimeter is 6. The script graphs
it and checks both numbers numerically: the area follows from
Green's theorem as the integral of x*y'(t).

Web/desktop:             paste the whole file into the entry, press Enter
The graph lines open the plot pane in the desktop, web and TUI apps;
the CLI transcript records them as "graph:" lines.
============================================================================ */

// ---- the curve -----------------------------------------------------------------
def ax(t) = cos(t) ^ 3
def ay(t) = sin(t) ^ 3

// ---- results -------------------------------------------------------------------
print("cusp on the x-axis (t = 0):", ax(0), ay(0))
print("area, exact 3*pi/8:", integral(cos(x) ^ 3 * 3 * sin(x) ^ 2 * cos(x), 0, pi / 2) * 4)
print("perimeter, exact 6:", integral(sqrt((0 - 3 * cos(x) ^ 2 * sin(x)) ^ 2 + (3 * sin(x) ^ 2 * cos(x)) ^ 2), 0, pi / 2) * 4)

// ---- the picture ---------------------------------------------------------------
graph param cos(t) ^ 3, sin(t) ^ 3 from 0 to 6.28318

/* ---- expected output ----
= cusp on the x-axis (t = 0): 1 0
= area, exact 3*pi/8: 1.1780972451
= perimeter, exact 6: 6
graph: param cos(t) ^ 3, sin(t) ^ 3 from 0 to 6.28318
*/

scripts.name: brachistochrone-arc
scripts.title: the cycloid beats the straight ramp
scripts.text:
/* ============================================================================
brachistochrone-arc.epher -- the cycloid beats the straight ramp

Of all curves from A down to a lower B, the cycloid is the fastest
ride (Johann Bernoulli's challenge of 1696, solved 1697 by Newton,
Leibniz, l'Hopital and the Bernoullis; Stewart, "Calculus", ch. 10.2,
project). Sliding frictionless, speed is sqrt(2*g*y), so the descent
time is the integral of ds / sqrt(2*g*y). On the cycloid
(t - sin(t), 1 - cos(t)) to the arch's half-way point (pi, 2) the
integrand collapses to the constant sqrt(2); on the straight ramp of
length L the time is L/sqrt(g). The script graphs both routes and
times them; the cycloid wins by about 16 percent.

Web/desktop:             paste the whole file into the entry, press Enter
The graph lines open the plot pane in the desktop, web and TUI apps;
the CLI transcript records them as "graph:" lines.
============================================================================ */

// ---- the model -----------------------------------------------------------------
const g = 9.80665   // standard gravity, m/s^2

// ---- results -------------------------------------------------------------------
print("cycloid time, exact pi/sqrt(g):", pi / sqrt(g))
print("straight-ramp time, L/sqrt(g):", sqrt(pi ^ 2 + 4) / sqrt(g))
print("the cycloid's advantage:", 1 - (pi / sqrt(g)) / (sqrt(pi ^ 2 + 4) / sqrt(g)))

// ---- the picture ---------------------------------------------------------------
graph param t - sin(t), 1 - cos(t) from 0 to 3.14159
graph param t, 2 * t / pi from 0 to 3.14159

/* ---- expected output ----
= cycloid time, exact pi/sqrt(g): 1.00320464629
= straight-ramp time, L/sqrt(g): 1.18924599959
= the cycloid's advantage: 0.156436391931
graph: param t - sin(t), 1 - cos(t) from 0 to 3.14159
graph: param t, 2 * t / pi from 0 to 3.14159
*/

scripts.name: folium-of-descartes
scripts.title: the leaf with the loop and the slant asymptote
scripts.text:
/* ============================================================================
folium-of-descartes.epher -- the leaf with the loop and the slant asymptote

The folium x^3 + y^3 = 3*x*y (Descartes, 1638, in his letters to
Fermat) unfurls a loop in the first quadrant and two wings that close
on the slant asymptote x + y + 1 = 0. The rational parametrisation
const x = 3*t / (1 + t^3), y = 3*t^2 / (1 + t^3) walks the whole curve with
one parameter t; the node sits at the origin and the loop's far
corner at t = 1 (Lockwood, "A Book of Curves", ch. 8). The script
graphs the loop and the wings separately - t = -1 is a pole - and
prints the landmarks.

Web/desktop:             paste the whole file into the entry, press Enter
The graph lines open the plot pane in the desktop, web and TUI apps;
the CLI transcript records them as "graph:" lines.
============================================================================ */

// ---- the curve -----------------------------------------------------------------
def fx(t) = 3 * t / (1 + t ^ 3)
def fy(t) = 3 * t ^ 2 / (1 + t ^ 3)

// ---- results -------------------------------------------------------------------
print("the node at t = 0:", fx(0), fy(0))
print("loop corner at t = 1:", fx(1), fy(1))
print("wings approach x + y = -1; at t = -1.5, x + y =", fx(-1.5) + fy(-1.5))
print("the curve meets its equation, at (1.5, 1.5):", 1.5 ^ 3 + 1.5 ^ 3 == 3 * 1.5 * 1.5)

// ---- the picture ---------------------------------------------------------------
graph param 3 * t / (1 + t ^ 3), 3 * t ^ 2 / (1 + t ^ 3) from -0.9 to 8
graph param 3 * t / (1 + t ^ 3), 3 * t ^ 2 / (1 + t ^ 3) from -8 to -1.3

/* ---- expected output ----
= the node at t = 0: 0 0
= loop corner at t = 1: 1.5 1.5
= wings approach x + y = -1; at t = -1.5, x + y = -18/19
= the curve meets its equation, at (1.5, 1.5): true
graph: param 3 * t / (1 + t ^ 3), 3 * t ^ 2 / (1 + t ^ 3) from -0.9 to 8
graph: param 3 * t / (1 + t ^ 3), 3 * t ^ 2 / (1 + t ^ 3) from -8 to -1.3
*/

scripts.name: lissajous-3-2
scripts.title: the 3:2 Lissajous figure
scripts.text:
/* ============================================================================
lissajous-3-2.epher -- the 3:2 Lissajous figure

Driving x with one sine and y with another produces the Lissajous
figures a oscilloscope shows when two pure tones feed its inputs
(Lissajous, 1857; the classic treatment is Rayleigh, "The Theory of
Sound", ch. 3). The figure closes exactly when the frequency ratio is
rational; a ratio of 3:2 gives a woven curve with 3 lobes one way and
2 the other, traversed in one period 2*pi. The script graphs the
curve, samples landmarks, and checks the closure numerically.

Web/desktop:             paste the whole file into the entry, press Enter
The graph lines open the plot pane in the desktop, web and TUI apps;
the CLI transcript records them as "graph:" lines.
============================================================================ */

// ---- the curve -----------------------------------------------------------------
def px(t) = sin(3 * t)
def py(t) = sin(2 * t)

// ---- results -------------------------------------------------------------------
print("start point (t = 0):", px(0), py(0))
print("at t = pi/2:", px(pi / 2), py(pi / 2))
print("closure, P(2*pi) vs P(0):", abs(px(2 * pi) - px(0)) < 1e-12 and abs(py(2 * pi) - py(0)) < 1e-12)
print("frequency ratio, a closed figure needs rational:", 3 / 2)

// ---- the picture ---------------------------------------------------------------
graph param sin(3 * t), sin(2 * t) from 0 to 6.28318

/* ---- expected output ----
= start point (t = 0): 0 0
= at t = pi/2: -1 0.000000000000000122464679915
= closure, P(2*pi) vs P(0): true
= frequency ratio, a closed figure needs rational: 1.5
graph: param sin(3 * t), sin(2 * t) from 0 to 6.28318
*/

scripts.name: witch-of-agnesi
scripts.title: Maria Agnesi's bell-shaped curve
scripts.text:
/* ============================================================================
witch-of-agnesi.epher -- Maria Agnesi's bell-shaped curve

Named (in mistranslation) after Maria Gaetana Agnesi, who treated it
in 1748: take the circle x^2 + (y - 1)^2 = 1, draw a line from the
origin to a point of the circle, and mark where it meets the
horizontal through that point. The traced curve is x = 2*tan(t),
const y = 2*cos(t)^2, bell-shaped with peak 2 and the x-axis as asymptote
(Lockwood, "A Book of Curves", ch. 4; MathWorld, "Witch of Agnesi").
The total area under it is 4*pi. The script graphs the bell, prints
landmarks, and checks the area numerically.

Web/desktop:             paste the whole file into the entry, press Enter
The graph lines open the plot pane in the desktop, web and TUI apps;
the CLI transcript records them as "graph:" lines.
============================================================================ */

// ---- the curve -----------------------------------------------------------------
def wx(t) = 2 * tan(t)
def wy(t) = 2 * cos(t) ^ 2

// ---- results -------------------------------------------------------------------
print("peak at t = 0:", wx(0), wy(0))
print("near the asymptote, t = 1.4:", wx(1.4), wy(1.4))
print("area under the bell to +-60:", integral(2 / (1 + x ^ 2 / 4), -60, 60))
print("full area, exact 4*pi:", 4 * pi)

// ---- the picture ---------------------------------------------------------------
graph param 2 * tan(t), 2 * cos(t) ^ 2 from -1.5 to 1.5
graph 8 / (x ^ 2 + 4) from -6 to 6

/* ---- expected output ----
= peak at t = 0: 0 2
= near the asymptote, t = 1.4: 11.595767431 0.0577776593313
= area under the bell to +-60: 12.2998026473
= full area, exact 4*pi: 12.5663706144
graph: param 2 * tan(t), 2 * cos(t) ^ 2 from -1.5 to 1.5
graph: 8 / (x ^ 2 + 4) from -6 to 6
*/

scripts.name: archimedean-spiral
scripts.title: r grows in lockstep with the angle
scripts.text:
/* ============================================================================
archimedean-spiral.epher -- r grows in lockstep with the angle

The spiral r = theta winds outward one fixed band per turn: successive
turns cut any ray exactly 2*pi apart, the property Archimedes proved
in "On Spirals" (c. 225 BC) when he squared the circle's motion. The
uniform spacing is what distinguishes it from the logarithmic spiral,
whose bands grow geometrically. The script graphs two turns and
checks the spacing and a radius along the axis.

Web/desktop:             paste the whole file into the entry, press Enter
The graph lines open the plot pane in the desktop, web and TUI apps;
the CLI transcript records them as "graph:" lines.
============================================================================ */

// ---- the curve -----------------------------------------------------------------
def r(t) = t

// ---- results -------------------------------------------------------------------
print("radius after one turn, 2*pi:", r(2 * pi))
print("radius after two turns, 4*pi:", r(4 * pi))
print("band spacing per turn, exact 2*pi:", r(4 * pi) - r(2 * pi))

// ---- the picture ---------------------------------------------------------------
graph polar theta from 0 to 12.566

/* ---- expected output ----
= radius after one turn, 2*pi: 6.28318530718
= radius after two turns, 4*pi: 12.5663706144
= band spacing per turn, exact 2*pi: 6.28318530718
graph: polar theta from 0 to 12.566
*/

scripts.name: cardioid-polar-area
scripts.title: the cardioid's area by the polar formula
scripts.text:
/* ============================================================================
cardioid-polar-area.epher -- the cardioid's area by the polar formula

The cardioid r = 1 + cos(theta) is a circle of radius 1/2 rolling
around an equal circle, heart first: a cusp at the origin, a dimple
facing left. The polar area formula, A = 1/2 * integral of r^2 over
the angle, gives exactly 3*pi/2 for the full sweep 0 to 2*pi (Stewart,
"Calculus", ch. 10.4, where this curve is the worked example). The
script graphs it and checks the area numerically, along with the
radial landmarks.

Web/desktop:             paste the whole file into the entry, press Enter
The graph lines open the plot pane in the desktop, web and TUI apps;
the CLI transcript records them as "graph:" lines.
============================================================================ */

// ---- the curve -----------------------------------------------------------------
def r(t) = 1 + cos(t)

// ---- results -------------------------------------------------------------------
print("the cusp, r at pi:", r(pi))
print("the far lobe, r at 0:", r(0))
print("area, exact 3*pi/2:", integral(r(x) ^ 2 / 2, 0, 2 * pi))

// ---- the picture ---------------------------------------------------------------
graph polar 1 + cos(theta)

/* ---- expected output ----
= the cusp, r at pi: 0
= the far lobe, r at 0: 2
= area, exact 3*pi/2: 4.18879020479
graph: polar 1 + cos(theta)
*/

scripts.name: lemniscate-area
scripts.title: the figure-eight r^2 = cos(2*theta)
scripts.text:
/* ============================================================================
lemniscate-area.epher -- the figure-eight r^2 = cos(2*theta)

Jakob Bernoulli's lemniscate (1694) is the locus where the product of
distances to the two foci (+-1/sqrt(2), 0) stays at 1/2: a stretched
figure eight. In polar form r^2 = a^2*cos(2*theta), each loop spans
45 deg on either side of the x-axis, and the area of ONE loop is
1/2 * integral of r^2 = 1/2 for a = 1 - so the whole curve encloses
exactly 1 (Stewart, "Calculus", ch. 10.4, example; MathWorld,
"Lemniscate"). The script graphs the eight and checks the total area.

Web/desktop:             paste the whole file into the entry, press Enter
The graph lines open the plot pane in the desktop, web and TUI apps;
the CLI transcript records them as "graph:" lines.
============================================================================ */

// ---- the curve -----------------------------------------------------------------
def r(t) = sqrt(cos(2 * t))

// ---- results -------------------------------------------------------------------
print("r on the axis, theta = 0:", r(0))
print("the loop pinches where cos(2*theta) = 0, at pi/4:", abs(cos(pi / 2)) < 1e-15)
print("both loops area, exact 1:", integral(cos(2 * x) / 2, -pi / 4, pi / 4) * 2)

// ---- the picture ---------------------------------------------------------------
graph polar sqrt(cos(2 * theta))

/* ---- expected output ----
= r on the axis, theta = 0: 1
= the loop pinches where cos(2*theta) = 0, at pi/4: true
= both loops area, exact 1: 1
graph: polar sqrt(cos(2 * theta))
*/

scripts.name: limacon-inner-loop
scripts.title: the snail with the inner loop
scripts.text:
/* ============================================================================
limacon-inner-loop.epher -- the snail with the inner loop

The limacon r = 1 + 2*cos(theta) (the name, "snail", is Roberval's)
crosses into itself when b > a: between theta = 2*pi/3 and 4*pi/3 the
radius is negative, which plots the small inner loop through the
origin (Stewart, "Calculus", ch. 10.3, "limacons with inner loops";
Lockwood, "A Book of Curves", ch. 10). The script graphs it, prints
the radial landmarks, and checks where the curve passes through the
pole.

Web/desktop:             paste the whole file into the entry, press Enter
The graph lines open the plot pane in the desktop, web and TUI apps;
the CLI transcript records them as "graph:" lines.
============================================================================ */

// ---- the curve -----------------------------------------------------------------
def r(t) = 1 + 2 * cos(t)

// ---- results -------------------------------------------------------------------
print("the far lip, r at 0:", r(0))
print("through the pole at 2*pi/3:", abs(r(2 * pi / 3)) < 1e-15)
print("inner loop tip, r at pi:", r(pi))
print("symmetry about the x-axis, r(pi/3) vs r(-pi/3):", r(pi / 3) == r(0 - pi / 3))

// ---- the picture ---------------------------------------------------------------
graph polar 1 + 2 * cos(theta)

/* ---- expected output ----
= the far lip, r at 0: 3
= through the pole at 2*pi/3: true
= inner loop tip, r at pi: -1
= symmetry about the x-axis, r(pi/3) vs r(-pi/3): true
graph: polar 1 + 2 * cos(theta)
*/

scripts.name: logarithmic-spiral-growth
scripts.title: the spira mirabilis grows by equal ratios
scripts.text:
/* ============================================================================
logarithmic-spiral-growth.epher -- the spira mirabilis grows by equal ratios

The logarithmic spiral r = e^(a*theta) doubles, or grows by any fixed
ratio, in a fixed angle: every turn scales the last by e^(2*pi*a).
The angle between the curve and the radius is the same everywhere,
which is why a moth flying at constant bearing to a lamp traces one
(Jakob Bernoulli, 1692, who called it the spira mirabilis and asked
it engraved on his tomb; Cooke, "The History of the Spiral"). With
a = 0.2 the per-turn growth is e^(0.4*pi), about 3.5. The script
graphs three turns and checks the growth ratio.

Web/desktop:             paste the whole file into the entry, press Enter
The graph lines open the plot pane in the desktop, web and TUI apps;
the CLI transcript records them as "graph:" lines.
============================================================================ */

// ---- the model -----------------------------------------------------------------
const a = 0.2    // the tightness of the wind

// ---- results -------------------------------------------------------------------
print("radius at theta = 0:", e^(0.2 * 0))
print("radius after one turn, e^(0.4*pi):", e^(0.2 * 2 * pi))
print("after two turns, e^(0.8*pi):", e^(0.2 * 4 * pi))
print("growth ratio per turn is constant:", e^(0.2 * 4 * pi) / e^(0.2 * 2 * pi) == e^(0.2 * 2 * pi) / e^(0.2 * 0))

// ---- the picture ---------------------------------------------------------------
graph polar e^(0.2 * theta) from 0 to 12.566

/* ---- expected output ----
= radius at theta = 0: 1
= radius after one turn, e^(0.4*pi): 3.51358562429
= after two turns, e^(0.8*pi): 12.3452839392
= growth ratio per turn is constant: true
graph: polar e^(0.2 * theta) from 0 to 12.566
*/

scripts.name: rose-four-petals
scripts.title: the four-petaled rose r = cos(2*theta)
scripts.text:
/* ============================================================================
rose-four-petals.epher -- the four-petaled rose r = cos(2*theta)

The rhodonea or rose r = a*cos(k*theta) opens k petals when k is odd
and 2k petals when k is even (Guido Grandi, who called the curves
"roses", 1723; Stewart, "Calculus", ch. 10.4). With k = 2 the rose
has four petals, tips at radius 1 on the axes, pinching to zero
between petals every 45 deg, and the total area is exactly pi/2 - one
quarter of the circumscribing circle. The script graphs the rose, samples the petal
tips, and checks the area with the polar formula.

Web/desktop:             paste the whole file into the entry, press Enter
The graph lines open the plot pane in the desktop, web and TUI apps;
the CLI transcript records them as "graph:" lines.
============================================================================ */

// ---- the curve -----------------------------------------------------------------
def r(t) = cos(2 * t)

// ---- results -------------------------------------------------------------------
print("petal tips at theta = 0, pi/2, pi:", r(0), r(pi / 2), r(pi))
print("between petals, theta = pi/4:", r(pi / 4))
print("area, exact pi/2:", integral(cos(2 * x) ^ 2 / 2, 0, 2 * pi))

// ---- the picture ---------------------------------------------------------------
graph polar cos(2 * theta)

/* ---- expected output ----
= petal tips at theta = 0, pi/2, pi: 1 -1 1
= between petals, theta = pi/4: 0.0000000000000000612323399574
= area, exact pi/2: 3.14159265359
graph: polar cos(2 * theta)
*/

scripts.name: circular-helix-pitch
scripts.title: the spring curve and its pitch
scripts.text:
/* ============================================================================
circular-helix-pitch.epher -- the spring curve and its pitch

The circular helix (cos(t), sin(t), t/6) wraps a unit circle around
the z-axis while climbing one pitch of 2*pi/6 per turn: the curve of
a coiled spring and of a spiral staircase both (do Carmo, "Differential
Geometry of Curves and Surfaces", ch. 1-2, the model curve whose
curvature and torsion are constant; Stewart, "Calculus", ch. 13.1).
The arc length of one turn is the hypotenuse of the unrolled circle
and pitch: sqrt((2*pi)^2 + (2*pi/6)^2). The script graphs two turns
and checks the pitch and length.

Web/desktop:             paste the whole file into the entry, press Enter
The graph lines open the 3D pane in the desktop, web and TUI apps;
the CLI transcript records them as "graph3d:" lines.
============================================================================ */

// ---- the curve -----------------------------------------------------------------
def hx(t) = cos(t)
def hy(t) = sin(t)
def hz(t) = t / 6

// ---- results -------------------------------------------------------------------
print("stays on the unit cylinder, x^2 + y^2:", hx(1.3) ^ 2 + hy(1.3) ^ 2)
print("pitch per turn, 2*pi/6:", hz(2 * pi) - hz(0))
print("one turn of wire, unrolled:", sqrt((2 * pi) ^ 2 + (2 * pi / 6) ^ 2))

// ---- the picture ---------------------------------------------------------------
graph3d param cos(t), sin(t), t / 6 from 0 to 12.566

/* ---- expected output ----
= stays on the unit cylinder, x^2 + y^2: 1
= pitch per turn, 2*pi/6: 1.0471975512
= one turn of wire, unrolled: 6.36985402624
graph3d: param cos(t), sin(t), t / 6 from 0 to 12.566
*/

scripts.name: conical-spiral
scripts.title: a helix whose radius grows as it climbs
scripts.text:
/* ============================================================================
conical-spiral.epher -- a helix whose radius grows as it climbs

Let the radius ride with the height and the helix opens into a
conical spiral: x = (t/6)*cos(2*t), y = (t/6)*sin(2*t), z = t/3.
The point stays on the cone z = 2*sqrt(x^2 + y^2) for every t, and
one full turn gains height 2*pi/3 while the radius grows 2*pi/6 -
the shape of a wound conical spring (space curves of this family are
standard exercises, e.g. Stewart, "Calculus", ch. 13.1, problems).
The script graphs it and checks the cone membership.

Web/desktop:             paste the whole file into the entry, press Enter
The graph lines open the 3D pane in the desktop, web and TUI apps;
the CLI transcript records them as "graph3d:" lines.
============================================================================ */

// ---- the curve -----------------------------------------------------------------
def cx(t) = t / 6 * cos(2 * t)
def cy(t) = t / 6 * sin(2 * t)
def cz(t) = t / 3

// ---- results -------------------------------------------------------------------
print("on the cone z = 2*r at t = 5:", cz(5) == 2 * sqrt(cx(5) ^ 2 + cy(5) ^ 2))
print("radius at t = 5:", sqrt(cx(5) ^ 2 + cy(5) ^ 2))
print("height gained per turn, 2*pi/3:", cz(2 * pi) - cz(0))

// ---- the picture ---------------------------------------------------------------
graph3d param t / 6 * cos(2 * t), t / 6 * sin(2 * t), t / 3 from 0 to 12.566

/* ---- expected output ----
= on the cone z = 2*r at t = 5: true
= radius at t = 5: 5/6
= height gained per turn, 2*pi/3: 2.09439510239
graph3d: param t / 6 * cos(2 * t), t / 6 * sin(2 * t), t / 3 from 0 to 12.566
*/

scripts.name: trefoil-torus-knot
scripts.title: the (2,3) torus knot, the simplest knot
scripts.text:
/* ============================================================================
trefoil-torus-knot.epher -- the (2,3) torus knot, the simplest knot

Wrap a string around a torus twice the long way and three times the
short way and it closes on itself as the trefoil: the only knot with
three crossings (Rolfsen, "Knots and Links", ch. 2; every knot table
starts with it). The parametrisation
const x = (2 + cos(3*t))*cos(2*t), y = (2 + cos(3*t))*sin(2*t),
const z = sin(3*t), scaled here by one half, rides on the torus of tube 1/2
around the ring of radius 1. The script graphs the knot and checks
closure and the torus membership.

Web/desktop:             paste the whole file into the entry, press Enter
The graph lines open the 3D pane in the desktop, web and TUI apps;
the CLI transcript records them as "graph3d:" lines.
============================================================================ */

// ---- the curve (half scale) ------------------------------------------------------
def tx(t) = (2 + cos(3 * t)) * cos(2 * t) / 2
def ty(t) = (2 + cos(3 * t)) * sin(2 * t) / 2
def tz(t) = sin(3 * t) / 2

// ---- results -------------------------------------------------------------------
print("closes after one lap, P(0) vs P(2*pi):", abs(tx(2 * pi) - tx(0)) < 1e-12 and abs(ty(2 * pi) - ty(0)) < 1e-12)
print("rides the torus: ring distance at t = 1.3:", sqrt(tx(1.3) ^ 2 + ty(1.3) ^ 2))
print("z stays inside the tube, max |z| = 1/2:", abs(tz(3 * pi / 2)))

// ---- the picture ---------------------------------------------------------------
graph3d param (2 + cos(3 * t)) * cos(2 * t) / 2, (2 + cos(3 * t)) * sin(2 * t) / 2, sin(3 * t) / 2 from 0 to 6.28318

/* ---- expected output ----
= closes after one lap, P(0) vs P(2*pi): true
= rides the torus: ring distance at t = 1.3: 0.6370338479
= z stays inside the tube, max |z| = 1/2: 0.5
graph3d: param (2 + cos(3 * t)) * cos(2 * t) / 2, (2 + cos(3 * t)) * sin(2 * t) / 2, sin(3 * t) / 2 from 0 to 6.28318
*/

scripts.name: cone-slope
scripts.title: the 45-degree cone z = sqrt(x^2 + y^2)
scripts.text:
/* ============================================================================
cone-slope.epher -- the 45-degree cone z = sqrt(x^2 + y^2)

Spinning the line z = x about the z-axis sweeps the right circular
cone with walls at 45 deg: every horizontal slice is a circle, every
vertical slice through the axis is a V (Apollonius again - slice it
with a plane at the right angle and the conics all fall out; Thomas,
"Thomas' Calculus", ch. 13.6). The script graphs the cone and prints
the slope and slice relations.

Web/desktop:             paste the whole file into the entry, press Enter
The graph lines open the 3D pane in the desktop, web and TUI apps;
the CLI transcript records them as "graph3d:" lines.
============================================================================ */

// ---- the surface ---------------------------------------------------------------
def z(x, y) = sqrt(x ^ 2 + y ^ 2)

// ---- results -------------------------------------------------------------------
print("wall slope along the x-axis:", derivative(sqrt(x ^ 2), 1))
print("z(3, 4), three-four-five on the wall:", z(3, 4))
print("slice z = 2 is the circle r = 2:", z(2, 0) == 2 and z(sqrt(2), sqrt(2)) == 2)

// ---- the picture ---------------------------------------------------------------
graph3d sqrt(x ^ 2 + y ^ 2) from -2.5 to 2.5

/* ---- expected output ----
= wall slope along the x-axis: 1
= z(3, 4), three-four-five on the wall: 5
= slice z = 2 is the circle r = 2: true
graph3d: sqrt(x ^ 2 + y ^ 2) from -2.5 to 2.5
*/

scripts.name: egg-crate-lattice
scripts.title: the periodic bump grid z = sin(3x)*sin(3y)
scripts.text:
/* ============================================================================
egg-crate-lattice.epher -- the periodic bump grid z = sin(3x)*sin(3y)

Multiplying two sines tiles the plane with a lattice of alternating
bumps and dents: peaks of height 1 over a grid of period 2*pi/3 in
both directions, peaks over pits like an egg crate (a standard
teaching surface for periodicity and symmetry, e.g. Thomas,
"Thomas' Calculus", ch. 13.1 on surfaces). The script graphs the
lattice and prints the grid spacing and sample extrema.

Web/desktop:             paste the whole file into the entry, press Enter
The graph lines open the 3D pane in the desktop, web and TUI apps;
the CLI transcript records them as "graph3d:" lines.
============================================================================ */

// ---- the surface ---------------------------------------------------------------
def z(x, y) = sin(3 * x) * sin(3 * y)

// ---- results -------------------------------------------------------------------
print("grid period, 2*pi/3:", 2 * pi / 3)
print("a peak at (pi/6, pi/6):", z(pi / 6, pi / 6))
print("a pit at (pi/2, pi/6):", z(pi / 2, pi / 6))
print("zero along both axes:", z(0, 1.23) == 0)

// ---- the picture ---------------------------------------------------------------
graph3d sin(3 * x) * sin(3 * y) from -3.2 to 3.2

/* ---- expected output ----
= grid period, 2*pi/3: 2.09439510239
= a peak at (pi/6, pi/6): 1
= a pit at (pi/2, pi/6): -1
= zero along both axes: true
graph3d: sin(3 * x) * sin(3 * y) from -3.2 to 3.2
*/

scripts.name: gaussian-bell-surface
scripts.title: the two-dimensional bell and its volume
scripts.text:
/* ============================================================================
gaussian-bell-surface.epher -- the two-dimensional bell and its volume

The radially symmetric bell z = e^(-(x^2 + y^2)) is the bivariate
normal kernel: every vertical slice is a 1D bell, and the whole
surface is generated by spinning one around the axis. Its volume is
the famous integral the 1D bell hides: shifting to polar coordinates,
V = 2*pi * integral r*e^(-r^2) dr, exactly pi (the trick of Poisson;
Stewart, "Calculus", ch. 14.4 on polar double integrals). The script
graphs the surface and reproduces the volume numerically.

Web/desktop:             paste the whole file into the entry, press Enter
The graph lines open the 3D pane in the desktop, web and TUI apps;
the CLI transcript records them as "graph3d:" lines.
============================================================================ */

// ---- the surface ---------------------------------------------------------------
def z(x, y) = e^(0 - x ^ 2 - y ^ 2)

// ---- results -------------------------------------------------------------------
print("peak at the origin:", z(0, 0))
print("slice along y = 0 is the 1D bell:", z(1, 0) == e^(0 - 1))
print("volume, exact pi:", integral(2 * pi * x * e^(0 - x ^ 2), 0, 6))

// ---- the picture ---------------------------------------------------------------
graph3d e^(0 - x ^ 2 - y ^ 2) from -2.5 to 2.5

/* ---- expected output ----
= peak at the origin: 1
= slice along y = 0 is the 1D bell: true
= volume, exact pi: 3.14159265366
graph3d: e^(0 - x ^ 2 - y ^ 2) from -2.5 to 2.5
*/

scripts.name: monkey-saddle
scripts.title: z = x^3 - 3*x*y^2, a saddle for three legs
scripts.text:
/* ============================================================================
monkey-saddle.epher -- z = x^3 - 3*x*y^2, a saddle for three legs

A horse needs two depressions for its legs; a monkey needs a third
for its tail. The polynomial z = x^3 - 3*x*y^2 = r^3*cos(3*theta)
in polar form supplies three symmetric valleys running down toward
theta = pi/3, pi and 5*pi/3, with three ridges between (Courant and
John, "Introduction to Calculus and Analysis", ch. 5; do Carmo,
ch. 3). The script graphs the surface and prints the height at the
six compass directions where the cosine decides.

Web/desktop:             paste the whole file into the entry, press Enter
The graph lines open the 3D pane in the desktop, web and TUI apps;
the CLI transcript records them as "graph3d:" lines.
============================================================================ */

// ---- the surface ---------------------------------------------------------------
def z(x, y) = x ^ 3 - 3 * x * y ^ 2

// ---- results -------------------------------------------------------------------
print("along theta = 0 (a ridge), z(1, 0):", z(1, 0))
print("along theta = pi/3 (a valley), z(0.5, 0.866):", z(0.5, sqrt(3) / 2))
print("along theta = 2*pi/3 (a ridge), z(-0.5, 0.866):", z(-0.5, sqrt(3) / 2))
print("polar form r^3*cos(3*theta) at r = 1, theta = pi:", cos(3 * pi))

// ---- the picture ---------------------------------------------------------------
graph3d x ^ 3 - 3 * x * y ^ 2 from -1.8 to 1.8

/* ---- expected output ----
= along theta = 0 (a ridge), z(1, 0): 1
= along theta = pi/3 (a valley), z(0.5, 0.866): -1
= along theta = 2*pi/3 (a ridge), z(-0.5, 0.866): 1
= polar form r^3*cos(3*theta) at r = 1, theta = pi: -1
graph3d: x ^ 3 - 3 * x * y ^ 2 from -1.8 to 1.8
*/

scripts.name: paraboloid-bowl
scripts.title: the bowl z = x^2 + y^2
scripts.text:
/* ============================================================================
paraboloid-bowl.epher -- the bowl z = x^2 + y^2

Rotating the parabola z = r^2 about its axis sweeps the elliptic
paraboloid, the shape of every satellite dish and radio telescope:
parallel rays falling on it reflect through one focus (Thomas,
"Thomas' Calculus", ch. 13.7, on quadratic surfaces; the reflection
law is in any optics text). Horizontal slices are circles of radius
sqrt(z), vertical slices are parabolas. The script graphs the bowl
and prints the slice relations.

Web/desktop:             paste the whole file into the entry, press Enter
The graph lines open the 3D pane in the desktop, web and TUI apps;
the CLI transcript records them as "graph3d:" lines.
============================================================================ */

// ---- the surface ---------------------------------------------------------------
def z(x, y) = x ^ 2 + y ^ 2

// ---- results -------------------------------------------------------------------
print("the bottom of the bowl:", z(0, 0))
print("radius of the z = 4 slice:", sqrt(4))
print("slice circle relation, z equals r^2:", z(2, 0) == 4 and abs(z(sqrt(2), sqrt(2)) - 4) < 1e-12)
print("height at the rim sample (1, 1):", z(1, 1))

// ---- the picture ---------------------------------------------------------------
graph3d x ^ 2 + y ^ 2 from -2.5 to 2.5

/* ---- expected output ----
= the bottom of the bowl: 0
= radius of the z = 4 slice: 2
= slice circle relation, z equals r^2: true
= height at the rim sample (1, 1): 2
graph3d: x ^ 2 + y ^ 2 from -2.5 to 2.5
*/

scripts.name: ripple-tank
scripts.title: circular waves from a point source
scripts.text:
/* ============================================================================
ripple-tank.epher -- circular waves from a point source

A stone in still water sends out rings whose height falls off as they
spread: z = sin(k*r) / (1 + r) oscillates with wavenumber k and
decays like 1/r, sharing its energy over the growing circumference
(the Huygens construction; Crawford, "Waves", Berkeley Physics
ch. 8, on circular waves). With k = 3 the crests sit where 3*r is an
odd multiple of pi/2, one every 2*pi/3 along a radius. The script
graphs the surface and prints the ring spacing.

Web/desktop:             paste the whole file into the entry, press Enter
The graph lines open the 3D pane in the desktop, web and TUI apps;
the CLI transcript records them as "graph3d:" lines.
============================================================================ */

// ---- the model -----------------------------------------------------------------
const k = 3    // wavenumber: crests every 2*pi/k of radius

// ---- results -------------------------------------------------------------------
print("the source stays calm in this model, sin(0) = 0:", sin(0) == 0)
print("first crest on the x-axis at r = pi/(2*k):", pi / (2 * k))
print("ring spacing, 2*pi/k:", 2 * pi / k)
print("decay from r = 1 to r = 4:", (1 / (1 + 1)) / (1 / (1 + 4)))

// ---- the picture ---------------------------------------------------------------
graph3d sin(3 * sqrt(x ^ 2 + y ^ 2)) / (1 + sqrt(x ^ 2 + y ^ 2)) from -6.3 to 6.3

/* ---- expected output ----
= the source stays calm in this model, sin(0) = 0: true
= first crest on the x-axis at r = pi/(2*k): 0.523598775598
= ring spacing, 2*pi/k: 2.09439510239
= decay from r = 1 to r = 4: 2.5
graph3d: sin(3 * sqrt(x ^ 2 + y ^ 2)) / (1 + sqrt(x ^ 2 + y ^ 2)) from -6.3 to 6.3
*/

scripts.name: saddle-surface
scripts.title: the hyperbolic paraboloid z = x^2 - y^2
scripts.text:
/* ============================================================================
saddle-surface.epher -- the hyperbolic paraboloid z = x^2 - y^2

The saddle rises along the x-axis and falls along the y-axis, so the
origin is simultaneously a minimum and a maximum: the classic saddle
point (Thomas, "Thomas' Calculus", ch. 13.7; do Carmo, "Differential
Geometry of Curves and Surfaces", ch. 3). Slicing by y = 0 gives the
upward parabola z = x^2; slicing by x = 0 gives the downward one
z = -y^2. Pringles are the food version. The script graphs the
surface and prints the slice values that exhibit the two parabolas.

Web/desktop:             paste the whole file into the entry, press Enter
The graph lines open the 3D pane in the desktop, web and TUI apps;
the CLI transcript records them as "graph3d:" lines.
============================================================================ */

// ---- the surface ---------------------------------------------------------------
def z(x, y) = x ^ 2 - y ^ 2

// ---- results -------------------------------------------------------------------
print("slice along the x-axis (y = 0), z(1, 0):", z(1, 0))
print("slice along the y-axis (x = 0), z(0, 1):", z(0, 1))
print("at the origin both slices meet:", z(0, 0))
print("on the diagonal x = y, z(2, 2):", z(2, 2))
print("a level curve z = 1 is the hyperbola x^2 - y^2 = 1")

// ---- the picture ---------------------------------------------------------------
graph3d x ^ 2 - y ^ 2 from -2.5 to 2.5

/* ---- expected output ----
= slice along the x-axis (y = 0), z(1, 0): 1
= slice along the y-axis (x = 0), z(0, 1): -1
= at the origin both slices meet: 0
= on the diagonal x = y, z(2, 2): 0
= a level curve z = 1 is the hyperbola x^2 - y^2 = 1
graph3d: x ^ 2 - y ^ 2 from -2.5 to 2.5
*/

scripts.name: arithmetic-across-bases
scripts.title: mixed-base sums and products
scripts.text:
/* ============================================================================
arithmetic-across-bases.epher -- mixed-base sums and products

Arithmetic mixes base spellings freely, because a prefix only changes
how a value is spelled, never what it is: 0xFF + 0b1 + 0o10 adds 255,
1 and 8 to 264. Results print in decimal, and the bin, oct and hex
builtins spell them back. The script only uses the builtins and
literals; it does not reimplement any conversion.

Source: standard numeral systems; positional notation in bases 2, 8
and 16. Every value here is small, so all arithmetic is exact.

Web/desktop:             paste the whole file into the entry, press Enter

There is no knob: the sample expressions are the point of the script.
============================================================================ */

// ---- one sum, spelled three ways ---------------------------------------------------------
print("255 + 1 + 8 = 264, in decimal:", 0xFF + 0b1 + 0o10)
print("264 spelled in binary, 0b100001000:", bin(264))
print("264 spelled in octal, 0o410:", oct(264))
print("264 spelled in hex, 0x108:", hex(264))
print("the literal 0x108 reads back as:", 0x108)          // the spelling reads back

// ---- a product across bases ----------------------------------------------------------------
print("10 * 10 = 100:", 0b1010 * 0o12)
print("100 spelled in hex, 0x64:", hex(100))
print("the literal 0x64 reads back as:", 0x64)

// ---- subtraction and powers -----------------------------------------------------------------
print("256 - 1 = 255:", 0x100 - 0b1)
print("2^8 = 256, written with a binary two:", 0b10 ^ 8)
/* ---- expected output ----
= 255 + 1 + 8 = 264, in decimal: 264
= 264 spelled in binary, 0b100001000: 0b100001000
= 264 spelled in octal, 0o410: 0o410
= 264 spelled in hex, 0x108: 0x108
= the literal 0x108 reads back as: 264
= 10 * 10 = 100: 100
= 100 spelled in hex, 0x64: 0x64
= the literal 0x64 reads back as: 100
= 256 - 1 = 255: 255
= 2^8 = 256, written with a binary two: 256
*/

scripts.name: binary-to-decimal
scripts.title: binary literals read as decimal values
scripts.text:
/* ============================================================================
binary-to-decimal.epher -- binary literals read as decimal values

Evaluates binary literals and prints their decimal values. A binary
literal is the prefix 0b followed by bits, and its value is the sum of
the powers of two in it: 0b101010 = 32 + 8 + 2 = 42. The prefix
changes the spelling, never the value, so the results below are plain
decimal numbers.

Source: standard numeral systems; positional notation in base 2, the
place values 1, 2, 4, 8, 16 and 32 made explicit under the first
check. Evaluation is exact for every value here.

Web/desktop:             paste the whole file into the entry, press Enter

There is no knob: the sample literals are the point of the script.
============================================================================ */

// ---- the place values -----------------------------------------------------------------
// 0b101010 has ones in the 32, 8 and 2 places, so it is 42.
print("32 + 8 + 2:", 32 + 8 + 2)
print("reads as 42:", 0b101010)
print("eight bits set, 128 + 64 + ... + 1 = 255:", 0b11111111)
print("2^10 = 1024:", 0b10000000000)
print("the largest four-bit value, 15:", 0b1111)

// ---- a list at a glance ---------------------------------------------------------------
print("0b1 reads as:", 0b1)
print("0b10 reads as:", 0b10)
print("0b101 reads as:", 0b101)
print("0b1111 reads as:", 0b1111)
print("0b101010 reads as:", 0b101010)
print("0b11111111 reads as:", 0b11111111)
/* ---- expected output ----
= 32 + 8 + 2: 42
= reads as 42: 42
= eight bits set, 128 + 64 + ... + 1 = 255: 255
= 2^10 = 1024: 1024
= the largest four-bit value, 15: 15
= 0b1 reads as: 1
= 0b10 reads as: 2
= 0b101 reads as: 5
= 0b1111 reads as: 15
= 0b101010 reads as: 42
= 0b11111111 reads as: 255
*/

scripts.title: how many 1 bits a number has, the popcount

scripts.name: decimal-to-binary
scripts.title: decimal values spelled in base 2
scripts.text:
/* ============================================================================
decimal-to-binary.epher -- decimal values spelled in base 2

Spells decimal integers in binary with the bin builtin. The spelling
is the language's binary literal form: the prefix 0b, then the bits,
so bin(42) prints 0b101010 and reads back as the literal 0b101010,
which is the same value 42. The script only calls the builtin; it does
not reimplement the conversion.

Source: standard numeral systems; positional notation in base 2, with
place values 1, 2, 4, 8, ... (the next script spells back the other
way). bin is exact for every integer the calculator can hold.

Web/desktop:             paste the whole file into the entry, press Enter

There is no knob: the sample values are the point of the script.
============================================================================ */

// ---- named spellings ---------------------------------------------------------------
print("42 = 32 + 8 + 2 = 0b101010:", bin(42))
print("eight bits set, 0b11111111:", bin(255))
print("2^10, a one and ten zeros:", bin(1024))
// ---- a list at a glance ---------------------------------------------------------------
for x in {0, 1, 2, 7, 8, 42, 255} do bin(x)
// ---- the spelling reads back -------------------------------------------------------------
print("the literal form of bin(42), same value:", 0b101010)
print("255, the largest eight-bit value:", 0b11111111)
print("the literal 0b101010 reads back as:", 0b101010)
/* ---- expected output ----
= 42 = 32 + 8 + 2 = 0b101010: 0b101010
= eight bits set, 0b11111111: 0b11111111
= 2^10, a one and ten zeros: 0b10000000000
= {0b0, 0b1, 0b10, 0b111, 0b1000, 0b101010, 0b11111111}
= the literal form of bin(42), same value: 42
= 255, the largest eight-bit value: 255
= the literal 0b101010 reads back as: 42
*/

scripts.name: decimal-to-hex
scripts.title: decimal values spelled in base 16
scripts.text:
/* ============================================================================
decimal-to-hex.epher -- decimal values spelled in base 16

Spells decimal integers in hexadecimal with the hex builtin. The
spelling is the language's hex literal form: the prefix 0x, then the
digits 0 to 9 and a to f in lowercase, so hex(255) prints 0xff and
reads back as the literal 0xff. The famous value 3735928559 spells as
0xdeadbeef. The script only calls the builtin; it does not reimplement
the conversion.

Source: standard numeral systems; positional notation in base 16, with
place values 1, 16, 256, ... . Hex is a compact binary shorthand: each
hex digit covers four bits. hex is exact for every integer the
calculator can hold.

Web/desktop:             paste the whole file into the entry, press Enter

There is no knob: the sample values are the point of the script.
============================================================================ */

// ---- named spellings ---------------------------------------------------------------
print("15 * 16 + 15 = 0xff:", hex(255))
print("the classic 0xdeadbeef:", hex(3735928559))
print("16^3, 0x1000:", hex(4096))
// ---- a list at a glance ---------------------------------------------------------------
for x in {0, 10, 16, 255, 4096} do hex(x)
// ---- the spelling reads back -------------------------------------------------------------
print("the literal form of hex(255), same value:", 0xff)
print("3735928559 again:", 0xdeadbeef)
print("the literal 0xff reads back as:", 0xff)
print("the literal 0xdeadbeef reads back as:", 0xdeadbeef)
/* ---- expected output ----
= 15 * 16 + 15 = 0xff: 0xff
= the classic 0xdeadbeef: 0xdeadbeef
= 16^3, 0x1000: 0x1000
= {0x0, 0xa, 0x10, 0xff, 0x1000}
= the literal form of hex(255), same value: 255
= 3735928559 again: 3735928559
= the literal 0xff reads back as: 255
= the literal 0xdeadbeef reads back as: 3735928559
*/

scripts.name: decimal-to-octal
scripts.title: decimal values spelled in base 8
scripts.text:
/* ============================================================================
decimal-to-octal.epher -- decimal values spelled in base 8

Spells decimal integers in octal with the oct builtin. The spelling is
the language's octal literal form: the prefix 0o, then the digits 0 to
7, so oct(42) prints 0o52 (four eights and two ones) and reads back as
the literal 0o52. The script only calls the builtin; it does not
reimplement the conversion.

Source: standard numeral systems; positional notation in base 8, with
place values 1, 8, 64, ... . Octal was a favourite shorthand for
binary on early computers, since each octal digit covers three bits.
oct is exact for every integer the calculator can hold.

Web/desktop:             paste the whole file into the entry, press Enter

There is no knob: the sample values are the point of the script.
============================================================================ */

// ---- named spellings ---------------------------------------------------------------
print("42 = 5 * 8 + 2 = 0o52:", oct(42))
print("8^2, 0o100:", oct(64))
print("7 * 64 + 7 * 8 + 7 = 0o777:", oct(511))
// ---- a list at a glance ---------------------------------------------------------------
for x in {0, 1, 7, 8, 42, 64, 511} do oct(x)
// ---- the spelling reads back -------------------------------------------------------------
print("the literal form of oct(42), same value:", 0o52)
print("64, the third power of 8:", 0o100)
print("the literal 0o52 reads back as:", 0o52)
/* ---- expected output ----
= 42 = 5 * 8 + 2 = 0o52: 0o52
= 8^2, 0o100: 0o100
= 7 * 64 + 7 * 8 + 7 = 0o777: 0o777
= {0o0, 0o1, 0o7, 0o10, 0o52, 0o100, 0o777}
= the literal form of oct(42), same value: 42
= 64, the third power of 8: 64
= the literal 0o52 reads back as: 42
*/

scripts.name: hexadecimal-to-decimal
scripts.title: hex literals read as decimal values
scripts.text:
/* ============================================================================
hexadecimal-to-decimal.epher -- hex literals read as decimal values

Evaluates hexadecimal literals and prints their decimal values. A hex
literal is the prefix 0x followed by digits 0 to 9 and a to f, and its
value is the sum of the powers of sixteen in it: 0xff = 15 * 16 + 15 =
255. The prefix changes the spelling, never the value, so the results
below are plain decimal numbers.

Source: standard numeral systems; positional notation in base 16, the
place values 1, 16, 256 and so on. Evaluation is exact for every value
here (the largest, 0xdeadbeef, stays far below the exactness limit).

Web/desktop:             paste the whole file into the entry, press Enter

There is no knob: the sample literals are the point of the script.
============================================================================ */

// ---- named values --------------------------------------------------------------------
print("fifteen, the largest single digit:", 0xF)
print("15 * 16 + 15 = 255:", 0xFF)
print("sixteen, 0x10, not ten:", 0x10)
print("the classic, 3735928559:", 0xdeadbeef)
// ---- a list at a glance ---------------------------------------------------------------
for x in {0x1, 0x9, 0xA, 0xF, 0x10, 0xFF, 0x100} do x
// ---- the place values -----------------------------------------------------------------
print("15 * 16 + 15:", 15 * 16 + 15)              // how 0xff reads
print("0xFF is 255:", 0xFF == 255)
print("0xA is 10:", 0xA == 10)
/* ---- expected output ----
= fifteen, the largest single digit: 15
= 15 * 16 + 15 = 255: 255
= sixteen, 0x10, not ten: 16
= the classic, 3735928559: 3735928559
= {1, 9, 10, 15, 16, 255, 256}
= 15 * 16 + 15: 255
= 0xFF is 255: true
= 0xA is 10: true
*/

scripts.name: octal-to-decimal
scripts.title: octal literals read as decimal values
scripts.text:

octal-to-decimal.epher -- octal literals read as decimal values

Evaluates octal literals and prints their decimal values. An octal

= 7 * 64 + 7 * 8 + 7: 511
= one eight and seven ones, 15: 15

= 0o1 reads as: 1

scripts.name: power-of-two-check
scripts.title: the bit trick n & (n - 1) == 0
scripts.text:
/* ============================================================================
power-of-two-check.epher -- the bit trick n & (n - 1) == 0

A positive integer is a power of two exactly when n & (n - 1) is 0:
subtracting 1 borrows through the trailing zeros, flipping the lowest
1 bit to 0 and everything below it to 1, so the and clears that one
bit and leaves the rest untouched. A pure power has only that one bit,
so the result is 0; any other n keeps a higher 1 bit. The guard n > 0
matters because 0 itself would pass the bit test. The script checks a
list of values with the bitwise builtin; it does not reimplement the
test.

Source: standard bit-twiddling lore; see Henry Warren, "Hacker's
Delight", 2nd ed., section 2.1. All values are small and exact.

Web/desktop:             paste the whole file into the entry, press Enter

There is no knob: the sample values are the point of the script.
============================================================================ */

// ---- the named checks ---------------------------------------------------------------
print("1024 is a power of two:", 1024 > 0 and (1024 & 1023) == 0)
print("1000 is a power of two:", 1000 > 0 and (1000 & 999) == 0)
print("256 is a power of two:", 256 > 0 and (256 & 255) == 0)
print("100 is a power of two:", 100 > 0 and (100 & 99) == 0)
// 0 would pass the bit test alone (0 & -1 is 0), which is why the
// positivity guard sits in every check above.
print("0 and the guard:", 0 > 0 and (0 & -1) == 0)

// ---- a list at a glance ---------------------------------------------------------------
for x in {1, 2, 3, 4, 16, 100, 255, 256, 1000, 1024} do print("is " + str(x) + " a power of two:", x > 0 and (x & (x - 1)) == 0)
/* ---- expected output ----
= 1024 is a power of two: true
= 1000 is a power of two: false
= 256 is a power of two: true
= 100 is a power of two: false
= 0 and the guard: false
= {is 1 a power of two: true, is 2 a power of two: true, is 3 a power of two: false, is 4 a power of two: true, is 16 a power of two: true, is 100 a power of two: false, is 255 a power of two: false, is 256 a power of two: true, is 1000 a power of two: false, is 1024 a power of two: true}
*/

scripts.name: roman-numerals
scripts.title: decimal to Roman and back, for 1 to 3999
scripts.text:
/* ============================================================================
roman-numerals.epher -- decimal to Roman and back, for 1 to 3999

Spells numbers in the classic subtractive Roman system, where fours
and nines write one before five or ten: 4 = IV, 9 = IX, 40 = XL,
90 = XC, 400 = CD, 900 = CM. The def roman(n) builds each digit place
from a small digit helper with the symbols of that place; checks:
1994 = MCMXCIV and 2026 = MMXXVI. A second def val(c) scores a single
Roman symbol, and a packed while loop (guide 1.30) parses a numeral
with the subtractive rule: when a symbol is smaller than the next one,
it subtracts instead of adding, so MCMXCIV reads as 1994.

Source: the standard Roman numeral convention, as tabulated in any
reference; the subtractive scheme is the one in common use since the
Middle Ages. All values are exact.

Web/desktop:             paste the whole file into the entry, press Enter

There is no knob: the sample numbers are the point of the script.
============================================================================ */

/* ---- the digit helper ----------------------------------------------------------------
digit(v, one, five, ten) spells one digit v with the place symbols:
1 to 3 repeat one, 4 is one before five, 5 is five, 6 to 8 put one to
three ones after five, and 9 is one before ten. */
def digit(v, one, five, ten) = if v == 0 then "" else if v < 4 then one + digit(v - 1, one, five, ten) else if v == 4 then one + five else if v == 5 then five else if v < 9 then five + digit(v - 5, one, five, ten) else one + ten
// roman(n) takes the thousands, hundreds, tens and units digits apart
// with floor and mod, and spells each with its place symbols.
def roman(n) = digit(floor(n / 1000), "M", "M", "M") + digit(mod(floor(n / 100), 10), "C", "D", "M") + digit(mod(floor(n / 10), 10), "X", "L", "C") + digit(mod(n, 10), "I", "V", "X")

// ---- decimal to Roman ------------------------------------------------------------------
print("1994 is", roman(1994))            // MCMXCIV: M CM XC IV
print("2026 is", roman(2026))            // MMXXVI
print("2024 is", roman(2024))            // MMXXIV
print("3999 is", roman(3999))            // MMMCMXCIX, the largest of the range
for x in {1, 4, 9, 49, 99, 1994, 2026, 3999} do roman(x)

/* ---- Roman to decimal ---------------------------------------------------------------------
val(c) is the value of one symbol; the while loop walks the numeral
and applies the subtractive rule: a smaller symbol before a larger one
is subtracted (I before V is one less, so IV is four). */
def val(c) = if c == "I" then 1 else if c == "V" then 5 else if c == "X" then 10 else if c == "L" then 50 else if c == "C" then 100 else if c == "D" then 500 else if c == "M" then 1000 else 0
const s = "MCMXCIV"
v = {1, 0}
while v[1] <= len(s) do v = {v[1] + 1, v[2] + (if v[1] < len(s) and val(s[v[1]]) < val(s[v[1] + 1]) then 0 - val(s[v[1]]) else val(s[v[1]]))}
print("MCMXCIV reads as:", v[2])         // 1994, the round trip of the first check
/* ---- expected output ----
= 1994 is MCMXCIV
= 2026 is MMXXVI
= 2024 is MMXXIV
= 3999 is MMMCMXCIX
= {I, IV, IX, XLIX, XCIX, MCMXCIV, MMXXVI, MMMCMXCIX}
= {1, 0}
= MCMXCIV reads as: 1994
*/
