*/

scripts.name: empirical-rule
scripts.title: 68, 95, 99.7 percent of a normal distribution
scripts.text:
/* ============================================================================
empirical-rule.epher -- 68, 95, 99.7 percent of a normal distribution

The empirical rule for a normal distribution, from the builtin
normcdf (guide 1.20): about 68 percent of the probability lies within
one standard deviation of the mean, 95 percent within two, and 99.7
percent within three. In standard units the three areas are
P(-1 < Z < 1), P(-2 < Z < 2) and P(-3 < Z < 3), each computed as
normcdf(k) - normcdf(-k) and shown as a percent below.

Web/desktop:             paste the whole file into the entry, press Enter
Everything also works line by line in the TUI.

No knobs: the rule is the demonstration.
============================================================================ */

// ---- the three bands, as probabilities and as percents ---------------------------------
print("P(mu - sigma < X < mu + sigma):", normcdf(1) - normcdf(-1))
print("within two standard deviations:", normcdf(2) - normcdf(-2))
print("within three standard deviations:", normcdf(3) - normcdf(-3))

print("within 1 sd:", (normcdf(1) - normcdf(-1)) * 100, "percent")
print("within 2 sd:", (normcdf(2) - normcdf(-2)) * 100, "percent")
print("within 3 sd:", (normcdf(3) - normcdf(-3)) * 100, "percent")

/* ---- expected output ----
= P(mu - sigma < X < mu + sigma): 0.682689492137
= within two standard deviations: 0.954499736104
= within three standard deviations: 0.997300203937
= within 1 sd: 68.2689492137 percent
= within 2 sd: 95.4499736104 percent
= within 3 sd: 99.7300203937 percent
*/

scripts.name: normal-areas
scripts.title: areas under the standard normal curve
scripts.text:
/* ============================================================================
normal-areas.epher -- areas under the standard normal curve

Three textbook areas under the standard normal density, from the
builtin normcdf (guide 1.20): the probability that Z lies below 1.5,
above -0.8, and between 0.5 and 1.5. The middle one uses the symmetry
of the curve: P(Z > -0.8) equals P(Z < 0.8), and the last subtracts
the two cumulative areas. normcdf(x) is the lower tail P(Z <= x).

Web/desktop:             paste the whole file into the entry, press Enter
Everything also works line by line in the TUI.

No knobs: the three cut points below are the demonstration.
============================================================================ */

// ---- P(Z < 1.5): most of the curve sits below 1.5 -------------------------------
print("the lower tail at 1.5:", normcdf(1.5))

// ---- P(Z > -0.8): the upper tail at -0.8, by symmetry the lower tail at 0.8 -------
print("the upper tail at -0.8, or equally normcdf(0.8):", 1 - normcdf(-0.8))

// ---- P(0.5 < Z < 1.5): between two cut points, subtract the lower tails ------------
print("between 0.5 and 1.5:", normcdf(1.5) - normcdf(0.5))

// ---- the two cut points for the last area, for the record ----------------------------
print("normcdf(1.5):", normcdf(1.5))
print("normcdf(0.5):", normcdf(0.5))

/* ---- expected output ----
= the lower tail at 1.5: 0.933192798731
= the upper tail at -0.8, or equally normcdf(0.8): 0.788144601417
= between 0.5 and 1.5: 0.241730337457
= normcdf(1.5): 0.933192798731
= normcdf(0.5): 0.691462461274
*/

normal-percentiles.epher -- cut points that leave a given area below

The standard normal percentiles z such that P(Z <= z) equals the
probability in `p`, from the builtin inverse normal invnorm(p, 0, 1)
(guide 1.20). The 90th percentile is the familiar 1.2816, the 97.5th
is the 1.96 of two-sided 95 percent intervals, and the 99th is 2.3263.
The last three lines feed each percentile back through normcdf: the

*/

poisson-approximation.epher -- the binomial for rare events as a Poisson

Approximates the binomial probability P(X <= 3) for X with num = 1000
trials and p = 0.002 (a rare event) by the Poisson with rate
lambda = num * p = 2, using the builtin poissoncdf (guide 1.20). The
rule of thumb: the Poisson approximates the binomial well when num is

scripts.name: choosing-a-fit
scripts.title: four curves on one growth dataset, compare the r
scripts.text:
/* ============================================================================
choosing-a-fit.epher -- four curves on one growth dataset, compare the r

Fits all four builtin curves to the same (hour, size) pairs in `xs`
and `ys` and lets the reported correlations pick the model. The sizes
grow by a nearly constant ratio each hour, the fingerprint of
exponential growth, so expreg should win: its r = 0.9999 beats the
linear 0.9312, the quadratic 0.9963, the power 0.9552 and the
logarithmic 0.8051. The manual Pearson r below recomputes the
correlation between x and ln(y) by the textbook formula; its square,
r^2 = 0.99984..., is the fraction of the log-variance the model
explains and agrees with the r in the expreg display.

Web/desktop:             paste the whole file into the entry, press Enter
Everything also works line by line in the TUI.

The knobs to edit are `xs` and `ys` below. Everything above the results
section is machinery you can leave alone.
============================================================================ */

// ---- the knobs -----------------------------------------------------------------
const xs = {1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8}   // hours since the culture was started
const ys = {2.5, 3.6, 5.4, 8.1, 12.2, 18.3, 27.5, 41.3}   // size, thousands

// ---- helpers: Pearson r of x against ln(y), textbook formula ----------------------
def lny(k) = ln(ys[k]) // natural log of the k-th size
def sumlny(k) = if k > len(ys) then 0 else lny(k) + sumlny(k + 1) // sum of the logs
def mlog() = sumlny(1) / len(ys) // mean of ln(y)
def slx(k) = if k > len(ys) then 0 else (xs[k] - mean(xs)) * (lny(k) - mlog()) + slx(k + 1)
def sll(k) = if k > len(ys) then 0 else (lny(k) - mlog()) ^ 2 + sll(k + 1)
def rlog() = slx(1) / sqrt(sum((xs - mean(xs)) ^ 2) * sll(1)) // r of x vs ln(y)

// ---- the four candidate models on the same data -------------------------------------
print("straight line, the worst of the four:", linreg(xs, ys))
print("parabola, good but not best:", quadreg(xs, ys))
print("exponential, the clear winner:", expreg(xs, ys))
print("power curve, which must pass through zero:", powreg(xs, ys))
print("logarithmic, badly bent the wrong way:", logreg(xs, ys))

// ---- the r^2 remark from the manual Pearson r -----------------------------------------
print("Pearson r of x against ln(y):", rlog())
print("and its square, r^2:", rlog() ^ 2)

/* ---- expected output ----
= straight line, the worst of the four: y = 5.1655*x + -8.3821 (r = 0.9312)
= parabola, good but not best: y = 0.9827*x^2 + -3.6792*x + 6.3589 (r = 0.9963)
= exponential, the clear winner: y = 1.6289*e^(0.4032*x) (r = 0.9999)
= power curve, which must pass through zero: y = 1.6892*x^1.3414 (r = 0.9552)
= logarithmic, badly bent the wrong way: y = -5.7535 + 15.5525*ln(x) (r = 0.8051)
= Pearson r of x against ln(y): 0.999920198771
= and its square, r^2: 0.99984040391
*/

scripts.name: linear-regression-prediction
scripts.title: least squares by hand, then predict
scripts.text:
/* ============================================================================
linear-regression-prediction.epher -- least squares by hand, then predict

Fits the least-squares line to the five (hours, score) pairs in `xs`
and `ys` with the classroom formulas: the slope is
const b1 = sum((x - xbar)(y - ybar)) / sum((x - xbar)^2) and the intercept
is b0 = ybar - b1 * xbar. epher's linreg fits the same line, so the
print of linreg below is the cross-check. The line then predicts the
score for six study hours, just past the data.

Web/desktop:             paste the whole file into the entry, press Enter
Everything also works line by line in the TUI.

The knobs to edit are `xs` and `ys` below. Everything above the results
section is machinery you can leave alone.
============================================================================ */

// ---- the knobs -----------------------------------------------------------------
const xs = {1, 2, 3, 4, 5}       // hours of study, one per student
const ys = {2.1, 3.8, 6.1, 7.9, 10.2}   // practice-test scores out of 15

// ---- helpers: the classroom least-squares formulas ------------------------------
def mx() = mean(xs) // mean of x
def my() = mean(ys) // mean of y
def sxy() = sum((xs - mx()) * (ys - my())) // sum of x-deviation times y-deviation
def sxx() = sum((xs - mx()) ^ 2) // sum of squared x-deviations
def b1() = sxy() / sxx() // the least-squares slope
def b0() = my() - b1() * mx() // the least-squares intercept

// ---- the pieces of the fit -----------------------------------------------------------
print("sum of x-deviation times y-deviation:", sxy())
print("sum of squared x-deviations:", sxx())
print("slope b1:", b1())
print("intercept b0:", b0())

// ---- prediction at a new x -------------------------------------------------------------
print("predicted score at 6 hours:", b0() + b1() * 6)
print("cross-check, the builtin reports the same line:", linreg(xs, ys))

/* ---- expected output ----
= sum of x-deviation times y-deviation: 20.3
= sum of squared x-deviations: 10
= slope b1: 2.03
= intercept b0: -0.07
= predicted score at 6 hours: 12.11
= cross-check, the builtin reports the same line: y = 2.03*x + -0.07 (r = 0.9988)
*/

Fits the least-squares logarithmic curve y = a + b * ln(x) to the

scripts.name: pearson-correlation
scripts.title: the correlation coefficient by its formula
scripts.text:
/* ============================================================================
pearson-correlation.epher -- the correlation coefficient by its formula

The Pearson correlation r of the seven (hours, score) pairs in `xs`
and `ys`, from the textbook formula r = sxy / sqrt(sxx * syy), where
each s is a sum of squared or paired deviations from the means. The
builtin linreg prints r inside its display string, and the number
below should agree with it. The syy term prints as the exact fraction
6424/7 because epher shows repeating decimals as fractions.

Web/desktop:             paste the whole file into the entry, press Enter
Everything also works line by line in the TUI.

The knobs to edit are `xs` and `ys` below. Everything above the results
section is machinery you can leave alone.
============================================================================ */

// ---- the knobs -----------------------------------------------------------------
const xs = {1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7}     // hours of study, one per student
const ys = {55, 63, 68, 74, 79, 85, 90}   // exam scores out of 100, same order

// ---- helpers: the sums behind the textbook formula --------------------------------
def mx() = mean(xs)
def my() = mean(ys)
def sxy() = sum((xs - mx()) * (ys - my())) // paired deviations, x and y
def sxx() = sum((xs - mx()) ^ 2) // x-deviations squared
def syy() = sum((ys - my()) ^ 2) // y-deviations squared
def r() = sxy() / sqrt(sxx() * syy()) // Pearson correlation

// ---- the formula, piece by piece ------------------------------------------------------
print("sxy:", sxy())
print("sxx:", sxx())
print("syy:", syy())
print("Pearson r:", r())
print("cross-check, its display string reports the same r:", linreg(xs, ys))

/* ---- expected output ----
= sxy: 160
= sxx: 28
= syy: 6424/7
= Pearson r: 0.998130257012
= cross-check, its display string reports the same r: y = 5.7143*x + 50.5714 (r = 0.9981)
*/

/* ============================================================================
quadratic-regression.epher -- fit a parabola to braking distance data

Fits the least-squares curve y = a * x^2 + b * x + c to the braking
distances in `ys` recorded at the speeds in `xs` with the builtin
quadreg (guide 1.20), which prints the fitted model and the
correlation r as a display string. Physics says braking distance grows
with the square of speed, so a parabola should fit well; r = 0.9985
confirms it. The data are illustrative example values.

Web/desktop:             paste the whole file into the entry, press Enter
Everything also works line by line in the TUI.

The knobs to edit are `xs` and `ys` below. Everything above the results
section is machinery you can leave alone.
============================================================================ */

// ---- the knobs -----------------------------------------------------------------
const xs = {20, 30, 40, 50, 60}   // speed, kilometers per hour
const ys = {6.4, 13.2, 25.8, 37.4, 58.1}   // braking distance, meters

// ---- the fitted parabola ------------------------------------------------------------
print("least-squares quadratic, with its correlation r:", quadreg(xs, ys))

/* ---- expected output ----
= least-squares quadratic, with its correlation r: y = 0.0191*x^2 + -0.2554*x + 3.94 (r = 0.9985)
*/

scripts.name: coefficient-of-variation
scripts.title: spread relative to the mean, as a percent
scripts.text:
/* ============================================================================
coefficient-of-variation.epher -- spread relative to the mean, as a percent

The coefficient of variation of two datasets, stdev / mean as a percent:
a unit-free spread measure that lets datasets with different means or
units be compared. Ten exam scores (mean 81.3) scatter more, relative
to their mean, than eight adult heights in centimeters (mean 174).
The stdev here is the population version (the builtin divides by n).

Web/desktop:             paste the whole file into the entry, press Enter
Everything also works line by line in the TUI.

The knobs to edit are `data` and `h` below. Everything above the results
section is machinery you can leave alone.
============================================================================ */

// ---- the knobs -----------------------------------------------------------------
const data = {72, 85, 91, 64, 88, 79, 83, 95, 70, 86}   // exam scores, out of 100
const h = {170, 175, 168, 182, 177, 171, 169, 180}   // adult heights, centimeters

// ---- the coefficient of variation as a percent -----------------------------------
print("exam scores, CV:", stdev(data) / mean(data) * 100, "percent")
print("heights, CV:", stdev(h) / mean(h) * 100, "percent")

// ---- what feeds it ------------------------------------------------------------------
print("exam scores, mean:", mean(data))
print("exam scores, stdev:", stdev(data))
print("heights, mean:", mean(h))
print("heights, stdev:", stdev(h))

/* ---- expected output ----
= exam scores, CV: 11.5653864678 percent
= heights, CV: 2.84468245305 percent
= exam scores, mean: 81.3
= exam scores, stdev: 9.40265919833
= heights, mean: 174
= heights, stdev: 4.94974746831
*/

scripts.name: five-number-summary
scripts.title: min, Q1, median, Q3, max of a dataset
scripts.text:
/* ============================================================================
five-number-summary.epher -- min, Q1, median, Q3, max of a dataset

The five-number summary of the ten exam scores in `data`: the minimum, the
first quartile, the median, the third quartile and the maximum. Quartiles
come from the builtin quartile(data, k), which follows the TI-83/84
convention: the median of the lower half for Q1, of the upper half for
Q3, and on an even count the median is the mean of the two middle values.

Web/desktop:             paste the whole file into the entry, press Enter
Everything also works line by line in the TUI.

The one knob to edit is `data` below. Everything above the results section
is machinery you can leave alone.
============================================================================ */

// ---- the knob -----------------------------------------------------------------
const data = {72, 85, 91, 64, 88, 79, 83, 95, 70, 86}   // exam scores, 10 students

// ---- the five numbers -----------------------------------------------------------
print("min:", min(data))              // smallest score
print("Q1:", quartile(data, 1))       // median of the lower half
print("median:", quartile(data, 2))   // the middle value (builtin median agrees)
print("Q3:", quartile(data, 3))       // median of the upper half
print("max:", max(data))              // largest score

/* ---- expected output ----
= min: 64
= Q1: 72
= median: 84
= Q3: 88
= max: 95
*/

scripts.name: geometric-mean
scripts.title: the average growth factor over several years
scripts.text:
/* ============================================================================
geometric-mean.epher -- the average growth factor over several years

The geometric mean of the yearly growth factors in `r`: the nth root of
the product, product(r) ^ (1 / len(r)). A fund that returned 5, 8, 3,
6 and 2 percent in five years grew by the factors 1.05, 1.08, 1.03,
1.06 and 1.02. The geometric mean 1.0478 is the factor that, applied
five times in a row, gives the same total growth; the arithmetic mean
1.048 slightly overstates it, as it always does for ratios.

Web/desktop:             paste the whole file into the entry, press Enter
Everything also works line by line in the TUI.

The one knob to edit is `r` below. Everything above the results section
is machinery you can leave alone.
============================================================================ */

// ---- the knob -----------------------------------------------------------------
const r = {1.05, 1.08, 1.03, 1.06, 1.02}   // yearly growth factors: 1 + return

// ---- helpers: the geometric mean --------------------------------------------------
def gmean(xs) = product(xs) ^ (1 / len(xs)) // nth root of the product

// ---- the average yearly growth ------------------------------------------------------
print("geometric mean of the five factors:", gmean(r))
print("total growth over the five years:", product(r))
print("arithmetic mean for contrast:", mean(r))
print("as an average yearly return, percent:", (gmean(r) - 1) * 100)

/* ---- expected output ----
= geometric mean of the five factors: 1.0477827959
= total growth over the five years: 1.262863224
= arithmetic mean for contrast: 1.048
= as an average yearly return, percent: 4.77827958955
*/

scripts.name: harmonic-mean
scripts.title: the right average for rates: 60 there, 40 back
scripts.text:
/* ============================================================================
harmonic-mean.epher -- the right average for rates: 60 there, 40 back

The harmonic mean of the speeds in `s`, len(s) / sum(1 / s): the
correct average for rates over equal amounts (here: two equal legs of
a trip, at 60 and 40 km/h). Because the slower leg takes longer, the
average speed is not 50 km/h but 2 / (1/60 + 1/40) = 48 km/h. The
harmonic mean is always at or below the arithmetic mean.

Web/desktop:             paste the whole file into the entry, press Enter
Everything also works line by line in the TUI.

The one knob to edit is `s` below. Everything above the results section
is machinery you can leave alone.
============================================================================ */

// ---- the knob -----------------------------------------------------------------
const s = {60, 40}   // km/h on the outward and return legs of a trip

// ---- helpers: the harmonic mean ---------------------------------------------------
def hmean(xs) = len(xs) / sum(1 / xs) // count over the sum of reciprocals

// ---- the average speed over the whole trip ------------------------------------------
print("harmonic mean, km/h:", hmean(s))
print("arithmetic mean, the wrong average here:", mean(s))
print("the textbook formula written out:", 2 / (1 / 60 + 1 / 40))

/* ---- expected output ----
= harmonic mean, km/h: 48
= arithmetic mean, the wrong average here: 50
= the textbook formula written out: 48
*/

scripts.name: iqr-outlier-fences
scripts.title: the 1.5 IQR rule for spotting outliers
scripts.text:
/* ============================================================================
iqr-outlier-fences.epher -- the 1.5 IQR rule for spotting outliers

The interquartile range of the scores in `data` (one of them is a 20, a
score far below the rest), and the outlier fences of the standard rule:
values below Q1 - 1.5 IQR or above Q3 + 1.5 IQR count as outliers
(Tukey's boxplot rule). Each score is then classified by counting, one
by one, how many fall outside the fences.

Web/desktop:             paste the whole file into the entry, press Enter
Everything also works line by line in the TUI.

The one knob to edit is `data` below. Everything above the results section
is machinery you can leave alone.
============================================================================ */

// ---- the knob -----------------------------------------------------------------
const data = {72, 85, 91, 64, 88, 79, 83, 95, 70, 20}   // exam scores; the 20 looks wrong

// ---- helpers: count values below or above a cut, one index at a time ------------
def below(xs, cut, k) = if k > len(xs) then 0 else (if xs[k] < cut then 1 else 0) + below(xs, cut, k + 1) // how many xs[k..] fall under cut
def above(xs, cut, k) = if k > len(xs) then 0 else (if xs[k] > cut then 1 else 0) + above(xs, cut, k + 1) // how many xs[k..] exceed cut
def iqr() = quartile(data, 3) - quartile(data, 1) // the interquartile range of data

// ---- quartiles and the fences (Tukey's 1.5 IQR rule) -----------------------------
print("Q1:", quartile(data, 1))
print("Q3:", quartile(data, 3))
print("IQR:", iqr())
print("lower fence Q1 - 1.5 IQR:", quartile(data, 1) - 1.5 * iqr())
print("upper fence Q3 + 1.5 IQR:", quartile(data, 3) + 1.5 * iqr())

// ---- the verdict: 64 up to 95 lie inside the fences, the 20 does not -------------
print("scores below the lower fence:", below(data, quartile(data, 1) - 1.5 * iqr(), 1))
print("scores above the upper fence:", above(data, quartile(data, 3) + 1.5 * iqr(), 1))

/* ---- expected output ----
= Q1: 70
= Q3: 88
= IQR: 18
= lower fence Q1 - 1.5 IQR: 43
= upper fence Q3 + 1.5 IQR: 115
= scores below the lower fence: 1
= scores above the upper fence: 0
*/

scripts.name: mean-of-data
scripts.title: arithmetic mean of a dataset, cross-checked as sum/n
scripts.text:
/* ============================================================================
mean-of-data.epher -- arithmetic mean of a dataset, cross-checked as sum/n

The arithmetic mean (average) of the ten exam scores in `step`, from the
builtin mean (guide 1.20) and independently as sum(step) / len(step). The two
must agree, which checks the builtin against the textbook definition.

Web/desktop:             paste the whole file into the entry, press Enter
Everything also works line by line in the TUI.

The one knob to edit is `step` below. Everything above the results section
is machinery you can leave alone.
============================================================================ */

// ---- the knob -----------------------------------------------------------------
const step = {72, 85, 91, 64, 88, 79, 83, 95, 70, 86}   // exam scores, 10 students, out of 100

// ---- mean by the builtin and by its definition (sum over count) ---------------
print("builtin arithmetic mean:", mean(step))
print("the textbook formula, sum(step) / len(step):", sum(step) / len(step))

// ---- the pieces of the formula ------------------------------------------------
print("total of all scores:", sum(step))
print("number of scores:", len(step))

/* ---- expected output ----
= builtin arithmetic mean: 81.3
= the textbook formula, sum(step) / len(step): 81.3
= total of all scores: 813
= number of scores: 10
*/

scripts.name: median-of-data
scripts.title: the middle of a dataset, even and odd counts
scripts.text:
/* ============================================================================
median-of-data.epher -- the middle of a dataset, even and odd counts

The median of ten exam scores (an even count: the mean of the two middle
values) and of a five-score set (an odd count: the middle value itself),
from the builtin median (guide 1.20) and by hand on the sorted list.

Web/desktop:             paste the whole file into the entry, press Enter
Everything also works line by line in the TUI.

The one knob to edit is `step` below. Everything above the results section
is machinery you can leave alone.
============================================================================ */

// ---- the knobs -----------------------------------------------------------------
const step = {72, 85, 91, 64, 88, 79, 83, 95, 70, 86}   // exam scores, 10 students (even count)
const od = {64, 70, 72, 79, 83}                      // a five-score set (odd count)

// ---- median of the even count: the mean of the two middle values ---------------
print("builtin median:", median(step))
const s = sort(step)                 // the sorted list; the two middle entries straddle
print("the 5th and 6th sorted scores, averaged by hand:", (s[5] + s[6]) / 2)

// ---- median of the odd count: the middle value itself ---------------------------
print("builtin median of the five scores:", median(od))

/* ---- expected output ----
= builtin median: 84
= the 5th and 6th sorted scores, averaged by hand: 84
= builtin median of the five scores: 72
*/

scripts.name: mode-of-data
scripts.title: the most frequent value, ties and all
scripts.text:
/* ============================================================================
mode-of-data.epher -- the most frequent value, ties and all

The mode of the exam scores in `data` from the builtin mode (guide 1.20):
the value that occurs most often. Two of the ten students scored 85, so
85 is the mode. A second dataset shows the tie rule: when two values
tie for the lead, the builtin reports the smaller one.

Web/desktop:             paste the whole file into the entry, press Enter
Everything also works line by line in the TUI.

The one knob to edit is `data` below. Everything above the results section
is machinery you can leave alone.
============================================================================ */

// ---- the knobs -----------------------------------------------------------------
const data = {72, 85, 91, 85, 88, 79, 83, 95, 70, 86}   // exam scores; 85 appears twice
const ties = {2, 2, 3, 3, 4}                            // 2 and 3 tie for most frequent

// ---- the mode of the scores ------------------------------------------------------
print("the mode of the scores:", mode(data))

// ---- the tie rule: smallest wins -------------------------------------------------
print("the tie rule, smallest wins:", mode(ties))

/* ---- expected output ----
= the mode of the scores: 85
= the tie rule, smallest wins: 2
*/

scripts.name: population-stdev
scripts.title: standard deviation of the ten scores, dividing by n
scripts.text:
/* ============================================================================
population-stdev.epher -- standard deviation of the ten scores, dividing by n

The population standard deviation of the exam scores in `step`, from the
builtin stdev and cross-checked as the square root of the population
variance. epher's stdev is the POPULATION version: variance divides by
the count n, and stdev is its square root (guide 1.20). When the data
are a sample, use the n - 1 version (sample-stdev.epher shows it).

Web/desktop:             paste the whole file into the entry, press Enter
Everything also works line by line in the TUI.

The one knob to edit is `step` below. Everything above the results section
is machinery you can leave alone.
============================================================================ */

// ---- the knob -----------------------------------------------------------------
const step = {72, 85, 91, 64, 88, 79, 83, 95, 70, 86}   // exam scores, 10 students

// ---- population standard deviation: sqrt of the population variance -------------
print("builtin stdev, population version (n):", stdev(step))
print("sqrt of the builtin variance:", sqrt(variance(step)))
print("the variance it comes from:", variance(step))

/* ---- expected output ----
= builtin stdev, population version (n): 9.40265919833
= sqrt of the builtin variance: 9.40265919833
= the variance it comes from: 88.41
*/

scripts.name: population-variance
scripts.title: variance of the ten scores, dividing by n
scripts.text:
/* ============================================================================
population-variance.epher -- variance of the ten scores, dividing by n

The variance of the exam scores in `step`, from the builtin variance and
from its defining formula, the mean squared deviation from the mean.
epher's variance is the POPULATION variance: it divides by the count n
(guide 1.20). When the data are a sample, use the n - 1 version instead
(sample-variance.epher shows it).

Web/desktop:             paste the whole file into the entry, press Enter
Everything also works line by line in the TUI.

The one knob to edit is `step` below. Everything above the results section
is machinery you can leave alone.
============================================================================ */

// ---- the knob -----------------------------------------------------------------
const step = {72, 85, 91, 64, 88, 79, 83, 95, 70, 86}   // exam scores, 10 students

// ---- population variance: mean squared deviation, divide by n -------------------
print("builtin variance, population version (n):", variance(step))
print("the formula, sum of squared deviations over n:", sum((step - mean(step)) ^ 2) / len(step))
print("the squared deviations in total:", sum((step - mean(step)) ^ 2))

/* ---- expected output ----
= builtin variance, population version (n): 88.41
= the formula, sum of squared deviations over n: 88.41
= the squared deviations in total: 884.1
*/

scripts.name: range-of-data
scripts.title: the spread from smallest to largest value
scripts.text:
/* ============================================================================
range-of-data.epher -- the spread from smallest to largest value

The range of the ten exam scores in `step`: the builtin range (guide 1.20),
cross-checked as max(step) - min(step), with the two endpoints shown. The
range is the crudest spread measure: it uses only the two extremes.

Web/desktop:             paste the whole file into the entry, press Enter
Everything also works line by line in the TUI.

The one knob to edit is `step` below. Everything above the results section
is machinery you can leave alone.
============================================================================ */

// ---- the knob -----------------------------------------------------------------
const step = {72, 85, 91, 64, 88, 79, 83, 95, 70, 86}   // exam scores, 10 students

// ---- the range and its definition -----------------------------------------------
print("builtin range, largest minus smallest:", range(step))
print("the textbook formula, max(step) - min(step):", max(step) - min(step))
print("the smallest score:", min(step))
print("the largest score:", max(step))

/* ---- expected output ----
= builtin range, largest minus smallest: 31
= the textbook formula, max(step) - min(step): 31
= the smallest score: 64
= the largest score: 95
*/

scripts.name: sample-stdev
scripts.title: standard deviation of a sample with the n - 1 correction
scripts.text:
/* ============================================================================
sample-stdev.epher -- standard deviation of a sample with the n - 1 correction

The sample standard deviation of the ten exam scores in `data`. The builtin
stdev is the population version (divides by n), so the sample version
(n - 1) is built from it as sqrt(variance(data) * n / (n - 1)); see
sample-variance.epher for the variance alone. With ten scores the result
is sqrt(2947/30), about 9.9113, against the population 9.4027 below.

Web/desktop:             paste the whole file into the entry, press Enter
Everything also works line by line in the TUI.

The one knob to edit is `data` below. Everything above the results section
is machinery you can leave alone.
============================================================================ */

// ---- the knob -----------------------------------------------------------------
const data = {72, 85, 91, 64, 88, 79, 83, 95, 70, 86}   // exam scores, 10 students

// ---- sample standard deviation: sqrt of the n - 1 variance ----------------------
print("the n - 1 version of stdev:", sqrt(variance(data) * len(data) / (len(data) - 1)))
print("the formula directly:", sqrt(sum((data - mean(data)) ^ 2) / (len(data) - 1)))
print("the population version for contrast:", stdev(data))

/* ---- expected output ----
= the n - 1 version of stdev: 9.91127304302
= the formula directly: 9.91127304302
= the population version for contrast: 9.40265919833
*/

scripts.name: sample-variance
scripts.title: variance of a sample with the n - 1 correction
scripts.text:
/* ============================================================================
sample-variance.epher -- variance of a sample with the n - 1 correction

The sample variance of the ten exam scores in `data`: the builtin variance
divides by n (population), while the sample version divides by n - 1
(Bessel's correction), so it is computed from the builtin as
variance(data) * n / (n - 1). There is no separate builtin for it. With
ten scores the population variance is 88.41 and the sample variance
88.41 * 10 / 9 = 98.23..., which epher shows as the exact fraction
2947/30 (its exact-fraction display: 98.2333... repeats).

Web/desktop:             paste the whole file into the entry, press Enter
Everything also works line by line in the TUI.

The one knob to edit is `data` below. Everything above the results section
is machinery you can leave alone.
============================================================================ */

// ---- the knob -----------------------------------------------------------------
const data = {72, 85, 91, 64, 88, 79, 83, 95, 70, 86}   // exam scores, 10 students

// ---- sample variance: sum of squared deviations over n - 1 -----------------------
print("population variance rescaled by n / (n - 1):", variance(data) * len(data) / (len(data) - 1))
print("the formula directly:", sum((data - mean(data)) ^ 2) / (len(data) - 1))
print("the population version for contrast:", variance(data))

/* ---- expected output ----
= population variance rescaled by n / (n - 1): 2947/30
= the formula directly: 2947/30
= the population version for contrast: 88.41
*/

scripts.name: weighted-mean
scripts.title: a grade average where credits set the weights
scripts.text:
/* ============================================================================
weighted-mean.epher -- a grade average where credits set the weights

The weighted mean of the grades in `g`, weighted by the course credits
in `w`: sum(w[k] * g[k]) / sum(w). A three-credit course counts three
times as much as a one-credit course, so the weighted mean 87.5 sits
above the plain mean 86.8, pulled up by the top grade in the heaviest
course.

Web/desktop:             paste the whole file into the entry, press Enter
Everything also works line by line in the TUI.

The knobs to edit are `g` and `w` below. Everything above the results
section is machinery you can leave alone.
============================================================================ */

// ---- the knobs -----------------------------------------------------------------
const g = {85, 92, 78, 88, 91}   // grades out of 100, one per course
const w = {3, 4, 2, 3, 2}        // course credits: 3, 4, 2, 3 and 2 credit hours

// ---- helpers: the weighted mean --------------------------------------------------
def wmean(xs, ws) = sum(xs * ws) / sum(ws) // sum of value times weight, over total weight

// ---- the grade point average by credits -------------------------------------------
print("weighted mean, sum(g * w) / sum(w):", wmean(g, w))
print("the weighted grade total:", sum(g * w))
print("the total credits:", sum(w))
print("the plain mean for contrast, every course equal:", mean(g))

/* ---- expected output ----
= weighted mean, sum(g * w) / sum(w): 87.5
= the weighted grade total: 1225
= the total credits: 14
= the plain mean for contrast, every course equal: 86.8
*/

scripts.name: z-scores
scripts.title: how many standard deviations a value sits from the mean
scripts.text:
/* ============================================================================
z-scores.epher -- how many standard deviations a value sits from the mean

The z-score of one exam score and of every score in `data`: z = (x - mean)
/ stdev, the distance from the mean in standard-deviation units. The
list form uses epher's elementwise arithmetic (guide 1.20), so one
expression standardizes the whole list. A z-score of 0.39 says the 85
sits 0.39 population standard deviations above the class mean of 81.3.
The stdev here is the population version (the builtin divides by n).

Web/desktop:             paste the whole file into the entry, press Enter
Everything also works line by line in the TUI.

The one knob to edit is `data` below. Everything above the results section
is machinery you can leave alone.
============================================================================ */

// ---- the knob -----------------------------------------------------------------
const data = {72, 85, 91, 64, 88, 79, 83, 95, 70, 86}   // exam scores, 10 students

// ---- helpers: z of one value and of the whole list -------------------------------
def z(x) = (x - mean(data)) / stdev(data) // z-score of score x against the class

// ---- z of a single score ---------------------------------------------------------
print("z of the score 85:", z(85))

// ---- z of the whole list: elementwise (data - mean(data)) / stdev(data) -------------------
print("the standardized scores, average 0 with sd 1:", (data - mean(data)) / stdev(data))

/* ---- expected output ----
= z of the score 85: 0.393505701095
= the standardized scores, average 0 with sd 1: {-0.989081897348, 0.393505701095, 1.03162305422, -1.83990503485, 0.712564377659, -0.244611652032, 0.180799916719, 1.45703462297, -1.20178768172, 0.499858593283}
*/

scripts.name: chi-square-goodness-of-fit
scripts.title: is the die fair?
scripts.text:
/* ============================================================================
chi-square-goodness-of-fit.epher -- is the die fair?

Tests whether the sixty rolls in `obs` fit the fair-die expectations
in `expected` (ten of each face) with the builtin chi-square goodness-of-fit
test chisq_gof(observed, expected) (guide 1.20), which prints the chi2
statistic and its p-value as a display string. The statistic is the
sum of (observed - expected)^2 / expected over the six faces; the
p-value is the upper tail of the chi2 distribution with 5 degrees of
freedom.

Web/desktop:             paste the whole file into the entry, press Enter
Everything also works line by line in the TUI.

The knobs to edit are `obs` and `expected` below. Everything above the
results section is machinery you can leave alone.
============================================================================ */

// ---- the knobs -----------------------------------------------------------------
const obs = {8, 12, 9, 11, 10, 10}   // how often each face came up in 60 rolls
const expected = {10, 10, 10, 10, 10, 10} // the fair-die expectation per face

// ---- the pieces of the statistic ---------------------------------------------------
print("total rolls:", sum(obs))
print("chi2 statistic:", sum((obs - expected) ^ 2 / expected))
print("degrees of freedom:", len(obs) - 1)

// ---- the test ------------------------------------------------------------------------
print("chi-square goodness-of-fit of the rolls against the fair-die expectation (chi2 and p):", chisq_gof(obs, expected))
// a chi2 this small (or smaller) happens 96% of the time with a fair
// die, so nothing here suggests unfairness

/* ---- expected output ----
= total rolls: 60
= chi2 statistic: 1
= degrees of freedom: 5
= chi-square goodness-of-fit of the rolls against the fair-die expectation (chi2 and p): chi2 = 1, p = 0.9626
*/

scripts.name: one-proportion-z-test
scripts.title: support for a change, against 25 percent
scripts.text:
/* ============================================================================
one-proportion-z-test.epher -- support for a change, against 25 percent

Tests whether the share of supporters differs from the claimed 25
percent when 42 of 200 people back a change, with the textbook one-
proportion z test: z = (phat - p0) / sqrt(p0 * (1 - p0) / num) and a
two-sided p-value from the normal tail, 2 * normcdf(z) for the
negative z below. There is no builtin proportion test, so the formula
is written out.

Web/desktop:             paste the whole file into the entry, press Enter
Everything also works line by line in the TUI.

The knobs to edit are `succ`, `num` and `p0` below. Everything above the
results section is machinery you can leave alone.
============================================================================ */

// ---- the knobs -----------------------------------------------------------------
const succ = 42    // supporters of the change in the sample
const num = 200   // people polled
const p0 = 0.25 // the claimed population proportion

// ---- the pieces of the statistic -----------------------------------------------------
print("sample proportion:", succ / num)
print("standard error under p0:", sqrt(p0 * (1 - p0) / num))
def zstat() = (succ / num - p0) / sqrt(p0 * (1 - p0) / num) // the z statistic
print("z:", zstat())

// ---- the two-sided p-value from the normal tail ---------------------------------------
print("two-sided p:", 2 * normcdf(zstat()))   // p = 0.191: 42 of 200 (21%) does
                                        // not differ significantly from 25%

/* ---- expected output ----
= sample proportion: 0.21
= standard error under p0: 0.0306186217848
= z: -1.30639452948
= two-sided p: 0.191418425238
*/

scripts.name: one-sample-t-test
scripts.title: is the class mean really 75?
scripts.text:
/* ============================================================================
one-sample-t-test.epher -- is the class mean really 75?

Tests whether the mean of the ten exam scores in `step` differs from the
claimed population mean 75 with the builtin one-sample t test
ttest(data, mu0) (guide 1.20), which prints the t statistic and the
two-sided p-value. The t statistic uses the sample standard deviation
(n - 1) under the mean, here about 9.9113. The test prints its result
as a display string; the lines above it show the pieces the statistic
is built from.

Web/desktop:             paste the whole file into the entry, press Enter
Everything also works line by line in the TUI.

The knob to edit is `mu0` (the claimed mean) below, or `step` for other
data. Everything above the results section is machinery you can leave
alone.
============================================================================ */

// ---- the knobs -----------------------------------------------------------------
const step = {72, 85, 91, 64, 88, 79, 83, 95, 70, 86}   // exam scores, 10 students
const mu0 = 75                                       // the claimed population mean

// ---- helpers: the pieces of the t statistic --------------------------------------
def sds() = sqrt(variance(step) * len(step) / (len(step) - 1)) // sample stdev, n - 1

// ---- what the test sees ------------------------------------------------------------
print("sample mean:", mean(step))
print("sample size:", len(step))
print("sample stdev (n - 1):", sds())

// ---- the test ------------------------------------------------------------------------

// at the 5% level the data do not firmly contradict the claimed mean
// of 75, though the sample mean of 81.3 sits 6.3 points above it

/* ---- expected output ----
= sample mean: 81.3
= sample size: 10
= sample stdev (n - 1): 9.91127304302
= one-sample t test of the scores against mu0 (t and p): t = 2.0101, p = 0.0753
*/

/* ============================================================================
one-way-anova.epher -- do three fertilizers grow the same yield?

Compares the plot yields under three fertilizers, the groups `a`, `b`
and `c`, with the builtin one-way analysis of variance anova(g1, g2,
...) (guide 1.20), which prints the F statistic and its p-value as a
display string. F compares the spread between the group means with the
spread within the groups; here the between-group spread is 14 times
the within-group spread, and p = 0.0007 says yields under the three
fertilizers differ clearly. The yields are example values.

Web/desktop:             paste the whole file into the entry, press Enter
Everything also works line by line in the TUI.

The knobs to edit are `a`, `b` and `c` below. Everything above the
results section is machinery you can leave alone.
============================================================================ */

// ---- the knobs -----------------------------------------------------------------
const a = {12, 14, 15, 13, 16}   // yield per plot, fertilizer A, kg
const b = {10, 9, 12, 11, 8}     // fertilizer B
const c = {15, 17, 14, 16, 13}   // fertilizer C

// ---- what the test sees ------------------------------------------------------------
print("mean yields, A B C:", mean(a), mean(b), mean(c))

// ---- the test --------------------------------------------------------------------------

// at any usual level the group means differ, so the fertilizers are not equivalent

/* ---- expected output ----
= mean yields, A B C: 14 10 15
= grand mean: 13
= one-way anova of the three fertilizer groups (F and p): F = 14, p = 0.0007
*/

1.20): one person, two measurements, so the test works on the seven

t-confidence-interval.epher -- where the class mean lies, with a t

Builds a confidence interval for the mean of the ten exam scores in
`step` with the builtin tinterval(data, level) (guide 1.20): the sample
mean plus or minus the t critical value times the sample standard
error. The level knob is the confidence level, 0.95 for a 95 percent
interval: about 95 percent of such intervals would capture the true
mean. Raising the level to 0.99 widens the interval.

Web/desktop:             paste the whole file into the entry, press Enter
Everything also works line by line in the TUI.

The knobs to edit are `level` below, or `step` for other data. Everything
above the results section is machinery you can leave alone.
============================================================================ */

// ---- the knobs -----------------------------------------------------------------
const step = {72, 85, 91, 64, 88, 79, 83, 95, 70, 86}   // exam scores, 10 students
const level = 0.95      // the confidence level, between 0 and 1

// ---- what feeds the interval ------------------------------------------------------------
print("sample mean:", mean(step))
print("sample stdev (n - 1):", sqrt(variance(step) * len(step) / (len(step) - 1)))

// ---- the interval at the chosen level, and a wider one for contrast --------------------
print("95% t interval for the mean:", tinterval(step, level))
print("the wider 99% t interval:", tinterval(step, 0.99))

/* ---- expected output ----
= sample mean: 81.3

scripts.name: two-sample-t-test
scripts.title: Welch's test for two independent groups
scripts.text:
/* ============================================================================
two-sample-t-test.epher -- Welch's test for two independent groups

Compares the mean scores of two teaching methods, groups `a` and `b`,
with Welch's two-sample t test: unequal variances are assumed, so the
standard error pools the two sample variances divided by their own
group sizes and the degrees of freedom come from the Satterthwaite
formula. There is no builtin two-sample t test, so the textbook
formulas are written out below; scipy's ttest_ind with
const equal_var = False reproduces these same numbers.

Web/desktop:             paste the whole file into the entry, press Enter
Everything also works line by line in the TUI.

The knobs to edit are `a` and `b` below. Everything above the results
section is machinery you can leave alone.
============================================================================ */

// ---- the knobs -----------------------------------------------------------------
const a = {78, 82, 84, 80, 79, 81, 83}   // method A scores, 7 students
const b = {76, 74, 79, 75, 78}           // method B scores, 5 students

// ---- helpers: Welch's formulas -----------------------------------------------------
def sva() = variance(a) * len(a) / (len(a) - 1) // sample variance of A, n - 1
def svb() = variance(b) * len(b) / (len(b) - 1) // sample variance of B, n - 1
def se() = sqrt(sva() / len(a) + svb() / len(b)) // the Welch standard error
def t() = (mean(a) - mean(b)) / se() // the t statistic
def df() = (sva() / len(a) + svb() / len(b)) ^ 2 / ((sva() / len(a)) ^ 2 / (len(a) - 1) + (svb() / len(b)) ^ 2 / (len(b) - 1)) // Satterthwaite df
def p() = 2 * (1 - tcdf(abs(t()), df())) // two-sided p-value

// ---- what the test sees ----------------------------------------------------------------
print("method A, n:", len(a))
print("method A, mean:", mean(a))
print("method A, sample variance:", sva())
print("method B, n:", len(b))
print("method B, mean:", mean(b))
print("method B, sample variance:", svb())
print("Welch standard error:", se())

// ---- the test -----------------------------------------------------------------------------
print("Welch t:", t())
print("Satterthwaite df:", df())
print("two-sided p:", p())      // p = 0.0047: method A scores significantly
                                // higher than method B in this sample

/* ---- expected output ----
= method A, n: 7
= method A, mean: 81
= method A, sample variance: 14/3
= method B, n: 5
= method B, mean: 76.4
= method B, sample variance: 4.3
= Welch standard error: 1.23558353286
= Welch t: 3.72293728241
= Satterthwaite df: 8.99978547831
= two-sided p: 0.00474921073903
*/

scripts.text:
/* ============================================================================
z-test-known-sigma.epher -- class mean against a known population spread

Tests whether the ten exam scores in `step` differ from the claimed mean
75 when the population standard deviation is known to be 9 from past
administrations of the exam, using the builtin z test ztest(data, mu0,
sigma) (guide 1.20), which prints the z statistic and the two-sided
p-value as a display string. With sigma known the standard error of
the mean is sigma / sqrt(n) and no sample standard deviation is needed.

Web/desktop:             paste the whole file into the entry, press Enter
Everything also works line by line in the TUI.

The knobs to edit are `mu0` and `sigma` below, or `step` for other data.
Everything above the results section is machinery you can leave alone.
============================================================================ */

// ---- the knobs -----------------------------------------------------------------
const step = {72, 85, 91, 64, 88, 79, 83, 95, 70, 86}   // exam scores, 10 students
const mu0 = 75      // the claimed population mean
const sigma = 9     // the population stdev, known from past exams

// ---- the pieces of the statistic -----------------------------------------------------
print("sample mean:", mean(step))
print("standard error sigma / sqrt(n):", sigma / sqrt(len(step)))
print("z by hand:", (mean(step) - mu0) / (sigma / sqrt(len(step))))

// ---- the test --------------------------------------------------------------------------
print("z test of the scores against mu0 with sigma known (z and p):", ztest(step, mu0, sigma))
// the sample mean of 81.3 is 2.21 standard errors above the claimed
// 75, significant at the 5% level

/* ---- expected output ----
= sample mean: 81.3
= standard error sigma / sqrt(n): 2.84604989415
= z by hand: 2.21359436212
= z test of the scores against mu0 with sigma known (z and p): z = 2.2136, p = 0.0269

scripts.name: clock-angle
scripts.title: the angle between the hands of a clock
scripts.text:
/* ============================================================================
clock-angle.epher -- the angle between the hands of a clock

At h hours and m minutes past twelve, the minute hand has swept 6 m
degrees (6 deg per minute) and the hour hand 30 h + 0.5 m degrees
(30 deg per hour, plus half a degree per minute of drift). The smaller
angle between them is the acute one: min(diff, 360 - diff), where diff
is the absolute difference of the two sweeps. The classic puzzle answer
for 3:00 is 90 deg and for 6:00 it is 180 deg; both fall out below.

Web/desktop:             paste the whole file into the entry, press Enter

The knobs to edit are the `hs` and `ms` lists below, one clock time per
column (hour 1-12, minute 0-59). Printed values carry about 12
significant digits.
============================================================================ */

// ---- the knobs ---------------------------------------------------------------
const hs = {3, 6, 12, 9, 2, 1}      // hours of the sample times
const ms = {0, 0, 30, 15, 47, 5}    // minutes of the sample times

// ---- helpers ----------------------------------------------------------------
def sweep_h(h, m) = 30 * mod(h, 12) + 0.5 * m   // hour hand, degrees past 12
def sweep_m(m) = 6 * m                            // minute hand, degrees past 12
def diff(h, m) = abs(sweep_h(h, m) - sweep_m(m))  // raw separation, <= 360
def hand_angle(h, m) = min(diff(h, m), 360 - diff(h, m))   // the smaller angle

// ---- results -----------------------------------------------------------------
// Hand angles for 3:00, 6:00, 12:30, 9:15, 2:47 and 1:05 (hs[k] with ms[k]).
// 12:30 is 165 deg, not 195: the smaller angle is the answer.
for k in 1 to 6 do hand_angle(hs[k], ms[k])

// The classic checks, labelled: 3:00 and 6:00 are quarter and half turns.
print("hands at 3:00:", hand_angle(3, 0), "deg")
print("hands at 6:00:", hand_angle(6, 0), "deg")
print("hands at 12:30:", hand_angle(12, 30), "deg")
print("hands at 9:15:", hand_angle(9, 15), "deg")
print("hands at 2:47:", hand_angle(2, 47), "deg")
print("hands at 1:05:", hand_angle(1, 5), "deg")
/* ---- expected output
= {90, 180, 165, 172.5, 161.5, 2.5}
= hands at 3:00: 90 deg
= hands at 6:00: 180 deg
= hands at 12:30: 165 deg
= hands at 9:15: 172.5 deg
= hands at 2:47: 161.5 deg
= hands at 1:05: 2.5 deg
*/

scripts.title: decimal degrees, DMS, and back again
scripts.text:
/* ============================================================================
degrees-minutes-seconds.epher -- decimal degrees, DMS, and back again

Nautical charts and hand sightings give bearings and positions as degrees,
minutes and seconds of arc (122 deg 32' 15"), while calculators, plotters
and GPS math want decimal degrees (122.5375). The conversion builtins are
deg2dms(x), which formats decimal degrees as a DMS string, and
dms2deg(d, m, s), which folds a DMS triple back into decimal degrees
(guide 1.16, the astronomy helpers). The worked example is the bearing of
a buoy from a harbor entrance; west or south bearings just take a minus
sign on the whole decimal value.

Web/desktop:             paste the whole file into the entry, press Enter

The knob to edit is `bearing` below (decimal degrees). Printed values
carry about 12 significant digits.
============================================================================ */

// ---- the knob ---------------------------------------------------------------
const bearing = 122.5375          // buoy bearing, decimal degrees

// ---- helpers: split a decimal degree value by hand ---------------------------
def degpart(x) = floor(x)                       // whole degrees
def minpart(x) = floor((x - degpart(x)) * 60)   // whole minutes
def secpart(x) = (x - degpart(x) - minpart(x) / 60) * 3600   // seconds, decimal

// ---- results -----------------------------------------------------------------
// The bearing as a chart would print it, then as a calculator wants it.
print("deg2dms(122.5375):", deg2dms(bearing))
print("dms2deg(122, 32, 15):", dms2deg(122, 32, 15))

// Same split, done with plain arithmetic so the parts can be checked.
print("by hand:", degpart(bearing), "deg", minpart(bearing), "min", secpart(bearing), "sec")

// The two directions agree: 122 + 32/60 + 15/3600 is 122.5375 exactly.
print("round trip:", abs(dms2deg(122, 32, 15) - bearing) < 1e-12)

// A latitude from the chart table: 37 deg 46' 30" north.
print("dms2deg(37, 46, 30):", dms2deg(37, 46, 30))

// A half minute more: 122 deg 32' 30", and deg2dms rounds to whole seconds.
print("deg2dms(122.541666666667):", deg2dms(122.541666666667))
/* ---- expected output
= deg2dms(122.5375): 122° 32' 15"
= dms2deg(122, 32, 15): 122.5375
= by hand: 122 deg 32 min 15 sec
= round trip: true
= dms2deg(37, 46, 30): 37.775
= deg2dms(122.541666666667): 122° 32' 30"
*/

scripts.name: quadrant-of-angle
scripts.title: which quadrant an angle lands in
scripts.text:
/* ============================================================================
quadrant-of-angle.epher -- which quadrant an angle lands in

An angle in standard position lands in one of four quadrants, or on an
axis when it is a multiple of 90 deg. The recipe: reduce the angle to
[0, 360) (see coterminal-angles.epher in this folder), then compare with
the four boundaries 0, 90, 180 and 270 deg. The boundaries are checked
first, so 90 deg reports the positive y-axis and 270 the negative one,
not a quadrant.

Web/desktop:             paste the whole file into the entry, press Enter

The one knob to edit is the `angs` list below (degrees); an axis angle,
a negative angle and an angle past a turn are included on purpose.
============================================================================ */

// ---- the knob ---------------------------------------------------------------
const angs = {45, 135, 225, 315, 0, 90, 180, 270, -90, 390}   // angles, in degrees

// ---- helpers ----------------------------------------------------------------
def reduce360(x) = x - 360 * floor(x / 360)   // angle into [0, 360)
def quad(x) = if reduce360(x) == 0 then "the positive x-axis" else if reduce360(x) == 90 then "the positive y-axis" else if reduce360(x) == 180 then "the negative x-axis" else if reduce360(x) == 270 then "the negative y-axis" else if reduce360(x) < 90 then "quadrant I" else if reduce360(x) < 180 then "quadrant II" else if reduce360(x) < 270 then "quadrant III" else "quadrant IV"

// ---- results -----------------------------------------------------------------
// One line per knob angle: the angle, then where it lands. -90 deg reduces
// to 270, the negative y-axis, and 390 deg reduces to 30, quadrant I.
print("at", angs[1], "deg:", quad(angs[1]))
print("at", angs[2], "deg:", quad(angs[2]))
print("at", angs[3], "deg:", quad(angs[3]))
print("at", angs[4], "deg:", quad(angs[4]))
print("at", angs[5], "deg:", quad(angs[5]))
print("at", angs[6], "deg:", quad(angs[6]))
print("at", angs[7], "deg:", quad(angs[7]))
print("at", angs[8], "deg:", quad(angs[8]))
print("at", angs[9], "deg:", quad(angs[9]))
print("at", angs[10], "deg:", quad(angs[10]))
/* ---- expected output
= at 45 deg: quadrant I
= at 135 deg: quadrant II
= at 225 deg: quadrant III
= at 315 deg: quadrant IV
= at 0 deg: the positive x-axis
= at 90 deg: the positive y-axis
= at 180 deg: the negative x-axis
= at 270 deg: the negative y-axis
= at -90 deg: the negative y-axis
= at 390 deg: quadrant I
*/

scripts.name: small-angle-approximation
scripts.title: sin x ~ x and tan x ~ x for tiny angles
scripts.text:
/* ============================================================================
small-angle-approximation.epher -- sin x ~ x and tan x ~ x for tiny angles

For a small angle in radians, sin(x) = x - x^3/6 + ... and
tan(x) = x + x^3/3 + ..., so both functions are well approximated by x
itself and the relative error grows like x^2. This is why the small-angle
approximation is always stated in radians: the x in the series is the
radian measure. The script prints the relative error
(approx - exact) / exact of sin(x) ~ x and tan(x) ~ x: positive for
both, since sin(x) < x < tan(x) for a positive angle.

Web/desktop:             paste the whole file into the entry, press Enter

The one knob to edit is the `xs` list below (radians; the file works in
radians on purpose, since the approximation is about radian measure).
Printed values are rounded to 11 significant digits: sin, cos and tan
come from the platform's math library, and platforms can disagree in
the twelfth digit (Linux and Apple silicon do, for tan at these
angles). The rounding keeps this transcript identical everywhere.
============================================================================ */

// ---- the knob ---------------------------------------------------------------
const xs = {0.5, 0.1, 0.01, 0.001}   // angles, in radians

// ---- helpers ----------------------------------------------------------------
def relerr_sin(t) = (t - sin(t)) / sin(t)    // relative error of sin(x) ~ x
def relerr_tan(t) = (tan(t) - t) / tan(t)    // relative error of tan(x) ~ x

// Round to 11 significant digits (see the header): the platform math
// libraries agree to about eleven digits, and the transcript should too.
def r11(x) = round(x * 10^(10 - floor(log(abs(x))))) * 10^(floor(log(abs(x))) - 10)

/* ---- results -----------------------------------------------------------------
Relative errors across the knob angles, biggest to smallest: at 0.5 rad
sine is about 4% low and tangent about 8% high, at 0.001 rad both are
within a few parts in 10^7. The errors fall off like x^2, as the series
predicts. */
for t in xs do r11(relerr_sin(t))
for t in xs do r11(relerr_tan(t))

// The promised close look at x = 0.01 rad (about 0.573 deg).
print("x =", 0.01, "rad")
print("sin(x) =", r11(sin(0.01)))
print("tan(x) =", r11(tan(0.01)))
print("relative error of sin(x) ~ x:", r11(relerr_sin(0.01)))
print("relative error of tan(x) ~ x:", r11(relerr_tan(0.01)))
/* ---- expected output
= {0.042914821467, 0.0016686131635, 0.000016666861113, 0.00000016666668612}
= {0.084756139144, 0.0033355576741, 0.000033333555558, 0.00000033333335562}
= x = 0.01 rad
= sin(x) = 0.0099998333342
= tan(x) = 0.010000333347
= relative error of sin(x) ~ x: 0.000016666861113
= relative error of tan(x) ~ x: 0.000033333555558
*/

scripts.name: law-of-cosines-angle
scripts.title: angle C from three sides (SSS)
scripts.text:
/* ============================================================================
law-of-cosines-angle.epher -- angle C from three sides (SSS)

Solving the law of cosines for the angle opposite side c,
cos C = (a^2 + b^2 - c^2) / (2ab), turns three known sides into the
angles of the triangle (the SSS case). The builtin acos is the inverse
of cosine on [0, pi], so C lands in (0, 180) deg, obtuse included: a
negative cosine means an obtuse angle. Angles are reported in degrees
with deg(). The sides are given in meters and are plain numbers here,
which is safe because the formula only uses their ratios and the units
cancel. Standard classroom material (e.g. Stewart, Redlin and Watson,
"Precalculus", ch. 6).

Web/desktop:             paste the whole file into the entry, press Enter

The knobs to edit are the two side triples below (meters). Printed
values carry about 12 significant digits.
============================================================================ */

// ---- the knobs ---------------------------------------------------------------
const t1a = 3    // first triangle: the 3-4-5, sides in meters
const t1b = 4
const t1c = 5
const t2a = 5    // second triangle: 5-7-9, sides in meters
const t2b = 7
const t2c = 9

// ---- helpers ----------------------------------------------------------------
def angc(a, b, c) = deg(acos(((a ^ 2) + (b ^ 2) - (c ^ 2)) / (2 * a * b)))   // angle opposite c
def anga(a, b, c) = deg(acos(((b ^ 2) + (c ^ 2) - (a ^ 2)) / (2 * b * c)))   // angle opposite a
def angb(a, b, c) = deg(acos(((a ^ 2) + (c ^ 2) - (b ^ 2)) / (2 * a * c)))   // angle opposite b

// ---- results -----------------------------------------------------------------
// The 3-4-5 triangle: the angle opposite the 5 m side is exactly 90 deg,
// because (9 + 16 - 25) / 24 = 0 and acos(0) = 90 deg.
print("3-4-5: angle opposite 5 m:", angc(t1a, t1b, t1c), "deg")

// All three angles of the 3-4-5, and their sum: 180 deg.
print("3-4-5 angles:", anga(t1a, t1b, t1c), "deg", angb(t1a, t1b, t1c), "deg", angc(t1a, t1b, t1c), "deg")
print("3-4-5 sum:", anga(t1a, t1b, t1c) + angb(t1a, t1b, t1c) + angc(t1a, t1b, t1c), "deg")

// The 5-7-9 triangle: (25 + 49 - 81) / 70 = -0.1, so the angle opposite
// the 9 m side is obtuse, about 95.74 deg.
print("5-7-9: angle opposite 9 m:", angc(t2a, t2b, t2c), "deg")

// The three angles of the 5-7-9 and their sum.
print("5-7-9 angles:", anga(t2a, t2b, t2c), "deg", angb(t2a, t2b, t2c), "deg", angc(t2a, t2b, t2c), "deg")
print("5-7-9 sum:", anga(t2a, t2b, t2c) + angb(t2a, t2b, t2c) + angc(t2a, t2b, t2c), "deg")
/* ---- expected output
= 3-4-5: angle opposite 5 m: 90 deg
= 3-4-5 angles: 36.8698976458 deg 53.1301023542 deg 90 deg
= 3-4-5 sum: 180 deg
= 5-7-9: angle opposite 9 m: 95.7391704773 deg
= 5-7-9 angles: 33.5573097619 deg 50.7035197608 deg 95.7391704773 deg
= 5-7-9 sum: 180 deg
*/

scripts.name: law-of-cosines-side
scripts.title: side c from a, b and the included angle C
scripts.text:
/* ============================================================================
law-of-cosines-side.epher -- side c from a, b and the included angle C

The law of cosines generalizes Pythagoras: c^2 = a^2 + b^2 - 2ab cos C
gives the third side of a triangle from two sides and the angle between
them (the SAS case). When C = 90 deg the cosine term vanishes and the
law reduces to c^2 = a^2 + b^2. Angles come in degrees through the
knobs and are converted with rad() for the builtin trig; the sides keep
meters, and the squares and products cancel back to meters under the
square root. Standard classroom material (e.g. Stewart, Redlin and
Watson, "Precalculus", ch. 6).

Web/desktop:             paste the whole file into the entry, press Enter

The knobs to edit are the two sides and the two angles below. Printed
values carry about 12 significant digits.
============================================================================ */

// ---- the knobs ---------------------------------------------------------------
const a = 5 m       // first side
const b = 7 m       // second side
const C = 43        // included angle, degrees
const C90 = 90      // included angle for the Pythagoras check, degrees

// ---- helpers ----------------------------------------------------------------
def sidec(a, b, C) = sqrt((a ^ 2) + (b ^ 2) - 2 * a * b * cos(rad(C)))   // c from SAS
def angc(a, b, c) = deg(acos(((a ^ 2) + (b ^ 2) - (c ^ 2)) / (2 * a * b)))   // angle C back out

// ---- results -----------------------------------------------------------------
// The SAS case: c^2 = 25 + 49 - 70 cos(43 deg), c ~ 4.7755 m. Surveying
// would call this "given two sides and the angle between them".
print("side c at C = 43 deg:", sidec(a, b, C))

// The right-angle case: cos(90 deg) = 0, so c = sqrt(25 + 49) = sqrt(74).
print("side c at C = 90 deg:", sidec(a, b, C90))

// The same 3-4-5 shape: a = 3 m, b = 4 m, C = 90 deg gives exactly 5 m.
print("side c of 3-4-5:", sidec(3 m, 4 m, C90))

// Round trip: the law of cosines for the angle recovers C from the side
// it just produced, so both directions of the law agree.
print("angle C back out:", angc(a, b, sidec(a, b, C)), "deg")
print("round trip:", abs(angc(a, b, sidec(a, b, C)) - C) < 1e-9)
/* ---- expected output
= side c at C = 43 deg: 4.77548331446 m
= side c at C = 90 deg: 8.60232526704 m
= side c of 3-4-5: 5 m
= angle C back out: 43 deg
= round trip: true
*/

scripts.name: law-of-sines-ambiguous
scripts.title: the SSA case: two, one, or no triangles
scripts.text:
/* ============================================================================
law-of-sines-ambiguous.epher -- the SSA case: two, one, or no triangles

Given angle A, side b and side a (side-side-angle), the law of sines
gives sin B = b sin A / a, and the number of triangles that fit depends
on how a compares with the altitude h = b sin A:

  a < h        no triangle: the side a never reaches the base line
  a = h        one right triangle: it just touches
  h < a < b    two triangles: B and 180 deg - B both work
  a = b        one triangle (the second candidate collapses)
  a > b        one triangle

This is the classic ambiguous case of any trigonometry course (e.g.
Stewart, Redlin and Watson, "Precalculus", ch. 6). The script compares
h against a with a 1e-12 slack, because sin(30 deg) is 0.5 to twelve
digits but not to the last binary bit.

Web/desktop:             paste the whole file into the entry, press Enter

The knobs to edit are A (degrees), bside and the five a-values below
(meters). Printed values carry about 12 significant digits.
============================================================================ */

// ---- the knobs ---------------------------------------------------------------
const A = 30            // given angle, degrees
const bside = 12 m      // given side b
const a1 = 4 m          // a shorter than h: no triangle
const a2 = 6 m          // a equal to h: one right triangle
const a3 = 8 m          // a between h and b: two triangles
const a4 = 12 m         // a equal to b: one triangle
const a5 = 16 m         // a longer than b: one triangle

/* ---- helpers ----------------------------------------------------------------
The altitude the far side must clear. A def body only sees names that
exist as consts or defs when it is written, so this is a const, not an
assignment. */
const hgt = bside * sin(rad(A))
def sinB(a) = bside * sin(rad(A)) / a       // law of sines for the candidate B
def b1(a) = deg(asin(sinB(a)))              // first candidate angle B
def b2(a) = 180 - b1(a)                     // second candidate angle B
def verdict(a) = if a / hgt < 1 then "no triangle (a < h)" else if a / hgt < 1 + 1e-12 then "one right triangle (a = h)" else if a >= bside then "one triangle (a >= b)" else "two triangles (h < a < b)"

// ---- results -----------------------------------------------------------------
// h = b sin A = 12 m x 0.5 = 6 m.
print("h = b sin A =", hgt)

// The five cases in order of growing a.
print("a = 4 m:", verdict(a1))
print("a = 6 m:", verdict(a2))
print("a = 8 m:", verdict(a3), "B =", b1(a3), "deg or", b2(a3), "deg")
print("then C =", 180 - A - b1(a3), "deg or", 180 - A - b2(a3), "deg")
print("a = 12 m:", verdict(a4), "with B =", b1(a4), "deg")
print("a = 16 m:", verdict(a5), "with B =", b1(a5), "deg")
/* ---- expected output
= h = b sin A = 6 m
= a = 4 m: no triangle (a < h)
= a = 6 m: one right triangle (a = h)
= a = 8 m: two triangles (h < a < b) B = 48.5903778907 deg or 131.409622109 deg
= then C = 101.409622109 deg or 18.5903778907 deg
= a = 12 m: one triangle (a >= b) with B = 30 deg
= a = 16 m: one triangle (a >= b) with B = 22.024312837 deg
*/

scripts.name: law-of-sines
scripts.title: two angles and one side (AAS and ASA)
scripts.text:
/* ============================================================================
law-of-sines.epher -- two angles and one side (AAS and ASA)

The law of sines, a / sin A = b / sin B = c / sin C, solves any triangle
once one side and its opposite angle are known. Given angles A and B and
side a (the AAS case), C = 180 - A - B follows from the angle sum and
then b = a sin B / sin A and c = a sin C / sin A. Given the side c
between A and B instead (the ASA case), the same C gives
const a = c sin A / sin C. Angles come in degrees through the knobs and are
converted with rad() for the builtin trig; the sides keep meters.

Web/desktop:             paste the whole file into the entry, press Enter

The knobs to edit are the angles A and B (degrees) and the two given
sides below. Printed values carry about 12 significant digits.
============================================================================ */

// ---- the knobs ---------------------------------------------------------------
const A = 40        // angle at A, degrees (shared by both problems)
const B = 60        // angle at B, degrees (shared by both problems)
const a_side = 10 m     // AAS: side a, opposite angle A
const c_side = 100 m    // ASA: side c, between angles A and B

// ---- helpers ----------------------------------------------------------------
def cang(A, B) = 180 - A - B             // angle C from the angle sum
def side_b(a, A, B) = a * sin(rad(B)) / sin(rad(A))   // b from AAS
def side_c(a, A, B) = a * sin(rad(cang(A, B))) / sin(rad(A))   // c from AAS
def side_a_asa(c, A, B) = c * sin(rad(A)) / sin(rad(cang(A, B)))   // a from ASA
def side_b_asa(c, A, B) = c * sin(rad(B)) / sin(rad(cang(A, B)))   // b from ASA

// ---- results -----------------------------------------------------------------
// The shared third angle: 40 + 60 + 80 = 180 deg.
print("angle C:", cang(A, B), "deg")

// AAS problem: angles A = 40 deg and B = 60 deg, side a = 10 m opposite A.
print("AAS: side b:", side_b(a_side, A, B))
print("AAS: side c:", side_c(a_side, A, B))

// The law of sines read as one shared ratio: a/sin A and b/sin B agree.
print("a / sin A =", a_side / sin(rad(A)))
print("b / sin B =", side_b(a_side, A, B) / sin(rad(B)))

// ASA problem: the same angles with the side between them, c = 100 m.
print("ASA: side a:", side_a_asa(c_side, A, B))
print("ASA: side b:", side_b_asa(c_side, A, B))
/* ---- expected output
= angle C: 80 deg
= AAS: side b: 13.4729635533 m
= AAS: side c: 15.3208888624 m
= a / sin A = 15.5572382686 m
= b / sin B = 15.5572382686 m
= ASA: side a: 65.2703644666 m
= ASA: side b: 87.9385241572 m
*/

scripts.name: right-triangle-solver
scripts.title: one side and one acute angle, find the rest
scripts.text:
/* ============================================================================
right-triangle-solver.epher -- one side and one acute angle, find the rest

In a right triangle with acute angle A and the leg a opposite it, the
definitions of sine and tangent give the other two sides directly:
sin A = a / c so the hypotenuse is c = a / sin A, and tan A = a / b so
the other leg is b = a / tan A; the remaining acute angle is
B = 90 deg - A. The sides keep meters through the arithmetic. Standard
classroom material (e.g. Stewart, Redlin and Watson, "Precalculus",
ch. 6); the builtin trig is used, in radians, so the degree knob is
converted with rad().

Web/desktop:             paste the whole file into the entry, press Enter

The knobs to edit are the two problems below. The first is the famous
3-4-5 triangle, written so that its angle comes out of the builtin
asin; the second is a 30-60-90 triangle. Printed values carry about 12
significant digits.
============================================================================ */

// ---- the knobs ---------------------------------------------------------------
const side_a = 3 m                    // leg opposite angle A
const angle_A = deg(asin(0.6))        // its angle: deg(asin(3/5)), the 3-4-5 triangle
const side_a2 = 2 m                   // second problem: leg opposite angle A2
const angle_A2 = 30                   // second problem: acute angle, degrees

// ---- helpers ----------------------------------------------------------------
def hyp(a, A) = a / sin(rad(A))      // hypotenuse from opposite leg and angle
def leg(a, A) = a / tan(rad(A))      // adjacent leg from opposite leg and angle
def pyth(a, A) = abs((hyp(a, A) ^ 2) / ((a ^ 2) + (leg(a, A) ^ 2)) - 1) < 1e-12   // c^2 = a^2 + b^2

// ---- results -----------------------------------------------------------------
// Problem 1: the 3-4-5 triangle. c comes out as 5 m and b as 4 m to full
// double precision, and the Pythagorean check confirms c^2 = a^2 + b^2.
print("hypotenuse c:", hyp(side_a, angle_A))
print("other leg b:", leg(side_a, angle_A))
print("angle B:", 90 - angle_A, "deg")
print("c^2 = a^2 + b^2:", pyth(side_a, angle_A))

// Problem 2: a 30-60-90 triangle with the short leg 2 m. The hypotenuse is
// exactly 4 m and the long leg is 2 sqrt(3) m ~ 3.4641016.
print("hypotenuse c:", hyp(side_a2, angle_A2))
print("other leg b:", leg(side_a2, angle_A2))
print("angle B:", 90 - angle_A2, "deg")
print("c^2 = a^2 + b^2:", pyth(side_a2, angle_A2))
/* ---- expected output
= hypotenuse c: 5 m
= other leg b: 4 m
= angle B: 53.1301023542 deg
= c^2 = a^2 + b^2: true
= hypotenuse c: 4 m
= other leg b: 3.46410161514 m
= angle B: 60 deg
= c^2 = a^2 + b^2: true
*/

scripts.name: vector-components
scripts.title: magnitude and direction into x/y, and back
scripts.text:
/* ============================================================================
vector-components.epher -- magnitude and direction into x/y, and back

A vector of magnitude m at angle t to the x-axis has components
const x = m cos t and y = m sin t; the builtin atan2(y, x) inverts the pair:
its argument is the direction the vector came from, and atan2 keeps the
signs straight, which the single-argument atan cannot do (t = 210 deg
below would look like 30 deg to atan). Rebuilding the magnitude with
sqrt(x^2 + y^2) closes the round trip. Angles are degrees through the
knobs, converted with rad() for the builtin trig; the vector keeps
meters.

Web/desktop:             paste the whole file into the entry, press Enter

The knobs to edit are the two vector pairs below (magnitude in meters,
direction in degrees). Printed values carry about 12 significant digits.
============================================================================ */

// ---- the knobs ---------------------------------------------------------------
const mag1 = 12.5 m   // first vector's magnitude
const t1 = 210        // first vector's direction, degrees (third quadrant)
const mag2 = 8 m      // second vector's magnitude
const t2 = 45         // second vector's direction, degrees

// ---- helpers ----------------------------------------------------------------
def vx(m, t) = m * cos(rad(t))      // x component of magnitude m at angle t
def vy(m, t) = m * sin(rad(t))      // y component of magnitude m at angle t
def vmag(x, y) = sqrt((x ^ 2) + (y ^ 2))   // magnitude back from components
def vdir(x, y) = if deg(atan2(y, x)) < 0 then deg(atan2(y, x)) + 360 else deg(atan2(y, x))   // direction back, in [0, 360)

// ---- results -----------------------------------------------------------------
// First vector: 12.5 m at 210 deg. Both components come out negative:
// cos(210 deg) = -sqrt(3)/2 and sin(210 deg) = -1/2.
print("x:", vx(mag1, t1))
print("y:", vy(mag1, t1))

// The round trip: atan2 returns -150 deg for the third-quadrant pair, so
// vdir adds 360 deg to land back on 210 deg.
print("magnitude back:", vmag(vx(mag1, t1), vy(mag1, t1)))
print("direction back:", vdir(vx(mag1, t1), vy(mag1, t1)), "deg")
print("round trip magnitude:", abs(vmag(vx(mag1, t1), vy(mag1, t1)) / mag1 - 1) < 1e-12)
print("round trip direction:", abs(vdir(vx(mag1, t1), vy(mag1, t1)) - t1) < 1e-9)

// Second vector: 8 m at 45 deg, where x = y = 8 sqrt(2)/2 ~ 5.6569 m.
print("x:", vx(mag2, t2))
print("y:", vy(mag2, t2))
print("magnitude back:", vmag(vx(mag2, t2), vy(mag2, t2)))
print("direction back:", vdir(vx(mag2, t2), vy(mag2, t2)), "deg")
/* ---- expected output
= x: -10.8253175473 m
= y: -6.25 m
= magnitude back: 12.5 m
= direction back: 210 deg
= round trip magnitude: true
= round trip direction: true
= x: 5.65685424949 m
= y: 5.65685424949 m
= magnitude back: 8 m
= direction back: 45 deg
*/
