scripts.name: pendulum-period
scripts.title: T = 2 pi sqrt(L / g) for a simple pendulum
scripts.text:
/* ============================================================================
pendulum-period.epher -- T = 2 pi sqrt(L / g) for a simple pendulum

A simple pendulum of length L swings with period T = 2 pi sqrt(L / g),
independent of the mass and, for small swings, of the amplitude
(Huygens, 1673; the formula is the small-angle solution of the pendulum
equation, good while the swing stays under a few degrees of arc). The
script keeps the units honest: L is a length and the builtin g is
9.80665 m/s^2, so L / g is a time squared and the square root lands in
seconds. Note the g builtin divides as a bare number, so the script
converts it with `in m/s^2` first to get a real quantity for the
division (see the units note in the README).

Web/desktop:             paste the whole file into the entry, press Enter

The knobs to edit are the two lengths below (meters). Printed values
carry about 12 significant digits.
============================================================================ */

// ---- the knobs ---------------------------------------------------------------
const L1 = 1 m     // a one-meter pendulum
const L2 = 4 m     // a four-meter pendulum

// ---- helpers ----------------------------------------------------------------
def period(L) = 2 * pi * sqrt(L / (g in m/s^2))   // T = 2 pi sqrt(L/g)

/* ---- results -----------------------------------------------------------------
The one-meter pendulum: T = 2 pi sqrt(1/9.80665) s ~ 2.0064 s. A useful
rule of thumb: a pendulum one meter long beats seconds (half a period
per swing, about one second per beat). */
print("T for L = 1 m:", period(L1))

// The four-meter pendulum: the length is four times as large, so the
// period doubles: sqrt(4) = 2.
print("T for L = 4 m:", period(L2))

/* The check that it really doubled, and the inverse use: the length of a
pendulum with a given period, L = g (T / 2 pi)^2. A two-second pendulum
(one beat per second) needs L = g / pi^2 ~ 0.9936 m, close to the
one-meter pendulum above: that closeness is why the seconds pendulum
was proposed as the first definition of the metre (Huygens, 1673). */
print("T(4 m) = 2 T(1 m):", abs(period(L2) / period(L1) - 2) < 1e-12)
print("L for T = 2 s:", (g in m/s^2) * (2 s / (2 * pi)) ^ 2)
/* ---- expected output
= T for L = 1 m: 2.00640929259 s
= T for L = 4 m: 4.01281858518 s
= T(4 m) = 2 T(1 m): true
= L for T = 2 s: 0.993621385566 m
*/

scripts.name: projectile-motion
scripts.title: range, height and flight time of a launch
scripts.text:
/* ============================================================================
projectile-motion.epher -- range, height and flight time of a launch

A projectile launched at speed v0 and angle theta over level ground
follows the ballistic parabola; neglecting air drag, the range, peak
height and flight time are

  R = v0^2 sin(2 theta) / g     H = v0^2 sin^2(theta) / (2 g)
  t = 2 v0 sin(theta) / g

At 45 deg, sin(2 theta) = sin(90 deg) = 1, so R = v0^2 / g: with
v0 = 20 m/s that is 400 / 9.80665 ~ 40.79 m, checkable by hand, and the
peak height is exactly a quarter of the range. The builtin g constant
is converted with `in m/s^2` so the units cancel properly: meters
squared per second squared over meters per second squared leaves
meters, and the flight time lands in seconds.

Web/desktop:             paste the whole file into the entry, press Enter

The knobs to edit are the launch speed and the two angles below
(degrees, converted with rad() for the builtin trig). Printed values
carry about 12 significant digits.
============================================================================ */

// ---- the knobs ---------------------------------------------------------------
const v0 = 20 m/s    // launch speed
const th1 = 45       // launch angle, degrees
const th2 = 30       // second launch angle, degrees

// ---- helpers ----------------------------------------------------------------
def rng(v, th) = (v ^ 2) * sin(2 * rad(th)) / (g in m/s^2)   // R = v0^2 sin(2 theta) / g
def hmax(v, th) = (v ^ 2) * (sin(rad(th)) ^ 2) / (2 * (g in m/s^2))   // peak height
def tfly(v, th) = 2 * v * sin(rad(th)) / (g in m/s^2)   // flight time

/* ---- results -----------------------------------------------------------------
Launch at 45 deg, v0 = 20 m/s. The range is v0^2 / g ~ 40.79 m (hand
check: 400 / 9.80665); the peak is R/4 ~ 10.20 m; the flight time is
2 v0 sin(45 deg) / g ~ 2.88 s. */
print("range at 45 deg:", rng(v0, th1))
print("max height at 45 deg:", hmax(v0, th1))
print("flight time at 45 deg:", tfly(v0, th1))

// The two clean identities of the 45 deg shot: R = v0^2/g exactly, since
// sin(90 deg) = 1, and H = R/4, since sin^2(45 deg) = 1/2.
print("range = v0^2/g:", abs(rng(v0, th1) / ((v0 ^ 2) / (g in m/s^2)) - 1) < 1e-12)
print("range = 4 x height:", abs(rng(v0, th1) / (4 * hmax(v0, th1)) - 1) < 1e-12)

// Same speed at 30 deg: the range drops to v0^2 sin(60 deg) / g ~ 35.32 m,
// the peak to H ~ 5.10 m (half the 45 deg height, since sin^2(30 deg) is
// 1/4 where sin^2(45 deg) is 1/2), and the flight time to ~2.04 s.
print("range at 30 deg:", rng(v0, th2))
print("max height at 30 deg:", hmax(v0, th2))
print("flight time at 30 deg:", tfly(v0, th2))
/* ---- expected output
= range at 45 deg: 40.7886485191 m
= max height at 45 deg: 10.1971621298 m
= flight time at 45 deg: 2.88419299633 s
= range = v0^2/g: true
= range = 4 x height: true
= range at 30 deg: 35.3240058036 m
= max height at 30 deg: 5.09858106489 m
= flight time at 30 deg: 2.03943242596 s
*/

scripts.name: simple-harmonic-motion
scripts.title: position, velocity and acceleration
scripts.text:
/* ============================================================================
simple-harmonic-motion.epher -- position, velocity and acceleration

A mass on a spring obeys x(tm) = A cos(omega tm) with angular frequency
omega = 2 pi / T for period T. Differentiating: v = -A omega sin(omega tm)
and a = -A omega^2 cos(omega tm) = -omega^2 x, which is Hooke's law
written as an acceleration. The script evaluates all three at a chosen
instant, with the units kept through the arithmetic: A in meters and
omega in 1/s (displayed as Hz) give x in m, v in m/s and a in m/s^2.
Two invariants are checked: a = -omega^2 x, and the energy identity
x^2 + (v/omega)^2 = A^2.

Web/desktop:             paste the whole file into the entry, press Enter

The knobs to edit are the amplitude, the period and the instant below.
Printed values carry about 12 significant digits.
============================================================================ */

// ---- the knobs ---------------------------------------------------------------
const A = 0.05 m    // amplitude of the motion
const T = 2 s       // period
const tm = 0.25 s    // instant to sample (one eighth of the period)

// ---- helpers ----------------------------------------------------------------
def omega(T) = 2 * pi / T                     // angular frequency, 1/s
def xof(tm) = A * cos(omega(T) * tm)            // position
def vof(tm) = -A * omega(T) * sin(omega(T) * tm)   // velocity
def aof(tm) = -A * (omega(T) ^ 2) * cos(omega(T) * tm)   // acceleration

// ---- results -----------------------------------------------------------------
// The angular frequency: omega = 2 pi / 2 s = pi /s (1/s displays as Hz).
print("omega = 2 pi / T =", omega(T))

/* Position, velocity and acceleration at tm = 0.25 s = T/8. With omega tm =
pi/4, x = A cos(pi/4) ~ 0.03536 m, v = -A omega sin(pi/4) ~ -0.1111 m/s
and a = -omega^2 x ~ -0.3489 m/s^2. The mass is on its way back through
the middle of the swing, so v is large and a points toward the origin. */
print("x(0.25 s) =", xof(tm))
print("v(0.25 s) =", vof(tm))
print("a(0.25 s) =", aof(tm))

/* The two invariants: acceleration tracks position with the minus sign of
a restoring force, and position plus velocity energy stay at A^2. Both
checks divide by one unit of the quantity first, because abs() takes
plain numbers, not quantities. */
print("a = -omega^2 x:", abs((aof(tm) + (omega(T) ^ 2) * xof(tm)) / (1 m/s^2)) < 1e-12)
print("x^2 + (v/omega)^2 = A^2:", abs(((xof(tm) ^ 2) + ((vof(tm) / omega(T)) ^ 2) - (A ^ 2)) / (1 m^2)) < 1e-15)

// The extremes at tm = 0: the mass sits at rest at +A (velocity exactly 0,
// since sin(0) = 0) and the acceleration is -omega^2 A at its most
// negative.
print("x(0) =", xof(0 s))
print("a(0) =", aof(0 s))
/* ---- expected output
= omega = 2 pi / T = 3.14159265359 Hz
= x(0.25 s) = 0.0353553390593 m
= v(0.25 s) = -0.111072073454 m/s
= a(0.25 s) = -0.348943209982 m/s^2
= a = -omega^2 x: true
= x^2 + (v/omega)^2 = A^2: true
= x(0) = 0.05 m
= a(0) = -0.493480220054 m/s^2
*/

scripts.name: sound-wavelength
scripts.title: wavelength = speed / frequency
scripts.text:
/* ============================================================================
sound-wavelength.epher -- wavelength = speed / frequency

A tone of frequency f in air at about 20 deg C travels at v = 343 m/s,
and one full cycle occupies one wavelength: lambda = v / f. The script
keeps the units in the arithmetic (343 m/s divided by 440 Hz is a
length) and converts the answer to centimeters with `in cm`. 440 Hz is
the standard tuning A; 220 Hz is the A an octave below, whose
wavelength is twice as long because the frequency is half.

Web/desktop:             paste the whole file into the entry, press Enter

The knobs to edit are the speed of sound and the two frequencies below.
Printed values carry about 12 significant digits.
============================================================================ */

// ---- the knobs ---------------------------------------------------------------
const vsnd = 343 m/s     // speed of sound in air, 20 deg C
const f1 = 440 Hz        // concert A4
const f2 = 220 Hz        // the A an octave below

// ---- helpers ----------------------------------------------------------------
def wavelength(v, f) = v / f   // lambda = v / f

// ---- results -----------------------------------------------------------------
// At 440 Hz the wavelength is 343/440 m ~ 0.7795 m, about 78 cm.
print("wavelength at 440 Hz:", wavelength(vsnd, f1), "=", wavelength(vsnd, f1) in cm)

// At 220 Hz it doubles to ~1.559 m, about 156 cm.
print("wavelength at 220 Hz:", wavelength(vsnd, f2), "=", wavelength(vsnd, f2) in cm)

// The relation inverts cleanly: lambda times f is the speed again.
print("lambda x f = v:", abs((wavelength(vsnd, f1) * f1) / vsnd - 1) < 1e-12)
